The graphics are decent and the game plays fairly well once you get into it BUT there is very little to guide the player as what to do.  The crafting system is on the complex side with new recipes randomly(seemingly) popping up but they seem to be more tied to resource gathering.
Resource gathering: a PITA.  While there is an autogather option that can be turned on, it SURPRISINGLY does NOT use the grabber tool and so only picks up what is on the spot that your character's feet cross.  The grabber used manually is easily blocked in ridiculous ways forcing more mining that one might want to do just to get at the originally mined resources.
The game menus are a complete and total mess.  Honestly it's the best way that I can describe them, illogically organized and arranged.  e.g. when wanting to strart a new game with a new world instead of offering a NEW FSCKING GAME menu option you are presented with CREATE AN FSCKING CHARACTER.  This as you might surmise allows the player to create a new character which is just a name  and very few character depiction options.  To create a new world/map in singleplayer(SP) you must dig down into the SANDBOX menu(WTF?!) where you will find the options to generate a new world.  THIS IS ALSO WHERE you can DELETE OLD FSCKING maps/worlds.  Yes I would've though that would be my first place to look.  This menu madness continues EVERYWHERE in the game.
Controls: while they work, they are clunky and dissimilar to ANY OTHER similar game.  Apparently like the menus they don't have a clue...
Development: EXTREMELY sssslllllloooooowww

I'll admit, I haven't played Grand Theft Auto 5 (when it comes to PC, I might check it out). with that concession, I consider this one the best GTA. The RPG elements were useful without being annoying (building up your gun/vehicle/hand-to-hand/etc skills was just fun and MUCH better than dragging your friends and family to friggin' leisure activities between every damn mission like GTA 4). The play control was better than VC (mouse looking in vehicles was a great addition), the characters are a little cliche (over the top, racial stereotypes), but all in all, it adds to the 90s flavor of the game. Also, the soundtrack can't be beat. After GTA 4, I switched over to Saints Row and haven't really looked back. I love GTA's dark sense of humor, but the play control in 4 was a massive step down from San Andreas.
It's not flawless, but it is a true sandbox. You can run missions, or just antogonize the local law enforcement and enjoy running across bone county runnin-n-gunnin'. I got to the point where I owned every territory, had turned in every illegal car, and was STILL finding stuff to mess around with! I also decided to just throw my own playlist together and just enjoy running around in/on various vehicles just to be able to floor it to my jams (so to speak) and see how long the car would hold together.
If you like games where your character can grow, but it dosn't mean their worthless to start, a halfway decent story, a TON of stuff to do, and a high amount of replayability, this game is for you!

Call of Duty meets Coips and Robbers.  APB Reloaded looked great to me at first glance, and the trailer sold it for me.  Then however......I started playing.
Don't get me wrong, this game does have a few good things that can be said about it.  They actually put some work into a base storyline, that I feel could have done well if it's gameplay counterpart wasn't a pile of sh*t.
1. There really are nearly infinte amounts of customization options.  If you're the kind of gamer who gets hot and bothered when you can change the shade of colours you never actually see, you'll be here a while....
2. Aesthetics.  The graphics in APB are pretty good, even above par in a few ways.  The voice acting is also better than most I've heard.
3. Options.  You can play the way you want.  Maybe grab a rifle and sit on a rooftop, or climb in a van with your buds, grab some SMG's and have a good ol' fashioned drive-by.
But, the negatives are there as well, and I feel they seriously outdo the pros.
1. Free to Play.......Pay to Win.  No matter how much In-game Cash you grind by doing missions and getting epic multi-kills, you can never actually buy a weapon.  You rent them for a week......a week!  One would think that this time limit would at least make the weapon worth your hard work right?  Wrong.  Shell out $20 real world and you can get a gun that takes the entire in game shop and blows it's face off.......forever.
2. Vehicles. Remember the drive-by I mentioned earlier? You might wanna forget that....because you can't call what you do in an APB vehicle driving.  Every vehicle is slow and unresponsive, on average it takes a second before the vehicle will start turning the direction you told it to.  And when it does turn, it's like being on a Canadian highway in December!
3. AI.  I know handicapped people with better mechanics than this.  Park your car in the middle of the road and the whole city is like a Sim avatar stuck behind a chair in the kitchen.
4.  Matchmaking.  This could be put in both pros and cons actually....  The matchmaking system is very intuitive.  It matches players based on in game "Threat-Level"  The higher this level, the better.  However, this only accounts for personal achievements.  Say you win 30 matches back to back, rockin' your starter rifle.  You'll get an impressive Threat-Level.  But some chotch who wins some and loses some might get put in a lobby with you, and he paid for his loadout.  You stand little chance and the sysytem has no clue.
There are probably more things I could say about APB Reloaded, but at this point....I'm ranting.  And you probably didn't even read this far anyway.

The reason to play this game is for the story. Don't be fooled by those that may say you have to make difficult choices during the game because, aside from the four possible endings, you are more of an observer that is thrust into difficult situations alongside Captain Walker, the protagonist. And when you do play the game through, you are sort of left to draw your own conclusions about the experience (or read some fan theories if your only conclusion was, "Uhh, what?").
The biggest downside to this game is the controls. Sprinting, in particular. I guess that's the "difficult decision" in this game, isn't it? You can choose when to begin sprinting. After that, you're just along for the ride until Walker decides when it's appropriate to stop...past the cover you wanted to duck behind. Great choice. Now you're dead. I also love when developers intentionally make certain parts of a game incredibly frustrating; here, it's Chapter 13 (just be sure to get the two Intel items the first time around so you never have to go back to that level again).
To quickly summarize: the story is good but not as great as some say it is, the controls can be irritating, and Chapter 13 is a pain. At the end of the day, I enjoyed it and think it's worth a playthrough.

I played the original Captain Forever and some of the alternative versions on Farbs website a few years back and thoroughly enjoyed them.  The retro graphics and quick on the fly ship modifications made for good game play.
The Remix has all the same fun of the original but now with a 'saturday morning cartoon' style and theme.  You progress level by level through the solar system to stop King Kevin and his horde of cranky mutants.  There are loads of weapons and ship parts to experiment with, as well as randomised obstacles enemies with their own randomised ships.  It is a fun jaunt, a retro arcade shooter with ship building that I thoroughly reccomend to fans of retro shooters or retro games in general.
Destroy others, take their left over parts and repeat the process until it's done to you. Super fun,

Captain Forever is a different game that I would recommend trying out, even if you're not into roguelike shooters. Its gameplay consists of on-the-go ship building, as well as a 2D shooter with the aim of destroying a ship as efficiently as possible, as doing more damage to anything other than a ship's core means having less parts to rebuild your own ship with.
Like many roguelikes, there is quite a steep difficulty curve, and will often leave you frustrated - but willing to try again.
That is, until the final level, where your impervious monster of a ship is torn to shreds in an instant, and the only way to win is to wedge the core of your ship in a spot that is able to hit the 'boss' whilst being dragged along by it, and not being hit by its own projectiles.
This game is great fun, has an interesting visual style, and must have been designed by a sadist...
But you should really check it out.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a metriodvania action platform game.  It also very immersive and has an impressive soundtrack.  Metriodvania's are my favorite genre so as a result this review may be very picky in some area's.
The story of Ori begins with a sombre note of loss and sadness.  You are a creature of the spirit tree a white rabbit type thing.  After getting swept up into a storm you are found by somebody who nurtures and takes care of you.  Sometime later the forest dies and it's up to you to save it.  I don't want to completely spoil the beginning but it's one of the most emotional beginning's I’ve experienced.  Metriodvania's are not known for having an interesting story but this game focused a lot more on it I feel.  The story is not told really in words.  The spirit tree says a bunch of things throughout the journey but maybe 20 sentences max.  Most of the story is shown to you and it's easy to understand without words.
I feel like this game is much more story centred, which in my mind takes away from the aspects I enjoy.  I wish the game were longer and had a lot more exploration which really makes the metroidvania genre for me.  I like how in metriod you would get upgrades and then at the end it would force you to use them all to get to certain area's.  I don't feel like this game brought that to the table, it just feels like a more casual metroidvania which is ok just not for me.  As for the movement, it feels really good.  The abilities like jumping climbing launching slamming, all feel perfect.  The slam for instance shakes the ground and has a big boom as if you are hitting the ground with force.  The launching although at first seemed a bit odd it becomes second nature and is really fun to use.  One thing I feel this game excels at is the ramping difficulty.  You get new abilities then the game askes you to do harder and harder things with it.  In the beginning it's just basic things you do but by the end you are doing much harder tasks that make you feel satisfied. The other ability in the game is the fireball.  Which is an attack you get right at the start for fighting enemies.  It's basic because it shoots at all angels and you don't have to aim it but it feels alright.  You also get a few abilities that add to the fireball but that’s not the games main focus.  There aren't any true boss fights just a few mini bosses.  As for the enemies I feel they fit the levels but are somewhat recycled, that being said each enemy that isn't recycled feels different.
This game has a level up feature.  You get experience from killing enemies and finding ability point orbs. You put your ability points into one of three separate categories.  Efficiency, Utility and Combat.  Efficiency helps you with finding all the hidden collectables.  Utility allows you to get more out of your healing abilities and soul power which allows you to save.  Combat which makes you do more damage and attack more enemies.  I feel it's alright but on a second play through you would avoid Efficiency because you would know where everything is.  Some of the abilities later in Utility are really strong giving you triple jump and the ability to breath underwater.  The combat ones don't do anything visual.  That being said the game does make you feel like you are gaining strength.  The collectables in this game are just HP and Soul power, there are not many of them either.  Most of the pickups are ability point orbs which if you want to max level are needed.
This games soundtrack is amazing.  At first it feels kind of slow and boring but as you go it starts to really pick up.  That being said I feel like the soundtrack always fit what was going on, on the screen.  Without the game I feel the soundtrack isn't the greatest, thats not a problem for me but it's just a thing.  During the intense parts the music is intense, during the sad parts sad it's just fits perfectly with the game.  There isn't much to say I feel as during the game it went together but on it's own it's not very memorable.
Overall as a complete package I think the game is perfect.  In it's: Length, sound, movement, action, platforming, fighting.  Everything just goes together completely.  Although as a metroidvania I feel it kind of misses it's mark in terms of exploration and length.  That being said, Ori and the Blind Forest made me feel emotions I didn't expect.  By the end of the journey even though it was short I felt like I had accomplished a big task.  At the end I felt a bit emotional because it felt like the end to a long journey and that makes me recommend it for sure.

First off, this is not for the casual gamer.  You will pretty much have to study this game in depth for quite a while just to understand the basics.  It's also very user-unfriendly.  However, I'm not giving it the thumbs-down simply for its complexity.  I would have probably come to appreciate it, except for the particularly awful and boring experience from the beginning.
I finally got tired of endless and ridiculously wordy tutorials full of spoken dialogue that didn't match the written dialogue on the screen, as well as having to go and find the tutorials in various locations in the game, and started searching for [exit/quit].  It took me two minutes of searching before I finally realized I'd have to search for some kind of guide, which took another minute, followed by another two minutes of pecking around at subjects, before reading that I had to find [camp,] then select among several potentially perilous options to camp, and which required anywhere from 30 to 120 seconds before the game finally closed.
Not to mention, during the game, I was subjected to endless popups asking me to buy stuff...right in the middle of the game!  They blocked or kept me from using various controls, including one time during a battle.  It was easy enough to close the window with the extremely dimunitive [x] provided, but the flow was interrupted.
The worst part was that there were FOUR LOADING STAGES.  The first one started when I clicked [play game] in Steam; this took 11 minutes on my laptop at cable internet speed.  The second one started when I tried to run the app, and took another 10 minutes.  The third one took over 30 minutes to complete, and was followed by a fourth stage that took another 15 minutes while the game apparently organized itself.  The total download was probably around 4 GB, with the longest download being during that 30-minute stretch.  I have games bigger than this that took maybe 15 mins tops to download and start.  My computer is not pokey or short on memory, either.
I'm not a stranger to free games, and I don't mean to look a gift horse in the mouth, but it just proved to not be worth the wait.  As soon as I finally got my laptop back from the game, I uninstalled the game and started writing this review.

EQ and EQ2 were my first and favorite MMORPGs.  I'm actually a huge fan of the franchise, though I'm afraid it is dead to me now. I'll give you the TL;DR below.  But, do I recommend this game?  Yes and no.  It was amazing at its inception.  Now, almost 14 years later, it has a lot of baggage.  For old players returning (like I would be), the mudflation bloat and changes may well seem unappealing.  For new players, I don't think you would find much community or support.  However, your style might not be my style and there is actually a lot of content if you just like adventuring alone or can find a friend or two.
TL;DR history and thoughts.
I've given SOE a ton of money over the last couple decades on a couple accounts since 1999.  (Approx $30 x 12 x 18 = $6,460 + expansion costs  + who knows how much more on marketplace fluff)  EQ was great, though raiding had me hating the game by the time EQ2 came out.
EQ2 was a more simple game than EQ1 and did away with a lot of un-fun brain damage BS that was in EQ1 (like... the cleric complete heal rotation cycle that had to be maintained for 5 hours in the plain of earth encounter).  EQ2 was a breath of fresh air and I never looked back to EQ1 despite the thousands of hours I had played from 1999 to 2004.  EQ2's graphics were great (for that time) and the world felt familar but brand new.  I banded up with a bunch of other new players and EQ1 migrants.  It was a ton of fun.  I made some wonderful friends and had all of those great experiences that made fond memories.
But, like EQ1, EQ2 eventually jumped the shark.  For me, it was about the Destiny of Velious days around 2011.  The content was still great but it was starting to get a bit 'gimicky' with the effort to keep all the players in the skinner box.  New game mechanics were introduced to keep things dangerous.  It only got worse in the expansions after that.  The loot became more formulaic and generic, catering to specific stats in more and more exaggerated ways.  That's nothing new of course.  But, the game became all about DPS.  The devs realized that it was one way to keep players feeling as if they were progressing without introducing as many new and confusing game mechanics.  Whatever it takes to get the player to buy the new expansion and get their new gear...  Anyhow, the DPS scale from a character went from single digits to triple digits to quadrupal digits in the golden age of the game.  Now, with these later expansions, the scale has become laughable.  Can you do the hundred of millions of DPS to kill that mid-tier mob?  It's great if you can.  But...  Yeah...  The magic is gone.
Anyhow, 20 years later in life.  I'm not a broke teenager anymore.  I have more money than time and don't give a crap about a monthly fee.  I spend way more on less entertaining hobbies.  Bring me something fresh and new in the franchise, maybe an EQ3 which I can hobby on without feeling like I just got a second job, and I'll put my money on the table.  All this trying to get creative to find ways to get gamers to part with their money is laughable.  Target the demographic with the money and give them something they'll enjoy.  All you devs with 'experience' are probably my age.  Stop making games for teenagers.  Target your demographic.  In fact, put some full frontal nudity in so that we can rule out ending up in the same party with some squeaky voice pre-pubescent kid right off the bat.  They need to be playing pokemon or something and not playing my legacy franchise.
And, a final note.  Daybreak.  You bunch of stooges.  You bought the old mare with the deliberate thought of riding her till she died.  The franchise is dead.  Daybreak is where old MMO's go to hospice.  It is my opinion that a modern and well done EQ3 would lure back the nostalgic.  Do us a favor and sell the EQ franchise to a more vibrant and forward thinking game development company.

An interesting game, but one that seems to be going nowhere. Right now there is too little in the game to make it a worthwhile purchase, and after years of development I have seen very little significant change. Here are the problems as I see it:
1. Too little content. I know this is early access, but, seriously, only one surface biome?
2. So many animals wandering around that I feel like I must be stepping in sheep dung with every step.
3. The limb movement system, while nice to look at, makes combat seem a little wonky. (Bow combat is the worst.)
4. There's no reason to build anything more than a one room cabin. In fact, just put up some walls and a roof to keep critters out while you craft. Back walls are optional.
5. The inventory system is messy. It looks like a throwback to Ultima 8, with everything piled on top of everything.
6. Survival is trivial. Food is unbelievably abundant.
It does have some nice features, such as a radar map system, and an actual plot (not finished.) And, to the devs' credit, they were quick to help when I had an issue with world generation that made my game unplayable. They do seem to be actively working on the game, adding new features occasionally. (Usually new weapons/armor.) But the games needs more to it. Right now, you will lose interest fairly quickly.
If/when this game ever gets better, I will change my review.

The reason to play this game is for the story. Don't be fooled by those that may say you have to make difficult choices during the game because, aside from the four possible endings, you are more of an observer that is thrust into difficult situations alongside Captain Walker, the protagonist. And when you do play the game through, you are sort of left to draw your own conclusions about the experience (or read some fan theories if your only conclusion was, "Uhh, what?").
The biggest downside to this game is the controls. Sprinting, in particular. I guess that's the "difficult decision" in this game, isn't it? You can choose when to begin sprinting. After that, you're just along for the ride until Walker decides when it's appropriate to stop...past the cover you wanted to duck behind. Great choice. Now you're dead. I also love when developers intentionally make certain parts of a game incredibly frustrating; here, it's Chapter 13 (just be sure to get the two Intel items the first time around so you never have to go back to that level again).
To quickly summarize: the story is good but not as great as some say it is, the controls can be irritating, and Chapter 13 is a pain. At the end of the day, I enjoyed it and think it's worth a playthrough.

Terratech in space, on speed and with permadeath.
Graphics: 90%
Audio: 80%
Gameplay: 85%
Replayability: 100%
Value for Money: 100%
Overall: 91%
Captain Forever Remix and Terratech is similar in the way you build your vehicle: You have a command module, which works on its own. And then you snap pieces you find or salvage to it, buildig a bigger and bigger craft. But there ends the similarity.
CFR is a fast paced spacecraft builder, where you must use what resources you find, and rebuild whenever you have the spare time. Because, if you wait untill the end of the round, you might have too little time. Often you get so wrecked, that you have to improvise to survive. That can often be a bit frustrating as you often have no way of recovering from a deady encounter. But that's the theme of the game: Childs' play. You smash your ship to bits and build it up again. Like at least I did when I was a kid.
Childs' play is also the theme of the game. A girl and her brother is playing the hero and the villain in a fantasy world. While it's very well made, both in graphics, comments and music, I miss the small parts. Maybe having a real voice would be the icing on the cake. But it could also have ruined the entire experience. The graphics is also very functional, only a few tidbits pulls the impression down.
As for gameplay and replayability, it's one of those games that you play again and again to see if you can build the perfect ship. Only to see it gets wrecked by a too tough opponent. And that is what pulls the score a bit down. I feel some of the opponents are impossible to beat, and if you are unlucky, you cannot outrun them either. When you compare them to some of the other variations you meet, you can also very lucky. Getting a cube without guns, or without thrusters. For the campaign, I feel that could have been a bit less random, as you also have the sandbox mode. A bit frustrating, but after playing too many a Rogue-like, I'm used to hitting dead ends.
Hectic, exciting, crazy fun. The mechanics feel extremely polished/tight and the core gameplay is just plain enjoyable.

Yep, I have to be one of those people again and find a game alot of peeps like, buy it, and hate every moment of it. Anyway I do have a ton of legitimate reasons as to why I thoroughly have not been able to enjoy this game even after 6 - 9 hours, read on if you actually care, do it for your own sake if you’re thinking of getting this.
First and foremost I was shocked when I first got into the game how absurdly hard and unfair it was right from the start. I really can't express in words just how frustratingly awkwardly difficult this game is. I don't think ive ever even played a rogue lite this hard before in my life! And All I do is play games, even see my steam library. The small tutorial barely tells you how to make ships properly, what good weapon combos their might be or how things work, how important ship balancing and equal thrusters are, nope just the controls and how to put parts on other parts making the game seem soooo simple and casual, but holy frick it so isn’t. It doesn’t even explain for a second that there is a colour system for higher tiered stuff! Yea sure that's maybe a given if you know anything about game rarity systems but I wanted to express just how pathetic of a tutorial there is. Expect to go in very confused, blind and lost, cas I could never figure out fully how to not dire horribly to stupid unbalanced crap over and over even after 6 hours. It tells you nothing and throws you into hell, pitted against bigger beefed ships you have no hope of winning against without some serious fire power, which you hardly ever find in decent amounts, and expects you to get anywhere, it's just such a silly, lazy development decision to do that. I get the whole 'just jump right in and play and learn as you go! No having to mess about in a stupid lame tutorial' concept, it's an interesting one to keep using in indie games but not for every game, it's mostly only ever felt right to me in survival games like Don't Starve and even then it can be hard to justify such lack of information to the player to get in and actually be able to play properly. This kind of humiliating and frustrating experience I have had so far has all been on the darn easiest difficulty too, easy! I do not even want to fathom the BS and aggravation that would have to be endured from higher difficulty levels, I wouldn’t wish it on my worst enemy. This game is making me feel like such an idiot that knows nothing about games every freaken run I try! it's depressing and frankly not fun in the slightest. =/ The visuals of the game make it seem so giddy, happy and casual but let me make it clear that it really, REALLY isn’t, this game will kick your archsloff and it won't care how bad it makes you feel every time it does it. Your expectations will be blown to hell after looking at this game every single time you die, and you will die alot until your either fed up and write a review, like me, smash your computer to pieces or cry in a corner, either one.
The devs need to do some serious overhauling of the game balance and expectations of you fighting higher level enemies to go up a stage cas right now it's just brutal and a joke. You don't have any other way to go up a stage by the way, you have to fight and absurdly powerful ship way higher level then you with way more firepower and armour and beat it, that's fine and all, if you were evenly matched with it, but you never are and never will be, so it's like jumping into a pit of snakes and dancing around hoping not to be bitten pretty much. I could go on about how stupidly, brutally unfair and hard the game is even on easy but you should probably get the point I’m trying to make. If you don't like hard games and were thinking of buying this well then I hope you were lucky enough to read this my friend and not go through the pain I’ve put myself through to make a point that's not even worthwhile making. I shouldn’t have to ever prove myself to a darn game, it should prove itself against me! I paid for the flipping thing, if I want an easy run so I can actually make progress then why can't I?! I just feel ripped off so much right now and that even buying this time waster on sale makes me feel like a sucker. =/
The entire budget clearly went into the art style and audio cas holy heck there is almost nothing to do in this game but shove pieces together hoping they work right and pew pew at other ships floating around hoping to kill them, that's it! There is almost no progression system either, you unlock new ship part kits by going up through the levels then unlock others by using new kits you unlocked to unlock the next one by getting to level x, it's actually frankly a pain in the tush cas if your new ship kit sucks and is made of parts that are almost downright useless, you are kinda stuck with them until you actually make it to the level it wants you to get to with them before you can get a better starting ship, what kind of annoying progression system is that crap?! Why not base it on kills? or how many parts you collect up? or if you make a cool big ship? nope, just boring get to this level and you get a kit. After 6 hours not only am I frustrated as hell with repeating such nonsense over and over, but I’m bored of it too and wish I had my money back to buy something enjoyable, ugh. The game may look great, has fantastic effects, voices and sound but my god the lack of gameplay absolutely kills it in every way, for me at least and alot of people without god like patience I’ll bet.
Death after death you rarely learn anything new because there IS nothing to learn new, the game is too simple, it's just float around and shoot so what am I darn missing?! The game will drive you crazy with it's somehow over complicated super simplified gameplay that doesn’t ever try to help you improve or LET you improve, it will just keep killing you over and over with bull crap and give you next to nothing for your wasted time, not a single, not a bit of advice, just a kick in the nuts and a restart as a brand new hunk of junk. If you’re looking for a repetitive, shallow rogue lite game that's hardly satisfying in any way, shape or form then look no further really!

Quick Review: Stellar game.  Totally worth $15.  Highly recommended if you like random generation or 2D space shooters.
Detailed Review: If you'd like to make an informed purchase, check out the original flash game for free
.  It'll provide about 2 hours of fun before you beat it and are thirsty for more.  So, apart from being incredibly faithful to the original, what more has been added to keep the game fresh?  Well, they've added:
- 12 new, incredibly varied weapons.
- 3 new types of stut (bulkhead) that all dramatically change how you think about ship design.
- 2 new types of thruster to mix things up.
- An augmentation system to upgrade your ships with.
- Much less waiting around for ships to show up, with the added ability to jump to the next level.
- The ability to repair your ship.
- Lot's of obstacles and bonuses floating in space.
- A sandbox mode where you can fly around in your past ship designs.
- A very welcome and well implemented difficulty setting.
- The game explains istelf a bit more and is easier to understand.
- An awesome cartoon style and great soundtrack.
I can't think of anything that they've missed.  This is the best remake of a free game I've ever played.  You can tell that this Captain Forever Remix was developed by big fans of the original game, and for the first time I can safely say that they completely captured what made the original so fun.

My god! It's been almost 10 years since this game was released! That was quite a long time ago. And to see it released after Vice City it was a big deal. Seriously, the game employed at least 10 times the area Vice City had. And here there are 3 different cities available not to mention the countryside in between these. This game is huge and just by completing all side missions you can easily go over a 100 hours of gameplay time!
This game still did not have any physics as in order to get the next gen feeling we needed to wait for the 4th instalment of the franchise. But this is not a problem as in case you look at it as Vice City's successor you can appreciate what San Andreas offers: greater playable area, hundreds of vehicles, minigames, car modifications, gang wars and the ability to purchase clothing, tattoos and even to have your own haircut.
I had only an issue with the game's RPG elements: for some reason some stunts are not available at first and you need to keep driving a car until you unlock the next level. To be able to sprint further or have stronger punches in melee you need to visit the gym often. From time to time you need to eat but junk food will soon make you obese. So you need to visit the gym again. These side activities stole some of my time and I never liked paying any attention to them but I had to. I liked how these were skipped in the next episode which, unfortunately, skipped the car modifications and this is the only GTA with bikes in it! And to date, in my opinion, this game has used the best voice actors in the series: Samuel L. Jackson, Chris Penn, Ice T and James Woods just to name a few.
This is a classic and if you like the "old" GTA games but for some reason skipped this one now is to time to purchase it. Or when it's discounted as 10 bucks is a bit too much for such a title but I'm sure the price will soon drop.

This game is fantastic! A must have for any platforming fan!
This game has a "Metroidvania" structure, with areas that open up as you increase your skillset, which include some very interesting moves (there's a move where you can use the enemies' projectiles to propel yourself, and at the same time you can redirect this projectile to harm enemies or destroy obstacles. This opens up a lot of mechanics that I haven't seen in other platformers).
It has tight controls (a must for this kind of game), a moving story (for me at least), it has some of the most gourgeous graphics I have seen for this kind of game, and a beautiful soundtrack, which fits the scene perfectly!
It also has a very interesting save system, in which there are no checkpoints but you can save anywhere you want, but to do so you spend energy points, which could be used for special moves instead.
The only downside I can think of is that it can be hard and frustrating for some, but this new Definitive Edition adds an easy mode, which might aleviate this issue.
So to sum it up, it's not for everyone, but if you're into this genre, it's essential! And even if you're not a fan of the genre, I think it's worth a shot!

As Max picked up a photo (history relic) of a teenager with a snowman, he commented:
"I can't remember the innocence... of snow, of man."
I feel like it described everything the wastelands was, a harsh world that snuffed out any hint of innocence or hope for the advancement of humankind. It was full of savages and survivors who considered getting through a day without harm a true win. In this world, there is no right or wrong, good or evil, only the strong, the weak and the unfortunate ghosts of the past. Then again, there's Max who just bulldozes through everything!
I liked the lore and world-building (though small) here. They handled that part of the game quite well in my opinion. I believe at one point I came to the realiziation some wastelanders were using human skin as leather.
It was really fun at first but got repetitive toward the middle/end of the game (though I did wipe out everything before the final mission). One qualm I did have was upgrading the Magnum Opus. The scrap collecting was easy but there were points where I had to finish a quest before obtaining the first of an upgrade. However, I'd be able to get the third, fourth or final stage by reducing the threat level of a territory. Didn't make a lick of sense, but I got them all anyway to complete the Archangels, which was one of my favorite parts of the Opus. Some of them were just plain cool.
As for the ending, I was left in a little bit of a daze because I felt mixed emotion. Like I understand it but wish it had not happened and went "oh well." You'll see or do know my meaning.
Despite some of its repetitive activities, the monotonous process of upgrading the Magnum Opus, and the rage-inducing combat, I really liked the game and some of its characters (Hope, Glory, Griffa, and Chumbucket for instance). I recommend the game, though on sale is best.
Now go on and corpse them War Boys! Happy gaming.

A fantastic game which has to be experienced first-hand, for some it may be repetitive and monotonous but I think there is something very soothing about the desolate nature of the game. All activities revolve around collecting scrap or combatting the various groups of bandits roaming the wasteland either on foot or in your car; the Magnum Opus. The story is very simple but suits the game and every character is acted and written superbly.
The hand to hand combat is very similar to the Arkham series but feels much more satisfying here probably due to the fact that Max has no qualms about plunging a knife into someone's eye socket. Fist fights are always entertaining and wince-inducing at their best.
Vehicular combat is great because of the variety of ways you can modify your car. Some upgrades are beneficial whilst others (despite also benefitting you) have their drawbacks. You can build a jack-of-all-trades with the most expensive components but that doesn't mean you will have a car that suits your playstyle. Car combat feels awesome, the visual feedback upon collision is satisfying and the multitude of weapons at your disposal make for some memorable moments. Once you reach the zenith in upgrades, vehicle combat does became a bit easy and the same goes for ground combat yet if you slip up you can still be easily overpowered.
Whilst the breadth of what Mad Max offers isn't as vast as other games I think that it really nails most of what it does do.

It's difficult to review this game as just positive or negative.  It's for times like this that we need a "Mixed" button.  I don't hate this game, nor do I love it.  I'll just judge it as whether or not I'd recommend it.  At this point in time, the answer is no, but it mainly comes down to your personal choice and willingness to wait for more content.*  I looked online to find out whether I should buy Signs of Life or Starbound.  Everywhere I looked, Signs of Life won in a landslide, saying it was more "Signs of Life = Something an adult made.  Starbound = a 2 year olds plaything."   What I actually saw in playing Signs of Life was more opposite than not, not that I'll go *that* far and say 2-year-olds created this.  However, a giant mech chicken?  That sounds like something out of old school DragonFable.  Also, the conrols are counter-intuitive and it needs controller support (or better mapping).  I think I was expecting more from this game.  Yes, it's in early access.  I'm happy to support a developer.  But to find out we can't even go off planet in this game?  It's a deal-breaker for me, at least at this point in time.  So I guess it boils down to: do you want a game where you can mine and build and explore buildings left by previous inhabitants but not talk to them?  Great!  Do you want to support a (judging by other reviews) helpful and attentive dev team?  Awesome!  But that's about all you can do.  Personally, I don't think I'll play this game until it gets something I can sink my teeth into.  I'm excited to find out what the devs will do with this game, though.  It has great potential.
TL;DR
Get it if you want to support a promising game, but as is, I can't recommend this game except to people who love sandboxes.*  I'm excited to see where it leads in the next few updates.
*review subject to change

The latest installment of the Hitman franchise is no let down, even if you were to have been impatient enough, like me, to have bought it from day one. Now that all the proposed 'episodes' have been released, I purchased the remaining episodes at a discounted price! I have to say I do not mind the episodic run, if it means we have more Hitman throughout the years. The story seems to be coherent and has moved from the linear yet telling rehash of the great movie LEON.
The freedom to roam in much larger areas is really immersive. The ability to track opportunities, make your own killings and try to solve the puzzles is a treat. Escalation, contracts and the elusive contracts make for a genuinely active replay of the mechanics in Hitman.
The mechanics are clever, ironic and dark in humor. Some of the targets certainly deserve what is coming to them. While the game looks lovely, some of the audio is lazy. The imersion comes from door signs and shop signs in the native languages of the area you are in, but the audio of the locals is a lazy america accent in italy. A cockney accent in Thailand. For me, this takes me out of the moment, but only for a moment - eventually it becomes funny rather than irritating.
All in all I think this is a good way to release this type of game. I don't think episodes are a lucrative or smart marketing means for some AAA titles, but for missions like assasination, it works!
Looking forward to more freedom, more immersion and the planning involved in escalation, elusive contracts and contracts mode, as well as more story!

I would give this game a definite 9.5/10. The character customization is ridculously in-depth. Although you can't have exact hairstyles, the game allows for a wide array of customizations to the hairs that are in the game, so it's not that big of a deal. Another great thing that the customization offers is the ability to truly modify characteristics. What this means is that you can angle your eyes, close or open your eyelids more or less, change your lip size, change your chin height and detail - a lot of in-depth customization that a lot of other games don't have, which is very nice. Not only does APB Reloaded have very detailed character customization, but it also allows for highly customizable clothing which is another excellent customization feature that a lot of games don't necessarily have. Saints Row IV had something to the same effect, but it feels as though APB Reloaded has a much wider possiblity for freeforming your own character in his/her own style.
Gameplay wise, the gameplay is relatively smooth. It sucks to start off the game as a weak player who gets blown up by an RPG, or shot to death by a shotgun at close range, but the mechanics aren't terribly difficult to learn. My one gripe with controls and gameplay is that driving is an issue when you first start out. Unless you buy a car, your handling will be the equivalant of not driving at all.
Chat functionalityis high; the ability to moderate your clan, your group, and chat all in one is a great, typical feature. My issue with the chat is that it's not very clear as to how to switch between chats. /help didn't tell me how to change between chats. You have to instinctively know that it's not a hotkey. Instead, you just type '/' and then the name of the group you want to talk to. For example '/district'.
Overall, awesome game. There were a few things that I didn't like that are mentioned above, but I still can't rate it below 9.5. It does seem like a game that demands you pay real money, but the free customization that I've seen so far is quite vast that it actually doesn't seem all too necessary.

Arguably the pinnacle of the series, and emphatically so. GTAIV and V may have deservedly won plaudits for a more mature storyline and graphical fidelity, respectively, yet the shadow of GTA: San Andreas looms heavily all these years later. SA still contains far more content and sheer fun than any of its successors, with all that was omitted in later instalments sorely missing; Niko's journey in Liberty City was tarnished by poor customisation options, a dearth of (fun) side-missions and unnecessarily difficult driving, whilst controlling Michael, Franklin, and Trevor in a revamped Los Santos, as technically accomplished as it is, suffers from an identity crisis by trying to relive CJ's glory days and telling a decent story at the same time, and ultimately not doing itself justice in either.
GTA: SA, on the other hand, managed to find that important balance perfectly the first time round, with a 90's setting in Los Santos, San Fierro, and Las Venturas within the greater state of San Andreas proving awe-inspiring in terms of its atmosphere, ambition and playability, accompanied by a plot that was never meant to be taken seriously aiding the enjoyability of the game's missions as they entered the realm of the ridiculous. The fact that the GTA IV add-on The Ballad of Gay Tony and GTA V rely so heavily on paying homage to, or rather reintroducing, what was present almost a decade earlier perhaps testifies to the significance and ever-present influence of San Andreas.
Vice City comes so close with its 80's aesthetic and amazing licenced soundtrack, along with perhaps the best humour and radio station chatter in the series, but San Andreas took GTA to a new level with the scale and explorability of its world and a far superior aiming system that isn't nearly as bad as it's made out to be. Along with, shall we say, a thing or two to do to pass the time.
You'll find an amazing abundance of activities to take part in ranging from, to merely scratch the surface, base jumping to gambling, committing home burglaries to driving semi-trailers across cities, playing pool to bulking up at the gym, dating love interests to expanding your 'hood in local gang wars, and in this PC version you'll get to experience it all the way it was meant to be, with a silky smooth framerate and excellent draw distance that brings Los Santos' skyscrapers into view as soon as you step out of CJ's house in the Grove.
But the real key to San Andreas' success? Amidst all the hidden gang graffiti tags, photo opportunities, and horseshoes, and the host of clothing stores, barbers and tattoo parlours littered around the map, not to mention the amazing choice of music whether it be West Coast rap or Rage Against The Machine, you'll also discover a remarkable soul - a real sense of purpose in the thick of all the chaos - that may possibly never be matched again. Not even, tellingly, by Rockstar itself.

This game has set my standards for gaming in general. There are but a few games that come close in freedom, diversity and creativity as Everquest (2). I've been hooked since launch and been playing EQ1 before that.
The hours I've spent playing this are uncountable. I have over 10,000 hours of playing time EASY, probably closer to 20,000.
-------------------------------------------
TLDR: This game is really good and will keep you busy for months if not years, unfortunately the game has been in its dying phase for years already and the player population is declining more year upon year. The game is virtually dead. There's the elite, the veterans, at the top who have their little group going and don't need anyone else. It is really hard for new/returning players to get into end-game content, if that's your sole purpose... well good luck with that, if not, there is also a TON of solo, group and raid content to be enjoyed at lower levels.
Overall I can only say that I really recommend this game and that it's too huge to review in a bit of text.
See for yourself.
-------------------------------------------
The motto 'Free-to-play. Your way', well they're right. You can really play your way.
Do you want to craft? Go ahead. Do you want to explore? Go ahead. Do you want to gather? Go ahead. Do you want to reset your character's advancements and try something new? Go ahead.
Do you have different advancement profiles you like and want to switch between them as often as you like? Go ahead. Do you want to play a healer whose advancement profile is build on maximum damage output? Go ahead.
Do you want to get filthy rich of selling collectibles and other stuff or do you want to collect everything you find? Go ahead.
Do you want to spend your time decorating (a) house(s)? Go ahead. Better yet, do you want to decorate an entire castle and meet your guild mates there? Go ahead.
Do you want to have all the prefix and suffix titles in the game? Good luck and go ahead. Do you want to be a froglok with the title Destroyer of Frogloks? Go ahead.
Do you want to have a name that is so big that it doesn't fit the screen? Go ahead. Do you want to play an evil shadowknight wearing a pink robe and riding a unicorn? Go ahead.
Pros
- The amount of content.
- The diversity of races, both playable and monster races.
- There's a class for everyone's playstyle.
- Character progression.
- Every MMO has it these days, but this game was the first to introduce a housing system and a very customizable one at that.
- Broker system.
- The user interface is extremely customizable.
- Mercenaries. Makes soloing a hell lot funner.
- Amount of quests and special quests such as signature, heritage, lore & legend and language quests.
- Zone design.
- Quite reasonable graphics for a game from 2004 (especially on extreme quality).
- Collectibles aka shinies.
Pro/Con
- Button mashing! There are so many spells, combat arts and other skills that can and need to be used in fights. Like it or not!
- Marketplace. Some people like this, some people don't.
- Many superficial quests, ie: Gather x amount of this, Kill x amount of that.
- Dumbing down of the game, making it 'noob friendly' too much.
Cons
- The amount of lower level content that has been created the last couple of years: virtually zero. Where as end-game gets all praise and glory. If I feel like creating a new character, I have to go through the same zones I have been hundreds of times already. It gets boring after a while. This doesn't count for new players or returning players who don't have too much experience.
- Server lag.
- Expensive expansion packs and subscription (considering the game's age).
- SOE -> DBG switch.
- EXTREME inflation.
- The game once was a product of passion, nowadays it seems the developers are just trying to milk the cashcow for as long as it still can.
The game, specifically the amount of content and features, can be quite overwhelming to new players so I recommend the use of EQ2 Wikia (
) and EQ2 Maps (
) for your own ease. These tools are very useful and recommended also to experienced players.
Overall I can only say that I really recommend this game and that it's too huge to review in a bit of text.
See for yourself. Also, give it some time before judging... the game has a learning curve and you really need to get used to it, especially in terms of user interface.

Like many guys, I was a bit skeptical about buying this game. I finally caved when I saw it discounted by half and reading some trusted opinions. So, this game used to have a lot of negative reviews but seems to be picking up recently. So what's the deal here?
What seems to have been the most controversial about the game was the episodic release model, where we were treated to each of the game's missions one at a time. Many folks had an understandable problem about it, because it gives no guarantees if, in the worst case scenario, the full game gets released at all.
Another controversial issue was the DRM which forced the player to stay online, essentially giving us all the hassle of multiplayer games and none of the benefits.
With that out of the way, I think it's a good time to let the game stand on its own and discuss its actual merits. All the missions for this season are out and are pretty polished.
So, for those of you who never played a Hitman game, the series is about a genetically engineered contract killer who works with a mysterious organization doing what hitmen do. Looking at the screenshots you might be lead to believe this is a third person shooter game. To an extent that's true, but the game is more about sneaking and observing patterns. A typical game goes like this: you're thrown into a game's level, you spend the first half an hour or so getting the feel of it - where are the targets, important items, other key points such as disguises and opportunities. You spend a lot of time skulking about and observing how the entire mechanism of NPC routines unfolds... and then you throw a wrench into it all and see what turns up.
The objective is of course to eliminate the indicated targets. The game is pretty good at providing you with numerous options to do that. Poisoning, explosion close combat or long range sniping? Or maybe an accident? And that's not all. The tutorial mission is pretty good at demonstrating the great many possibilities. You will stalk your prey, changing disguises to blend in and get close. It needs to be said at this point that your targets aren't good people. Some are mobsters, some are terrorists, others managed to get away with dirty deeds and feel smug about it. The ethics involved are of course questionable, so if you have a problem justifying this, perhaps this isn't a good game for you.
With that out of the way, the game's levels are overall very well designed. They are pretty varied and each one offers a unique feel (although you are likely to like some and loathe others). There are numerous opportunities (and rewards) for exploration. The overall presentation is superb, the very first "real" mission gives a great feel of a crowded fashion event that feels very alive and organic.
All in all, the game's appeal is in replayability. There aren't a lot of missions and it's very possible to "finish" them in under 20 hours - just let yourself be guided by the first opportunity you run into and put a bullet in each target's head. This is of course the simplest and least rewarding way to play this game - the levels were meant to be replayed, explored and savored; otherwise, you are robbing yourself of the game. There are always multiple ways to get to the target and multiple ways of doing them in, 90% of the fun is exploring all this and getting the timing right. The game does a good job at promoting this through listed Opportunities and Challenges (some of which are pretty straightforward, others are hidden and quite absurd in nature).
Once you had enough of the main targets, you are free to try custom contracts and escalations where you get a different set of targets (often with special conditions to satisfy along the way) and the map can be altered in a subtle way. There's quite a lot do in this game after you've scratched the surface.
For veterans of the series, I am sure the real question is this: how does it stand in comparison to the previous entries. As a fan, I am pleased to observe that the game doesn't follow in the footsteps of Absolution. I felt at home immediately during the tutorial mission - no railroading, fully freeform approach, lots of little details that make it seem alive. If you can get over the episodic release and forgive the DRM, you're in for a treat. Getting Silent Assassin Suit Only is as satisfying as ever, and the difficulty is fully customizable. There's a few hand-holding options which can be switched off in the menu. The only thing missing in this regard are limited saves, but this is partially fixed in Escalation contracts where no saving is allowed.
There are of course some low points, they don't retract too much from the overall experience, but they're there.
The controls don't feel very fluid, especially when shooting and climbing, and the player character sometimes has problems navigating simple looking obstacles. I'm not too keen on the quick time events in hand to hand combat either. On the other hand, Hitman games were also slightly crude when it comes to controls, so it doesn't stand out that much.
The AI sometimes behaves oddly, immediately homing in on your location after you make a shot with a silenced weapon, other times it spots bodies through vegetation, it also doesn't seem bothered by blood marks at all. All in all, the game is pretty decent at communicating what went south and why, so it doesn't feel cheap or unfair.
Fans of the series will notice a few of missing features like taking hostages, gun customization and rifle cases. Myself, I am missing custom guns the most, but the game gives you an ersatz in unlocking various pieces of equipment through mission mastery - the more challenges you do, the more stuff you open up - different starting locations and disguises, hidden caches, new equipment that you can use for all other missions, some of them being customized weapons. Another personal favorite was the newspaper articles from Blood Money which followed your exploits and reacted to your playstyle.
All in all, the game manages to deliver what I believe to be a Hitman experience, therefore I recommend this game.

Awesome game. It's not one of those doomed game tie in's to Fury Road. Which I suspect made this game fizzle out sooner than it shoud have. It is its own thing, but has elements taken from all the of the Mad Max films.
It's very similar to the Batman Arkham games and Shadow of Mordor series. So if you like them you'll probably enjoy this too.
However the setting is completely different in this. You'd think how can you make a desert wasteland varied and interesting? The simple thing of changing the colour tone and enviroment lighting along with added places to explore as you enter the new areas. It's subtle and very cleverly done. The graphics even to this day are excellent. The debris scattered across the wasteland is the best i've ever seen in a game (and some of it is destructable).
The game comes with your bog standard upgrade system. Character progression (moves/attire etc..) You can also customise your car all the way down to what type of suspension you want, your engine, tyres, bumper, colour scheme etc. You're not confined to one car, however you're most likely going to use the one that game wants you to play with the most as you wont be able to progress without it. The only thing that lets it down a bit is the story which feels a bit hammy at times and feels especially rushed towards the end. Regardless of that though its a good ride.

This was a good game. If you like open world, cars, apocalypse, and combat, you'll probably enjoy it for many hours.
The game is a like combination of Far Cry 3 and the Arkham series. The world is based on the Far Cry 3 engine, with various regions that you can explore by riding a hot air balloon (the equivalent of far cry's radio towers), then liberate by clearing out camps and strongholds, weakening enemy positions, as well as collecting artifacts and money (here called scrap). Fighting is like Arkham, where you can chain together a number of combinations and do some special moves with proper timing and keystrokes. Mad Max fights a lot like Batman, it turns out.
There's a good enough story here to follow, and a few twists in the story that will likely impact you. A few characters are memorable and interesting. And upgrading Max's car is fun and will fuel your efforts to clear out certain regions. It does get a bit repetitive toward the end. I found that about the 25% point I had mastered the hand to hand combat (and it doesn't really get tougher), but it takes the whole game to unlock all the vehicle upgrades. That was entertaininng.
All said, enjoyable. Got it on sale, and no regrets. A couple necessary hints: Max can jump (ctrl on my game), and you need it a few times; the car harpoon can force a ladder to drop, and you need this a few times. It took me forever to realize this and I wish I knew it sooner. Have fun!

As Max picked up a photo (history relic) of a teenager with a snowman, he commented:
"I can't remember the innocence... of snow, of man."
I feel like it described everything the wastelands was, a harsh world that snuffed out any hint of innocence or hope for the advancement of humankind. It was full of savages and survivors who considered getting through a day without harm a true win. In this world, there is no right or wrong, good or evil, only the strong, the weak and the unfortunate ghosts of the past. Then again, there's Max who just bulldozes through everything!
I liked the lore and world-building (though small) here. They handled that part of the game quite well in my opinion. I believe at one point I came to the realiziation some wastelanders were using human skin as leather.
It was really fun at first but got repetitive toward the middle/end of the game (though I did wipe out everything before the final mission). One qualm I did have was upgrading the Magnum Opus. The scrap collecting was easy but there were points where I had to finish a quest before obtaining the first of an upgrade. However, I'd be able to get the third, fourth or final stage by reducing the threat level of a territory. Didn't make a lick of sense, but I got them all anyway to complete the Archangels, which was one of my favorite parts of the Opus. Some of them were just plain cool.
As for the ending, I was left in a little bit of a daze because I felt mixed emotion. Like I understand it but wish it had not happened and went "oh well." You'll see or do know my meaning.
Despite some of its repetitive activities, the monotonous process of upgrading the Magnum Opus, and the rage-inducing combat, I really liked the game and some of its characters (Hope, Glory, Griffa, and Chumbucket for instance). I recommend the game, though on sale is best.
Now go on and corpse them War Boys! Happy gaming.

I got this prequel to the ever sucessful Arkham series, hoping it'd be better than what critics have made it out to be. But as it turns out, the game is more of an overall disappointment to what it could have been a signifciant improvement to Arkham City. While AC was so flawlessly free of technicalities, this game is still riddled with quite a few glitches and bugs the devs couldn't be bothered with. Nothing so game-breaking at least.
Where the games shine, the combat system, AO does away by making for slightly more challenging enemies and variations. This is surely a good thing, if not for the numerous control input problems and fight inconsistencies that simply ends up screwing up the enjoyment of gameplay. Especially annoying when the game expects you to perform up to task for the stupid Dark Knight System and ranked challenge maps.
Thankfully there's the very unbalanaced and overpowered Shock Gloves, to compensate for this. A new and important gadget to this game, it makes you wonder why the heck wasn't Batman using this OP weapon in Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. I mean it helped
. It's so glorious, there's no reason to abandon it.
There's only one thing AO has made the biggest improvement from the past games. The main story missions are now more noticeably fun and interesting to get through, despite the silly premise which mainly serves as a subtle excuse in order to chuck a whole bunch of notable Batman villians in this one single game.
It's also slightly longer and less than straightforward, compared to AC's main campaign, which is nice..
The dark cinematics and presentation are also brilliantly well done in coveying the tone of the game. If only the actual game looked as good... Boss fights are exceptionally great fun as well but makes Batman look too darn overpowered for someone just starting on an early vigilante career.
The open world of Gotham is much bigger than the Arkham City in Arkham City, many similiar buildings stand out, being bigger in size, and the layout is mostly different enough to distinguish as being unique. It's also as completely unrealistic as ever, as a city completely void of civilians. Another ridiculous excuse to prevent Batman from making "social interations" with civilians. What a bummer.
Collectibles still remain the same, data packs replacing riddler trophies this time and the number of packs hidden and are spread around the city. Finding or acquiring them isn't as hard as before, with less puzzles and challenges to solve. A show of leniency to completionists, or just a lack of effort on the devs' part in rushing this game.
- Game presentation is great, some areas of gameplay is an improvement, others is a thumbs down. A great game regardless, nevertheless, but nothing much so noteworhy for the upcoming Arkham Knight to follow and adapt from.

Better every day.
Functionality: A bit of a rocky start led to some mixed reviews up front, but the dev team is very actively seeking out feedback and implementing changes accordingly. The list of bugs is quickly depleting with every patch and update, and it's great to see their team responding to feedback in a positive manner and looking into the issues as quickly as they can.
Physics: Looking through the reviews, there are many notes on the physics and flight characteristics of the rigs used in the game. Personally, I think the system emulating the flight characteristics of the Racer3 flies quite well. It's certainly very far from absolutely unfliable, as other reviewers have called it. Is it perfect? Not quite yet, but again the devs are aware that it doesn't represent an absolutely identical experience to that of flying the 1200g Racer3 IRL and they're on it. There's also a garage mode coming soon, through which pilots will hopefully be able to choose between various options for their drones that offer a different flight experience. We'll presumably be able to better find something that flies in game closer to how our actual quads fly in real life. It's very important to keep in mind that the Racer3 weighs nearly three times that of some of our personal racing drones.
Tryouts: This is the portion of the game that has really sucked me in. Offering a tryouts tournament with a substantial financial contract and a position as a pilot on the show is absolutely phenomenal. I think this is a great way for those of us who are interested to really sit down and bust our asses to prove that we're capable of holding our own against the best of the best and chase that dream. This also provides a very significant incentive to hop into the game; there's nothing better than pitting yourself against all of the best sim pilots in the world to really see how you stack up to the competition. It's absolutely addictive, and I'm having a blast with it.

Let me just start by saying this game is NOT 'just another Minecraft clone.'
This game was recommended to me by a friend who had just purchased the mobile version and was showing it to me. I bought the game myself the next day, and I've been a fan ever since. Heck, my profile picture features a boss from the game itself.
While the graphics and vague fighting style may mislead you, the true beauty of this game resides in whatever else it has to offer. Enemies have different ways of attacking you. Crafting materials can be found anywhere. Items sometimes have the ability to be combined to make another new item. You can even wear clothes over your armor!
I've played Terraria for so long that it's extremely difficult to find what the downsides are. It depends on how you play the game. If you prefer to build, that's fine. If you prefer to fight, that's fine too.
I recommend this game because it has a lot more than you'd expect from a typical sandbox game. Terraria isn't 'typical' at all. Players have built houses, castles, and worlds, all with immense amounts of detail. Some have created large multiplayer servers for others to have fun.
Terraria is an open door to imagination and creativity. And if you like digging, fighting and building, then this game is for you.

Absolutely terrible.  I mean so impossibly terrible I can't get over it.  Been flying drones over 2 years now and I assure you its nothing like the real thing.  They have soiled the good name of Betaflight with their terrible attempt to duplicate it here.  I put in the same settings I use on all of my real drones and get an inoperable POS, even with the same Taranis.  Rate adjustments are basically a choice between too fast and too slow, tweak the sliders all you want.  Throttle is much the same, its either dead stick or rocket launch with little middle ground.  And the basic gravity settings on this game are not even close.  Obviously A-Nub is not the only 'self taught engineer' over at DRL.  Ever been stuck to a ceiling doing anything under any circumstances whatsoever?  Get ready to be stuck to them here.  Even at zero throttle.  Punch straight up and cut throttle to zero and a 2 lb drone will take 5-10 seconds to float gently to earth.  DO NOT try to duplicate this by jumping off a real building.  Real gravity works much differently .  My 300gram drone falls in a fraction of that time here in reality even with airmode on.  The yaw/pitch/roll blending is impossible to get close to anything I'd call realistic and the rendering in response to it is nauseating.  In fact all the rendering is nauseating.  Floors jump up at you, walls jump out at you and ceilings hold you.  I play this game for an hour then it takes me another hour to relearn how to fly my real drones.   Maybe its a great 'almost the real thing' for gamers who are used to terrible rendering, sluggish controls, and nauseating tilts and pans, but you will not become a real or good drone racer using this.  You may however vomit profusely.  Its just awful.   I recall old PS1 games that had better controls (and rendering) than I have after playing and tweaking this game for weeks.  Finally giving up now.  $20 down the drain that I could have spent on parts for my real drone.  Terrible.

Altho the game doesnt state it, this is a digging game.  You dig...and dig...and dig.  The game only progresses when you dig.  It slows the game down to a boring crawl.  Can't make steel until you find anthracite...and that one is VERY far underground.  Funny thing - you can build a laser pistol, but you cant make steel.
Combat just plain ole sucks.   Weaponry, when you can make something useful,  is laughably  underpowered.  Three shots from a pistol to kill a crawling slug,  anything bigger and you better be climbing...if you get caught on a straight run, you're dead.  Not because you dont have something that will do the job - you just can't access it fast enough in the clunky UI before the monsters kill you.
Crafting recipes, while seeming to be balanced, hit an invisible wall because of two things: a required "Project" and the correct materials.  Recipes show up based on what you pick up, meaning that you may get a recipe you can't use, because you're not sure what the resource is from.   Add in that you may have the materials, but can't use a recipe because you can't complete a required Project, and frustration ensues.
Also, prepare to restart again and again...with nothing.  When you die, and you WILL die because of the poor game mechanics, you drop everything you own.  Everything...right down to your sandals.   Then you get restarted back on the surface sans anything.  Which means totally resupplying yourself and a long run back to where you died to reclaim all your swag before you can try anything else....which is totally unecessary and totally boring.  And of course you can't build anything to help with the restart process because the resources are too rare.  Catch-22.  For me, that was the thing which made the game more trouble than it was worth.
Go spend your ten bucks on something else..stay away from this one.

Furthermore, as the quad moves along I could move the throttle stick + or - 45 degrees without the quad moving up or down hardly at all. I checked the curve and it was not extreme enough for that and even with heavy curve it would have still responded with some movement. This is also not even close to real life or even a decent attempt at simulation. Mind you i'm flying this with a Taranis well configured. I double checked settings. This is so painfully bad in terms of a sim that I just could not keep playing even though I wanted to try to win the gates.
If you are reading this and you are not a real life quad pilot yet, I would recommend lift off. It's gravity is not quite either but its a LOT closer to real life.

I started playing this game about a year ago due to nostalgia of remembering playing this on trial in my childhood days. Honestly I didn't think it'd hold up, much less suck me in like it did. It's definitely not an MMO for everyone, especially not for people used to convenience that modern MMOs have. It offers an experience of what MMORPGs were like back in the day of Vanilla WoW with few modern touches here and there. Many quests don't even have markers on the map, but for me that's a plus. There is a group finder, but on my server nobody uses it and we just talk to each other to find groups. The most important thing is the game gets constantly updated, every year it gets a new expansion and in the meantime there are a lot of patches with new content. I don't have many bad things to say about Everquest 2 as I really enjoy it. One thing that bothers me is the ability to exchange tokens buyable for real money for gametime, which leads to buyable currency, but that seems to be in every MMO nowadays, after Blizzard implemented it in WoW and probably won't go away anytime soon.
Tl;dr    I really like this game and would recommend MMO fans to at least try it, you may be surprised by how much it has to offer, just like I was.

Have well over 300 hours of play time on this game and I absolutely love it. Used to play WoW but it got so boring, felt like I just sat in Org all the time with nothing to do and dungeon finder took a lot away from the game. EQ2 has so much to the game, I have played for 300 hours and have barely even scratched the surface with so much more to explore and see and do. It is free to play but you need to buy the latest expansion to unlock that content, but theres tons to do before you even get to that point. It isn't like wow where if you don't have the expasion there is no point in playing. The monthly membership is a nice perk but definately not needed, and the store items are mostly cosmetic or frill items, its definately not a pay to win game. Anything you can buy in the store you can get better in game, even xp potions will be gotten over time if you dont want to buy. after a week, month, 3 months, 6 months, and then yearly intervals you get awesome rewards by typing /claim (also how you get your perks from any collector edition expansions you buy or preorder bonuses you get). I would definately recommend this game to someone who is looking for a MMO that is new but still has a classic feel to it. Even the graphics have held up pretty well for its age, but it won't compare to games like black desert online. But I'll take a slight dip in graphic quality for a huge, well fleshed game that is a ton of fun. Most criticisms of the game from when it was first released have been fixed since and improved.

While the sandbox element accounts for that somewhat, if you've played Arkham City you've played Origins and more. The combat is exactly the same except for the addition of the Shock Gloves (which are damn cool.) The new detective segments are an interesting concept but instead of making each investigation unique they all end with the "fly over and beat up the thugs at the last know location of the perp."
I have yet to play the DLC, but the collectables were a nightmare. They were MUCH easier to obtain than they were in City, and while I thought they were a headache at the time back then I now know that the challenge was everything. In this game, collectables are as challenging as using google.
Additionally, the switchover from the classic (90s) voiceactors was jarring, but it's not worthy of complaint as the acting is good.
In closing, if you think the price is good for a playthough of the main storyline, go for it; the rest of the gameplay won't add value outside what you got from Arkham City.

The story of Captain Forever Remix is short, sweet and endearing. Your brother, Kevin, wants to play a game and you agree to play with him if you can play the hero! Little Kevin wants to destroy the Solar System and you’re the only one who can stop him!
I can’t lie, I really enjoyed the intro and thought it was cute as hell. When we were kids our imagination was our greatest tool and that seems to be the basis of the story. You must create your own awesome spaceship and traverse the universe destroying anyone in your path so you can stop Kevin once and for all before he destroys everything.
The gameplay of Captain Forever Remix is simple but very addictive. You’ll be fighting your way through the various planets wiping out any ships who dare to cross you. Your ship is created by you before playing and can be customized and shaped in any way you want using the parts provided. You only start with a few bits and pieces but as you progress further you’ll unlock new ship starter packs with different (and often stronger) parts. Once your ship is created you’ll be plunged into the universe and will be faced with various enemies, all with their own ships which can be destroyed. When you destroy a ship some, or all of the parts become available for you to combine with your own ship, so you’ll able to get bigger and stronger as you play through the game. If you’ve played TerraTech the ability to build as you play will feel very familiar and is just as fluent. Some enemies also drop chests with parts for your ship as an additional bonus so you can get some pretty cool and unique customization going. You’ll find things from weapons, to shields to boosters, everything you’ll want and need to build yourself a total death machine.
Each stage will have a quest to complete which is usually along the lines of destroying a certain level enemy and once you complete it you’ll be able to travel to the next planet in the solar system on your way to Pluto and to stop Kevin destroying the universe!
The graphics are fab, your ship will soon be bursting with color as you traverse the beautiful solar system backdrops. I like the music too, it reminded me of retroish style games that I played when I was younger.
--- Full ship customization.
--- Fun addictive gameplay
--- Customization WHILST playing.
--- True to the original whilst adding more content.
--- Simple progression allowing you to unlock new ship and ship parts.
--- Enemies ship parts can become yours for awesome upgrade possibilities.
--- Randomly generated enemies.
--- Feels like there could be more to do than just build and destroy.
--- Not a lot of customization on start.
--- No actual quests or goal as such.
--- I actually feel the price is a tad steep for the content,.
--- Can’t combine different ship starter pack parts.
Captain Forever Remix really is great. The simple game-play is addictive and the customization and building of your own ships as you play really is a brilliant selling point. The price point I feel is a little high for the content you get but on sale the game would be a steal and is well worth trying. If you enjoyed the original Captain Forever then you’ll love this, it’s bigger, brighter and all round better.

Captain Forever Remix is an amazing update to the original Captain Forever
