When you're out destroying ships, it's just too easy to get carried away and go mad with power, slapping pieces everywhere and before you know it, you're dead. That's fine though, there are 9 different starter kits to choose from which for the most part require different styles of play. This IS a roguelike (roguelite?), so I guess you should be thankful for those options.
The appearance of the game is also really charming too. Lots of people have compared it to a Saturday morning cartoon and I feel the same way too. The art style, music, and dialogue all blends together so nicely. It's kinda hard to get too mad at this game from how cutesy everything looks, even if that last enemy called me a butt. Meh.
Really though, give this or the original a try, they're both really fun.. OUO

Mad Max is a decent vehicles customization and driving game that sorely lacks content that takes advantage of your decked out car. Remember in Fury Road when Max was chasing down a big semi hauling gas and women destined for breeding? Or how about the stretches of road where people are jumping on the car, throwing explosive, and just flat out rying to kill you? Very little of that stuff - the reason we enjoy the movies - is in the game; or it is in the game, but it feels watered down.
Sure, there are 'convey routes' where you need to blow up the "boss" vehicle, and these can be a bit of a challenge if only because you are outnumbered and the AI rubberbands, but at no point are you hanging off the side of a big semi or rescuing women. You will encounter the occasional free roaming enemy vehilcle, and some guys will jump on your car or try to run you off the road, but I found that what mostly happens is everyone inevitabbly slows to a stop and you and the AI drive around in small circles playing bumper cars until someone gives up. But even when outnumbered by other vehicles decked out with spikes and flames, there are just too many ways to defeat them: shotgun, grappling hook, explosives, etc. You do have limited ammo, but It remains so easy that the encounters actually end up becoming frustrating because you just want to get to the mission objective without being reminded of how much better the driving portion of the game should be.
Another problem is the size of the map. Yes, it's big, but you are never blasting along a long stretch of desert to chase down something important, or racing along an old asphalt road, weaving between debris. Instead, you drive along some defined paths that let your car go faster. Veer off the path and your car goes a bit slower. There are rocky hills and you do need to naviagate around some occasional difficult terrain, but on the whole, the landscape, overall, is boring.
So, for being a car-centric game, there isn't a whole lot of stuff to do with your car. The main story missions require that you do have to go on foot to fight the bad guys, and this is when things start to fall apart. All around the map are oppertunities to do different things, which mostly amount to driving to the place (fun) get out (not fun) and mash the X button. Occasionaly hit Y to dodge. Before entering these locations you can talke to people that will give you information about how to get into an area without ramming the front gate, but I found that geing in guns blazing works best as this is not a stealth game by any means.
Then there is the occaisonal boss encounter with lots of fire to contend with, and this adds some much needed variety, but once you figure out how they move and attack, you can quickly exploit their weakness. Secondary to this, these boss locations follow a similiar formula of sameness. Again, there is the occasional variety to the design, but everything inbetween looks and feels the same; climb some ladders, kick open a door, blow something up, fight enemies, and repeat.
The game does try to challenge you by making you manage your food, water, and fuel. But as you level up you character, these resources begin to matter less, and less, and less, until you find yourself passing oppertunities to claim a new water source because why does it matter? The same is true for enemy encounters. After a few hours, you level up your strength and defenses, and you become so powerful that when surrounded by enemies you can take them all out with zero effort.
Oh, and yes, the bases. You can upgrade these, but in order to to do this, you need parts. The parts are scattered around the map. To get these, drive to the place, get out, and start punching people. I found that it wasn't worth the time or effort, even for the bonuses or to see the base with more people.
I picked the game up for under 5$. For a movie-based tie-in game that is just basically a clever reskin of the Arkham and Morder games, it's worth the money.
The game is polished and relatively good looking - considering it is an empty, brown, apocalyptic environment. There are some props, like fallen windmills and collapsed bridges that make you wonder what happened. Character models are solid. The voice acting works.
I turned on Netflix when I played the game because I did want to progress in the game, but I couldn't help from becoming bored. It's probably best to avoid trying to do all the side missions and instead focus on finishing the main story.
Summary:
The game has a handful of clever and fun ideas that get run into a sand bank as a result of its limited scope. A sequel would be welcome, as there is much that could be expanded upon. But as it stands, pick it up for under $10 during a sale. It operated like the Arkham and Mordor games while still being its own thing, so all the underlying mechanics work well enough. I wouldn't say it is on the same level as those two properties, but Avalanche did a fine given the source material.

I really enjoyed the challenges each map offered, It has a ton of replayability; the main thing everyone wants in a Hitman game. It has both manual saving and autosaving for you to work with.
Unfortunately the AI is not exactly the smartest but there's lots of room for improvement which I hope IOI concentrates on for the next season. Performance wise it could be better, some maps run very smooth and others not so smooth, mostly in very specific parts. The graphics are nice but Hitman is not really a game where graphics are paramount.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. I will say however the DRM is over the top and I understand why people would skip this game for that reason as well as episodic release method. The game disconnected me a few times which was annoying. A recent patch has allowed you to use your unlocks offline, however you still have to be online to actually unlock them. Hopefully Squenix/IOI tone that aspect down some for the next season.

The population isn't too bad either for an old MMO, the new zones are usually crowded and somebody always seems to be in every overland zone.
It's pretty fun to run around as an old player for nostalgia sake, and anybody can login now that it's free-to-play.
However, the economy is definitely messed up and not good for new players, lowlevel items can be very expensive and no newbie would ever have the amount of money needed for some stuff on the market (though they could easily join a guild and ask for help and gear).
A lot has changed over the years, but if you're a former-EQ2 player looking for nostalgia or a new player looking for a game to kill time in you should definitely give this game a try.

Version reviewed: 0.6.
I understand this is early access, but I was still expecting a lot more from this game. A few things in the trailer don't seem to exist in the current version of the game (e.g. starting in a base, a jump-jet with unlimited fuel, a moon environment... it actually looks like the early parts of the trailer... that's supposed to be backstory, but presenting it in the form of actual gameplay that we the players don't get to experience is a dirty trick. Though there is still a very playable (if incomplete) game here with most of the demonstrated features. I still, though, have other criticisms.
First of all, the inventory management system is a serious pain. With no auto-organizing, optional snap-to-grid placements, and the inefficent sort/organize functions for containers... at least being able to carry an unlimited number of nested containers and label them though, helps organize things. But something tells me the final version of the game is going to do away with that.
Secondly, the controls. In addition to the difficulty of successfully picking up smaller/thinner items, there's also the awkward and clumsy movement that gives me lots of frustration trying to make jumps. It's also hard to attack exactly where you want to attack. Singling out the right item you want to use in automatic mode takes a long time if you've got a lot of stuff (and an effective unlimited inventory means you can and should get as many toys on your person as possible) and manual mode is impractical since the hotbar is limited to seven slots plus two quick slots.
Thirdly is the fake difficulty. Death is cheap (you drop everything and respawn, and I don't think items ever disappear from the world) but it can be really irritating to get back to where you dropped all your stuff -- especially when you respawn with a partial bar of health, an empty stomach (you only regenerate health when you've had something to eat), and no armor. And many monsters that stand in your way can kill you in precisely two hits in that state. And then there's the frustration of having to re-organize your main inventory -- since whenever you pick something up with the grab laser (the fastest way to pick stuff up) it just gets thrown into a random spot in your bag.
Fourth -- the progression. It just doesn't feel right. This is clearly a space-age survival game, but the metals available to use don't even include titanium. Steel is the second-best metal there is, with the tier after that being practical post-game equipment. Also, why the heck is bronze stronger than iron?
Fifth, everything that's missing. No music. No way to quickly switch ammo types on a held weapon (you need to select the item in question which you probably have in a nested container in your inventory to change its used ammo).  No mechanism wiring systems (no designing elaborate traps or light switches). No liquids (water/lava/etc).
I haven't even tried to build a base of my own because the game gives you a prefabricated base from the start, and building structures is made a lot more complicated than it has to be as every building material has like 8 different types of blocks, and the clunky interface and crafting required would make it more of a chore than it's worth. I dread having to build anything creatively in this game.
I've clocked 31 hours into this game (as of this writing) and I feel like I've basically seen everything there is to see. That's depressingly low for a survival game. You're better off going for Starbound -- this game has a long way to go before it can even hold a candle to it.
Maybe I'll check back in a few versions and see how it's advanced.

This game is really good.  The controls are tight and the artwork is very pretty.  It's like Edge of Space except this is executed properly.  Both games have similar descriptions but 'Signs of Life' has the fundamentals down pat.  If you were apprehensive about buying this game because of past disappoints with other games in the genre, don't worry.  The Devs are focusing on the right areas for this game's design and will put more of the content in later, as opposed to some other games out there with all the bells and whistles but have artwork that clashes and mushy controls.

If you played Terraria or Starbound, then you'll feel right at home here.  The mechanics are pretty similar with the occasional tweak here and there. There's a fairly typical mix of old and new weapons, swords vs guns and so on. It's nice that to have an early armor options that require minimal killing of things, although some of the plants can be deadly, since some of the critters that drop leather are kinda dangerous.
At this point (0.6?) the limited story is a bit of a downside in my opinion. It feels disconnected, kind of like my experience in Starbound up to the initial starbase and thereabouts. Terraria has a stronger, but looser narrative. I think it'd be nice to tie the player in a bit more, since whatever the lore is aside, it feels like the player crash landed and then stumbled into stuff. So, there's not much attachment or concern for the back story people except to hope they had some good stuff you can loot and take not of any warnings about what to avoid... Not sure why I've crashed on a planet in an escape pod.
Regarding the UI:
I do think that the inventory is not a strong point as is. It's interesting, but stuff visually overlaps, which is a little annoying when you have to click on things and having to manually request auto-arrange/auto-sort can be annoying at times. The auto-bar which groups items into a small set of categories and provides access via scroll to all items of a certain type through a particular bar is, however, a nifty feature, even if it occasionally leads to unintended shooting (you know, like of your foot!) and food consumption... One of the more interesting notions is how the map works. You don't get a map by default or even by passive exploration, you've got to actively build one with the scanner. I'd strongly recommend upgrading it at least one step before engaging in a serious world mapping attempt, though, it'll make it a fair bit easier.
TL;DR
Fun to play and fairly engaging, but there's not pressure to build anything more than a minimal shelter before heading off to explore. The AI communications are annoying in a way, but a nice touch even if it's kinda of telling you that you're an idiot the entire time and implying that you wouldn't even survive without it's help. Some things to get used to with the user interface (UI) and movement. Also, try not to fall too far, it's kind of painful.
P.S.
Giant Robot Chicken is a plus. Surprised that it's peaceful if you don't attack it though. Might be funny if there was a base in the game somewhere that looked like the chicken gave it a hard time...

At launch, I bought the first episode of Hitman and greatly enjoyed it. The training missions were fun and interesting, and Paris was absolutely fantastic, easily on par with a good Blood Money level.
I then went onto the Steam page and left a scathingly negative review because, despite the level-design brilliance on display, the experience was constantly hampered by an always-online requirement. The server connectivity in those early days, like with most games, was spotty at best and non-functional at worst. When the connection dropped, I found myself bereft of all of my unlockables and unable to do any challenges. Thus, thanks to a rather draconian DRM scheme, I felt compelled to leave a negative review.
The big November patch changed things. While the online requirement still unfortunately exists if you wish to make progress on challenges and unlock items, the items you unlocked online can now be used offline as well. It's not perfect, not by any means, but it takes the worst of the sting out of my early frustrations with the game and its DRM.
Aside from the DRM, people have been singing this game's praises, and rightfully so. The Sapienza mission in particular far outshines most instances of level design in recent memory, and both Paris and Hokkaido are up there with Blood Money's best missions. Even the weakest levels - for me, Marrakesh and Bangkok - are significantly better than the weakest of the older Hitman games' levels. All six main missions are exceptionally replayable, with new mission-start locations and smuggled item drop-offs exponentially increasing your options as they are made available. This, in conjunction with the lively target AI that wanders the map, interacting with the environment and reacting to a number of different variables, creates a well-realized social stealth and assassination experience.
Overall, Hitman is now an extremely solid and entertaining game, a standout title in the stealth genre, and well worth its price tag. Here's hoping Season 2 is every bit as good.

HITMEME™, the new exciting game in the Hitman series brings a new refreshing touch by using an episodic system that makes you wait half a year until you actually get to play the whole, rich experience of 6 missions.
Square Enix, the small indie company behind recent gems such as Deus Ex: Memekind Divided, featuring the amazing concept of purchaseable skill points that disappear once you start a new savegame, or that other game with the episodic system, Life is Strange, that nobody except YouTubers actually bothered to finish, has yet again scored another homerun for their wallets by making another game of an already famous franchise.
You follow the rich and developed backstory of Soldier 47, world class assassin that can't enter supermarkets because the barcode scanner keeps picking up on the backside of his head. The gameplay mainly consists of following the little markers the "opportunity system" sets for you and getting near perfect scores without knowing what you doing. There's also a little easter egg where you turn the opportunity system off to unlock the actual game.
The game also features a lot of incentives to keep you playing, for example you can use the mastery system which makes the missions progressively more easy the more often you have completed them. This is the complete opposite of what you would expect a mastery system to do, so it serves as a plot twist to compliment the story.
There is also user generated missions ranging from difficulties between Bronze League of Legends and competitive NEKOPARA. Some of the missions in the escalation system and user generated contracts also require you to basically have the entire layout of the map in your head, as well as the movement of every person at any given time, but you can also circumvent this prerequisite by using 10 savestates a minute.
All in all, I think HITMEME™ is a very good game if your PC can run it, don't buy the intro pack and complain about not having all the missions u dum fuks, its really not that hard of a concept to understand.

So after nearly 1k hours in this game it's about time to write a review. I'm by no means one of the so called legacy players and can only offer an opinion from around January this year until now. I'll give two perspectives before and after the new BP update.
Component system:
the component system was probably the worst time to play the game. Zergs dominated. People had aks and full Metal gear in a few minutes on a high pop fresh wipe then proceeded to massacre any naked they could get their hands on. Pvp was terrible for newbies and servers died within a day of the wipe and unless you were on a you tubers server along with all the 13 year old fan boys servers died off in a day thanks to certain servers with daily wipes. This was probably the worst time for rust and if I had written this review based on this alone I would not recommend it.
New BP system:
I didn't play the old BP system so I was curious about what people found so fascinating. This new system may change the game honestly. But it's not a type of system that's solo friendly. The whole group mentality is even more so into play. Encouraging larger groups to grind scrap. But the good news of this is that server don't die as quick, in fact you'll get max pop 3 days into a wipe with some servers even having queues. I like this system although it's grindy as he'll you need to be good at early game pvp cuz the best you'll get is whatever an air drop will give making airdrops even more crucial. Bow pvp and early game guns such as the revolvers and pipe shotgun gun should be a major focus for any new players.
Performance:
I run this game at 30 or so fps on max servers using potato but get a lot of lag and such as I also have 200-300 ping on the nearest zone (Eu) servers. Mainly in combat it kicks in but I have a Nvidia GeForce 950m which for all non tech savvy people is a laptop gpu that is one of the most potato of potato graphics cards. Game runs smoothly other than the rage inducing stutters.
Conclusion:
All in all this game is a lot less worse than made out to be. Sure the community is more toxic than a nuclear wasteland and has a ton of salty people, squeakers, trolls, zergs,hackers, imbeciles, etc. But this new update may open a whole world of possibilities and in time hopefully the community spends less time against each other and trying to work together to accomplish goals. This is by no means a solo game as this game is boring and nearly impossible solo. Gl and hf whoever buys it. You'll need it.

The DRL sim is a great way to get flying and keep your practice schedule regardless of weather, lighting, or time available. I'm not serious about racing, so I'm going to write this review from a freestyle pilot's perspective.
- Setup and Configuration -
The simulator is easy to set up using the Frsky Taranis radio with its integrated USB port. If you're using another brand of radio with a simulator cable (I tried it with a Futaba) it is a bit more involved. This is largely not the game's fault, as most of the additional setup needs to be done in the Windows control panel, but may still take a bit longer to get going if you're using Spektrum/Futaba. I didn't try practicing with an xbox controller, as IMO that is not how this game is designed to be played.
- Physics -
The sim physics are accurate for the quads available in the game, but those quads are not necessarily representative of what most pilots fly. The default quad (DRL racer 3) is a large 5S quad that weighs around 1kg. That's 3x what my personal builds weigh. While I have not flown the racer 3, I have flown heavy quads on 5S and they are much closer to the "feel" experienced in the simulator than my personal builds. Some of the other quads (such as the mifune) do have a feel closer to what I generally fly. I'm hoping that the workshop feature, when added, will allow us to tailor the quads to more closely match our individual setups. This change alone will be an enormous improvement as a training aid.
I found it difficult to match my rates in the simulator to the rates I fly in the real world. It is not a direct plug-in from Betaflight, as it may seem on first inspection. This also contributes to the "different" feel that a lot of other viewers have alluded to.
-- Maps --
In addition to all the maps from first and second DRL seasons, the simulator offers its own "gates of hell" map, which is more geared towards freestyle. This map has a large container ship port, a factory, a city, some woods, and a tunnel with trains. The map is massive, both in extents and in its physical scale. It's difficult to grasp the scale of the map as you don't really have any reference points to your body, but most of the areas I practice in with my real quads are a fraction of the size of even one of the map "areas". This naturally changes the feel of the quad, since you're using a much larger area than you normally would.
-- Interface --
The "tile" interface for the menus and settings selection is difficult and kind of confusing, but doesn't impact gameplay once you start flying. This is definitely an area that needs some improvement in future updates.
Though I may have seemed a bit harsh, I believe that the DRL sim is currently the best, most complete, and most accurate sim available (for freestyle flying at least). It's also a great way to practice or learn to fly without breaking gear or risking damage / loss. Most of my issues are not fundamental, and they will most likely be addressed in future updates. Give it a shot; it has a few quirks still left to be ironed out but all in all it's a good experience and a valuable tool for practice.

I've spent a great deal of time now in Signs of Life over the last few weeks and months, and I feel it's now a decent time to update my review of it.
I still think the game deserves a thumbs up becasue it is definitely heading in a very good direction. From the mystery of Pioneer One and its inhabitants to the very well designed alien ruins, the game has an amazing allure that simply cannot be ignored.
However......
I must say that I purchased this game for a friend on the sole basis of showing him exactly how bad the inventory system is. I'm fairly certain he is now seeking extensive therapy. The game's inventory is so bad that I just couldn't NOT show it off. While the game itself is geting very good, the inventory could be better put to use in tech schools across the globe teaching new developers how not to design an inventory system. Simply put, it is a creature of pure madness. I'm quite sure there is a special place reserved in Hell where people will simply sift through an inventory system just like this to find a sweater for eternity, and that poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is going to find it faster than the player. I literally wish that just like the tablet, I could turn my shotgun or pistol on my own face in-game with a right click and just end it all after a few minutes of searching for that one item I just picked up. Yes, it highlights, no, you cannot see it behind the wall of crap already in there. Who thought ovelapping items after a sort would be helpful? So I have bags that auto-sort various items out, but a lot of good those do when they, too, become so cluster ♥♥♥♥ed that finding an apple is... how did I say it before? A chore.
I literally could go days on how bad this inventory is, but that's probably enough bashing to get the point across. Besides, we have more to talk about here.
But first... I can't humiliate the inventory system without making some suggestions to lighten the load. So, with that in mind, I would pose the idea of not overlapping items in the containers. Slotted bags may be in every game, but I assure you there is a damn good reason for it. You need a clear and concise view of every item in a bag. At this point, I would even welcome a text based inventory menu. Even something exactly like the crafting menu but for inventory would increase the usuability and efficiency of this inventory system by 3000%.
On to other things... Datapads. I have one word for datapads.
W H Y ?
Why is there no journal? Why am I sifting through 15 identical datapads (amongst 500 other items blocking my view, mind you) to find that one datapad I just picked up that holds crucial information on where to get multipass lvl 2? Seriously?
Though shalt use a journal. Bind it to a key, let me read past messages in one simple to use window on the interface. Don't throw me to the hounds of hell in that tiny white box of nightmare in the corner of my screen to find crucial data to progress the game.
Now I know everyone might think this review is all bad, but by no means should it be viewed that way. I wouldn't take all this time if I didn't actually care. I really do think this game has LOADS of potential, and I'm not sorry I bought it. I finally got to experience the multiplayer aspects and, although I couldn't find a way to toggle off friendly fire, the framework performed quite well. Exceedingly well, perhaps. It's a fun game, with an incredible alluring mystery about it that you just want to know more about.
I find myself wishing I could scan things with a query tool to learn about them, because exploration in this game is very unique. I can't wait to see what else gets added.
I know she's still on the drawing board. So I say keep up the good work, and please, for the love of almighty Zuess and pals, rethink inventory. It's the worst aspect of the game right now.
Side note to people thinking about buying and playing the game, you gotta give it a chance. It seems wonky at first, but it gets better. Just don't get sucked into the 9th dimension of hell that is inventory management.
(PS, you should make those cracked bricks in Pioneer one look more cracked and noticable... had to google that one.)

I love the game so far with over 35+ hours invested and look forward to future updates with more content towards release, please keep in mind this is an early access review of the game in it's current state. As well my personal opinion and first impression, as I only write selective reviews on refreshing game experiences. So the only real issue that I have encountered is the fact that the world is a small place after all and loops around back towards the players starting position, which can be completed around ten minutes or less. That aside it is large enough in terms of depth, the surface world as well an ecological underground world where time has no meaning. I have also been informed  by the developer that "world-generator" is not limited to the previously mentioned constraint, and that is temporarily due to creating quality content to fill the void.
That fact aside there is plenty of content to keep the player occupied for many hours. As a game about exploration, this allows the player a rewarding experience. I dislike the linear trends of most games, feeding the player non-vital information through tutorials leaving nothing else to discovery. Games only need a few mechanics to be great, a storyline is just the icing on the cake. The game starts abrutly as your escape pod crashes downward into the atmosphere of an unkown planet with a limited fuel supply, you land safely upon flattened terrian with nothing remote of a civilization around as you gaze through the glass upon your new surroundings, you step fourth...
AGIS, your "friendly" artificially "intelligent" friend! This is your A.I. companion, and although it's moral programming is limited, AGIS will allow you to learn crafting reciepes,and reverse engineer as you discover new resources to survive. You will find from time to time, that AGIS is able to lighten your mood during convexing times upon the desolate planet, that or you have gone past the breaking point of your sanity. :D
AGIS is part of your MEG Tool, that's the name of the device attached to your wrist. This multifunctional tool will allow you the player, topographical mapping functions, illumination, traction beam, and laser extraction, powered by a battery capacitor and lens. All of which are upgradable through precious gemstones, and salvage discovered on the planet.(Sapphire, Topaz, Amethyst, Ruby,etc.) in varied conditions affect functionality of your MEG. If you so desire, forgo all of the techology as decreed by the gods! And manually work the planet with your barehands (pick axe, gardening hoe, regular axe, shears, hammer, and seeds).
If your preferred genre of gaming and in general is sci-fi, for $10.99 you won't have any regrets, especially for a game that's currently in the early stages of it's development. Do not try to compare this gem to what's available on the market. If there is an aspect of the game you wish to have included, removed , or improved upon, offer a suggestion on the forums for the game, I'm sure the developers would appreciate it. I whole-heartedly recommend "Signs Of Life" if you are looking for a 2D side scroller with simple build and exploration mechanics. On a personal note this game satsifies my missing nostalgia for the 90's (SNES,SEGA,ETC.) .

At launch, I bought the first episode of Hitman and greatly enjoyed it. The training missions were fun and interesting, and Paris was absolutely fantastic, easily on par with a good Blood Money level.
I then went onto the Steam page and left a scathingly negative review because, despite the level-design brilliance on display, the experience was constantly hampered by an always-online requirement. The server connectivity in those early days, like with most games, was spotty at best and non-functional at worst. When the connection dropped, I found myself bereft of all of my unlockables and unable to do any challenges. Thus, thanks to a rather draconian DRM scheme, I felt compelled to leave a negative review.
The big November patch changed things. While the online requirement still unfortunately exists if you wish to make progress on challenges and unlock items, the items you unlocked online can now be used offline as well. It's not perfect, not by any means, but it takes the worst of the sting out of my early frustrations with the game and its DRM.
Aside from the DRM, people have been singing this game's praises, and rightfully so. The Sapienza mission in particular far outshines most instances of level design in recent memory, and both Paris and Hokkaido are up there with Blood Money's best missions. Even the weakest levels - for me, Marrakesh and Bangkok - are significantly better than the weakest of the older Hitman games' levels. All six main missions are exceptionally replayable, with new mission-start locations and smuggled item drop-offs exponentially increasing your options as they are made available. This, in conjunction with the lively target AI that wanders the map, interacting with the environment and reacting to a number of different variables, creates a well-realized social stealth and assassination experience.
Overall, Hitman is now an extremely solid and entertaining game, a standout title in the stealth genre, and well worth its price tag. Here's hoping Season 2 is every bit as good.

HITMEME™, the new exciting game in the Hitman series brings a new refreshing touch by using an episodic system that makes you wait half a year until you actually get to play the whole, rich experience of 6 missions.
Square Enix, the small indie company behind recent gems such as Deus Ex: Memekind Divided, featuring the amazing concept of purchaseable skill points that disappear once you start a new savegame, or that other game with the episodic system, Life is Strange, that nobody except YouTubers actually bothered to finish, has yet again scored another homerun for their wallets by making another game of an already famous franchise.
You follow the rich and developed backstory of Soldier 47, world class assassin that can't enter supermarkets because the barcode scanner keeps picking up on the backside of his head. The gameplay mainly consists of following the little markers the "opportunity system" sets for you and getting near perfect scores without knowing what you doing. There's also a little easter egg where you turn the opportunity system off to unlock the actual game.
The game also features a lot of incentives to keep you playing, for example you can use the mastery system which makes the missions progressively more easy the more often you have completed them. This is the complete opposite of what you would expect a mastery system to do, so it serves as a plot twist to compliment the story.
There is also user generated missions ranging from difficulties between Bronze League of Legends and competitive NEKOPARA. Some of the missions in the escalation system and user generated contracts also require you to basically have the entire layout of the map in your head, as well as the movement of every person at any given time, but you can also circumvent this prerequisite by using 10 savestates a minute.
All in all, I think HITMEME™ is a very good game if your PC can run it, don't buy the intro pack and complain about not having all the missions u dum fuks, its really not that hard of a concept to understand.

-Story; its ♥♥♥♥ing wonderful. All the characters are memorable, the lengths and breadths you have to go to are maddening its... I don't want to spoil anything but gods, it is one of the best game stories I've seen in a long time.
-The world: Harsh and beautiful, this part of the Wasteland is full of so many fantastical landscapes. It's a unique experience to be speeding through a long-dry sea bed, using a shipwreck as a jump- all en route to an offshore windfarm turned into a massive enemy camp.
-Upgrade system: You can upgrade both Max himself and the car, the Magnum Opus, in a wild amount of ways. While having all the upgrades on max don't really effect your gameplay but make it better, the Opus actually requires some balancing depending on how you play. I prefer a quick, heavy weapons Opus- fun stuff.
-Capture system: As it's such a theatrical game, it has a quick system to catch the most brutal screenshots you can get, even with a selection of modifiers and filters. Its a great touch.
THE BAD: There's not much, but I'll list it here so you know what to be prepared for.
-The Archangels: A preset system for the Magnum Opus... and its basically useless. You only have to use it twice in the story, and gosh its annoying. Especially if you have obviously better upgrades and have to downgrade to get further. For the second one you need for the story, you even need to kill a specific Big Dog to get a war paint... which leads me to the next topic.
-The Big Dogs: There's about half a dozen of these guys in the game; all are basically commanders of the enemy factions... and all of them are the same guy, just recolored. the first fight was exciting, trying to dodge that huge mace. Eventually unlocked a really garrish bright warpaint for my Opus (its a new paintjob) and kept moving. To unlock other paintjobs, you need to kill Big Dogs; all of them litterally the same guy, killed the same wya, jsut with different arenas. It gets boring, and sometimes really annoying.
-Bugs: There's a few. Do not try to minimize from full screen, it will ♥♥♥♥ with your game in some odd ways (And it wont minimize). Also, sometimes the upgrade menus will freeze, sounds may vanish, or indeed you'll have overlapping dialogues which are annoying as all hell. Lastly, try not to get sandwiched between two cars while on foot; it happened to me and I was shot fifty feet straight up in the air to just land and die. It's... odd.
THE VERDICT: 9/10.

TL:DR >  Watching Batman movies and reading Batman comics is great and all, but if you really want to feel like you are the Dark Knight, playing Arkham Origins is probably as close as you can get without becoming a billionaire and having your parents murdered.
What makes the game so great is that it features all the elements of being Batman: Detective work, awesome gadgets, martial artistry, chasing crazy people, wearing your underpants on the outside, and so on.
Long review:
Graphics: Excellent, well tuned to NVIDIA GPUs, notably DX11 Tesselation and PhysX. AMD guys may have a different story to tell.
Gameplay: For these new to the game, some boss fight scenes will be a considerable challenge, so prepare to die and restart the game from that point and get taunted for failing.
Story: Well-developed characters and story line that explains a lot about the prequels, and dropping subtle hints that allows the Batman universe to intertwine in all the three games. This is one of the strongest points in the game; Take for instance, the origin of Mr. Freeze, Bane's breakdown, the relationship between Bruce Wayne and his butler, and the Joker's over the line insanity.
Tips: Get the season pass to access the rest of the DLCs. If you don't need online play, the season pass has you covered with the rest, such as the Initiation DLC and stuff. That adds extra hours of immersive gameplay that'll keep you practising and on edge to keep up with your enemies.
Length:Well balanced. On average, it is possible to pull off both the main and side missions without being sidetracked too far from the game, and also offers sweet upgrade points which reward the gamer's time spent on the side missions.
Replay value: Owing to the excellent challenge mode(s) and extra game play modes, you8 cannot play this game once.
Overall rating: 10/10. This game is perfect.
PS: Did I mention there were Ninjas? Yes, I did.
Overall: 10/10. Gameplay reminiscent of Batman Arkham City.
Extra notes for AMD users: On DirectX 11 tesselation, use normal settings and avoid all NVIDIA "enhanced" settings, they can cripple the game's performance. The same aplies to people using NVIDIA GPUs priot to Kepler.

This is primarily a hidden object game with a variety of additional mini-games throughout, plus a puzzle you complete in between each of the game's chapters.
Pros:
+ It's cheap, and if you get it on sale the already low price is even nicer.
+ The game music is pretty and soothing.
+ Lovely hand-drawn artwork.
+ There's a somewhat helpful in-game hint system. Collect the little blue bugs and eventually you'll earn enough that you can use a little red bug to find whatever's on the screen that you've missed (or confirm that there's nothing there to find). You can also use the hint system to get what are often necessary hints as to what to do in the mini-games. In fact, sometimes you're given full solutions - but be aware that sometimes these "solutions" are actually lies.
Cons:
- Badly designed. It's quite possible to leave an area forever without collecting all of the area's puzzle pieces, and some areas somehow have too many. Granted, this didn't cause any problems later on (you'll always have enough puzzle pieces to build the World puzzle), but it still annoyed me.
- I loathed several of the mini-games, in particular the two fake arcade games and the water wheel puzzle. Unlike some reviewers, I did feel that the game provided enough information to figure out what to do with the various puzzles, but sometimes those puzzles were just plain annoying. With the water wheel puzzle, I got too frustrated trying to figure out the pipe paths, and the arcade games had terrible controls and were a chore to get through.
- It was a good thing that the World puzzle pieces stuck in place when they were in the correct spot, because the colors of several of them were off (mainly the all blue and white ones) and I'd never have figured out where they were supposed to go otherwise.
- Full-screen mode is glitchy and not truly full-screen with my screen resolution (1920 x 1080) - there were black bars around the image and everything was a little stretched. Display settings were very basic, so there was no way to even try to fix these issues. I ended up playing in windowed mode.
- I actually checked a walkthrough to make sure I'd really finished the game. The ending came very suddenly and looked like it might potentially be some kind of epilogue, but not so much. You could listen to any music track from the game and replay the mini-games and that was it. The mini-games didn't have good replay value, so it felt pretty pointless.
Overall, this was a disappointment. The atmosphere is great and the puzzle difficulty level is usually pretty good, but it has some appalling design issues and I hated the first arcade mini-game so much that I almost rage-quit when I came across the second one.

"It takes a strong man to deny what's right in front of him...."
Spec Ops: The Line is, without question, a game that revels in it's amazing story despite it looking like a generic third person shooter at first glance. You play as Martin Walker. You are sent into Dubai, along with your comrades Adams and Lugo, to find any survivors and to uncover what happened to the original rescue and evacuation team led by Lt. Colonel John Konrad.
As said, the game's best aspect has to be it's story, a story that evolves as you play it, a story that truly shows you how war can affect you and others. The actions that Walker carries out, spiral him into a state that is truly representative of real life interaction with warfare. How your character's attitude and motives alternate throughout the story is something that is only seen in  few games, but those small details add so much to the immersiveness of the game.
Nolan North as Walker is one of the best, if not the best, voice acting in the history of games, he does so well to live the character that is Walker. Further on the small details mentioned above, is the way your character changes his way of speaking. During the beginning, Walker uses professional military terminology such as "Enemy down" or "target is neutralized." But as the game proceeds, your character's words alter drastically because of what he has witnessed and experienced, the dialogue turns to more sociopathic and immoral such "Kill is f***ing confirmed!" and "Got the f***er!."
Now the game does involve some rather disturbing scenes, one of which tasks the player with using White Phosphorus, A chemical that is known for it's ability to burn people alive, to eradicate a camp of opposing soldiers. After the attack, players are forced to walk through the remains of the camp, and are exposed to frightening scenes of soldiers crawling while letting off screams of pain and proceeding to die as you witness. This is made even worse by the fact that players then run into innocent civilians who have also suffered the same fate. The scene, in my opinion, really does question both the morals of you and your character, and I even asked myself if what I'm doing is really what had to be done. When compared to the infamous 'No Russian' mission from Modern Warfare 2, this is just as controversial and affecting, and even more so in showing how war really is, not something glamorized by being a hero or receiving medals for courage.
Another aspect I really liked was decisions that you are given throughout the game. Even if these decisions don't affect the ending, they still made me feel like I was important and I had control over the story, instead of it already being set out for you from the start. These decisions also affect your character's mood and other's perceptions of you, as you will be treated and viewed differently depending on which of the options you took.
In short, Spec Ops: The Line is nothing short of spectacular in my eyes, and I would recommend that anyone who enjoys a strong narrative over other aspects to give it a go and see how you fare. The game will definitely hold a high place on my list of favourite games, and will stay there for a long long time.

Fun, original, colorful, rogue elements, modular shipbuilding...REALTIME modular shipbuilding...what's not to love here?!
+Gameplay: Fast and satisfying. It feels just as good to destroy as it does to narrowly win.
+Graphics: Loving those neon blocks and creative color palettes!
+Audio: The music is good and blowing things up is satisfying.
+UI: Beautifully minimal and efficient.
+Roguelite: Embrace death, and do better next time. It's fun to die!
+Genius: Why has there never been a game where you have to build in real time while fighting?
+Charm: It's cute, and knowing it is a made up game between two kids makes it a little easier to take deaths less seriously.
-Progression: Sometimes the balance is a bit off on kits, potentially even just because you won't get enemy parts due to blowing them all up.
-Story: Could be slightly more engaging/structured.
+/-There needs to be more! This concept could be pushed SO far!
Captain Forever Remix is a game that makes no pretense; it is all about the gameplay. If you like games where you get to custom build your ships, salvage enemy parts, and experiment with various designs to wreak havoc in creative ways, it is the game for you.
The most distinct feature of Captain Forever Remix is the modular ship building, much like legos, you pop on blocks and parts with various purposes. Unlike everything else, however, you do it in realtime, while any enemy could walk up and attack you. You may be fighting two enemies, kill one, and then quickly pop on the weapons or armor gained from it to kill the other.
This is a really fun, engaging, and original concept, and I'd love to see it go above and beyond this game to potential future titles or projects from the developer. It is one of those pieces that amounts to more than its individual worth in tandem with other parts, and it increases the worth of other parts, too.
At any rate, you will be kept on your toes, at times enraged, and at times filled with adrenaline while trying to hastily add to or rebuild your ship in the middle of chaos. The mechanics for momentum are quite nice, as you can use various types of boosters to propel yourself forward, turn more efficiently, or brake yourself or your turns. You could also put boosters on all sides of your ship and it can be omnidirectional.
There are a good mix of weapons present, each of them satisfying in their own way, and encounters are most of the time quick and fun. There are just a few problems, though. If you don't keep your ship very fast at turning, you can end up in perpetual spinfights, sometimes destroying all of everyone's pieces (but there being a couple left) they will eternally run away from you becasue they have 3 strong boosters sitting around. Another issue is that you can at times get ships two levels above you, that will completely wreck you, or say, when you use mines, at first it spawns in all ships that use mostly mines, and you just end up blowing each other up. Little things like that, usually easy to work around, or can be avoided if you get good, but present and slightly annoying nonetheless. All in all, it's very fun, though!
So to start with, the backgrounds used in Captain Forever Remix are beautiful, and I love the brightly colored neon blocks. The character designs are also cute and colorful, although a bit simplistic. The weapon effects are distinguishable and satisfying. The particle effects are also quite colorful and lovely. Everything is very bright, colorful, kid friendly, and looks good...and that's about all there is to say about that, really.
I really like the music in Captain Forever Remix. It reminds me of Birdy Nam Nam a bit. Some more tracks definitely wouldn't hurt, though, and some of the weapon sounds are a bit loud, and can drown out other sounds.
The audio present in CFR is pretty sparse, though, so that's all I can think of to mention!
Your kids will love this. The kid in you will love this. It's happy, colorful, bright, and fun. You can't go wrong with purchasing this title. The story should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours to complete and unlock all kits. I'd like to see additional gamemodes in the future to add to the longevity, but either way, you will get your money's worth!

A fun open-world, post apocalyptic game with some great nods to the movie franchise, even if it's not always 100% true to the canon.
The story will be familiar to movie fans, being somewhat of an amalgamation of most of them.  A tortured Max is on a journey to find the Plains of Silence, where he hopes to ease his troubled mind, when he is attacked by a group of Warboys led by the current warlord of the wasteland, Scabarous Scrotus (son of Immortan Joe, from Fury Road).  Beaten, his car stolen, left for dead, he begins his quest to construct a new vehicle capable of taking him to his destination.
By completing numerous missions and challenges, Max can secure a plethora of upgrades, taking his new vehicle from♥♥♥♥♥♥box status all the way up to a monster killing machine.  The diverstity of upgrades, plus the ability to unlock specific rigs (called Archangels) allows for a satisfying amount of experimentation;  sacrificing endurance for speed as an example, or attack capability in lieu of handling.  This allows the player to customize their rig to their own preferences, or make modifications on-the-fly to meet quest-specific requirements.
The same upgrade process applies to Max as well.  Starting out as a rather pathetic 'road warrior', by end-game he is a well-equipped one man wrecking crew.  I found both the melee and vehicular combat to be great fun, and I particularly enjoyed the simplicity of the mechanics, mastery of which doesn't require uber-reflexes or split-second timing on multiple key-combos.  The animations are fluid and look good, and I never tired of the joy  of an exploding enemy vehicle.
The environment can get a little drab in it's repetition, but there is a vast array of characters to either help or hinder Max on his quest, and by visiting different locations and finding relics (usually letters and photos), one gets a feeling for what once was.  This results in a pervading sense of loss, which is the main theme of the game, and I thought it was done very well, adding to my immersion in the game world.
I personally enjoyed spending many hours blazing thru the wasteland in my custom rig, trying to complete all challenges, which can get a bit tedious for achievement hunters.  But that is by no means a requirement, and simply sticking to the main story-line results in 30-40 hours of car-wrecking, head-bashing, convoy-chasing fun.
I do feel the need to warn you that the ending...is a little weak, to put it mildly (some reviewers say it actually sucks so hard it warrants a thumbs down for the entire game).  I'm not that harsh about it, and while I agree it could have been better, it was the journey that made it worth-while.  I'm not sure I'd recommend paying full price for Mad Max, but since it's fairly common to find it on sale for $5 then by all means, you should pick it up.  You wont be disappointed.

Nameless as this protagonist may be, his story is largely told by your imagination. As a sandbox game, you are free to assassinate your targets in myriad fashion. Do you poison, stab, electrocute, shoot, or perfectly time a chandellier to come crashing down on your target? Hitman lets you decide for yourself; and as you do so, you largely decide who Agent 47 really is.
This is an episodic tale that trots the globe, placing you in vastly different, beautifully designed environments with each episode. The game is openly designed to encourage exploration and planning, as there are so many ways to skin the cat - do you cut from the hind legs or slice from the shoulders? And because there is so much room for experimentation, Hitman has absolutely tremendous replayability. Each episode begs to be played more than once, if only to experiment with the interesting ways to execute your targets.
Mechanically, Hitman is solid. Combat is responsive, and NPC interaction is mostly believable, with characters picking up on the peculiars of your actions quite quickly - are you crouching behind a desk (this might raise suspicion, for instance) - that help to build immersion. Likewise, the way you execute your enemies can greatly impact the subtlety (or lack thereof) of your planned escape.
A solid all around game, with few, if any, real shortcomings. If you're interested in taking on the virtual role of a nameless Assassin, Agent 47 is likely to fit your shoes.

My initial review for this game was negative but honestly I cannot say I feel the same having spent more time with this sim. It's not perfect but it has a lot to offer. Great visuals, great music, multiple quad choices (only the racer 3 puts you on the leaderboard and cool tracks. What I would like to see is a lot more easy tracks, there's only one so far!
Just a few thoughts... (the "- "doesn't mean a negative)
-It feels like the quad is a little too big in the virtual world... not sure how to describe it but the gaps feel tighter than it does in real life.
-I initially found there was a delay to the controls, this actually had to do with the fact I was using my computer with a tv and despite it being on game mode, it just isn't as fast as my monitor.
- The floatyness is the main aspect that I find rather unrealistic, the quad should drop faster when cutting the throttle.
-The side collision effect was very aggressive initially: the lightest touch spun you completely around or upside down even, however, it seems like it was changed a little since my last review.
-The quad seems like it has a very grippy rubber bottom because it will always flip over if you touch the ground even on smooth surfaces. We should be able to scrape along the ground
-The beta had a crash detection, this version has none and it's a little weird flying full tilt into a wall with no consequence.
There is a steep learning curve for sure, even if you've flown FPV for a long time as a lot of the tracks are SUPER tight, nothing like the quad races i've been to, but i think it's rewarding overall and helps with the real life stuff. I got over the frustrations and put myself in 10th place on project noob, yaaay!

A fun open-world, post apocalyptic game with some great nods to the movie franchise, even if it's not always 100% true to the canon.
The story will be familiar to movie fans, being somewhat of an amalgamation of most of them.  A tortured Max is on a journey to find the Plains of Silence, where he hopes to ease his troubled mind, when he is attacked by a group of Warboys led by the current warlord of the wasteland, Scabarous Scrotus (son of Immortan Joe, from Fury Road).  Beaten, his car stolen, left for dead, he begins his quest to construct a new vehicle capable of taking him to his destination.
By completing numerous missions and challenges, Max can secure a plethora of upgrades, taking his new vehicle from♥♥♥♥♥♥box status all the way up to a monster killing machine.  The diverstity of upgrades, plus the ability to unlock specific rigs (called Archangels) allows for a satisfying amount of experimentation;  sacrificing endurance for speed as an example, or attack capability in lieu of handling.  This allows the player to customize their rig to their own preferences, or make modifications on-the-fly to meet quest-specific requirements.
The same upgrade process applies to Max as well.  Starting out as a rather pathetic 'road warrior', by end-game he is a well-equipped one man wrecking crew.  I found both the melee and vehicular combat to be great fun, and I particularly enjoyed the simplicity of the mechanics, mastery of which doesn't require uber-reflexes or split-second timing on multiple key-combos.  The animations are fluid and look good, and I never tired of the joy  of an exploding enemy vehicle.
The environment can get a little drab in it's repetition, but there is a vast array of characters to either help or hinder Max on his quest, and by visiting different locations and finding relics (usually letters and photos), one gets a feeling for what once was.  This results in a pervading sense of loss, which is the main theme of the game, and I thought it was done very well, adding to my immersion in the game world.
I personally enjoyed spending many hours blazing thru the wasteland in my custom rig, trying to complete all challenges, which can get a bit tedious for achievement hunters.  But that is by no means a requirement, and simply sticking to the main story-line results in 30-40 hours of car-wrecking, head-bashing, convoy-chasing fun.
I do feel the need to warn you that the ending...is a little weak, to put it mildly (some reviewers say it actually sucks so hard it warrants a thumbs down for the entire game).  I'm not that harsh about it, and while I agree it could have been better, it was the journey that made it worth-while.  I'm not sure I'd recommend paying full price for Mad Max, but since it's fairly common to find it on sale for $5 then by all means, you should pick it up.  You wont be disappointed.

Nameless as this protagonist may be, his story is largely told by your imagination. As a sandbox game, you are free to assassinate your targets in myriad fashion. Do you poison, stab, electrocute, shoot, or perfectly time a chandellier to come crashing down on your target? Hitman lets you decide for yourself; and as you do so, you largely decide who Agent 47 really is.
This is an episodic tale that trots the globe, placing you in vastly different, beautifully designed environments with each episode. The game is openly designed to encourage exploration and planning, as there are so many ways to skin the cat - do you cut from the hind legs or slice from the shoulders? And because there is so much room for experimentation, Hitman has absolutely tremendous replayability. Each episode begs to be played more than once, if only to experiment with the interesting ways to execute your targets.
Mechanically, Hitman is solid. Combat is responsive, and NPC interaction is mostly believable, with characters picking up on the peculiars of your actions quite quickly - are you crouching behind a desk (this might raise suspicion, for instance) - that help to build immersion. Likewise, the way you execute your enemies can greatly impact the subtlety (or lack thereof) of your planned escape.
A solid all around game, with few, if any, real shortcomings. If you're interested in taking on the virtual role of a nameless Assassin, Agent 47 is likely to fit your shoes.

Summary: A solid engaging, and thoroughly enjoyable experience; definitely a purchase for anyone who enjoys games of Terraria’s kind. The complaints I have with this game are not too noticeably and will hopefully be fixed as it heads closer to completion.
Long Review: At first glance it looks like another Terraria clone, which I’ve played but never hit off with. Signs of Life is similar in the aspect of Terraria, but possess a more serious theme with a heavy emphasis on exploration. The game is tough in the beginning due to the lack of a tutorial and new users might be deterred like I was at first. The only source of information was AGIS the AI which squats in your wrist device, and he is about as helpful as he is insensitive. Alright, I’m being a little harsh. He’s my only companion and I depend on him to discover crafting recipes. For that I can overlook his jabs and would-be-delight at my coming misfortunes. However I must put a negative on his dialogue. Some parts feel too much like no writing effort was made and instead was just words slapped together to convey the basic intention of his attitude. Tsk, tsk, shame on you developers.
The graphics are pleasing; bright and vibrant. I enjoyed the design of the characters and environment. It has more realism than you would expect from this type of game; none of Terraria’s pixelated approach. A plus in my books.
The crafting system made my brain twirl a bit in the beginning and AGIS being the help he is, only kept piling more recipes for my brain to work out, into my already flooded list. Though once you learn how the gears tick and get the basic tools up and running, it is bloody damn enjoyabe!
The soundtrack I hardly noticed. So far the songs I’ve heard when I pay attention to it, fit the whole atmosphere quite well; Peaceful and lulling, perhaps too much so as it tends to flow in one ear and out the other. I actually heard more of Terraria’s music than I did here. The lack of combat oriented soundtracks for when you engage monsters makes me give this edge of the game a slight negative.
The monsters are interesting and for the most part, well imagined and thought out. Some are the only source for certain crafting ingredients thereby forcing you into the dark reaches of the earth to hunt them down. I have my issues with their current behavior in combat. They can be a threat, especially in the early stages where you’re just learning to stand on your feet, but once you get decent gear, it is disappointing. They are also encountered sparsely, this makes it easier for new poorly equipped players, but subtracts the danger feel as you explore. However they do spawn in more numbers as you go deeper, but not enough to make you feel satisfied. The lack of types, numbers, and ease of which you can eliminate them as you get better gear subtracts from this aspect of the game. Now while I’m being a spoiled kid and bashing the hard work of the poor developers, let me just add that the lack of dangerous creatures above ground, apart from that one special chicken, is disappointing to me.
Now onto the developers, the charming creators of this experience I am so enjoying. I’ve read a number of negative reviews and nearly each of them they have responded to with grace and factuality to the criticism and gripes people have of this game. They are also active on the Community Hub and welcoming to ideas. Get ready because I will hit you with a list of mine as well as issues. Ugh, when I’m actually energetic enough to write it out. Currently they are my second favorite, a big round of applause to them. Their involvement with the community was a factor in encouraging me to buy Signs of Life.
Now the game has some lore which adds a nice touch. In a way it helps drive you on to discover the full story as you explore and craft. However it is currently lacking in content. Understandable since this is still early access, but please bear that fact in mind. Newcomers, if they are slow minded dimwits like me, can expect to have enough content to work through and learn the ropes for 24.8 hours before it gets dull. Progression till then is perfectly enjoyable if you’ve managed to work out how to proceed. Good news is that a tutorial is in the works. This will transform it into a smoother experience for rookies. However, currently there is only one world, or in Terraria terms, one biome. And that is the green lush forest grassland. I do hope more locations with varieties in animals and flora will be added later. Fingers crossed.
Now that Signs of Life has had Co-op multiplayer added, it is even more fun. This game is another little gem lost in the swirling mass of titles being thrown into Steam since the Greenlight feature, and I find most of them to be very dreary. Don’t pass Signs of Life up if you are into the style. Perhaps genre would be a better term, but oh well.
PS: It is a pity you don’t know how lazy I can be. That I managed to force myself to write a review of this game means it is worth having a gander at. Oh well, oh well. No one will believe me. That’s fine. I know myself. That’s good enough.

The thought of delivering cargo in a trucking game, sounds extremely boring. That's what I thought when I initially seen this game, however after only owning it for a month and logging in over 150 Hours I can safely say it's beyond addictive.
There are many attributes to making this game appeal to many people.
- Modding; There is a MASSIVE modding community, with new trucks, skins, engines, maps, literal overhaul mods that change every aspect of this already wonderful game to give it that extra spice that you may want.
- Progression; My issue when playing games is that I only play games, that offer some sort of replayabilty. I want to invest hundreds and hundreds of hours into something and still have more to do. This game offers that. With the ability to start off with taking out a loan and buying a garage, then hiring drivers, to then bring in additional income to comtinue building up your trucking empire throughout Europe. Or you can start out taking small jobs from other companies, build income slowly buy your first big rig then launch your own company and hire truckers. You and each driver has a skill tree that you can progress into. Deliver heavier cargo, deliver further distances etc.
- Map; The map is 1:19 in most of the map, 1:15 in the UK, and 1:3 in cities scaling = real world. In short, going from one side of the map to the other takes around an hour and a half.
- Driving; The tucks have weight to them, you have to take into account the weigt of the cargo otherwise when going around a corner you may tip over and ruin your cargo. Mastering sharp corners is a challenge in of itself.
- Online; TruckersMP has a simple yet intuitive tool you can use (Third Party Application) to play online. This offers a whole new relam of fun. Hopping online with almost all of the time a full server of 2,300 People is amazing. You come across convoys of hundreds as they all journey through the world and deliver cargo. You can stop at cities and show off your rig, chat with people via voice/text and this is where most of my time is spent.
Overall my review doesn't even tap into the sheer amount of content in this game. I just thought I'd share some of my thoughts and perhaps get you to give this game a go. It's a 10/10 for me.
They've recently released American Truck Simulator which is basically the same thing but in America, with new trucks. However it's quite new and is very, very small. It becomes quite boring very fast. However they're rescaling the maps so maybe this time next year it'll be complete with new DLC's to add to it.
If you've thought about getting this game, but are on the fence. I would 100% buy it, download the multiplayer mod right away and play for a few hours. Don't like it, issue a refund.

Being a completely new drone pilot here's my take:
The training missions are good, fantastic even.
Within 2 hours I was flying in noob/toy/hold mode
Within 4 I was flying in intermediate and acro but not abe to do anything short of wide open spaces to flail about in.
Within 6 I was able to actually to control myself to the same level as 2 hours of noob mode.
I still have 3/4 left of the intermediate mode training missions left.
So the training missions work. They're interesting and progression is challenging but not discouragingly hard.
The maps are great, they're large and each map encompasses a huge variety of sections to fly around in each offering varying levels of challenge. I'm very surprised at how detailed and wide open they are. I never feel like i'm being boxed in by the game.
The drones are varied but with a small selection. There are plans to add a garage mode so you can tweak your drone to presumably perform closer to your real drone but this is yet to be implemented in the game. As of writing this came out of early access less than 24 hours ago.
There's a heap of other modes too. You can have freestyle flying, racing and multiplayer.
The race modes each have multiple courses per map including the DRL 2016 campaign races and you can race combinations of ghosts from the worlds top 10 to rivals and yourself.
The controller support is great, they seem to be supporting a lot of the major drone controllers so you have your taranis, your futuba, your frsky, etc. They also support the console controllers and my XBONE controller worked out of the box.
So you can get flying before even ordering a transmitter.
Overall I reccomend this purely on the quality of the maps and the training modules. I can train here with specific training courses or just freestyle it all conveniently from my PC without any battery charging, travel or money spent on broken parts.

The mainstream reviewer criticisms of this game caused me some concern before playing it, as I knew it must be hard for a different studio to match the level of excellence Rocksteady had achieved with Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. All these concerns were steadily laid to rest as I delved into Arkham Origins.
I don't know what these whiners are complaining about! WB Montreal did such an amazing job of duplicating all the excellence of Rocksteady's first two Batman games, that had I not KNOWN it was a different studio going into this I wouldn't have even noticed that it wasn't Rocksteady that made this game. All the little polishes, sound effects, menu mechanics, controls, combat, gadgets, all of it has been amazingly re-created in Arkham Origins AND expanded upon.
In my opinion, they also did a fantastic job in portraying Batman in such a way that he really does seem like a less experienced Batman. The ONLY thing that doesn't make sense is the fact that he has access to more gadgets than he does in Asylum and City. While it is understandable that WB Montreal wanted to expand the Batman experience by doing this, it doesn't fit as well into the plot of a younger, less experienced Batman.

I should mention that I played Arkham City with maximum graphical settings and benchmarked at an average of 30 FPS, so the fact that I had graphical issues and slowdown was interesting to me.
Within minutes of beginning the game I began to notice graphical issues. During the first boss-encounter with "Killer Croc" was a memorable one, since while I'm lead to believe that Croc's special abilities include making him extremely large and strong - the file negates to mention that apparently he has the ability to flicker in and out of visibility. This left Batman looking like he'd made a wrong turn on the way to ninja school and had taken up the art of mime instead.
More graphical errors started when I got into a more open world environment, as less than 5 minutes later I was treated to a display of Batman's amazing aerodynamic prowess - gliding gently through the air while symultaneously forward flipping in a fashion resembling a hamster in a washing machine. It was quite entertaining actually.
I also have to report that the combat system is what you would expect from this latest generation of Batman:Arkham games - because it's copy&pasted from Batman:Arkham Asylum. From what I can see there have been no changes to the combat engine, Batmans animations or the AI of the... AI.
Almost all simple fights can be won by spamming the "punch, punch, punch, counter, punch, counter, punch, takedown" sequence and when faced with tougher opponents with knives, body armour or guns, it becomes "Punch, punch, punch, cape sweep, rapid punches, counter, cape sweep, rapid punches, counter, repeat as necessary until victory."
The aiming system is still rather ham-fisted, in that when there are multiple enemies attacking in close proximity to each other it can be very difficult to judge which of them will be struck. This is especially irritating when one of said enemies is charging their attack (when you would want to counter, if you wouldn't strike them before their blow landed) and hit his buddy instead - losing your combat multiplier in the process. In addition, a ground takedown still can't be interupted in order to counter a standing attack - maybe that's by design but it doesn't feel right to me.
I'd also love to know why that "bat effect" which occurs on the last punch of every combat decides that my FPS should drop from my average 30 down to 1 or 2 for around 5 seconds? It's been like that since Arkham Asylum and it baffles me as to why it happens.
The RPG aspects also feel out of place to me, as they did in Arkham City. It really feels like the whole leveling up system is shoe-horned into the game in order to add play-time to it. Since I have yet to encounter any true "time limits" in the game, I see no reason why Batman wouldn't fly around the beginning area, beating up random thugs until he reached maximum level before going out to tackle Gothams meanest and ugliest. I was under the impression that was what his pre-game training was for, but oh well.
All in all, if you thought that Batman:Arkham City was a great game, you'll think that Batman:Arkham Origins is also a great game. But if you were, like I was, underwhelmed by the sequel to Batman:Arkham Asylum, then you will be left disappointed by this title.
Oh, one last note for the developers: Batman, being the superhero who refuses to kill, would not drop a thug from the top of a building, even if there were a christmas tree to potentially break his fall. It's very out of character and completely broke my immersion in the part - I was from that point onwards playing as Wayce Brune - the cheap Batman knockoff from China, whom evaded customs on the back of a banana shipment.

'Signs of life' is another one of 'dem ol' Sanbox games. But unlike most sandbox games, Signs of life has a lot more of a better feel to it, such as characters bending this way and that to look in the mouse's direction, pickaxes colliding with rock in it's swing arc regardless of whether or not that's the one you aim your cursor at, running and walking aminations are great, and all in all it brings a lot of life to the character. You're not some blocky dude, or a sprite that looks like it was ripped from Final fantasy, you play as a detailed human being.
You begin your journey alone, save for your trusty wrist device's AI (Whom may or may not have zero sympathy for human life), aboard a pod freshly landed on some alien planet that isn't too different from earth, save for the fact that you can probably walk along it's surface in like, 15 minutes. But you aren't quite so alone, with sheep, tapirs, and other generally peaceful wildlife decorating the planet's surface, while deep underground, you'll find things that you'll need to shake more than just a stick at.
With plenty of weapons, armors, parts, items, objects, and basically a whole metric sh-tton of other stuff, this game is packed with crafting materials. And you don't just use some logs to make things like a chair. No, you saw them into planks, use cotton and thread to make padding, and craft nails that you require a hammer to use to assamble the entire thing. Crafting isn't just slapping a few pieces together, you craft all of the parts needed to assemble what you need. And there's lots of things to be made. Need guns? SMGs, handguns, shotguns, rifles and more are a lengthy mining trip away. Want to hit things? Swords, clubs, bats, and even weapons made from pieces of your foes can be made to give your target a good beating or cut them down to size. Want to protect your delicate babyflesh? Armors can be made out of anything, from wood and twine, to bone, to iron, to silver, to some of the rarest minerals you can find.
The game is still in alpha when this review is/was made, but it's still a fantastic game so far, with multiplayer now built in and more amazing things on the way. Keep it up, developers, this one may just set a trend for a whole new generation of sandbox games.
