I've only started playing, mainly due to what I've seen as the developer's genuine care and involvement for their community. I've been burned out by other EAs where the devs seem to just drop out, even if it had such a good foundation, and this has happened frequently in 2D side-scroller crafting/adventure games. The devs (I don't know how many there are, if there's multiple) seem to frequently update, are involved in the community, and don't come off as defensive rather open to anything. Even negative reviewers have commented positively on the Devs.
Now, onto the game in a simple pros/cons list with overall review:
Pros:

-Simple, yet lovely graphics. This is a smooth looking game for EA, nothing exceptional, but its extremely easy on the eyes.
-AI isn't aggressive at appropriate times. I don't feel like I'm constantly under danger, which I appreciate when I'm trying to build/explore.
-The technology in the game, although I'm barely in, seems great. As you come in a landing pod, you can guide it to land, and (as per story) the battery begins to die out, I landed on top of an animal splatting it. I actually laughed out loud when it happened, I'm not the type to laugh, rather smile at these situations, and I've come across a few more like it.
-I think the Devs listening to feedback is obvious, in other reviews they talk about crafting issues, and as I've just begun to play this game, every ingredient you get opens a recipe, and it seems rather clear cut. While there is some struggle, (pickaxe, for example, I though I'd know how to make it from copper ore, but it took making boards to open the recipe), its not really a pain at all. Its an effort, as I feel there should be with some games. They've also included what seems to be a basic tutorial, again compared to other reviewers, there may've not been one before, and this is representative of the Devs involvement.
-Ton of potential, for early access, its incredibly well-done, and considering they just added multiplayer, I think there's a ton of room for this game, and as the devs have proven themselves with this, I look forward to other games from them in the future. The pricing is just right for this.
Cons:
I'm only early on, I haven't really seen as many, so this is a nitpick attempt.
-You start off with a multitool that can mine blocks and cut down trees. This isn't bad at all, I like it, but there's instances where a pickaxe or an axe may be necessary in the future, and that kinda gets lost on me. I've come across what seems to be deposits that I can only mine with a pickaxe (I haven't even gone really underground yet), but I don't know what the significant difference is. Again, this is a nitpick attempt, and nothing really critical of the game. As I advance in the game, I may add more cons here, of which I'll note it was edited in, but otherwise.. Not much. Its a really solid EA.
Summary:
This is what I had wanted from my other sidescrolling sci-fi EAs, except not only is it being properly and consistently executed, its being done so by an engaged Dev who seems to care for community feedback and does it at a extremely decent price. For thsoe who've been burned out by EAs that may've fit this bill, I can only try to assure you in that, I feel this is the one sure time we won't get burned. I'm crossing my fingers, but the devs are making a reputation for themselves and have passion behind this game that is all ready a solid foundation.

Just finished the Tiny Bang Story game and I can say it was very enjoyable.  I place a high value on the visuals of a game.  This one was outstanding in its artistic presentation.  If you enjoy finding hidden shapes inside a complex picture you will enjoy this game as well.  It also offers a chance to place puzzle pieces after every level of the game for those jigsaw puzzle fans.  Many puzzles were a bit reminiscent of a family favorite game from Microsoft called "Pandora's Box,"  although others were downright engineering in nature.  Overall, it took me just 7 hours to complete the game and I imagine a quicker study might do it in 4-5 hrs.  I bought this on sale, in a bundle, so it was well worth the $0.62 I paid.  I believe the artwork alone is well worth the regular retail price.  One comment for those beginning to play the game.  There are obvious shapes to collect that you will see right away, but you often need to complete the collection of an earlier shape before you can start to collect the others (complete the early quest first).  Completion of each quest often opens new rooms to explore which is where that last piece or two may be hiding.  So, I recommend looking forward before over-analyzing existing areas.

The Tiny Bang Story is a good few hours of fun. If you enjoy searching for objects and solving puzzles, this game will probably be good for you. Some of the puzzles did seem a little frustrating as I wasn't sure what the objective was. I would say the replayablity is low. So you might want to pick this one up on sale.

I also crashed 2-3 times at certain points in the game (same levefl) so I'm wondering if there's a bug, but auto save is great as I opened right back where I left off. (I'm a lazy person so auto save is wonderful in this way).
Overall I would recommend this game, easy play through, great graphics, quite relaxing and great at sale price. If you are stuck on any puzzles there are walkthroughs available, but I don't think it's necessary if you're willing to guess it out. The horrors of the human mind are on display in the most grounded way possible. The genius of the game is the darkness wrapped on an easily digestible shell, you don't know what's wrong until it's too late. Of all the amazing, and I use that term lightly, moments in this game it's the little touches that get you. A good portion into the game you are given the option of executing two men. One stole water rations for his family, the other killed the man's family but he only did so under orders. Who do you choose? When you get to the end you understand what that choice means but in the moment you must weigh your options. I did what don't think most people know about, I shot the snipers who were waiting for me to choose. The two men died in the crossfire but I believed I had done the right thing. That is truly your first step into the madness. Most FPS games hardly tackle the atrocities of war but SO: The Line forces you to confront it, forces you to experience hell. As you descend further into depravity you will undoubtedly question yourself, and the game tries to reassure you, 'You are still a good person', yet in the next breath chastises you, 'Do you feel like a hero yet?'. This leads to the player ultimately coming to grips with the terrible things they've done, and for what? A man back home and a medal that gathers dust, never mind those whose life bled into that godforsaken sand. Never mind the mother clutching her child in a desperate attempt to safe them. Never mind that there was always a choice. There is always a choice, in the moment it might not seem like it but after the dust settles you have to live with the choice you made. You have to live with the blood on your hands, haunted by the sights that are forever burned into your mind so that every second is a nightmare. War is hell. And hell is human. Humanity feared the monsters they believed lurked in the trees, lakes, mountains, and deserts, but the true monster, the one we should all fear, is the monster inside each and every one of us. The darkness that claws and howls to be let loose, the beast that begs for blood, we all have it. Some are more in touch with it and give in, while others are scarred and forever changed by giving into their demons and living with the consequences. Spec Ops explores that beautifully and it can't be praised enough.﻿ I don't feel like a hero. Not in the slightest.

The thought of delivering cargo in a trucking game, sounds extremely boring. That's what I thought when I initially seen this game, however after only owning it for a month and logging in over 150 Hours I can safely say it's beyond addictive.
There are many attributes to making this game appeal to many people.
- Modding; There is a MASSIVE modding community, with new trucks, skins, engines, maps, literal overhaul mods that change every aspect of this already wonderful game to give it that extra spice that you may want.
- Progression; My issue when playing games is that I only play games, that offer some sort of replayabilty. I want to invest hundreds and hundreds of hours into something and still have more to do. This game offers that. With the ability to start off with taking out a loan and buying a garage, then hiring drivers, to then bring in additional income to comtinue building up your trucking empire throughout Europe. Or you can start out taking small jobs from other companies, build income slowly buy your first big rig then launch your own company and hire truckers. You and each driver has a skill tree that you can progress into. Deliver heavier cargo, deliver further distances etc.
- Map; The map is 1:19 in most of the map, 1:15 in the UK, and 1:3 in cities scaling = real world. In short, going from one side of the map to the other takes around an hour and a half.
- Driving; The tucks have weight to them, you have to take into account the weigt of the cargo otherwise when going around a corner you may tip over and ruin your cargo. Mastering sharp corners is a challenge in of itself.
- Online; TruckersMP has a simple yet intuitive tool you can use (Third Party Application) to play online. This offers a whole new relam of fun. Hopping online with almost all of the time a full server of 2,300 People is amazing. You come across convoys of hundreds as they all journey through the world and deliver cargo. You can stop at cities and show off your rig, chat with people via voice/text and this is where most of my time is spent.
Overall my review doesn't even tap into the sheer amount of content in this game. I just thought I'd share some of my thoughts and perhaps get you to give this game a go. It's a 10/10 for me.

WTH have they done?!
I only just found that DRL was on steam and thought I'd give the latest version a go after 10+hrs practice in Beta V1.1.1.
It's so bad and unrealistic now, I'd say it's almost useless as a simulator and is likely to teach you more bad habits than good.
As far as I could tell there is no way of setting gravity (I set mine to 14m/s in v1.1.1) and feel like I'm flying on the moon in the latest version. It takes an eternity to dive a tall building in 'Gates of Hell' and if you use this "simulator" as an indication of what you can do in reality, your IRL quad will be smashed to pieces in no time.
You can also crash into a building at full speed and just bounce off it with no consequences at all. A slight correction of trajectory and you are on your merry way again.
If you get used to doing that, and take those habits to real life, your quad flying hobby will be over in seconds.
Another thing DRL messed up is the sound. v1.1.1 is acceptable if not good. But, in this version the motors make a constant 'weeeooowwweeeooooweeeeoooow' sound (at constant throttle) that is extremely annoying.
Also, they took away mouse support for navigating the menu!? Who thought that was a good idea?
Fortunately it's not all bad. Setup of the transmitter works well and is easy. Reset quad via custom transmitter switch is great.
But, unfortunately they improved the least important aspects of the sim, and ruined the core!
I'm guessing the devs have made the quad easier to control and way too 'floaty' (and 'arcady') to make it easy for the filthy casuals to fly.
I use this program for practicing new tricks and training muscle memory so I can bring it to real life and minimise the chances of exploding my quad.
Until DRL goes back to it's intended purpose, I can't recommend this.
Instead, download v1.1.1 and set gravity to 14m/s for something that resembles reality.

Preface: I've only played Hitman: Absolution before this one, so I'm not familiar with the rest of the Hitman games.
Stealth is one of my favorite genres, and Hitman is one of my favorites in it. I enjoyed this iteration overall with its replayability, and it really feels like each level is a carefully crafted and thought out set piece.
PROS:
+ Sandbox-esque level designs encourage players to replay missions and explore every nook and cranny to figure out all the different paths and methods to eliminate targets.
+ Disguises are actually useful now, as opposed to Absolution. The only NPCs that suspect you are ones in supervising-type positions (e.g. if you're at a military base disguised as a soldier, other soldiers won't suspect you but commanding officers will).
+ Graphically, it is impressive, and missions take place in different countries, each offering their own unique aesthetic - Japan, France, and Thailand, to name a few places.
+ The concept of Elusive Targets is very interesting and is great for an extra challenge after finishing the story missions. Elusive Target missions are only available during limited windows of time. At the start of the mission, the target is not immediately visible to you, and it is completely up to you to locate them and gather intel about them. On top of that, you only have one chance at taking them out (no saving or restarting).
CONS:
- Why do I need an Internet connection to play a singleplayer game?
- The absence of an inventory hotbar means I can't tell what I have at a glance without opening the inventory menu.
- AI is still not very intelligent, making NPCs very easy to predict and exploit.
- The story is significantly less coherent than Absolution's. Things feel loosely connected by cutscenes between missions, and they don't really make a whole lot of sense until the pieces come together in the final two missions. Plus, the characters didn't have a whole lot of personality overall. At least in Absolution, almost all the enemies were well-established ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and it felt good to take them down.
- Can't dual-wield silverballers (or any weapon for that matter).

Hitman: SuperModel looking European man, who works as an Assassin.
Environments: Beautyfull, diverse, allot of possibilities, overall great map designs.
NPC's/Characters: Allot of different/diverse characters, which makes the game allot more alive.
You dont have to buy the complete game, so you can choose which maps you want to buy/play.

It have also had player housing for quite some time now, remember the first time i played back in 2004 on another account i bought a house in Qeynos and filled it with stuff. Prestiege houses are also available to purchase in the ingame store (zero rent) and you can use your steam wallet to purchase things.
Regular monthly City festivals that go from town to town and themed events (Christmas, Valentines day) etc lets you get nice stuff to decorate your house with, or earn a couple of new mounts, or other stuff you can sell on the broker for tonnes of platinum.
You can play it free, but you can't experience it fully free. You can chose to unlock certain features (classes, broker credits, character slots) or go full in and get a monthly subscription. This is my review or impressions of HITMAN. I played all the original games as well as Hitman Absolution. I am torn on this game whether to give it a thumbs up or down.
PC Specs
6700k OC to 4.5ghz
ROG Hero Alpha Z170
16GB DDR4 G Skill Trident Z 3200mhz
GTX 1080 MSI SEAHAWK EK Custom
Samsung Evo 850 500GB 2x in RAID 0
Full Custom Swiftech Loop Dual 240mm Rads (Too many parts to List Here Just know temps are wayyy down)
2560 x 1440p Asus Monitor
Game Played MAXED OUT everything DX 11 not DX 12. Wating for my 960 Evo M.2 drive to install windows 10 fresh install then I will test out DX12
Graphics- The game looks down right beautiful. The enviroments are so detailed as well as the density of the levels have NPC's everywhere. Feels so alive. Smooth gameplay no major FPS drops or graphical mishaps. ( I played the game with a 4770k and 980ti and turned a few settings down but still smooth gameplay)
Gameplay- Hitman Veteran Players will feel right at home. Mechanics and gameplay feel very intuative if you have played the others. Not hard to get a grasp of if a new player either.
Now the whole play the level over and over to get used to NPC behaviours and doing different kills is something your either going to love or hate. In my opinion I was more of a fan of the linear level style of Hitman Absoution. I am most likely one of few that feel this way. I just felt like was more of a story in absolution, more levels, and the game had momentum that led me to want to keep playing that next section. I did play the game a few times (back on PS3 in 2012) and also played through on PC in 2015 and was fun to try a different playstyle through the new playthrough. I never did find myself repeating a level right after finishing though.
So in conclusion the game runs very well, at least on higher end hardware 4770k 6700k 980ti 1080, but cannot speak to other configurations as I have not tested. The world is alive, well done graphically, details and mechanics of game work well.
Just be aware of the type of game this is. It is a game of repetition. You become the badass 47 by playing level over and over and over. First time on a level will be a mess of you fumbing around being spotted and screwing up. After a few tries you become the badass 47 and can do a flawless play not being spotted by anyone and making your escape. I just felt no motivation to keep playing the levels. Lost intrest quick. I ended up finishing all the levels (episodes) and the bonus missions in about 17hrs. Just in my opinion I wish there was a more compelling story to keep me playing, but that is my personal preference.
Good luck to those who purchase! Hopefully this helps you know what you getting into!

A really great game, offering plenty of replayability and satisfying ship building. Both the building and fighting systems are very intuitive and complement each other nicely. The art style is also nice and colorful, fitting the theme perfectly.
I have only two very minor concerns (see below). Note that the game is still in early access at the time of writing, and the changes may therefore either have been implemented at a later stage or they are made unsuitable/redundant due to other changes to the game. Whether they are addressed or not, please do not let this discourage you from buying the game, as it is already a fantastic experience.
My first nitpick is with the timer limiting the available time one may spend rebuilding the ship after finishing a stage. Nowadays I pretty much exclusively use the super kit with a fully upgraded build time (210 seconds), but for the last 2-3 stages even this isn't enough to allow me to really think my design through properly (which for me is perhaps the most enjoyable aspect of the game). Also, I can't imagine ever going back to playing a kit which does not offer upgrades to build time, and are therefore limited to the original 60 seconds. While I understand the idea of adding a sense of urgency to the game even between stages, I think the enjoyment of figuring out a particularly interesting ship design outweighs it. An alternative would be to simplify replacing a module with a higher level one (without having to rebuild the entire branch of the ship connected to that module), but I think that would present a large number of difficult design choices.
My second issue is with the zoom function. In the later stages there are weapon modules where the range of the weapon is longer than the distance from your ship to the top/bottom of the screen, even when zoomed all the way out. This makes it very difficult to utilize the weapons efficiently in those directions. As there are also enemies that use said modules, suddenly you may be attacked by someone from off-screen. The simple solution (from a design perspective that is, I obviously have no idea how difficult it would be to implement it in this particular game) to this would be to make it possible to zoom out further. Tweaking the range increases for late stage weapons could also work, but would probably affect the balance between different weapon classes quite a bit.
As stated previously, this is a really fun experience and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys a bit of creativity in their games.

I just want to first say that the idea behind Captain Forever Remix is solid. Building your own space ship, blowing up other spaceships and then using their parts to add onto your own ship sounds like a really cool idea to me, but I struggled to get into the actual game play mechanics.
There is next to no tutorial to explain what all the different building blocks of ship you get actually do, although most can be quiet self explanatory, it was hard at first to actually be able to build a ship that would move correctly. I found myself a times not being able to move around at all because I couldn't work out how to place the boosters on my ship to get enough power, but maybe that is just me being stupid.
I did like the feature where you can unlock differen "starter packs", which are essentialy the first set of space ship parts you get at the start of each game, obviously as you progress, the better these starter packs are.  I also enjoyed the art style here, some really nicely drawn 2d characters too.
I have to say, building the ships and making them look awesome is a really satisfying aspect, sadly though for me the gameplay didn't quite hit the marker I was expecting.  Thankfully the game is still in Early Access so I expect alot of these issues to be ironed out before the full release, I'll definately be keeping an eye on CFR, but for right now, I can't really recommend this title.

Signs of Life is a game very much focused on exploration and creation, and it does both very well. You start off in a pod filled with only the basics(such as a gun and a single bullet, if being the only one on a planet gets too boring) and a sassy artificial intelligence that doesn't quite understand the meaning of empathy. From there, you must run, punch, and scream your way to a better home.
The graphics and soundtrack are both very pleasing, the crafting system is delightful once you build yourself a nice workshop, and the general building mechanics are pretty well executed. The combat, however, lacks in a way that most sidescrollers do: It's not very dynamic. Despite this, the enemies, or at least the ones that are a threat, are well designed. You can power through them, but their gimmicks enable you to employ some neat tactics to make it a bit more fun.
Signs of Life also does not hold your hand. There's no real tutorial and you're mostly left to figure out everything yourself. Most people I've seen get confused with(what I'd call) the story progression of the game, though there are enough hints left about it to where you can eventually figure it out, and be mad at yourself for not doing so sooner.
The developer is fantastic. They're very engaged with the community, and get right on any issues you may be having. It's worth noting that I had no issues at all until I opted into the beta, and the issues I had there were patched an hour after I contacted them. For an early access game, Signs of Life is incredibly stable and well thought out.
Overall, 9/10 Easily.

I wouldn't recommend buying this because there are better games out there that follow a similar idea.
Try Terraria or Don't Starve as they are both survival games that are better laid out and thought out.
It's not that this game is bad per se but that there are better options out there if you want to buy a game in this genre.
Normally I would end the review here but for the developer here are things that I think you should work on.
1) Don't try so hard to be funny. It doesn't come off right. I found it more annoying than funny.
2) The crafting system is confusing. I was told that I could make an ingot but I couldn't look at the metal in my inventory to figure out how to make an ingot. The AI said I could use a smelter but I had no way of looking up the smelter recipe to figure out what I needed. I had to go to the wiki to find out which really breaks immersion. Either things need to be intuitive or there needs to be a way to look it up in game without needing to exit the game.
3) Similarly with cooking meat. It wasn't exactly an intuitive process. I tried starting a fire and throwing the meat onto it because there didn't seem to be a way to interact with the fire to cook the meat.
4) When you start cutting the trees with the laser, there was no indication that anything was happening. Even if it is something like making the tree shudder a bit like in Don't Starve or having little bits come off like Terraria, there needs to be some sort of visual feedback that something is happening.
5) I also wasn't impressed that I needed to make a wooden sword and club to start out with. For a fantasy game, those are the ideal sorts of weapons but for a sci-fi game they don't seem to fit. I know that it's hard to come up with a simple low level weapon that sticks with the sci-fi theme but perhaps if you already had something like a light saber but needed you to generate energy to make the battery work? This way you stick with the theme but still create a need for exploration and gathering so you can't insta-stomp the local flora/fauna.
6) Not being able to pick up things unless you use the grab laser is also annoying.
7) The pacing of the game is too slow. It doesn't feel like you are achieving anything or getting anywhere, especially at the start of the game when you are new.
8) The inventory system also needs work. We should be allowed to put whatever we want in the hotbar, not have it restricted to what you think is ideal and having to scroll through things.
That's about it. I just don't feel this game is fun enough to recommend to anyone.
Good luck in the future.

Prison Architect is the game that proves that you don't need flashy 3D graphics to have a great game.   The 2D visuals are still attractive nonetheless.  The only graphic deawback is the people but if you can look past that, you're in for a treat.
Let's start by saying that good prison games are hard to find.  and this one is the best prison simulator we will have for the next 10 years and here's why...
The detail of building your prison is immense.  You can design and build everything from a dormitory detention center to a full blown supermax prison complete with death row (yes, there is an electric chair).   You can even build female prisons!  Some women come complete with babies and need places to care for them.
After you get the prison constructed enough to begin housing prisoners, you then dive into running the place.  This is where the real fun begins.
You'll manage food distribution, finances, the daily schedule, reform programs, drug addicted losers, staff, guards, what offences get what penalties,  the list goes on and on.
That's not all, there is a full weather system so you'll need to supply heat to your prison or your inmates will complain about being cold.    Find and confiscate contraband from cigarettes and booze to weapons and escape tools.  These people will smuggle in all sorts of stuff from the visitation room from mom and dad to their buddy throwing drugs over the yard wall!     Got a prisoner doing time in solitary for getting caught with a knife?   see if he is willing to be a confidential informant in exchange for his release from solitary (not the prison).   Now he will sing like a bird and tell you who is carry what contraband (that he knows of).   He'll tell you if he knows of an upcoming trade or drug deal.  He'll fill you in on when a drop over the wall was arranged or if Joe Smith has a tunnel started under his toilet!
Best of all are gangs!  The confidential informant will also tell you who are gang members and gand leaders (that they know of).   They'll tell you who is strong, volitile, fearless, etc.   Gangs will take over territory in your prison.  The red gang might have control over the yard and the blue gang grabbed the common room.  The gangs will extort money from regular prisoners to use the room's facilities.  (Charge an inmate to use the weights in the yard for example.)  You must stop these gangs from taking over your prison!   Deploy guards, armed guards, K-9 dog handlers to take back territory.  The K-9 can sniff out drugs as well as find tunnels.
This is so much more than a building game.  The designing and building is very fun but the real fun begins when you get a lot of prisoners and especially if you have gangs enabled and they begin taking over parts of your precious creation!
Once you get your prison escape proof,  load it up in "Escape Mode" and be a prisoner yourself!   That's right,  you can be a prisoner in your own prison!   Now you can test just how easy (or hard) your prison is to get out of.   Recruit a team of buddies, get in fights,  smuggle a weapon from the workshop,  dig under your cell to find freedom!
There are loads of mods in the Steam Workshop that make this game even better.  There are graphic mods that remove the "cartoon" look of the game and add more "HD" looks to it.  There are mods that completely add new reform programs, objects, building materials, people and staff,  etc, etc..  The game is very British,  which is ok.  But there are mods for other languages as well as American terminology.
The developers are finished adding new content and will be tying everything up in a few months with a completed, bug-free version, or so they say.   So the game is near completion.
The best prison simulator on the market,  hands down.   If you own any (or all) of the Prison Tycoon games,  they have been executed and will rest in peace.   Throw them all away and buy Prison Architect right now.   You will not be disappointed!

Before I review this game, I have to make a very important note: This is not a good representation of real events or a representation of the army in general. This is a fictional story. By playing this game, you're walking into a "War is bad" propaganda campaign with some unrealistic consequences. I am reviewing this game for what it is, a game, and nothing more.
So basically, you're playing Captain Walker, a Commander Shepard lookalike who leads a 3 man squad (including himself) through Dubai in order to evecuate the city. What follows is a series of bad choices and some action scenes taken directly from a Michael Bay movie. Without revealing too much, I'll let you know, the game is quite thrilling. The combat is somewhat enjoyable, it's challenging (on suicide mission difficulty, at least), the overall feel is very hurt-lockerish and the voice acting is solid.
As I was mentioning before, the plot is completely bonkers and serves one purpose only: to shove anti war agenda up your♥♥♥♥♥by forcing choices down your throat, that basically, doesn't really matter. We get it, "War is bad", "Killing innocents is bad". Why do you have to spell it out for us? at one point the game clearly mocks you for events occuring in the game and asks you if "You're a feeling like a hero yet?", or tells you that "It's just a game, you shouldn't really care". Mixed signals, game! Mixed signals. You're making everything so god damn dramatic, but then tells us nothing matters, so which is it?
Other than this pretentious plot, I recommend playing the game if you're into cover shooters. It doesn't offer anything new, it isn't mind-blowing or anything, but it does provide a challenge, and most probably it's also fun in multiplayer (but I'll have to say almost anything is better with a multiplayer).
I wish I could give this a mixed rating, and at this point I still am unsure of whether I should recommend it or not...
I guess I'll have to say, play it, but only if you get it in a deal.

Preface: I've only played Hitman: Absolution before this one, so I'm not familiar with the rest of the Hitman games.
Stealth is one of my favorite genres, and Hitman is one of my favorites in it. I enjoyed this iteration overall with its replayability, and it really feels like each level is a carefully crafted and thought out set piece.
PROS:
+ Sandbox-esque level designs encourage players to replay missions and explore every nook and cranny to figure out all the different paths and methods to eliminate targets.
+ Disguises are actually useful now, as opposed to Absolution. The only NPCs that suspect you are ones in supervising-type positions (e.g. if you're at a military base disguised as a soldier, other soldiers won't suspect you but commanding officers will).
+ Graphically, it is impressive, and missions take place in different countries, each offering their own unique aesthetic - Japan, France, and Thailand, to name a few places.
+ The concept of Elusive Targets is very interesting and is great for an extra challenge after finishing the story missions. Elusive Target missions are only available during limited windows of time. At the start of the mission, the target is not immediately visible to you, and it is completely up to you to locate them and gather intel about them. On top of that, you only have one chance at taking them out (no saving or restarting).
CONS:

Borderlands 2 is a FPS RPG hybrid that uses the physical gameplay of an FPS but the mechanics of an RPG (Such as Level Systems, item systems, boss fights, etc.) with an emphasis on 4 player co-op action.
The story is you are a Vault Hunter (which is, in essence, an intergalactic badass trained to be a badass, and looking for the legendary "Vault" which is said to house ancient alien loot, and namely super awesome weapons) on board to Pandora, a barren desert planet where humans scrape by a life and the local wildlife hunts everything in sight... even if it's itself. However, on route the person who brought you to Pandora, Head of the Hyperion Weapons Corporation: Handsome Jack, reveals it was all a trap to lure and kill any and all Vault Hunters. From there you make it your mission to hunt down Handsome Jack, look for the ancient Vault, blow stuff up, and get paid.
In terms of actual gameplay, it is a really good mix of both RPG's and FPS's. It controls like an FPS, and extremely well at that. You rarely find a moment that you're losing because something happened in the game, but rather because you are missing, didn't plan well enough, or otherwise are just screwing up. On the other hand, the RPG elements are blended in really smoothly. You have a level up and skill based system, more health, and the ability to equip better gear. That mixed with the loot system adds a unique experience in the FPS genre.
In combat it's your classic "shoot enemies and they die", but with more than a handful of twists. These include unique weak spots, as well as type variants that can boost or detriment your damage, forcing you to be ready to change your plans. This adds a lot of little mixes that keep you on your toes. You yourself have Shields and Health. Shields recharge over time if not taking damage, while health doesn't naturally. Managing this while exchanging fire with enemies is a key part of making sure they die and you don't.
But the combat would still get boring if there wasn't enemy variety. However, there is more than PLENTY of that. This doesn't account for the different sub-types. Each enemy has their own unique fighting styles and in turn you need to make a plan for each, especially when they are all mixed together in a group, mixing up combat all the time
The item system is also a pretty neat gimmick. You can hold multiple weapons at a time, and this allows you to customize how you want to be equipped.
The variety of weapons in and of themselves are pretty interesting too. Weapons themselves are randomly generated from various parts, of various weapon types (from Rocket Launchers to Snipers to SMGs). In addition to that, there are various different traits you can get. There's different elements (Electric, Fire, Corrosive, Explosive and Slag which itself doesn't do much, but boosts non-slag damage), and different Companies that give unique traits. These also get divided by Rarity, rarer weapons being more powerful.
The skill system also adds a lot of varied gameplay. There are 4 (non-DLC) characters, and each character has 3 trees, each with it's unique traits.  You can do 3 playthroughs with the same character and do each playthrough entirely differently.
The story is simply amazing. It keeps you guessing what will happen next. The story gives you a lot of good context as to what you are doing without really being intrusive of the game itself, something not common in most games.
The game looks and sounds gorgeous in action. The soundtrack, while maybe not memoriable, is definately suiting for whatever situation your in. And the places you visit, well even though you're on a desert planet, there's a lot of variety to the locals you visit. And to top it off the great use of Cel Shading pieces it together, giving the game a unique look and feel.
The character's are all amazing with their own charm. Psycho's will cry out random banter while rushing you , Skag's will growl at players, Handsome Jack sometimes phones you just to taunt you, your characters will even shout stuff as you activate abilities, kill a tough enemy, etc. and it all pieces the world together so well. You'll learn to love virtually all of the characters.
The game itself has a lot of replayability. Maybe you want to go and fight that super tough boss that usually requires 4 players to beat at max level. Maybe you just want to try and get that super rare loot. Maybe you want to do a second playthrough with a higher difficulty. Maybe you just want a different character. In any case, there's lots to come back to, especially if you mix things up.
A quick note on the DLC for this game. For the most part this is what I would call "Good" DLC: It adds a lot of replayability. However, the Head Hunter packs are only really for those looking to scrounge more hours into this game.
The co-op is also a great mix, and working with your allies to accomplish an otherwise challenging mission or boss is extremely gratifying.
Alright, now you've heard me praise the game for almost every aspect, so what can I complain about?
Well for one the final boss. Now don't get me wrong, it's a pretty amazing fight in and of itself. However it can drag on for too long, easily.
Some side-quests are also pretty underwhelming, You go to do __, buddy says thanks, gives you reward, you leave. Often times you are already heading to the area anyway, so it's less of a "Side Quest" as much as "Do this while you're there".
It'd also be nice to be able to see what my options were when turning in "multi-end" quests, so I know what reward I would get from which path I take.
However these are mostly minor gripes with an otherwise amazing game.
Overall, a great game you should add to your collection if you are looking for a unique twist on both the FPS and RPG genres.

Tiny Bang Story is a cute little mouse-only point-and-click puzzle game with mechanics similar to Machinarium and other type games. It's pretty short, but it's got a pretty good spread of puzzles. Nothing you probably haven't seem before: lots of jigsaw puzzles, sliding piece puzzle to make a picture, move-all-the-pieces-to-the-correct-spot-with-only-one-free-space, some old-school arcade games like fly-your-ship-down-a-maze-and-don't-run-into-walls, and your generic hunt-for-10-components hidden object puzzles. But even when you immediately know what to do (i.e. all the Tetris-looking blocks need to fit into a rectangular space with no holes), actually doing them can take quite a bit of effort.
This game also does a couple of interesting things, though although these are all positives, they also become rather tedious after a while:
1) the hint system. You have a bar to fill up to get a hint (normal), but you have to collect little flying insects to fill up the bar (interesting). However, it takes a LOT of them, and if you're stuck on two different items you're trying to find, expect to do a lot of clicking.
2) It's linear, but non-linear (if that makes sense). You definitely have a certain sequence to follow (e.g. find 10 of these things to unlock a puzzle, which gives you a key, which opens a door, which reveals another puzzle that needs 15 of this other thing to open, etc.) However, you can have multiple TYPES of things to search for at any given time, and for each of those TYPES, there are tons of actual ITEMS to find. However, since there is some linearity to it, you'll start to notice a ton of a given item but be unable to pick them up until you find the machine or door that requires all those items. This makes for a lot of "Now, where did I see that thing earlier?" hunting.
It's got cute art, and a neat (but simple) story of you trying to put back your tiny little world. Putting back the world is actually a puzzle in itself (a literal jigsaw puzzle), which is a nice little detail.
So, is this game groundbreaking? Hell no. Is it worth full price? Probably not. But is it worth the $1 I spent on it? I think so. Despite some minor annoyances, I got my dollar's worth.

As Captain Forever, you piece together a spaceship out of parts given to you through kits. You can unlock different kits as you play. Once you have built your spaceship you fly through different levels of space, destroying other ships and stealing the parts for yourself.

You need to plan how you are going to destroy your enemies, trying not to blow up too many parts of their ships but ultimately winning each battle by destroying the enemies cores causing them to break apart, rendering their parts usable.

Below you'll find a written and video impression on the game.
Captain Forever Remix melds the idea of perma death and random generation from the roguelike games and the customization of ship builder games. An interesting hybrid, one that I feel worked out!
When you first jump into the game you'll be able to do a quick build of your ship from an assortment of different starting kits. Each kit will have their own type of blocks, and already in it's early access form, there is a large variety of blocks and gizmos to discover and build out of. Once the ship is ready to go, you'll head out into space to do battle with other ships. If you managed to destroy the enemy, what parts they had left over you'll be able to scavenge and use for your own ship to grow it in power and performance. But be aware, this game is all real time, so you'll have to quickly attach parts, often while under enemy fire. This help keep the game feeling frantic, and multitasking skills will be tested.
The controls of the game will take some getting used to. The game has a physics system that takes into account your ship's weight, balance, and inertia. Because of this, depending on how you build your ship, it can move very sluggish, and can feel floaty. But once you get adjusted and can factor it's physics you'll be sailing the 7 galaxies in no time!
The visuals and audio is just fantastic in this game. I love the cartoon style, and the audio is great as well. Wonderful music with all the appropriate beeps and boops that you would expect.
I don't have too much negatives to point out about the game so far (this is a good thing of course), but I do have a couple of suggestions. Though the game works perfectly fine as a single player game, I can also envision this game as multiplayer and imagine it to be a lot of fun! Shooting each other's parts off, building from your enemy's ships. I think the game would be well suited for it. Of course, at this time it is only single player, and I don't think there is any plans for multiplayer, but it is something I would love to see in Captain Forever Remix.
Overall, Captain Forever Remix is an interesting blend of genres that looks great, plays great, and really taps into the player's creativity when constructing a ship. For an early access, the game feels very complete and polished.
Pros:
- Great visual and audio design
- Fun, creative, and challenging
-  Accessible and easy to learn
- Feels very complete and polished for an early access
Cons:
- Could use a better options menu
- Lacks extra features

Fun game overall, I think I'm about done with it though.
+ Sandbox mode
+ Fine-grain control over almost everything
+ Custom character bios can be amusing
+ Can't just leave overnight, requires constant attention for escapes, etc
- Not much replayability
- AI for staff can be really dumb
- Limited customization (textures, etc)
- Performance is bad with larger prisons
I've sunk quite a bit of time into the game at this point, building several prisons as I figure out how everything works. Once you've got that worked out, though, the game gets fairly boring.
but after you know what will keep prisoners happy, you build until your prison is complete (or until performance sucks - I've gotten up to ~2000 cells and it seems to happen around ~1500) and then there isn't much to do aside from sit and watch.
One major complaint is that the staff AI is idiotic at times. If you're building, say, a 5x5 room, the game will pull 25 staff members to build one piece each - even if a few staff members are right there and the others are across the map. The few that were there could have completed the room by the time the others got to it had they built more than one piece. Multiply that on a large scale and it can take forever to get things done.
Legendary prisoners can be difficult to handle - hopefully you've researched permanent solitary before they arrive, and build a separate SuperMax wing just for them. Annoying that they can repeatedly murder prisoners and staff and it just adds to their sentence (i.e. you get to deal with them for even longer) instead of promoting them to Death Row at some point.
Lots of other minor gripes about how some things need to be built a certain way to function correctly.
Overall, though, I've spent a lot of time building things and it was definitely entertaining at times. I'd recommend the game (on sale, for sure) if you like the architect/tycoon genres.

Lets look at spec ops: the line and see if it is a good. I will go over the game in a pro con style while trying to provid as much detail as i can to get my point across.
Pro:
Enjoyable story. At times the game will throw you a curve ball making the player reaccess what is going on through the game. You might think you know the story but with twist thrown in making the player keep thinking about actions or choices they have done.
Music is very combat orientated. It is complicated to explain but the music is good and fits moments of dispare or high octane moments where you are in the battle field.
Gunplay is good, guns have a sense of recoil and ammo depending on the difficulty is scarce. So need to get those headshots.
No clown boxes for the most part. I found 1 clown box but it was very minor and easily blazed right through it. So dont expect moments like in call of duty where you kill a dude and 1 min later a dude replaces the gunned down enemy up till the player passes an invisible line to stop the respawns. That isnt in this game.
Ai support orders are a unique mechanic to this game since if the player is stuck in a heavy fire the game would sometimes say press the squad button to throw a flash bang or used the squad button to mark out a sniper to be taken out by the ai.
Some environment hazzards. The player can shoot some objects like explosive barrels but that is really casual for shooter games to have that. Here you can shoot glass that has trapped sand. So what some might say but what is cool is that this is one of the ways to kill off your enemies. Yes this is pressent is very few locations but it is a mechanic worth mentioning allowing players to save ammo and have an alternative to killing enemies with bullets.
Con:
Poor Ai. The ai do some really stupid things like moving forward while under heavy fire or moving out of cover to apply suppressive fire. These moments will cause the ai to go into bleed out. What sucks is when the ai's bleed out timer runs out then its game over. Most of the time you will get a game over from the ai rather than you dying personally.
Enemys throw gernades like mad at times and really accurate at it too. This is very apparent on the hardest difficulty called FUBAR (♥♥♥♥ed Up Beyond All Repair). The enemies would toss gernades right at you many times, what would be nice is if we had the ability to toss the gernades back. Another thing gernades are very weird on how they work. Sometimes you survive gernades your not suppose to and die from some your were not suppose to.
Conclusion:
Spec Ops: The line is a great game, is it perfect no. The Ai is really bad and will go to bleed out alot and in some really bad locations but what the game has it does well. The gunplay is fun to do, story was awsome, and the music really emphasised what was going on. Was the player suppose to feel sad or what? I would reccomend this game to all who are interested in shooting games and i offer one advice you cover. This isnt like call of duty where you can rush into combat with no real worries here you need to use cover to survive and take enemies one by one making a safer passage to move up to the next cover.

Weird controls. There is one button which is used for sprinting and taking cover. Which means you are never really in control. Sometimes you just want to sprint but the game places you in cover. Other times you really want to take cover but the game forgets to do this so you die. The same button is used to get you out of cover or to quickly switch from one piece of cover to another. At any rate; way to often I find myself being unintentionally out of cover and sprinting somewhere is annoying since the character auto runs to any cover in the direction you are sprinting.
There is another button which is for jumping over stuff and melee. I won't get into how odd that is.
The game has no map or objectives marker. Which I don't mind but there is only 1 path to the objective and there are invisible walls everywhere. Also some decor can not be used for cover. And a lot of decor can not be jumped over.
I am 80 minutes in and do not see a reason to return to the game. The combat is lacklustre because of the weird controls and so far there is not really a story. Sure, stuff happens but the main character knows more then me, the player. Which makes me question why he actually does things. You pick up intel which gives some extra story stuff but you can only read it immediately when you pick it up and not later. I picked up intel in a quiet part, was about to read it and then the enemy showed up and killed me. I was unable to read the intel after the game loaded the checkpoint.
The game has more of these sloppy things. Like small graphic glitches or no ability to change your mouse sensitivity separately for aiming down the sights. Or friendly AI frozen out of cover. Speaking about AI; it is horrible. Both enemy and friendly; it is  the same as in games from 15 years ago.
The maps allow you to flank sometimes but since there are invisible walls everywhere you instantly learn not to try this. And having your character not really be controllable while sprinting doesn't invite straying from the path either.
There is stealth but I think this is only when the game wants you to be stealthy. It does not seem to work in other segments of the game.
Conclusion after 80 minutes: This is just a simple on rails cover shooter where you play as an American soldier with a cut scene here and there and lacklustre controls and bad AI set in a desert city. If it were not for the graphics this game could have been made 15 years ago.

PROS:
It has open levels with tons of ways to dispose of the target.
The Right amount of cutscenes to not delay you from playing, yet keep You interested in the story.
Possibility to discover more about Your targets and reasons why they need to kick the bucket.
Smart enough AI with peripheral vision.
Most of your targets have evacuation plan in case you blow your cover. NPC routines change during the level.
Stealth depends more on disguises again (unlike in absolution, which relied more on "traditional" sneaking).
Locations are diverse with lot of details and interesting things to discover.
Escalation side missions, Elusive targets, Location mastery and User contracts will keep you playing long after finishing the main story.
Challenges are tough, if You want to kill just the targets.
It quickly became my most favourite Hitman game (and I've played the series since the first game).
After the latest patch, there is no need to be always online to play with Your unlocks. So who hesitated to buy the game because of it, might want to reconsider.
CONS:
I really miss the suitcase and other items that could be used to conceal a bigger weapons. The fact that You can walk around with a sniper rifle in Your hands while disguissed as a guard is just weird.
AI does not react to blood splatters.
When AI is going to check some strange noise and radio it to HQ, there is no reprecussions for taking him down before he gives the "all clear" signal.
Good game with loads of stuff to do, like running around as a clown with a fire extinguisher smacking people over the head!

Hitman 2016 honestly fufills itself as the rightful successor to Blood Money. It is way more detailed than Absolution or Blood Money, allowing you to emerse yourself in a more life-like world. The game goes even so far to include details such as Dalia Mangolis' awareness of her surroundings when you take out one of the guards, commenting there is one guard short. It also brings back the extra content that is contracts mode, giving players more post-game content. While there may be minor faults (SUCH AS WHETHER THAT GUARD IN SAPIENZA WHO IS GUARDING THAT CASTLE LIKE BUILDING IS DEAF AND WHY MY OPTION TO SUBDUE HIM ONLY COMES UP WHEN I RUN INTO HIM) it is still a great game. Yes, while the title is very demanding performance-wise and is not to well optimized for lower end systems (yet) it is still a fantastic game and is worth a buy.

The first two early access games I got into were the early access versions of Minecraft and Terraria. They were both great in their own ways. I've since tried other early access games and have had many disappointments.
Fortunately, Signs Of Life did not disappoint. There is a lot of exploring to do, many things to do in this game and a lot of things to make. The game is stable and the gameplay is very smooth and polished.
Development is a little slow, but it is steady. As of this review, I think we've been waiting on the next 'big update' for maybe over a year now. However, the devs are active. They chat on the forum. Occasionally they've put out an update which adds something interesting. I should probably add that the dev team only has a few people. So, progress is probably good and steady for a team of this size.
Overall, the $9 price tag is well worth it. This feels like one of those games that someone made because it was something they really wanted to do, not just to make a quick buck.
Also, there has been an Alien Artifacts update which is pretty nifty.

3 out of 6 stars. I'm on the edge here, but ultimately not reccomended. Mostly ebcause of low replayability.
Pros:
- nice graphics in comparison with similar titles
- clearly SF-themed and oriented
- some interesting objects and animals that do make you feel like its an alien world.
- has some background story and its interesting to play it the first time
Cons:
- short, you can reach top range gear quickly and not much left to do from that point on
- while the world is procedurally generated, the amount of biomes and objects is very limited. So playing it the second time feels entierly the same as playing it teh first time.
- building options are frankly very limited in comparison to let's say terraria or minecraft. For such an SF-themed game, you will be unable to build the nice futuristic style buildings that you can see in the game (these are NPC ones and mostly cannot be removed or rebult).
- Same main missions, same boss etc in each playthrough.
- Low overall replayability. This is sadly not what one would expect from minecraft-ish style procedurally generated world games.
Overall teh game can be enjoyable in you first playthough, but once you pass it once you ill have no reason to play it again. Sluggish development doesn't help.

Got this for $7.50 on the summer sale and worth every penny. I wouldn't have spent $30 though. While I sunk 22 hours into it in the span of 3 days, by the end of the campaign I was feeling a bit worn.
Sure, it's average gaming binge issues but it comes largely with looking at the same thing for hours and hours. If you're inclined to managing and micromanaging, absolutely buy this game, though. I realize I don't have the patience for that level of nitty gritty.
As a lover of "tycoon" games I'd like a little more variety in items, walls, decoration, and placement. Some items you can't face the direction you want, and while most work fine facing the wrong way, sometimes they don't.
I did love the story that went with the campaign/tutorial and would love to see updates or DLC that brings more stories and items to the game, but it seems like they update it pretty frequently, so that's nice.

Not really my thing, considering just how rapidly you're bombarded by slimes, zombies, and other enemies, even if you've boarded up a hideaway. Enemies will still manage to appear from either side of the screen leading to your large base suddenly being overrun if you make it too wide. You always revive at the start position, too, regardless of whether it's the beginning or middle of night and how far you have to treck in the dark with the enemies. Logging also became a menial process because I couldn't cut down a single tree without being swarmed by slimes who flee and return after being "killed." I'm not the only one who couldn't keep up with the onslaught of enemies, either; my guide, an NPC that spawned with me, and is apparently important in some way, managed to get himself eliminated before the first night even began due to the slime-slaught.
Still, probably something to loo into if you like bit-crafting. I personally don't and only really checked it out due to the hype, so I'm aware I'm probably nitpicking. You could probably make a decent base to protect from the get-go if you know these sort of things ahead of time. I'd probably give it a four or five out of ten because of it wasn't really a good match for me but other people, who are cool with the endless barrage of enemies might like it. Still, there's no "meh" Steam option, so "Yeah, maybe to the right crowd" will have to do.
Besides, I'm slightly biased; I'm also a bit peaked since Steam refuses to refund it on the basis of "2 hours" worth of playtime, despite only having played 93 minutes, which is a bit over 1 and a half hours of time, not 2 hours. Not really Terraria's fault, though. Only five dollars worth of an investment lost, but still annoying due to the princile of the thing.

(This review is mostly copy-pasted from the non-Definitive version of the game)
Ori and the Blind Forest has earned its stripes in more ways than one.
The first ten minutes of the game are a heart-touching series of beautifully animated scenes between two characters that don't need a word of dialog; all set to a soundtrack that's on par with the best of indie composers. While technically there's a narrator speaking through parts of it in vague, riddlish sentences, it still represents a superb example of showing rather than telling.
The game does not simply rest on some status as an artistic, classic-gameplay adventure though. You may have heard mentions that the game is hard; I don't rank it among Super Meat Boy's levels of masochism, but unique platforming challenges and coordination are some of the staples of its gameplay. This would be a lot more annoying were it not for an inventive checkpoint system; you can essentially save anywhere by using up one expandable "Energy" point; as a Metroidvania, there are also true save points that refill both your health and Energy. I really hope for the difficulty not to put people off; at the very least, it will make those reward moments so much sweeter when you finally escape the flooding of the Ginso Tree.
Every room in the game always seems to have the detail of a painting; the fantasy wonder of a game like Trine, but seemingly almost all of it hand-painted instead of 3D (many times, it's hard to tell the difference!) With some of the game's more cinematic set-piece moments, it's almost hard to fathom the kind of work that went into the visuals. You could pretty much hit the screenshot button at any time and have yourself a new wallpaper.
While there are some excellent reveals in the storyline, overall the strongest emotional points are the ones closest to the beginning. In some ways this makes sense, letting the story serve as a "hook" to get you to keep playing, rather than starting with baffling mysteries that you can't even theorize an answer to.
Out of the storytelling, animation, soundtrack, challenge, and overall cinematic presentation; Ori would be a highlight of the year for mastering just *one* of these elements to the degree they've managed. Had I known what I do about this game prior to buying it, I easily would have accepted a starting price of $60. The only possible detractor that might ward some people off of playing this game is its difficulty, but the Definitive Edition has added difficulty selection that may make this less of a concern. Easily one of the best indie games of the past few years.

Creamy-center-chocolate-space-muffin-surgeon-simulator 2015. Buy this game!
Early access stability:
A few minor bugs will still pop up (but this review was written in early-early access). Some collision issues and some minor crashes but other than that totally playable and fun as s**t!
Story:
A very neat premise in which you play the older sister to a younger brother who went and messed up the universe. It's extremely charming and heartwarmingly 90's
Mechanics:
The original Captain Forever took an approach to space combat that was utterly original and dynamic. As every space-craft is centered around a fairly weak control module which, when destroyed, allows the player to remod their ship with salvage from fallen enemy ships. This means you will want to attack as much of the creamy center as possible, without doing too much damage to your enemy's hull, weapons, shields and thrusters, so that you may use these parts to become the greatest creamy center chocolate space muffin surgeon known in the solar system.
In spite of the cute child-like presentation, this game is nothing short of "Dark Souls level" hard-core. Nothing comes easy and you'll end up fighting for every piece of salvage like it's a bread-crumb in a 1930's Polish trainstation. Trying to remod your ship while frantically dodging three, if you're lucky, incoming enemies is nerverackingly fun.
The best part:
The way you choose to design your ship is as dynamic as you'll find in games like Space Engineers, and doing so is a lot less dull. Every "block (hull modules, shields, weapons, CHAINSAWS!!!!!!!!, laser beams etc) has a "mass" value which influences your ship's balance. Putting a truster or weapon slightly off center will spin your ship into fatal inertia, but after a bit of practise you will build the most bad mofo of swiss army space crafts fully equiped with lasers, sniper shots, missles, AND MODDERFORKING SPACE-CHAIN-SAWS!!!! It's rediculously fun!
You can build big and sluggish, small and agile, small and sluggish, bulky and fast like a Coventry girl trying to get a council house. Build a lopsided flying missle♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ a triangular spinning sniper craft, or a tiny little ship that can fly its way straight the middle while dodgin torpedoes, or a fat ship that can take a million punches: it's all viable, it's all fun and you'll die anyway so why even bother.
Long story short:
If MineCraft scoodilypooped Asteroids (while Surgeon Simulator was ball-gagged and made to watch) you'd get a horrible game that nobody should ever play and your money would be much better spent on buying "Captain Forever Remix" twice. It's that good.

What is there to say about this game.. hmmm..  APB is a mixed bag of nuts so to speak. There's some in there you want and some you wish were never in the bag. This game has tons of depth in terms of customization, but lacks in more important areas such as matchmaking and weaponry. A lot of people say this game is Pay 2 Win. It's true, but at the same time it's false. You can easily purchase a new weapon in 3-5 missions. Even the stock weapons can prove their usefulness up against a $30 G1C(Real Life Money) Weapon. I've been playing this game for a really long time, around 2 year On and Off. I can safetly say the server's stability has definitely increased and fixing the FpS lag is as simple as deleting a folder or disabling Realtek. PunkBuster is one of the crappiest HackShields available, thus hackers are abundant, however, from my latest experiences, I haven't noticed any. In fact, I've been called a hacker more times than I've actually faced one. Honestly, on a scale of 1 to 10 on how pro i am, I'd say 6.5 flat. This game has so much potential, but just lacks the key components to really make it successful. I JUST recently dropped $40 into this game and only because they had a 50% off sale. Also, my Threat level is Gold, so apparently the game thinks I'm good. (Threat levels range from Weakest to Most Skilled as Green, Bronze, Silver, Gold ).
Key Factors in this game that keep me interested and to why I'd recommend it :
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#1 - Ragdoll is numbah one-san.
#2 - The Customization makes me drool.
#3 - Open World PvP Combat ( You can even see other players fighting without being in that mission ).
#4 - The Storyline is pretty unique.
#5 - A lot of fun when you play with friends or find a decent group of players.
#6 - You don't HAVE to spend real $ to be good.
#7 - The selection of vehicles if quite vivid, each being specialized in different areas. Driving takes a while to get a hold of however, especially a select few vehicles.
#8 - Modifications to enhance your weaponry, character and vehicle to your liking whenever you unlock them. Mods are thankfully permanent.
#9 - Great in-game soundtrack featuring popular artists such as Clutch & Pendulum.
#10 - You can arrest people? That's the ultimate troll pwng power possible! P's!!
Reasons to avoid this game :
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#1 -Rare Occassions - There's hackers.
#2 - It's not very new user friendly which can immediately turn someone off. Lacking a legitimate tutorial, though the objectives are pretty obvious, it's not THAT difficult to understand what to do.
#3 -Matchmaking is awful, don't expect to go up against new players or players around the same level as you.
#4 -Broken Guns : This one i'll have to explain. Some weapons in this game seem to excel far beyond other weapons in certain specifications. Example, a slow firing SMG should not be able to take out a fast shooting LMG at 5 meters.
#5 - Character models don't move in the most fluent way, so aiming at opponents can prove very difficult, especially when lag factors in, causing them to teleport.
#6 - Weapons and certain Vehicles only last 7 days. Pretty stupid.( UNLESS you pay real $ for a permanent one. Which i'd say is another reason i wouldnt recommend this game ).
Overall, the game deserves credit where credit is due, but hate where it's mostly needed.

Before we get into the nitty gritty, heres a nice little synopsis. Is this game worth the asking price? Yes, if you're a fan of this style game it most certainly is, though I would still say wait for a sale like the most recent 50% off one. You may move on now if you so wish.
The Nitty Gritty: I have a very basic set of rules to determine if I think a game is worth recommending to other people, or even not feeling ripped off by my purchase. Is the game fun, and do I get a decent amount of gameplay per dollar.
Is the game fun: As is likely obvious by the recommendation and me saying it is worth the asking price, the game is very fun. The mechanics are smooth, the controls are fluid, and I have yet to see a complaint about the actual gameplay of the game.
Gameplay per Dollar: Heres a big one that so many modern games fail. I believe a game should give me at least 1 hour of gameplay for each dollar I spent before I feel ripped off. If I buy it on sale it has to at least hit the sale price. I spent 43 dollars on Hitman The Complete First Season, as I'm writing this I currently have 53.8 hours of gametime. I am nowhere near done as I still have Colorado and Hokkaido to finish, and a mountain of challenges and escalations across every stage still to do. I'll easily break 100 hours before I am done with this game without including the forthcoming Season 2 and before I reach the player-made Contracts.
There has been complaints about this game and I thought I'd address those as well to give my opinion on them. The most obvious complaint I've seen across the negative reviews has been its Always Online feature. I see a lot of "This game is so much fun, but you have to always be online so negative review" usually by people with 60+ Hours in the game. This is an issue I agree but not a deal breaker and the developers have taken steps to ease the pain when they released The Chef Elusive Target. Now you retain all your upgrades you've gained from online play when you play the game in offline mode. I haven't seen any mention of it going the opposite way so likely you won't be able to unlock anything new from a offline run of a mission. Despite that I have had a single connection issue in my time playing the game and that was likely caused by my PoS router going out so I can't hold the "outages" many have brought up. Sadly, Always Online is the way games are going and I just hope for further steps to make the eventual death of the servers easier on those of us who will continue playing it single player.
The only other major complaint I've seen with this game has been its episodic nature. Honestly I don't see the complaint, noone has been able to truly articulate to me why the episodic nature is bad. What is the cost of a full price game Triple A game: $60. What is the cost of Hitman: The Complete First Season if bought as a bundle: $60. What is the cost if you buy it piecemail: $65. If I hadn't bought it on sale I'd be paying the same amount for this game as the guy down the street would be paying for the latest Call of Duty. That and theres benefits to an episodic release schedule. It gives the developers more time to hash out each stage, as well as fix errors they didn't find in their playtesting. On top of this it lowers the price-point for "I'm not sure"s. I don't know if I'll like Hitman, its a type of game I usually don't play, so I pick up Episode 1. 15 bucks gives me the prologue and the first mission, plenty of content for someone to wet their toes and determine if its their type of game. They love it they can then upgrade to the full season, if they hate it they're only out 15 bucks.
As this review is getting obnoxiously long I'll end it here. Final opinion stated again: Yes, its worth your money.

The Good:
-Graphics and animations are gorgeous
-Handheld multitool you start with feels like something a crashed ship survivor might actually have, high tech without being game-breaking, and scales up nicely over the course of the game
-Imaginative enemies with an AI that, while simplistic, knows what it can do and how to accomplish it, and will even outmaneuver and trap you
-Story (what there is of it, I'll get to that in a moment), while not all that new, is handled better than most triple-A titles do it, paced so you learn more as you advance
-Tech scales up nicely from primitive constructs assembled with sticks and vines to plasma cannons, and the transition actually feels pretty natural
The Bad:
-Not much variety.  It's very easy to reach a point at which the game has nothing new to show you, or where there is more content but you're completely stuck as to how to advance or just plain don't realize there is more.
-Rare updates.  It was doing very well, but the last update was two months ago, and didn't add much.  Even if it's just the odd new weapon or another bit of the story revealed, I'd love to see more frequent updates.
The Verdict: If you like Terraria, this is like Terraria but in my opinion better fleshed out.  There's less content than in other games, but what there is has been polished to a mirror shine, with the promise of more on the horizon (even if that horizon is sometimes frustratingly far away).  A brilliantly executed take on the sci-fi survival game that I sincerely hope will keep growing and realize its potential.

When you play a game that exists in a genre that’s already heavily populated with awesome titles, it’s easy to jump to negative comparisons. In the case of Sweet Dogs Studios’s Signs of Life, you’ll be having too much fun to think about how games like Terraria or Starbound may be more expansive.
Signs of Life is what Sweet Dogs Studios defines as a “sci-fi survival sandbox platformer”. It mixes different elements of crafting games while adding an adventure game feel through the storyline. The premise of this game is that you’re one of the lone survivors of a devastating incident which left most of your crew lost or dead. Your task is to land on the planet (which is conveniently Earth-like) your crew originally intended to investigate and survive long enough to find out what happened to them. In spite of the morbid implications left through the clues about your crew that you’ll find throughout the world, Signs of Life manages to stay light-hearted and keep you focused on exploration and fun.
When you first start out, you’re given several character creation options. Since the game is still in its Early Access stage, your options are limited but the developers have promised to expand on the character creation system in the future. I simply opted to make the most girly-looking dude possible and ended up with pink slippers and a super-saiyan haircut. You then make your landing on the planet via your escape pod and quickly discover that you’re going to have to improvise in order to make it.
The crafting options in Signs of Life were a lot more intuitive and varied than I initially expected. You have dozens of options from the very beginning, and as you discover new areas and objects, your virtual companion AGIS compiles new recipes for you. AGIS is only one component of your infinitely useful wrist-laser device, which is what you use to break blocks and collect items. The only thing the wrist-laser can’t be is a weapon – you’ll have to just settle for guns, crossbows, swords, and a plethora of other weapons you can craft based on your preferences.
One of the more difficult aspects of the crafting is perhaps the gathering of the actual materials. Although some of the materials require a common-sense driven gathering process (picking up rocks from the ground, chopping down trees for wood) others require exploration (you probably won’t find a battery in a tree). You’ll also have to get used to figuring out the base components of certain objects by looking through their recipes and trailing backwards in order to achieve crafting that item. That may seem cumbersome at first, but the crafting menus are built in such a way so that everything is easily sorted and found.
My personal favorite thing about Signs of Life has to be the art style. The backgrounds that seem to move with you are beautifully done and serve as a contrast to the blockier style of the actual playing space. The graphics give an overall sense of polish to the game that may not always be present since it is still an Early Access game. The music that plays in the background is mostly non-intrusive and peaceful. While it serves to make sure that the planet you’re on isn’t entirely silent, it’s not enough to make you feel like you’re not alone – which was probably the point. Signs of Life really emphasizes the fact that you’re a lone survivor, isn’t always pleasant. The game will definitely benefit from the eventual implementation of multiplayer, as do games like Minecraft and Terraria.
With Signs of Life, Space Dog Studios has created a game with plenty of character. It’s through intuitive gameplay and special attention to detail that this game will stand out in the eyes of those who play it. When Signs of Life is finally finished and out of Early Access, it will likely have the potential to be a contender among the Terrarias and Starbounds of the genre. Signs of Life is worth the investment. It’s not a perfect game, but it’s definitely a lot of fun.

Seinfeld is an American television sitcom that ran for nine seasons on NBC, from 1989 to 1998. It was created by Larry David and Jerry Seinfeld, with the latter starring as a fictionalized version of himself. Set predominantly in an apartment building in Manhattan's Upper West Side in New York City, the show features a handful of Jerry's friends and acquaintances, particularly best friend George Costanza (Jason Alexander), former girlfriend Elaine Benes (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), and neighbor across the hall Cosmo Kramer (Michael Richards). It is often described as being "a show about nothing", as many of its episodes are about the minutiae of daily life.
Seinfeld was produced by Castle Rock Entertainment. In syndication, the series has been distributed by Sony Pictures Television since 2002. It was largely written by David and Seinfeld with script writers who included Larry Charles, Peter Mehlman, Gregg Kavet, Carol Leifer, David Mandel, Jeff Schaffer, Steve Koren, Jennifer Crittenden, Tom Gammill, Max Pross, Dan O'Keefe, Charlie Rubin, Marjorie Gross, Alec Berg, Elaine Pope, and Spike Feresten. A favorite among critics, the series led the Nielsen ratings in seasons six and nine, and finished among the top two (with NBC's ER) every year from 1994 to 1998.
Seinfeld is widely considered to be one of the greatest and most influential sitcoms ever made. It has been ranked among the best television shows of all time in publications such as Entertainment Weekly, Rolling Stone, and TV Guide. The show's most renowned episodes include "The Chinese Restaurant", "The Parking Garage", and "The Contest". In 2013, the Writers Guild of America voted it the No. 2 Best Written TV Series of All Time (second to The Sopranos). E! named the series the "number 1 reason the '90s ruled", and quotes from numerous episodes have become catchphrases in popular culture.
