Spec Ops: The Line is an excellent example of why I no longer trust video game reviewers. Somewhere along The Line between entertainment and art, curators and plebs alike decided that a game with a point was somehow exempt from basic rules of gaming. It’s like if Mona Lisa spat on everyone who looked at it we’d still consider it genre-breaking. Except, Spec Ops isn’t Mona Lisa, it’s a trite piece of undercooked antiwar masturbation that appears to fear rupturing an aneurism if it avoids a cliché. Admittedly, I am comparing it to my larger recollections of war stories, not the current state of the subject within games. Compare Spec Ops to Stanley Kubrick’s Paths of Glory and the chasm between entertainment and pacifism Spec Ops apparently thinks unavoidable appears more of an artificial border. That is to say, Paths of Glory is every bit as cynical as Spec Ops but with half the tedium.
I am not the first to point out that Spec Ops is a horrible game. Its benefactors admit this with the caveat that it somehow lends credence to its message. The Cynical Brit said it “isn’t a good game per se, it’s deliberately mundane 3rd person shooter which makes you think about the horrors of war.” It’s the “deliberately mundane” that irritates me. A deliberately mundane game is often indistinguishable from an incompetently mundane one. Cover-based gunfights that can be best described as soggy could be a statement about the stupidity of war, or a testament to how hard it is to make crisp-feeling third-person firefights. Considering that Gears of War is the only successful such attempt in recent memory, it’s all too convenient to say the gameplay was supposed to be bland. The blurb from its Steam store page describes this allegedly meaningful mediocrity as “tactical squad-based Delta Force gameplay throughout a horizontally and vertically oriented world”. Perhaps I expect too much, but anyone who pens prose such as this should not be trusted to make any adaptation of the Heart of Darkness. The memorable part of the gameplay is being constantly overwhelmed by hugely boring enemies who appear to be completely fungible with the exception of a single heavy type, who by describing as ‘heavy’ I have already imparted more information about their humanity than the game ever bothers to. Which is another issue with the deliberately mundane hypothesis. The storyline meshes with the gameplay precisely not at all. As I stand knee-deep in American soliders I shot to death because they stood between me and the next cutscene I’m expected to find my accidental shelling of a few dozen civilians the moral low point and story high point of the entire affair. Why? Ten minutes ago I intentionally killed men whose principal crime was proximity, and now I’m expected to feel remorse over the ones I offed on accident? Perhaps the convenience of intentionality ran dry by this point in the plot, because apparently designing mundane gameplay does matter yet designing to murder does not. Who’s ever heard of manslaughter anyway?
While I’m worrying about intentions, this game does an impressively bad job of concerning itself with mine. Sometimes, I was killed by the nameless faceless ‘baddies’ because I was too bored to be bothered to think about any kind of tactics. The rest of the time, I was killed because the game figures “run headlong into the enemy” and “cower beneath chest-high wall” are basically synonymous. Neither was any quick recovery possible, because unlike in Gears of War, the far superior gameplay progenitor of Spec Ops, I could not reverse my inertia with the tap of the ‘don’t-get-killed’ button. Instead, I stood to my full height, rearing my all-American chest to their all-American steel, slowly reoriented myself to our homeland and attempted to correct the game’s mistake.
But allow me to judge this “Story Rich” and “Political” game by its story and politics. Besides the name Conrad, the only feature Spec Ops retains from the Heart of Darkness is inexplicable motivations. And I don’t particularly appreciate that in the original text. Why does the protagonist continue on? That his unwilling companions constantly question him only compounds the issue by making it apparent. The complete lack of confusion on his part lulls the player into a blind acceptance of the plot, as we are presumably supposed to feel about the soldier’s acceptance of their mission drift. If you’re wondering where the plot holes are, just list the plot points. Why does he continue on into the city despite his orders about the retaining wall? To save the soldiers he watched die? What about the rebels who kill those soldiers; why do they vanish? Why does he accept the CIA so readily, while accepting that his fellow soldiers must die? And at no point do his Delta force underlings question him. These are men who are better educated and generally older than the average soldier: Men who are trained to question things normal soldiers aren’t. Even at the end, the last underling can’t bring himself to actually defy the protagonist. He merely won’t go with him any longer. Apparently, Conrad’s existence is enough to throw the protagonist into a fit of vengeance but his murdering of fellow soldiers, disregard of common sense, morality, and orders isn’t enough to inspire anything but words from his compatriots. I suppose they made the mistake of not being player-controlled characters.
The Heart of Darkness doesn’t work without xenophobia. Chinua Achebe was right to point out that the text portrays Africans as inhuman, but it’s a necessary literary move for the text to work as a whole. It may be wrong, but you can’t just take the xenophobia out and expect the story to survive. Unless you’re Spec Ops. There are no foils for “good” Europeans to be compared to within the game. No “savages” on the shore to provide a visceral reminder of what the main characters are pretending not to be. All that’s left is people acting strangely. The ideology of imperialism cannot even be mocked if there are no apparent victims to it. And the handful of quivering refugees are as easily regarded the victims of the sandstorms as they are of the American military industrial complex.
My principal emotions from playing the entirety of this quagmire of a game were frustration, confusion, and apathy. Frustration with the gameplay which clearly hated itself, confusion as to why any of the characters were doing almost anything they did, and apathy at the results of the decisions I didn’t understand. If this game is political, what political views should I take away from it? That we should be careful before dropping mortars on thermal signatures? That Delta Force commanders should not have total jurisdiction over places at which they just arrived? There is no political message here that is any less tedious or obvious than the game itself. Unless you need an eight-hour reminder that killing is bad (m’kay), stick to Bioshock for literature-inspired gaming.

Everquest 2 is the biggest mmo ever made. The amount of content in this game is overwhelming. You can play for hundreds of hours and barely scratch the surface of all the different things that you can do, see and achieve.
Of course there is the stright-line play, go from lvl 1 to 100 as fast as possible then do raids for great gear and accumulate riches that will allow you to play as a subscriber without paying real money, thats a perfectly viable playstyle, but there is an ocean of content that you will miss.
There is a lot of easily available filler content, mostly aimed for fast leveling or casual fast play, but there are also tonns of hidden stuff and elaborate quests for the players that are more curious, and who like exploring and investing more effort.
More often than not, the rewards for pursuing some of the strange questlines found in remote areas are quite surprising.
Playing Everquest 2 is like getting lost in a jungle. No matter where you decide to go and what you decide to do, you will find adventure....or adventure will find you as the case may be.
This game offers lots of content for every taste.
You want to solo from start to finish and still get great gear and do dungeons? No problem, game offers plenty of ways to do just that.
You like direction and hand-holding, gps quests and casual stuff? Lots of that in the game.
You like to break your head with difficult quests that require some inquisitive thinking, time and dedication? Hundreds of hours worth of this kind of content.
You like crafting? You'll be overwhelmed, crafting is insane in this game, its more content in the EQ2 crafting sphere alone than in the whole worlds of other mmos.
The character progression has no equal. Just the alternate achievement skill-trees alone are way and beyond the whole progression system of other games. You decide how you divide the experience gained between the character leveling and the AA (alternate achievement) level. Personally i like to channel all the exp into AA, that way i get quite overpowered at low levels, which for me is quite satisfying.
This game was never very appealing to the younger players, nor to the ones that only come to talk random stuff in world chat as is the case in other games.
As a result the game seems quiet and tranquil, which for me is a good thing. I dont need a lot of players jumping around aimlessly in the start areas and talking smack ( i call them cheerleaders cuz thats what they really do in these games).
Sadly there are a lot of players who need these cheerleaders to consider the game as being "alive" and not "dead".
There is a lot of poison thrown around on the internet regarding this game, and its a shame because many players will miss out one of the best mmos ever made and definitely the biggest one.

I’ve been a fan of the previous games playing the first Hitman until Blood Money, I did not really play Absolution just the first level and did not find it as fun as the previous iterations so that is where I stand in the series.
Hitman is not a perfect game by any stretch as it has always online components which is a bit annoying and prevent saving offline; framerate drops due to poor optimisation; long load times (I advise installing it on an SSD drive to avoid most of this issue) and poor story (who really cared about the Hitman story before? Still nicely rendered cut-sense). If you loved the classic Hitman games and longed for the sandbox kill, then the latest Hitman is a fantastic addition to the game with each level offering a whole host of ways for you to complete in this fun puzzle-box game of assassination.
I completed the main story including the two extra missions in around 15hours but still have a lot of challenges to do and side objects to unlock new items. The levels offer a lot of personalisation as you move around looking for new methods to kill.
I don’t write many reviews on Steam but I felt that Hitman is the sleeper hit of this year, I feel many will pass it up due to Square messing around and lack of buzz around the title but this game really does deserve your time.

As i write this review, on June 29th 2016. There are still a couple bugs within the game which i've encountered personally.
1. An item menu got stuck on my screen one time after i'd clicked the plus icon to expand it.
I fixed that by simply saving my game and reloading the save.
2. I built extra buildings during the Campaign which i shouldn't have (until absolutely necessary).
3. The CCTV system seems a bit wonky, but i'm quite sure it works.
4. During my own prison-running within the game i was bulk-building foundation-and-furniture-ready luxury cells, and one of which got stuck in the foundation stage, resulting in the cell turning out as incomplete & transparent.
This was fixed by placing a new foundation within the exact perimiter of the cell and adding a door of course, so the cell would get finalized.
5. One thing that bothered me was the fact nobody ever told me there was a difference between a foundation and a wall.
So. If you're building a huge prison block, but it keeps ♥♥♥♥ing itself up, then there's your reason. External walls: Foundation. Internal walls: Walls.
All in all, a very entertaining game, with a good, decently capturing storyline/campaign.
I'll definitely be on the lookout for more games by this developer in the future.

I have many thousands of hours more in this game than is on my Steam record, and I have played a wide variety of other MMORPGs including WoW, Rift, AoC, Eve, LOTRO and TESO.  None of which are a patch on EQ2 (LOTRO does come close though).
I have been playing since 2004 (a month after release) and had 3 years out in 2010 due to work, so I have seen the game evolution, the server merges and all the other schizzle that has been going down over the course of its life.
You will have read about the gameplay in many other reviews so I wont duplicate what has already been written except to say a few things:
- Free to play is ok to try out, but dont judge the game from a F2P perspective.  I agree with other reviewers that to take the game seriously you will need to subscribe.  For the price of a couple of pints a month though, it is worth it in my mind.
- Join a guild as soon as you can.  You will not get the same out of the game if you dont.  The guild system is player based, easy to follow and use and can help a new player enormously.  Look for guilds which have a reputation for helping new players.
- To compare EQ2 to WoW (and I have played both), EQ2 is a much more grown up world.  The people are friendlier, more helpful and more adult.
The Negatives:
- Some of the best zones are in the lower levels which, after this amount of time, are empty.  There are mercenaries available and the levelling system is much quicker than it used to be so getting to level cap is not so much of a slog.  With agnostic dungeons being available now for lower level characters to run with other higher level characters (all player levels are "normalised") there is opportunity for lower levels to experience groups and dungeons.
- The game, at high end, can be a bit "rinse and repeat".  Running the same dungeons over and over to get the good gear.  Raids and levelling new characters mixes things up a bit though.
There are many, many more things going on in this game (its HUGE!!!) than any one person can write in a review like this.  This is the game I keep coming back to having tried a lot of the other MMOs that are out there and if you like the genre, you will like this.

There is like over 20 classes to choose from which are each very customizable with your talent trees. Plenty of races to choose from too. The game is huge. Much bigger than WOW and many more dungeons to go in to. Open and private. Each class has a ton of spells and attacks to use so that you can feel like a real hero. Some people say players have too many abilities but I love blasting off 15 different attacks to defeat my foes. If you don't want to use all your spells you certainly don't have to so that solves that issue if it is an issue for you. The 55 hours shown here is only Steam play. I have well over 10 years of game play in Everquest 2 within multiple accounts. This game does require a good computer to run smooth. A video card with at least 2 gigs of RAM in my experience if you want the game to look good. 4 gigs if you want it to look smashing. You can turn the settings way down if your computer is that deficient but it will look like a 15 year old game.
One other note: I only played this game in free-to-play mode while on Steam and I noticed things may be different than if you have a sub. The alt character looks are better than the default looks for sure. If they changed that then that is great. My review is based on subbing not free-to-play but I have played free to play and I had a great time too but with some limitations which they recently may have done away with, hopefully. Try the game out anyhow and give it a good trial. Not 1 hour of play time. The community was always good to me and I suspect that has not changed although with free to play you never know who will play the game. Enjoy.

While the glory days are behind this game. It's still a solid game to take for a spin.
Graphics are definitely dated, but this game is a perfect example of why that doesn't always matter. There is content...and after that MORE CONTENT.
Difficulty has been scaled back, which some might find appealing while other's will be immediately be turned off. I personally, find it appealing. I grew up in the era of "sit on a spawn for hours", but I'm older now. I have other things I can do (either by choice or by necessity).
Final Verdict:
Game's still fun to hop in and play a bit. But it'll leave you a bit sad if you know the history, knowing you missed out on a truly exciting time in the Gaming Industry with this new genre called 'MMORPG'; now it's a common sight.
...so, come, come play a bit of history -- In the world of Norrath.

Everquest 2 is a standard, serviceable MMO.  There is no lack of contact to play through and the levelling is quite enjoyable, I would rate the levelling as even more enjoyable than World of Warcraft, being that there is a cohesive plot line and flow between the quests as well as a wealth of concisely delivered lore given in readable speach bubbles and not a forgettible quest accept window.  The story is about the world of Norrath, not the player hero.
Pros:
+EQ2 offers one of the widest selections of playable races and classes with few to no restrictions (2 races and 2 classes are premium only).
+The game also looks pretty good for a 2004 title and as you go to higher level areas the art only improves.
+Skills are very cool with a wide variety of available playstyles.
+Free to play up until the latest expansion (level 95).
Cons:
-Combat animations are not smooth, but it's a 2004 game so I'll give it a pass.
-Player is not well guided to enter dungeons, I was fairly unaware of their existence during most of my play time.
-Game does not seem to encourage co-op for the first 25 levels.

This is a very easy game to get into with a great story and fantastic gameplay, one of the best racing type games I actually enjoy, but it can be repetitive, especially if you are a completionist. The wasteland area is massive but it is riddled with very similiar objectives I could compare to AC1's flags. The only difference is these flags (scarecrows) are eventually upgraded into stronger ones that require better gear to take down. There are countless other objectives like camps and strongholds but these aren't as repetitive in the aspect of how it is liberated. Some require every enemy killed, others require the base destroyed. I greatly enjoyed doing almost everything in this game on my console when the game was released, and all over again on my PC. I chose to play it all over again for the fact I highly enjoy the game personally, and that the Magnum Opus has so much customization that I felt compelled to take it from the top and do it all over differently. The combat is as smooth as an Arkham title before Knight. There are times when you go into rage mode and 1v10 so damn hard you want to find another 10 and do it again. There is character and car progression that I think is the greatest part of a free roam game, you have different options from face, to beard, to body. The car starts off as a raggedy base with wheels and an engine, and by the end of it, you give it a complete overhaul with defense systems, body armor, and engine power. Everything you do in Mad Max is rewarded in some way, whether you are able to unlock more gear, or further decrease and eventually eliminate how many enemies roam the map, nothing really goes unsatisfied when I play, it's the best reason for replayability.

There has been a lot of controversy about this game with Squares decision to create it with always online DRM and personally I did not like the idea of it being released as episodes over several months, as a result I held off until the final product and then when it was in the sale I decided to grab it. I’ve been a fan of the previous games playing the first Hitman until Blood Money, I did not really play Absolution just the first level and did not find it as fun as the previous iterations so that is where I stand in the series.
Hitman is not a perfect game by any stretch as it has always online components which is a bit annoying and prevent saving offline; framerate drops due to poor optimisation; long load times (I advise installing it on an SSD drive to avoid most of this issue) and poor story (who really cared about the Hitman story before? Still nicely rendered cut-sense). If you loved the classic Hitman games and longed for the sandbox kill, then the latest Hitman is a fantastic addition to the game with each level offering a whole host of ways for you to complete in this fun puzzle-box game of assassination.
I completed the main story including the two extra missions in around 15hours but still have a lot of challenges to do and side objects to unlock new items. The levels offer a lot of personalisation as you move around looking for new methods to kill.
I don’t write many reviews on Steam but I felt that Hitman is the sleeper hit of this year, I feel many will pass it up due to Square messing around and lack of buzz around the title but this game really does deserve your time.

Borderlands 2 takes the fantastic co-op gameplay, cel-shaded visuals and charming humour from the first game and improves on it in every single way. The whole world is no longer a wasteland with environments such as glaciers, highlands and cities mixing things up a bit. Interaction has improved too, as players can trade weapons and money in-game with each other, or if they wish, they can duel for it all.
There are plenty of other subtle things that make the game much better than the original Borderlands, such as being able to move around when you're fighting for life, but there are way too many of those to cover. Borderlands 2 is a well-deserved upgrade from the original. Grab some friends, buy it and play the heck out of it.

I never write reviews on games, so perhaps that speaks to this game because here I am.
After the first two hours, I really enjoyed this game. The art style is lovely and unique (many p&c games look as if they use the same assets, not here) and the music is relaxing. There doesn't seem to be much of a story, and the puzzles are standard fare - find so many of this object, slider puzzles, color matching, etc. If you get stumped, you can collect flies that periodically show up on screen to fill up your hint bubble, though hints will only work if you're on the correct screen where the object you're looking for resides. Clicking the hint bubble on a screen where there are no objects yields nothing, and no tooltip or anything to let you know to move along.
Where the game started go to sour for me was the arcade-style minigames. They are very slow, moving frame by frame every second. In one you move a boat through water, avoiding whales and mines. It took a few tries to get the hang of, but it wasn't too bad. Not exactly what I had in mind when I bought the game, and it felt like it went on a bit longer than necessary, but I could look past it. The second arcade-style minigame, though... I find quite frustrating. You move a plane left to right as it's flying down, avoiding the bad black planes as well as obstacles in the form of trees. This minigame is much more difficult, and is where I stopped playing. If you don't move at the exact right moment, or choose the wrong path, you crash and have to start over. I'm only in the third chapter of the game, so I don't know how many more minigames of this style are waiting for me, and I don't much care to find out. I had to take a break out of frustration, and wonder if the frustration is even worth continuing to play.
For this reason, I would not recommend this game. It has a lot more going for it than the few annoying arcade minigames, but those stand out quite a bit if they're not your cup of tea (as is the case for me). It's such a shame as the art style is so nice. This game may be worth checking out when it's significantly on sale, if you are at all curious about it.

"The Tiny Bang Story" presents you with a small but fun world that you need to rebuild after a football (soccer ball) accidentally breaks apart.  This game contains several types of puzzles that you need to figure out in order to go through each level:  finding hidden object, matching patterns, discovering hidden areas,...  So if you like puzzle games, "The Tiny Bang Story" will be a lot of fun.
But there is more!  Each panel of hand-drawn art offers a beautiful background for all your puzzling fun.  The music is pleasant and happy (instead of annoying, cheesy, or elevator-like); the characters help you out; the big jigsaw puzzle fun to put together.  This game even has a built-in hint system.  Catch enough fireflies and the hint button in the upper right corner will fill up with blue, available to you in most areas of the game when you just need a small nudge to finish a challenge.
Overall, I love "The Tiny Bang Story" and I recommend it for all puzzle lovers.

The second season of Sam & Max is one of TellTale’s best point ‘n’ click adventure; a series that managed to elevate beyond the confines of its budget and the somewhat self-repeating TellTale formula to become one of the most definite nonsensical adventures to date.
TellTale’s Sam & Max trilogy has a plethora of ideas crammed into it, but in the end, it still follows the classic trilogy formula: the second season mostly reuses the recipe of the first, only adds a little more of everything.
In this case, everything means more wacky adventures and even crazier setups; from Santa Claus to the Bermuda triangle or outer space, the Freelance Police wreaks havoc wherever it goes in the typical Sam & Max fashion.
These adventures are confined to the old engine, meaning only a handful of locations per episode and game mechanics restricted to a Use and Look button. The simplicity is compensated by typical Sam & Max puzzles, where things make little sense, but you can find the twisted, zany logic behind the tasks.
Said tasks are somewhat held back by the typical TellTale game design, meaning each episode has the exact same structure: short introductory puzzle leading to the central plot, which then gets divided into a set of sub-tasks that you need to finish to start the final sequence. (The game also relies way too much on the triaé-and-error combination hunting puzzle type.)
Because the developers knew they were repeating themselves, they did everything to hide it behind great writing that strikes a perfect balance between self-contained stories and arcing plot, creating one of TellTale’s best point ‘n’ clicks and a must-have game for Sam & Max fans.

Don't recommend.  Maybe it will get better as the EA progresses, but so far I found myself binge playing this game once then putting it down and never picking it back up again.
Why?  Is it a bad game?  No.  But neither is a very engrossing game.  There really isn't much here that's new and unique.  It features a few small touches that are intriguing (such as the wearable holographic mini-map that must be filled in by manual scanning), but largely none of these made me really feel all that engaged.
The art and presentation is fine, if bland.  Only real complaint I had was that the high-rez, high-saturation pixel art made it hard to figure out what is an actual user interface element and what are just little visual doodads that serve no purpose.   But you learn quickly enough what is clickable and what isn't, so it's not like it prevents you from playing the game.  It's just a style I don't particularly care for in a game.  (Starbound had the same issue, though it featured low-rez pixel art.)
The trailer showed all kinds of nifty items, such as lasers, flying ships, etc.  But after seven hours of play, I had nothing to show for my time save the same standard progression of items that you find in these games.  I had yet to craft anything that was cool and exciting;  All I saw in my future was an ever-progressing grind.  Replacing my copper items with iron, and so on.  I'm sure I'd get flying laser ships eventually but the incentive isn't there for me to try, particularly when you die very far away from your spawn and must back-track quite a long way to recover your items -- Without even a marker to indicate where you died.  A lot of work for too little reward, IMHO.
Crafting is okay, and like that it's implemented via a list.  (Though it's annoying that you cannot mass open or close categories.)
I think this has signs of life (pun!) but for now I would recommend you wait.

I was originally somewhat skeptical of Signs of Life, as the trailer and screenshots I'd seen hinted at what I would probably call a "Baby's First Terraria".  After recently being disappointed with Darkout, I decided to give this one a shot.
The first thing I noticed was your AI companion and the giver of what amounts to the game's tutorial (unfinished as it is).  Namely, I noticed that I actually grunt-chuckled a bit at one or two of his lines, which is something I'm not used to experiencing...  I mean, sure, he's no comedic god, but how often is it where you honestly make some audible expulsion of breath when playing something by yourself?
...the second thing I noticed was just how helpless and left to your own devices you are in the beginning.  Not to say the game is particularly difficult, it really isn't...  But the learning curve for figuring out what you're supposed to do and how you're supposed to do it is quite a tricky slope.  It does somewhat help that AGIS is as snarky as he is, so those first flailing hours of trying to work out how to do and craft things really makes you feel like the self-destructive primitive fleshbag AGIS thinks you are.  Still, it really helps to be very patient with this game in the beginning...  It doesn't so much hold your hand as thrust it into a fire and then smack you for getting yourself burned.
Perservere through the liftoff phase, and you'll find an actually quite pretty, engaging environment with lovely lighting effects, a great deal of playstyle customization, and an atmosphere that manages to be irreverently tongue-in-cheek and yet still bizarrely creepy and tense at times.
The game is still quite unfinished however, the "tech tree" and progression of the game is hamhanded at its absolute best, and a confusing maze that turns in on itself at all other times.  It's frequently very difficult to find out "where do I go next?" or, worse, "what do I *DO*?".  As well, the game currently just sort of peters off as there's no real indication that you've accessed most or all the recipes and enemies it has to offer at this point.  But it will certainly give you plenty of hours of exploration and running like a coward before that time comes.
All in all, I would very much recommend this title.  It's different enough from Terraria to stand alone as its own game, similar enough to not be completely alien, and in my opinion actually does a few of the gameplay mechanics better than the genre's poster child.

A misunderstood game with a bumpy start, Arkham Origins is an often-maligned yet fun and gripping prequel to Arkham Asylum and Arkham City. Visually, the game is superb. Even on low settings, the snow-covered streets of Gotham are a sight to behold. The gameplay is smooth and responsive, and taking on rooms of thugs and mercenaries by yourself is still as fun as it first was back in 2009. You actually feel like Batman at certain moments in the game, and the side-quests (which involve tracking down and stopping crimes in progress and the schemes of minor villains) are fun distractions from the main story.
Multiplayer is finnicky, but it might appeal to some people. I would recommend the game for the singleplayer alone, as you're guaranteed to get a lot of time out of that. All-in-all, I would give this an 8.5 out of 10, docking points for the disappointing plot twist halfway through the game, user-unfriendly multiplayer, and occasional bugs that pop up in free roam.
Buy it on sale if you're hesitant about the game or new to the series. Only buy it full-price if you're a fan of the other Arkham games or a diehard Batman fan.

This is a great hitman,  I have found myself doing a lot of exploring in the first two levels. There are so many interesting ways to kill your target, and when you get used the wonky controls you can pull off some cool movie scene like hits. Some of the best kills are not even the environmental or opportunistic ones, for me it's smuggling in the sniper rifle to the best vantage point and dropping my victim like a sack of potatoes, then watching the pandimonium as the crowd goes nuts, then I walk right into the crowd and vanish. As with every game, however, there are some flaws to this excellent piece.
First let's look at the Positives:
+ Level design is superb, well detailed and very large. There are a multitude of ways to start off your mission... I'm not talking about the different starting points either, I'm talking just starting the level "vanilla". I entered the first real level in 5 different ways... some which were much easier than others, but it's fun to try difffernt approaches and the game encourages it.
+ They finally have it nailed as far as how NPCs react to you. Instead of instantly opening fire if you are in the wrong uniform, or seeing through walls etc. It took the enhancements the game has received since the first iteration and expanded on them tremendously. There was an annoying bit where I picked up a butcher knife while being a waiter and everyone freaked out and started trying to kill me which was sort of funy. While in my next try I picked up a a different big♥♥♥♥♥kitchen knife and walked around the entire mansion and nobody thought that odd. On the positive end, I shot someone in the head through a window and drape then hid quick and the entire map didn't immediately converge on my position which took a while to plan out. But the guards were more edgy obviously after this for what seemed like the rest of the level and were talking about it over their radios and alarms were going off while pedestrians were being evacuated etc.
+ Lots of AI reactions depending on your behavior throughout the level. The fact you can influence the behavior and reactions of others in a much more dynamic way makes this game seem a lot more "alive". I wish the Assassin's Creed games would blend their open worlds and badass fighting with sequences of actual stealthy assassinations.
+Speaking of NPCs, they aren't totally dumb anymore! No longer can you just wait at the end of a hallway and headshot them all as they come barreling down the hall of death... While admittedly that is a good stress reliever, I am ultimately happy at the enhanced AI.
+ Weapons feel great. Clobbering someone with a monkey wrench makes a flinch inducing sound.
+ Graphics are pretty nice, not the best, but definitely nice to look at. I have a mid range system and it runs with very few frame drops.
+ Lots of challenges and large level designs with multiple objectives means that each level has a lot of replayability, Add to that a slew of different contracts on the same level and this game certainly has a fair amount of content.
+ overall stealth mechanics feel a lot better.
The Negatives:
- Controls feel extremely awkward and non-intuitive. There are some redundant keys that could have been combined together. This makes it difficult to pull some cool combos smoothly without playing for a long time just to get the hang of the controls.
- Why the heck do I automatically switch to whatever I pick up?! It's quite frustrating. Just because I picked up rat poison doesn't mean I want it equipped.
- Wich brings us to inventory management... the inventory selection is outdated and not very well designed. Just do a rotary wheel.... hold a button, move to your selection, let go. This one is just annoying.
- This is the biggest one for me... the game has opened up a lot and gives you many new opportunities to carry out contracts, however, it has now pretty much limited you to a stealth approach... sometimes when♥♥♥♥♥♥goes south and you are up close, in previous games you fealt like you were a powerful fighter and could do some cool melee attacks which were actually effective, here if you get into a scuffle with two guards you pretty much have to be leathal because your punches seem to tickle the AI instead of doing any damage to them. I also did like the whole splinter cell mark targets and drop them in a cinematic way thing in Absolution... why take it out? I like to play the hit man games in two ways, one as the stealthy assassain and another as the James Bond ultimate killing badass. With the enhanced difficulty of the AI, this could have been a lot of fun!
- You can save which is great... I have enough self-control to try to run through the missions without a save , I like the fluidity of it, but I also like the save feature when doing my first few runs while I get to learn the level. Why not add a quicksave feature then?! That's just silly!
- No "difficulty" challenges. Comeon, anyone who has ever played ANY OTHER HITMAN game has done this. They start the mission really careful and stealthy, then there is one slip up, then you KILL EVERYONE on the level, then explore all the different ways to approach it and try it again. Now, chances are, you aren't going to kill everyone on the map anymore, direct firefights are difficult and have a Tom Clancy vibe to it where one well placed shot and your dead. I like that... but now that the game is more difficult to explore, I would hope for some challenges for playing without the see through walls mechanic, or for playing a level through in one go and not saving. I'm still going to do it just for my own challenge, but it takes away the goal of being the best and having a perfect runthrough.
- Objective markers. NO! That's not the Hitman way! I like the idea of overhearing a conversation, or reading a letter or something and piecing together an opportunity. I even like the fact that Dianna might give you more data on the opportunity. You aren't a cyborg though, and the HUD markers make it a bit too easy. Also you can see through walls... maybe you are actually a cyborg who knows what they did to 47 in that lab.
The Negatives we already know, but it still needs to be said:
- Episodic Release: Dumb. They missed out on someone who would have paid full price on release (me) as a big fan, but after waiting a while I was able to pick up the game half off and chock full of content.
- Always online connection. I've yet to run into an issue with it... but are you serious? C'mon. If this was Hitman: The Online Adventure sure, but thats a bit insane for a single player game, and I agree with the "up in arms" reaction to this. My buddy is deployed, and can't play the game he spent money on because he isn't connected to the internet. Didn't steam take care of most of the hackers/torrent people anyway? You have to account for that happening anyway, don't♥♥♥♥♥♥off your loyal customers because you have a few crooks out there.
Conclusion: MUST HAVE FOR FANS
This game is a must have if you are a fan of the series. Even with the GLARING flaws of needing a constant connection and the episodic release (which shouldn't be an influencing factor any more). It has improved AI, Graphics, Physics, and Immersion in every way from it's predecessors, though by changing things up they removed some of the nice gameplay elements from past iterations. The game's biggest hinderences come in the form of the User Interface, Controls, and required internet connection. If you are a fan of Stealth games in general, you will like this, but wait for a sale which wil prolly be this summer.

Rating with the online requirement and release sechedule: 6/10

I don't recommend this game unless you're a fan of the HITMAN (don't forget the tm!) series and are willing to look past the negatives below. That being said, the gameplay itself isn't terrible, the negativity mostly come from how the game is packaged and sold.
If you don't get what is so bad about always online, remember that not only do you need to be online--their servers do. The server routinely goes down for maintenance, scheduled and unscheduled, and when that happens you're forced to play in "offline mode". Also, there will eventually be a day when the server is taken offline for good and there's no garuntee you'll ever get to play the game again. You are not purchasing this game, you're buying temporary access to their server to play it.
When you can't connect to the server you can play in "offline mode" which is basically a different version of the game. You cannot unlock anything in offline mode and are forced to play the standard missions with the default loadout and starting locations. You will also have to replay all the missions again as progress made in online mode doesn't carry over.
Every once in a while an "Elusive Target" is added to the online game for a short period of time. During this time period, the elusive target has a chance of showing up in a mission and you will have one chance to assassinate them for unique bonus rewards. This sounds great but at the time of writing, 14 of these targets have been added and all 14 are no longer available. This means these unique bonus rewards are now unattainable because you didn't buy the game early enough. Sucks for you!
Each mission, called an episode, is released as its own DLC that you must purchase if you want to play it. Groups of missions are clumped together into "seasons" which you can purchase at a slightly reduced cost. However, each season must be purchased individually as they are released. Essentially you have to pay everytime an update is made to the game if you want to play it.
Because of the above issues, I can't recommend you buy this game. However, the gameplay itself is good if you can put up with the money milking the devs and publishers are doing.

My one complaint about the games overall is that there is a little too much going back and forth between the several locations that comprise each episode, trying to solve the main puzzle (or puzzles) in each location, in order to get something you'll need to go solve another location's puzzles. When you get stuck, you do a lot of visiting each of the locations, looking for the one thing you missed that will let you proceed.

Still love Sam and Max and their priceless adventures, that and also just like Season one can't get enough of these two. Orh how much the games brought out my point and click love that was hidden for a long bit since of... Sometimes you miss the good ol' days. :3

Sam & Max Season Two is made of five episodes and continues insane adventure of Sam and Max in this point'n'click "old-school" adventure game. "Old-school" stands for "has nonsense puzzles".
It didn't make any big change to the series formula, still having same system. You will notice it in the graphics the most, as they are on same technical level, which would start to feel outdated in 2008. Then again, Season One was kinda outdated too. But hey, it still looks nice artistically.
Positive thing that was added was hints system. You can choose how frequent you want to have main character throw hints at you, from none to often. They come from subtle to insultingly direct. Max may say to go somewhere else, he may hint you "remember how we did it the last time" or Sam may exclaim "Ah, I get it, it's <something that directly solves the puzzle>".
It's still helpful to have them as rare.
And well, the first half of season isn't exactly amazing. It's original, yet something you kinda expect from comedical adventure games, while it also has adventure games sin: mini-games! Thanfully, they are easy and nice. Most hate cheap'n'hard minigames in such games after all.
Then as the second half of season comes, it completely throws mini-games away and focuses on much more exciting setting. No spoilers, but you will get some fun things to do. Wink wink, time.
And episodes felt a bit longer than expected too.
So, if you nejoyed Season One, it will be worth it. And worth it for others too. Almost. Puzzles are still stupid at times. Not as stupid as some "classics" though, it's still weird at times. And not always hinted. Well, aside from straight hints from main characters.

I have been with this franchise since the very beginning and own all of the games (except the 4th just never bought it) and I have to say that this was one of my favorites.
I have seen many playthroughs of this game and even played it myself and it gave me all that I hoped for. I love that in this game we get to look past our normal Fazbear  friends and see some new faces as well as hear about more characters. This game is easier to play, but gives you a different experience. Unlike the other games you don't just sit in a room and look at cameras until 6 AM or check doors and lights. Another thing about the gameplay is that it locks together more aspects than the other games. This game focuses more on the follow the leader, listening, and patience aspects in each "minigame".

The best puzzle/hidden object game you can get for 1,24€ - I bought it on sale, just to make things clear - and this is coming from a person who utterly despises the hidden object concept.
Everything about this game oozes charm and uniqueness. The world is beautifully drawn, the music will help you relax after a long and difficult day, while the puzzles are not very difficult to solve. There are a few puzzles that might get you stuck, but there's no shame in checking the Internet for walkthroughs when it comes to this game.
As for finding the hidden objects/puzzle pieces - as with every other game in the genre, some are instantly detectable, while others blend with the game background, so you will have to do the occasional click-all-over-the-screen thing. Even though I hate this element in games, The Tiny Bang Story is an exception - its atmosphere, music and style kept me going.
The hint system in this game is interesting - Other than showing you what you're supposed to do with the puzzles through illustrations, you can use it ONCE after you get enough mosquitoes and it will reveal the location of a puzzle piece you're supposed to collect. Then, it's getting mosquitoes all over again.
Unfortunately, once you finish The Tiny Bang Story, there's no replay value whatsoever. Still, I thoroughly enjoyed the 4.7 hours I spent playing it and recommend it to every gamer out there.

EQ2 is one of those old MMOs that have stood around and other games have copied bits and pieces from. As one of the originals, there's something to be said for putting effort into it. Sortof how you would feel playing an old playstation one game that had a good story or you felt some nostalgia about. You won't get the same hardcore base as you have with WoW and FFXIV, but it is good to have an MMO that is rather laid back. Not paying means you aren't obligated to play every day, you can go at your own pace.
That said, it could be considered too laid back for some people. Alot of group content and no working in game group finder tool can make most playtime solo, or duo if you grab a friend. There's npcs you can hire for in game gold that do decently well too. So you can take on most things by yourself if you have enough gusto to quest around. This game is called everQUEST for a reason, there will forever be quests for you to do. Not just daily ones, but class and profession ones as well. Even as you level there are quests that bring you back to older content to run a dungeon or somesuch and get a sizable reward.
The downside to this game is that there isn't really much presence of a fanmade guide to things, and there are so many things to do that keeping track of them all can be really tiresome and just about impossible. There are some old sites around that explain events and tell you where to go, but support has been dropped with the new developer buyout. Of course some things that come with it being old, the player models arent impressive nor is the armor.
The upside to this game though, again, you don't need to pay for things. There is player and guild housing, as well as items you can loot from in game objects in dungeons and put on display. Taking the heads of raid bosses and mounting them in your guild hall, making it into a small city. There are plenty of expansions to explore, and there is as much crafting as there is slashing. Crafting everything from ability improvements to house decorations, seasonal ones as well.
All in all, the game has alot to offer but takes time to show it. There still is a devout player base around, just have to look.

TL;DR: SoL is one of the best Sandbox games out there if you are willing to put the time into it, and I can not recommend it more if you are into that genre.
-----
Signs of Life is a breath of fresh air (for me, at least) in the survival-sandbox genre. Most games in said genre tend to visually resemble eachother, or play identically (i.e. make a crafting table, then furnace, etc...).
SoL manages to differentiate itself from the lot, mostly thanks to it's (although minor) storyline and lore.
Sure, it has pickaxes, mining, 2D voxel worlds and the likes, but it offers much more than the run-of-the-mill sandbox game.
Having played for a good couple of hours now, I've made it to the point where I've acquired the Level 2 Access Card, and have explored the 4 structures that I've found (I'm certain there are more that I've yet to discover), and am starting to get a nice collection of gadgets, and technologically advanced items.
However, at multiple points during my current playthrough, I started getting afraid that I might have gone through all of the content, due to the fact that I had no new recipes that seemed interesting, nor could find anything of interest that I had access to either. Though, I will admit that when I 'did' discover new recipes and the likes, I couldn't help but pull a massive smile, knowing that my playthrough wouldn't be done anytime soon.
In it's current state, the game has huge amounts of content (most of which I haven't even discovered yet), and quite a bit of potential. I'm hoping that the content shown on the trailer will be soon added -if not already-, as I'd love to find larger bases, ruins, and more content to explore.
SoL is by far one of my favourite games in the sandbox genre, and could easily compete with, or even surpass games like Edge of Space, Starbound or Terraria, if enough work is put into it in the coming months of it's development.

Batman: Arkham Origins is definitely the most hated of the Arkham series (not that that's saying much, considering the other 2 are considered amazing), so frankly when I picked this up and saw it had already dropped to $20 in the course of a few months...I was prepared for an awful game that tainted the Arkham series.
I'm happy to say, I was wrong. Fans of the series will notice a distinct lack of innovation in Arkham Origins, but at the same time, it's not like WB Games Montreal "ruined" any of the mechanics. Plus the game does take quite a few steps forward, all though to varying degrees of success.
The best way I can describe it is, while Arkham City and Asylum were both revolutionary in many areas, Arkham Origins just evolves their formula slightly.
Running the game on a GTX 660, everything maxed out (including PhysX) and FXAA High enabled, I was getting a stable 60fps and above for most of the game. A few areas and fights (especially one fight with Bane on a rooftop) I noticed some drops but nothing too bad.  The FoV is just fine, really nothing to complain about. Runs solid and looks solid. My only issues would have to be the stuttering when you first boot up the game as Unreal 3 loads in the rest of the world, and the sudden changes to pre-rendered footage at times.
The game maintains that dark Arkham feeling, as the snow comes down on Gotham on Christmas Eve. It looks great, in a gloomy kinda way. The Nvidia effects in the game are really nice looking, smoke moves out of your way as you pass by, paper and money flies around in fights, and Batman himself looks really well detailed. It's quite impressive for an Unreal 3 game, but it's still obvious this is Unreal 3 and that engine is aging. Textures will pop in at close distances and that can look pretty bad at times. Also, there are some odd animations when characters talk in game, especially Alfred. Hard to explain, but it just looks...wrong.   However, I have to say I believe this is probably the best looking Unreal 3 game to date. And with Arkham Knight being made in Unreal 4, I think this IS the best looking Unreal 3 game we'll get.
Wow...the story in this game is actually really good! After the rather strange ending to Arkham Asylum, and cluttered mess of a story that happened in Arkham City (not saying I didn't like them, but their stories weren't exactly the selling point of the game) I didn't expect much from this game. Especially when I heard Mark Hamill and Kevin Conroy would not be making an appearance as the Joker and Batman in this game, unlike in Arkham City and Asylum. However, to my surprise both actors that replaced them do a great job, especially Troy Baker's Joker. The story manages to be just as chaotic as Arkham City, while having a central goal: Track down the assassins. And it's delivered very well. The game is more of a origin story for Joker and Batman's relationship though, instead of Batman himself. And it's quite neat to see the first time Batman and Joker have that "connection", where they realize they were in some odd way, meant to meet. I have to say, I was very impressed with this story, and there were some truly emotional moments in it. All though it is pretty predictable at times, there are still a good chunk of twists that keep the story moving at a good pace. Also, I really enjoy how tough and angry this Batman is compared to the more experienced and calm Arkham City and Asylum Batman. Arkham Origin's Batman is the type of guy that leaves some criminal hanging on top of a building, then comes back to the guy in a police station, just to beat him up again.
Batman: Arkham City 2.0 basically. There are some neat additions, such as the ability to use your zipline to attach enemies to each other, or throw fire extinguishers at them. However, other than that gameplay is identical. They did add in a more advanced crime scene investigation detective mode, but it's only used maybe 3-4 times total, and most of the time you're just looking for the red arrow instead of actually figuring out what happened yourself. This mechanic is pretty awesome in the Deadshot side mission, but since at E3 2013 they showed it off already, it kinda spoiled the whole expereince of that side mission.
Part of Gotham City, the bat cave, and Black Gate prison are the locations the game takes place in, all on Christmas eve. The world feels VERY similar to Arkham City. The northern part of the map (or Old Gotham) is basically straight out of Arkham City, Wonder Tower is even in the center of it. That doesn't change the fact the setting works really well for the game, it's just a bit of a shame to not see them try to expand Gotham besides adding in an absurdly long bridge and a little bit of land in the south. Plus, citizens are just no where to be seen. There is a curfew going on which could explain it I guess, but it just makes the world feel lifeless.
Just making this a category from now on in my reviews. So the music is great, it keeps with the whole dark and heavy tone the Christopher Nolan Batman movies soundtracks have. Also, whoever decided to have that remix of "Carol of the Bells" as the Joker's main theme...kudos to you.

It's a good time, don't get me wrong. I'd definitely recommend picking it up in the upcoming Fall sale. Also, anybody see the new Arkham Knight footage? HOLY CRAP! 2015 just can't get here fast enough.

There are parts in Arkham Origins - which were advertised heavily before the game came out, so no spoilers here - where you can "be an actual detective" and "recreate a crime scene" that you can play back and rewind at your own leisure to find the answers to what exactly happened at the scene. They're flashy and feature impressive scripted sequences, but really just amount to being pixel hunts. They're kind of representative of AO as a whole.
People praise AO for its writing a lot, and I'm not really sure why. If I had to guess, it's probably because AA and AC were the trademark kinds of turds produced by Paul Dini post-2000, and because of its really, really flashy setpieces. Batman falls from a skyscraper punching the Joker, with the most impresive graphics the franchise has ever seen, which looks great - but winds up being the beginning of the game completely abandoning its "EIGHT ASSASSINS! ONE NIGHT! PAY FOR YOUR SEAT BUT YOU'LL ONLY NEED THE EDGE EDGE EDGE" hook before it could even be a third of the way finished.
It's downright impressive how many things this game ripped off from previous Arkham games. A surprise section where you play as a different character was console-exclusive bonus content for another Arkham game, animations copy-pasted and all. Shock gloves (which instantly trivialize any and all combat) are just the super mode from the Wii U version of Arkham City. Mad Hatter is here, for some Goddamn reason, and he's got yet another hallucinogenic trip to send Batman on. Etcetera.
When the gameplay isn't stolen, it just doesn't work. There's still bugs with the Concussion Detonator (which is basically worse than AC's REC in every way) breaking combo constantly, due to the delayed nature of its explosion. Batman will occasionally just outright fail to counter enemies, and a lot of animations that were cancelable in AC aren't in AO. The island is the most lazy expansion I've seen on a previous open world, with areas broken up into segments that are broken off by either a hilariously long bridge where nothing happens, or massive buildings that you inexplicably cannot grapple or climb. Martial arts enemies don't add variety as much as they add busywork, and the bosses are a huge step back from even AC's basic Zelda-esque bosses.
It's probably the prettiest game in my Steam account, though, and the challenge rooms are still a great time. It's worth $7.50 if you REALLY love the Arkham games, but it's the weakest entry so far, and you'd be totally fine by just replaying City's challenge rooms and waiting for Knight to hit instead.

This is a great hitman,  I have found myself doing a lot of exploring in the first two levels. There are so many interesting ways to kill your target, and when you get used the wonky controls you can pull off some cool movie scene like hits. Some of the best kills are not even the environmental or opportunistic ones, for me it's smuggling in the sniper rifle to the best vantage point and dropping my victim like a sack of potatoes, then watching the pandimonium as the crowd goes nuts, then I walk right into the crowd and vanish. As with every game, however, there are some flaws to this excellent piece.
First let's look at the Positives:
+ Level design is superb, well detailed and very large. There are a multitude of ways to start off your mission... I'm not talking about the different starting points either, I'm talking just starting the level "vanilla". I entered the first real level in 5 different ways... some which were much easier than others, but it's fun to try difffernt approaches and the game encourages it.
+ They finally have it nailed as far as how NPCs react to you. Instead of instantly opening fire if you are in the wrong uniform, or seeing through walls etc. It took the enhancements the game has received since the first iteration and expanded on them tremendously. There was an annoying bit where I picked up a butcher knife while being a waiter and everyone freaked out and started trying to kill me which was sort of funy. While in my next try I picked up a a different big♥♥♥♥♥kitchen knife and walked around the entire mansion and nobody thought that odd. On the positive end, I shot someone in the head through a window and drape then hid quick and the entire map didn't immediately converge on my position which took a while to plan out. But the guards were more edgy obviously after this for what seemed like the rest of the level and were talking about it over their radios and alarms were going off while pedestrians were being evacuated etc.
+ Lots of AI reactions depending on your behavior throughout the level. The fact you can influence the behavior and reactions of others in a much more dynamic way makes this game seem a lot more "alive". I wish the Assassin's Creed games would blend their open worlds and badass fighting with sequences of actual stealthy assassinations.
+Speaking of NPCs, they aren't totally dumb anymore! No longer can you just wait at the end of a hallway and headshot them all as they come barreling down the hall of death... While admittedly that is a good stress reliever, I am ultimately happy at the enhanced AI.
+ Weapons feel great. Clobbering someone with a monkey wrench makes a flinch inducing sound.
+ Graphics are pretty nice, not the best, but definitely nice to look at. I have a mid range system and it runs with very few frame drops.
+ Lots of challenges and large level designs with multiple objectives means that each level has a lot of replayability, Add to that a slew of different contracts on the same level and this game certainly has a fair amount of content.
+ overall stealth mechanics feel a lot better.
The Negatives:
- Controls feel extremely awkward and non-intuitive. There are some redundant keys that could have been combined together. This makes it difficult to pull some cool combos smoothly without playing for a long time just to get the hang of the controls.
- Why the heck do I automatically switch to whatever I pick up?! It's quite frustrating. Just because I picked up rat poison doesn't mean I want it equipped.
- Wich brings us to inventory management... the inventory selection is outdated and not very well designed. Just do a rotary wheel.... hold a button, move to your selection, let go. This one is just annoying.
- This is the biggest one for me... the game has opened up a lot and gives you many new opportunities to carry out contracts, however, it has now pretty much limited you to a stealth approach... sometimes when♥♥♥♥♥♥goes south and you are up close, in previous games you fealt like you were a powerful fighter and could do some cool melee attacks which were actually effective, here if you get into a scuffle with two guards you pretty much have to be leathal because your punches seem to tickle the AI instead of doing any damage to them. I also did like the whole splinter cell mark targets and drop them in a cinematic way thing in Absolution... why take it out? I like to play the hit man games in two ways, one as the stealthy assassain and another as the James Bond ultimate killing badass. With the enhanced difficulty of the AI, this could have been a lot of fun!
- You can save which is great... I have enough self-control to try to run through the missions without a save , I like the fluidity of it, but I also like the save feature when doing my first few runs while I get to learn the level. Why not add a quicksave feature then?! That's just silly!
- No "difficulty" challenges. Comeon, anyone who has ever played ANY OTHER HITMAN game has done this. They start the mission really careful and stealthy, then there is one slip up, then you KILL EVERYONE on the level, then explore all the different ways to approach it and try it again. Now, chances are, you aren't going to kill everyone on the map anymore, direct firefights are difficult and have a Tom Clancy vibe to it where one well placed shot and your dead. I like that... but now that the game is more difficult to explore, I would hope for some challenges for playing without the see through walls mechanic, or for playing a level through in one go and not saving. I'm still going to do it just for my own challenge, but it takes away the goal of being the best and having a perfect runthrough.
- Objective markers. NO! That's not the Hitman way! I like the idea of overhearing a conversation, or reading a letter or something and piecing together an opportunity. I even like the fact that Dianna might give you more data on the opportunity. You aren't a cyborg though, and the HUD markers make it a bit too easy. Also you can see through walls... maybe you are actually a cyborg who knows what they did to 47 in that lab.
The Negatives we already know, but it still needs to be said:
- Episodic Release: Dumb. They missed out on someone who would have paid full price on release (me) as a big fan, but after waiting a while I was able to pick up the game half off and chock full of content.
- Always online connection. I've yet to run into an issue with it... but are you serious? C'mon. If this was Hitman: The Online Adventure sure, but thats a bit insane for a single player game, and I agree with the "up in arms" reaction to this. My buddy is deployed, and can't play the game he spent money on because he isn't connected to the internet. Didn't steam take care of most of the hackers/torrent people anyway? You have to account for that happening anyway, don't♥♥♥♥♥♥off your loyal customers because you have a few crooks out there.
Conclusion: MUST HAVE FOR FANS
This game is a must have if you are a fan of the series. Even with the GLARING flaws of needing a constant connection and the episodic release (which shouldn't be an influencing factor any more). It has improved AI, Graphics, Physics, and Immersion in every way from it's predecessors, though by changing things up they removed some of the nice gameplay elements from past iterations. The game's biggest hinderences come in the form of the User Interface, Controls, and required internet connection. If you are a fan of Stealth games in general, you will like this, but wait for a sale which wil prolly be this summer.

I don't recommend this game unless you're a fan of the HITMAN (don't forget the tm!) series and are willing to look past the negatives below. That being said, the gameplay itself isn't terrible, the negativity mostly come from how the game is packaged and sold.
If you don't get what is so bad about always online, remember that not only do you need to be online--their servers do. The server routinely goes down for maintenance, scheduled and unscheduled, and when that happens you're forced to play in "offline mode". Also, there will eventually be a day when the server is taken offline for good and there's no garuntee you'll ever get to play the game again. You are not purchasing this game, you're buying temporary access to their server to play it.
When you can't connect to the server you can play in "offline mode" which is basically a different version of the game. You cannot unlock anything in offline mode and are forced to play the standard missions with the default loadout and starting locations. You will also have to replay all the missions again as progress made in online mode doesn't carry over.
Every once in a while an "Elusive Target" is added to the online game for a short period of time. During this time period, the elusive target has a chance of showing up in a mission and you will have one chance to assassinate them for unique bonus rewards. This sounds great but at the time of writing, 14 of these targets have been added and all 14 are no longer available. This means these unique bonus rewards are now unattainable because you didn't buy the game early enough. Sucks for you!
Each mission, called an episode, is released as its own DLC that you must purchase if you want to play it. Groups of missions are clumped together into "seasons" which you can purchase at a slightly reduced cost. However, each season must be purchased individually as they are released. Essentially you have to pay everytime an update is made to the game if you want to play it.
Because of the above issues, I can't recommend you buy this game. However, the gameplay itself is good if you can put up with the money milking the devs and publishers are doing.

Here's the bottom line, Hitman puts you on a nice honeymoon period and then drops you flat on your face.

I was blind to this at first because I turned off any "help" the game offers you, but it dawned on me after 8 hours of playing the game. After turning on the "help" I saw how A+B=C this game was.
So now I beg the question: Why is it so hard to make a game that is truly a sandbox?

TBS is a delicate adventure that combines hidden object games with puzzle-solving. On starting each chapter you're shown a beautifully hand-drawn environment that usually requires finding a number of objects. As you click on these objects they are collected and stored. Before long you'll realise to progress, and see another funny/peculiar screen, you have to dig around. The goal of each chapter is usually to find an ultimate component that sets some sort of mechanism in motion. Puzzles and games were perfectly-pitched being neither too easy nor too hard and the well-designed environments always made the experience a fun an enjoyable one.There is a very good hint system - where you fill up the question mark meter by clicking on the buzzing flies - but I still had to resort to a couple of visits to YouTube. However, these occurrences were few and didn't ruin immersion.
TBS is not only a very well-presented production but an inventive one as well. The hand-drawn environments are like those beautiful picture books you stared at and found so intriguing when you were a child. Massive attention to detail has been made in the artwork department and the sound also suits the visual tone harmoniously. A delicate, melodic piece is heard as you play; subtle enough to be enjoyed but not intrusive enough to put you off. Sound effects are spot-on as well. The game consists of about five or six chapters that might take about an hour each to complete. At the end of each chapter you get to fill in daytime pieces of a globe that cleverly shows your progression. It's a good system as it divides the game into five or six parts and, like a book, allows you to take a break at convenient points.
There are text-heavy adventure games that require you to wade through mountains of dialogue and then there are breezier adventure games with the emphasis on actually playing a game! The Tiny Bang Story may not be for everyone as it will certainly make you stop to think and may even bring in mild frustration as you search maddeningly for that last elusive piece but, for me, I put it at one of my personal favourite adventure games.

This is a hidden object/puzzle/minigame game all in one. While those terms tend to reflectlow quality, this ones hand drawn beautifully painted scenes serve to make the world interesting to witness.
The puzzles are quite enjoyable, and the game's polish makes it something I come back to again and again.  Honestly I wish more "hidden object" games would take this as a lesson to do more with the seemingly simple genre.

Locating various recurring objects is required to access locked areas or repair machines. You can't collect these series until they're explicitly needed. Each chapter is reasonably sized so backtracking through scenes is simple enough. You can usually tell in advance when certain objects will be required eventually upon spotting their multiplicity.
Delightfully detailed backgrounds with a lovely surreal Eastern European vibe can be favorably compared to some of Amanita Design's excellent games, more specifically
.
Accessible UI keeps track of the items you've collected and how many more you need, with a reminder of where they'll be useful once you have a completed set. Acquire conventional puzzle pieces throughout each of the 5 chapters to put the world map back together. Most of them blend quite well with the environment.
Puzzles range from a variety of simple jigsaws to fine variations on common logic puzzles. You will put a lot of things back together. There's nothing truly revolutionary here but everything is well presented and only a few puzzles are really difficult. Hints are available on demand but they sometimes directly reveal the answer or are not helpful at all.
It turns out to be a very relaxing and pleasant experience, except for arcade sequences that feel out of place and defiantly ruin the mood with their needlessly poor controls. Thankfully they are short and few.
I initially gave this game a negative score because it constantly presented a blank screen and subsequent exit to desktop, without any way to fix it despite clean reinstalls.
The game did run fine on my secondary work laptop, but I never attempted the full screen option for fear of locking myself out of a potentially good game. You too may be forced to play on a tiny window since the game runs in a very low resolution on today's HD monitors.

A nice, if unspectacular point and click, hidden object game. Throughout five chapters, each made up of about four screens filled with things to interact with, you'll click on various people or mechanisms to initiate quests to find some hidden items they require. Once found and brought back, it will typically trigger a mini puzzle of some kind and give you another item upon completion that'll help you progress further. That's basically the long and short of it.
There is some kind of story about a meteor hitting "Tiny Planet" and scattering the world apart in the form of jigsaw pieces which are hidden all over the place, but it's largely inconsequential and serves only to back up a puzzle mechanic and explain how you access each chapter in turn (even though the jigsaw pieces aren't actually necessary to move on). There also seems to be a recurring character that appears in paintings and photographs showing him at different stages as he grows up, but the significance of this is never explained. Presumably we're retracing his steps in places that either he had an impact on, or which had an impact on him. It's hard to tell, and to be perfectly honest, even harder to care, since this is never expanded upon in any meaningful way or as any clear goal for the player.
Most of the puzzles and hidden objects are pretty fun and fair deals, but occasionally there's the odd obscure one that will have you either losing all faith in humanity, or else looking up a guide. I'm also really not a fan of them messing with the scale of the hidden objects, like having large jigsaw pieces in one place, then other, much small ones in other places yet still at the same distance away from the camera perspective. More consistancy of scale with the objects would be appreciated.
You'll have a fun, if not somewhat forgettable, two or so hours with the game, and have the option to replay any puzzle when you reach the end... which is possibly the most anti-climactic end I've ever experienced in a game. But I'd still recommend it for anyone looking for a quick break through a visually pretty world with some fun and engaging puzzles.

- You can do the above two points with friends
- Some scope to change the skins of assets/models
Negatives:

I looked around the google sphere to find out why I couldn't customise my avatar, or if there was a way to change it (even if I had to create and pay for a private server) and I came across this article (link below) with reasons stated by the devs for the lack of character/avatar customisation.
To me, the developers reasons make no sense to me. If a certain player was to grief other players, generally being a nuisance, exploiting a game glitch, trigger botting etc, this is the territory of the ubiquitous "report player" ticket which invariably in some games lead to admin bans or the vaunted "VAC ban".
TLDR; Rust is what it is what it is and as a result of lack of character/avatar customisation, I recommend the following two options:
1) if you don't care/it doesn't bother you that a game chooses your character for you, in-game players ridiculing you over a player avatar you had no choice in making, getting ganked within 5 minutes of joining a server and you enjoy the survival game genre; then this game is for you.
2) if character customisation is a lynch pin of keeping you immersed and enjoying a game, then steer clear of this one.
