Now, I'm a decently sized Hitfan, and this might not just be my favourite game of 2016,
but my fav Hitman game? Which is dangerously high praise, I know, considering Blood Money is
and 2016 has been a excellent year for games.
It's just a legitimately amazing game! Occasionally astonishing in its breadth & depth:
Both in bespoke scripted events and dynamic systems, and in its gorgeous, lovingly crafted environments. Though a lot of it would be moot if the core gameplay was not as solid and uproariously enjoyable as it is.
IO has succeeded in crafting a delicious murder sandbox: a variety of tools and weapons, dynamic AI and various systems that you can experiment and play with,
leading to spontaneous fun and emergent gameplay. This allows you the freedom be the perfect ghost that does not leave a trace, or a sort of bumbling, homocidial Mr. Bean.
Listen, the game rocks. If you have any interest in stealth-action sandbox-goodness, HITMAN is your jam!
The game continues to be
, and IO has done a fantastic job maintaining it. The new Patient Zero & GOTY Ed.-additions are short but sweet, and has some fun variations on the standard gameplay. (I quite enjoy how one of the Patient Zero missions is, straight up, a new Hitman Sniper Challenge level)

It's Blood Money with a bunch of user generated content. Nuff said.

In more detail, Hitman (tm) is a return to form after the disappointing Absolution. It's classic Hitman, with the costumes, tools and accidents that have made it stand out as the best assassination simulator that the games industry has to offer. The set-peices, while few in number are beautiful and detailed and are filled with myriad means to eliminate targets.

While the story targets have the more entertaining means of assassination that can be found by listening in on conversations and nabbing certain items which reveal 'opportunities', the game allows users to create contracts on any NPC within each of the levels. These are definitely the more difficult, as fellow players are far more demanding than the developers. The contract's creator can add additional requirements which are necessary to successfully complete the contract. How are you going to kill that security guard, sat in a room with three other security guards, unseen and unheard? And how are you going to do so without the body being discovered? And all while never changing from 47's iconic suit? And using an explosive duck as the murder weapon?
Not that the developers have stinted on content themselves. They have included a wealth of challenges for each of the story missions and locales, which when completed add to your mastery of that level. Gaining higher mastery with unlock additional mission starting points, weapon drop-points and disguises for that locale, or unlock new assassin tools which can be used in any destination. These challenges encourage the player to tackle assassination in a number of different ways and help showcase the versatility of their sandbox for players wishing to create their own contracts. The game also has 'Elusive Targets' which are contracts made by the developer that only last for a limited time and feature new special NPCs with their own behavior patterns. Failure in these contracts are permanent and is included in your player record, making them tense, high stakes affairs. Unfortunately new players are unable to access past Elusive Targets, so will find their assassin resume filled with lots of 'MISSED' in big red letters. This however, only adds to the prestige and challenge of completing these contracts successfully.
All-in-all, an impressive stealth assassination game with plenty of content, whose only real downside is the need to constantly be online while being played, despite the lack of multiplayer. Unless you have frequent loss of internet, that is a small price to pay for a game of this quality.

With time I've mellowed to the game so I now recommend it. My pros and cons still apply though.
Pros.
- Does not follow the trend of absolution
- The gameplay is great

- The graphics and visual feedback is good

Cons.

- Also when you jump down/climb (more like step down/up) the tiniest ledge everyone will instantly scream "DON'T CLIMB AROUND!" and 5 second later "WHAT IS IT WITH THIS GUY" another five "YOU DON'T LOOK LIKE A GARDENER!" and then they shoot you/call guards.
- Too short with only 6 missions + 2 prologue & 2 small bonus missions.
- Always online, I have good internet but that's beside the point. Also at the time of this review the servers is undergoing maintenance. ON A SINGLEPLAYER GAME!!!
- The textures load at a dreadful speed.
- All the gimmicks with the escalation missions "Kill this random npc, now this guy too, now do it with an axe dressed as vampire". And note this takes up ~80% of the "content" this game has to offer.
- The gimmick that is elusive targets with its "oh boy it's so real, you only have one chance during these 50 hours or the target is gone forever" This is plainly good content wasted, this is what the secondary missions you should have had instead of escalation where you kill generic npc #1725. - The grinding you have to do to unlock better equipment on missions and by that time you've probably done everything already twice.
- The season 1 campaign end with a CLIFFHANGER! Are you serious?
So to conclude, at 50% off; at 25€ it is worth it. At full price? I doubt any of the problems I have with the game will go away aside from maybe the texture problem (fingers crossed) so it's not gonna get any better.

I was very excited to come back to EQ2.  I was there pre-launch when we all lived on the forums speculating and planning our new guilds and played for a couple of years everyday until my first kid was born; I was amongst the first group to betray from evil to good (back when it was a long involved quest) I think I was the very first Ogre to do so.
I was even there when Sony made the pvp release announcements, deleted every thread and post they'd ever made saying they would only concentrate on pve in order to make it the best it ever could be, then flat out called everyone who protested a liar - challenging them to find the now deleted posts.
So, after a good few years away I come back and to be honest I was underwhelmed.  I still had my old toons (not that I could access them all), still had my fancy house filled with many objects, decorations and pets, some of which are probably pretty rare now.  But as I walked around, revisiting the places where I fought for days on end for tier 1 nodes and generally having a nostalgia trip, I just felt that it had changed too much for the negative.
I can't quite put my finger on it, I revisited EQ1 too and was grinning to myself the whole time wielding my now collectible Sceptre of Destruction, so it's not because it's dated.  I don't know what it is, but there's nothing exciting there for me as a returning player.  It seemed too easy and linear now maybe?
So why the positve review?  I can see that if you give this game a chance, pay to play and find a good guild, you could well find it a brilliant alternative to WoW.  Generally there's fewer idiots, fewer overly serious manchildren and a better community in general.  'Go back to WoW' was an oft heard slur aimed at those that whined about difficulty in the early days and rightly so.  EQ2 is a bit grittier and less cartoony.
It should have beaten WoW as the number 1, of that I'm sure.  Lack of advertising hurt it, even finding somewhere that sold the discs could be a challenge, so it was never to be.  But this is the better game.
I never got in to high end raiding on EQ, EQ2 or WoW, so I can't comment on which is best for the serious guys.  But for the rest of the people, the ones that just want to play, EQ2 is recommended.
Just don't expect the same level of teary eyed joy as you get from EQ1 if you're a returning visitor to both.

To summarise my major emotion about TTBS: it's frustrating.
The game has a sharp, yet storybook-like art style, catchy (though quickly monotonous) music, and a hidden object/puzzle/adventure gameplay. I love all of these features, then what went wrong?
The game basically doesn't contain any written or spoken text, and any hints it gives about objectives or solutions are extremely sparse and unhelpful. Thus a significant portion of my playtime was spent wandering around the same handful of screens, trying to figure out
.
Once you
figure it out, the rest of the time is spent either hunting minute objects that you've passed many times before, but only become collectable when the game decides to do so, or doing one of the quite difficult puzzles (without a skip function and barely a single hint! annoying!) or one of the timed minigames (which really don't fit to the otherwise quite laidback gameplay).
To acquire any kind of help from the game, you have to collect 30 little floating bugs for each use of the hint button, and even then it only showed a hint to me on puzzle screens, not when I spent ages looking for the last few tiny objects in the general game screens.
Despite the art style being pleasant, the game seems to have quite a confusion on what visual theme it wants to pursue - the end result is a haphazard mix of fairytale, steampunk-ish and retro-futuristic elements.
Another noticeable thing for me was the lack of "player character". There's no body through which a player acts, feeling like I was some invisible disembodied force which still needed lifts and ladders to get to various places, resulting in the weird, empty feeling of both being there and not being there. It was probably one of the reasons why I didn't connect emotionally with the game at all - it felt like a soulless exercise of cookie-cutter charm.
Through my playtime the game felt more and more like a chore that I just wanted to be over and done with - then I remembered that games are supposed to be fun, and just dropped it altogether. A disappointment!
PS: I recommend to either use a walkthrough, or go play a game with actual charm, character and way less frustrating gameplay, like Botanicula or Samorost.

A city full of sand. A few very angry Americans, and a few things that don't seem right.
I had orignally wrote up a 6000+ characters review about this... That obviously wasn't gonna fit, I trimmed it as best I could but it still wouldn't work out. Instead, I've opted for the only reasonable course of action I can think of. A very simple and small review.
This is based solely on the campaign, I did not play Multiplayer nor Co-op.
It's an action shooter game that plays in the veil of Rainbow Six: Vegas.
It's based in the city of Dubai, which is full of sand and angry people.
The gameplay is very straight foward and basic, reminiscent of common Western shooters - You have two guns, duck and cover gameplay, and you gotta wipe jam off your face constantly. You command two other teammates who can take minor actions that you wish. Most of the time it's all on you.
Dubai itself is cool, very apocalyptic.
But onto the story, which seems to be what everyone was talking about.
I myself was told by friends and others alike that this game was simply, 2deep4them.
While most of the original review was all about the story, I figured it really wasn't focusing on what a review should be about. I'm to talk about the gameplay and it's other aspects, and how I felt along with it.
So I'll just give crib notes and my reactions (all completely spoilers):
Onto my reaction of it - I wasn't satisfied with any of it. I like what Spec Ops tries to attempt, but everything you've done now has just been invalidated and is pointless,
So you just ask yourself why you wasted all this time on it.
And I'll just give this one piece right here,
If you want something of similar gameplay, go play Rainbow Six: Vegas - If you want something of a different, but relatable story, I dunno, go play MGS or something.
tl;dr - It's a common action shooter, with a tries-to-be deeper than normal story. You'll like it if it's your first. But not if it's your second or more.

Rust will never be forgotten, and it will never be at peace. I told myself I would wait to do this review, that I would let it settle, that it would one day be finished and then I could write my thoughts. Well, too much time has passed for me to wait any longer, and for some reason, today seems to be the day.
I'm not even sure now how I discovered this, "new game with a cool idea". A friend, DayZ-exploring, a flashing Steam store page, who knows. But once I installed it, and loaded it up, I had found a new, exciting video game. The music when loading was incredible, eerie and atmospheric; and this was 'alpha' music? Once I loaded into the world, an island of apparently great size, I enjoyed the experience from the start. Nature, trees, vast distances, animals, ruins, and...people.
For that is what makes Rust tick, people. The first moment, not knowing whether to hide, fight, or try to communicate, is telling, and this is a common thread. And with these first moments, come the first deaths, both expected and not. And so comes the first rule of Rust, don't trust anyone. And with this rule comes the choice you have to make, do you strive to live a solo life? Do you have Steam friends that play and can band together? Or do you try to find some team to take you in? Be ready, you are going to die, a lot.
I made a shelter, and built, and harvested, and hunted. I ventured into dangerous places and survived. Or died. In the end, it was a great experience. Then came the version changes, at first it was good, bugs were fixed. Then, they started over from scratch, and things started getting different from what made it good in the first place. It was good, then bad, then good, then bad.
The game today is worse than it was, a new thing we are seeing in games when they are made to be a service. A game with a golden age, something we used to only see in MMOs. That is why I can no longer recommend this game. I am going to give it a thumbs up, because of my experiences, and that it was worth the money I paid, but now is a different time. Rust is over for me.
Graphics:
Apart from certain updates and small periods, Rust has always looked fantastic. As they moved into Beta and the modern Rust era, the game both looks great, and takes a great system to run. It's one of the games that gets my PC as hot as it can get. Beware!
Sound:
Great music and sounds at first, but inconsistent sound production. Seemed like the staff never settled on consistant sounds/music during the process. To me, this shows a lack of focus, which has been clear from every player since the beta started. This developmental blurriness seems to coincide with when Rust had already made huge sales. Pretty much the team had success, and just went in slow-patch mode. It was less about a work of art, a work that could have defined the team of producers and developers for the rest of their lives, and more about making the project akin to updating the software in automatically flushing toilets.
Community:
It's a multiplayer game, and the community can be tight-knit if you're in good, but overall it's as toxic as it gets. The sadness with Rust comes from both the community and the developers. Nobody is happy, ever. This has bred conflict between players I've never witnessed before. In short, Rust has the worst community of players I have ever seen, and the clear lack of maturity in most players is almost depressing.
Overall:
Rust was a pioneer, and flagship in a tattered lot, but what made it great also destroyed it. When new games are made in its shadow, I hope that someone can capture that essence just once again, and hold it tight until a perfect time to share it with the world.

This game was pretty cool, about an 6.5 out of 10.  The game play was very similar to Batman Arkham City.  It pretty much consisted of the same main missions and side missions as Arkham City except with different bad Superheros.  Gadgets pretty much performed the same  actions as the ones in Arkham City except these "new" ones had different names and minor tweaks (i.e. new glue gernade instead of the old ice gernade.)  The old Riddler Trophies are now Enigma data packs but they involve almost identical puzzles as to Arkham City.  I could go on about this forever but you pretty much get the point.
However, if you are able to play the game on the ultra settings, it is a sight to behold.  I played Arkham City on PS3 but my visual expierence on my new self built computer was a lot better.  The character and city textures and shadows are amazing.  I couldn't believe how the snow on top of buildies realistically reacted to enemies and my footprints when sneeking and fighting.  Knocked down enemies leave body shaped dents in fresh snow cover and each foot print looks like real as if someone was walking through 4-6 inches of snow.  When inside buildings, debris and trash reacts realistically to the enemies that walk through it like ive never seen in a video game.  The texture details really made the game a more enjoyable than the similar one I played on the consul.
However, stunning graphics and texture detials comes the need for a powerful unit to process them.  I do not know the exact specificaitons of the game but I tried playing the game on the lowest settings on my middle market laptop and it absolutely sucked.  Now I know that only specific laptops are made for gaming and mine was not made for it but even dumbing down the graphics and reslolution to its minimum wouldnt even get me past the first character interaction.  I then decided to play it on the computer i just built (Intel I5-4430 Quad core, 8GB DDR3 RAM, Sapphire Radeon R9 280 3GB GDDR5 Grahpics Card) and it was able to process everything just find on all Ultra settings.
All in all I would not reccomend this game if you previously played Batman Arkham City.  The story lines between the two games are almost identical along with the gadgets and side missions.  Even though the Ultra graphics settings and the texture detials are quite impressive, it is not worth picking up unless you know 100% that you have the hardware required to play the game on Ultra.  Also, I would not buy this game at all for its original price, the only way I would MAYBE get this game was if it goes on sale for very cheap.

During it's launch, most of us criticized it because of its episodic format (me included). But by the time I bought the 1st episode my opinion about the new HITMAN game changed. The game is still great and reminds me more of Blood Money. The always online nature of the game is a bit of a letdown but it doesn't bother me that much. The graphics are okay and it stays true to that signature Hitman look.
But what surprises me the most and what makes the episodic nature of the game reasonable is that each level is huge and chokeful of challenges and miscellaneous things that you can do. Escalation Missions are also a joy to play and will give you that extra challenge you long for in a Hitman game. Sure you can complete the campaign/story mode of one level in less than an hour, but that's just scratching the surface of a very large game that invites you to be creative and think outside the box every time you play a mission.
Now that season 1 is complete I can say that most of us we're all wrong in judging the game way too early. HITMAN is a success, and I can't wait for season 2 to start.

Although I was curious about Hitman for several months, I was initially turned off by the relatively low user review score on its Steam page (sitting at 65% positive at the time of writing).  I'd heard inklings of an icky episodic payment model, as well as resentment directed towards the game's always-online policy.  However, a podcast I listen to (Idle Thumbs) consistently praised Hitman, and had story after emergent story to tell about the game.  Finally, I saw the game on sale for 50% off, so I decided to pull the trigger and get the Intro Pack.
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is
.  Each of the 3 levels I've played at the time of writing is a deliberately-constructed, dense space to explore, replayable but not repetitive, much like Metal Gear Solid 5: Ground Zeroes.  Levels are intelligently constructed sandboxes, with various opportunities presenting themselves as you sneak around in the forms of notes and conversations between NPC's.
About the conversations - the voice work in this game is
good.  When you overhear an NPC speaking to another character on a cell phone, the person they are speaking to is likely in the level, and is carrying on the conversation in real-time; if you were eavesdropping on the other person, you'd hear the other side of the conversation.  Guards communicate effectively with each other, too - if you are spotted, but elude your pursuer, you may overhear them describing "a white, bald, 40-something male" to their fellow guards.  These are small things, but they create a sense of permanence within the game that is incredibly immersive.  I just finished spending roughly 20 hours completing every challenge on the Paris level, and I was consistently hearing entirely new voice lines right up until the end.  There's just
going on in each level.
As for the rest of the level design, it's consistently outstanding.  There are multiple ways to do pretty much everything in the game, from sneaking into a particular restricted area, to knocking out a particular guard, to stealing a particular item.  The only area where Hitman falls short is the gunplay - handling the heavier guns doesn't feel particularly satisfying.  Once you are spotted and get into a firefight, the guards are far too accurate for you to stand a chance.  However, it's a stealth game, not an action game, so I'm absolutely willing to overlook the weak gunplay.
The only other strike against Hitman is its enforcement of an unnecessary always-online policy, and it's this policy that has generated the vast majority of the negative Steam reviews for the game.  For the uninitiated, always-online means that Hitman locks you out of the vast majority of the game's content if you are not connected to the Hitman servers.  It's a single-player game, so why do I need to be online to play it?  However, I've only ever encountered one problem with this (a 20-minute timeframe when the servers were down and I wanted to play).
After playing through the Paris level many times, I did end up getting the Upgrade Pack (also 50% off).  I highly recommend Hitman, particularly if you enjoyed Ground Zeroes.  I'm really glad I took a chance on buying Hitman, because it's honestly fantastic.

HITMAN has completely changed my opinion on episodic content. The steady drip of quality content has kept me entertained since the initial release in March with new maps, and new contracts to fulfill. I cannot think of a better melding of gameplay, and content distribution than this game. The rate at which new areas are released keeps the current crop exciting, while elusive "exclusive" targets, which only stick around for so long, entice you to revisit each sprawling map. This combined with the escalation missions gives you reasons to explore the vast riches of each area.
I have enjoyed this game like any person would enjoy a new television series, if only they we able to go back to previous episodes and discover new content.
HITMAN has surprised me, and I couldn't be more excited for episode 2!

Hitman has always been a niche series, with this entry the managed to make it to the big boys league. Last Hitman game was a disaster luckily you do not need to play it to enjoy this entry. It's sorts of a reboot. And a great one at that!

THIS is how you make a modern stealth game. Each episode feels like an episode of a intense TV drama with twists and turn around any corner.  The game is brimming with an overwhelming atmosphere from A to Z throughout the entire game, something I/O Interactive (almost) always has been known for. The attention to detail, conversation lines, opportunities and ways to perform each mission is staggering to say the least, and will provide you with tons of things to do even after the 6 main episodes. You can even create your own contracts for others to play.
All in all, it's a fantastic game. Incredibly well voice acted, the music is superb and gameplay that puts YOU in control. I've yet to encounter any major bugs. So for the most part, if you fark up, you have yourself to blame. The only downside I can think of is the Marrakesh episode, which was quite uninsteresting except for some small segments.
Even if you haven't played a single Hitman game before or played them all, this is one for everyone. Sure, fans of the series will get some more out of the story, but you can come in not knowing much at all. And for those who've been along since 2000, there are some nice nods to the original games along with other games I/O Interactive have made. Hello, Tobias Rieper!

If the Call of Duty franchise is a well-oiled machine, Black Ops III is the replacement part that keeps the wheels moving into yet another year. It introduces minor changes to an established formula, and in some aspects, this is developer Treyarch near its peak. But in other areas, Call of Duty: Black Ops 3 lacks inspiration.
Treyarch has set a high bar with its contributions to the Call of Duty series. The first Black Ops introduced a twisting, engaging campaign with vivid characters and historical conspiracies. Black Ops II revamped multiplayer customization, lending deeper player choice to a fine-tuned competitive experience. And now there's Call of Duty: Black Ops III, a shooter reaching in several different directions with vastly different results.

The rare AAA game that manages to grasp for the vaunted (phantom?) classification of "art", Spec Ops the Line is mechanically simple, but its presentation and narrative elevate it to something greater. On paper a straight forward 3rd person cover shooter bringing little new to the table, Spec Ops manages to build an identity by masterfully subverting one of action gaming's sacred cows: the lionization of the military, and of heroic adventurism in particular. Although there is a meta-commentary running through on the player's implicit guilt in the entire affair that doesn't always hit the mark, the in-world narrative has more than enough meat to provide a refreshing take on armed conflict in games, and the reliability of narrators in an interactive medium.

Spec Ops: The Line is best described by a metaphor. It is an AKM in the hands of a first-year philosophy student at UCLA. The story hates itself for what it's doing, hates you because you're in this situation too, and hates the society that has made doing these things normal because if we all just put the gun down and talked none of this would be necessary.
"If we could all just stop being self-interested, stop being selfish and angry and thinking only about what we want," says Spec Ops: The Line, "maybe the world would be a better place and you wouldn't have to listen to me preach at you about ethics and how your choices don't matter, you filthy murderer."

Well first off the npcs are what you would expect. Some have stores and there own personalities. Each npc has a specific way you must unlock them, be it killing some boss or getting so far into the game. Or even just finding them while spelunking!
But before you can even unlock these gentlepeople you must have a viable room for each one, you wouldn't want there poor innocent souls lounging around outside would you? You now have to build a house (or several sepperate houses) make it whatever you want. Like a huge glowing mushroom or a secret base in a mountain, the limit is your imagination. My favorite thing to do is creating minecart tracks to travel quickly to different parts of the map where i've built different things like, for example, a boss fighting arena which you should probably invest some time in building, it helps.
Now the bosses. I think the bosses, or rather all the enemies are balanced. The first time you encounter enemies you'll have a hard time fighting even zombies and floating eyes. Now all the new enemies have their ways with you! But don't worry when you get the better weapons, whether from killing bosses or creating them yourself, you'll start to adapt. For the exploration, its pretty good. From floating islands to secret underground jungle temples, all with there own fair share of things to kill. And you will be killing alot! And the moment you get your first of several types of wings, its the funnest thing ever.
I think overall its an amazing game and its completely worth the $10 if you ask me. Mostly when you get some friends on with you. Like i said earlier it has great replay value and i see myself doing stupid challenges and speedrunning bosses.

Hitman has always been a niche series, with this entry the managed to make it to the big boys league. Last Hitman game was a disaster luckily you do not need to play it to enjoy this entry. It's sorts of a reboot. And a great one at that!

THIS is how you make a modern stealth game. Each episode feels like an episode of a intense TV drama with twists and turn around any corner.  The game is brimming with an overwhelming atmosphere from A to Z throughout the entire game, something I/O Interactive (almost) always has been known for. The attention to detail, conversation lines, opportunities and ways to perform each mission is staggering to say the least, and will provide you with tons of things to do even after the 6 main episodes. You can even create your own contracts for others to play.
All in all, it's a fantastic game. Incredibly well voice acted, the music is superb and gameplay that puts YOU in control. I've yet to encounter any major bugs. So for the most part, if you fark up, you have yourself to blame. The only downside I can think of is the Marrakesh episode, which was quite uninsteresting except for some small segments.
Even if you haven't played a single Hitman game before or played them all, this is one for everyone. Sure, fans of the series will get some more out of the story, but you can come in not knowing much at all. And for those who've been along since 2000, there are some nice nods to the original games along with other games I/O Interactive have made. Hello, Tobias Rieper!

I heard this game was different from all the other MMOs.
It's not.
The biggest unique thing I noticed was that there's an excessive amount of races and classes to choose from. There's like 15 races and 20 classes or something like that. To me that's a downside, I dislike when a game puts limitations on you before the game starts. I highly prefer games where you make no class choices at all, but rather your 'class' is somehow determined by your own choices during the gameplay.
Anyway, after the excessive choices pre-game, you're thrown into the same thing that you're thrown into in any other MMO: kill monsters to levelup, move to the next area, rinse and repeat. Quests are just that; kill monsters, collect items from monsters, walk back and forth from NPC to another clicking through uninteresting dialogue. Receive new generic items, sell old ones.
Graphics are not very interesting either, everything is large scaled so the world looks vast in scale, but this just equates to a bland unmemorable landscape and more walking in the end. Houses seem to be copy pasted quite a bit, every single door looks the same and you'll run into buildings that are a carbon copy of another building. I suppose that happens when you try to make the world too big.
I should disclose though, that I'm not interested of endgame content and therefore did not look into it. I play MMOs for the journey, not for the goal.
On a technical note, opening the game resets my monitor calibrations, and closing the game restarts all my tabs on firefox. Really bizzare and obnoxious behavior.

Let me just start by saying I recieved this game from a friend as a gift. So if that lessens my review you might as well scroll down to the next review.
This game is so fresh and pure; in it's story, characters and gameplay. What I mean by that is this is not your average RPG. You don't have to kill anything; not a single creature. It was so refreshing when I found out I didn't have to kill anything in this game.
The story can become a little head turning at times. There are multiple endings; all each with their own criteria. So if you literally want the whole story; get ready to press that reset button a few times. (SPOILERS: I recommend doing the true pacifist run first; even though it is considered the hardest).
The soundtrack might I add, is amazing. This is the first game soundtrack that I listen to outside of gameplay. They are all so gosh darn catchy and fit each scene perfectly. Although that is not surprising considering there 103 tracks on the album release.
At first I wasn't so sure of the controls. I thought they were clunchy, fidgety and sometimes to senstive (when using a controller). But I found them to mostly work. I did have to switch from controller to keyboard quite a few times cause it registered movement when I didn't touch the control stick. Especailly when in menus(!!!). To be honest, you might be better playing on keyboard, even though the layout is weird (that's why I used a controller).
The visual are quirky and have a certain charm. You quickly learn to love it; in fact I quiet enjoyed it.
Overall I woudl say this is a great buy for the money; you're sure to get a good play out of it. Makes me wish it was avilable on other platforms like mobile; that way i could play it on the go.

If you've played the previous Batman games, it will be easy to get frustrated with Arkham Origins. The real center of these games is hand-to-hand combat with large groups of thugs. That's what you'll be spending a large portion of the game doing, and it's never been more frustrating.
In past games, you were able to cancel out of any long animation Batman might be in the middle of in order to counter an attack coming from a thug behind you. In this game, not only do your animations have priority over your commands, but enemies can slide from a good distance away right up next to you to lay a sudden smack-down on the Bat, the whole while you are helpless to defend yourself. This makes the "Bat sense" warning signals above enemies' heads useless at least half of the time, since it will be impossible for you to counter them.
This is more or less emblematic of the problems with Arkham Origins: changes were made that make little sense and do a lot to detract from the experience. There's some fun to be had here for anyone desperate for more Batman after Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, but if you can hold out, you'd be better off waiting for Arkham Knight next year.

The Arkham series has been a strong favourite of mine in recent years. From Asylum’s fantastic story to City’s excellent free roaming mechanics and combat, they have really set the standard for both licensed games and 3rd person action games. It’s therefore fair to say that Origins is disappointing. Given that it's a prequel, the common synonym for "cash-in", it's fairly predictable that this game would be a little substandard.
Origins is based short while after Bruce Wayne has become Batman. He is still seen as a criminal, the police are after him and he has no allies. He has a lot of work to do, with gangs ruling Gotham, systemic police corruption and a massive bounty on his head. The goal is to defeat the many assassins coming to collect, while trying to stop the villain who's posted the bounty.
Along the way Batman learns a bit about teamwork and making allies. It's a story that has been told many times before, but it serves well enough as a way to move things along.
It's pretty obvious that this game falls into the category of "more of the same". The game is familiar; you can roam Gotham as Batman, stalking criminals, solving murders and fighting gangs, but Origins takes the copy-paste plan a little too far. For one, many of the assets are literally identical to City, with unchanged NPC models and a good portion of the map cloned from the previous game, though in fairness the rest of the map is very well designed. Gameplay is similarly unoriginal, with very little to distinguish it from City, though in this instance I can't complain. Apart from the combat feeling a little clunky this round, the core mechanics still hold up very well. I greatly enjoyed prowling around as Batman and found the predator sections, where you are called on to stealthily clear a room of hostiles, to be immensely satisfying.
There's plenty to do aside from the main campaign, with a couple of NG+ modes that ramp up the difficulty, as well as the challenge maps to pad things out. There are the usual Riddler Trophy collectibles where the challenge is less in finding them, more in solving the puzzle to grab them. What I liked the most were the side quests; there are several crimes around the city that need solving, usually in the form of a murder. What is new here is the ability to recreate the crime scene in the detective vision mode, where you calculate the trajectory of the bullet from the blood splatter and so on. It’s used a couple of times in the main story but I enjoyed it more in the various side missions.
Arkham Origin's is a fairly mediocre game by Arkham standards, but it's still an Arkham game which puts it way ahead of other games in the genre. It's worth a play for fans of the series, but I'd recommend waiting for Arkham Knight.

It's Christmas night in Gotham. There are rumors in the streets of a new masked vigilante called Batman, but that's just an urban legend. After a few hours Batman discovers that the Black mask has put a hit out for Batman, and a handful of pretty tough villians are the Assassins. The longer the night goes, the more publicity the Batman gets, people realize that he is more than a myth he is the real deal, and you experience it all.
That's the main story, with a few twists that I won't spoil. Overall the main story took me 17 hours on easy mode and the main story is only 30% of the game, after completing it you must defeat another handful of villians I.E. The riddler, the penguin, etc. in order to get 100%. After you complete the game entirely I think there is a bonus ending. The game's mechanics are great, basing the combat on real martial arts and there is nothing like a big sandbox Gotham where you can glide around kicking the crap out of bad guys all night.
I did have a few issues with the game though. Though the combat is great and always helped me feel like Batman, a baddas bat straight outa hell, there were a few parts of the game that were just plain boring. The boss battles, some of them epic, but some bosses you have to fight in multiple parts of the game and they don't change anything about the boss to make it different. Those boss battles become monotinous, not like "I'm grinding for XP" kinda way, more like "I have to do this again?!" Kind of way. Another thing I've noticed about the game is a bunch of the levels are obviously recycled from Batman Arkham Asylum, they were linear and with the TV's hanging while the villian talks to you from them is straight from that game but they just change the decor.
Overall it was an enjoyable experience, I played on easy mode so I could just enjoy the story  and not have to try very hard. The story and the combat mechanics is what makes this game great, oh, not to mention you're mother♥♥♥♥in' Batman.

Good harvesting, crafting, and trapping.
Forage bushes for berries to eat or to bait traps with (raw meat can also work). Cook meat near a fire. Use stones and obsidian to make heads. Fell trees with axe for logs to fuel fire and sticks and feathers for traps, arrows, bows, fire starter, and axe handle. The character needs to eat meat, as berries alone will not sustain him, and they can not be harvested in the cold seasons.

On My Own is an outdoor survival game featuring exceptional production values, pixel art, and calming music. With little fanfare, you’re thrust into the wildness, tasked with surviving on your own. The ultimate goal is to survive long enough to climb the mountain.
On My Own is dubbed a woodland survival adventure game by Beach Interactive and Close Studios. Released on Steam last month, the game is now making its way to iOS, Android, and soon consoles. Before I start this review, I’ll just mention that I personally know the designer and artist Kyle Weik. I hail from Fargo, North Dakota, where Beach Interactive resides. I’d talked to Kyle about the game for months before it released, so naturally I was a bit disposed toward liking this game.
That said, the subject matter itself was a natural draw. Ever since I was a kid I’ve gone camping with my family. As I got older, we did more extreme camping; I’ve been on about a dozen canoe and backpacking adventures over the years.
At an early age I fell in love with books like My Side of the Mountain and The Hatchet. I was also a Boy Scout, and trained in wilderness survival. Part of me has always longed to strike out on my own, to be alone in the wilderness with nothing but my wits and wisdom. While being marooned in the wilderness would obviously be a terrifying experience—especially for loved ones left behind—I’ve always wondered, Could I survive in the wilderness if I had to?
I’ll likely never know the answer to that. While I’ll always have a love of camping, the modern world is such that it’s nigh-impossible, without immense sacrifice that I’m unwilling to endure, to just drop everything and go into the wilderness. I’d leave too many loved ones behind, for one.
On My Own (OMO), though, afforded me a few hours to think through that possibility. You choose the sex of your character, read a brief letter about why you’re going into the wilderness, and then you’re there. You have a cabin, a hatchet, and a backpack. With little guidance, the game forces you to trap and hunt your own food, sew clothing from hides, construct weapons and tools, and start and maintain fires.
There’s a fair amount of variety to the activities, but time moves quickly through the seasons, which adds a welcome challenge. Berries only grow in the summer. Plants, needed for making bows, are only available in the summer and fall. The winters are cold, limiting how far you can venture from camp before your energy is depleted.
The first couple winters were brutal for me. I didn’t construct a bow that first winter, and berries barely provide any energy. My hunger meter gradually decreased as the winter wore on: I wasn’t prepared, and I thought I might starve at one point.
The second summer I worked hard to gather the materials for a bow so that I could shoot a deer. But the bow broke as I hunted a deer. Then my second bow broke. The rabbits closest to my home were already harvested. I entered another winter unprepared.
As the game progressed through the years (playing a year takes about 40 minutes), I got better at surviving. Soon I had a surplus of food and rabbit skins. The game is a bit unbalanced at times, where you might gather a ton of certain resources and then lack other resources. And time can move a bit fast—both the length of day, and the number of days in a season (ranging from 2-4 days for each season) could be extended.
But for your money, the game is still a great adventure. There isn’t a lot of variety to the music, but the twangy banjo music is uplifting and never gets old.
Conflict is minimal. The need to eat is an ever-present drive, and occasionally you might get mauled by a bear (I learned right away how close I could safely get to the grizzly bear, and where that line was!). The game does not present nature as an enemy, or as something to fear. Nature simply exists, I alongside the myriad animals.
Human contact is minimal, but I never felt alone or lonely. I felt content, satisfied. Often while I played my breath with hitch and I would deeply sigh, relaxed, fulfilled.
The loading screens are peppered with quotes about the natural world. For example,
Seeking means to have a goal; but finding means: to be free, to be receptive, to have no goal.
~Herman Hesse
The game doesn’t hold your hand, and provides very few hints on how to craft new items. I resisted looking up a wiki how to progress. When I finally discovered how to make a longbow, one that wouldn’t break like my bundle bow, I felt so accomplished!
If you are looking for an end-goal, the game provides one in the form of different environments. You can camp in four landscapes, the last being the bleak and lonely mountain. Make it to the mountain and you “beat the game.” This is a game, though, where the destination isn’t as important as the journey. Any woodsman will tell you that being in nature, in and of itself, is enough.
For all the challenges those first two years posed to me, eventually I fell into a rut. Harvesting deer and rabbits became easy. I stocked up on berries, fish, hides, feathers, and wood. I accumulated so much that surviving was no longer difficult. As I played the game, I became complacent. I dared walk closer to the grizzly bears, knowing that even if they attacked me, it wouldn’t seriously set back my efforts.
To me, survival games are always most enjoyable in the beginning, when the danger is real. The first time I played Minecraft, back when it was in beta, I had no idea what to do. The first couple nights were actually frightening to me. I had no shelter, and I died over and over again by the slings of arrows from skeletons that I could not see.
But then I learned to build a shelter, mine iron, and craft weapons and armor. I started over many times in Minecraft, and the first few hours are always the most enjoyable. I eventually reach the point where I know how to craft everything, and the challenge is gone.
By the time I got to the third camp of OMO, I had so much stuff that I had nowhere to store it. I just left it on the ground, scattered around my lean-to. I had become rich.
The same thing happened to Sam Gribley in the My Side of the Mountain series, and Brian in The Hatchet series. The first books of those series are the best, when the boys are just learning how to survive. By the later books, they, too, become rich.
And I suppose that’s the natural way of the wilderness. Even alone, you are truly on your own for only a very short time. Then you have your stuff as company.

On My Own:
~~~~~~~~~~
Nature can be so beautiful, majestic and peaceful. However, when you are by yourself and need to survive in it, nature can be tough on anyone. And you will be on your own!
On My Own is an adventure / survival game in a pixel world type of graphics. At the start of the game you will be able to choose if you would like to be a female or a male survivor stuck in the middle of nowhere. Upon choosing your gender, you will start the game in the beautiful and hot season of summer. Plenty of fruits and flowers are available for the picking in this season and you should take advantage of it. Starting in the summer is great but you will need to get through the next summer without dying, which could be a slight challenge shall we say.
The game is set in seasons and each season has turns:  summer has four turns, fall has two, winter has four and spring has two.  This game is all about your resources via hunting animals and picking picking fruits. No Zombies or other baddies to kill in this game.
You will find boxes here and there; make sure you actually look in them as they have valuable information on how to craft new items.
You will use W,A,S,D to move your character and the mouse to pick up or use items. Good Pixel artwork.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Good pixel artwork
-	Interesting survival game without Zombies
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Not much action
On My Own is a nice survival type of game based on accumulating resources.
7/10

Although I doubt anything I say will really change anyone's minds given the buzz Undertale's had for the past two years, I felt I might as well put in my own two cents.
First off, when I first booted up the game and realized what I'd just bought was a 2D shooter with pixel graphics, I was expecting the graphics to really annoy me. Surprisingly, it didn't. If anything, it just added more to the atmosphere of the game. I think that if it had been made as a fully animated 3D game, it would have lost some of its charm, and certainly the emotion. A lot of Undertale's charm is that it makes you think for yourself, instead of telling you what to think. The graphics help with that.
The next thing I thought, mostly from watching playthroughs and then in the first few fights, is that Undertale would be easy. Although it's not horrifically difficult, nonstop, the bosses will give you trouble- especially if you're a heartless individual who decides to try the Genocide Route. The Neutral Route's boss will become slightly easier after a certain number of deaths, but other than that, the game is entirely skill-based. You have to win through your own merit, and not because the game is giving you pity-points.
There's a ton more that could be said about the characters, the thematic elements, the soundtrack, general gameplay, and other things, but that would take way too much time. Probably the only thing I'd want different is the amount and difficulty of the puzzles. If I'm going to die 30+ times to some of the bosses, I think it's only fair the puzzles give me more than thirty second's pause.
TL;DR: I definitely recommend this game! Although it's much better going into it blind, I think it's still worth a go even after watching playthroughs of it. There's something to be said for doing it yourself.

Now that the whole game is out, minus one small bonus mission coming January, I think it's a good time to buy. There is a Season 2 coming next year, though.
The good:
Large, open levels reward exploration and creativity
Restricted loadout system allows you to make more interesting decisions about what to bring with you
Unlockable gear system is cool even if some of the gear is a bit useless (why would I want a plain combat knife that can't even go through frisks?)
Lots and lots of opportunities; some are spelled out for you and others are more subtle
Handholding mechanics can be turned OFF for veterans
Performance issues have mostly been fixed since release
Elusive targets and the suits they unlock provide a reason to keep coming back
The disguise and suspicion system feels much less arbitrary than in Blood Money
The bad:
Uses both Denuvo and an always-online system (this is the worst thing about the game)
There are simply too many ways to disable or kill NPCs, and it's too easy, compared to Blood Money
Aim-down-sights system means it's almost impossible to pull a gun and quickly kill someone before they react; once they react they start moving their head all over the place, making it hard to get a kill shot
Killing someone immediately after being spotted doesn't remove the penalty for being spotted (even if he only saw you a moment before the knife you threw entered his skull)
The score system is only interesting if you are speedrunning; it's something I don't even look at because it's boring and inferior in every way to Blood Money's ranking system (but there's no reason we can't have both wink wink nudge nudge please add it IOI)
You can carry any weapon while disguised as a guard, making it trivial to e.g. get into position with a sniper rifle.
One of the levels has a truly obnoxious, unskippable non-assassination objective
Throwing weapons lock on like in Absolution so they're absurdly OP
Overall it's a good game, and I don't regret buying the full package back in March.

Whoa.. THIS GAME! It is absoulutely amazing! First of all i love platformers, i grew up with Donkey Kong Country, Banjo Kazooie and Super Mario games. The things important to make a great 2d platformer now is a couple of things:
1. Great gameplay! Any game is trash if the gameplay isnt good, Ori & The Blind Forest has great gameplay, a skill based system, its difficult but not too hard, and it has a great collaboration of everything you unlock throughout the game.
2. Collecting stuff! Like bananas, jiggies or stars, every platformer with development throughout the game need stuff to collect, in this game it is orbs, health and soul crystals, which works perfectly in my opinion!
3. Puzzles! Its important to have a map in a game like this that is filled with different things, you don't want to run through an empty map (sorry assassins creed) just doing nothing but its OK cause it looks cool. In Ori you have to collect stuff, do puzzles to access the collectables, and the ENTIRE game is filled with something for you to do.
4. Graphics! This is not very important, i would always want great gameplay over great graphics, but this game offers both, an own artstyle with great movement and a living feel to the map, the graphics are AMAZING!
5. STORY! This is without a doubt the top two most important things, gameplay and story. This game, it's going to make you cry, its gonna make you smile, and feel appreciated. The story in this game is just absolutely stunning.
Now for my personal opinion.
This game is an easy 10/10 for me, it has everything i can appreciate in a 2d platformer.

The Dark Knight. Part of the Arkham series of games. This is the third in the series however it is a prequel to them. The game skips most of the origin story and dives right into Batman's first year. You play as the Dark Knight on Christmas Eve. A bounty has been placed on your head and you must now not only survive the regular trouble in Gotham but also the threat of the bounty hunters. Can you survive one of the most daunting nights in Batman's life?
The game is visually beautiful. Dark and gritty world filled with the scum of the world. You have almost complete free roaming ability from the beginning of the game. There is a handful of places that will require specialized equipment but for the most part you can wander as you wish. There is an easy to navigate system that will help you find your next goal. The game itself is one part open world and one part mission hunting. Not as open as say Skyrim but still a rather open game.
You take control of the Dark Knight himself. You have minimal equipment but as you advance you acquire and create new equipment. One of your most used abilities is gliding and hooking. It gets pretty redundant with movement and combat grows dull rather quickly. The missions are fairly straight forward and don't often create a new challenge. You will glide from mission to mission and occasionally find some unusual to do or require some unusual gear.
The steam achievements for this game are pretty daunting. You will likely have to beat the game multiple times on varying difficulties. You will also have to master the various skill paths as well as perform various challenges. The achievements are rather difficult and in all honest its not worth it.
This game is a great deal of fun. I would highly recommend anyone who enjoys open world, action-RPG, and/or Batman should get this game. That being said I would hold out for a seasonal sale or some kind of bundle.

A worthwhile third installment in the Arkham series, but pulled down by a combat system less responsive than the one in Arkham City, mostly forgetable and weak boss fights, and a truely worthless New Game Plus mode. Story wise, AO gives a lot of back story to the previous two games, and is mostly well written and composed. This is taken further by the Cold, Cold Heart DLC, focusing on Mr. Freeze. Also worth getting.
If you liked the semi open setting of Arkham City, the free flow combat system and gadget heavy brawling, you'll enjoy this as well. The weaknesses, while being annoying when you encounter them, shouldn't keep gamers away.

What a let down.  I preordered this on the strength of the previous games - what I didn't know is that they'd used a different developer for this prequel.  And sadly, it shows.  The greatest strength of the Arkham series is the sharp, fluid combat system.  Origins loses the smoothness, and introduces mechanics which break the flow of combat, reducing it from best-in-class to merely passable.  The storytelling, extremely strong in Asylum and still decent in City, is clumsy and formulaic in Origins, with none of the psychological introspection that made Arkham Asylum great.  The stealth sections are still nearly as good as the previous titles, but lack the extreme polish, quality and attention to detail that the other two had.
It's not actually that bad a game, but such a disappointment.  The new features in Origins don't add anything interesting, and a lot is lost in quality.  I uninstalled this and went back to Arkham City for the combat challenges.  If you're thinking of buying this game, I would instead suggest you buy Arkham City, or Arkham Asylum if you care more about story and atmosphere.  If you have those games already, play through them again rather than getting this; you will be disappointed.

Rust will never be forgotten, and it will never be at peace. I told myself I would wait to do this review, that I would let it settle, that it would one day be finished and then I could write my thoughts. Well, too much time has passed for me to wait any longer, and for some reason, today seems to be the day.
I'm not even sure now how I discovered this, "new game with a cool idea". A friend, DayZ-exploring, a flashing Steam store page, who knows. But once I installed it, and loaded it up, I had found a new, exciting video game. The music when loading was incredible, eerie and atmospheric; and this was 'alpha' music? Once I loaded into the world, an island of apparently great size, I enjoyed the experience from the start. Nature, trees, vast distances, animals, ruins, and...people.
For that is what makes Rust tick, people. The first moment, not knowing whether to hide, fight, or try to communicate, is telling, and this is a common thread. And with these first moments, come the first deaths, both expected and not. And so comes the first rule of Rust, don't trust anyone. And with this rule comes the choice you have to make, do you strive to live a solo life? Do you have Steam friends that play and can band together? Or do you try to find some team to take you in? Be ready, you are going to die, a lot.
I made a shelter, and built, and harvested, and hunted. I ventured into dangerous places and survived. Or died. In the end, it was a great experience. Then came the version changes, at first it was good, bugs were fixed. Then, they started over from scratch, and things started getting different from what made it good in the first place. It was good, then bad, then good, then bad.
The game today is worse than it was, a new thing we are seeing in games when they are made to be a service. A game with a golden age, something we used to only see in MMOs. That is why I can no longer recommend this game. I am going to give it a thumbs up, because of my experiences, and that it was worth the money I paid, but now is a different time. Rust is over for me.
Graphics:
Apart from certain updates and small periods, Rust has always looked fantastic. As they moved into Beta and the modern Rust era, the game both looks great, and takes a great system to run. It's one of the games that gets my PC as hot as it can get. Beware!
Sound:
Great music and sounds at first, but inconsistent sound production. Seemed like the staff never settled on consistant sounds/music during the process. To me, this shows a lack of focus, which has been clear from every player since the beta started. This developmental blurriness seems to coincide with when Rust had already made huge sales. Pretty much the team had success, and just went in slow-patch mode. It was less about a work of art, a work that could have defined the team of producers and developers for the rest of their lives, and more about making the project akin to updating the software in automatically flushing toilets.
Community:
It's a multiplayer game, and the community can be tight-knit if you're in good, but overall it's as toxic as it gets. The sadness with Rust comes from both the community and the developers. Nobody is happy, ever. This has bred conflict between players I've never witnessed before. In short, Rust has the worst community of players I have ever seen, and the clear lack of maturity in most players is almost depressing.
Overall:
Rust was a pioneer, and flagship in a tattered lot, but what made it great also destroyed it. When new games are made in its shadow, I hope that someone can capture that essence just once again, and hold it tight until a perfect time to share it with the world.

This is a suprisingly good licensed title, and a very good PC port (to the point you might wonder if it was just built around PC in the first place). The vehicle combat is earth shaking & rattling when you ram & harpoon other vehicles in the desert sands and you do get a real feeling of speed. The ground combat is brutal & visceral in the Arkham Knight Batman style. While it suffers a bit from an open world that is far more empty than games like GTA 5, you can derive a lot of fun from zooming around the map.
It went criminally under the radar on release, as many people would likely have seen it as a rushed licensed tie-in and didn't give it a chance. This game was apparently being made for quite a while before even getting the license, and the care taken shows. The storyline is functional, but it has some good flavourful characterisation that matches with the wider franchise. It also contains some good character customisation & there are a few "bases" you can work on.
If you are a big fan of open world games then buy it. If they aren't you cup of tea put it on a wishlist and wait until it's deeply discouted below the $10 USD mark & give it a shot even if it's just the motor oil soaked doomsday asthetic that you might be attracted by. I bought it around the time that GTA & Metal Gear Solid 5 came out, and this was as fun for me as GTA 5 and a lot more enjoyable than MGS.
Now for a point that is outside the normal realm of reviewing the game itself. Mad Max has an insanely good screenshot/camera feature where you can stop the action & play with the scene with things like photoshop or instagram filters to take high res screenshots. If you have a PC like mine which can do very high specs at a high res you can get some gorgeous customised wallpapers, while a lot of the map is bare desert & moutains like a muted Bob Ross painting the asthetic can work if you're taking shots of a vehicle going at high speed, but it also has some nice peaks, caves & valleys, dust storms & pre-war locations, and extremely impressive graphics for explosions & combat scenes.
Stop things at the right point and you can get an exploding vehicle covered in billowing flames, or snap a shot with Max right in the middle of delivering a stunning fist or knife strike to a crazed cultist mutant, in super high detail. It's not a feature that will sway people to buy it, but don't overlook it if you do get the game, play around with it and see what you can come up with. Features like these that aren't really at all "neccessary" to the gameplay should be praised when develoeprs add them to a game in a way that works so well, a loving touch that helps elevate the game as a whole.
By far this most disapointing thing about Mad Max is that the developers Avalanche followed up Mad Max with the extremely disapointing Just Cause 3, and haven't taken the good things that Mad Max did and find a way to improve & expand them into an independent new franchise that they could make a lot more money from than a licensed title or games developed under contract to other publishers.

APB Reloaded is not a very good game for a few reasons.
One: driving. Driving in this game is a chore. The streets must be made of solid sheets of ice, because cars slide around on turns. They're very hard to control, especially for beginners.
Two: unfair advantages. This game features microtransactions, which, when done properly, are not a problem at all. APB does it wrong. The more expensive guns are clearly better than others, putting inexperienced players or those who don't want to spend money on this game at a severe disadvantage to those who do. There is also no skill match mechanic, meaning that new players have a chance at going up against top-level players much of the time. This quickly leads to much frustration at not being able to do anything. For the new player, the only way to advance is to get lucky, which is not a good first impression.
Three: the game constantly pushes these purchases on you. If I wanted to buy something from this game, I would visit the marketplace myself. You don't need to constantly remind me that something's on sale. If I cared enough, I would check the sales out myself.
Four: the gameplay itself. Gameplay is unbalanced and frustrating, leading to much confusion for the new player. Objectives are hard to find, and the instructions vague at best. Rest assured most of it involves killing.
There is only one possibly redeeming quality about this game, and that is that there are good customization options for your character. This is dragged down by the fact that to get these customization options, you need money, which is earned by either trudging through the impossible missions or buying currency.
All in all, this game is only playable if you're willing to spend hundreds of dollars on it, and even then, it's mediocre at best. This game left a bad taste in my mouth, and you can be sure I won't be coming back for another bite.

Now that the whole game is out, minus one small bonus mission coming January, I think it's a good time to buy. There is a Season 2 coming next year, though.
The good:
Large, open levels reward exploration and creativity
Restricted loadout system allows you to make more interesting decisions about what to bring with you
Unlockable gear system is cool even if some of the gear is a bit useless (why would I want a plain combat knife that can't even go through frisks?)
Lots and lots of opportunities; some are spelled out for you and others are more subtle
Handholding mechanics can be turned OFF for veterans
Performance issues have mostly been fixed since release
Elusive targets and the suits they unlock provide a reason to keep coming back
The disguise and suspicion system feels much less arbitrary than in Blood Money
The bad:
Uses both Denuvo and an always-online system (this is the worst thing about the game)
There are simply too many ways to disable or kill NPCs, and it's too easy, compared to Blood Money
Aim-down-sights system means it's almost impossible to pull a gun and quickly kill someone before they react; once they react they start moving their head all over the place, making it hard to get a kill shot
Killing someone immediately after being spotted doesn't remove the penalty for being spotted (even if he only saw you a moment before the knife you threw entered his skull)
The score system is only interesting if you are speedrunning; it's something I don't even look at because it's boring and inferior in every way to Blood Money's ranking system (but there's no reason we can't have both wink wink nudge nudge please add it IOI)
You can carry any weapon while disguised as a guard, making it trivial to e.g. get into position with a sniper rifle.
One of the levels has a truly obnoxious, unskippable non-assassination objective
Throwing weapons lock on like in Absolution so they're absurdly OP
Overall it's a good game, and I don't regret buying the full package back in March.

I just returned to EQ2 after a several year hiatus.
I joined as f2p and all of my toons and their inventories were still availalbe (I did have to delete one of them due to character slot limitations...but there are plenty of slots---I just had too many toons).
I deleted another, low-level toon, so I could start over and get reacquianted with the game.  I have to say the play is still very engaging and fun. The graphics are a bit dated..but I am not that concerned if the game can grab my attention and stay fun. Also this is one of the few games, out there, that can accomodate my close group of friends in a single group. We normally have 6 players, and most games limit you to 4 (maybe 5) person teams.  EQ2 supports 6 - for us this is a BIG bonus.
I was leary of SOEs implementaion of free-to-play (f2p), having been irritated by many titles being f2p (free to PAY AND OFTEN) instead of f2p (free to play). Sony has this one set (imho) perfectly.  I have run into very little restrictions (text chat in game is frustratingly gimped for f2p, but after dealing with the foul-mouth trolls that commonly make the chat useless, I FULLY approve!)
I do understand that at the highest tier (I mean 80+ level here) there is money involved if you are f2p, and I am absolutely OK with that.  If I have played on their servers, over their network, and enjoyed their hard work for that long, then they damn good-and-well deserve something from me in return.
There are also two races, and classes that you pay to have access to, that is OK too. These are mostly cosmetic and have a fun idea behind them. There are still so many free choices that if I decide I want to play one of those other races or classes I can (again) pay for them and not feel I am having my credit card ransomed. Fianlly you will get pop-ups when you log in for things to purchase, and another shortly to take advantage of the Sony All Access. Again this is a minor annoyance and easily closed. (Also at $10 a month for subscription access to most SOE titles and more coming online it sure beats $15 a month for most paid MMOs)

In theory, "The Tiny Bang Story" is a Hidden Object Game (HOG).  In reality, it's not.  Yes.  There are teeny tiny little objects to be found throughout the game.  But, that's not what a HOG is.  It's not really that important since other things swamp my rating.  But, it's something to be aware of.  The big thing that hurts the game is that nothing (absolutely nothing) is explained.  We're dumped into a setting with no idea what we're supposed to do, how to do it, or why.  The next biggest issues is somewhat related:  once we figure out what we're doing, we get into mini-puzzles.  But, once again, we're given no idea what to do with them.  Most of them can be figured out with the hint they give us.  But, some of them remain entirely opaque (I finished several by blindly flailing around with the mouse and never understood what I'd done to "succeed").  Next, as we move around the screen looking for those hidden objects or the secret areas they might be in, the cursor doesn't change to indicate any "hot" zones.  Basically, the game turns into a click-fest because we have to click on every single thing we see in case it's important.  And finally, the puzzles and objects aren't necessarily "necessary" to the game.  In the second area, I skipped a puzzle so I could come back to it later.  I ended up brute-forcing another puzzle which, I think, the puzzle I skipped was supposed to open.  The game happily let me do this and leave the area without ever finishing that puzzle.  In the third area, I finished the last puzzle before gathering the last hidden puzzle piece.  When I placed the object from that last puzzle where it belonged, the game happily moved me from the area and gave me all the puzzle pieces I needed for the world-puzzle.
I got 4.0 hours of game-play out of this.  So, the list price is a bit high purely from a dollar-per-hour aspect.  But, even if the game were much cheaper (heck, I paid 50 cents for it), the issues I noted above just put the game into the Not-Recommended area.

One of those few games that WB absolutly did right. Everything worked, it's easy enough to grasp, but it's an adventure of finding goodies, smashing things up, and weathering some of the most extreme sand storm systems you're ever going to witness.
It's like taking some of the more recent Batman games, tossing it into the MadMax universe, which inspired huge chunks of Fallout from the start, and tosses you into sandstorms that feel almost as threatening as radiation storms from STALKER or Fallout 4, only you can actually surivive standing out in the sandstorm, if you're lucky and vigilent. But it's often wise to take shelter or be in the car much of the time tracking down the rare chest and loot that fly about in said sandstorms with a gorgious harpoon mechanic that really makes the vehicular play work great. Not to mention uncovering obsticles to find more hidden away shelters like Zelda mini dungeons.
If any of this even tremotely seems interesting to you, and you don't have it yet, pick it up when you can. As of this writing it's on sale for a little more than a breakfast sandwitch. Treat yourself, it's very well optimized and if for some reason you don't have a PC that can run it, at least pick it up for a console. It works good on just about any platform it's available on.

When you’ve managed to create an unexpectedly great first entry for a franchise, it begs the question: What the hell do you do with the sequel? In the case of Borderlands 2 developer Gearbox has decided to largely stick with what worked the first time around, while implementing a host of tweaks that make it an overall superior game. A few relatively minor complaints aside, Borderlands 2 improves not only the narrative, but almost every major game system. If you’ve been itching for a reason to jump back into the world of Pandora, Borderlands 2 provides a more than ample supply.
The hook of Borderlands 2, the very reason that I found myself thinking about it when I worked or tried to fall asleep, is the loot. Guns, ammo, character skins, grenade mods, class mods -- there’s always something just a bit better, something you so desperately didn’t even know you needed until you found it in Borderlands 2. Just like Diablo or a number of other action RPGs, the hunt for loot becomes intoxicating because of the tiny rush you get each time a rare colored item spills out of a chest or is dropped by a recently slain enemy. Every firefight and intense boss battle becomes all the more rewarding, because, though you might die a few times and want to crush something near you in real life, it suddenly feels like everything is going to be OK when you’re blasting away enemies with a newly looted gun.
Guns really do make up the bulk of the loot, and that’s great because you’re going to spend most of your time in Borderlands 2 staring down a gun sight. No matter the quest, at some point something or someone is getting pounded with lead. Thankfully, snappy shooting and lots of environmental hazards combine with each class’s unique ability to turn every skirmish into a playground. You simply have to decide the best -- or most entertaining -- way to kill everyone.
While many guns operate similarly to one another, the stats and augmentations are just complex enough to create a seemingly endless number of combinations, without being so diverse that they’re hard to understand at a glance. You roll in, you kill anything that looks at you the wrong way, and then you walk around and look at items, utilizing the handy on-screen comparison tools to see if you’ve found something at all better than what you’re already holding. It keeps things from dragging, and drives you rapidly onward in the never-ending quest for loot.
Seeing as how Borderlands 2 takes cues from numerous RPGs, I still find myself disappointed with the lack of visual customization options (Borderlands 2 features the ability to reskin your character, but only with blanket skins that change the look of their body and their head). However, when it comes to class skill customization, Borderlands 2 is heading in the right direction. Like the first game, Borderlands 2’s four classes each have a unique ability. Unlike the original, though, a lot of options have been added to the skill trees to make it possible to create much more diverse builds...at least to a point. No matter what, every Commando will be about using turrets, every Gunzerker about raging out and blasting people with two weapons at once, every Siren about using a stun ability called Phase Lock, and every Assassin about temporarily cloaking and unleashing devastating surprise attacks. But how those abilities and characters function can be tailored to your playstyle (and can be changed over and over again for a negligible fee on a whim). For instance your Assassin might be focused on sniping and avoiding damage, while mine could be tailored to get in close and melee enemies while taking it on the chin. On the surface two people’s takes on a class might seem similar, but the new, more filled out skill trees allow you to create a version of a class that better suits your style.
