This is a suprisingly good licensed title, and a very good PC port (to the point you might wonder if it was just built around PC in the first place). The vehicle combat is earth shaking & rattling when you ram & harpoon other vehicles in the desert sands and you do get a real feeling of speed. The ground combat is brutal & visceral in the Arkham Knight Batman style. While it suffers a bit from an open world that is far more empty than games like GTA 5, you can derive a lot of fun from zooming around the map.
It went criminally under the radar on release, as many people would likely have seen it as a rushed licensed tie-in and didn't give it a chance. This game was apparently being made for quite a while before even getting the license, and the care taken shows. The storyline is functional, but it has some good flavourful characterisation that matches with the wider franchise. It also contains some good character customisation & there are a few "bases" you can work on.
If you are a big fan of open world games then buy it. If they aren't you cup of tea put it on a wishlist and wait until it's deeply discouted below the $10 USD mark & give it a shot even if it's just the motor oil soaked doomsday asthetic that you might be attracted by. I bought it around the time that GTA & Metal Gear Solid 5 came out, and this was as fun for me as GTA 5 and a lot more enjoyable than MGS.
Now for a point that is outside the normal realm of reviewing the game itself. Mad Max has an insanely good screenshot/camera feature where you can stop the action & play with the scene with things like photoshop or instagram filters to take high res screenshots. If you have a PC like mine which can do very high specs at a high res you can get some gorgeous customised wallpapers, while a lot of the map is bare desert & moutains like a muted Bob Ross painting the asthetic can work if you're taking shots of a vehicle going at high speed, but it also has some nice peaks, caves & valleys, dust storms & pre-war locations, and extremely impressive graphics for explosions & combat scenes.
Stop things at the right point and you can get an exploding vehicle covered in billowing flames, or snap a shot with Max right in the middle of delivering a stunning fist or knife strike to a crazed cultist mutant, in super high detail. It's not a feature that will sway people to buy it, but don't overlook it if you do get the game, play around with it and see what you can come up with. Features like these that aren't really at all "neccessary" to the gameplay should be praised when develoeprs add them to a game in a way that works so well, a loving touch that helps elevate the game as a whole.
By far this most disapointing thing about Mad Max is that the developers Avalanche followed up Mad Max with the extremely disapointing Just Cause 3, and haven't taken the good things that Mad Max did and find a way to improve & expand them into an independent new franchise that they could make a lot more money from than a licensed title or games developed under contract to other publishers.

I really, really wanted to like this game. It's exactly the kind of game I like to play, and I did enjoy my first few minutes of wandering around. However, after about five minutes, I grew increasingly frustrated with the crafting/inventory UI, which appears above and below the player. I consequently found it difficult to move items from my inventory into the world – quite often, the UI was in the way. There was a clunkiness to the user controls in general – I felt like I had to focus entirely on figuring out how to actually play the game, and couldn't focus on the world itself. I played for about 20 minutes, ragequit, and requested a refund.
Maybe one day I'll check it out again, because, aside from the terrible UI, the game itself seems really solid. There's definitely a lot of merit to this game, but in the end I didn't find the frustration worth it.

Amazing game. A return to form after the terrible game that was hitman absolution. I prefer this one over blood money too.
The maps are designed very well and intelligently where it's fun to explore them and figure how it connects together. Great little details in the maps and general atmosphere of them make them feel authentic. The gameplay is simple but solid. I would recommend turning off 'opportunities' for a first play of a map as otherwise the game holds your hand too much. Has great music that fits the game. Story is non existent but it doesn't matter at all. Always online is not an issue, stop crying about it you window lickers.
The game is small if you don't replay the maps. The maps themselves are big enough with different ways to kill targets. Still, with only 6 maps it does feel short. At least 2 more maps would have been the ideal length.
AI is very dumb and you get away with things you really shouldn't but you begin to forgive this when you start to see the game as more of a puzzle game than a stealth game. Optimization isn't great, it's a very demanding game.
Overall this is a must play for any stealth fan or 'trial and error hitman' fan. It really is what absolution should have been.

I don't know what to think of this game, if you can call it that, so lets do the typical thing and break it down into pros and cons.
+Good looking game, considering 4 years of age
+B+ gunplay, but definitely made for consoles
+Noticable, meaningful character progression
+..."Interesting" story
-Lip syncing is quite poor at times
-Controls, like gunplay, were made for consoles
-Characters fit archetypes a little too strongly
And now, for the BIGGEST con....
-Choice is an illusion.
There are a few small choices that change the half-second snippets you see in the end cutscene, but the real perpetrator is a doozy.... The focal point of the game is just that: a point. While it gives the potential for an immense decision, and a companion mentions that it IS a choice, the protag simply states that it is not, and he was right; it was coded not to be. Not following the path laid out for you faces you with an infinite onslaught of soldiers, snipers, and sub-par cover. Worst of all is that the game expects you to feel responsible for this decision and all repercussions of it, but it WASN'T a decision, it was just the given script.
While this one, MAJOR issue does detract heavily from enjoyment(?) of the game(???), the story that IS presented to players is one I was quite content with seeing the conclusion of, (if not a bit obvious of an ending). I recommend this game as an... "experience", which has probably been said before, but STRONGLY urge people to not expect one that respects your choices: You're only here for the ride.

Hidden object games have never been my thing, but after playing through this exquisite little gem, I may have to branch out a little. From the music to the charming little puzzles interspersed throughout, you'll find much more than a time waster on your hands.
With no conventional story to be had, the whole plot basically revolves around collecting the puzzle pieces that make up the world. You'll encounter an individual character in each area, and you'll see a broad narrative of a young boy's adventures as you go, but it's mainly background. Everything in this game is hidden in plain site, but a keen eye can spot the majority of the items often before you even need to pick them up. This is all bundled in an absolutely gorgeous art style that makes use of pastels to give an authentic painting look. Every puzzle has its own twist, and there was only one puzzle out of the dozens I encountered that seemed to not follow any discernable logic. Some of the puzzles you encounter are often more mini-games than anything, from a simon-says challenge to some challenges that look like they came straight from a Commodore 64. Variety isn't something I was expecting with this, but by god is there a lot.
The only hiccups in design is that once you leave an area, you can't return. Not that I found anyway. The early areas indicate the ending through obvious cues, but some of the last areas aren't as obvious, and it led to me leaving behind a few as yet unfound puzzle pieces (I think 3 in all). Curiously, I was still able to put the world back together without a single piece left out so it's not a big deal, but my OCD aches that I couldn't get the other pieces. That, and the hint system is nearly worthless, and kind of a pain in the butt to charge. You have to collect dozens of bugs for one use, and no matter if it's charged or not they still litter the screen. You won't need the hint system generally though, so it's all minor gripes, but a desire to turn off the bug hints was rather high for me.
There are few games that can put me at piece as easily as this one did, and it served as a wonderful sleepaid after work and the like. For something a little different that harkens back to the Pajama Sam days but with a sense of grace to it, it's really a genuinely pleasant experience, and that is hard to come by these days. Absolutely worth it.

This is a platformer game taken to the extreme. And even so, you'd be better off playing the Brutal Mario hacked game for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System for entertainment value than this.
From the twisted mind of the guy that is so prominently featured in Indie Game: The Movie, you get a meat cube that loves a girl made of bandages and has to rescue her from the infamous Dr. Fetus, a pre-born that is loved by no one. Dejá-vu, the awkward nihilistic tendencies depicted in The Binding of Isaac years later.
But really, it is basically Mario Bros all over again, with the added wall-jump capabilities and a time-based e-peen measurement of how unrealistically good you are at timing-based jumps and devising of plans (if you are actually trying to solve each and every level on your own, of course). The concept isn't new, and what does matter is if you feel pride after completing a challenging level.
Also like The Binding of Isaac, but to great detrimental effect, Super Meat Boy (== SMB != SMB == Super Mario Bros, oh wait, full circle...?) is based on the flash engine if I'm not entirely mistaken, and is a slight upgrade to a version of absolutely free-to-play-ness. Add a few extras and it's all good... right? Not really. And the reason this is detrimental is because of how the input of keys lags sometimes. Needed to jump just a bit earlier? Too bad, the input lagged out and you have to waste another 30 seconds of pure geniously awesome perfection to reach that point you died all over again. And again, and again, and again...
Mind you, Super Meat Boy is not at all a bad game. But Super Meat Boy is annoying on many different levels, and few will actually like it unless they like a) platformer games in a market that refuses to produce high quality and interesting 2D platformers, b) seeing blood squishing out and poluting a level every time your little meat cube golem runs into just about anything the level is made out of (sawblades, needles, fire, you name it) on your next attempt, c) improving your coordination and reaction skills to the point of becoming a mechanically operated robot or d) don't feel like playing anything else at the time.
Also, for the record, my time clocked into the game is not accurate. I used to play Super Meat Boy a lot when it came out, but on a friend's computer. I already had 87 bandages and completed over half of Pink World's normal level, a few of them with bandage. I remember how annoying it was to unlock The Guy/Boy/person that is totally ripped off (presumably with permission) from I Want to be the Guy game, more than two hours of my life. And that's the reason I can't really be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to play this game again now that I own it on my account, even if I would like to increase my achievement percentage to about 50. I've also always resented the ingame suggestion of playing it with a controller; I think it was Super Meat Boy that said something along the lines of "A gamepad is optional, but so is showers. Think about it.": might not be such a bad advice, saving everyone's precious water AND forcing everyone to learn a little something about tolerance towards another, instead of shoving the irrational "good advice" that you're only a "pro gamer" IF you use a controller to play on your computer.
So many things anger me about this game that I simply choose to not recommend it, even if it's a fun game when you don't overthink it and are moderately to highly skilled in platformers. Otherwise avoid like the plague.

I'm not going to judge HITMAN on it's business practices, but judge the game itself. Yes , DRM is annoying, but it's not what bothers me most about this game. It has some excellent pros, but a LOT of horrible cons that make it really far worse than BM or contracts were.
Pros :
- Disguise system is back and improved from BM
- Plenty of ways to complete contracts
- Lots of dialogues to hear
- Good controls
- Good graphics
- Windows of opportunity that disappear if you're not fast enough add tension to the game.
- Voice acting is top notch (aside from the fact there aren't enough VAs) and CG cutscenes are amazing.
Cons :
- Maps are just big for the sake of being big, and 95% of them is irrelevant fodder. BM and contracts had a LOT of interactions that were removed in HITMAN. (Carrying boxes, using cameras, more frequent use of poisons, etc)
- AI is stupid. Extremely stupid. It just goes from A to B with no subtlety , doesn't detect blood, sees bodies through walls sometimes, etc.
- Music is awful. Jesper Kyd asked to be the composer for this game and squeenix refused for some stupid reason , now you're stuck with really forgivable crappy music.
- 47 is no more the "scary cold killer" he used to be. Now he just does his job and his cold-bloodedness now appears as an overall lack of enthusiasm.
- Out of the 4-5 ways that are there to kill the targets , only one or two are effective/risk free in most cases.
- LACK OF CHARACTER. Seriously. The level design just feels off in absolutely every level . The maps are just full of nothing. You barely interact with your enemies anymore , and stuff is just thrown around in places you wouldn't expect.
- Opportunities are either directly pointed at or impossible to find because the maps are ridiculously ♥♥♥♥huge with no good way to find your bearings other than playing them over and over and over and over again.
- Snail pacing . everything is super slow and you spend most of your time waiting for your targets.
- Everyone speaks english in every country ; completely breaks the immersion.
Neutral points :
- If you kill anyone who's not your target , you lose a bunch of points. Going psycho killer isn't possible anymore, at least until you've perfected the mission.
- Bunch of content , but it's non content : elusives, escalation, etc. They're litterally basic missions with less content.
All in all my second least favorite Hitman game, absolution being the first. If you loved blood money, don't expect to relive the same thing here.

I first heard of the 'Borderlands' series when I watched an episode of Game Theory about Handsome Jack (FYI go watch that it's great), and it seemed like fun to me. Eventually, the game was on sale and I gave it a try... Holy cow it didn't disappoint! The story made me care for the characters, the NPC's are funny and making people explode by shooting them never gets old.
Although I personally haven't played it with friends, I noticed many places where co-op would be great. For example: having to go through the Raid on Digistruct Peak by yourself multiple times might get boring (should you not like making people explode), but with a friend or two it becomes more challenging, which could make it more fun to play, and more bearable to play through more than once.
Some games get criticised for their DLC's. Sure, Borderlands 2 has very many, but most of them are character skins and outfits. The playable DLC's, however, are a blast. The wacky yet immersive story of Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon's Keep and the challenges of Mister Torgue's Campaign of Carnage were the most fun for me personally. You might think otherwise, but these are the ones I'd recommend.
No game is perfect, and this one is no different. If you try to defeat a Raid Boss on your own, you have to be quite overleveled (I was lvl 39 when taking on the lvl 32 Hyperius the Invincible, and still had trouble). However, this might also be because I'm just not that great at the game ;). The timed missions are impossible for me to beat (might also be because I'm bad).
All in all, I would most certainly recommend this game. It's a fun experience for you on your own or with some friends. Giant bosses, memorable characters, fun storyline, epic DLC, cool soundtrack... and Handsome Jack.

EverQuest 2 is an MMORPG that has come free to play on Steam in December of 2011. Originally it was a subscription based MMO that released in November of 2004. Before it came onto Steam, you could get a very limited access, free to play account. Now that it's on Steam, the limitations have mostly been lifted.
With 21 races and a whopping 26 classes to choose from, you can be just about anything! Well not with out a little bit of effort. There are Good races and Good classes that require a good race, and the same goes for Evil races and Evil classes. Additionally there are neutral races that can pick any of the classes. But what if you want to be an evil race with a good class? Through the process of a lengthy and repititious quest chain (Which can be started once you hit level 10), you can turn your Ogre Shadowknight to an Ogre Paladin!
With your Ogre Paladin at your command, you are ready to start adventuring! Don't worry, you can further customize your Paladin with the use of Alternate Advancement (AA)! You have, quite literally, hundreds of AAs to choose from to enhance and shape the way your Paladin plays. What's the catch? In order to get these points, you have to fill an AA experience bar, which siphons regular experience from your character as you kill monsters and complete quests. With the free to play account, you're left having to put 50% of your experience gained to the AA points, which will really slow you down and put you behind other leveling zones. In order to remove this restriction, you have to pay the monthly subscrition fee.
Don't want to pay? Well don't worry, you have plenty of areas to level in! There are plenty of quests to do, along with shiny collectable objects lying on the ground for you to acquire and complete collections, which can then be turned in as mini quests. Additionally you can also group up with other people and tackle dungeons to acquire loot and experience, in the typical MMO fassion.
If adventuring is not your thing, you can take up a profession, or tradeskill! You have 11 to choose from, from Weaponsmith to Alchemist, Tinkerer and Carpenter. Carpentry? Yes, it's a thing. Carpentry is used to make furniture for your very own house or guild hall in game!
How is the customer service? Amazing. For the longest time I had shared an account with my Father, and eventually I had several high level characters. Recently he had pushed me to get my own account. I agreed, but I didn't want to sacrifice my characters. So I contacted customer support and of course, for a fee, I was able to get my characters transfered within a day of submitting in a ticket. I was incredibly happy with the customer support from SOE, as they were very kind and understanding.
EverQuest 2 is everything you might expect out of an MMORPG, but with the free to play version, there are a few things I wish they would lighten up on, mainly the Alternative Advancement slider. That's really the biggest turn off from this game for not just myself, but many others as well. It reminds me of a pay-to-win model which is nothing anyone enjoys. You could also argue that it encourages you to go to different zones to quest to get up to level, and it is easy enough to get to one of the zones in question within 5 or 10 minutes, but not everyone wants to leave a quest chain in the middle of it to go half way across the virtual world to level up a little before coming back.
One more thing to mention is that not all of the races and classes are available to play with out paying for them. Out of the 21 races, 19 of them are playable for free. Out of the 26 classes, 24 of them are playable. This really doesn't sound too bad but it is $20 dollars per race*, and $25 dollars per class.
If you don't want to start off with a level 1 character, you can spend $35 dollars on a level 90 character with 320 AA points, equipped powerful gear. Once again the pay-to-win model comes to mind.
Is this game any good? For the amount of content and what you can get out of this game as is, it is definitely worth it. The AA slider issue is something you can work around and can be a blessing. Where some are higher level than you, you may be just as powerful because you have more AAs. Additionally it encourages you to check out other zones. You can be just about anything, you can do just about anything, and yet it all cost next to nothing. Why not give it a try?
*Some races come with extra bundles that costs an extra sum of money.

The insane amount of ways to assassinate your targets alone is well worth the full price of the best Hitman game to date. Other things have been done better on previous entries in the series, but so much is better, that it comes out on top. And, I'm actually a fan of the bold move to make it episodic to listen to the community before launching more episodes.
I'm only two episodes in, and I'm already looking forward to replaying the remaining episodes to death (pun intended etc yada yada and so forth).
Pros
+ Large levels with tons of ways to reach your target
+ Challenge system with XP that rewards players who perfect their gameplay
+ Suberb character handling for a 3rd person game. All the minor flaws in that area from their earlier games are gone.
+ Awards all kinds of psychopaths, whether they like to kill their victims from afar or close up with a screw driver. Almost anything can function as a weapon or killing device.
+ NPC reaction are pretty decent, although dumb enough that you can actually get away with murder. Realistic NPC's would probably just ruin the game.
+ Written to really enjoy replaying. Replaying is actually better than playing the first time. Also the unlock system gives each new replay some added joy and/or subtracted grinding.
+ All play styles have their own rewards.
+ Elusive targets. Targets you can only kill once in seven days, and then they're gone for ever. Might be the most exiciting gameplay I've ever played.
Cons
- Players who don't like doing stuff over and over will finish the game in about three hours.
- Network connection is required, although I have encounter that problem only once in 35 hours of gameplay.
- Big Picture crashes every time I play. This never happens in other games. But I don't know with whom this flaw lies. This forces me to change which screen to use as my primary to play it.
- Jesper Kyd's music is not nearly as good as in Contracts and Blood Money.
- The levels are too clean, too beautiful; I want some grittier atmosphere.
Although I'm just two sixths into the game, I think it's safe to give the game 9 out of 10 stars. There's even a season two pending - I might be inclined to bump it up to ten after that.

A fictional war game where the carrot of choice is dangled in front of the player frequently. The graphics and setting, to me, were the best part of this game. The attention to detail is great and lends a real element of immersion to the world. However, the gameplay, which is where I'd put the most emphasis, I found to be incredibly lackluster. I found myself fighting the controls more than the enemies in the game. This game relies heavily on a cover mechanic (that is also mapped to two other functions) and often times is unresponsive or downright broken. More times than I would have liked to count, I was in cover, was moving along cover, and then all of a sudden would be out of cover and get shot to death. A GAME WITH A COVER FEATURE SHOULD ONLY UNCOVER WHEN I PRESS A BUTTON. OTHERWISE, DON'T FORCE COVER. It could honestly only be a problem with the PC version if the game was designed around consoles, but regardless, it happened enough times to sour my taste to it by the end. The next gripe about gameplay is the ammo system. The devs clearly didn't program this aspect of the game well at all. If 30 enemies are bearing down on you with automatic weapons nonstop, you'd think they'd have a few magazines worth of ammo on them, eh? But no, if you fight 30 guys and go to collect ammo after a fight, they will have like 4 different varieties of guns amongst them and if you are lucky, you will find about 20 rounds of ammo for a gun that suits your current needs. All the immersion the graphics and attention to world-detail that were brought really just collapsed under this awful system. To sort of strengthen this point, the ammo cap for all weapons is ridiculously low for the amount of enemies per section. So, the game is really designed around keeping you low on ammo the whole time for arbitrary reasons. The gunplay by itself, though, is fine and actually enjoyed it a fair amount. The story is nothing to write home about, although it's what everyone who plays this game talks about. They were going for a Fight Club vibe where everything you do makes sense in a sane and insane context. Otherwise, it's obvious early on you have a soldier going rogue that you can't do anything about (oreders at the outset were to radio for more troops. They get disobeyed like 30 minutes into the game) unless you just quit the game. The main protag's name is Walker, too, which I find highly ironic considering how many cinematic, slow walking scenes are incorporated throughout the gameplay. It didn't add anything to the story for me and could have just as easily been achieved by a cutscene. I think my overall impression of this game is that it should have a been a decent movie, but instead they made a mediocre game out of it. I would personally not recommend anyone I know to play this game, hence the score, but if you are absolutely dead set on playing this, it's worth maybe one playthrough with Flawless Widescreen on PC to bump up the FOV. I also wouldn't pay the full $30+ asking price; definitely check it out on sale if you must.

Overall a very good post apocalyptic game, a very good
game, but not without some minor flaws.
Pros:
+ Very well optimized, performance was optimum the vast majority of the time.
+ Game has really nice graphics.
+ Each area is distinctive from the others and have their own challenges.
+ Chumbucket is a great NPC
+ A solid story with, by even
standards, some dark moments.
+ Camps are all unique in design and present their own challenges
+ Taking down convoys is fantastic, although maybe the game could have had more.
+ The storms are absolutely wild.
+ A great variety in enemy and enemy vehicles.
Cons:
- The camp Top Dogs are all the same and all have to be defeated in pretty much the same way. I would have liked  more variety.
- The Archangel cars seemed insignificant in the context of the game. Apart from 1 mission where it was necessary to use an Archangel, I stuck with the main car, the Magnum Opus for the vast majority of the game.
- Balancing issues. I maxed out Max's skills in the 2nd area, so the rest of the combat in the game became a formality.  Camp difficulty made no difference because of how powerful Max was. In contrast, the car seemed to more balanced with each new area being difficult at first when it came to car combat.
If I had a choice in playing a modern post apocalyptic game between Mad Max or Fallout 4, it would be Mad Max.

Being one of the most played games in my steam library, I feel I owe this game a review. Unfortunatly, due to my inability to review, here's my personal pros and cons:
Pros:
+ Really active dev team, I've been with this game since alpha 13 and it's amazing how much work the devs have put in even after all these years.
+ I love the ability to play it your way, you can develop a massive prison working closely with each individual inmate to keep them happy and work hard to reform and rehabilitate them so they are ready for the world on realse. Alternatively, you can get 1000 max-security prisoners, 20 armed guards, turn on freefire and wait.
+ Great amounts of polish that just make the game that much better
+ Mod support, the best way to ensure a game stands the test of time. Being able to dowload such a wide varity of mods from texture packs to complete mechanic changes keeps the game alive and fresh so no two prisons ever develop the same way.
+ Downloadable maps allow even the most innept of architects to feel acomplished by maintaining someone elses (often considerably better) prision.
+ Time lapse camera built in is a really nice touch, especally when building massive prisions in the sandbox mode.
+ Escape mode, not very polished but still a really good addition, more so now that you can escape from community prisions.
Cons:
- Optimisation is poor. My largest prision has about 700 innmates but after that the game was quite simply unplayable. I was hitting 20 FPS max with my RX 480 with a highly inconsistant frame rate which is a real shame as making massive prisions is one of the most fun things to do.
- Starting conditions, you always start with $30k, no matter what unless you mod the game. For newer players it would be nice if there were different starting conditions, i.e: on easy you get more money and some basic buildings already in play, medium starts the game how it is currently and hard could give you less money to start with or remove the ability to change prisoner flow.
- More of a challenge needed. This is sort of linking to my last point but after 300+ hours (at the time of this review), even max security prisoners are easy to look after, we need the option to take in super max or increase the percentage of prisoners who are in gangs.
TL;DR: Get this game, it is one of the best sandboxes I have ever played.

The mechanics are a bit confusing at first, but very easy to learn. For instance, to start a fire you need to cut down a tree with your ax, then place the log in the firepit near the cabin and add a match. You can use this fire to cook things you shoot with your bow and arrow (in winter) or trap (3 small sticks and a rock).
Definitely worth checking out if you are looking for a bit of nostalgia, but a lot more than depth than old-school 8-bit games.

defenitely recommend, especially if you like platformers, or metroidvania games of any kind.

This is an addictive simulator in which you are tasked to manage a prison. There is a decent tutorial at the start which brings you up to speed on the basics of running the prison, as well as having a story with it which was a nice touch. If you are a player that enjoys micromanagement, then this game is definitely one that you'll enjoy, as you have control over almost every aspect of the prison. However, this can also be a deterrent for those that can't quite be bothered because if you don't keep some particular things in check, it will lead to problems in your prison which you'll end up having to solve and deal with the consequences. The graphics are simplistic but suits the style, as is allows for easy tracking of what's going on, and the sounds are nice to. There are many online guides to this game which is good because after the tutorial, the game doesn't hold you hand. In addition to this, they have integrated steam workshop which has allowed for many mods and prebuilt prisons to be experimented with. The developers have been great since early access, constantly pushing updates for the game that fixes issues for the game and adds new features. If you're looking to get sucked away for many hours into a simulator, then i'd definitely recommend this one.

Ok, so what is this game? Well, you build prisons, with an available minigame to escape any of the prisons you or the internet have made. Pretty simple.
Now simple, does generally describe the graphics, but that's really just art styling, and it is generally appealing to look at. Nothing flashy, nothing eye-damaging. A+ here.
The gameplay is deviously complex however. The devs went through a painstaking process to get all these details, and I think it shows. You can learn more on the development of this game via the dev's youtube channel:
You can micromanage a lot of your prison, and you don't have too, either. There is also the choice of whether you're going to be a hardass and make your prisoners never want to commit crimes again, or if you want to reform them and give them the tools to live a prosperous life on the outside. A+++.
Now, why on Earth would I give a very slim description on this game? Well, I thought the thing I really needed to focus on is the developers. I was pleasantly surprised by Arkham Origins and it eased the bad taste of disappointment Arkham City left in its wake.  Seeing Gotham ‘pre-Arkham City’ felt like a warm trip down ‘Nostalgia Boulevard’ and the plot of taking place during a snowy Christmas Eve brought back memories of some of the old classic Batman tales.  Combat has changed little from the previous two games except possibly being a little easier and with more powerful abilities; and the game is better for it.
I expected it to feel claustrophobic with villains like ‘City’ but fortunately they balanced it nicely.  Origin stories are done to death these days but that seemed handled properly as well.  Even with all the side quests and Riddler nonsense the game ended just before the mark where it begins to get old…a lesson probably learned from its predecessor’s mistake of never-ending collectibles.
Most people hold Arkham City as ‘the’ Batman game but I think this one comes out on top.

The sequel to Black Ops met some expectations with flying colors, but let others fall miserably.
PROS:
+Campaign introduces a new RTS-like gamemode for "special operations," a welcome idea and fine game mode to play.
+Customizable loadouts in the Campaign!
+You can make decisions in the campaign to affect the ending.
+Highly balanced multiplayer (again!) with only one or two really overpowered guns (again!)
+Multiplayer with Bots! (In almost all modes, now!)
+Far more customizable emblems!
+Secondary weapon/knife camo in multiplayer!
+CODpoints replaced with unlock tokens, a better representation of what CODpoints on Black Ops 1 should've been.
+Nazi Zombies!
CONS:
-While the story is good, it's far from the narrative in Black Ops 1.
-The story in BO2 ignores the epilogue from BO1, which would've made for a far better introduction.
-No dedicated servers
-DLC pack unlocks a weapon for use in Multiplayer.
-Significant downgrade in the quality of Zombies maps.
A disappointment after Black Ops 1, but a solid game nonetheless.

This game returns to the fundamentals of Hitman by giving the player a well rounded stealth mechanic, gorgeous environments and a target.
Each episode features a new area (Prologue has 2 smaller separate areas) for the player to experiment with and an objective. Within each location, the player will encounter a variety of "Opportunities" leading them towards one of the many ways to execute a target, often with humorous or explosive results. This help guide new players through the map, but can be disabled at any time for players who prefer to discover things on their own.
After the intial mission on each map, replayability comes in the flavor of "Challenges" and "Escalations".
The "Challenges" are used as suggestions to alter play style and entice players in finding new and interesting ways into areas or different methods of executing a target (Weapon, Outfit, Map specific accidents...).
"Escalations" are repeatable missions with increasing difficulty. After each escalation you are presented with the same scenario, but with an added objective (additional target) or encumbrance (Surveillance Cameras, Time limits...).
The overarching story is limited to a few interaction between the player, Agent 47, and their handler, Diana Burnwood, the remaining narration is limited to target briefings from Burnwood before every missing.
This game does not feature a story campaign like Hitman: Absolution nor does it have multiplayer, but does bring back its "Contracts" mode.
"Contracts" allows you to create and share a contract with other users and friends with your own selection of objectives, on the map of your liking, to compete on the leaderboards.
This title also adds "Elusive Targets" which are unique targets release for a limited time and can be restarted as many times as you please as long as the mission does not end. Once ended, regardless of the outcome, the mission can never be restarted.
The game does not take itself seriously and you will be deeply disappointed if that is what you are hoping going in. The main interaction, the AI NPCs, are not the sharpest and given the lack of difficulty settings, which were present in the previous iteration, your success will be determined by your flow of execution and not your precision. The game is therefore much more lenient and the pleasure will be had by coming up with solutions on the fly as opposed to perfect execution and planning. This will still allow players who love perfection to restart and rerun their steps dozens of times, but won't aggrevate players who simply want to get through the game.
But to those players who simply want to play through the game, be warned that the majority of the content of the game is reused content. From "Challenges" to "Contracts", if the fundamental mechanics are not something you would see yourself enjoying then stay away from this title.
As for the rest of the players, the episodic development flow will keep you satiated with new content every few months and have you come back every few weeks to put your skills to work on "Elusive Targets".
For people who like stealth action and have that "OCD" itch, this game is definetly for you, but for those who are seeking for a more standard triple "A" title, I would point you in another direction (Deus Ex: Mankind Divided or Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain).

Now that all episodes are finished and the game is complete this is definitely a great game. It goes back to how the original Hitman titles were: more open, sandbox type games in a specific setting, instead of being a single player/checkpoint design.
A WORD ON ASSASSINATION OPTIONS:
There are 6 primary locations to play in for the story. Each one has 1-3 targets and a couple have secondary objectives besides just assassination. How you go about assassinating targets is up to you.
As far as gameplay, I'm really just going to focus on the method of going about figuring out what to do on each level. There are so many options on each level to play in different ways that the game developers created a system called "opportunities". You can go into your menu and start tracking an oportunity and the game becomes a directed experience where you can follow an on screen display to figure out what to do to accomplish a certain type of assassination. The on screen display will direct you towards conversations that you can overhear, or a specific disguise that you have to get to infiltrate an area, things like that. This system really helps to teach you what is possible on each level.
You can also play and figure things out yourself by not tracking the opportunities, which is what I did, but your assassinations will likely be a lot more messy.
CONTENT TO KEEP YOU BUSY:
As for content in the game there is a single player experience which has you killing specific story targets and between each level a movie plays that furthers a loose story. Like I said there is a lot of different things to do on each level so a lot of the content revolves around that aspect. You're supposed to play the same level in different ways to gain experience and unlock items, disguises, and different entry points to begin a stage at.
Other types of content are: contracts, which are player made assassinations on the same 6 stages. Players can decide which NPCs to assinate and how. Playing and beating these will result in experience. There are also escalating targets which also take place on the same 6 stages, but the targets are different than in single player and it gets more difficult with each stage, of which there are 5 stages for each escalation mission/map. Elusive targets are a one chance assassination that comes around every couple weeks. These are made by IO Interactive and finishing them gains you points toward new suit unlocks.
BOTTOM LINE:
Basically all the content, no matter what it is, is just about different methods to assassinate different NPCs on the same 6 maps. If you find the general gameplay fun, and want to experience all the different options available to assassinate targets, then you'll like doing all those extra things I mentioned and the game could be played for a long time. If you just want to experience each of the 6 levels, get the assassinations done in whatever way, and see the story then the game is about 6-8 hours long.

Solid game if you can get it on sale. I can't recommend it at full price because of the length. It comes with a whole lot of replayable content, different ways to assassinate, but again it's replayed/rehashed. Theres 6 unique places, and two extra that are prologue content. You don't get any weapons except a 1911 silenced and your piano wire garrote, but doing missions and completing achievements unlocks additional weapons, starting locations, and suits. The original story is pretty engaging and not on rails like absolution was. You're able to take targets from any angle and however you choose. The game has a story, but it's not focused on a linear progression level by level model. You're given an area, a sandbox, and you can kill your targets however you choose.
My only complaint is more content for it's price. Again don't buy this at full price. I was able to get it for $27 with all DLC. Which reminds me, all of the missions are split into DLC. I'm not sure why they chose to do this, it's a game, not a TV show. It was probably frustrating to have bought the game when it first came out and have only a couple missions to do. I still largely enjoyed the game.
The other thing I liked is that this iteration was more true to stealth game form. Where absolution was more lenient on getting hit, and killing people, in Hitman you get overwhelmed quickly when guards are alerted. You won't find yourself in large gun fights simply because you're more likely to die. Non-Target kills will reduce your score, and some killing blows will make more noise than others. Throwing knives, axes, or whatever else, or punching someone will be audible. Then there is the disguise mechanic so you can hide in plain sight so long as you don't blow the cover. Speaking of disguises, many disguises will be required to pass through different areas of the mission site. Some areas are blocked off by low security, others higher security, requiring you to adapt and find a secret way past or get a disguise fitting of the location you're in.
I've sunk 12 hours into the game just going through the missions. I'll probably go back through some and do some of challenges. I've also heard they are creating a season 2... which I still hate the DLC model, but at this point I'd buy into season 2 for the gameplay and new areas.

I went into this game warily. I had heard how it wasn't nearly as good as its predecessors, but after completing the game I'm not sure what all the hate was about.
The cons of this game: Yes, it is glitchy. But only sometimes and nothing at all that would make the game unplayable. They had one instance in the game where the dialogue should have been a cutscene, but instead used the player models.
The improvements: The unlock-system for abilities I really liked. It allowed you to buy all the later/better abilities after you've bought the ones before it (all abilities are connected and buying one unlocks a few others). The shock gloves are a "gadget" that make you much stronger that you can active after racking up hits on enemies, and they are GREAT.
As far as story goes, I thought the Arkham Origins story was pretty good. I really loved the Arkham City story and it kept me interested and wanting to progress in the game. This game's story felt shorter, but it seemed to be more well polished. Batman actually learns a moral lesson (no spoiling what it is) and the sudden plot twists in the story were very cool.
When it comes to side quests, I think overall I liked Arkham City's slightly better. Origins had half really good side quests and half not-great side quests. In City they were all just pretty good side quests, so it averaged out to be little better than Origins.
Riddler Challenges. in Arkham City there were 282 Riddler Trophies, and then a bunch more scanning riddles besides that. As a person who likes collecting things and 100%ing games, this was even a little too much for me. In Origins I am SO GLAD they took down the count, with only 200 trophies (called Datapacks in this game) to be found, and no scanning things.
Overall, this game was pretty good. No, it was not as good as City, but it was still a good game and got a lot more hate than it deserved. The only thing I wish is that the creators had ironed out the glitches BEFORE initially releasing the game.

+Highly balanced multiplayer (again!) with only one or two really overpowered guns (again!)
+Multiplayer with Bots! (In almost all modes, now!)
+Far more customizable emblems!
+Secondary weapon/knife camo in multiplayer!
+CODpoints replaced with unlock tokens, a better representation of what CODpoints on Black Ops 1 should've been.
+Nazi Zombies!
CONS:
-While the story is good, it's far from the narrative in Black Ops 1.
-The story in BO2 ignores the epilogue from BO1, which would've made for a far better introduction.
-No dedicated servers
-DLC pack unlocks a weapon for use in Multiplayer.
-Significant downgrade in the quality of Zombies maps.
A disappointment after Black Ops 1, but a solid game nonetheless.

Solid game if you can get it on sale. I can't recommend it at full price because of the length. It comes with a whole lot of replayable content, different ways to assassinate, but again it's replayed/rehashed. Theres 6 unique places, and two extra that are prologue content. You don't get any weapons except a 1911 silenced and your piano wire garrote, but doing missions and completing achievements unlocks additional weapons, starting locations, and suits. The original story is pretty engaging and not on rails like absolution was. You're able to take targets from any angle and however you choose. The game has a story, but it's not focused on a linear progression level by level model. You're given an area, a sandbox, and you can kill your targets however you choose.
My only complaint is more content for it's price. Again don't buy this at full price. I was able to get it for $27 with all DLC. Which reminds me, all of the missions are split into DLC. I'm not sure why they chose to do this, it's a game, not a TV show. It was probably frustrating to have bought the game when it first came out and have only a couple missions to do. I still largely enjoyed the game.
The other thing I liked is that this iteration was more true to stealth game form. Where absolution was more lenient on getting hit, and killing people, in Hitman you get overwhelmed quickly when guards are alerted. You won't find yourself in large gun fights simply because you're more likely to die. Non-Target kills will reduce your score, and some killing blows will make more noise than others. Throwing knives, axes, or whatever else, or punching someone will be audible. Then there is the disguise mechanic so you can hide in plain sight so long as you don't blow the cover. Speaking of disguises, many disguises will be required to pass through different areas of the mission site. Some areas are blocked off by low security, others higher security, requiring you to adapt and find a secret way past or get a disguise fitting of the location you're in.
I've sunk 12 hours into the game just going through the missions. I'll probably go back through some and do some of challenges. I've also heard they are creating a season 2... which I still hate the DLC model, but at this point I'd buy into season 2 for the gameplay and new areas.
Hitman is the best stealth game I've ever played.

So after playing 25 hours (as of this review) I can safely say that the game is worth buying. I bought it from bundlestars for $6, and I can say it is definitely well worth the price. I would have even bought it at full price and would feel the same about the game. Yes the game is heavily grindy, and quite linear, but it's a very fun linear. The game runs well, and while there is a bug here and there, it is quite smooth. The bug in specific that only really annoys me, is when you're in the garage menu and you click on an option, it  freezes and cannot be closed. The game itself is still working, the menu just freezes up, so it requires a restart.
Pros:
Exploration
Beat 'em up style combat (really simple, no fancy movements like Chivalry, as an example)
Driving (While quite arcadesque, still very fun.)
Customization (Limited, but not very limited.)
Cons:
Linear
Extremely short story, and quite boring.
Repetitive grinding. (Go to location A for scrap, location B for scrap, location C for parts for strongholds, rinse and repeat)
There are more pros and cons, but these are the ones that came to mind that stood out quite a bit at the time of this review. Otherwise I would rate this game (personally) an 8.5/10.
If you want to grind for all the upgrades go ahead. The game is fun and worth a ton of hours but it does get stale at a point.

Best simulator game EVER.  I would give it 9/10.
Editing my review while closing up one 300hr's. I will tell you about it.
So, first you have like two roads to go. You can either go down the singleplayer or the multiplayer road. I either of them you will have to start a new company, deliver some loads, take a loan, buy a truck and try not to loose it all. The first part will be quite interesting in both of the roads, but it will be harder in multiplayer if you choose a crowded place to start in because there are a lot of people that ram you. Let's say you've gaven back the loan and are running smoothly with a steady amount of money. This is where it changes. In singleplayer you should probably buy another truck and get workers, so you basically don't really need to do much, but in multiplayer you can't have workers (tehnically you can, but they don't do anything) so you probably upgrade your own truck or just buy a new one for yourself. That's about the interesting part.
Things that I very much like about this game-
*A very nice trucking comunity to interact with, and you can see it in multiplayer (Stuck? No worries, someone will help you even if they break their truck in the end)
*Updates pretty reguraly, you get new trucks and lots of other new stuff
*It is very relaxing at most of the time. Sit back, listen to music and drive.
*You can play it on a potato that is about to fry. When I started to play this game, I had a laptop. Still was very fun.
*Lot's of DLC's to get, gotta get them all. And the best part of it is that they don't tease you and put pressure on you to buy them like Ubisoft and EA does.
*Mods, lot's of them. Want to drive an Optimus prime with like 3000hp? Yes, you get to do it. Want to drive an Opel? Also possible.
At the end, I suggest you buying it but, ofcourse,  it's not for everyone.

Contrary to my steam play time I have well over 1,000hrs invested in EQ2 with my 3 endgame characters. This was by far the most fun I've ever had in a generic style MMORPG.
I did play WoW for a while but the graphical style of WoW and the over simplified skill system kinda bored me to death.
Everquest utilizes an in depth skill system that requires you think before using points in a particular tree. Granted classes are not really open like in some of the new MMOS but the class itself has a lot of customization.
Example: A wizard has class restrictions forbidding the use of heavy armor and a variety of weapons. But it allows a rounded out skill selection including element proficiency and damage/debuff modifiers.
All in all I strongly recommend this game for any and all MMO players. F2Players are not restricted like in many other F2Play games. Level cap is 85 and the auctionhouse requires F2Play auction tickets to use otherwise buying the All access pass makes most everything free besides Expansion stuff.

Batman: Arkham Origins is a prequel to Arkham Asylum and a sequel to The Land Before Time.
You play as a younger and less handsome Batman, when he was just starting his career of ILLEGAL vigilantism and his parents were slightly less dead. But still very dead by normal human standards. The game takes place on Christmas eve, a time for celebration and also a time when the diner turns on its heater in the alley and I can be warm at night. A man called Roman Sionis,  Negrodomis aka: the Black Mask and totally the main villain for the entire game has hired several assassins to come make Batman like his parents for the low low price of 50 million Vietnamese Dongs. These villains include Bane, Deathstroke, Deadshot, and several villains you've never actually heard of.
The combat is much the same as it was the last two games, only with a few more features, such as electric gloves that also double as a nifty way to power your cellphone. Much like a microwave. It also adds a few new enemy types, such as discount Jet Li, and roid-monsters. But old enemies return as well like the random mook, and of course those creatures I am deathly of: girls.
Stealth is pretty much the same, only this time you also get an upgrade to your spider-man web in the form of a gun that allows you to strap people to gargoyles so you can wrap them up and suck out their juicy goo like the evil man-spider you are. You awful, awful monster.
The collectible riddler side-mission returns, only this time it reminds me of my high-school years: long and heartbreaking. The riddles and Batman trivia is gone in favor of collecting datapacks that I spent more time doing than I care to admit. There are also these invisible icons left behind by some chump called Anarky, and much like the gay agenda, they are everywhere.
The game itself is rather jarring compared to the first two Arkham games. While Rocksteady made a rather loving tribute to the Dark Knights in comic and cartoon, Arkham Origins feels much like the movies, taking many assets from the Dark Knight trilogy and clashing themes together much like the skin tone between me and my African twin. Though you can use one of the many skins for Batman after you complete the game, most of them tend to not fit with the theme the game is going for, so you're left out like a DnD nerd at a Fantasy Football meet up.
The game also gives you the option of playing as Deathstroke in the challenge maps, a character that is rather easy to beat even on the hard difficulty and only shows up maybe twice through the entire thing. And even then, he's just a re-skin of Robin from Arkham City. So you're basically just playing as Robin during his rebellious teenage years.
This all being said, would I actually recommend Batman's third crusade through the streets of Angsty Metropolis? I guess, if you liked the first two. The side missions are unfulfilling and the Riddler missions make me want to rethink my life choice as a professional street Luchadore. But the game still held my attention for longer than I care to admit, and I still like to look at Bruce's chisled jaw and amazing abs.
That still doesn't make me gay.

When I played this game, I had very mixed feelings on it. On one hand, you had the combat and stealth systems whose only real change since 'City' have been the implementation of more gadgets. On the other, you have something that previous game was kind of lacking in; a long, fulfilling story and characters. Villains, both major and minor, are introduced in a way that makes them feel as new as they are meant to be.
Unfortunately, there is a big catch with this game. Small bugs still remain in the game, the kind that should've been fixed ages ago but haven't - and at least one big whopper which is quite the common encounter for many in the smack middle of the game; related to an elevator.
Still I recommend this game if you've enjoyed the other two in the Arkham series, but due to the number of aggravating bugs present I'd suggest grabbing it on a sale.

Creative, fun, expansive, and with frequent updates to improve all those fronts.
It's inexpensive at worst and fantastically cheap at best. It has quality, polish, and everything else a game should have.
The only reason not to consider it is if you just hate the genre - it, reduced to its simplest form, is MineCraft fused with a bit of bullet hell and dungeon crawler. If you dislike that sort of game, perhaps avoid this.
If not, it's a sure purchase, and one of the few you can make.
Otherwise, it's great fun. A large world and adventure, lots of different ways to arrange gear for best effect, 3 major character classes to build around (though it's totally free what you do) challenging bosses and it really is just nice and varied.
MineCraft suffers from becoming somewhat boring after a while due to lack of variety. Terraria has a fantastic amount of variety - I use the game only for comparison in terms of style, not in terms of substance.
Consider it. Even if you do dislike the genre, I really doubt you can go wrong for the price.

I'm still extremely iffy about recommending Prison Architect, mostly because it took the develops a whole FOUR MONTHS after releasing the game fully; not just in Early Access, but after releasing the goddämn motherfûcking 1.0 VERSION of it to add some ACTUAL optimization to what was an absolutely unplayable mess beforehand.
But then again, I think back on the time I've spent with this game, and I can't really NOT recommend it and keep what tiny excuse for a conscience that I have intact.
There is no music in it, and the sound is nothing to cheer for either, but neither factor is a deal-breaker.
The graphics are charming at best, and somewhat awkward and backwards at worst. However, that's no deal-breaker either.
Now, what CAN be a deal-breaker is the rather extremely unfair difficulty level of the game. Even if you start out on Easy, all you've got to spend at the start are a few grand, and with this meager amount of money, you're expected to build/achieve the following in just ONE DAY:
A canteen and a kitchen (latter being extremely expensive). A shower room. A holding cell and/or a fully fledged cellblock. Some form of a utilities structure for your power generator and water pump. A staff room. A common room. A visitation room. An isolation cellblock. A reception area. A set of offices for ALL of your administrators (minimum of 4 for your essential dudes). A chapel. A parole court.
And all of that while managing your finances and balancing the rather enormous amount of money you'll be spending on wages, vs the ludicrously TINY amounts of money you gain from taking on new prisoners.
Granted, you can start out each of the rooms I mentioned earlier as fairly small structures, but that still leaves you with at least one of two problems: you'll either have to continuously expand on an already established structure in order to accomodate a growing prisoner population, OR you'll have to continuously demolish your smaller structures and rebuild them elsewhere as larger ones, in order to make room for expanding the other ones, because you didn't plan 15 years ahead.
Simply put, the economical aspects of this game are absolutely INSANE. There is challenging gameplay in management games, such as starting out on Hard in SimCity 4, and then there's just extremely poor balancing.
There really is no room for newbies in Prison Architect, reader, so unless you're HIGHLY experienced with this sorta game, you may find this title a bit TOO much to handle. (And yes, I KNOW THAT GRANTS EXIST, but they give you a ONE-TIME chunk of money, not a continuous flow of income, so in the long run, they do just about dïck!)
But putting aside the pretty fûcking retärdedly poor balance issues, the game DOES offer a truly unique game with a very distinct style, with enough similarities to other management titles such as Theme Hospital or StarTopia, to make it at least SOMEWHAT accessible to "outside" players as well.
And lemme tell you, very few games can manage to make a situation like a prison riot or a fire feel equal parts frustratingly hectic, and equal parts adrenaline-inducingly exhilarating! Sending your armed guards into a particularly violent canteen to sort out the baddies with brute force has an almost cruel, oppressive feel to it, and this may just be my evilness speaking: I LIKE IT!
Adding to that, the prisoners are quite annoyingly stupid at times, as is the AI in general, but they're also frighteningly clever. They do extremely dumb things at times, like attacking snitches right near armed guards (despite not being the Fearless types), but I guess they would'nt be in prison if they truly were criminal masterminds.
What I'd like to see being added to the game, though, would be a significant boost to the GUARDS' AI as well. They behave extremely stupidly, and this without fault. Say a fight breaks out between 8 prisoners, for some contrived reason, and only 1 guard is present. What does he do? Does he shout at the prisoners to stop? Does he call for back-up? Does he try to separate the prisoners and simply keep them away from each other until help arrives? No, no and a huge resounding NO.
Instead, the dumbäss motherfûcker just charges in, baton in hand, and starts beating up one and only ONE prisoner at a time, ignoring the fact that if it's a 6 vs 2 scenario, the 2 are gonna be dead long before the guard has subdued even the FIRST of the damn convicts. So that's fûcking dumb. Personally, I'm hoping the devs will add some sort of a radio or walkie-talkie to the guards' arsenal, maybe unlockable through "research" (or buraeucracy as it's called in-game), that'll let them call for reinforcements during particularly nasty fights.
Anyway, all in all, PA is a game that's fairly unique, so I can't trash on it TOO much, but it has some pretty major issues still. So all in all, I'm giving it a VERY tentative recommendation here. If it's on a, say... 50% sale, it's definitely worth it. But full price? Nope, not even close to worth it. 6.4/10

Let me start this off by saying i have played this game far more than most other people or reviewers so i feel i have more experience with this game and hence ability to comment on it than most others. This is also the only negative review i've ever written on something.
I fell in love with the "concept" and "potential" of the game early on hence why i bought it. Sadly, the game has SERIOUS flaws and bugs, many of which have existed for YEARS without being fixed. Don't get me wrong, they have ATTEMPTED to fix many of the core systems but they are still broken to various degrees and i expect always will be. They moved development staff off a long time ago onto other things. The bugs are lucky to get addressed, if you check the bug tracker tons of them have been unaddressed for years.
Some of the bugs are small, some are large, some are game breaking. Most you won't really notice if you keep your prison to 25-50 people and only start showing up the larger your prison. But where is the fun in a small prison? I have large 500 inmate + prisons, including a master one i've been working on that would support thousands. Well good luck with that, what are small issues in small prisons, only amplify to be huge game breaking issues in larger ones.
It is extraordinarily frustrating for me having seen the potential for this title early on, to have gotten my hopes so high, and then seeing how the development has been handled by this studio. They pretty much seem to have 1-2 part time developers on it while they rake in millions off the concept. Other game studios re-invest money to staff to fix things and release new features, not Introversion. They just keep your money and ignore outstanding bugs that have existed for years.
Now with the new launch of the xbox version they finally come out and admit they haven't handled bugs properly. But the truth of the matter is nothing is going to change, it would have years ago if it was going to. This is a pure PR move as they weren't seeing the sales they wanted and were seeing people upset with the purchase and negative reviews. They are only going to be fixing small things in the newest systems like temp/weather, still ignoring the real issues with the actual core systems that all prisons require like cooking/food, laundry, prison danger that leads to rioting, janitorial, etc.
So in the end let me say this, the concept is great, the execution is poor. If you keep your prisons small you'll be mostly fine. But when you play the game, you'll want to build bigger and better. You too will start seeing problems. If you get too big they will be game breaking, and you will be beating your head up against a wall, frustrated,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off, and wishing for years they'd just fix it for you, and in the end being disappointed and heart broken when they don't.

Like the previous Black Ops, this game is basically 3 items: campaign, multiplayer and zombies. All of which offer some really satisfying gameplay but have their ups and downs. Across all modes, I got all achievements and have spent over 200 hours total. (42 hours in campaign, 108 hours in zombies and 89 hours in multiplayer.) So definitely worth the money/time, however I would only buy this on a sale, especially since the base price has not gone down since this launched. Also, definitely buy the Digital Deluxe edition, as it includes World at War. Side tip for Canadians: if you can pick up a boxed copy of this game, I've seen it heavily discounted at many places. I found a copy for 10$ at Staples (they were clearing out inventory) which is much cheaper than it's lowest price on Steam. And yes, this boxed copy can get redeemed on Steam too.
Campaign: while at times the story was a bit cluttered, I really applaud Treyarch for the direction they went in. It's how you evolve an annualized franchise. I was genuinely interested in seeing the different endings and how to accomplish them. And although the strike force missions weren't that well executed, it's also a really fresh idea. One thing that did drive me bananas was the quality of the cutscenes. It's all pre-rendered but at a lower resolution so it looks like♥♥♥♥♥ Apart from that, there were some great scenes and levels in the game, and a really good villain that almost made me feel sorry for him rather than just hate him.
Multiplayer: Overall, it's kind of more of the same, but it didn't suck me in as much as the multiplayer in the first Black Ops. The fact that they updated killstreaks to scorestreaks is great, that's all I would wish on the original. And the pick 10 system is also pretty well done. It's just the core part didn't feel as good. I disliked a lot of  maps, and grinding for better unlocks is yet again such a ♥♥♥♥ing pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Overall, the game was balanced which is obviously great, but I don't know, there was just something about it that didn't really capture me as much.
Zombies: the base game comes with one map, Tranzit, and I think it's pretty bad. A lot of really interesting ideas but very poorly implemented; these ideas were much more annoying than being remotely close to fun. There are a few new game modes, but absolutely nobody plays them and they weren't really fun to begin with. The DLC maps are MUCH better however, and take many of the features first introduced in Tranzit and make them fantastic.
Overall, I'd give this game a 7.0/10. It's a good package. Great campaign, decent multiplayer and okay zombies mode. If you are interested in the Season Pass (which I would say is a must for zombies) buy it on a sale, (where it's hit 50% off) and it'll be worth it. Honestly, I didn't get a chance to play the new multiplayer maps that much because of population issues. I ended up disabling my Season Pass every time I played multiplayer just so I could get into matches. I'd give the Season Pass about a 5.8/10. It's definitely above average; great zombies maps, and the multiplayer maps I did play were pretty good, but it's just so expensive.

After the success of Ori and the blind Forest, Moon Studios release the Definitive Edition of Ori, a subtle addition to the original game that doesn't detract from the original. It takes what made Ori great and added new movement tech and a new area to explore as well as some additional story involving Naru. If you played the original and loved it, then it's definitely worth it to pick up the Definitive Edition to relive the fun.

Ori and the Blind Forest is a platformer that I can't recommend enough. The story is deep and engaging, platforming tight and difficult, and overall, it's a ton of fun. This game is one of more difficult platformers I've played as of late, but it has a pleasant charm to everything.
The story follows your character known as Ori from where you're tasked with the aide of your light friend Sein to restore the forest of Nibel back to it's former glory after a cataclysmic event happens that ends up killing everything. The main antagonist is a huge owl known as Kuro who exists to make your day a little worse each time you meet her. There's more to her than meets the eye though. I'm not going to spoil anything here. There is a small amount of narration and the rest is animation and imagery that sells the emotions of it all very well.
The graphics are quite good. Everything is 2D, but it has this painted and brushed look that bursts with color where it needs to. The scenery of each major area varies just enough to stand out and everything matches. The game really does look like a painting.
As aforementioned, this game is a platformer and a difficult one at that. You will die, A LOT. Having that said, there weren't too many times that I was actually frustrated with it. Gameplay can be broken up into two categories: Free-roaming and chase/escape sequences. There are important plot points that describe why each chase/escape sequence happens, so I'll not go into that. Just know that they're there. Now where the gameplay really shines is in all of the abilities you get. You have the standard ones such as Double Jump, Wall Climb, Swim without a breath meter... but then there are the unique ones, my favorite being Bash. This is a skill where you slow down time and latch onto an enemy or projectile. During this time, you're given a direction to choose and that's the direction you'll launch yourself. As a result, the projectile or enemy you caught will be launched in the opposite direction which leads to great puzzle solutions and just an excellent way to keep safe. Moving on, I should mention that there's a unique energy system that you consume a point for either a powerful attack, to throw a light ball for puzzle solving, and even to save. Save often. There is NO auto-saving, which can be jarring and sometimes they throw you into a situation where you can't get enough energy back to save and have to tread lightly. Did I mention this game was hard? You're made of paper practically, because it's very easy to die. Just some food for thought. :)
TL;DR:
Pros:
- Excellent graphics that remind me of a painting
- Fun and engaging gameplay with unique abilities to protect yourself
- Tight platforming and stellar level design
- Emotional and deep story
Cons:
- This game is HARD. You will die often.
- No auto-save through areas. You must manually save and consume energy to do so. You can find yourself being brought far back if you didn't save for a bit
- Short. The main story could probably be beaten in under 3 hours; in fact, there's an achievement to do so!
Overall rating: 9/10. I wish it was longer because I'd love to keep playing. It's fantastic and I hope they come out with a sequel. The story could allude to there being a sequel depending on how you interpret it.

Years ago I picked up a old snes title by the title of Outlander. That game blew my preteen mind away as the closest thing to a mad max game that we would see for the next 20 years. We saw the Fallout series and Rage hit land but while great games in their own sense, they never managed to capture the whole road warrior feel to me.
This game is awesome. It is everything I ever wanted in a road warrior themed video game. I didn't even care that I wasnt Mel Gibson or Master Blaster never making an appearence. The world, car customization, combat, score and graphics just sucked me in. Speaking of graphics I have an old rig and ran this game on the lowest settings and it still looked beautiful. I can only imagine this game on higher settings on a modern computer.
While it does have its flaws, though none that made it unbearable or painful to play, the game was a well recieved surprise to a guy who grew up on Indiana Jones and Mad Max. I was not expecting anything groundbreaking when I got this title on sale but I can honestly say this was one of the rare games I would pay full price for and still say is 100% worth it. On the opposite side of the spectrum this game can get a bit repetitive at times as well as certain points in combat feeling unresponsive. Car physics can be a bit sluggish at times but nothing unbearable like the driving segments in Rage for example.
In conclusion I found this purchase to be worth the full price to anyone who is craving a true road warrior experiance. I'm usually not one for rehashed movies from the past and even less interested when its a video games based on said rehashed film. This game has actual made me want to go out and rent the new Mad Max movie considering the very deep scars that the most recent Indiana Jones flic traumatized me with.
If you've ever wondered why they call him "Mad" Max: this dude will literally murder an army with his bare hands and blow up all of their bases just to get his hands on a V8 engine.
Unbeleiveably fun!!! Haven't been drawn in by a games story in years, THIS got my attention. This is MadMax done right. I hope they put out more like this, it could be a good series.

This game might be a good game, if Sony Online Entertainment (SOE) would actually let you play it. To play, you need to get a (free) account with SOE. Chances are, however, that when you then try to log in, you'll get a 'Wrong Username or Password' error.
Theoretically you'd then submit a support ticket, but to do that you need to log in to their website—which is exactly what you can't do because of the aforementioned error message. SOE's suggestion on their website: create a temporary second account and use that to contact Support. Guess what: you get the same error, so you still can't file a support ticket. Same thing with a third account and the fourth account (for which I pretended to live in the US, in case it might help).
SOE Support doesn't have an email address, but if you can't log in, you can either contact them by phone (which adds up quickly if you have to call from abroad), or contact them through Twitter (@SOEHelp). Unfortunately, the help they provide through Twitter is limited to 'contact us through our website.' Yeah, very helpful if being unable to log in is why you try to contact them in the first place.
I've spent almost two weeks trying to get some actual help from SOE Support. Then I gave up and removed the game from my computer. I'm sure the higher-ups will be thrilled to hear that their support staff has cost them a customer.
So, there's a good chance you won't be able to play EverQuest II at all, and if you're one of the fortunate who do get to play it, don't expect any help from SOE Support.

I first heard of the 'Borderlands' series when I watched an episode of Game Theory about Handsome Jack (FYI go watch that it's great), and it seemed like fun to me. Eventually, the game was on sale and I gave it a try... Holy cow it didn't disappoint! The story made me care for the characters, the NPC's are funny and making people explode by shooting them never gets old.
Although I personally haven't played it with friends, I noticed many places where co-op would be great. For example: having to go through the Raid on Digistruct Peak by yourself multiple times might get boring (should you not like making people explode), but with a friend or two it becomes more challenging, which could make it more fun to play, and more bearable to play through more than once.
Some games get criticised for their DLC's. Sure, Borderlands 2 has very many, but most of them are character skins and outfits. The playable DLC's, however, are a blast. The wacky yet immersive story of Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon's Keep and the challenges of Mister Torgue's Campaign of Carnage were the most fun for me personally. You might think otherwise, but these are the ones I'd recommend.
No game is perfect, and this one is no different. If you try to defeat a Raid Boss on your own, you have to be quite overleveled (I was lvl 39 when taking on the lvl 32 Hyperius the Invincible, and still had trouble). However, this might also be because I'm just not that great at the game ;). The timed missions are impossible for me to beat (might also be because I'm bad).
All in all, I would most certainly recommend this game. It's a fun experience for you on your own or with some friends. Giant bosses, memorable characters, fun storyline, epic DLC, cool soundtrack... and Handsome Jack.
