EDIT (2/1/15): I just found out about something called heroic characters. This is a great feature for where EQ2 is in its lifetime. It allows you to pay to get a level 90 character of any class/race along with appropriate gear and 320 alternate advancement points.
You don't have to pay to try out any race/class combination. There is a try before you buy option which lets you play for as long as you want with that class at level 85, but once you reach level 86 the character becomes locked.
Since the strong point of the game was always the classes as I stated in my initial review I think this is a great opportunity to give EQ2 a try. You'll be able to experience a lot of different classes and explore a lot of the world.
I plan to play this off and on until EQ Next just to see some of the lore and great locations the game has to offer. I am changing my initial review. I definitely recommend jumping in and just exploring and trying out the different classes for free at level 85. I'll continue to post updates to this review on what I actually think of the content.
Original Review (6/21/14):
EverQuest 2, the sequel to the best MMORPG of all time. For me this game came out at a bad time because I was still heavily into EverQuest 1 so when I first played it I found it so different that it made it hard to like it. It just didn't feel like EverQuest; the classes were extremely different and the agro and combat system was different. Looking back, this is to be expected and is probably a positive now, but at the time I couldn't get used to it. I ended up playing EQ2 for maybe a month or two past the free month and got close to level 40. It was fun visiting old zones from EQ1, but they didn't resemble the zones much and some of them didn't connect like they did in EQ1 so it made it even more confusing expecting a certain zone to be nearby and it wasn't.
This is a review for EQ2 in its own right though, not a review of the transition from EQ1 to EQ2. Since my initial time with EQ2 I did revisit the game on multiple occassions and it continued to grow and continued to get better. The zones are really interesting, but don't quite have the charm of EQ1 zones. I like the combat, but I could never get into the agro system where NPCs are grouped together. The art style I found to be ugly at times, the game has some weird blur effect to it. The class system is great and honestly is the sole reason I would recommend playing this game, to try out different classes. The housing system has also gotten really good over time and even though I haven't really taken part in this aspect I've toured some homes of friends and you can do some pretty impressive stuff. I have no experience in end game with EQ2, but like EQ1 there is a dedicated few still active and I'm sure the lore is top notch like EQ1 was.
If EQ2 would have came around a year or two later I may have been really into it, but I think it was released too early when I was still into EQ1, and ultimately EQ1 is the superior game. I am impressed with where they took EQ2 over the years and some of the stuff I've seen looks really cool, but I can't recommend this game due to my lack of experience with it so I can honestly say I don't know everything it has to offer, but I will say what I did experience was pretty good. It won't be that difficult to jump into EQ2 because it is more up to date as far as MMORPG mechanics go, so should be a smooth transition if you choose to try it.
I would recommend skipping this one and looking for EverQuest Next sometime in 2015 (probably), it looks to be doing really good things in the MMORPG genre.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of the best games you've never played. It generally flew under the radar at the time of its release due to obvious reasons. Reasons such as this: it looked like yet another generic military shooter where you play as a white American soldier shooting nameless baddies that WASN'T Call of Duty or Battlefield. So right off the bat, hardcore CoD and Battlefield fans strayed far away from it, and those that saw the stigma associated with CoD and generic military shooters (older players, hipsters, etc.) also stayed as far away as possible. Only the few that decided to investigate the game further than surface value allowed discovered what it truly is: a dark, intellectual thriller that isn't so much a generic third person shooter as much as it is a complete and total meta-experience that turns everything on its head, skewering conventions, all the while in the
of a generic third person shooter.
If that doesn't make sense, it's okay, it probably shouldn't. That's what kind of game this is.
If you're familiar with Apocalypse Now, or Heart of Darkness, than you're already two steps ahead of everyone else. Spec Ops: The Line is an adaptation of Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, and shares the theme and many messages therein, but it still has its own story and message to deliver.
DO NOT look up anything about this game. It plays exactly like it looks here in the Steam store. It's a generic third person shooter. But at the same time, it is anything but.
Pros
+ One of the best stories you'll ever experience in a video game; just don't let anyone spoil ANYTHING.
+ Gameplay is incredibly solid; it doesn't try anything new, but it was never supposed to.
+ Terrific voice performances from Nolan North (the protagonist) and Jake Busey (Radioman, you'll hear him a lot).
+ Soundtrack includes original and licensed music, and is terrific and well implemented
+ Atmosphere is palpable and akin to Bioshock.
+ Great collectables that actually share insight into the story.
Cons
- The graphics are looking dated
- Multiplayer is dead
Don't look anything up about this game, don't watch any videos, just buy it if you:
* Liked the original Bioshock
* Liked Apocalypse Now or Heart of Darkness
* Like your shooters with a side of story
* Want something

I purchased this game back and 2008 and only played the 30 day free trial but didnt feel like it was worth the subscription fee at the time as I probably didnt put enough time into. When everquest 2 extended came out I downloaded it too but never ended up really playing it as I just couldnt get into it.
Finally I decided to play it again now that it was Free to Play. Fist I downloaded the standalone client and played for quite sometime and began enjoying the what I was able to do in this game and what the future had in store for this game. When I noticed it was on steam I reinstalled it on here and Iv been playing non stop eversince.
One of the huge perks I found as I was playing was I had recieved tons of free ingame goods such as housing items, 500 Station Cash I didnt know I had and tons and tons of other bonuses I had recieved from purchasing and registering the game back on 08. This really had me sucked in now as even though most of the goods were not entirly powerful or usful for adventuring it really gave me a glimps of what I could do in the game. Especially with housing.
Graphics:
This is obviously a game that is getting up in age and the graphics do show in this way, however it seems like this was the perfect time for graphics engines because a lot of these games still look really good. Its not all blocky and cluncky like a ps1 game or everquest one but its smooth and has really nice looking landscapes, armor sets ect. It all just rolls out to look so good for its age. There are tons of settings that you can dink with to make it look as good good as you need it and its garenteed youll probably be able to find what looks best for you depending on your pc spec.
In some of the main hub towns, especially freeport, the frames dropped crazy low. Im not sure if its a server issue or my internet. Its not so laggy that its unplayable by any means especially due to the fact that main cities are more or less used for grabbing quest, crafting, trading which means you wont need as many frames anyways to do these smaller faster taskes.
Gameplay:
Iv sunk so much time into this game so fast too. I dont think iv been able to dedicate myself to an mmo from the start as quick as I did with this game; despite me not giving it the chance in the first place. Im still not even at the level cap of 95... Wait I read they raised it to 100 hahaha. Thats pretty awesome in itself to me because it means i still have a ton of content to buzz through plus the latest expansion pack. So far as of this review Im level 54 and I dont even really feel the game is a grind. It just leaves me wanting to play more.
The questing type for the most part is standard kill so and so or get me this many of this thing but it does thow in some quests where unique items are given to you and that item is used to summon a boss for instance or special goggles to help you find clues. Even though it has so many of the standard quests I actually prefer them over the other quests wheree the special items are required. There usually less tetius and go quicker and this results in faster xp and gold and sick♥♥♥♥♥quest item rewards. This being said I still love the bit of variety it does have and it keeps me wanting more.
This game has made me fall in love with running dungeons. In the Guildwars games dungeons were always pretty fun with friends or a good group but they generally require you to wait around for a group or use there sick♥♥♥♥♥dungeon finder to get a group together. This is all well and sweet and pretty flawless for guildwars 2 but I like how I can freely run a dungeon alone or with a group here in everquest 2. It just depends on your level and ability. Theres the flipside to that. You can also run the dungeons with people when your at a lower level or whatever so that option is obviously still there I guess the problem with it is though, is finding a group of people around who want to help you and not just clear the whole place out a few seconds before you. I tuely feel that there dungeon matchmaking needs to be improved because I find it confusing as♥♥♥♥♥♥or not very functional at the time. It would be amazing if they incorperated a mega server type idea like Guildwars 2 as that solution in my opinion is ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant. I swear if Everquest 2 and Guildwars 2 had some awesome♥♥♥♥♥sex, that would be my dream game born.

I also sub'd last month and this month so I could adjust my alternate experience slider to give me more adventure xp for a few months but this was just something I wanted to test and it is a nice added feature but the free 50 percent option is still more the viable and works behind the scenes so you dont even need to think about it. Some games can work with the whole "You control all players on your team with one controller" thing ok, but this game absolutely can not.  This game is all about positioning and beating the "goalie" on angles, but since your characters constantly bounce off the other team and most likely all get crammed up together, you just end up moving as one big clump. Also "shoot" "pass" "charge" and "goalie" (even after playing a bunch of rounds i still have no idea exactly what "goalie" does) are all mapped to one button, while there are 3 jump buttons. all 3 of your players jump at the press of one button so I don't understand why there are 3 buttons for jump and NO options to change controls.
Maybe this game is better with a group of friends to play with, but I was hoping the single player would be worth it, and it really isn't in its current state.

I don't know why people have mixed feelings about this game. The 5 or so hours that I have now spent in it have been the best I've had in any of the Hitman series (this is my first one). I'd like to debunk some cons that people here have said about this game based on my brief experience with it. Hitman servers have never went down during my playtime, there have been no lagging/fps drops and I'm running with highest settings. There they were. The pros outweigh the cons by a longshot. The episodes are well made meaning that they have a lot of different ways to assassinate your targets, just got playing through Sapienza and it was beautiful. The graphics are good and there's lots AI doing their own stuff giving the game a feeling of immersion. Now I would like to note that I wouldn't enjoy it as much if I had payed the full price for it. The game really feels like an assassination game. You can't run and gun your way through. Well sometimes you can but most of the time not. My advice, have good internet and go into the game thinking that it's gonna suck and you'll be surprised how good it is.
P.S. While I don't mind about the always online thingy, it would be better if they ditched that idea in season 2.

PRO: Game itself is good, map is expansive, multiple ways to complete the mission. If you are hoping to get the longevity and feel of Dishonored 2 (taking out targets non-lethally, meaningful story or sense of progression), then this game won't have it. It feels like a collection of level sandboxes that you play multiple times just to see how many ways the targets can be killed. It can be fun. Many different locales and the graphic is very good. I also did not have any technical issues so far in-game. Personally, I do not have any problem with episodic nature of this game. If any, it just feels like any other Telltale adventure game.
CON: Let me start by saying that
Why the dev is doing this is beyond me and I hope this practice does not continue in season 2!
. Nobody cares about the leaderboards, and the server connection is hit/miss. If you do want to play offline, you can, but it's main story campaign only with default starting positions, weapon loadout, and no, you cannot customize any of it. No ratings, no unlocks, no escalations, no nothing. Oh, and the saves are also separate between online/offline. This will be a big NO NO for a lot of player, including myself (yes, I received the game for free, and I'm writing this to warn potential buyers). If you plan to play offline, or do not have stable internet, stay away until they take out the always online requirement (which is silly), because you should be able to do pretty much everything I mentioned you couldn't in offline.
Few other things:
- No effect on subsequent levels/story if you play silent assassin/mass murderer, like Blood Money
- Everywhere everyone speaks PERFECT ENGLISH, except maybe a computer in Japan, and Diana.
- AI is quite abusable and exploitable
- Something wrong with the blood
- While I did not experience any issues, I read a lot of people experiencing technical issues, crashing, and performance problems. After half a year, I thought they'd fixed most of these, but apparently not...
I'm giving this game a NO, primarily because of the always online BS for essentially a single player game. Please be mindful of that before you purchase. I hope devs see this and take this into consideration for season 2. I will not hesitate to purchase full price season 2 if the stupid always online is taken out.

A pedigree entry in the point and click adventure genre. With an absence of main character to control, this game presents a return to the now less prominent fixed perspective style, but to great effect.
Simple, blissful point and click mechanics supported by an intuitive hint system. Each element of the world responds in a slick, responsive way, for a modern and refined feel.
Beautiful art drives the entire experience, with varied and fascinatingly detailed worlds rewarding each step forward. Truly memorable, prepare to be lost in this game's dreamlike wonder.
Nostalgic, relaxing and mesmerising music throughout, perfectly capturing the feel of the world. High quality sound effects also give weight to the experience.
If you are looking for a solid point and click adventure, puzzle, or relaxing game then this is highly recommended. If you appreciate quality art and music in video games, then this game is a must buy.

This game is alright - it is quite repetitive, and the actual driving doesn't feel very great which is sad because of the whole theme of the game.
I would recommend it on sale EXCEPT for the story mission "Gastown Death Race"
There's too many terrible design decisions for this mission to even list, it's not worth the time. It's the WORST experience in an otherwise OK game I have ever had, period. An hour of fighting RNG and losing. There's ONE good tactic, no skill involved, just luck, and you have to intentionally lose the race as quick as possible after it fails to try again. And unskippable dialogue each time. I wasted an hour trying and at this point, I find it hard to believe the rest of the game is worth trying again.
So I guess if you want to pick it up on sale for $5 to experience some interesting world exploring, mediocre driving and combat, and then stop playing before the end of the main story, then go for it. Otherwise, invest that $5 in something better
Update: I opened the game back up to go try something else in it and it loaded into the race (apparently where the checkpoint was). The guy you have to destroy got instantly stuck on one of the random pixel protrusions that normally end your attempt and just sat there while getting destroyed. That's a good example of the best possible outcome for that mission, hope the AI glitches and you beat it instantly.
The rest of the game is fine, really, more-of-more-of-the-same with some tropey contrived ending bit to make it tie into the movie, I guess?
Overall, the game falls short. It has a lot of potential in it and I honestly WANT to like it, but it's too bloated and the experience is too... mediocre, in the end. Sometimes it captures the feeling of Mad Max quite well but those moments are few and far between.

So as literally nobody expected, the new Hitman game (HITMAN™, get it right), was actually ♥♥♥♥ing better than Blood Money. I have no idea how that happened but it's glorious.
I've just done one runthrough of the game so far and already, I can tell I'll be doing another 10 or 20. It's THAT replayable. I just chose one solution each time, and usually my solution wasn't even that advanced. The target happens to walk into a slightly secluded place? Give them a quick shot in the head and get right the ♥♥♥♥ out of there. But other times, I went the whole way, killing the targets in a completely accidental way.
And then there's the parts in between, like sniping them through a crowd of people, or trying to predict their paths and lead them down the one that's rigged with ♥♥♥♥ing bombs.
And then came the last mission, where I literally just ♥♥♥♥ing killed everyone.
It took every single aspect of Blood Money's strategic freedom and just expanded upon it, so much. Way bigger levels, more disguises, more solutions, more fun. Combat is satisfying as ♥♥♥♥, difficult, fast-paced and really lets you take the upper hand. You really feel like a scientifically-enhanced super-agent and it's all just sooooo well done.
Stealth is great. It took Blood Money, where the only stealth was hiding in plain sight, and then took Absolution, where most of the stealth was just creeping around in cover, and then it just merged them together. You can still use disguises to get around just fine, but it's not the core of the experience. The level design is so well done that you can still sneak around without even having the right disguise, and it's not laid out in Absolution-style paths, where you can see exactly where the game is trying to tell you to go.
The graphics are actually pretty good. I don't know what's up, but everything seems to look really sharp and refined. I think the lighting has to do with that. The music is on point. It works ♥♥♥♥ing PERFECTLY. For every single action, phase of alert or other significant event, the audio kicks in just perfectly to suit the mood. A LOT of effort went into this stuff, and it pays off so ♥♥♥♥ing much.
I've had moments where I did something really cool, kinda sat back and made a "ooohhhhhhh" sound, wondering if I actually got away with what I just did. And then I just watched as the chaos ensued, as the AI runs around, confused as ♥♥♥♥, wondering what just happened, while a completely nonchalant gardener makes his way downtown right next to them. (Note: That's NOT the gardener. He's currently on the top floor, stripped naked, out-cold and stuck in a bathtub.)
And beyond the six main missions, there's still a load of other side content that I haven't even explored yet.
Beyond the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ episodic scheme, the always-online DRM and the kinda meh performance, the game is a ♥♥♥♥ing 10/10, by far. It's literally Blood Money, the best game in the Hitman series, by far, except even better, by far. I didn't even think that was possible.
EDIT: 52 hours in and it's still no less fun than it was when I started. IT'S SO GOOD

An incredible. I bought it for just $10 pesos (like $0.99 dollars or even less).
I expected it to be very simple and boring, basically a broken game coded in one day or so. I could not be more wrong.
Here, the flaws of the game:
- It doesn't support high resolutions. At least in my machine, it can run only on 1024x768, even on fullscreen.
Here, the good things about the game:
- Very good music. Is very relaxing. I loved the main title music, is just... good, soft, I can't describe it.
- Well made puzzles. Some of the puzzles presented are easy, even trivial, but others (like the Worl Map or the Tetris Like pieces)... oh boy, they are complex, even when you know what you need to do. A couple of puzzles, I think, need more explanation to really know what you are supposed to do, but they are still very good.
- Pieces very well hidden. You need to find puzzle pieces. To do it, you need to solve some problems. To solve the problems, you need to find other pieces. To find other pieces, you need to solve other problems. A very interesting way to play, I think.
- Makes you think about your actions. Mostly at the two last levels, I learned, the hard way, that you need to first search for all the puzzle pieces that you can fin *before* completing a problem, because the problem for which you already have the needed pieces might be the las problem to solve and you will be transported to the next level, even when you have not found the remaining puzzle pieces yet.
I truly recommend this game. If you can afford the game, have time to spend, like to think about problems and have a big screen (to compensate the more or less low resolution), then, you need to buy it.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS (review will be edited once I'm finished):
I'm currently on World 3 of this game, and I'd highly reccomend it.
This game is a love letter to classic NES/SNES games. I'd say this game is a way to do references right. They're not in your face and a person who hasn't played one of those games wouldn't be confused.
This game is also how to do hard games right. A lot of hard games are just unfair.
EXAMPLE: Mario: The Lost Levels. You can get something that looks like a powerup but will actually kill you. How are we supposed to know that will kill you? It's the game's fault you got killed.
Super Meat Boy doesn't have that. Every time you die it's your own fault. Plus each level is really short so it isn't frustrating that you have to go back to the beginning of the level.
The controls are really tight and great. I'd say the controls are better on the gamepad but the keyboard has great controls too.
Also, the amount of content in the game is amazing. I've spent up to 8 hours on the game and I only just began World 3. Each level has a dark world counterpart which makes the game even harder. There's also warp zones. Some are 8-16 bit warp zones and some are character warp zones.
Did I mention that you can use characters from other games? This game introduced me to the BIT.TRIP series (which is awesome by the way).
In other words, BUY THIS GAME. IT IS AWESOME.

I have invested many hours into this game, and there are so many things I love about it. Simply put, Borderlands 2 is one of THE BEST co-op games available. Grab some friends, shoot some baddies, and snag sweet loot. If you liked the original Borderlands, this is in most aspects a huge improvement.
+Overhauled story. One of the prime complaints of BL1 was its confusing story and underwhelming ending. BL2 remedies this with an action packed story filled with vibrantly written characters and a conclusive ending.
+Unique visuals. Continuing the cel-shaded comic book style of the original, BL2 looks stunning without being hardware demanding.
+MMO style raid bosses. Those who like to invest in endgame like me should be content with what BL2 offers. Post-game bosses are gruelling difficult but rewarding.
+Good humor. Although it might not be everyone’s cup of tea.
+Dragon Keep is one of the best DLCs I’ve ever played
-No more revolver weapon type
-Loot system feels unfair, not as fun or sporadic as BL1
-Humor can be hit or miss
If you have a group of friends willing to pitch in, definitely purchase a pack of Borderlands 2. It’s a rootin’ tootin’ co-op experience fun for the whole family (minus the dog).

Everquest 2 is in the same league as World of Warcraft, Guild Wars 2, and even the new Final Fantasy MMO, but none of these other games are so evolved they’ve revolutionized the overall experience. This results in an overload of similar content presented through different layers of graphics, lore, classes, creatures and underlying support systems (such as crafting and raiding). Don’t get me wrong, many of the games have “unique perk features” (e.g. GW2 allows you to dodge attacks), but these perk features don’t qualify as bringing MMOGs to the next level of gaming experience.
EQ2 trumps the competition when it comes to overall content, playability, many features and functionality; and in some cases far beyond the other games.
1. Mercenary, which is like having another player with you, a single character can solo most of the dungeons and heroic areas/monsters of the game. This opens all players who use a mercenary up to the majority of the content without having to look for a group and rely on others to play.
2. Alternate Advancement, a system that allows the player to decide what percentage (up to 100%) of their experience they want to go to this secondary point system, which opens some new skills.
3. Quests, EQ2 has an unique balance of presentation for it's quests. The players can quickly and blindly click through things to move on through the next step whereas players who are heavy into a storyline/lore can interact and engage with the NPC. The rewards are also well designed and refined imo.
4. Guild, EQ2's guild system brings their players together, sharing their accomplishments and keeping them connected better than any other MMO.  The guild system with automatic notifications toward the player's achievements, level gains, and finding valuable items. It also has a built in Voice Chat which works great. EQ2 has the best Guild system out of all mmo games. Period. EQ2's guild system also have the Guild Hall (home of the guild). No other mmo game comes remotely close afaik.

Story time. My mission was simple: Kill a general set up in an abandoned school, and a diplomat in the Swedish embassy. Easy mode for 47.
I'll spare the details about the general, and tell the beautiful tale about how practicing your throwing arm will save you.
I started stranging a guard to get his uniform, but his friend saw me. I threw a sword in his face, and hid both of them in a trash can. So good so far, right? I then go downstairs, where I am immediately recognized by another soldier. I engage in glorious melee combat, and end it by snapping his neck. His friend then arrives, and I throw my sword at him (again), and hide both of them in a locker. This is going to be a thing, isn't it?
I manage to get inside the embassy, where I instantly get spotted by a security guard. I somehow draw him into a small corridor without alerting anyone else, and proceed to throw my sword, which I was somehow still allowed to carry. I switch clothes, and decide that maybe it's time to ditch the sword. Then I find a screwdriver...
I proceed to, one-by-one, surgically kill so many people with a single throw of the screwdriver that I lost count towards the end. If 47 ever entered the javelin toss Olympics, he would be unstoppable. He would probably also kill all the opponents before the event even began, but that's a different story for, hopefully, a mission in the next game.
After killing the general and his men, this time with the sword AND the screwdriver, I swap back to my neat black Italian wool suit, and escape.
My score according to the game? Zero. None, zip, zilch, nada, nothing. Absolutely ♥♥♥♥-all

You will feel like a bad person after finishing this game. Immediately after beating it I started another game so I could try making better choices, but there are no good choices to be made. Spec Ops will move you like no other.

There is a scene about an hour into Spec Ops: The Line, generally the one people who have already played the game will recognise as the "game changer" scene, that forces you to walk through a landscape of smouldering, writhing soldiers. Some beg for help, others just quietly choke on their own oozing fluids. And its around about this time that the average player will have an epiphany.
"It takes a real cold hearted psycho of unimaginable cruelty to do something like this," they will think.
Of course, the fact it was THE PLAYER that did it is exactly what makes this game unique. (THE PLAYER, an American soldier, NOT a Saturday morning cartoon villain who twirls his moustache, cackling gleefully as he kicks puppies and heils the swastika, or shouts "JIHAD!", or whatever is most fitting these days.)
You see, Spec Ops: The Line is the anti-Call of Duty. And it doesn't so much deconstruct the Call of Duty games as it does strip them down to their bare reality, shove them right up the player's♥♥♥♥♥ and ask: "Just how cool do you think war is now?"
The above mentioned scene in Spec Ops: The Line very obviously mimics a scene from CoD, involving bombing soldiers from an airborne drone. At least, it mimics the bombing people part. The moments after, where you witness the results of the bombing, are very specifically added. And this is the purpose of the game.
Many will have noticed that in the Call of Duty series the focus of the games are entirely on the fast paced, pulse pounding, fifty-soldier-a-second-murder-rate action part of war, and never once do the games force you to witness the consequences of your actions. (Except for that "Crawling through the city nuke scene," but really, that was many years ago, and the tones of the games have changed drastically since then.) Spec Ops: The Line is happy to give you the pulse pounding action, and it even does so with similar over the top spectacle as can be found in the CoD series, but it never strays far from making you stare the horrific results of those actions square in the face. Likewise, the characters in Spec Ops: The Line grow ever more twisted, tortured and insane, clearly reflecting the reality of the horror around them. The player, be he or she a person of reasonable intelligence and not a sexually frustrated teenager, (you know who you are,) should hate themselves by the end of the game, not feel like a hero.
"This game doesn't sound like much fun," I hear you say, "What about the actual game part of the game?"
Fair enough. Lets talk gameplay.  In terms of gameplay, I must be honest, Spec Ops: The Line isn't a perfect, and certainly isn't much to write home about. Its a reasonable third person shooter with functonal cover mechancis, reflecting Gears of War more than CoD, in point of fact. Even these basic mechanics, however, are a bit flimsy at times. On curved walls it seems a bit ambigous as to whether Walker, the protagonist character, will shift up the wall upon you moving the thumbstick to the right, or leap up out of cover like a man doing an interprative dance of a meerkat on the lookout for predators. These instances are rare, however, and the gameplay is for the most part fast paced, epic, and enjoyable. The gameplay really is, however, just a means to drive the wheels of the story forward.
Lastly I would like to add that Spec Ops: The Line is also hands down the most breathtakingly beautiful game I have ever played. The sheer amount effort that must have gone into making the enviroments, that turn a war-torn Dubai into an artistic masterpiece, more then makes up for the average gamelplay, and then some. This game, a shooter that has you blowing off heads, simultaneously makes love to your eyes with an absolutely stunning gallery of gorgeous level designs.

There is another scene I'd like to mention now, before ending this already overly long review, where you and your soldiers drop down into a cave, the floor of which is a carpet of hundreds of lit candles. And, as you and your soldiers walk over these candles, your clumping boots extinguishing the little pinpoints of light, leaving paths of darkness in your collective wakes. This visual metaphor of these soldiers and their purpose, (soldiers snuff out lives beneath their mighty tread and leave darkness behind them, for those sexually frustrated teenagers who didn't get it,) created in such am original and strikingly beautiful way, is why Spec Ops: The Line is one of my personal favourite games. This massively overlooked game, indeed not perfect by any means, was a risky project of passion by a group of developers I feel should have got more recognition for it. The game is good, but buggy as hell. To clarify, I recommend it only if you can ignore those bugs and overall problems (and believe me, sometimes they're frustating).
The worst problem I've found was a pretty good think as an idea, but was apparently badly executed, which is the camera. The angles are really cool and could make it look great, if it didn't interfere so much in clicking the scenario to run or walk. Long story short. you're running from the monster in a corridor, then you want to click on a door to enter it, but when you click it once, the character starts walking, so you have to click it twice to keep running (remember there is a monster on your trail). The problem is, the camera is following the character, so you click one time, and when you're about to double click, the camera "walks" a little bit and you lose the click spot (don't know how it's called). To end it up, it's terrible to turn around when you're in this "escape mode", where you're running from the monster and the gameplay changes a bit, so yeah, if you miss the door, you'll probably have to fight it, and if the character is tired, bye my life.
And also, the character gets tired REALLY quickly, even to a girl (I can understand Monica since she's drunk and for her shoes, but Roony?).
About the bugs, they usually don't interfere much with the gameplay, it's more visual, like the character's hair being alive and having it's own physics, or then you open a door and the character teleports to the other side, that type of bugs.
So yeah, the big problem here is the camara, combined with the 3D point and click thing, it didn't work that well, even though the camera are really nice and could be really useful for a movie, or even a usual third person game (like Silent Hill or Resident Evil), it could work much better that way. Even so, it's still really cool to have a new Clock Tower (yes, that's basically a new Clock Tower), following the old style and everything, that's awesome.
Some points about the game:
>Storyline is pretty interesting, though there's some points that are let unexplained. I felt a major "plothole" feeling when I finished the game, it gives the impression that the developers forgot about some things they put in the plot.
>Graphics are good, specially shadows, they're really well done. Bug sometimes they let you down a bit, specially the "white borders" around objects and doors, the hair thing I said earlier and some details in characters (facial expression for example). Also, it's not well optmized, I had to play it on "good" because "beautiful" don't work well in my PC, even though I play other games with better or equal graphics without any problem. Even so, the game is still clunky, even on "good" or "medium", proving that it's optimization problem.
>Sound is good too, but sometimes buggy. Many times when I was playing, the sound came first and only after a couple of seconds, came the images that the audio belong for. Besides that, soundtrack is good, general audio is good and immersive, and the voice acting are not bad (some exceptions though).
>Good variety of endings and things to do, might be entertaining for collectors (such as myself, that hates to get away of a game that is not 100% completed).
So, Nightcry is a good game, but sadly, doesn't seem like a finished one. It's more like a alpha or beta of a in-development game. Really doesn't seem fully polished and I think that, for some reason, the developers released it in a hurry or something like that, because I can't think of other explanation. Well, I really hope they decide to remaster (or even remake, who knows) that game, because it deserves. If they could improve the camera gameplay and bugs, it would already be great. (and yes, they already corrected a lot of bugs, seems like this game was barely playable at it's release,...)
Then, if you can ignore the bugs, that camera problem, and the bad optimization (I don't know if this will count for everyone but I've seen other reviews complaining about it), then I recommend it, but I would recommend even more in a sale. In case you regret, there's always the refund, but I'd recommend you give it a chance for the max time you can. In any case, just pretend it's a PS2 game and you'll be fine.
I'll give it a 7/10, mostly for entertainment and storyline, it could be a lot better but it was still a pretty fun experience, and a welcome Clock Tower return, a franchise that I love with all my heart.

Color Chaos is a seemingly simple yet thoroughly fun, little 3D casual shooter. Its objective is equally straightforward: obtain and always strive to increase your high score by obliterating as many enemies as possible. The difficulty is well scaled and by going from Classic to Chaos Mode, you can substantially increase the challenge while the Turbo modes, up the ante even further. The presence of Achievements, Cards and even a Leaderboard, make this small competitive title, a good break from the complexity of other games. The beautiful neon glows and chromatic diversity are sadly not complemented by a worthwhile soundtrack. Being part of the twin-stick shooter subgenre, means that Color Chaos is obviously best played on a controller, but I had little difficulty enjoying it on the traditional mouse & keyboard layout. While I noticed that some buyers have complained, I do not think that this game is overpriced given the overall state and functionality in which Color Chaos is to be found right now. Dubstep music aside, I had a lot of fun with it and I do hope it shall receive further support in the future.

To me this "game" seems more like a tech demo than a real video game, for the following reasons:
The gameplay mechanics are poor. In a typical game, there are only two kinds of enemies. Once you reach the stage where a 3rd type of enemy starts to appear, the game changes from extremely easy to insanely difficult. And it's not about me being a poor player, I made it to top-10 on global ranking, but apparently, there hasn't been much gameplay testing, because it's just not very fun this way.
This game is basically about dodging bullets, the enemies spawn at fixed intervals at the edges of the screen, and if you happen to be there at that time, game over. You have to have a hunch of when the new wave might appear, and be at the center. Your ship seems to have mass, because there's a delay in steering. Which could be undestandable in a simulator type game, but in a bullet-dodging game, it's not that great. Sometimes 5 (or more) shooting enemies spawn at the same time, and if you decided to stop moving after clearing a wave, well... you get the idea. Also, having about a second of delay in shooting doesn't help much in an arcade shooter. Call it consistency if you want.
That's about it regarding the classic mode. The chaos mode seemed to be truly chaotic, because you would get updates for your weapon or more speed at random times, overpowering a wave or two completely and then returning to the gameplay of the classic mode.
As icing on the cake, scoring is also flawed. As you shoot your enemies, the combo-bar builds up, and if you shoot frequent enough, your multiplier rises. But, if you happen to finish one wave off too quickly, the pause between the next one gets so long, that you lose the multiplier! So you have to be careful not to shoot too much...
I bought this game for 1.50€, wouldn't recommend the game for that price.

I am a fan of games that have a simple concept that prove to be a lot of fun that they are the very definition of ‘turn on and play.’ Allow me to introduce you to Daniel Riley and his Steam developer debut title, Color Chaos. Twin stick shooters aren’t quite the rage that they used to be but they can be some of the most entertaining games on Steam. Fans of the genre may have thought that they had seen it all but the color swapping component of the game provides a freshness that revitalizes the genre.
It’s one of those score attack games that you will find yourself returning to again and again for short bursts of game play. If you return home from work or school and only have fifteen minutes before you need to do things at home or return to studying then you’ll find yourself playing a round or two of this. Of course, if you have hours of time you may find yourself addicted to climbing up the global leaderboards and playing until you’ve achieved a personal high score that you didn’t think was possible. The game is addictive.
There are two game modes. Classic and chaos mode. Personally, I find classic to be a little bit on the boring side. However, it is a reasonable way to learn the basics of the game without the action being too frantic. On the other hand, I adored the fast paced action that is chaos mode. It becomes very twitchy but it’s awesome. You will learn patterns early on that will build you up to a certain level of success and other times you’ll curse your luck. But I never felt that the game cheated me of my death in either mode and that is a real tribute to the well programmed hit box.  Chaos mode is more frantic because there are power ups that power up your weapons and the enemies come at you faster.
A great well designed score attack game that I highly recommend.

is a challenging twin-stick shooter which provides an intense experience of both gameplay and visuals.
As the title suggests,
provides quite a lot of hectic elements which is majorly seen throughout the gameplay. Your aim is to survive as long as you can in a world filled with vibrant enemies either trying to eliminate you via being rather intimate, or shooting you down. No colour the same as yours can destroy you, and the same rule applies to your enemies. One of the most unique aspects of the gameplay is the colour-swapping feature, where you can swap your colour to be able to defeat the hoards of similar-coloured enemies, or protect yourself from other intimidating ones.  Powerups can be found in the 'Chaos' gamemode, adding some slightly refreshing gameplay.
A slight problem with all of that is the excessive difficulty of it all. You will die many times due to usually to the same reason of being unable to move away from a cluster of enemies while trying to dodge the newly spawning ones. It tends to feel a bit unfair and makes the game slightly repetitive when starting over again and again with little progress of inching up to a greater highscore. Still, overrall it's fun mix of action and chaos, spread across four different gamemodes that provide equally entertaining content.
As you can tell by the screenshots, the visuals add to the madness of the game and whilst not being absolutely amazing, they are (mostly) nice, bearable to look at and suit the chaotic style of the game. Unfortunately, in the centre of the screen the background tends to get blurry and distracts from the gameplay.

The price seems relatively fair, as $4 isn't really too much, but for the amount of content received you may like to get it on sale.

Color Chaos is an interesting kind of twin stick shooter that requires you to be precious and accurate with your shooting. It was developed and published by a guy called Daniel Riley. The game itself is very fun and addicting to play and is hard to stop playing even when you tell yourself that this will be the last run.
The game itself is very simple and easy to understand. You have your shooting and movement keys that comes prior to every shooter game. Your main mission is to stay alive for as long as possible and try to get the highest score as possible, and that's pretty  much the whole gameplay. But the main difference between Color Chaos and other twin stick shooter is the colours that the enemy shooters are and the colour that you are. In order to destroy the other shooters that are trying to destroy you, you will need to be a different colour prior to what colour they are. But something that is helpful if you are the same colour as them is that if they hit into you they can't hurt you. So if you are the same colour as the enemy then you will not destroy them, this requires you to pay a bit more attention to the game and what colour you are prior to their colour. I find that this mechanic is really interesting to play with throughout each time that you play through this game. I really enjoy this mechanic that I haven't seen before in the classic twin shooter games, this really makes this game unique.
Now there are a few types of game modes that you can play through, which make the game a bit more interesting and adds more replayability to the game itself. You have the classic mode that is a endless wave upon wave of enemies that spawn more and more frequently prior to the longer that you stay alive throughout the run. You're trying to get the highest possible score and survive the longest to achieve that.
Chaos mode is basically like classic mode, but there are more enemies, more shooting and of course more chaos the longer you survive. You will find a variety of powerups that will help you increase your firepower to make the odds a bit more in your favour. Turbo Classic mode is more of a quick reaction test as you fight waves thick and fast in classic mode. Turbo Chaos mode is basically Chaos mode but is much more quicker, with more enemies and firepower. I really like the amount of different game modes that this game has, it really pushes your ability of this game at different levels to see how good you are at the game.
The graphics of this game are very vibrant and colourful, which shouldn't be that much of a surprise as this game focuses upon colours. You might be old enough to remember those brightly lit and colorful vector style games from the early 80's arcades...ones which ignited your imagination with awe & wonder as they hypnotically called out for you to drop a quarter inside so that you could go head to head against both this marvelous machine, as well as fellow players, to see who would come out on top with the highest score.
I now introduce you to Color Chaos created by Daniel Riley, an old-school styled twin-stick shooter which seeks to capture and mimic that very magic of years gone by in those gathering rooms for teens which could best be described as an electronic wonderland for those fortunate enough to experience it.
I found the gameplay dynamic of this particular title to be rather unqiue & intriguing. And the way it works, is that you are able to shoot enemy ships of any color except your own, and they in turn adhere to the very same principle when firing upon you. Two exact colors cannot harm one another here, but it becomes even more interesting still because both you and they have the ability to shift current colors to a different one, which adds an entirely new element of tactical play in this game.
There are also 2 game modes present by the way, 'Classic' (progressively harder and more numerous enemies the longer you stay alive) and 'Chaos' (described as more enemies, more firepower and more chaos), so as to inject a greater amount of variety into the gameplay.
Furthermore, also present is a nifty power-up system in place which allows you to temporarily increase your ships' abilities in various ways, by simply moving toward & collecting the item whenever it appears on the screen.
I spent a reasonable amount of time experimenting with and playing Color Chaos to develop a good feel for it...in order to ascertain what its strengths and inherent weaknesses were. And in the end, I felt it was somewhat of a mixed bag. A very admirable effort to be sure, which, if tweaked in a couple specific ways could be even more fun.
Firstly, I will go over some aspects of it which I wasn't a particularly big fan of. I felt that there was simply an excessive amount of color bloom present, especially toward the center of the screen, where it all blended together into a hazy semi-translucent morass which wasn't very easy on the eyes I might add. It might have instead been optimal to leave the inner gameplay area a largely pitch black star-field to more nicely contrast with the pretty colors of the ships and boundary lines. That would have actually looked rather sharp and pleasing. It isn't to say that the the current effect is poor by any stretch, I just feel that it isn't necessarily ideal, and this is only my personal opinion on the matter. Others may or may not agree with this.
Secondly, Color Chaos is exceedingly difficult, especially when using a mouse & keyboard. It was definitely designed for the hardcore enthusiast of this genre in mind....with each game typically measured in several white-knuckle seconds for the typical gamer, and certainly not in minutes unless you are perhaps a seasoned veteran who practices relentlessly. And because of it being sudden death, once you are dead then that's it - you'll need to start over again to strive for a new high score, which is clearly the main objective here incidentally. The difficulty stems from the fact that enemies are chasing you continuously & relentlessly at all times, forcing you to mostly move in a wide circular pattern so as to avoid them, while also firing upon you with bullets which travel at a surprisingly fast pace. It was difficult to establish any kind of rhythm or groove since each individual game simply didn't last very long. Perhaps making the enemies sometimes change direction in a more random manner might have added even more to the satisfaction of the gameplay dynamic. As it was however, I just couldn't imagine myself sinking hours at a time into this, and thus it's more ideally suited to being played in short controlled bursts.
Now onto the decidedly positive side of things, I will say that the game itself runs exceptionally well with no framerate issues and even includes the ability to play with both keyboard & mouse, or a controller...with remappable keys for the former.
Additionally, both the background music (ambient electronica) and sound effects were superbly implemented, and it is definitely one of the highlights to be found here. Together they both generated a very mellow and relaxing vibe to the game, which counter-balanced nicely against the sheer challenge of it. Somehow it works, and works very well.
Overall, I would say that this is a fairly good game for the price point it is at, especially for those who appreciate this specific type of challenge and its old-school feel. It's one that I could definitely see myself playing here & there in small bursts if I'm not up for a lengthy session playing something else, or if I simply don't have the time to do so. It could be better in a couple ways, sure, but nonetheless it's still very fun, and I applaud the developer for attempting to capture the magic of those games which we used to play way back in the day...transporting us to those happy times when our world was filled with row upon row of chaotic flickering color.
I'll rate this one 3.5 out of 5 stars, while at the same time giving a smiling nod to nostalgia.

I was VERY wary of the always-online requirements but for no cause at all: Connection with the servers has been broken two times but each time the game pauses and lets you try to fix the issue instead of booting you out of the game. If you can't fix it, you go to the menu and either restart offline or wait for the connection to come back (always done for mere seconds for me) and then you reload your preferred save. This is a very short game, but entertaining enough for the price.  The art is very pretty and the puzzles had a lot of variety; my only quibble is that there is not a skip option for puzzles.  For someone like me, who likes certain types of puzzles and completely abhors others, it's grating to have to struggle through the irritating ones.
The bulk of the game, aside from the minigame puzzles, is "hidden-object" style with a set number of puzzle pieces in each level, along with a variety of other objects to find to complete objectives (i.e. finding all the mail packages to load on a plane before you can take off).  The hidden items are legitimately challenging; the puzzle pieces especially blend in very well to the backdrop and that's a refreshing change from the typical "here's a pile of junk, find stuff in it" style of HO games.
With the length of the game, I'm not sure if it's worth the full price, but I did find it enjoyable.  If you like HO games and puzzlers, you'll probably like this one; you'll have to decide whether or not to wait for a sale!

The developers learned from their mistakes in Hitman Absolution, which wasn't a Hitman game true to the franchise, but rather a Splinter Cell like game spent mostly hiding behind chest high walls. Hitman does what the older games did right, hiding in plain sight. This game even improves on the mechanics of the best game in the series, Blood Money, by making the disguise system more believable. Now certain NPCs can see through your disguise even if you're disguised as one of them, like the head of security knows his staff, etc. which feels more realistic than the older games.
The locations are good in the beginning but in my opinion get less interesting as you progress in the game. I haven't yet played the last few missions even though the locations are interesting on paper, they just aren't that interesting (tried them though). If the mission is in Thailand, you'd want the mission to be somewhere recognizable, not a luxury hotel that could be in any part of the world. Likewise you'd expect the Japan mission to be somewhere more familiar instead of some high tech facility. This makes the last missions feel a bit uncreative since they could be placed anywhere in the world, really. Feels like they didn't put as much thought into them than the first ones.
The biggest minus comes from the low effort that has gone into voice acting. You don't really feel immersed in most levels since the same voices are present regardless of locale. NPCs have British or American voices even in Morocco or Thailand or wherever you are. This makes it all feel more like a simulation or training mission like the first missions in this game.
The gameplay is great and feels like a Hitman game should. Better voice acting and different languages for NPCs would make this almost perfect, but right now it feels like they ran out of money or time despite the episodic system (which I like btw, makes it much more likely I'll finish the game).

Pros: Good storyline, lots of side missions, fast travel, new gadgets
Con: frustrating combat system, ridiculous unlockable upgrades
The new stuff they decided to add were great additions to the game, such as fast travel system. Only makes sense that Batman doesn't glide everywhere when he's going from one place to another. The new gadgets are fun to use, if not very useful, and adds new elements to the game. The storyline is good with nice voice acting. And of course, there's lots to do aside from the main questline.
However, what they decided to tweak was for the worst. The unlockable upgrades forces you to do specific challenges only after you've unlocked a previous challenge, instead of the "do whichever challenge you like whenever you want" from the previous game. This doesn't sound so bad until you run into missable challenges, which quite literally is not accomplishable unless your restart your game, or do a new game plus (Worst Nightmare 5, I'm looking at you).
And why did they have to change the free flow combat system? Arkham City's combat was smooth and felt rewarding. Origins is just plain frustrating. Batman's targeting is flawed and you'd constantly end up punching the air. Villians attacks teleport across the screen to hit you. Batman's attack animations are locked in so countering feels hit or miss. Camera angles during fights would constantly shift, making it hard to see where the enemies are - you end up getting hit randomly from villians off screen.
If you love Batman, which I do, you'll get the game anyway and force your way through it. Then end up uninstalling it and going back to Arkham City for the better combat system.

"Spec Ops - The Line" is a competent TP cover shooter with standard, but reliable mechanics, unassuming yet crisp and in places beautiful graphics and art style, and even great music.
But first and foremost the game is standing out of the crowd due to its bold take on the genre. Which is not the usual way of making the player feel like a badass. Without spoiling too much, "Spec Ops - The Line" is more akin to movies like "Apocalypse Now": It shows us shooter fans how gruesome war and fighting actually is, does not let us neatly discern "good guys" from "bad guys", and never allows us to actually feel good doing what we think we "must". There are almost never "right" choices available, just different ways to get our hands dirty.
Oh, and don't listen to those who claim the game has clunky controls, for that's simply not true. At least with a gamepad, controls are responsive and precise. It's basically the same as "Gears of War", so if you're used to this control scheme, you should be very ok. Whenever my character suffered from a mishap going in or out of cover, I always knew in my heart it was my own fault because I accidentally pressed the wrong button at the wrong time. I suspect that the negative reviews come from people who usually only play first person shooters.
Absolutely get it, you'll miss something special if you don't.

Rather than talking about some of things other people have talked about, I want to cover exploration and discovery within this game. I've always been the kind of person who likes to go off the beaten trail and explore every nook and cranny a game has to offer. This game may be quite linear and not have many too many secret pathways and rooms (although it still has quite a bit to explore in that regard), but it definitely rewards the person who's of the mind to deviate from the story in search of extras. Almost anytime you decide to turn back and go explore previous areas, you'll end up finding new pieces of dialogue, new NPCs, or easter eggs. Now this definitely isn't something that anyone would want to do, as there is no run feature or fast travel in this game, so it requires some old-fashioned leg work if you want to actually find any of these things.
It's not just in the world where you can find this hidden goodies but in the combat as well. The combat can appear to be quite straightforward, either kill or spare your opponent. However, you'll often find that there are multiple ways to get towards your goals. Sometimes using certain items can have an effect on your ability to spare an individual, other times there may just be a little easter egg of text even if it has no actual impact on the fight. And one of my favourite things about these fights is if you choose to stick around after you're already able to spare the monster. Even though these interactions rarely lead to anything of value, these moments are usually more than worth it. One of the more well known instances of this is in the case of Lesser Dog, but there are others as well.
There are other ways in which you can uncover new bits of dialogue and secrets, but that might drift into spoiler territory so I'll leave it up to you figure that out. Anyway, if you look at other reviews, you'll see there's already so much to love in this game, but I wanted to take the time to cover the wealth of little extras, easter eggs and goodies that really add to the experience.

Undertale is truly incredible. Never before has an RPG used the very nuances of video games to tell such a rich, deep and compelling story, to the point where the player themselves feel like a part of the world, where every character is so charming and quirky, yet feel so real. While other RPGs at most give you "good" and "evil" options, this game really tests your conviction to stay on either path, and delivers a rich, satisfying and uplifting conclusion for the former, and nightmare-inducing, disturbing and permanent conclusion for the latter.
The game may not look like much on the surface, with its simple graphics and relatively simple gameplay mechanics. However, the simple graphics in my opinion allow the game to be truly immersive, as it's so wacky, goofy and fourth wall breaking that the graphics pull you into the world very quickly. And yet, despite the graphics, the characters are so expressive at all times, and nearly every character/enemy is very memorable from both their personalities and their designs.
The gameplay also offers a lot of unique ways to play, as you find out with each new boss. In Pacificst route, the game is mostly a game of dodging incoming projectiles and solving the battle via interacting peacefully with the enemy, which is definitely more absorbing and fulfilling than simply fighting. Each boss varies this formula, and changes to styles like platformer, 2D shooter, pointing a shield to block projectiles, answering a quiz show, defusing bombs, deadly dodging... the list goes on. I'd say the gameplay and the graphics are the weaker parts of the game, not that they are bad, but the story and characters are so incredible that I'd say the graphics and gameplay are "very good".
The music... my god the music. Every major characters has their own theme that suits them perfectly, and its hard not to smile when these guys are on screen. The music nearly everywhere perfectly portrays how you feel at that exact moment, from cozy but awkward, laid back and carefree, mysterious and downtrodden, to extremely disturbing and terrifying tracks when you actually are terrified, to heartbreaking final tracks that nearly always leave me in tears when I hear them. The story wouldn't be half of what it is without the music.
I can't say much about the story and characters without giving much away. The story is that good that I would try and avoid any forums/discussion/fanart of the game until you get the true ending. The game also has a no mercy route, but... whether you should play that or not depends on how attached you are to the game after the true ending. I could never play the no mercy route... even watching someone else play it left me quite disturbed and sick to my stomach. Suffice to say though - the true ending makes you feel like a true hero, back in your childhood, when the hero faces overwhelming odds against an powerful foe, and their powers of friendship and determination get them through? The game makes you that hero. Not the player character in the game. YOU. Sitting wherever you are, playing this. No other RPG has ever done this for me, and that's why I cannot recommend this game enough for anyone who likes story/character driven RPGs. Hell, if you like story-based games in general.
Thank you, Toby Fox. Games like this remind of how wonderful games, and humans... even monsters... can be.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a very non-simulator like simulator. I feel as though is this game didn't have simulator slapped at tthe end of its name it would have a better reputation, so do not ley that word fool you.

Pros:

-Realistically driving trucks
-Living, breathing Europe
-Steering wheel, game pad, and even joystick support
-Intuitive AI
-Cheap price
-Relaxing gameplay

-Great money system
-Challenging progression
Cons:
-Unlocks based on level progresssion
-Small cities

-Nothing, besides the vehicles, is dynamic

Overall, a great game, would for sure reccomend this.

Oh Nightcry.... As a big fan of the Clock Tower series I had to play this game no matter how bad the reviews were. Let me put it this way: I am overjoyed and very grateful that the creators are playing around with the series again BUT I really wish they had put a bit more effort into this. Allow me to explain: my biggest complaint is the crashes. I have a gaming desktop so this game shouldn't be a problem for it.  But boy did it crash. Not every single time. But quite often and at the worst times (like in the middle of a chase).  That aside, the characters movements were... Interesting. I applaud the creators for making each character model unique and organic looking (as in not all characters look the same with different hair and eyes).  But when it came to the Faithful, the character models looked like early Rockstar material.  The storyline was subpar for a Clock Tower game. Not even interesting enough to make me want to finish playing despite being minutes from finishing. To sum up all my feelings about this one let me say this-- what makes this game a no for me is ultimately the fact that the story just wasn't interesting. As a lover of old PC games from the FMV era even, the graphics were not a deal breaker in the slightest, but the lackluster storyline? Yeah, you betcha. All that being said, I implore the creators to try again and make a remake of the original games, ir some kind of sequel or prequel that honors the feeling of uneasiness the old games provoked.

Second, performance is pretty bad. The game is very unoptimized. The only way to change graphics options are through the launcher defaults of Poor through Beautiful (the launcher is actually the default launcher for a game built in Unity, so they didn't even supply customizable graphics options). On a more than capable system, I run the game at the second highest setting "Good" and often fall to 20 FPS, which really slows the game down and makes it feel clunky, which probably nobody will appreciate. This performance should just not happen in a game with requirements such as NightCry's.
Third, general quirks that other people have noted. Sometimes, (while I still don't believe to be gamebreaking), the camera makes it hard to control the character. What I hate is often in some hallways, the camera will point at the character's front, so that they are moving towards the player's view. With click to move controls, it makes it awkward to try to keep the character moving straight. I often find I am clicking the lower half of the screen rapidly to keep them moving, which tends to frustrate me. A lot of people also mention bad graphics and animations. Graphics could be better, the poor performance I experience doesn't really make sense for the quality. Animations I haven't been too concerned with other than little weird things like the character rapidly zigzagging as they approach a door for whatever reason.
All in all, the game is fun to me. I personally like exploring all the possible endings, as the game gives you a nice tree detailing why the story path went good or bad, making it easy to go back with a walkthrough (the first result on a quick Google search returns a fantastic one) and figure out what to do differently. I personally don't like walkthroughs, but some key story events to trigger different paths are things I don't think I'd ever try without pure luck.
I don't like the lack of finish and performance issues with the game. I definitely understand why those would turn people away from the game (and probably should).
As with any Steam game, I wouldn't purchase this for full price, wait for a good sale to maybe give it a shot, but be prepared to grin and bear through a good number of quirks throughout. I personally seem to enjoy it easily, but I tend to have lower standards with games and put up with issues many others wouldn't.

Let's start from the end: Ori is difficult as hell, but not for the good reasons: Its mechanics are simply horrible -- hard to aim jumps and hard to combine multiple keys for specific combos\actions. There are too many keys to control in a short sequence to simply get from point A to B. If you have weak nerves, DON'T PLAY IT because in Ori you'll die a lot, and I mean A LOT (200+ times !!!). The mechanics are extremely inconvenient and it leads to pure frustration. Moreover, the "health bar" in Ori means nothing  -- most of the obstacles will kill you in single touch even if your health is full (because they are "dead end" obstacles). The game is one of the hardest I ever played, on "normal" difficulty. On the other hand, it's so wonderful in terms of graphics, riddles, and story, that's why I continue playing. But eventually it's more of a suffering rather than playing.

Edit: This is only a review of the Definite Edition and it's difficulty settings!
I've played the Original Version and quit it in frustration at some totally unimportant series of obstacles. I simply suck at any game that requires coordination and pressing combinations of buttons. I got the Definitive Edition because it promised the option to change the difficulty and I was hoping that I'd be able to complete the game in Easy Mode (yes, that's how bad I am). Well, the stuff that got easier is fighting enemies (which was never a problem for me) and making it through the big bad escape sequences (which I had never reached anyway). Well...I just quit out of frustration early into the game again.
The game is absolutely stunning. I love the visuals, the story and the soundtrack. But I can't ♥♥♥♥ing play this, even on easy. For me, this game just means stress and frustration.
If you've played the Original Version and were too frustrated by the regular obstacles...don't get this. The difficulty settings simply won't help enough.
Edit:
To make this a bit clearer since Steam forces me to chose between recommending this game or not:
Get this game if you:
- enjoyed the original edition of Ori
- are determined/persistent, even if that means spending a long time trying to overcome one obstacle
- do not easily get frustrated
- have a high drive to complete a game
Do not get this game if you:
- struggled with the original edition of Ori
- get frustrated easily
- are bad at coordination
- are a more casual gamer who just wants to relax

Absolutely incredible game in every sense of the word. The original was a masterpiece, and the Definitive Edition was even more so. Truly an amazing game.
The art design and overall mood of the game is breathtaking. It's very visually appealing, with unique graphics and beautiful artwork. The moods it creates resonate with the player very well, and it is very immersive.
The music is simply spectacular. Before I even owned the game I listened to the music on repeat for days, I was captivated. The music adds to the mood making it at times feel lighthearted, and other times feel mysterious and mystical. Truly amazing soundtrack and overall sound design.
The gameplay, similarly, is very rewarding and thrilling. While it is a 2D platformer, there are numerous movement abilities you can gain through playing that allow you to control Ori in all sorts of ways. While the game is difficult, it is not frustrating. You have to be good with a new ability to use it to its fullest potential, and you have to really think about what you are doing at times. The gameplay is very interactive, and the combat (while slightly repetitive) is very fun as well. Once you get bash, a whole WORLD of possibilities opens up for you.
Lastly, the story is very immersive and full of emotion. The studio really did a wonderful job of conveying emotion and atmosphere in this game with little dialogue, and it is beautifully done. The characters are fun and dynamic, and really add a lot to the game.
Overall, I cannot recommend this game enough to anyone and everyone. It is truly a masterpiece. I've spent many hours playing this game and I have no plans to stop now. If you love video games at all, you're truly missing out by not playing this game.

Arkham Origins is perfectly fine. It looks great, plays smoothly, music & voice acting are superb. However, Rocksteady has pretty much beat this series to death now. You’ll feel cheated if you played Arkham City, because Origins re-uses the maps from it with only slight differences. The reason I can’t recommend it is that it’s the weakest one yet. Even if you have never played an Arkham game before, you’re better off playing one of the first two.
There’s very little new in Origins for series vets. You jaunt from pack of mobs to pack of mobs, they get incrementally tougher as the story progresses, and there are challenge maps on the side. There are a few minor changes, such as the handy dandy shock gloves, but nothing to write home about. If you had your fill of the combat system in the previous two titles, nothing here is going to excite you.
The story is the only chance this game could have of being something special but it, too, is uninspired. In fact, the story in these games gets more self-satirical as they go along. I’d have to get into spoilers and moral philosophy to explain further. Suffice it to say I felt like Rocksteady’s writers were purposefully goofing on Batman during this narrative.
Arkham Origins feels like a game that didn’t need to be made. The story is forgettable and you’ll be doing all the same stuff you’ve done in previous games, right down to collecting an ungodly amount of Riddler thingies. I’d only recommend it if you’re a diehard DC fanboy.

I'm going to recommend this overall, especially since the price literally amounts to pocket change, but there are plenty of issues that mar the experience. On the plus side, it is a streamlined, quaintly charming, and quietly beautiful point-and-click game that will probably provide more hours of enjoyment than most of its type (for reference, I'm only about halfway through). For the price, it's still well worth it, but like I said, you'll be in for a few growls. The biggest issue is that there is no option to skip puzzles, and some of them are just of the time-consuming, trial-and-error variety. In the same vein, there are a few clumsy (and completely incongruous) attempts at retro video game segments you have to wade through to return to the core game. The hint system could also use a revamp - a superficially clever way to "earn" your hints by collecting a series of buzzing bugs is no more than a mindless click-fest, and the hints often don't even activate on demand, leaving you to flounder around the current section until you stumble upon the interactive bit of it that opens up the next step. But don't let these gripes color your perception TOO much - like I said, it's still a lovely game for an unbeatable price.

As a fan of the series, this Hitman is one of the best for me. The open, beautiful levels are filled with many ways to kill to the point where it can get overwhelming. Luckily, the quality of life improvements established in this game helps focus your attention on what you can do. Opportunities are a nice way of introducing you to not only the map, but the target's route and behavior. Challenges are good milestones and markers that are sometimes just vague enough to make you buckle down and find out the best or easiest way to accomplish them. And the addition of unlocking different drop points for unlocked gear and new starting points keeps the game from getting dull from repeating the same opening every time you open up a level.
But there are some issues that can bring some caution to interested assassins. The game is very demanding on PCs. If you haven't had to upgrade your CPU in a while, this game might be the one to make you start to question your rig. Anisotropic x4 might sound like a low end spec you can handle, but set that option to literally any other option and your framerate will improve anywhere from 8-12 frames. DirectX 12 is taxing, also, but generally has more stable framerates than DX11. Technical aspects aside, the game also suffers from fairly common bugs, usually around the AI. An NPC will occasionally break their routine and stand still caught up in some technolimbo until something jostles them free, most of which involved me running into them or shooting somebody near them. There have also been some mention of NPCs seeing takedowns and kills through walls, but I have yet to encounter that.
One other caveat you might have is the always online requirement. I myself have never had a problem with it, but loads of others have and is a serious issue they consider when purchasing a new game. There have been some times when the servers have been slow to connect to or have crashed all together, but that is usually around the time an update or Ellusive Target has come out. I have never been booted from the game if the servers ever crashed.

HiTMAN is the sort of Hitman game I never imagined we'd see again after Absolution but here it is, Hitman is back and better than ever. Everything that Absolution did wrong has been corrected for this sequel and everything the series did right until that point returns, has been improved or replaced outright with something better. 6 large maps, offering near-complete freedom for players to go about completing the missions in their own way. At the end of season 1 it's clear IO took the criticisms of Absolution to heart and have gone above and beyond to return the franchise to what it was.
However, the always online requirement of the game is some of the most extreme and anti-consumer DRM I've seen in a game. It leaves you with the bare minimum of single player and disables ALL progress for weapon/item unlocks essentially locking you at level 1 unless you can get online and even then any offline progress you've made will not be carried over. I can only hope that as they took criticism of Absolution to heart when designing its sequel, they will see the overwhelmingly negative response to this DRM and remove the restrictions for season 2.
With hundreds of hours of gameplay and as many missions, this game is an awesome value.
