After playing around 12 hours of the game, getting all but two endings (got the best ending), and seeing a majority of the content, I'd say I'm ready to give my opinion of this game.
I came into this wanting a new Clock Tower game. Not in the likes of some odd magical girl fantasy or weird fetish horror like Haunting Ground/Demento. No, I wanted to relive the experience I had being chased and tormented by a sinister creature wielding a giant pair of scissors. And this game delivers in that aspect.
In the first chapter, I was taken right back to when I played the original games as a kid. Too nervous to look around, afraid any noise would attract the Scissorwalker's attention, and went through things quickly just to avoid encountering that thing. (Ended up getting a bad ending as a result. lol)
Admittedly, the fear diminished a bit when I soon learned in the third chapter the Scissorwalker more utilizes the formula of the First Fear. That being, she only appears in certain areas upon examining things as the way Bobby (first Scissorman) worked.
Even so, don't think you can just avoid her. Unlike being able to go all of First Fear without ever encountering Bobby (other than the beginning and until the end of the game anyway), there are certain areas and items you will be required to investigate that can bring her to you. While it is slightly disappointing the Scissorwalker is more scripted, it does encourage exploration, and daring you to take chances. I can say that even though I felt a little at ease knowing the Scissorwalker doesn't show up at random, I did still get nervous and a little freaked in some places, and especially when I did need to escape her.
The Clock Tower series never really had any great stories. Using a basic plot just to get the horror show going. You're a young girl who under unfortunate circumstances ended up in the clutches of the Scissorman and now must survive and escape. NightCry is a continuation of this basic premise.
The three main characters you get are two college girls, Monica Flores and Rooney Simpson, and their Professor, Leonard Cosgrove, who were boarding a cruise liner called the "Oceanus". You start as Monica, whose goal is to hopefully meet a rich man and fall in love (don't get the wrong idea, there's more to it than what you may think), then switches over to Leonard who is a cultural anthropologist and a very eccentric man, and finally the melancholic and withdrawn outcast Rooney. All three have their own chapters and offer different point of views of going about this nightmare, all helping to tie things together in the last act.
The lack of ambience is a little bit of a turn-off for some, and I guess I understand why. But in my opinion, the music more than makes up for it. The soundtrack is gorgeous, delivering a creepy, tension-heightening sound that makes you not want to see what could be around the corner. It's some of the best horror music I've heard since the Silent Hill series, some of my favorite tracks being "Close Behind", "Voyager", "The Cave", "The Cult", and many others. The only thing that disappointed me about the OST was the Scissorwalker's theme. It starts out with a scare chord, but then goes kind of mellow and slow. Maybe it's nostalgia talking, but I always enjoyed the fast paced theme of the Scissorman, "Don't Cry Jennifer". Nonetheless, the OST as a whole still does its job of creating a great atmosphere.
Some of the deaths and gore may be considered over-the-top, but that's always been how the Clock Tower series rolled. I, for one, loved them to pieces. They can get comical to creative to disturbing. One scene in particular comes to mind where something awful happens to a very unfortunate character that was really messed up. But it certainly added to the horror of what these people involved with the Scissorwalker are up to.
Now, having said all of this, the game isn't perfect. In fact, it suffers a lot of flaws that I can see many turning their nose up at it for.
*The graphics. They're not that bad to me, however, I know people of today love their pretty graphics and when you compare NightCry to the appearance of say Until Dawn, it certainly looks ugly. Not helped that it tends to shift. There're times they look passable, to uncanny valley.
*The animations. I will say, this is one of the more disappointing aspects. The animations sometimes are done well enough, but other times so sloppy I wonder how it was deemed "ready". Sometimes the lips don't even move, and while I got over it, I can't blame anyone who finds it jarring.
*The voice acting. Now, in my opinion about 90% of the voice acting was fine by me. Monica, Leonard and Jerome all got decent voices, but Rooney's was the big let-down. She sometimes overacts, and sometimes barely acts, making Rooney's important scenes rather cheesy. Fortunately, there is an option to switch it to the Japanese track if you can't bear the English track. I will say though, I wasn't fond of all the Jp voices either, personally. (But at least Rooney got a better portrayal.)
*The story. I mentioned earlier that the Clock Tower series's stories were nothing to write home about, and NightCry isn't doing much else either. The basic premise is all right (murder on board a ship, try to survive it, you are winner), but it's kind of not fleshed out. It seems to prefer to be a little too vague. There are some largely unexplained parts of the plot that may require you to do some extra investigating and theorizing after. Now, I just came off the game, so a replay may be in order to piece it together. But for now, I got to mark against it that it almost feels "incomplete" at times.
*Jank, camera, and controls. This game is quite unpolished. It uses the old-style point and click that the older Clock Tower games did. For me, I was quickly able to adapt and understand the controls, but I know this won't be the case for everyone else. The camera angles can be a bit awkward as well, causing you to struggle between it and getting the hang of the controls, especially when the Scissorwalker is chasing you. Like I said, I was able to adapt after a bit, but I realize this may be a turn-off for others. And there were times I did fumble with it as well.
*Bugs and glitches. As many people have reported, this game has a lot of bugs. Fortunately, none that really broke the game. Often closing and reopening the game fixed the problem, but it does tend to take away from the experience. The most jarring examples being that sometimes the music and/or sound effects cut out. However, the development team, from what I understand, is hard at work to patch all this up. So hopefully this will remedy the problem. It's barely two weeks old, so it kinda comes with the territory.
Despite naming these flaws and, admittedly, I wish this game could have been more than what it is, I still loved it for what it set out to do. This game worked on a small budget, only just barely above 300 grand, and was lucky to get what it got, so I wasn't expecting too much, but I did enjoy what they were able to do. I don't see a lot of people being very understanding of this though, so this game definitely falls under the "either love it or hate it" category. NightCry was definitely made for Clock Tower fans of the first two original. Following the same dynamics and principles. If the first two games didn't appeal to you, or old school Japanese horror (we're talking PSX/PS2-era) isn't your cup of tea, then there's a chance you might not be able to appreciate it.
If nothing else, wait for the patches and at least give it a try. Maybe it just might surprise you.
Speaking for myself as a Clock Tower fan, I was overall pleased with NightCry and feel it is a worthy successor to the original titles. I didn't regret my time at all with this game, and I hope that it improves to be even better in the near future.
Overall score: 7.6/10.

I cannot recommend this.
While it is amusing to begin with, the mechanics are inherently weak as is shown in later levels. Power is not truly transferable(meaning you cannot indirectly project power), and several of the later levels are designed in such a way that the natural outcome is a "deadlock". Meaning, for example, that there's a choke-point of 2 planets, and you can direct 5 planets worth of power there, and the AI can project 5 or 6 planets worth of power there. The result is that even if you manage to focus down one of those planets, it is now further in the AI territory and it can bring additional 3 planets worth of power to bear against it, instantly taking it back.
For some of these levels, there are supposedly Youtube-walkthroughs from the creator. The problem is that either the enemy got smarter, some mechanics changed, or they are immensely luck-based. (e.g. level 35, even if I try to copy the walkthrough exactly to bypass the deadlock, the AI is always smart enough to "save" against backdoor intrusion, and thus ultimately has sufficient planets available to force the deadlock again.
Other annoying aspects: There's obstacles that cause seemingly randomized pathfinding(meaning doing the exact same thing 2 times in a row produces different results), Enemies seem to focus on you(more obvious in a few maps featuring above-mentioned deadlocks), and seemingly "mirrored" maps are not(meaning the AI can reach a planet from a position where you cannot on your side of map, giving it an advantage).
Most annoying, though, is the fact that all that excess power is lost. While i understand that this is part of the mechanic, it also turns some maps into slugfests, where you clearly have an advantage but have to battle it out for, depending on your individual skill, quite a long time. A more elegant mechanic would have been preferable here.
Even if "boosting" a planet would just work as a tiebreaker against an unboosted enemy planet projecting power somewhere.
All in all, it is amusing for a while and the price is low. But it is a source of great frustration in some later levels, which is why I cannot recommend this. From its simplicity and tone, it aims to be similar to a number of games it lists in the store page. But it fails in providing that same fair and enjoyable playstyle.
TL:DR: Several shortcomings and map design make this game infuriating in later levels, with luck-based and seemingly random success-chance, rather than strategy. As such, cannot recommend even at this price. If you pick it up in a bundle, go ahead and give the first couple levels a try-those are fine.

Mad Max is a game of style over substance. Normally, that's a bad thing. Games that focus on how cool it is or how good it looks can sometimes make for a bad game. Not for Mad Max. The world is amazing. It's deep and weird and fun and horrible and brutal. It feels like you are in this world and you have to build up and get better or else you won't make it.
It's very grind-centric. You will have to go roaming and find things to do or else you can't progress. I thought I would hate that, but I've grown to love it. It's like the game told me, "Don't worry, the story isn't important. Just go explore. Do some fun stuff. Blow stuff up. You'll love it." I'm the type of guy to go and beat the story as soon as possible. But this game made me WANT to explore and find hidden items, go raid outposts, save people.
The combat on foot is fun and challenging. It has that standard Batman Arkham style system of endless combos, but even more brutal at times. The shotgun is essentially worthless until midgame when you build up a stronghold. But once you get going, you are a shotgun toating, fist fighting, face shanking bad♥♥♥♥♥with plenty of sweet combos and finishers at your disposal. The fighting is tough and gritty and brutal and fun.
But this is Mad Max! You want to be driving, right? Well, vehicle combat is not that great. It turns into "When will my harpoon reload" and not much else. Sometimes it's a blast to chase down a convoy and really do some damage and feel that Fury Road type chase, but most of the time it boils down to your harpoon doing work. But for the most part, driving is fun and it's just great to sometimes just go and cruise and see what type of trouble you can get yourself into. The car upgrades really make your car a unique project for everyone and really drives you to keep doing things so you can make it even better than it was. Wish there was a handbrake though for some of those nasty turns.
There's so much to do and so much to explore. If you want to just go have fun in an amazing sandbox, just pick this up. I can't rec this enough. The world is deep and you can just get lost for hours. It takes a bit, but once you get to a certain point, this game turns into something you can't put down.

I've seen a lot of indie games with smaller budgets that weren't so messy on the technical side. This is what happens when somebody tries to do something they can't possibly accomplish. I mean, seriously, why even go for 3D if you can't make it look good? Just take a look at
,
,
,
– they all are 2D and they benefit from it, because their developers had spare time to work on the aspects that matter. But, even if you go for 3D, why butcher the player's experience by shoving in so much more tech than you can handle? Yeah, hair physics and dynamic shadows look great, but 30 fps and aliased edges absolutely do not.
What about modding? It's a definitive aspect of PC gaming. This game would've gained so much more longevity and popularity if it had at least SOME kind of modding support. All the design flaws could've been dealt with if full support was introduced – while still not sacrificing the original creative ideas, since mods are optional.
This was just technical stuff. Don't even get me started on completely nonsensical and counterproductive design decisions, laughably contrived story, and utterly horrendous controls (in a
game, how can anyone screw that up?). This is simply not acceptable in 2016.
Despite all this, NightCry is oddly captivating. I'm yet to finish the game, and it will take me some time (since I keep stumbling into bugs I report only to be told it's all intentional), but, as it is, I can't stop playing it. The atmosphere of this game is only comparable to that of
or

series, which I, sadly, was not able to play).
Don't buy this game for $15. Wait until it drops to $5 or $8, then give it a try.

Those hardly take away from the enjoyment of the game, however. The game manages to create a great atmosphere, and the story is very good, very Mad Max-y. It's a bit short, however, there's a TON of stuff to do in the world. The side-objectives do get a bit repetitive, but the sheer act of driving in thes game is so great, you don't feel it. Hand-to-hand combat is also fantastic - a slightly simplified, more "realistic" version of the Arkham system. It's very visceral, and very fun. Definitely recommend it.

I Kickstarted this game, I was really looking forward to it. But it falls flat on it's face.
1) first thing I'm going to bring up is the controls, Like the original clock tower game, this relies on a point and click control scheme, No other buttons are used (Except escape to quit, and P to pause) That might not sound like a terrible thing, and in some cases it isnt, But when you're being chased by a maniac with a giant pair of scisors, you need responsive quick controls. The mouse doesn't offer what you need in the 3d world, which brings me to problem 2. It's in desperate need of controller support.
2) Bad camera angles. Like the resident evil games of yesteryear, this game relies on a fixed camera angle to give both tension and dramatic flare. This in and of itself isn't terrible, but with the pont and click control scheme mentioned above, it makes it very difficult some times to get to certain areas quickly, because you can't really click on it, To make it worse, you're being chased during certain points, and can't see where the monster is, meaning lights out.
3) the monster. The monster itself is exactly what i was expecting, Scary and mysterious, and relentless. Perfect for this kind of game. But with the camera angles and bad controls, it makes it difficult to get away from in a hurry. He's usually pretty easily evaded until you can find a spot to hide, Unfortunately, You can only hide in a spot once before he destroys it, giving you limited encounters, You don't know whats going to trigger the encounter, so when you are just looking for items to complete the area, you could unintentionally get him after you. It feels as though if you get him chasing you more then once, you may as well start the game over, cause you're gonna get cut.
4)  Lack of direction. Right from the start, there didn't seem to be any real sense of direction, not a lot of subtle hints, just click around and hope you find something that gives you a clue. This isn't a bad thing either in and of itself, but because clicking on certain things causes the monster to spawn, and you only have limited hiding spots to get away, it means that if you don't know what you're doing and your clicking willy nilly through trial and error, you're gonna run out of hiding spots and once again, get cut.
5) WTF. Seriously, WTF. Warning, this part contains early game spoilers, Don't scroll on down if you're worried about it.
The characters don't seem to react properly to the WTF ness. Early game the owner of the cruise ship asks you for a lighter...to boil his prosthetic eye, which he has out, in the open, on a bunsun berner, in the middle of the freakin' bar. Not only does your character, who is some eye candy blond in a backless, gravity defying sloot dress, help with this predicament, She seems completely okay with this, like thats just a thing people do. The game is full of moments where it just seems normal to be surrounded by the bizarr, A little WTF reaction would have gone a long way.

I am a huge survival horror/Clock Tower fan, and I did go into this game both based on my love for Clock Tower and with people's negative opinions fresh on my mind. With that said, I'll make a simple list.
You SHOULD play this game if:
-You can appreciate the classic frustration of an old game... but on a new game
-You can look past cringey, but tolerable voice acting
-You love horror games of all shapes and sizes
-You like multiple endings and alternate ways to die
-You like strong, independent ladies who kick♥♥♥♥♥(don't underestimate Monica!)
-You like a challenge and have patience
-You can work past stupid glitches and don't mind a check point system
-You like running from a single monster, who you somehow grow to like over time (just me?)
You SHOULD NOT play this game if:
-You are a new gen gamer who never knew or got to appreciate the hardships and struggles of an old horror/adventure game, believe me you will hate it
-You are a ragequitter
-You hate bad voice acting
-You are a Clock Tower fan! Seriously, don't play this if you are expecting something close to Clock Tower, its NOTHING like it. While playing this, nothing gave me even a hint of anything reminiscent of Clock Tower.
-You can't stand check points or obnoxious glitches
With all that in mind, I DO actually reccommend this game. Here's to hoping they will fix the bugs though, I had at least 4 stupid glitches that caused me to have to restart an area. AND MAKE SURE YOU CLICK EVERYTHING MULTIPLE TIMES! You will regret it and cry tears of blood when you have to start a whole area over because you forgot something or didnt trigger something correctly.
Also, there are a lot of plot holes. If you are someone like me who analyzes the scenario as a whole, a lot doesnt make sense story-wise. BUT, I don't know if this is just because of the route I took? Maybe if you take a different route in the story on another playthrough, you might fill the gaps. I don't know though.

Disappointment is sitting through an installer for over an hour only to find out this game plays like a clunkier version of every other MMORPG out there.
Now, let me clear a few things up.  I have no nostalgia coming into this game.  I never played Everquest when it was popular, as I was way more into consoles at that time.  I did get a chance to play Champions of Norrath 1 & 2 (probably still two of my favorite hack & slashers) on PS2.  Lately, I've been playing a lot of free-to-play MMORPGs and this was on my list of things to try out.
I couldn't even make it past the first beach with the crabs.  Combat is clunkier than every title I've played in this genre so far.  I wasn't even sure if I was hitting the crab and who was winning.  The health bars all kept disappearing behind terrain and some fantastic glitches, my swings were choppy and there was no noise to signify connecting, and (without lag, trust me) combat moved so slow that combined with those horrible controls I have to rate this experience as painful.  I have no comment on the epic tiered equipment as I have no desire to get to level 2.
If you've never played before, pick up a different MMORPG.  There have to be at least 5 in the fantasy genre on Steam, and you'd be doing yourself a favor not starting with this title.
I don't need to recommend this if you've played it before and enjoyed it, so if that's you, keep enjoying it.  This was a top game at one point, and there is a reason for that.  I just don't think it's as fun as some of the other free-to-plays on Steam right now.

I've never really gotten into the previous games in the Hitman series. Too much sensitivity around the stealth mechanics, and funky controls were usually the items that would have me running out of interest quickly. That all changed with this entry.
The controls make sense and are pretty responsive overall. They can be a bit cumbersome at times, but I found myself getting accustomed after a couple of missions. I've enjoyed the episodic release schedule for the game as it keeps me coming back pretty much on a monthly basis and gets me playing again when I otherwise probably would have beaten it once and forgotten about it within 2-3 weeks of release. I also appreciate that the development team has kept a pretty timely release schedule throughout the first season as some other episodic games have been stretched out over more than a year and can be difficult to find the drive to return to.
I haven't run into any issues with the always online requirement, so that's been smooth for me, but I can easily see where that could turn into a hassle and a point of frustration.
This game is definitely recommended if the series has ever even had a remote appeal to you and there haven't been any major flags that came up when looking at reviews.

most of the reviews are complaining about the online-only aspect. it's not fully online-only; you can still play offline. however, i can't say that their complaints aren't fair (especially if you have crappy internet).
anyway, the game is a true hitman sequel. it is like blood money and absolution merged together.... in a good way. it seeks to be blood money 2.0, by being a game about hiding in plain sight rather than hiding behind cover like in absolution, while at the same time it is not afraid to borrow the good aspects from absolution. i think the game accomplished this. for example, the maps are huge, and not only are they very replayable for the story mode, but also the contracts mode. in fact this game has the most replayability of any hitman game. my personal favorite is sapienza, because it's a great map for both the story mode and the contracts mode.
the story is solid too. it is the best story in a hitman game imo. the shadow client and that providence guy are interesting characters.
pretty much everything about this game is great. my only two complaints are the combat system and the rating system. they're not terrible or anything, but it seems that IO did not put a lot of work into those two things compared to the rest of the game, where they put a whole lot of effort into making the game right to please the fans. regardless, i give this game a 9/10. if you are a hitman fan this is a MUST.

GTA games have always had their place. And although San Andreas is supposedly the most fully-featured release to date, it is deficient in almost all areas.
Graphics- The game is graphically inferior, for the time it was released on the PC. Low quality textures, models and low view distance make this game a mediocre entry at best.
Sound- The farcical dialogue can sometimes be funny, and the radios feature good songs. But all the stereotypical voice acting is grating and obnoxious, and the gun sounds and other sound effects are mediocre at best.
Gameplay- Clearly, no effort was made to port this game to PC, although whether or not it should have been remains up for debate. At it's core its a TPS with driving elements but the aiming system is clumsy, the driving controls are downright drunken, and the consolized save system ( you can only save in "your house") is incredibly outdated, even for 2005 standards. In addition, the story and characters are incredibly annoying. Annoying isn't a strong enough word. I'm all for crime films and games IF they have compelling characters. There is nothing compelling about anyone you meet in this game. Nearly everyone who is your ally is despicable, and have no redeeming qualities. Maybe it's just me, but I find no reason to do missions involving tagging and lowriders, especially for people who give me no reason to like them. I understand this game is gang themed, but despite its sandbox gameplay, the missions themselves are quite linear and offer nearly no reason to complete them.
A good deal of my criticisms are subjective, but I believe this game is not only better suited on console, but better suited for a specific type of gamer that has little in common with me. I'm all for morally dark or straight up evil characters, but they have to be interesting, and the opportunity for role-playing has to be there. There's nothing interesting about ordinary criminals and gang scum.
Whether you agree or not, This game is off my hard drive for a long time.

With its distinct visual style and humorous dialogue, Borderlands 2 is an absolute joy to play! Equipment, level progression, and skill perks are all expertly balanced from start to end, and a wide variety of weapons, enemy types, and environments keep gameplay mixed up and interesting.
On the first playthrough.
This is not a bad thing except the game will eventually come to an end later or sooner depending on your level of skill, at which point you'll be faced with a choice... to start over or go New Game+.
With multiple job classes, starting a new game isn't bad but the storyline remains static. By the fourth or sixth (depending on if you got the DLCs or not) playthrough, even the most enthusiastic gamer might start feeling tedium creeping around the edges of the same jokes that you swore were so witty the first time around (and they were!).
Problems really start to arise on the New Game+ option, however, for those that are attempting to go for 100% completion. The issue above still arises (in that, you'll need to start the game over and make your way through the whole story multiple times), but it's compounded by the fact that the enemy difficulty begins to outpace your character strength. By the end-end game, and even kitted with the most powerful equipment, the most basic enemies will pose a serious threat to life and limb and bosses will soak up tens of thousands of rounds, usually far in excess of the amount of ammunition you can carry into the fight.
The only solution is to utilize very specific skill and gear combinations that enjoy stacking and complimentary effects. Normally this wouldn't be much of an issue except that the gear required is at this point nigh impossibly difficult to acquire and, second, that a primary joy of Borderlands 2 was the freedom to use the weapons that had the right "feel". That goes out the window in the end-end-game, where raw damage output and effects bordering on broken or glitched become necessary to survive.
But it's still great fun, who am I kidding? Give it a go, play it through, but don't try to really complete the game without knowing what's in store.

I backed this game over a year ago and was really looking forward to a game that catered to my nostalgia. There is definitely a serviceable game there, but it NEEDS more time in the oven. First off, the game defaulted to my onboard graphics card rather than my gaming one. I fixed this by launching via Explorer with a right-click rather than via Steam. They aren't fancy by any means, but I am perfectly fine with the graphics as they are presented. That being said, the game managed to turn me off within the first twenty seconds - a buxom blonde walks through a door and her hair ripples in every direction, clipping through her softball-size chest multiple times. She takes a step and the ends of her hair violently whip into the air like Medusa's snakes. I'm watching an in-engine cutscene, and I'm surprised that no one looked at this and thought it needed some polish. I take some painfully slow steps around the room (she walks like a satyr, but that's either because she's drunk, in heels, a combination of both, or just some inhuman animation,) and talk to the coatcheck. The voice acting seems perfectly acceptable. I click on him again, and the woman stares at him while he continues focusing on his work. They apparently have a conversation as diagloue appears along the bottom, but the voice acting is gone and they aren't moving their mouths or even displaying some type of speaking animation. I'm okay having voice acting only in major scenes, ala Parasite Eve, but two people standing motionless just boring holes into each other with their eyes while dialogue runs is a major turn-off. The silence becomes maddening - I understand that the Kickstarter didn't raise enough money for ambient noise, but it's odd and a bit boring wandering around a giant cruise ship kept company only by your footsteps. I do exploring around and discover that I can run somewhere by double-clicking, but I notice that in the 3D environment the game will grossly misinterpret where I want to run and I end up in a wall or doing an about-face. I went down a long hallway and was doing okay, but when I turned around I was at the mercy of the camera; it never shifted when I turned around, so there were only about three feet (to scale) between my character and the edge of the screen. As a result, a hallway that took me six clicks to get down (12, actually, because I was running,) took me 24 (48, because I was running) to get back down because I could only move three feet at a time until the camera finally changed. The Scissorwalker looks great, but I couldn't find the time for fear because I was so busy drunkenly careening through the ship fighting the camera and the poor navigation with the point-and-click interface. I REALLY would like to play this game as it was envisioned, but it needs A LOT of polish, and since it has been already been released, I'm not very hopeful.

I had been looking forward to this game for over a year. I'm very sorry to say that it's not just that I'm merely disappointed: I'm rather displeased. This game is borderline unplayable. It's unpolished and the controls don't feel right, and this is coming from a longtime fan of point-and-click adventure games (let alone the Clock Tower series, having started with the Super Famicom classic). But I just didn't have much fun with the twelve hours I've spent.
I'm only writing this review now because I've reached an unwinnable situation: NightCry has literally pulled a "Duck Amuck" (yes, from Looney Tunes) and erased much of the scenery, to the point where I can't progress. I'm stuck. I could reload a checkpoint and try again, but overall this game simply does not feel like a finished product. It feels like a work-in-progress, and I'm very disappointed with the results.
There are some things of merit, to be sure. I love the design of the Scissorwalker, but it's a shame that she often gets stuck in doorways, giving me plenty of time to recover stamina and evade. The chapter with Leonard was the most interesting to me, and some of the visuals look good... while other parts look more drab.
But the glitches have rendered NightCry pretty much unplayable to me. The controls are so awkward (again, this is coming from a longtime fan of the genre) that I DREADED the Scissorwalker sequences, but not because I was scared--because I didn't want to get even more frustrated. The unpolished vibe that surrounds this game, along with the horrendous glitches, all thoroughly ruin the horror and tension that a true Clock Tower successor needs.
I'm very sad to say--and I mean it, because I really wanted to like this game--that I'm strongly disappointed. I appreciate the idea of a Clock Tower successor, but I'm dissatisfied.

At it's launch state, I can only give this a "nope". While it does definitely have the atmosphere of a classic survival horror game, it suffers a lack of playtesting and illogical event progression. It has potential, but to call the release premature would be an understatement. While they are already busy patching things, some of the issues run deep enough that there can be no fix beyond a re-think of the core approach. I seriously advise looking deeper into the game's state before you risk a purchase.
Those of you who are familiar with older gems are probably no stranger to awkward cameras, high profile bugs and nonsensical triggers, but we usually forgave them because the game managed to outshine it's flaws. However in this game, the camera is such an issue that it can really get in the way of losing yourself to the game. The controls are point-and-click based, but if the camera doesn't change to allow you to near your desired destination, you will simply be unable to go there. For example, if a corridor forks in two directions but the camera nests itself inside one path, you may simply have no ground to click on (and clicking too close to the walls may send you in only god knows what direction). You will have to wrestle with the camera, as well as occasional invisible walls or no-walk zones. This can easily happen while an antagonist is chasing you.
Thankfully your cursor has a forgiving area for revealing interaction points, but memories of pixel-hunting come back when things hide themselves just outside of your strangled camera, or when one interactible's field blocks another, or when one intercepts your attempted click to move somewhere. Then there is the game progression. What the creators wanted you trigger before you can progress is often very hard to understand. Forgetting to repeatedly interact with even token scenery items can cost you a lot of pointless wandering and backtracking, made worse if there is no reasonable way to discern the requirements. Deliberately re-interacting with everything until you run out of new text will become second nature, even though each interaction causes a pause for a blink of fade-to-black (both before and afterwards), and there isn't always a way to skip individual lines of description (only the whole thing, sans the fade).
I don't mind a chapter's progression being linear, as that lets the creators write in a much more controlled manner, but NightCry falls too far into the trial and error side of things. Initially, interacting with certain objects will give you typical "nothing to do here" responses that suggests they are just props. I'm sure you know the kind. "Nothing out of the ordinary", "Just a clean table", "A stack of magazines. I never read these" and "I can't waste time here!" Only later on you may be required to re-check one of these 'prop' items to cause the story to proceed, even when nothing immediately suggests you should do so. I hate hand-holding as much as the next gamer, but breadcrumbs in a maze are always a godsend. Too much time lost and you simply disengage. Those footprints? Yeah. Go back and interact with them twice more for some flavour text, otherwise you're going nowhere.
For instance : (minor?) SPOILERS for chapter 1 ahead.
An initial pass of some nearly identical rooms will tell you (paraphrased) "This briefcase is stuck shut, no need to open it anyway". Each room has a briefcase with the same reactions. However you will need to re-check one of them later, and you will be unable to progress unless you do so. I only knew to do this because the game eventually took mercy and gave me a hint phonecall after hobble-wandering the corridors forever. Another example was having a set of keys to a cafe, only the cafe was already open access. The cafe had a second floor and she even notes "the stairs are only blocked with a rope cordon" but then says "but I have no reason to go up there", despite the current goal being to search for a way to a different floor. Yeah.

I have played both Ori and the Blind Forest first and then bought the DE (=Definitive Edition) afterwards for 5€ (25€ total). You should definitely buy this because it is one of the best games I have ever played. After the list about pros and cons of the original I only compare the two games but since you'll receive both anyway you don't really need to go trough everything.
I never used anything but a gamepad to play but I recommend using one if possible as other reviews complain about complicated controls which isn't the case when using a controler.
difficult platformer (neither too hard, nor too easy)
good graphical design
good story
game mechanics I haven't seen in any other game before
appropriate length (it took me about 8 hours for my first playthrough but I also managed to do it in less than 3 hours)
I assume it's rather well optimized (could play it on my previous rather bad PC) but I'm not an expert
can't really think of anything now
new game mechanics
well designed new area(s)
quick travel system
changeable difficulties
extended story (Naru's past)
reaccessing older areas (Ginso Tree, etc.)
new mechanics and area(s) are optional to use/explore
Naru's past not as satisfying as many expected
I love those games and you should try them but I expected more changes from the DE. Everything they claimed to be new to the game is a part of the game but that's already it. Changable difficulties are a great thing and the quick travel to a few locations is useful too. And in case you missed out on a secret location you can reaccess some areas.
All of this is nice to have but not a big deal.
The biggest problem is that the two new areas - which could also be one single area insted - are optinal. The first time I played I didn't notice the first area until I was already far enough through the game to just follow it up with the second area. You're able to learn one ability in each area but since it's all optional to the story those abilities aren't made use of later on. Other than using them in order to make everything else a little easier you can only unlock little secret zones for steam achivements with them. A lot of potential in terms of new challenges wherever you are seems to be wasted now.
I can hardly say the Definitive Edition was worth the extra 5€ I had to pay.
But as I mentioned earlier, this doesn't matter to you becasue your only choice is to buy both for the price of one. Have fun playing

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Hitman has seen many different implementations over the years with various levels of success. This itteration of the storied franchise throws everything out and rebuilds the game from the ground up, taking the finest ingredients from previous games and works them into a forward-thinking and modern title that stands on the shoulders of giants.
Its 'Opportunities' system for every hit make sure the player is always aware of how to proceed and never gets stuck, while dozens of 'Challenges' layer on top to provide hints at other ways they can complete their mission. Released episodically, the game is a triumph, allowing players the time to go back and attempt each level from hundreds of different angles, playing each map's mechanics to their advantage.
With a system of unlocks to reward exploration and experimentation, and a host of community-made contracts and time-limited ellusive targets released every few weeks, the first season is astonishing value for money and is a standout game of the year for me. Well Recommended for fans of the series as one of the strongest, if not THE strongest installment to date.

It's important to know that the majority of negative reviews for this game are because of two things:
1) This game has online DRM.
2) This game has scheduled "elusive targets" side-missions that are time-gated (only available for a few days) and reward cosmetic suits. Note that these missions are essentially the same as user-made "contracts" would be, and don't offer meaningful content (or achievements). Just some flashy suits.
Now, if either of those factors are an absolute deal-breaker for you - if you're adamant on never supporting online DRM, or are crazy about completion - then this game might not be for you. And I'm honestly very sorry you won't be experiencing this gem of a game.
On the other hand, if you're like me and are only mildly concerned about both those issues, then I wholeheartedly recommend this game. The game itself is incredible, has in insane amount of content and replayability, and is no doubt worth what I paid for (30usd). At the end of the day, you must do your own research to determine it suits your needs, but know that in my opinion this is the most satisfying stealth game I've played in years.

Here's the deal.
Let us put to the side the fact that Spec Ops The Line hits every cliché of shooters of its time, almost as if there was a rule book the developers had to follow. Let us put aside the excessive light bloom, the awkward controls and the B-movie action. Let us put all of it to the side because I was prepared to. I was prepared to do so because this game did have a number of things done well, it had a number of things going for it. However, there is a point in the game, where you have a large unsuspecting enemy camp in your way, and you are given a white phosphorus mortar to use.
…No.
See, I know that it is against international laws to use WP directly against people, and I bet even those without legal training understand this. But in case you didn't, the game shows to you what WP does to people in one of the previous scenes. And by this moment in the game, I can tell quite well that the game is setting me up in order to preach to me. Spec Ops has been marketed as having choices, but it is all bullsh*t. Aside from a few insignificant choices, it does not give me a choice of not being a victim of its linear preaching. It won't let me proceed without doing this thing it commands me to do.
So I won't proceed. F*ck you, game.
See, there are many games out there that are linear, but those games generally don't push you over the line, don’t treat you like crap. You are usually following orders and/or the objectives are honorable, or at the very least the bad consequences of your actions are not clear. That is how games are. You know, the things that people play for pleasure?
This game has a lot of cool stuff, but the things I have to go through to get to that cool stuff have just gotten too much for me. I wish you better luck. As for me, I reached the point at which I turned around and walked into the desert and the game ended for me.

Violence, bloodshed, and cruelty are unfortunate, likely indelible parts of our reality. As widespread as they are, it’s only natural they’re reflected in expressive media. Guns, for example, are always a hot topic, and a good fit for video games: point, shoot, be visually and technically rewarded. First and third-person shooting can provide such a compelling feedback loop for players that hundreds of these games are developed, and millions of copies are sold. Series like Call of Duty and Gears of War set the pace for the modern shooter. In a medium, in a society, so acclimated to this kind of violence, it is, in turn, only natural that opposing commentary arises. See Heart of Darkness, Apocalypse Now, and Spec Ops: The Line.
A third-person shooter set in the near future or an alternate present, Spec Ops: The Line puts players in the shoes of Captain Martin Walker, an American soldier sent to Dubai with two companions to evacuate survivors from the city, long in ruins from hellish sandstorms. Upon arrival, the group picks up a distress signal from Walker’s old commander, Colonel John Konrad, apparently holed up in the city with his battalion, the 33rd. Walker decides to search him out, only to be met with extreme opposition from crazed members of the 33rd itself. Over the course of the game, Walker and his fellow soldiers cross paths with the CIA, cross swords with the 33rd, and make decisions that will change the lives of thousands.
From minute one, the influence of Conrad and Coppola is clearer than a summer sky. Konrad (like, come on) may as well be named Kurtz; Walker, Marlow or Willard. The trek through Dubai is as hellish as the Conrad’s Congo or Coppola’s Vietnam. It is certainly a fitting setting for a modern retelling. Dubai is a rich man’s paradise built on the backs of thousands in a position no better than slavery. It’s in close proximity to areas heavily occupied by US armed forces for the last two or three decades; it’d believably be a point of interest and interference for our troops if such disastrous storms ever did strike. While The Line does hit these points, the classic story beats, and more, it’s held back by a lack of subtlety and a few key, sloppy moments. Narrative choices are peppered throughout, typically deciding between the life or death of nameless characters - only the final choice matters counts towards your ending, as far as I can tell. Those choices are further undercut by narrative choices you have no say in. This is summed up in an early chapter: you have a choice to save an informant or some civilians. One of your squadmates pushes for the informant and the mission, while the other wants to protect innocent lives - I went with the civilians. Hardly ten minutes later, your path is blocked with considerable forces, but there just happens to be white phosphorus mortars nearby. Now, strangely, your squadmates’ roles swap - the one who argued for the civilians now argues for completing the mission by any means necessary, while the other now vouches for finding another way. “There’s always a choice,” he says. Apparently not, because you’re promptly forced to melt a couple hundred people to continue towards your goal. This is made all the more baffling when, in later chapters, load screens directly chastise the player for killing without caring. I do appreciate that The Line asks these questions and poses them to players, many of which may be expecting just another action-packed military shooter. I’m just sure there’s a way to do so with more finesse and, ultimately, impact.
Gameplay is serviceable, though drab. The closest comparison is probably Gears of War, owing to the focus on cover, roadie run, visible grenade arcs, and other nuances. Level and encounter design is, again, just serviceable. There are in-game challenges that offer a bit of engagement - get a hundred headshots, kill twenty rappelling enemies. I suspect this feature is a self-aware genre jab, juxtaposing arcade-like objectives with horrific and widespread death, but it ended up as the only thing maintaining my interest in each firefight. That’s the thing about this game: much like Apocalypse Now, it can feel like just another example of what it’s trying to criticize. It can come off as a cheap Gears clone made to sell units, and there isn’t always enough evidence present to say otherwise.
I’ve been hard on it, but I do have a lot of respect for Spec Ops: The Line. Amidst the ocean of Duty, Battle, and Honor, this game stands out as a genuine effort to make these audiences, and this industry, to consider genre standards we may be too comfortable with. It’s worth attention, despite its missteps. Apparently, development was repeatedly delayed, some of it owing to story changes; with more time and a unified vision, Yager Development could’ve made something truly great. For now, we have a solid attempt at a Heart of Darkness for the modern age that deserves recognition for confronting complacency to violence.

I have played both Ori and the Blind Forest first and then bought the DE (=Definitive Edition) afterwards for 5€ (25€ total). You should definitely buy this because it is one of the best games I have ever played. After the list about pros and cons of the original I only compare the two games but since you'll receive both anyway you don't really need to go trough everything.
I never used anything but a gamepad to play but I recommend using one if possible as other reviews complain about complicated controls which isn't the case when using a controler.
difficult platformer (neither too hard, nor too easy)
good graphical design
good story
game mechanics I haven't seen in any other game before
appropriate length (it took me about 8 hours for my first playthrough but I also managed to do it in less than 3 hours)
I assume it's rather well optimized (could play it on my previous rather bad PC) but I'm not an expert
can't really think of anything now
new game mechanics
well designed new area(s)
quick travel system
changeable difficulties
extended story (Naru's past)
reaccessing older areas (Ginso Tree, etc.)
new mechanics and area(s) are optional to use/explore
Naru's past not as satisfying as many expected
I love those games and you should try them but I expected more changes from the DE. Everything they claimed to be new to the game is a part of the game but that's already it. Changable difficulties are a great thing and the quick travel to a few locations is useful too. And in case you missed out on a secret location you can reaccess some areas.
All of this is nice to have but not a big deal.
The biggest problem is that the two new areas - which could also be one single area insted - are optinal. The first time I played I didn't notice the first area until I was already far enough through the game to just follow it up with the second area. You're able to learn one ability in each area but since it's all optional to the story those abilities aren't made use of later on. Other than using them in order to make everything else a little easier you can only unlock little secret zones for steam achivements with them. A lot of potential in terms of new challenges wherever you are seems to be wasted now.
I can hardly say the Definitive Edition was worth the extra 5€ I had to pay.
But as I mentioned earlier, this doesn't matter to you becasue your only choice is to buy both for the price of one. Have fun playing

NightCry comes at me as one of the most disappointing, frustrating, illogically designed horror and point and click games I've played in the past decade. This game gets so much wrong and with the talent behind the game is why I'm shocked as I was expecting a higher standards product.
Let's get this out the way. NightCry isn't a good game - at all - and in fact crossed over to be unplayabley buggy. The controls... what on Earth were the developers thinking? This is bare bones point and click, no confirmation selection and the horrendous, inaccurate reading of where I click my mouse and where the character moves is awful. This is especially the case when turning sharp corners, clicking on the perimeter of the screen, or wanting to do a 180 degree turn. It isn't unplayable, but it's frustrating, this feels more like an after thought. This can be solved by allowing WASD movement, controller support, and learning how to code.
The puzzles... what possessed these people when they were designing them? Not only will you pick up useless, distracting items, but most puzzles involve just clicking the item in your "inventory" (which isn't actually an inventory, just a lazily-drew on-screen box with the picture and title of the item) and click the thing in front of you. There's a couple of puzzles that require thinking outside the box, such as the suitcase and call-for-help, which were pretty okay. When you look at the previous Clock Tower games, incl. Haunting Ground, they had actual puzzles beyond drag'n'drop or click an item to use it.
Furthermore, and probably the most hair-ripping, depressing-inducing, mind-acheing mechanic of the game is the finite stamina system. ♥♥♥♥ me sideways, this is one of the worst stamina-use mechanics I've ever ever seen, worse than The Evil Within's. You'll fall over automatically when you're out of stamina and it takes a second to five or so seconds just to get back up whilst you're sitting there holding left-click barking at the screen to get up. By the time you do - whilst now being on low stamina - there is an extra second delay where the character just for no ♥♥♥♥ing reason freezes; allowing the scissorman to catch up to you. Then there's the "hiding spots" which are far between, and the "traps" which I never used because I just kept reloading my previous save. Why did I reload? Because being stalked by the scissorman is a chore, it's not fun, in fact it's so infuriating that I hit my head on the desk out of sheer temperament. There's little excitement as per previous entries in this franchise, it's far too slow paced and repetitive for me to be excited and enthralled being stalked by a scissorman who will insta-kill you for being curious about exploration. Which was a mistake in hindsight, never ever extremely punish the player for exploring - especially in a survival horror game.
Next... is why the game is unplayabley buggy. I encountered a game-breaking glitch right at the very end of chapter 2 when you walk out the exit door. I won't spoil beyond that, but I know that once the cutscenes are over you're onto chapter 3 as a new character. However, with me, it breaks to a game over screen after the third cutscene and I'm back in the last room. I've tried replaying scene 2 again - which didn't work - and then the entirety of chapter 2 which again: didn't work. I tried everything except a complete restart because I don't think my sanity can handle chapter 2 again. By the way, which is one of the worst sub-plot, protagonist-switches that I've ever seen; topping both Metal Gear Solid 2 and Tomb Raider: Angel of Darkness. That's right, Clock Tower, the series known to take its inspirations and game design influences from Giallo horror, Japanese horror, and plays on the dismal-in-distress trope, is nowhere to be seen in this game. The game cuts chapter 1 where the story only just began to pickup and you're now playing some old jackass nobody ever cared about, neither did the developers ever mention Leonard prior to release. Thrown into a horribly written, pointless, filler sub-plot that doesn't add to the current events, but backstory which could have been told in a minute or two. I hate Leonard, I hate chapter 2 and I hate the game-breaking glitch I've hit right at the end of chapter 2.
Other annoyances incl. the graphics. It doesn't know whether it wants to be high fidelity, or a mix of some kind of cel-shade or not. This inconsistency is plagued throughout the game, both gameplay and graphics. And inconsistent is what this game is. It's a mix of what were popular genres, but doesn't stylise or , ahem, "fuse" these together to create an original, unique, coherent product.
Survival horror and point and click are two favourites of mine, as well as old school movement with fixed cameras, and I even consider the first Clock Tower and Haunting Ground to be masterpieces. But no way in Hell does this game live up to any of them, or any horror game released up to this point. This game shames the Clock Tower series and is an embarrassment similar games ala Silent Hill, Siren, etc. I'm also a Kickstarter backer, and the key members of this project are people I love, and it is gut-wrenching that I'm saying this game is pretty awful. But I'm mentally sick of this game now, so much frustration and hype, all for nothing. The future of survival horror is looking bleak right now if even the masterminds of the genre can't get it right.
Now, there are positives to this game. The music, which is under-used, is right on spot. It'll send a chill down your spine as did mine, the musician did an amazing job at fitting her work to this game. Also the copy-pasted male character model that looks like DmC Dante was unintentionally hilarious, and totally not immersive breaking, which added light comedy elements. But seriously, all I can think this game has going for it is its soundtrack, which you should totally download.
All in all, I hate myself for saying this, but NightCry isn't a worthy successor to a masterful series, neither does it do justice to the horror genre, and gets about everything wrong with trying to mimic it. These types of games are right up my alley, but I need to call products out that don't meet expectations after so much hype I created for myself given the circumstances. My final score is 2/10, I don't even recommend this to fans of Clock Tower, unless you want to just see how bad this game is in comparison.

So, having put 14-15 hours into the game, having experienced 7/8 of the endings (including the true ending), 8/11 of the horror scenes, and 14/25 of the death scenes, here's my breakdown:
TOP-LINE: This is a new Clock Tower game. It is unpolished and janky even by the series standards, but it's not incredibly buggy or anything, and literally feels like an old-school horror game from yesteryear that just fell out of a worm hole and released. It can stand proud among the company it comes from, is unapologetic of how old-school and cryptic it sometimes is, but chances are if you liked the Clock Tower games, you'll like this game. It takes a bit to get going, but when it hits its stride you may find yourself hooked.
PROS:
-Unapologetically Old-School. This won't be a pro for everyone, but the game targeted a niche fanbase of the Clock Tower games, and this game delivers what it promises to that fanbase. It feels like an old-school horror game, a Clock Tower game specifically, and it can stand proud with them since it's a good Clock Tower game. It has most of the same flaws the rest of the series does, but also the same strengths, and there is some new stuff sprinkled in, but it also doesn't modernize its vision.
-There are some really cool/creepy scenes. I wouldn't define this game as scary (I didn't find the other Clock Tower games especially scary either I should mention, though), but there is some beautifully morbid scenes in this game. Some more surreal, some more gruesome. The gore is over the top. The game has a tendency of coming out of nowhere with a particularly nasty or horrific scene and sucker-punch you with it into some over-the-top horror scene (in a good way!). The game manages to tie everything nicely, while still feeling like it's creative enough to get away with what it wants. Notably, the game gets more twisted in the last fourth of the game compared to the rest of the journey.
-The story: It's not going to win any awards or blow anyone away, but the story is actually quite nice. It's got a lot of subtle details, things in the environment, hidden double meanings in some dialogue or small touches to bring it together. The story is extravagant (as Clock Tower stories usually go), but told in a hushed, more mannered way. It is a multi-layered story with a lot of elements it manages to bring together, but not with a bang, but a whisper, and some of it may stick with you. I didn't find any of the characters unlikable, and it's telling I would often look forward to the voiced cutscenes (that were often the more cinematic ones). If you pay attention, you may get more out of the story than others. The true ending is a bit brief, but supported with everything else the game says.
-The audio. The music is nice, with some stand-out tracks (maybe with the only disappointment I had being that the Scissorwalker's theme was a bit simple and repetitive), the voice acting is actually solid, hammy, but enjoyable. There's some very nice audio ques and sounds used to good effect in the game.
-It's campy: Between over-the-top deaths, hammy voicing in some places, some silly scenes and dialogue exchanges, there is enjoyable camp here, and camp that fits perfectly with what was present in past installments of the series.
MIDDLE:
-The graphics. It actually looks a lot better than I was expecting, but the visual consistency is all over the place. Some areas look really good, while others look kind of bad.
-Animations. Just like the graphics, the animation is all over the place. Some of scenes are actually expertly animated, there is some parts where they move like humans and respond and move in a realistic or creepy way... and then other times they look like dead-eyed fish people with no lip sync or sometimes movement that look like creepy dummies trying to imitate humans, or flailing about unrealistically or stiffly. It's some of the broadest in terms of quality animation I have ever seen, some of it looks great, some of it looks terrible.
-Bugs: The game is unpolished, but it's actually not all that buggy. It has a few bugs, but nothing that's game breaking I found (sometimes you may need to reload a previous save though). I put this in the middle since while there are 3-4 bugs I ran into, none of them were major, and for playing the game for 16 hours, there were far less than I was expecting.
-Scissorwalker: Maybe it's only because I've played the whole series before this, but I feel the Scissorwalker was less of a threat in this game than the other Clock Tower games. Not in such a huge way, I did die and he did threaten me, but it felt a bit more scripted here than usual, and I found it to not have quite the same presence as the Scissorman in previous games, but still an effective, cool, and interesting stalker antagonist.
-Obtuse: Expect to replay segments of the game because you missed some easily missable key item that, without it, you will end up at a dead end or bad end in the game. It's unforgiving & stays true to this from the Clock Tower games. One new aid is when you go to load your game, there's a 'level flow' chart that shows the key points it branches at.
CONS:
-It's unpolished: The game is incredibly rough around the edges and unpolished. Fluctuating frame rate, small visual bugs, technical things, missing some options (Edit: Quit and return to menu have been added to the game as of Patch 1.02), jankiness... It's the game's biggest flaw for sure.
-The controls are sometimes finicky: While I found the controls fine most of the time, there are some scenes you really need to fight with the controls. The worst would be sometimes when you needed to go to another fixed camera angle but it was hard to walk into it since you needed to click the very sides of the screen to get there.
-Maybe the game is a bit too cryptic: The game doesn't explain much to you, it doesn't explain how to save, it hardly explains the stamina system, you can miss some minor thing and have to replay segments and try to figure out where it might be in long stretches of game; while they have a helpful flowchart on the load game screen, the game maybe is a bit too cryptic for its own good sometimes.
---
OVERALL: Liked it quite a bit, I feel like I'll want to replay this someday, I plan to get the last ending and find some more scenes I missed. I feel this stands tall with the rest of the series, and would look forward to replaying it in any sort of marathon replay of the whole Clock Tower series. It feels like a nice addition to Clock Tower, which is the biggest compliment I can give it. It's a good Clock Tower game, and one I think can stand with the rest of the series.
AN ASIDE: I can't imagine people who never played these older horror/Clock Tower games to jump on this and fall in love with it immediately, it's a bit demanding and doesn't ease new players into the sort of game it is. It's a required taste and may only find a niche audience (I imagine trying to get someone who was grown and raised on modern horror games like Outlast, Slender, Amnesia, etc., may not quite understand this game's appeal, like trying to show someone raised on newer horror movies to enjoy some of the early classics of horror films), but for those who've wanted more games like this in their life, this is probably the truest old-school horror game to have released in years. Jank and all, you'll have a hard time finding a horror game that's this true to the old-school design philosophies of horror games like NightCry released in the last several years. I imagine this title will gain a cult status down the line, and be brought up as part of the Clock Tower series.
BEST PART OF THE GAME: Chapter 3, and some of the twisted horror moments in that chapter, interesting rooms and hidden scenes, some of the visceral imagery in some of the bad endings.
WORST PART OF THE GAME: All of its technical problems and general roughness that hopefully gets patched out some.

Time to change my old review:
It´s going to be very long, so I make a lot of subdivisions, to make it look cleaner. First and
foremost why I still can´t recommend this game:
-It´s unpolished in a lot of ways.
-Neither the endings nor the death scenes are that great. (I got all endings, don´t care for the last 5 deaths I still need..)
-Only the third Chapter is good, that means half of the game is very annoying and boring
- Branch System that could have been WAAAY better. There are good points, but it´s so boring to go trough all the possibilities. I go further into detail later.
- You still have to click 3 to 5 times on a person/ object to get the absolutely important Items/ Information for the true end.
- If you skip all cutscenes and know what to do, then the game is finished in about 1 hour.
| I can only recommend this game to people who are very forgiving to games and don´t get frustrated very fast.! |
-> I gave up this game about 3 times, until I hit Chapter 3, then it actually made a lot of fun. But why is that? Let´s sum it up:
chapter 1: VERY annoying, you do die a lot, but it´s actually never your fault. But this Chapter has the best atmosphere from them all.
Chapter 2: the most boring part of the game. No atmosphere, no horror, very stupid quick time events (I only got further because I looked it up on yt and i recommend this method to everyone who needs more than 10 minutes and still can´t get further).
Now why Chapter 3 is the best part of the game:
- A lot of Characters. Only Rooney has some kind of a story, but it´s still nice to see more (side) chars.
- A lot of puzzles. To be honest, they were too easy for me, but It´s still a lot more fun than being killed in a badly presented Cutscene.
- The Story comes togehter. After not understand anything, the third chapter binds everything togehter very nicely. I might say that the Story presentation is a lot better than the acutal story. I think it might have been a very interesting way to always switch between the characters, after some decisions, instead of Ch1, Ch2, Ch3.
- I didn´t die nearly as often as in Chapter 1 and 2, because the scissorman doesn´t appear randomly and chases you until you´re dead and there are a lot more useable hideouts. So there was like 0 frustration compared to Ch1 and 2.
- The true ending could be called a "Corpse Party" (yes, i played and liked that PSP game^^)
Now about the Branch System
I like it a lot. Instead of the 0815 "Choose a or b", you have to find Items, post stuff, search for clues etc. It feels a lot more natural than the branch systems from western RPGs (for example). BUT, my problem with this is:
- There is absolutely no reason to experiment. The Story CAN NOT be changed. It doesn´t matter in which Branch you are, the decisions, the way, the outcome, EVERYTHING will stay the same. So theoretically, if you made one branch, you did them all with the same decisions. There is SADLY no point in experimenting. I replayed Ch3 so often, just to see the same endings over and over again. It was such an extreme waste of time, just so I could find out the first ending, that i didn´t got in Ch1... The developers could make it so that if you clear one branch, it´s cleared on all 3 Branches, it would be a lot cleaner that way.
All in all the game is half good, half boring and annoying. Who can deal with that, can buy this game, after seeing some trailers (just make sure what you are going to buy). It saddens me to see that aside from the graphics there has been made no changes from the first trailers. If I compare the first trailer from hyper light drifter to what I got in the game... Can´t argue whether that´s a good thing or not though.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now for whoever want´s to read my old review (4 hours in, only in Ch2). Maybe you will understand my frustration better, because I went more into detail there.
The true horror
Where do I even start? Oh, yes, how about the beginning! The first thing that you can do when you start the game is chosing the graphics, the resolution, which screen and windowed. Of course the graphics option has 4 levels: poor, fast, good, beautiful. The game doesn´t look "good" on any of them and you can´t change anything (like AA, Shadows- or texture level etc.). In the game you can only change the volume and language (dual audio: eng, jap). This is already the first fail. The game is locked at 30fps. The second problem was that the game was running on my onboard graphicchip, instead of my graphiccard, so i was playing with 7fps. I had to change it, so that the game runs with my graphiccard myself...
In the game the true horror starts. I am not talking about the genre,  but about everything else. I can´t choose what the worst part of this game is: animations, camera angles at exploration and escaping, the controls, the HORRIBLE level design or the mechanics. Everything is far from good. It feels kinda like something between an alpha and beta. Only very few cutscenes have audio and the characters repeat their animations every 3 seconds, while talking with closed mouths. There are also a LOT of bugs with the cutscenes, the camera and the mechanics. Examples: The scissorman can be stuck at a wall. Cutscenes being skipped just for fun. You can´t move, because your smartphone light is on. You can´t move because of the camera angle. The camera angle is so rtd that the characters always runs in the wrong direction. etc.
About the game itself:
At first I thought: Yes! Now it´s getting intense, but soon after that I was annoyed as hell. The game explains absolutely nothing, aside from running away and Items (you can skip cutscenes by pressing space and pause by pressing P). The scissorman can appear randomly, hideouts can be used only once, after that he will automatically kill you, if you use it a second time. The death scenes are extremly unpolished, bad and boring. You will die a lot, because the game is stupid. No, seriously. How the hell am I supposed to know whether I have to go in a room with my ligt on. How the hell am I supposed to know whether he is going to find me at the hideout or not. How the hell am I supposed to know what to do when there is a red exclamation mark? It could simply mean that there is danger nearby or a quicktime sequence is about to happen, OR LITERALLY ANYHTING! How the hell am I going to escape the scissorman, if I already used all hideouts? How the hell I am supposed to know when he appears? He can appear out of lockers or fridges, so the exploration part is completely rtd. The game rewards you with the scissorman if you want to look up everything. There is simply WAAAY too much trial and error within the gameplay.
What else is there to say? Oh yes, the characters run like complete idiots, you have no stamina bar, so you never know when you´re exhausted or fall to the ground.
Even if you know exactly what to do, the game won´t let you do it, because you haven´t clicked like 3 times on an object.
The pain you will suffer while playing this unfinished, broken, boring, annoying and bad game can´t be described with words.
THERE IS NO SAVING! I had to redo the first chapter about 10 times to get all 3 branches to the second chapter. So it took me about 4 hours to get further and now I completely lost my motivation for this game, there is also no hope left, it´s absolutely bad, unpolished and annoying af.
The game is a HUGE pia, the only two good things I can mention are:
Camera angles at cutscenes: they are sometimes okay, sometimes good and even sometimes very good.
The option to play with english or japanese voices.
Sound and Music are ok.
That´s it.

The bulk of Tiny Bang Story is a hidden objects game. You start out searching for jigsaw puzzle pieces, and as you interact with things you are informed of other things you need to find in order to access puzzles. When you complete enough puzzles on the few screens for each level, you are taken to the world screen to place the jigsaw pieces. There are five levels, and 25 puzzles.
The art direction for this game is fantastic, and the music, while repetitive, is rather soothing. This is definitely a game to play for relaxation and puzzle solving; there is no hardcore setting in Tiny Bang Story. There's also no story once you start playing. I streamed the game expecting something engaging, and did not get that.
The hidden objects portion of the game is tedious, but there are little blue flies you can click on to fill up your hint ball. Once the hint ball is full, you can click on it to send a red hint fly around the screen to orbit an item you haven't yet clicked on. If there are no such items on that screen, nothing happens, and you know you haven't missed anything on that screen.
Most of the actual puzzles are fairly rudimentary, and are things you've seen before. There are a couple that are very good though, most notably the water pipe puzzle in the last level. It is absolutely possible to solve it from scratch, and it is easily the most challenging puzzle in the game.
The worst puzzle is the astrolabe puzzle in level 3, which isn't a puzzle at all: you just rotate the thing until the lines all line up. Level 2 has what's basically a Simon machine, which is also not really a puzzle, and there are a handful of minigames scattered throughout as well.
