I finished it in 4 hours, and a fair portion of that was on level 1 while I was still getting used to the game mechanics. There's also no replay value, especially considering what the ending is. I give it a 6.5/10, and I'd say it's worth playing if you can get it on sale.

Tiny Bang Story is a tiny point-and-click adventure -- less than 3 hours for me -- that is partly a puzzle game and partly a hidden objects game. There are no words, very little instruction, and almost no replayability. But the artwork is enchanting and, despite the (very minimal) backstory of repairing a shattered planet, the ambience is cheerful and soothing. It felt endearing and unexpectedly satisfying to jigsaw puzzle a broken planet back together again, section by section. If you can get it on sale and enjoy finding hidden objects and solving puzzles, this little game will take you on a charming, bite-sized adventure.

For anyone who might be avoiding this thinking "oh, a movie tie-in game"... It isn't. It is an original Max Rockatansky story, though the main bad guy IS a son of Immortan Joe from Fury Road, and Gas Town from the beginning of that film is one of the locations. Not only is it not based on any of the movies, but, the game play is fantastic, unlike most film video games. The ground combat and brawling remind me of the Arkham games, and the game is open world with a ton of side missions, a la Assassin's Creed. The combat is simplistic but feels brutal, and the car combat just shines. I hate car games. HATE. THEM. But, Trying to take down on of the war rigs to reduce threat and collect hood ornaments often feels like a scene from Fury Road and is actually a lot of fun. Upgrading the car is central to the story. The very rich story, by the way, with a ton of lore items and dossiers you can read to flesh out the Plains of Silence and the apocalypse that left Max wandering the wastes of Australia, in addition to the storyline and side missions themselves. If you see this game on sale, definitely buy it. Double definitely if you're already a Road Warrior fan.

This is a very well made game.  For those of you that come from World of Warcraft(WoW), it has some of the same qualities; raids, PvP, and Guilds.  The one thing that surpasses WoW is its races and styles to choose from.  It has more the blah 4 or 5 races on each side to choose from and the basic 5 styles to play.  It has three sections to pick from as well instead of horde or alliance.  It has your three basic Dungeon and Dragon alliances, chaotic good, neutral or evil.  Within those there are a variety of races to pick from each with their own speciality, but not restrictions, so pick away the style you want.  After that the 5 basic styles are there but each has 2-3 sub-styles to choose from.  So just from the start you can build you hero/villian any way you want that would fit your way of play.
The Advanced GUI Experience:
The next big thing is the GUI format.  It has way ahead of WoW, you can move everything want for starters, putting things where you would like them.  A big plus for this is towards us druids and spellcaster alike.  You can not only move the hotbars around, you can also scale them.  For example you can make them nice and big if you only have a few spells, or when you get into the game and I am only talking about level 20(when you can start doing raids/dungeons[the only downfall I see from WoW where you can raid anytime you like at any level]) you can make them soo small that you casn have 5 hotbars and they barley take up any room on the screen(like WoW were when you get into a raid you can barley see what is going on, only a variety of colorful hotbars covering your screen[this is without any mods of course]).  Another nice factor that blow WoW out of the water is the ease of editing your hotbar.  You no longer have to delete the whole hotbar in order to make your own.  You have two choices; 1. you have to right-click the spell to get rid and click delete or if you are just replacing one spell then drag and drop your spell of choice from the spell menu and drop it on the one you want to replace. 2.  You can choose a setting that lets you slide the spells around freely whenever you like.  So now you can just click-hold and drag the spell to a new slot and if a spell is there that one is now automatically grapped to be placed anywhere and soo on.  It does like WoW have a local hotbar delete all button.(just to point out, each hotbar has its own settings, so though one might be small the next one on the screen will be big.  after making one however, every new hotbar you make from here on out will be the size of the last one you have.  Now this is just the GUI.  Now the real game begins.
Basic Leveling and The Amazing Skill Choices:
So like any other MMO you do you missions, grinding out farm kills, etc.  The interesting point to this pre-level edit.  So when you go to choose the passive skills and all that good stuff, you notice a dropdown box in the right hand corner.  It already has 3 pre-made settings; solo, PvP, and Group(raids/dungeons).  Now those are for those purposes only and are role specific.  For example, if you pick a druid-substyle-fury, you will have three styles of play, healer, tank and dps.  It is a good for being stable during solo play, which is mainly dps and healer for the most part.  But in group it will mostly go go down healer with some tanking. If you go PvP mostly DPS with basic healing and tanking to just be sustainable. Surpise though, you can make your 3 custom slots as well.  When you do this it will give you the MAX amount of points that you will get.  These points however are seperate to your normal leveling.  They are points you get every so often(I will be honest forgot the exact name but when you look at the bar with your experience recieved and to go, the button on the right will have three different options and one shows the bar for these attribute points) and are used for your tree build, spell specific passives, your trade skill, etc.  You will start off with 321 and you can either use the points you think you have or just use them all.  Now caution be warned, the order you put those points in will be the order they are used when you are leveling. So try to think what you will need. But don't worry if you do not like what you have then just go back and restart from the point you think it all went wrong.  But another caution, some of these come with extra spells, so if you do not go down the path of before then you will loose that spell but it will yet remain on you hotbar.(the only bad thing I saw when it came to leveling and the hotbar spells. Going on, you will notice that when you pick these points you have 4 choices at the top of the window, these is for your subclass, spell specific passives and one that the DLC is needed.(btw the premades use the DLC but they are not added to you sooo keep an eye out on that because you will be wasting points early on)Then you also have choices along the side and each one of these has its own points to use and will also be given when you level in that category, so remember to harvest, gather etc so you get points for that.  Now basic levling will come with its own set of spells, but it also has passives, this is your basic leveling again. Every so often you get a point to use for you character specific passives(usually is every 9 for some. every 10 for others(total of 10 for 9 and 9 for 10.) And these are usefull so check them out before hand to see if they will work with the skill points you have chosen.
Now the rest is up to you.  Go out and game, level, join up with others and farm away.  The game in itself is a great game.  It has great grpahics and you can zoom in and out of first person(think of skyrim).  If you are a fan of WoW then you will love this game.  It is free-2-play(outside of that you can choose silver member for $5 and get two more character slots plus can use expert level spells and make your own guild or your basic WoW charge for 2 more slots, Master level spells, and more) But really it is not needed.  You might only have 2 slots for character off the bat, but $5 for 2 more and expert level skills and make your own guild(you can join any guild however without having to pay anything.)you can not go wrong.  I will say it is fine with out going silver.  You have everything you need if you are just someone who makes one character and just plays the crap out of it.  While you are playing go into the settings and write a Bio of your character(has a limit) and let people know who you are, how you play, and what you wish to attain.  So go live it up!! Make your character now and get started, and it is all for free, how can you go wrong?!

A decent MMORPG. It's pretty much the first RPG I ever played, and I've been playing it since 2006. It's gameplay is kinda like WoW's, although it wasn't always that way. The combat system is what you'd expect from an '04 MMO: button clicking and cooldown timer watching. Population has declined greatly from when I first started playing, but with the ever-improving F2P model numbers are slowly rising again.
That being said, what, aside from my nostalgia, makes me like this game? It has a TES-like amount of lore and backstory, interesting world design, great music, an engaging active story, interesting quest timelines (although it also has a lot of "kill 10 rats" type stuff), and a large amount of character customization, with 20 races, 32 classes, and an Alternate Advancement tree that allows you to further refine your stats and abilities. To the experienced MMO player this game seems a little generic, but if you've never played an MMO before this one is a pretty good one to begin with.

Now that the 2016 season is concluded, it can be said without doubt that Hitman is a stealth action game very worthy of your time. Even if it's not 2016 best game, it's definatelly the most innovative one.
The six episodes are diverse enough to make the single player campaign satisfying for anyone remotely interested in the genre, but it's the large sanbdox levels and additional unlock challanges that encourage replaying and mastering your skills. The "elusive targets" introduced here for the first time are perhaps the highlights of the Hitman series: these contracts are released about twice a month and give you only a short window of opportunity to eleminate a newly introduced target, with no checkpoints or saved games and with a real world countdown timer. Time's up or you died because you mistakenly electrocuted yourself trying to set up a trap? Game over and that specific target is lost forever.
This type of real consequences "hardcore" gameplay is something entirely new and fresh, and it forces you to behave in a more calculated way and really evaluate every situation you're about to get into. It's perhaps the purest Agent 47 experience there ever was, and this mode alone justifies the "always online" requirment for stats tracking that frutsrated a few people (although after 30+ hours in the game I have yet to encounter a single connection issue).
Hitman 2016 is definatelly bigger than the sum of it's parts, and IO Interactive's risky and innovative vision for a AAA game seems to have really paid off. Recommended for series veterans and newcomers alike.

Super Meat Boy is a fantastic platformer, perhaps one of the best of the indie ones out there at the moment.
The game has a lot of challenging and fun content that will keep you occupied for hours. Each of the 7 chapters is divided into two worlds (the Dark and Light worlds) equalling a whopping 287 stages. And then there's the custom stages made by other players. Sadly, the stages in Light world often are stripped down versions of the Dark world's equivalents, which you are forced to fully clear before gaining access to the "real" content that is the Dark world.
The game is rather challenging and you will most like die over and over again, but rarely does it feel like it's the game's fault. The controls are tight (please rebind the keys if you are planning on using the keyboard), but getting used to Meat Boy's unique momentum takes some time.
For people looking to perfect the game there are tons of achievements that encourage just that. But, unfortunately, the leaderboards for each stage are dominated by hackers.
Overall, Super Meat Boy is a great platformer, and one that is certainly worth getting for any platformer fan out there.

If you grew up playing 2D platformers you probably remember just how difficult the genre can be. Well, Super Meat Boy takes that difficulty and pumps it full of rocket fuel, steroids, and enough saw blades to cut down the Amazon. The controls are precise and responsive enough to handle those last-second twitches you'll inevitably end up making in the late game, sometimes even in the mid-game. The soundtrack is amazingly catchy, varied, and never gets dull. The level, design is top notch and allows for various ways to approach any given obstacle in your path, further helped by all the unlockable characters with differing gameplay styles, all of whom are from other famous games, indie and not. If you complete the entirity main game's seven worlds, "if" being the key word, then there's always "Teh Internet", the game's central hub for user-generated levels. Overall the game combines steep challange, slick controls, and just the right amount of frustration that keeps you going into one memorable platformer that surely ranks up there with the likes of Super Mario World, Donkey Kong Country 2, Sonic the Hedgehog 3, and all the others in the pantheon of 2D platforming.

One of my friends was giving out copies of this game if we agree to write a review for the game. When looking for the game's page (aka this one), I found the NES-esque visuals quite appealing and it seemed quite fun. Now, it's time to write a review for Space Cat.
From my playtime with this game, it has been entertaining in classic mode, as well as in adventure mode. I couldn't test out multiplayer, as it was local only and doesn't have anyone to play with irl (unless there's an online mode that I'm being oblivious to), but I still had fun in solo.
In classic mode, projectiles are flying at you, while your objective it to get as many points as possible without falling off. The longer the game is, the harder it gets. It offers a challenge, which can become a bit chaotic at times (reminder that it's still in one-player mode). The jetpack offers a recovery option, even though I rarely use it.
In adventure mode, you go through a series of side-scrollers, while trying to survive and get to the end, with dog enemies in your way. This mode is best suited for those who are familliar with Classic mode, so it's best if you play it first instead of jumping straight in adventure mode. The themes are varied, from what I had played.
In both modes (including the giant mode, which is basically classic mode, but with a bigger stage), you can obtain a collectible (a hat coin-thing?) that can be used to unlock hats and, at one point, outline colors. You can customize your cat with a hat, its fur and outline color. Try styling your cat to your liking.
So tl;dr, this game is fun, even in solo. It has its sets of challanges, keeping the player's attention. You're not gonna regret this game; it has a low cost, so it's a good use of your money.

Space Cat feels nostalgic from the very beginning. It features 8-bit art (with a bit of modern cheating) and music which harkens back to arcade boards like Pac Man and Dig Dug, with the modern flair afforded by progressive technology and design. It feels like a Game Boy game being enhanced on the Super Game Boy; this comes from its customizable SGB-like border, in the presentation of cutscenes, and the simplicity of its colors and shapes. It doesn't chain itself to the limitations of the past, though! It has beautiful but simple parallax effects, comical detail (just wait until you meet Biggie Frost!) and clearly distinguishes between over a dozen enemies through color and function.
Under the hood Space Cat contains simple and intuitive mechanics, which combine into a deceptively challenging experience in Adventure Mode (the hot young star of the game). The titular hero Space Cat can run, double jump, cling to walls and jump from them, attack enemies with his claws, and use a jet pack which recharges fuel when you are on the ground. He can also choose from a few items littered throughout the level: a melee-range hammer to deflect bullets, a gun to shoot enemies at range in four directions, or an umbrella to slow his descent. If you plan to see Space Cat through to the end of his adventure, you'll need to learn to do it all.
Levels scroll automatically, which adds both tension and difficulty to the experience. Instead of being able to rush past enemies, you have to deal with them, at least for a short amount of time. Some enemies are beyond reach, others are hiding in the background and waiting to pounce. Then at the end of each level Space Cat must learn the mechanics of the unique stage boss. None of the levels ever feel unfair, because the way forward is clear and there is milk spaced throughout the stage that space cat can use to recover his health. The bosses can be stressful because if you die, you have to start the whole level over. But I was never frustrated with the game for anything but my inability to complete a level.
On the technical side, this game is far from perfect. On more than one occasion keyboard inputs were dropped, but it thankfully never made anything impossible - the versatility of the character makes it easy to work around this. There are no control customizations, so multiplayer on a single keyboard is tough, and not all controllers are supported so you will need to manually map controls to the given keyboard controls. There is also no netplay, so if you want something like that you'll have to get REALLY creative.
Even with everything I've highlighted, there's so much to this game worth praising:
* A traversable menu, where you move Space Cat around to access its modes and customizations
* Like 100 unlockable hats
* A 2-player basketball game and a playable game in the credits menu
* Arcade mode, with all the same mechanics present, formerly known as Space Cat 1.0
* 4-player local co-op or competitive play in adventure and arcade modes
* Stage Select mode after you beat the adventure for the first time
At the end of the day for the content, price, and the care and dedication put into it, Space Cat is a lovely gem for arcade enthusiasts, indie lovers, and nostalgia hunters alike.

A true Mad Max video game. Very enjoyable experience. The story follows Max as usual who journeys in a post-apocalyptic world in search of supplies while also running into trouble along the way, Max also runs into others along the way willing to help him while also discovering more about himself.
The key features I liked about this video game, include the atmospheric Mad Max world, combat system, vehicle, and character upgrades.
Notable features that I am neutral about: vehicle fuel system, and water canteen health rejuvenation. Fuel isn't as scarce as I believed it might be before I played the game. You can build fuel stations at strongholds to fuel up your vehicle completely at no charge, or you can win Death Run races, which when completed always have fuel at their starting lines. Fuel can also be stored on the back of your vehicle so you can later refuel.
This video game has a combat system similar to Batman and Middle Earth, the combat is fluid and responsive, you also get rewarded for chaining combos together. You can also upgrade Max's abilities that allow for more devestating moves that can be performed and allow you to take on more enemies easier.
Vehicle upgrades as I mentioned earlier are a plus, you have the ability to add nitros to your vehicle, add weapons, upgrade armor, and change the paint of your car. It's very enjoyable to use a grappling hook and pull the doors off an enemies vehicle and yank them out of the car, or even pull down a sniper's nest.
There's a specific aspect of the game I'm not too ecstatic about, but it doesn't ruin the experience; when liberating enemy locations a lot of them begin to feel very similar to each other and a bit repetitive. This doesn't affect the game too much since most of them are different enough that they feel like many different places, but you will notice similarities and may feel a bit tired of having to do the same thing over and over again.
I believe I named the key features of the game, and don't want to spoil anymore. If you don't have the game, I recommend getting it.

I'll make a longer review on my blog once I've gotten 100 percent completion, but I figured I'd throw in my two cents while the game's still pretty new.
Let's  get the negatives out of the way first:
If you're wanting something closer to a AAA experience, you should steer clear, because you'll only end up disappointed. NightCry is about as indie as it gets, and it shows in the presentation. The graphics aren't fully polished (Monica's 'scared' face looks halfway between a blow-job robot and a Macy's mannequin), the controls take a little bit of time to get used to, the optimization isn't perfect, and there are occasional framerate spikes. Also, the game doesn't tell you how to save, and you have to either ALT-F4 or ALT-Tab + Close in order to exit the game. NightCry has a very rough start, too, and takes a little bit to really reel the player in.
If these things are a dealbreaker, I can understand. It didn't scare me off, but it isn't for everyone.
Now, let's look at the positives.
This game is gloriously cheesy. Yeah, I consider that a positive. The voice acting is purposely bad, with silly death scenes and spooks right out of an 80's slasher or goresploitation movie. The soundtrack only adds to this, with one track directly referencing the Friday the 13th chase theme (You know the one). This is a game made by horror and slasher movie fans for other horror and slasher movie fans, and the enthusiasm and love for the genre is infectious, and never fails to put a smile on my face.
The way the game is structured isn't that bad, either. For as much as I see complaints about the game's checkpoint system, I think it's a good idea. In harder areas, it gets downright generous with those save points, and if you're diligent enough to save after every major event / getting a new item, then you will never have to worry about retracing your steps to get certain items after you die. The puzzles are (mostly) straightforward, and the use of social media and cell phones is pretty clever in a game of this type.
Also...this game's a Clock Tower sequel in all but name. It feels like a Clock Tower game, controls like a Clock Tower game, and is rough around the edges like a Clock Tower game. Clock Tower fans will have little to no trouble adjusting to the Scissorwalker, and new players will learn pretty quickly.
I love this game to death, but I know it isn't for everyone. I was a little disappointed at first, but I warmed up to it, and it now sits proudly with the other (good) Clock Tower games in that special shelf in my heart dedicated to spooky horror fun.
Check it out if you want to find a new Halloween favorite. Just don't mind the cobwebs.

There are moments where the characters will be in a ackward stiff looking pose and appear lifeless or move in some unnatural looking ways that lack a feeling of weight and balance. And in addition to that, is when you hear a character speak, sometimes you'll see their mouths move, and other times you wont. Also, the same can be said about facial expressions. Sometimes its animated, other times its non existent.
And to touch on another part about the visuals, there are some areas with glaringly bad texture seams in the game. Most notibly on the Island.
Apart from that are the Text Sequences, which i feel scrolls too fast. Whether you're a fast reader or not shouldnt matter.. I just feel it'd be better if the game were to let the player scroll through and end text sequences on their own terms rather than letting the game dictate that for you.
And lastly are the Controls. Which I dont have too much issues with. Just some unresponsiveness at times. But other than that, the control scheme is ok.
Please dont think I am being nitpicky. Its just that these are things that are easily noticable to me whenever I play any game and it tends to break my immersion. For other people however, they may not notice as much nor have a problem with it.
The Devs at Nude Maker definitley know what they're doing. However, there are areas of the game that lacks polish in which I feel it is in much need of so far. With that said though, I still like this game and hope for it to succeed so that some of the issues I have with it will not affect future projects from these Devs.

After that, the game crash..... Yes it crash, end of story. Fix all of this, please!!!! What I feel about this game?  It feel like I'm dating with my new girlfriend, but I keep thinking my ex-girlfriend (Original Clock Tower). Make me feel like I'm a terrible person.

So 15 or so hours has given me more time to think about how I really look at this game.
Pros: It's very reminiscent of the original clocktower games, evasion/hiding spots, cursor controls, intense chase scenes. I really liked that and it felt really cool to see this concept in modern day. And while the point-and-click controls were a little wonky at times, it wasn't too bad.
Cons: Other reviews have gone into detail about the bugs and such so I won't go into it. Although at one point in-game you open up  the upper floor to a balcony which has a hiding spot, but if you are being chased, the character won't go up the stairs as if it's still closed off. Meaning if you get chased more than once in that chapter, you're screwed.
Next, I feel that the "did you do this?" system is very flawed. While previous clock tower games (Clock Tower 2 had this issue too) had item/action requirements that affected the outcome of the game, it wasn't this heavy handed. Having me die in some ridiculous fashion every 8 minutes because I didn't do some vague action becomes tiring and immersion breaking. There needs to be a period of non-consequential gameplay so I don't have to worry if turnng not a handle 3 times just got me a instant bad ending. (Just a made-up example, not a spoiler.)
And lastly, the game fails to explain very important features. Mainly the save system/and continue system. Phone chargers are explained as able to "charge the in-game phones battery" and nothing more, so I didn't think about it as anything else. And for the continue system, I didn't know the game checkpoints at certain segments so all I was left to go off of was a new chapter button showing up on the save data pathways.
This translated to at one point in the game me repeating half of chapter 2 and the beginning of chapter 3 multiple times because the game didn't display a new button for chapter 3. It doesn't until you complete the first section of that chapter. And with an initial chase that can easily lead you to a dead end and die for lack of stamina, it came to multiple retries until I found out through the discussion board about saving and continuing.
So, in the end, do I recommend this game? It does capture a concept I loved very much from the clocktower games and I love how intense and high-stake the chase segments are. The scisssorwalker character is so well done design wise and is very intimidating. It is effective in pulling me in. I recommend this game for it's on-point concepts but without proper directions about basic elements in the game implemented, I don't know if I should entirely.

Should you buy/play terraria.
tl:dr ... yes.
You start with a sword, a pickaxe and an axe in the middle of a world wooded and peacefull but which by nightfall will turn ugly, quickly.
Your first day is prep, your first night, survival. Your first death, inevitable. Your victories, glorious.
If you play single player or invite friends to your world, if you go melee, ranged or magic, if you find it or craft it, if you build elaborate arenas for event grinders or if you just wing it as they come, if you just sit and fish, this game will surprise you, delight you and entertain you and keep you coming back for longer than you thought a game could.
If you're not into this type of game I honestly feel sorry for you. You will miss out on one of the defining games of the current era.
But what is Terraria like?
I would compare Terraria to games like Dwarf fortress, Sids' Civ series, and yes, Minecraft. It's RPG, it's 'Rogue like' (though the world levels or progresses while you just produce/find better weapons armour to deal with it), it's world building (and restructuring) and it is anything but linear.
Inevitably the game is most compared to minecraft, a 2D minecraft. But that is not a comparison that does either game justice. Terraria has more depth in 2D than Minecraft has in 3.
Yes, it is a world composed of blocks which the user explores and mines to gain resourses to craft and reshape the world as they see fit but that's where the comparison ends. In MC the user has to constantly grind just to maintain the only two weapons in the game; a bow and a sword.
In terraria there are more weapons, armours and loot than I can count and once you have one you have it forever and it is progress in an ever expanding world of foes and bosses and events and loot. Lots and lots of loot.
Swords, scythes, bows, repeaters (crossbows), spears, boomerangs, yoyos, flails, magic weapons, magic tomes, summoning weapons, minions to fight for you, guns, rifles, grenades, grenade launchers, rocket launchers,   I've been playing since this game came out and I still find new ways to despatch the multitudes of foes present on each world.
... and the foes ...
From simple slimes by day and night roaming zombies to world eating bosses and events that will rip you a new one if you are unprepared, this game keeps you thinking and wondering what's around the next block.
... and the world itself ...
Forests to deserts to snow covered ice to underground jungles to skeleton infested dungeons to oceans to caverns to sky islands to the very pits of hell itself this games world is as much a friend as it is an enemy. Each area rich in unique life and drops and traps and foes, waiting for the unwary.
The depth and replayability of this game is often mentioned but still underestimated. If you enjoy it, you will enjoy it for many, many, many years. There is that much depth. It is that much value. No extra dlc to pay for. Right from the start it's all yours and it is still being added to, for free, nearly seven years later.
Buy it.

While I enjoyed Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, I found it to be indistinct from other games in the franchise. The gameplay remained strong and overly interesting but was largely the same from game to game. The missions have a tendency to all bleed into one without enough distinct features which distinguish them apart from each other and it seemed at times that all any developer would have to do to make a new mission would be to cut and paste the objectives from the missions before it. The story also feels indistinct at times. The motivation of each Grand Theft Auto hero is essentially the same (to control all crime in the city and exact revenge on those whom opposed the protagonist) and have little depth to them. Consequently, I was never really playing the game for the story (which, I suppose, says a lot about the quality of the gameplay which the Grand Theft Auto series has considering the time I spent playing it).
The violence and sexual content is obviously a concern for anybody who is concerned about the effect that it might pose on the impressionable, but this is the reason there are game rating systems, and consequentlly anybody reading this review will have to determine what their level of acceptance is concerning such adult content for themselves.
A minor complaint I have about San Andreas is that the controls can be difficult to use on a computer. Flying certain types of aircraft was frustrating and I suspect that it was much easier to play on a console.
Overly, I recommend the game, but if you're looking for an entirely new and distinct experience in gameplay from other Grand Theft Auto games, you will be disappointed.

Visually-stunning. The musical score was beautiful and appropriate for the atmosphere. The developers skillfully avoided interrupting gameplay with lengthy dialogue or cutscenes, but trimmed the storyline down to bare bones. This game drives gameplay and visuals far more than story. You will not have the chance to get attached to any character (including Ori). Some of the platforming is frustrating and you will die a lot, but the game tries very hard not to delay the player from getting back to try again. Everything is doable with practice. Lastly, the game has too many points of no return where items and upgrades cannot be acquired later once an area is cleared. All that aside, I found the game enjoyable.

Now here is a game I did not expect to enjoy ... let alone as much as I have up until now. At first I had set this game on my ignore list because I am not so much into platform games. And this is very much a platform game with it's share of puzzles as well.
The thing that usually puts me off with most games is the "you died, try again...from the beginning!" With Ori you will get your fair share of "you died" but if you are smart about where and when you place your Soul Links (save games) you will be able to progress in spite of death and even learn bit by bit how to overcome the most difficult stages.
I have had stages where I was convinced I would never be able to pass... and then... I did.
So, somehow the engineers of this game got me hooked. I suppose the stunning graphics and the beautifull music are partly the reason for this but I doubt these are the only reasons I am unable to quit the game at times.
But be warned... this game can be very hard even when played at the easiest level.

I'm a big fan of the original Clock Tower and this game sounded interesting, so I decided to back the Kickstarter. Now the day comes and it releases, so I decided to give it a try!
Well... it's not good. It's not BAD, either? It's just not good. It functions, I didn't hit anything I'd really describe as a bug (other than perhaps a performance issue), it didn't crash, and the controls more or less work the way they seem to be intended to work.
The problem is that the difference between a bad game and a good game is often just polish, and this game has no polish anywhere. It's all jank and awkward camera angles and unclear objectives and just plain unpleasant gameplay. If executed correctly, this game could be good, but right now there's tons of stuff they need to fix/change and I can't imagine they'd release it for sale if they had a serious plan to fix those things anytime soon - why risk a bad launch?
During my couple hours with the game I died a few different ways, saw a few people get murdered, interacted with some NPCs, got some phone calls, and explored a couple floors of the ship. There were some jump scares mixed in there and small amounts of narrative - the one puzzle they threw at me worked fine and I found it straightforward to solve instead of annoying. So that's nice. But otherwise... none of it really worked. The game never spooked me, I never felt any real tension, just annoyance at the camera and the awkwardness of the control scheme. The last straw was that I hit the first 'ending' and it's the most pathetic fart of a denouement I've ever seen. I had to go back and replay it because I couldn't comprehend what had just happened.
If this game were more competently executed, I'd say it's at least worth a look for Clock Tower fans... but right now nobody should buy this game. Don't buy this game.

Note: I have only reached chapter 2.
For the most part the game is good. The graphics are okay, but not cutting edge. The voice acting is good. The controls can be a little difficult to deal with at first, but you'll ween yourself into them after walking around for a few minutes.
The game does not tell you the controls, as far as my experience goes, so you'll need to teach yourself before getting to the first chapter (technically you start in the prologue). Once the first chapter starts, the game will give you instructions on how to move and interact while being chased. The game does not point you in any directions other than through interacting with objects or dialogue during cutscenes, so pay attention and attempt to not skip any details.
There is no menu in the game, or at least I couldn't figure out which key opened the menu. You can pause the game by using the P key. You can skip cutscenes by using the SPACEBAR. The inventory becomes available as you find items. The only real flaw with the exclusion of a menu is that there is no way to escape the game, even from the main menu. If you are in window mode you can just close the window, but if you are in full screen mode, you either have to Tab+Alt out of the game and close it, or Alt+F4.
The only bug I've encountered is during a struggle with the main enemy of the game. You have to click a button quickly in order to push off your pursuer, however, if an object that is interactable is behind that button, your character will interact with it and die immediately afterwords. For example, this bug occured while in room 301, in the bedroom, where I got cornered and somehow interacted with the bed while fighting off the Scissorwalker. There may be other bugs, I do not know yet.
There seems to be a graphical issue with the main character's hair and the lighting that causes FPS to drop. This may not occur for everyone, as I did not experience this issue, however, some people I know, and some in the community are reporting this issue.
The story is suspensful as it sets up multiple suspects to being the Scissorwalker (my money is on grandma in the elevator). The gameplay is very similar to it's predecessors of the Clock Tower franchise: running from an unkillable enemy, hiding, and solving puzzles. The horror is strong in this game as well. Fighting off the Scissorwalker sometimes becomes necessary, but it will quickly drain your stamina and eventually kill you. Even with full stamina, you can still fall to the floor and end up spending your extra stamina picking yourself back up. If you fall and have no stamina, you're likely to die. Sometimes you have to solve a puzzle while the Scissorwalker is chasing you, and sometimes you have to interact with a "difficult to click on" object. The Scissorwalker's name is also ironic, considering it's walking speed is that of your running speed, and it can occasionally run after you to close any large gaps you may have made between it and yourself.
Hopefully, in a future patch, we can see at least some of these issues dealt with.
EDIT: I forgot to mention three things.
1.) You auto save during checkpoints, but you can manually save using a "phone charger." You get access to your phone later in the game, which gives you a light, and allows you to communicate with your friends, or at least the ones still alive.
2.) The history section of the main menu displays all the outcomes of important choices you made, and you can see the path you've taken in the save menu.
3.) When hiding, a heart will be displayed. The game does not mention what it's used for, but you must keep the heart as centered as possible to keep yourself from being discovered by the Scissorwalker. Some hiding spots will not always display the heart, which means the Scissorwalker will ignore those spots.

Prison Architect brings back some of the old school nostalgia from tycoon/simulation games the likes of Sim Hospital, Roller Coaster Tycoon, and Railroad Tycoon. Introversion takes on a rather unique art style and combines it with equally artful sound and UI design that makes the classical tycoon and simulation gameplay that much more enjoyable without feeling like "just another sim game".
The challenge of managing dangerous prisoners while turning a profit avoids becoming too difficult by giving the player several tools like a routine planner, guard shift planner, and building cloning tool. Despite the complexities, the learning curve remains relatively flat.
I purchased this game when it was in Early Access and had the pleasure of watching it grow into the great time-spender that it is now. Many great features were implemented along the way such as thorough mod support and "escape mode", and a good deal of bugs were squished too. My only reservation here is that several high profile bugs remained in the game when the developers decided to go 1.0, and while it has been some time since I've looked at their bug tracker, quite a few were still left.
It makes me a little sad that the original fiery passion and support the developers had for this game back in E.A. seems to be tapering, but I suppose that they can't continue working on the core game forever, as they're aiming for mobile and console releases now. Introversion has produced a shining example of how early access can be a success. I would absolutely recommend this game in its current released state.

I can hardly begin this review. I devoured this game in one sitting which does not happen often for me, so that is a start.
If you like war games and shooters, you need to play this game. Not because the action is intense and brutal (which it is), but because the story is intense and brutal.	 Never in a game before had I felt the atrocities of war so acutely. This game made me not only realize how horrible we can be, but how EASILY we can slip into hell, especially on a battlefield. That type of statement pulled off in a game that was fun to play is in my mind a genre changer. God help other military shooters for what they will have to do to keep up with this.
I have a few gripes about the game, they are not small, but they are demonstrably overshadowed by the storytelling.  The cover system sometimes is very inadequate, you step away from walls you did not mean to and get shot in the face. And sometimes you cover to walls you did not mean to and expose yourself in that way too. I feel they could have made the order system better as well as you have no control over where your team members go, just what targets they kill, and if you are lucky enough to get the prompt, who gets a flashbang before getting gunned down. The order system does have the benefit of being simple and therefore keeping you focused on the pace of the story, but this gets countered a bit in a few sections where your friendly AI gets killed by running ahead of you and into the open.   You do have to save them which puts you in terrible spots. I can only think of 2 spots this happened to me more than once, so it’s not that big of a deal. What is a bigger deal is that towards the end of the game the checkpoint saves get ludicrously far apart in my opinion. I would have to play one section over and over, just because the guy (a very heavy trooper) at the end of the section what giving me issues. In another section, the same sort of thing happened but I had next to no ammo when it put me at the checkpoint (I was not low on ammo when it saved)…that was a bit of a drag.
ALL of that said, on a scale of one to ten the game would be in the high 9s no problem for how well done everything else was done. Buy this game, play this game…but by something happy for yourself too. You are going to need it after the war.

Ah, Super Meat Boy. It's one of the most classic platformers I've ever played. You can switch CHARACTERS? You can even go into a DARK WORLD? To me, this sounds like stuff that's already been made, but this game is probably one of the best indie platformers you can probably get.
So, to the review: The puzzles can be quite challenging at times and it might cost you some time, or your patience. Some of them seem simple but hard. Here's an example: Jump over saws while you avoid these crawly slime things and get a key to unlock a door. It seems simple enough, but it's just difficult. Not sure if any of the levels did that concept, but it's just a example. Anyway, the difficulty can be just plain stupid at times. The puzzles are just stupid in these levels, such as Hell's boss. Seriously, who's going to go and remember these patterns?
The concept of character-changing blows my mind, I've never seen it before, so it's a huge bonus to this game's simplicity and fun. Ever heard of a game where you can pick the Headcrab from HL2 and The Kid from I wanna be the guy as a character? Heck, even Steve makes an appearance! Did I ever tell you that there was a level editor?
This game's plot isn't very cliche, but who saves a bandage girl? Whatever, beats me. This "Dr Fetus" guy seems as if he was a baby in a space pilot helmet, and that's pretty funny to me.
In general, this game is really worth your money, however you might want to not play it if you have a problem with difficult games.

Everquest II is an open-world MMORPG whose basic controls are similar to World of Warcraft, but whose integral mechanics and interface are quite different (and really, dramatically superior.)
As an SOE game, Everquest II shares its Station Cash currency with all other SOE games: Everquest 1, DC Universe Online, PlanetSide 2, and even Free Realms. Because of this, taking advantage of SC-related offers in one game is redeemable in any other game.
LORE AND SETTING
Everquest II takes place in a low-mid-fantasy world. Although it has fairies and lizard people and other stuff, they are portrayed relatively realistically. Early locations in particular are quite grounded and not really all that fantastic or colorful.
Fortunately, Everquest II doesn't take its seemingly-serious setting very seriously, especially compared to WoW, and much of the setting is self-deprecating (try learning Faerlie.) Despite that, it has a few rules in its lore that limit the player just a smidgen.
For instance, the playable classes are aligned good, neutral, or evil... as are the races. If you pick a "good" class, you can't pick an "evil" race, and vice versa; even though you can Betray your alignment and play as the opposite once you reach level 10. This is a bit of a bummer.
On the plus side, you will automatically start with knowledge of your race's language (in addition to "Common") and thus not have to do a quest to learn it.
COMBAT
Like World of Warcraft, you have strafe and turn buttons, left-click turns the camera without turning you, and right-click turns the camera while turning you. You must target -before- using a skill and are subject to "implied target" (e.g. casting heal on an enemy will heal your friend being attacked by said enemy instead), two things I've never been fond of. However, you don't have to be facing an enemy at the time you choose to attack it - your character will just turn and face them before attacking.
Some enemies are linked together in parties called encounters, and attacking one of them will cause -all- of them to retaliate. Encounters can get into the dozens for creatures like herd animals and raiders.
Your character's "auto-attacks" are a bit slow, especially at the start of the game. Your primary means of sustained damage will therefore be skill spams. Although skills consume Power, it's very rare (at least in the early levels) to run out of it, as it isn't spent very quickly and it renegerates more rapidly when not in combat.
The game uses the logically questionable hate / threat system wherein you can force NPC enemies to only ever attack your tank despite any reasonable combatant knowing that your healer or mage would be better to take out first.
Developing your character's combat abilities relies on several factors.
- Ordinary experience gain and level, which will give you most of your skills and raise their Rank;
- Character and Focus traits, earned on level multiples and giving you further boosts to certain skills or stats;
- Alternate Advancement (Lv 10+), earned alongside of but separately to level and spent to obtain new skills and power up existing ones; and
- Research (Lv 20+), allowing you to increase skill Mastery (separate from Rank but every bit as important.) You can research at any time but it will take hours to days to finish research.
- Prestige (much higher than Lv. 20) is basically badder♥♥♥♥♥AA.
Your account status determines how high you can raise your skill Masteries via Research.
- Free accounts can only raise up to Adept (3rd level of mastery.)
- Silver account (one-time $5.00 charge to keep permanently) can raise up to Expert (4th level of mastery.)
- Gold account (subscription) can research up to Grandmaster (6th and final level of mastery.)
You don't have to have these account status to USE the skills at that mastery, or to acquire them through non-Research means - you just need that status to Research up to that level.
MENTORING & CHRONOMAGE
Got a friend to play? Already level 60 when your friend just started at level 1?
NO PROBLEM.
Party with them and you can temporarily lower yourself to match their level. Your skills and gear will power down too, but it will still be better than a natural of the target level.
What's that? You want to go hunt low-level gear for Transmute but you're too high so they don't drop? And you don't have a friend of that level?
NO PROBLEM.
Go find the Chronomages in Qeynos and temporarily level down to any multiple of 5.
CRAFTING
Of all MMO's I have played, Everquest II plays second in its crafting system only to Vanguard. Like Vanguard, crafting level is separate from adventure level and the player participates in a small minigame to craft, but it isn't anywhere near as engaging or strategic - you merely craft in four-second increments and press one of your six skill buttons to counter problems. Unlike Vanguard, crafting of any kind is integrally tied to adventure, or else you won't be able to safely gather ingredients yourself. You will also more or less be unable to mastercraft.
Crafting also benefits from its own separate Alternate Advancement, and with Chains of Eternity you can also get Crafting Prestige. However, these AA's are earned with crafting experience and not adventure experience.
MOUNTS AND AESTHETIC
Guess what? You can use mounts in combat. No worries!
Everquest II is also smart enough to realize that costume items shouldn't give you any stats, so they don't.
Anything you can put in an equipment slot that changes your appearance can be put in the equivalent appearance slot (including mounts.) The only drawback? You can't put "nothing" in your appearance slot unless you purchase the invisible costume items during a city festival (e.g. invisible gloves so your hands look bare.) However, you can toggle on and off your headgear, your cape, and your mount (Character window --> Options.)
Upon reaching level 20, you can give your character a last name, which can be changed for free once a week. You can also change your prefix and / or suffix title whenever you want, assuming you've earned one.
CLOSING
Everquest II is a fine game by modern standards, though it has a few quirks I would change.
Remember to Transmute all equipment you no longer need or else you will be gimped in Transmute until you can chronomage at level 20.

It's charming, quaint, and relaxing, but overall I can't recommend it.
For me, the worst aspect was the hint system. If you get stuck and need a hint (and you probably will), you have to stop what you're doing and click on these flies that buzz in from offscreen. It takes a good minute or two to fill up the hint meter, and when you need another hint you have to repeat the process. It would have been better if the meter gradually filled on its own, or if items collected gave you some meter. But if you try to use the hint and the object you need isn't visible on the screen (hidden behind a door), the hint won't activate. It's useful for not wasting hints on screens where there are no items, but I got stuck when the item I needed was behind a window that had to be opened by clicking on a tiny lever half the screen away. No hints for that, just frustrated spam-clicking.
After that, there's the puzzles. Most of them are super easy: some even tell you the answer in the hint. But lots of them rely on color recognition, a big no-no in game design. There are no options for color-blindness.
Finally, scattered throughout each chapter are puzzle pieces which are used to rebuild the world. But you don't actually need to collect all of the pieces to finish a level, or even the game. I was missing two pieces on the final level, and it just ended. Then I suddenly had all of them to finish the big puzzle. Then the game just ended. Just like that. There was no fanfare, no "You did it!" The game just ended and you get to replay puzzles.
The game has its good points, but overall I was disappointed. A good timekiller, but not a well-made one.

Prison Architect brings back some of the old school nostalgia from tycoon/simulation games the likes of Sim Hospital, Roller Coaster Tycoon, and Railroad Tycoon. Introversion takes on a rather unique art style and combines it with equally artful sound and UI design that makes the classical tycoon and simulation gameplay that much more enjoyable without feeling like "just another sim game".
The challenge of managing dangerous prisoners while turning a profit avoids becoming too difficult by giving the player several tools like a routine planner, guard shift planner, and building cloning tool. Despite the complexities, the learning curve remains relatively flat.
I purchased this game when it was in Early Access and had the pleasure of watching it grow into the great time-spender that it is now. Many great features were implemented along the way such as thorough mod support and "escape mode", and a good deal of bugs were squished too. My only reservation here is that several high profile bugs remained in the game when the developers decided to go 1.0, and while it has been some time since I've looked at their bug tracker, quite a few were still left.

Introversion has produced a shining example of how early access can be a success. I would absolutely recommend this game in its current released state.

This game, is the best game i'v ever played (And yes, iv played Fallout 4, GTA V, and  JC2), just a personal preference of course. At first, when i bought this game it was VERY early in development and i didnt know how big it was going to become. I had hesitations to buy the game, it was 14.99 i believe, and i thought "What if its just a boring game. What if its repetitve. What if the Dev's abondoned the game. What if its too easy. What if its too hard. What if its boring."
What if.....
What if.....
What if.....
What if the game was good. What if the game was exciting. What if the game was fun. We never think about that.
The game is EXTREMELY good, especially for a 2D game. It is not just repetitive, because you are EVERYTHING. You build the prison, you manage it, you watch it grow, you watch it burn :(, you watch it evolved, you watch your prisoners get rehabilited, you watch them kill :/, get locked up, kill a Armed Gaurd, take his shotgun, kill 3 gaurds and run out of the prisoner rambo style....yes, that happened, yes i watched it. Yes, i loved it. The game is not an average simulation game. Prisoners have personalities. Some, like the Supermax imate i had, thought getting shot at was part of everyones daily life, others love fighting the system, and most, want to get the hell outta there. The game, in no way is easy, even with cheats/unlimited money. Theres planning. LOTS AND LOTS OF PLANNING. You dont want your prisoners going to the canteen and whe they get there lunch is over. But in no way is it hard.
I love this game. I keep mental track of the prisoners just because i have nothing els to do. I watch prisoners go on their daily life. If try to pick out the bad ones, and sadly put them on 24hr lockdown on a 1x3 cell. A bed, a toilet, and a shower over the toilet. Then i pick out the good ones, the ones that go to the reformation programs, that read, that have no History of Misconduct, and hook em up with a 6x6 cell in Protective Custody. IT IS YOUR PRISON YOU CAN DO WHAT YOU WANT. Then theres the gangs....gangs...the Red....The Blue....and the Green! Dont even get me started on those! Those gangs have started Riots, have killed 1/3 of my staff, have burned down my Canteen and have dealt so many drugs Paublo Escobar gets jealous. Now, look, the game is $30 right now, and even i would be a little hesitant for a 2D game thats $30, i would say wait for it to go on sale, but if you love video games, if you've been looking for that one game were you decidie the fate of a prisoner, you watch your world evolve, you have no boundries, and yet you will go beyond them, i'd pay $100 for this game.

That sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, he joined Red gang, killed a gaurd, Started a riot in Protective Custody Area. I sent my armed gaurds to kill everyone there...every dies except ABU. Ah, Super Meat Boy. It's one of the most classic platformers I've ever played. You can switch CHARACTERS? You can even go into a DARK WORLD? To me, this sounds like stuff that's already been made, but this game is probably one of the best indie platformers you can probably get.
So, to the review: The puzzles can be quite challenging at times and it might cost you some time, or your patience. Some of them seem simple but hard. Here's an example: Jump over saws while you avoid these crawly slime things and get a key to unlock a door. It seems simple enough, but it's just difficult. Not sure if any of the levels did that concept, but it's just a example. Anyway, the difficulty can be just plain stupid at times. The puzzles are just stupid in these levels, such as Hell's boss. Seriously, who's going to go and remember these patterns?
The concept of character-changing blows my mind, I've never seen it before, so it's a huge bonus to this game's simplicity and fun. Ever heard of a game where you can pick the Headcrab from HL2 and The Kid from I wanna be the guy as a character? Heck, even Steve makes an appearance! Did I ever tell you that there was a level editor?
This game's plot isn't very cliche, but who saves a bandage girl? Whatever, beats me. This "Dr Fetus" guy seems as if he was a baby in a space pilot helmet, and that's pretty funny to me.
In general, this game is really worth your money, however you might want to not play it if you have a problem with difficult games.
Super Meat Boy taught me a very important life lesson: You can't get an A+ in everything.

A triumphant return to the hitman formula that made the older games so amazing and unique. Hitman was always about an open environment with targets the many ways to eliminate them. Absolution took a hard turn away from that formula but this game returns to that. They also improved on that formula by increasing the replay value even further. It's no longer about killing the same target in whatever way you can imagine, there are also escalations and elusive targets that take the same level and spin it an entirely different way. I was skeptical about the episodic release of the levels but now I can see that it ensures that the levels they release are the most polished and thoroughly worked out levels and characters that they can make.
2017 Update: The game has had its rough times that it has gone through. However, I believe that with IOI behind the wheel as an indepedent studio that there will be much better features in the time before the second season (or the next game, kinda unclear whats going to happen). This is already proven true with the new Patient Zero content. The UI is a little uglier with the color change from red to gray IMO but the rest of the content feels fresh in already used maps.

Annoying always online DRM aside, this game is as good a 2016 Hitman game as one could ask for. Extensive levels, a crisp style, interesting kill opportunities using various gadgets or the series' trademark semi-improvised hijinks... The six levels boast serious replayability and alternative modes & challenges. While the DRM still remains the thorn in the game's side (next to the random headturning), the episodic release has become widely embraced by the playerbase. Hitman has brought the series back to it's sandbox-y roots, allowing you to become the impeccable silent assassin once more, if you're up for the task. Can't wait for season 2.

With its distinct visual style and humorous dialogue, Borderlands 2 is an absolute joy to play! Equipment, level progression, and skill perks are all expertly balanced from start to end, and a wide variety of weapons, enemy types, and environments keep gameplay mixed up and interesting.
On the first playthrough.
This is not a bad thing except the game will eventually come to an end later or sooner depending on your level of skill, at which point you'll be faced with a choice... to start over or go New Game+.
With multiple job classes, starting a new game isn't bad but the storyline remains static. By the fourth or sixth (depending on if you got the DLCs or not) playthrough, even the most enthusiastic gamer might start feeling tedium creeping around the edges of the same jokes that you swore were so witty the first time around (and they were!).
Problems really start to arise on the New Game+ option, however, for those that are attempting to go for 100% completion. The issue above still arises (in that, you'll need to start the game over and make your way through the whole story multiple times), but it's compounded by the fact that the enemy difficulty begins to outpace your character strength. By the end-end game, and even kitted with the most powerful equipment, the most basic enemies will pose a serious threat to life and limb and bosses will soak up tens of thousands of rounds, usually far in excess of the amount of ammunition you can carry into the fight.
The only solution is to utilize very specific skill and gear combinations that enjoy stacking and complimentary effects. Normally this wouldn't be much of an issue except that the gear required is at this point nigh impossibly difficult to acquire and, second, that a primary joy of Borderlands 2 was the freedom to use the weapons that had the right "feel". That goes out the window in the end-end-game, where raw damage output and effects bordering on broken or glitched become necessary to survive.
But it's still great fun, who am I kidding? Give it a go, play it through, but don't try to really complete the game without knowing what's in store.

Let's start with the good.
Origins tells an awesome story.  The campaign itself if really well done, better so than City's campaign, imo.  Not only is the writing better, but the pacing, the boss battles, and the cut-scenes were all so much batter.  That's not to say that City had a bad campaign, it was great, I just think Origins did it better.  If you are someone who keeps playing these games for the storytelling(like me), then you should not be disappointed.
The graphics look really good, and imo, better in some ways.  I can actually use DX11 effects and PhysX while still maintaining a very constant 60 fps.  I did get some drops here and there in very demanding PhysX areas, but I'd certainly call it playable.  With City I had to turn off DX11 effects, unless I wanted to play at 30 fps all the time.  Origins looks gorgeous, and while I do miss the very colorful style of City, this game gets the visuals right in a lot of other ways.
Now for the bad.
Origins is buggy.  A few persistent bugs I'd experienced were: not being able to finish off enemies on the ground at times, and not being able to grapple to some object FOR NO REASON.  When a gargoyle statue is right next to me, I should be able to grapple to it.  There were loads of other bugs I'd encountered, thankfully none of them game-breaking.  However, one that nearly broke the game was a bug that makes it minimize every time I click the mouse.  This happens when loading up the game, and the only fix I found was to close out of Origins completely, open the multiplayer game, exit out of that at the title screen, and then reopen the single player game again.  And I had to do this nearly every time I played!  Really annoying.
I suspect these bugs are due to the multiplayer that was thrown in.  It's bad, and the shouldn't be in the game.  If WB had not decided to include multiplayer, they could have spent that time and money testing and polishing the game.  I don't blame the dev studio for the bugs, they are clearly talented and put a lot of effort into the Origins.  I blame the publisher for shoe-horning in a pointless multiplayer mode.  I think this game could have easily been as polished as the other 2 Arkham games if they would have allowed for it.
Overall, Origins is worth playing for fans of the Arkham style of storytelling.  The campaign was so good that I can even look past all of the bugs.  Very glad I got the game, I'd be missing out on another awesome Batman adventure if I hadn't.

Videogames are still a rather young art-form mostly catering to an adolescent or adolescent-minded main audience which works both as a benefit and a detriment. On the one hand videogames are very free in how they express themselves compared to e.g. movies because your role as the player is a uniquely interactive one and the unhinged nature of many games has proven inspiring for decades of aspiring artists. However this playfulness becomes troubling when games start to depict real events, namely wars. While you could make a case for WWII-era shooters like the older Medal of Honor parts as "documentary games" the only reason they could get away with showing war, argueably the most horrific thing humans are capable of, as entertaining and fun is that the world wars have for the most part been delegated to the history books now and its millions of victims are brought up in a discussion more in a way that you would discuss a gripping chess game.
With modern shooters the situation is a bit different. The moral implications of portraying currently ongoing human tragedies as entertainment for the youth of the nations that are responsibly for quite many of them is very troubling. I don't believe the games we play have such a huge impact on us that they would convince an otherwise stable human being that brown people are inherently our enemies and more animal than man, but they contribute to a society that turns a blind eye to catastrophies unless they happen in their backyard.
Enter Spec Ops: the line. What is superficially a typical military cover-shooter is actually more of a psychological horror game with action elements (not that you could tell from the terrible trailers). You follow a soldier's quest for glory and victory which turns into a downward spiral into madness. In the end the soldier's incentive to be a hero in this story (and in extension the player's motivation too) are dwarfed by the atrocities he has commited. I won't spoil anything but many scenes of horrific violence made me feel rather sick and it's very rare that a game ever gets to me on such a level. Other games have tried to do similar things and tug our heartstrings and guts, yet in my opinion these scenes come off as pretentious and clumsy at best. In Spec Ops: the line the descent into madness of our main character feels a lot more genuine and cleverly made, starting with the subtitle "the line". It can refer to several memorable moments in the game or basically the line you cross when you go into a war game trying to be a hero, a narrative that as mentioned before is cleverly and drastically dismantled. In the end it's made clear that the only moral choice you can make is not to play.
The only downside to the game is the very standard gameplay. It's necessary to lure you in with the similarities to other modern shooters and then hit you repeatedly over the head with a hellish experience but many people will unfortunately be turned off and never even get to the bits that make Spec Ops a memorable and important game. The action set-pieces are not really the game's strength but the thick atmosphere more than makes up for it.
Play it, think about it and then reevaluate its peers, the call of dutys and battlefields of this world - it's like going from apocalypse now to michael bay's pearl harbor.

A beautiful, colorful, fun shooter with an expertly crafted plot (You travel to Dubai to save it and everything gets messed up.) that unfortunately ends on an awful nihilistic theme that all valor is pointless and all heroism doomed to failure.
So in a sense it's gaming's version of The Watchmen, only less of a game-changer.
Heartily recommend for all the things it does right though. Good, challenging regen health cover shooting, satisfying gunplay, absolutely beautiful environments, and the story is certainly very good at what it does.

If you can look past the always-online requirement and episodic release (which to me isn't a bad thing at all), it is as Hitman as Hitman gets. Great looking game, endless possibilities for experimentation, tons of fun. Episodic releases made me focus on getting as many achievements as I could before moving to the next level, so as far as I'm concerned, I'm getting my money's worth for it.

HITMAN is the latest installment of the action/stealth franchise, following the fairly mediocre Hitman : Absolution.
While Absolution opted for a more linear approach akin to Splinter Cell, HiTMAN fixes that mistake by going back to the Blood Money style of gameplay.
HITMAN features 6 very detailed levels that will take hours to fully explore and master, and 8 more being bonus levels that reimagine previous locations with different targets and settings. While it seems like a pretty low number of levels the level of details more than make up for it, as well as the user-made contracts and regularly added "escalation" missions taking place in these levels.
These levels are, in my opinion, some of the best in the whole franchise so far, some beating even Blood Money's. They're big, colorful, and incredibly detailed. They are filled with NPCs with lots of dialogue, telling small stories as you explore the level and listen to their conversations, making the locations feel "alive".
A new opportunity system allows you to easily find ways to get past guards or take out your targets, but it can be disabled if you'd rather find these out by yourself. In addition to the opportunities there are tons of ways to take out your targets in less scripted manners, giving the levels a lot of replay value. These ties into the new challenge system, keeping track of various feats you've accomplished so far, rewarding you with mastery points, which in turn unlock loadout options like starting locations, weapons and gadgets that lets you mess around with the levels even more.
Contract mode from Absolution is back, letting you go around the level and selecting targets to kill with specific weapons and outfits and challenging other players to finish your contract and beat your score.
Now to the bad bits,
Jesper Kyd noticeably didn't compose the soundtrack to this game, and it shows. The eerie orchestrated score from previous hitman games is gone, being replaced by a rather generic sounding synth-heavy soundtrack (hope you like that inception horn!).
Gameplay-wise, a lot of it is completely wasted because of the elusive targets, special missions only available for 2 days to 1 week being removed from the game after that. It's especially disappointing as they all include new characters (One of the target was Gary Busey, with Gary Cole making an appearance) and changes to the level, but unless you play them as they come out, you'll never get to see these ingame.
The game got a lot of hate for being always online, which I can somewhat understand, but personally I've never had any problems with it, especially as the developpers added a button to reconnect without losing any progress from your current run, but your experience may vary. Same with the optimization, I didn't have many problems with it but others had a lot, directX12 being by far the most problematic.
Overall I think hitman is worth checking out but mostly if you're a completionist, the levels can be played through quite quickly but the game gets a ton of replayability from the very detailed levels offering a lot of different ways to take out your targets.

A triumphant return to the hitman formula that made the older games so amazing and unique. Hitman was always about an open environment with targets the many ways to eliminate them. Absolution took a hard turn away from that formula but this game returns to that. They also improved on that formula by increasing the replay value even further. It's no longer about killing the same target in whatever way you can imagine, there are also escalations and elusive targets that take the same level and spin it an entirely different way. I was skeptical about the episodic release of the levels but now I can see that it ensures that the levels they release are the most polished and thoroughly worked out levels and characters that they can make.
2017 Update: The game has had its rough times that it has gone through. However, I believe that with IOI behind the wheel as an indepedent studio that there will be much better features in the time before the second season (or the next game, kinda unclear whats going to happen). This is already proven true with the new Patient Zero content. The UI is a little uglier with the color change from red to gray IMO but the rest of the content feels fresh in already used maps.

Annoying always online DRM aside, this game is as good a 2016 Hitman game as one could ask for. Extensive levels, a crisp style, interesting kill opportunities using various gadgets or the series' trademark semi-improvised hijinks... The six levels boast serious replayability and alternative modes & challenges. While the DRM still remains the thorn in the game's side (next to the random headturning), the episodic release has become widely embraced by the playerbase. Hitman has brought the series back to it's sandbox-y roots, allowing you to become the impeccable silent assassin once more, if you're up for the task. Can't wait for season 2.

In terms of gameplay the game is exactly what you'd expect. A realistic prison simulation that you control. Be a cold and ruthless warden that runs your prison with fear or be a generous and passionate rehabilitationist that helps your inmates improve themselves for society. Satisfy their needs and keep the rioting to a minimum. The story is great too and works well as a tutorial for new players! And the mods are amazing! So much potential has been given to the players to modify the game however they want. You can turn the prison into a Fallout Vault! Or a Star Wars space station keeping Rebel prisoners.
This is truly one of the best games on steam simply for it's continued support from the developers. You're truly getting your money's worth when you buy this game.

- Some bugs and tehnical issues, nothing gamebreaking. The AI got stuck a few ( running in place ), a few FPS drops with Physics on ( even if i have a pretty good rig )
- It's short, even shorter than the first two games.
- Not enough new stuff ( gadgets, mission types, moves and so on )
It's an excellent game but not of the quality i got used to by Rocksteady. But still for a new studio this is really an great effort.

A psychologically traumitizing game whose combat mechanics start at what other games call "bloody hard" (but what it calls a walk in the park) and escalates to realms that I have yet to even attempt.
The game is completely linear, with only a few relatively unimportant decisions actually being required for the whole game. The most important decisions are made for you.
I can't decide whether to recommend the game or not. I'll go with a tentative "yes". But it's a bit of a toss-up.
[edit] having replayed the game a couple of times to make different "choices", I've come to the conclusion that no, it's not a good game. It's a pretty good story, yes. Probably would have made a good short film, if done right. But that's it - it's a film, not a game. As a GAME, I'd have to say that it's not that good. Completely linear, "moral decisions" that amount to nothing at all and change nothing in the game itself, and even goes from "OK, no respawning of enemies" to "infinite respawn because we actually don't want to give you a choice even though we're pretending you have one".
So as a film, OK. As a story, OK. As a game, failure.

This game had huge expections to live up to and unfortunately it didn't.  Stand alone it would've been a great game, but following on from Arkham City it left me a bit wanting.  The progress from Arkham Asylum to City was amazing, the controls were more fluid, the gadgets more intuitive and the story more involving.  Origins felt like a bit of a step back from city.  Although it appears to be a very direct clone, within 10 minutes playing the game I could tell it had been done by a different studio and I was right.  Unfortunately this meant the studio had obviously lost the lessons learned from progressing from Asylum to City.
Here's the things I found frustrating:
1. The Gadgets - This was supposed to be a prequel yet you had all the gadgets from Arkham City, which didn't really make sense.  Also some of them were changed for little to no reason.  The Shock Gun had change to shock gloves but the most confusing change was the Ice Grenade changing to a completely identical Glue Grenade.  Also some of the gadgets just made combat too easy, like the shock gloves - once activated you just keep hitting X until everyone is dead.  The gadgets didn't add to the flow of the game like the original did.
2. Story is not as involved as City - In Arkham city the story had amazing flow, taking you from place to place and sometimes back again exploring new areas. They had managed to achieve the feeling of an open universe within a linear story line.  Origins didn't achieve this and the story was too short to really cover off all the areas in such a huge city.
3. Upgrade Tree - The gadget upgrade tree is so linear it's pointless. When you have points to upgrade you often have 1 or 2 choices that you can spend them on.
4. The Batwing - The concept of the batwing to move between places sounded cool, but in the end it really didn't live up to any sort of expectations.
5. Little evolution from City  - The game is so close to being a clone of city but even just falls short of that. Combat and everything else is identical but still doesn't feel as mature.
Here's what I liked about the game:
1. More Batman - Arkham City was my favourite game of all time, so it was good to get behind the controls again.
So essentially this game would've been great as a sequel to Asylum or as a Stand Alone game, but following on from City it just didn't hit the very high mark set.  It's still worthwhile playing, but I regret buying it on launch day rather than waiting for the price to drop.
