As compared to the other two Rocksteady games in this franchise, Batman: Arham Origins (by WB games) has aspects which are less well done than the others titles, but also some beautiful aspects that make it even more enjoyable than the previous two.
As game play goes, it is virtually identical to Arkham City, with same/simliar commands. There are some different types of enemies, those which require special stun attacks and those which need careful and quick response of counters to avoid rapid beatdowns. Side quests are largely the same: a series of timed events which require fast, long distance gliding to groups of enemies; searchs for trophies; destruction of certain kinds of items.
Internal areas are slighty more varied than the other titles, but the city design is virtually the same as that of Arkham City, if expanded. This is both a good and a bad thing.  Seeing the before and after of the same map, with expanded sections is pretty cool, but it can get a little frustrating to be negotiating the exact areas you've done before. This becomes especially noticible due to a lessening of the interactive ability of the landscape. Many things that would have been scalable or climbable or grapple(able?) are not. Additionally, it seems to take longer for grapple points to show as available when gliding and this can result in some choppy, unsatifying movement.
Additional bugs are indescriminate crashing of the game (other players have reported this; there seems to be no rhyme or reason to it) and a very annoying video bug where Batman's cape stutters repeatedly when gliding. The visual doesn't effect the actual flight but is very distracting, breaks immersion and if it goes on long enough, can even inspire low level nausea.
Now, to the very very good.  While I prefer not to include spoilers, I will simply say that I was only marginally satisfied with the game until Joker showed up. From  there on, the story took on new life.  The masterful voicework and beautiful cut scenes are thrilling and had me fangirling all over the place. The interaction between Batman & Joker and the subsequent peeks into Joker's head are gorgeously done and I can't praise them enough.
All in all, the good parts of this game are so good, they do make up for some of the lesser portions. I would be even happier if the bugs were worked out. A solid title, if a little samey in side quests and combat, but with a beautiful story mode that's worth the play through, especially if you are a comics Batman fan. There are little treats hidden all over the place; Easter eggs wherever you look.

I bought Undertale recently while it was on sale. I had heard good things about the game and I finally had the money to buy it, so I did. And I loved it. Easily 10/10 if you’re here just for the number.
Undertale is an RPG set in the Underground. A land below the surface of the earth, filled with monsters. You learn very quickly that some monsters are nice, and some aren’t. While the game does have a tutorial, it’s up to you to learn about the bullet-hell that you’ll have to go through in your adventures throughout the Underground in your attempts to leave. The graphics can be seen as simple, and you wouldn’t be wrong for saying so, but they fit the game perfectly. And then there are the characters, every character is developed nicely. Even your traditional grind fodder has been well-thought about.
One thing I want to make clear though, is that Undertale is a smart game. Yes, I do mean in the ways I’ve mentioned above, but I also mean intellectually, it’s smart. Undertale remembers things you’ve done between saves, so don’t think you’re outsmarting the game by killing someone then reloading your save to save them. It knows.
(I’m about to go into detail about each route in Undertale, if you’re looking to avoid spoilers, please ignore the rest of the review)
Neutral - This is the easiest path of Undertale to complete. Your only goal is to finish the game, letting you spare or kill anyone you want, making it the more "diverse" path to play (especially with the most endings)
True Pacifist - This path is slightly harder than Neutral, as you have to figure out how to avoid killing each enemy and boss, which doesn’t increase your LV by the way, so those later enemies are going to be harder to handle, as they’ll be able to finish you in a few blows. Though the main advantage there is that you only need the game's basic healing items. As for the story, it’s the same as Neutral for the most part, but later on, you learn a lot more about what’s been going on in the Underground, and why some things have happened. There is a major disappointment here for me, while the final battle in this route is definitely amazing, you’re actually fully incapable of dying to it. The ending is terrific though, and due to the credits afterward, is believed to be the canonical ending
Genocide - This ending is something you’re highly unlikely to find accidentally (unless you play those RPGs where you have to be at an insanely high level before you reach the first miniboss). So I’ll say this now, It’s the most boring of them all. There’s very little in the way of a plot or story information, you just sit in one room killing everything until nothing shows up, all of the puzzles have been solved already, and you immediately kill all the bosses. There are a few things stopping it being the easiest route (I won’t say it here). Be warned though, as going to the very end of a Genocide route will poison your future runs, causing events to happen that didn’t happen before. Because while you might want to... Undertale will never let you forget that you once killed all the people. And even without that reminder, it doesn’t feel that satisfying to kill them. I personally felt empty throughout this entire route, and even in the celebrations of those hard struggles I had mentioned, those were shortly followed by sadness. This route was made to make you feel like a bad person, and it does that well.

In a world where indie titles seem  to have cornered the avant garde and ofputting side of the market e.g Binding of Isaac, Limbo, This War of Mine it's neat to see such a high value title go in such a different direction from other mainstream shooters.
The overall look of The Line can be summarized as a typical shooter set in present day Middle East but with a slight saturation to the lens. It's not overdone and it seems to fit the mood of the game. Almost a sort of festering humidity at the edges of your vision. It becomes an unsettling contrast later in the game I find.

And yet it's the only way to progress. Once the gears are in motion it's either continue playing or uninstall the game. And it's too good to uninstall.
Sounds of weapons and enemies feel kind of flat and repatitive but the dialogue more than makes up for it. I'd put this squad dialogue as probably the best I've ever heard. Right up there with Alyx Vance or The Sands of Time narration. It just fits and is so well delivered. It kept me way more interested than all the firefights I was engaged in.
Single playthrough had me at six hours which is more than enough to feel sick about yourself. Also there are a lot of choices in the game which lead to an alternate ending which I'd love to tackle someday. For now, I'll take to heart the horrible lessons of modern day war and stick to playing Renowned Explorers: International Society, a game where I can suceed while being predominantly friendly.

Does playing a game through a screen like this justify everything we do? All the harmful actions we perform, all the lives we've taken away, all the lives we've ruined from such chaos? Few games will ever actually ask that question, and fewer still will tell you that it doesn't. At some points in this game, it almost feels like it DOESN'T want you to play it. It wants you to turn around from the monitor, walk away, be a better person than who you're watching in the story.
What appeared to be another generic shooter to perhaps many people, was a wolf in sheep's clothing. While some people are right, yes, the gameplay is nothing special, it's decently polished. No gamebreaking bugs, or even small ones really (As far as I saw), and yeah you might enjoy some parts. But after a while, you may find yourseff weighed down...weighed down by the horrors you've seen...horrors that aren't even real, but they still stay with you.
This game is like going into University, where you've accepted a certain truth your whole life. In this case, the truth is that you're a hero and every game makes you a hero. But like that surly university professor you take without realizing his nature, it tells you one thing. Question what's around you. Is everything really what you think it is?
Do you feel like a hero yet?

Full Review: Read at your own risk
I have to be honest, this game got to me, got inside my head and made me feel things I didn't think a basic, cliché, third person shooter could. There are plenty of games that show you violence, plenty of games have you run through all sorts of firefights and battles that are visually stunning making you feel awesome. You walk away from most firefights in this game feeling many feelings; sadness, guilt, horror and sickness. You start the game as a strapping commander of a small team of Special Forces, the serious "Captain America" type and sarcastic joker. You are entering the city of Dubai, struck by devastating dust storms trapping the 33rd and all the civilians they were trying to evacuate and of course, you know the CO of that unit, he was a good man who helped you in a past theater of war. All very, run of the mill story of a canned modern shooter. This is remarkably misleading. As you work your way through the city you find that order has utterly collapsed, you help soldiers under fire from apparent insurgents and as you go farther, you find American soldiers rounding up and gunning down civilians. You are forced to defend yourself when the turn their fire on you. It tears your team up and it is simply the beginning. The game constantly confronts you with choices between one evil or another. No one is the good guy, each side commits atrocities against each other, and if you hope to survive, you have to do the same. There are literally a pair of achievements named "Damned if you do" and "Damned if you don't". The game drags you through the mud watching soldiers, civilians and even your own team die. Your character's dialogue slowly devolves from in control tactical commands to screaming obscenities at the enemy and eventual hallucinations. This game brings themes from Apocalypse Now and The Heart of Darkness into the gaming world and confronts us with the true horrors of this level of violence. You don't walk away from this game feeling good about playing it, the game even goes meta, insinuating that you caused this violence; you could have shut it down and walked away at any time, why did you keep going? They are questions that demand answers. It is a game I think all gamers should play; it rocks you, makes you feel uneasy and forces you to appreciate the true nature of violence. The gameplay itself is smooth and user friendly. Basic squad commands and different guns give you multiple approaches to different combat scenarios. The gameplay is linear and simply escalated as different guns and enemies are introduced with smarter AI and better fighters, much like most of the Call of Duty franchise, although this game, I enjoyed more. Overall, this game is deeply dark and challenges you to confront its own violence. Been playing APB on and off since the RTW beta, and I think I've finally quit for good. As I post this, server lag is worse than ever with rubber-banding ocurring every 5 minutes. Cheaters are still rampant and unchecked, and probably G1's biggest real-money customers to boot. Sweet bloody victory ripped from the jaws of a thousand snarling hellhounds, friendships forged in the hottest flames known to man, hatred so pure it would make a sith lord weep. You will be fondly remembered for what you were.

If you are looking for a house building simulator.. this isn't your game.
Ask yourself these questions and you decide if you would enjoy this style of game.
1. Do you like to grind for resources like trees, stone, and metal to build a base for protection while logging off for the night and to come back with the chance of it not being there anymore?  This is Rust
2. Do you like to be attacked and have to fight for your life almost 100% of the time when you see another player? This is Rust
3. Can you deal with monthly wipes (some being weekly on private servers) and starting over from scratch? This is Rust
4. Want to hear 13 year olds (ages can very from 11-55 doing the same thing) run up to your base and call you the "N" word till you open your front door? This is Rust
5. Would you like to run around naked most of your time till you learn to play? This is rust
All of the above are things that I have had happen to me while playing Rust and I don't regret buying this game. The game isn't for everyone, keep that in mind and watch some YouTube footage before you make your decision.

This was until I watched a few playthroughs on YouTube and decided that this game actually looked really fun. I would totally recommend Undertale to anyone for the soundtrack, gameplay, plot, and humor. Toby Fox has really outdone himself with the amount of time and effort he put into developing this game, delaying the game for almost 3 years after the originally release date and gaining more than 10x the amount he had set as his goal on Kickstarter. The game itself has a similar art and music style to other indie games, drawing much of its inspiration from Earthbound. Undertale follows the journey of a human child that has fell down into the “Underground”. We learn that humans and monsters used to coexist with each other before the humans saw the monsters as a threat and sealed them with a magical barrier in the Underground. Your primary goal is to get past the king of the Underground, Asgore, and return home through the barrier. Along the way you meet several quirky and lovable characters and make choices that impact how your story unfolds as you progress. What makes this game so unique from other rpg’s is Undertale’s combat system. Toby Fox designed the battle system so that you have the choice to either kill or spare your enemies. By doing so, every action you make affects the gameplay. You can either take the pacifist route, neutral route, or the genocide route. This is why I’ve played Undertale thoroughly almost 7 times and purchased the complete soundtrack. The game is packed full of easter eggs and secrets that you can find from exploring every area, or from replaying the game. The character development is tremendous, and the subtle humor along with the music helps the player to bond with the characters. Every single character is designed in a way where almost anyone could relate to one of them in some way. Trust me when I say this, this game is one of the most greatest games ever for its story. You won’t regret buying it.

For once, I didn't really pay to the story, so here is a brief summary of the sequel of another solitaire game: a dragon is terrorizing the region and you set out on a journey to find it and to confront it. During this long journey accross mountain, desert, forest, villages, dark areas and many others, you'll meet companions willing to help you.
This is a card game. You draw a card and you have to make suits with those available on the board. You have 40 stages, with 10 levels in each. If at first, you choose a companion with a specific power, more will join you during the journey. Once they're used, they're respleneshing themselves with cards you're putting in a suit. The store will also provide you with bonus and with items that can be used in some levels (a potion to extinguish fire and a key to open a lock). Usually, the lock levels have a hidden key card while the fire (either put at the beginning or by a dragon card hidden in the stack) will extinguish itself after a few cards if you don't have any potion on you. Other cards are hidden like money (to increase your wallet) or a wild card that can help you to finish a level or to continue a combo. Some cards need some weapons to reveal themselves.
To keep on going, you need to meet the objectives for the whole stage (accumulate a certain ammount of gold during it, manage to do some perfect levels - where no card stays on board -, gather a certain ammount of stars - each level is rated -, fill the dragon bar and make combos). These can vary depending on the difficulty chosen.
I must say that despite being in casual, I've got an hard time to finish some stages. However, I found a work-around: before playing the last level, I can play another one to have another chance for the combos, but mainly, for the gold challenge. Sometimes, the AI throws you hard levels where you'll put in the stack only a few cards, so, make sure to use your companions and your wild cards at a good moment. Another little problem is that you can't carry more than a key and a potion, meaning that you have to get often in the store if you don't forget about it.
While the graphics are just fantasy backgrounds, the rest is just the cards designs. I've played with the default one, which is nice but if you have an hard time to distinguish cards, you have also the set with only the numbers or letters. About the soundtrack, it was fitting, however, I wish that one track wasn't reminding me of 12 Labours of Hercules as it's the main track of that game - I suppose that it was taken in a free of rights sites. The story is also voiced but the narrator was so boring that I never payed attention to the story. I just wanted to play the game.
I also found the "Continue" button placed at the worst place. It's not in first place but after "New Game" and I suppose that some players will reset their progression by being too fast.
I've also crashed a few times with an level exception access error or something like that.
The game is good, as you have at least 400 levels and minigames on side. But with the crashes, I wouldn't advice you to buy it at full price. The story is perhaps boring but it's not the point here - you're here to play cards. Anyway, I recommend it.

It's not solitaire as MS Windows defines it, you're not shuffling cards around, you're looking for cards in sequence - up or down, regardless of color.
To spice it up, there's a few modifiers - the stacks are sometimes not accessible until you find a tool to free it.
(Or buy the tool with money gained in previous levels.)
Also, unlike the solitaire that probably came with your computer, the stacks aren't ordered, they're all over the screen, blocking each other.
A nice touch are the wildcards you can find - basically, a free card to use if you're stuck and need just THAT card to continue. (The wildcard will have a fixed number, though. So you really need to need THAT card, not just ANY card :-)
There's a story told that is OK, though the game obviously has no influence upon it.
You're winning money, so there is a store where you can buy upgrades and items to help you play. Unfortunately, there's only a few of them, so you'll soon have bought everything there is, leaving you to play for the sake of playing.
(Which should be enough, after all. Though I admit I'd rather have something to grind towards while playing, the story alone isn't really enough for me.)

Full Review: Read at your own risk
I have to be honest, this game got to me, got inside my head and made me feel things I didn't think a basic, cliché, third person shooter could. There are plenty of games that show you violence, plenty of games have you run through all sorts of firefights and battles that are visually stunning making you feel awesome. You walk away from most firefights in this game feeling many feelings; sadness, guilt, horror and sickness. You start the game as a strapping commander of a small team of Special Forces, the serious "Captain America" type and sarcastic joker. You are entering the city of Dubai, struck by devastating dust storms trapping the 33rd and all the civilians they were trying to evacuate and of course, you know the CO of that unit, he was a good man who helped you in a past theater of war. All very, run of the mill story of a canned modern shooter. This is remarkably misleading. As you work your way through the city you find that order has utterly collapsed, you help soldiers under fire from apparent insurgents and as you go farther, you find American soldiers rounding up and gunning down civilians. You are forced to defend yourself when the turn their fire on you. It tears your team up and it is simply the beginning. The game constantly confronts you with choices between one evil or another. No one is the good guy, each side commits atrocities against each other, and if you hope to survive, you have to do the same. There are literally a pair of achievements named "Damned if you do" and "Damned if you don't". The game drags you through the mud watching soldiers, civilians and even your own team die. Your character's dialogue slowly devolves from in control tactical commands to screaming obscenities at the enemy and eventual hallucinations. This game brings themes from Apocalypse Now and The Heart of Darkness into the gaming world and confronts us with the true horrors of this level of violence. You don't walk away from this game feeling good about playing it, the game even goes meta, insinuating that you caused this violence; you could have shut it down and walked away at any time, why did you keep going? They are questions that demand answers. It is a game I think all gamers should play; it rocks you, makes you feel uneasy and forces you to appreciate the true nature of violence. The gameplay itself is smooth and user friendly. Basic squad commands and different guns give you multiple approaches to different combat scenarios. The gameplay is linear and simply escalated as different guns and enemies are introduced with smarter AI and better fighters, much like most of the Call of Duty franchise, although this game, I enjoyed more. Overall, this game is deeply dark and challenges you to confront its own violence. I believe that anyone who plays shooters should play this game to remind them how horrific true violence is; there is nothing wrong with playing our video games that are violent, we just can't become numb to it and this game keeps us grounded.

I've finished the game, so I'll oblige with a short review:

+ Beautiful art
+ Nice soundtrack
+ Smooth mechanics
+ Some unique puzzles
- No real story
- Repetitive tasks
- No instructions for puzzles/minigames
- No choice to skip puzzles/minigames
- Includes 2 short but stressful 8-bit 'obstacle-avoidance' action minigames (not what P&Cers are looking to play)
- Hint system not very good
- Anticlimactic and unsatisfying "ending" (if it can be called one)
- No replay value.
__________________________________
My feelings towards this game are mixed. I bought it based on all the positive reviews, and while I did enjoy it (mostly), and I do recommend the game (on sale), I still have a bunch of curmudgeonly gripes.
It didn't feel like there was much of a story. The wordless intro clip only show a basic scenario: meteor hits planet, planet breaks into puzzle pieces, you need to find them all and fix the planet. Not much of a plotline, just an excuse for the player to do stuff. The store description says that the world "fell apart" and "its future depends on you", but I honestly expected a bit more for the main objective than
putting a picture puzzle back together. And aside from the puzzle pieces, the actual game feels disconnected from the initial "story" idea; it doesn't seem like there's any dire trouble to tackle in the world - just finding misplaced parts and accessing new areas. There's not much that connects the minigames, puzzles, and hidden object bits to an actual story, anyway. Yes, the puzzle pieces fix the planet. But how does anything else in the game itself factor into the "story"? I know that's being nitpicky, but if "Story" is in your title, there should at least be more plot-like connections between the tasks a player must complete.
You get a couple of initial tutorial arrows showing what to click on, but then you're on your own. The puzzle piece hunt is obvious, but you still have to click around to find out what parts of the scene need "fixing". Those bits give you an secondary objective to find a certain number of objects (gears, pipes, dice, etc) to fix the broken part. Sort of a semi-hidden-object hunt. After fixing your ladder/panel/door/whatever, you either unlock another area, or are presented with a minigame/puzzle to complete in order to get the last piece for
secondary objective. Basically, "Find all the _____, or else you'll never get that last _____." At least clicks are precise, and the movement between scenes/areas is very fluid.
Many of the puzzles were very familiar/common in other games. But there are a handful I haven't seen in P&Cs/HoGs before, and the difficulty varied, which was nice. Either way, you get NO instructions once you start. Some are intuitive - like the "Simon Says" levers, or a version of that tube puzzle where you rotate pipes to complete a network. But many have you scratching your head before you realize what you're supposed to be doing in the first place. (I spent far too long on the Compass "puzzle" until I looked up the solution out of frustration.) At least you can click the red X to exit and reset everything if you mess up.
I
didn't like the action 'video game' minigames you're forced to play to continue, and was very glad there were only two. They're 8-bit obstacle games: one guiding a boat up and down to avoid walls, and one moving a plane left and right to avoid trees and planes. If you crash even once, you start over. They're not all that difficult, but they introduce an unwelcome level of stress that I generally play P&Cs/HoGs to
.
Oh, and forget about finishing the game if you get stuck. You can't skip a single thing. Not cool.
The hint system is cute, but iffy. Click on the blue flies to fill the "?" meter. Once it's full and clicked, a red bug will fly out and circle around whatever you're supposed to click or focus on next. The problem is that if you're in the wrong scene within a level, the bug will simply fly to the edge of the screen to the signpost arrow. I understand that means the next 'piece' or whatever is not in the current scene, but when you move to the next scene the bug disappears. So all you really got as a hint was "Nope, it's not here". Then the hint bar won't release a bug again for quite a while, even when full. I don't know what the timer is on it, but it's annoying to unknowingly "waste" hints like that. It's not difficult to refill the meter, but that really doesn't do much good if you can't use it.
The description calls each chapter "vastly different". I disagree with most of that. Different, somewhat. Vastly, no. Any major differences between levels are purely cosmetic. It's just different scenes, music, and what type of objects you need to find. The minigames/puzzles themselves are obviously going to be different, but that's expected for any game like this, so I wouldn't consider that a "vast" difference.
The tasks in each level are pretty much the same:
1) Find all the hidden puzzle pieces.
2) Find multiple objects to "fix" things so you can progress. Objects are hidden in similar ways in each level (behind panels, overlaying a similar shape, blending into the background, etc).
3) Help some random person (usually just a version of "find this many ____").
4) Solve a handful of minigames or puzzles.
5) Put the puzzle pieces together at the end of each level.
That said, it didn't take long for it to feel a little repetitive.
ending?
It's very anticlimactic and unfulfilling.
None whatsoever. You can't complete a level if you don't find/solve everything, so once you play through, you're done.
it has replay value if you want to revisit a minigame. But I don't see myself loading this up again just to play a puzzle with a 1-minute-or-less solution.
Despite my nitpicking, I do recommend the game to PoC/HoG fans (wait for a sale though - save the $5 for a latte or something). The lovely art and music are worth a look, at the very least. If the game was any more expensive, I'd probably just go look at some nice galleries on deviantART instead. But honestly I can't comment/complain about value, since I got it on sale for $0.49.
Developers: Beautiful game, nice puzzles, but if you advertise it as a story, it needs more plot depth to be "immersive" or feel that I'm saving or helping anyone.

Keep in mind that I haven't really played 2D Sidescrolling MetroidVania platforming games, or whatever genre this is.
My thoughts on this game - mixed, but generally positive
Starting the game you are blasted by a beautiful soundtrack which stays that way throughout the game. Further, the art-style is gorgeous to look at. It's a charming game.
The opening cinematic story sections are heartfelt and get you motivated to keep playing the game as it does have an air of mystery about it. Consider the world of Avatar and the way that world had an atmosphere of 'magic' about it - the viewer, or player in this case, wanting to immerse themselves in that world - this game achieves that.
Playing through as Ori to restore life to the forest you will go through many areas and mazes, conquer many traps and upgrade your abilities over time as well as even hunt and locate secrets to further boost those upgrades. The upgrades themselves exist on 3 'trees' where, as you obtain skill points through combat and secret boosts you can adavnce along any and all increasing your attack damage, gaining additional mid-air jumps, increasing the effect of life restoration, revealing some secrets on the map, and so on. The secrets are not too out of the way and over the course of the game I didn't need to 'grind' for skill points which is good. It's a very casual game as without necessarily intending to, I found that I located most of the secrets. Some I did want to find just because I wanted to master my abilities which also works to the game's advantage. The story is pleasant and magical and the tense moments are just that.
However. (Keep in mind this is my first venture into these types of games)
Mouse and keyboard - you will be jumping a LOT. Be prepared for aching fingers and you might need a thimble for your thumb on the spacebar. At one point I picked up my controller because of this, but found I had to move BACK to mouse and keyboard because of the rather silly way in which some abilities are implemented and not being particularly suited to the D-Pad of a controller. (I didn't use sticks as I would find that I would be going up or down unintentionally).
Maybe I'm impatient, maybe I'm easily frustrated, but some levels and their designs are infuriating. WHen you have so many control systems and abilities to juggle the level design can be very tricky to navigate without some abilities getting in the way or not working necessarily as intended.
As someone with a visual impairment, sometimes the art-style to the game, while fantastic, was a drawback because it made seeing where I could stand and where I could not quite hard leading to many deaths on my part.
Then there are the tense climax/chase moments in the game. These should be fast, exciting, but ultimately just turn into trial and error 50, 100-attempt sections that by the end you have lost all your excitement and just want to get the section over with.
Most of the game is relatively straight-forward however and was only really frustrating to me outside of the things I mentioned already when I just found controls, level design, or Ori's movement to be unintutive or temperamental.
Having said this, overall I would recommend the game, it's a charming experience and I imagine would be much more enjoyable to those more experienced with 2D side-scrolling platformers. As my first step into the genre, I'd say it was worth the time and money, although it isn't too long - maybe pick it up when it's on sale. Worth a second play-through, perhaps not for me. But I will be picking up that soundtrack, and that opening will probably stay with me a good while.

I have played the previous two Arkham games in the series and I felt both were friggin' awesome. I went into this one, after reading a  lot of the reviews for it and had a negative outlook on it. But, after my first ten minutes with the game I knew that all of those negative reviews were written to get traffic and in no way actaully reflect the game itself. Yes, it is not that much of an Origin story, unless you play it and realize its an Origin of Arkham and of the Joker's relationship with the Bat. The gameplay, combat, and mechanics truly have been taken straight from Arkham City and with the addition of some other gadgets it can become quite interesting. First of all, I am a huge Batman fan. That doesn't mean this review will be a fanboy galore, as it most certainly is not. First thing is first though and I need to get this off my chest; people who say this 'feels repetative' is dumbfounding. how many times does Batman suddenly decide to overhaul how he fights?
Anyway, the game has a superb atmosphere. Year one and Killing Joke are clearly inspirations for the story. On top of that, Gotham is eerily quiet, as it should be on Christmas eve late at night, in a city full of corruption to the point where Black Mask has a hold of the police comissioner on his payroll, SWAT teams in his pocket and criminals running the streets. Ontop of that, you have the GPD issuing emergency broadcasts that citizens stay inside. THIS is why there are very few citizens out and about. Its a complaint I see from people who just do not think about the game and the situation. Why would you be out late on christmas even when theres 8 assassins and countless more gang members out for blood?
Theres quite abit of 'Tim Burton' to the atmosphere. The portrayal of Joker and bane are especially brilliant. Bane here is done justice unlike the previous two games. I loved the boss fights too. For me, the gameplay isn't bland. Its slower than in Arkham City, but for me that represents the inexperienced Bruce in a much bulkier and heavily armored suit combined with Bruce's attacks being more raw and powerful. it feels asif im dealing more damage, theres more aggression and power behind the blows. This is why Batman moves slower in comparison to the lightweight armoured experienced Batman from AA and AC.
Batman makes mistakes in this, his interrogations aren't always fruitful, he goes blind in for the punch and gets hit and is learning the hard way. This is THE first time he is taking on super criminals, and it clearly shows.One of the most telling things about the character of Bruce is how charming he is with Vicki Vale at the start of AC, yet at the start of AO she says one thing and he is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and is so up himself he goes 'interview over'.
The graphics are great in this game, Some say its not 'christmassy' enough. In a town that is so corrupt, its citizens so oppressed, officials in the pocket of mob bosses, I like that we get to see more 'christmassy' decorations and tones in some parts of Gotham than in others, for me it represents the class division within Gotham City and the disparity between the poor and the rich, which was always a key theme within many Batman stories.
The Crime Scene investigation is a massive step up. I love it. Some people have criticised how you just press and hold a Button and it does it all for you, which to me is exactly what I would've thought would happen. You find the clues and the batcomputer, just like in AC pieces it together within the cowel. Its much more detailed and advanced and It adds to the experience.the multiplayer expiriance is oalso awesome.so overall ARKHAM ORIGINS ROCKS!!

(semi)-SPOILERS
I get what the game was trying to do here, but for me, at least, it just doesn't work.
The game REQUIRES you to treat it like a CoD or Battlefield game, otherwise it doesn't make any sense.
The plot railroads you into situations where you might logically just sit down and say "Hey, guys, why are you shooting us? We literally haven't done anything to you." But, hoping that the audience is used to shooters where you just shoot people for poorly explained reasons, the game just hopes you don't think for more than two seconds about what's happening.
Likewise, the fact that the character (and game)-defining moments railroad you into a 'choice' removes all feelings of personal responsibility and empathy that they spend so long building up. Call me cynical, but if you give me a game and force me to do something to progress, that has the same impact as follows:
"Hey, you literally -have- to kick that puppy to continue the story"
"Okay, I guess."
"OH MY GOD HOW COULD YOU, YOU MONSTER"
Of course, these forced 'choices' are required, because barely anyone would actually chose to do it this way if they were given the choice. Most people aren't ♥♥♥♥ing psychopaths.
BUT the story requires you to act like a psychopath in order to make sense. This lead to me, trodding along acting fairly sensibly, then the game forcing me to do something horrid, then scolding me for doing that thing that it forced me to do.
There were one or two moments that actually let you choose what to do at some points, and when one of them went wrong, that was when I actually felt terrible, because it was MY choice that lead to this, and not the the plot railroading me.
I came out of this experience a bit unfufilled, really. I had acted sensibly, trying to make logical choices where I could; not killing civillians, trying to stop people from shooting me on sight, even going as far to flashbang soldiers to see if I could just get their attention for a moment. Of course, this doesn't work, because the plot demands that you kill people. Frankly, this gave me some cognitive dissonance, because, to me, it was abundantly clear that we were fighting the 'bad guys' for no reason, and yet there was no way of acting on this understanding. Then, later, the game shouts at you "WHY DID YOU KILL ALL THESE PEOPLE?" Gee, I don't know, because you didn't give me a choice?
I almost feel as though Spec Ops plays it's hand too soon, immediately trying to make you feel guilty for the people that you were forced to kill not ten seconds ago. This results in that cognitive dissonance I mentioned earlier. I know I'm fighting these guys for no reason, and that I just killed them in a super-not-okay way, but I had to, because the plot demands it.
I think the story would have made so much more sense had they acted more like a modern shooter, romanticising things like WP, or drones, biological weapons or something, and giving you the choice to use them, but tricking the players into doing so because why wouldn't you? It's way more fun, cooler and easier than having to shoot everyone yourself, right? Instead, the game actively dissuades the player from using WP, which detracts from what it's trying to do, which is trick players into becoming a psychopathic war criminal.
Compared to something like CoD or Battlefield, this game is definitely leagues ahead in terms of story. Maybe people who are really into the shooter genre might get more involved in this story, but me, coming from more RPG-esque games, where choice is commonplace, this just felt linear and annoying, because I knew what I wanted to do, but I just wasn't given the option. Still, points for trying to reverse some genre tropes and using your shooter knowledge against you.

First and foremost, this is an "adventure" game. No, not an "adventure game." In those you pick up a stick shaped like an "F" and use it to open an oversized lock on a chest full of bubblegum that you'll soon need to throw at some dogs so you can sneak past them to get to the... no. This is an "adventure" game. The game is an adventure.
A real adventure. Like when you take a shortcut through the wilderness, but end up further and further off path as you follow a stream, looking for a good place to cross.
A real adventure. Like when you go hiking in the mountains and get lost. Only to realize it'll be quicker to get back to civilization by continuing forward, rather than returning the way you came.
A real adventure. Like when you find yourself some place you've never been before, and with just a few tools, build yourself a makeshift home and defend it from zombies at night while exploring the world around you during the day. Eventually working your way underground into chasms filled with treasure and the occasional abandoned dwelling. Perhaps running across a giant beehive in an underground jungle or a buried pyramid under the desert. Finding your way deep into the darkness where the dead wander freely and mushrooms fluoresce brightly. Going deeper and deeper yet; to the point where the molten core of the planet lights up your eyes in a way only the sun had previously done.
The hard part of writing a review for a game like this is not spoiling too much while still letting people know how deep the game actually is. So much of what I enjoyed about my first playthrough of this game was discovery. Terraria might seem too simple when you first start out, and then possibly even overwhelming. But you'll be glad you spent effort to follow the stream or continue forward through the mountains.
There's weapons and magic, but you never pick a class, like warrior or archer. Due to the wide range of weapons, accessories, and armor choices you'll suddenly realize at some point, perhaps when surrounded by your minions, that you've specialized as a summoner. Or that you're a wizard, or explosives expert. Or perhaps you're some unique archer-warrior hybrid. But your choices and discoveries have slowly lead you into your role; you never chose it from a drop down list.
There's a multitude of biomes to discover. Each with their own unique enemies, and of course, epic boss fights. There's an incredible number of things you can do as you progress through the game. And while it plays fine single player, if you have a friend or two you can bring with you on this journey, you'll have that much more fun and they will thank you for it.
Sure, you can spend hours upon hours building elaborate castles decorated with furniture you've crafted or statues you've collected from around the world. You can reshape the terrain around you - spreading biomes you like or cutting down those you don't. You can even bring biomes up from deep in the earth and set up the perfect potion mushroom farm right next to your base. One of my favorite things to do is to use the wiring system to set elaborate boobie traps around my fortifications. But you don't have to do any of that to progress. It's really all up to you. Although even if none of that is "your thing," you might be so drawn in that you find yourself happily engaged in such activities.
And yes, a big part of the game is digging, but it's primarily a means of exploration. A means of reaching that next treasure chest, or cluster of gems. A means of reaching the next deep fissure in the earth. A great adventure awaits you.

Would I buy this again?  Probably not.  Would I pay the asking price ($8.99)?  Absolutely not.
We're all pretty familiar with the way that solitaire works.  The rules for this one -- you have to choose cards that are sequential, not necessarily alternating between red and black suits.  The sequence can move up or down -- for example, when you have a "four" exposed you can either play a three or a five on it.
You get bonus points for the number of cards you can play in sequence.  You also achieve bonus points for various combinations and permutations.
For me -- there are so many free versions of solitaire out there that this one isn't necessary.  Yes, there is an overarching plot -- you are a group of fantasy adventurers journeying through the dangerous countryside, fighting orcs and dragons as you go.  But truly the requirements from advancing one level to another are pretty arbitrary.  And anyone who plays solitaire knows that your ultimate success is largely based on luck.
Games based on luck, for me, begin to feel tedious.  Grinding is an unpleasant label you might apply to it.  Listen, I've had my fill of grinding after playing WoW for seven years.  The title "The Insane" was enough to convience me that I was wasting my life on sh*t that didn't matter.
So I get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at games that essentially become grinding episodes.  The graphics are cool, the sound is passable, and the game enjoyable enough.  It's just that I think that there are plenty of free versions out there that makes me conclude that this one isn't worth spending money on.
As always, readers should view what I write seen through the lens of the casual gamer -- that is, someone who has limited time due to family, a career, and soul-crushing student loan debt.
Save yourself $9.  Buy your kids some cookies at Target.

A good game, though not without flaws, and a decent follow up to the Hero of Kendrickstone.  If you enjoyed HoK, you'll probably enjoy this.
The beginning and ending are too brief.  If your character has a mentor from the first game, why do they let you head off on this adventure?  For my knight character, where's my horse and squire?  That sort of thing is left unanswered.  (I think the tendency for CoG games to start
hurts the game here too, but that's more of my personal preference.)  The ending is basically your character saying "Well that happened" and setting off back to Kendrickstone.  You do know -in gerenal terms- how things will shake out in Hallowford after you leave, but you don't get to see or hear about it so the ending doesn't provide much closure to me.  Hopefully the next game in the series will fill in the gaps, but it'll presumably be a while until we see it.
A lot of side-characters are hard to keep track of.  They get introduced very quickly, half of them you might miss talking too unless you go out of your way to do so, and the some of the ones I actually could remember exit the story with no notice.  Two of them are in-universe famous heros that your character recognizes, but the game doesn't tell us
exactly they are famous.  Maybe if I had talked to them more/whenever I had the chance I would find out, but that would've meant not doing others things that made more sense to me.  I also feel those particular two characters are only really here to be introduced for future games, as their actual roles in this story could've been filled by any random adventurers.
Replayability.  This is also where having played the previous game and importing a save file (or 7 in my case) really pays off.  My well educated wizard carrying a tome of eldritch horror had unique opportunities to find out information and act on it, but my famous warrior was instantly recognized by villagers and fellow adventuers alike.  Puzzles, fights, traps and information gathering all have different ways to succeed.  You also have plenty of opportunity to decide who you're working for and why.

Hero of Kendrickstone is LOADED with easy to understand decisions that affect the development of your character, which are completely lacking in this game. Batman: Arkham Origins is the origins or prequel story to the current generation of Batman games (Arkham Asylum, Arkham City). Similar to City, Origins is an open-world game action/beat-em-up featuring a main story line, many, many side quests/stories, and included in this game are events called "Crimes in Progress" allowing for a brawl and quick gain of exp. One of your 3 mastery trees requires completing these crimes in progress through each of the zones in Gotham City. Your mastery trees include your abilities to fight (Shadow Vigilante), your abilities to maneuver the open world (Gotham Protector), and take down set "Predator" rooms (Worst Nightmare). These trees are different from skill tress as you achieve only a single goal in each tree to advance to the next goal. Each achievement grants new abilities and/or experience. Your fighting abilities include use of gadgets, combo multipliers, landing critical strikes, and receiving good ratings on fights with minimum requirements. Your Gotham Protector tree includes many gliding, diving, and flying challenges, almost exclusively used in the open world. The last and highly challenging tree is your ability to act as a Predator in set rooms throughout the game where you're given multiple opportunities for take downs and major environmental advantages- floor grates, destructible walls, wall mounted vantage points. I always challenged myself to complete each of these rooms without ever being spotted :).
Let's start with the story- it was great! Truly enjoyable, felt genuine, and is really the shining star of the game. The boss fights were sometimes overly gimmicky and would require a few tries, which honestly was enjoyable to re-try sometimes because each death shot has a taunt from your current opponent, content you'd otherwise miss. Most the gadgets return from the previous games and the newly added "Shock Gloves" were by far my favorite. Activate these babies during a brawl and you not only are attacking in super speed, but riot shields, shock batons, and "enforcers" were open targets without having to set them up with a cape stun or some other mechanic.
Ok, now for the crappy part- the collectibles were a complete waste of time. You can't get many until the end of the game because of missing gadgets, and the audio clip rewards are only 10-60 seconds long- you can probably find them on YouTube.
There were many game breaking bugs (bugs which prevented advancement of the game). I experienced multiple CTDs (crash to desktop) while playing the game and the side mission boss fight with Deadshot required a restart when I did a beatdown on him and he ended up falling through the stairs and getting stuck there. I opened the door out of Penguin's Boiler Deck arena and was greeted with a completely black screen with only Batman's model visible, and he was constantly falling, like I had fallen through the ground, again a restart fixed it. Many brawls ended with 1 enemy following you around in a defensive stance, but you can't interact with him and he's actually beaten and knocked out somewhere. Combat was often sloppy and occasionally you'd find yourself with every enemy on the ground so your combo dies because it wasn't high enough to do a multi-ground takedown. Controls felt optimized for a controller (go figure).
The short recommendation- blast through the story of the game skipping collectibles. The side bosses are ok, but not critical. I enjoyed the main bulk of the game and would recommend playing it while skipping all the collectibles and side missions.
It lacks the greatness of the previous two installments, but that's not to say it isn't worth playing.

Let's start with the short review:
The third entry in the Arkham franchise is good, but it's also superfluous. If you're looking for more Arkham, then by all means don't skip this game. That's what I was looking for when I started Origins, and I wasn't disappointed. I consider this game superfluous because it really doesn't do anything better than Arkham City. Indeed, in some cases it's pretty lacking.
And now for the long review:
The story to Arkham Origins is...well I'll be vague here. There's a bounty on the Dark Knight's head and eight villains are looking to collect. It's up to the player to put a stop to this nonsense and save the day. The pacing and story are a bit uneven, with a number of segments feeling like they're not really going anywhere. There's a distinct lack of great set-pieces, those moments that really define the Batman experience. That's not to say there isn't any, but they tend to get clumped together. It's like wow give me a chance to breathe here. There are even a couple objectives that seem to exist, solely to make sure Batman is in a particular place, so it doesn't break the next objective. Still the story definitely has its moments, the characters are well-done, and by the end I had a good sense of what WB Montreal was going for with the plot.
Next up there is the city. On one hand I like that unlike Arkham City, Gotham doesn't have The Riddler's ????? fetish on display around every corner. His trademark riddles are around, but they blend in a bit better with the surroundings. It's less guady, which counts for a lot. There are some nice details throughout the city. Overall though I can't say I'm too fond of it. Arkham City's..uh...city is more stylized, which is understandable since its villainous inhabitants have dressed it up to fit their personality. Still, I was expecting something a bit more gothic and ornate. There are elements of that and yet sometimes the city can look just plain. Aside from the aesthetics, Arkham City simply had a better design and "flow" to it. It felt like more time was spent creating a slice of Gotham that the player could really move around in. Origins on the other hand, can feel just a little bit clunky.
Then there is the combat. The Arkham games are divided into two styles of action. There are the melee-oriented "Vigilante" brawls and the stealthy "Predator" rooms. The goal is typically to defeat all the bad guys, with better experience rewards doled out to stylish players who take advantage of Batman's numerous abilities and gadgets. WB Montreal has done a fine job with both styles. In some cases the brawls aren't quite as tight, and I've had some odd dropped combos, but nothing really stands out as poor. Predator encounters are pretty much 1:1 with the previous Arkham games. There are also the occasional boss-fights, which can take elements from the core styles, or be a little unique.
Now then, the big complaint I have with Origins is that they didn't really add anything new. There are a handful of new gadgets for handling Batman's foes, but nothing really inventive. There's the shock gloves sure, but they're ridiculously strong. They chew through every possible defense and add to the combo multiplier at a rapid rate. As fans are well aware, successful vigilante is constantly changing things up, using all of Batman's maneuvers, and keeping a flawless combo going. The gloves simplify things a bit too much. Batman also gets a few new gadgets for his predator encounters, including the ability to string up three criminals to gargoyles from a safe distance. They're not nearly as overpowered, but I have to restrain myself just a bit more to keep things from getting too easy.
Of course this is all balanced by the bad guys getting a bunch of new equipment....right? Oh, oh no. This is where the lack of fresh content sticks out. There really aren't any new types of bad guys, nor are any new methods developed to help them spot Batman when he's stalking them. Everyone is still wielding bats or pipes, late-game guys get stun batons, and it's certain they'll get the bright idea to carry riot shields or car doors around. The combat is still good, but it's just more of the same.
This feeling of sameness extends to other moments in Arkham Origins. An encounter with Deadshot is oddly reminiscent of the final battle between Catwoman and Two-face, the boss-fight with Firefly is eerily similar to the one with Poison Ivy back in Arkham Asylum. As these battles play out I get that familiarity that really shouldn't be there. It's difficult to feel that sense of accomplishment when there's a little voice in the back of my brain saying "What are you celebrating about? You've done this before." The names and locations change, but too many other elements don't.
As far as concerns the rest of Arkham Origins content. There is the usual collection of vigilante and predator challenge maps, additional playable characters, and...multiplayer? I'll be brutally honest here, I played one multiplayer match, and that was it. What can I say? I'm not much of a competitive MP person. The multiplayer seems to be retaining its popularity well, as I got into a full match within seconds of starting up. Honestly I'd be satisfied with something a bit more simple and direct, Batman & Robin teaming up to put the hurt on some thugs. Maybe there could be some more advanced vigilante and predator maps to keep things balanced.
All in all, despite Arkham Origins not really doing anything new or improving on its predecessors, I still recommend it. Why? Simply because it's more Arkham. Yes, really, that's absolutely it. Am I shallow or what? Rocksteady struck gold when they developed Arkham Asylum. Now they have a model that can be applied to any and all future Batman games and I'm likely to eat it up everytime. As long as the quality remains at moderately-high level I'll remain a fan. Although I hope that with Rocksteady developing the next game, they include a slew of fresh game-design changes and additions. If the fifth Arkham game turns out to be a retread, I hope it's at least a retread of Arkham Knight and not Arkham City.

With its distinct visual style and humorous dialogue, Borderlands 2 is an absolute joy to play! Equipment, level progression, and skill perks are all expertly balanced from start to end, and a wide variety of weapons, enemy types, and environments keep gameplay mixed up and interesting.
On the first playthrough.
This is not a bad thing except the game will eventually come to an end later or sooner depending on your level of skill, at which point you'll be faced with a choice... to start over or go New Game+.
With multiple job classes, starting a new game isn't bad but the storyline remains static. By the fourth or sixth (depending on if you got the DLCs or not) playthrough, even the most enthusiastic gamer might start feeling tedium creeping around the edges of the same jokes that you swore were so witty the first time around (and they were!).
Problems really start to arise on the New Game+ option, however, for those that are attempting to go for 100% completion. The issue above still arises (in that, you'll need to start the game over and make your way through the whole story multiple times), but it's compounded by the fact that the enemy difficulty begins to outpace your character strength. By the end-end game, and even kitted with the most powerful equipment, the most basic enemies will pose a serious threat to life and limb and bosses will soak up tens of thousands of rounds, usually far in excess of the amount of ammunition you can carry into the fight.
The only solution is to utilize very specific skill and gear combinations that enjoy stacking and complimentary effects. Normally this wouldn't be much of an issue except that the gear required is at this point nigh impossibly difficult to acquire and, second, that a primary joy of Borderlands 2 was the freedom to use the weapons that had the right "feel". That goes out the window in the end-end-game, where raw damage output and effects bordering on broken or glitched become necessary to survive.
But it's still great fun, who am I kidding? Give it a go, play it through, but don't try to really complete the game without knowing what's in store.

Yager Development has created art. Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter that takes so many unique directions that it is a wonder 2K approved it. The game takes place in Dubai after being destroyed by sandstorms (rather than war) and the city is substantially distinctive from other Middle Eastern locales frequented in military shooters. Dubai is full of giant skyscrapers with beautiful interiors and an insane amount of sand thanks to the sandstorms. The enemy is a welcome change because it is not the typical terrorist cell or communist army. The combat is generic but that is by design – it is meant to lure you into thinking you are playing an average war game. Whether or not that is a poor excuse, Spec Ops: The Line is still fun. The only problem I had was that the difference between weapons felt scarce; I didn’t feel obligated to pick up a new weapon because the starting weapon sufficed and ammo boxes seemed to be around every corner. Of course, what makes this game so notorious is the narrative. I do not want to spoil anything so just take my word for it: it is beyond fantastic. I was impressed with the characters, how they change over the course of the game and how that was reflected in gameplay. Executions become more brutal and the characters angrily yell when confirming a kill rather than the calm “enemy neutralized” you hear in the beginning hours of the game. As for performance it ran well on my PC and I do not recall any specific performance or graphical issues. I did not even bother with multiplayer and neither should you. Even the developers thought it was a “cancerous growth”. If you are looking for a fun military shooter to play with friends – this isn’t for you. Spec Ops: The Line is less of a game and more of an experience.
I paid $6 for Spec Ops: The Line during a sale in June 2014.

I came into Spec Ops expecting something great behind the bland gameplay.
The internet told me all about how this game made them see war from a new perspective.
Yet at the end of my playthrough I sat in my room thinking about how much time I wasted on this game. The game wants introduce the idea of "What if you are the bad guy?" to it's players, but I've thought about this plenty of times before. This entire Heart of Darkness remake taught me absolutely nothing that I didn't already know.
From the moment I started playing I held hope that the game would redeem itself, but it never did (other than the Deep Purple section). Even when I was given the "choice" to fire white phosphorous into a crowd of "enemies" I felt underwhelmed. Especially when the game tried to guilt trip me for doing what it told me to do. It's not like other games haven't told me to commit horrible acts before.
I'm not suggesting the story is bad at all. For me it's just nothing new, but I can see the effect it might have on someone who's never thought of the ideas that it has to offer.

Everquest II is the sequel of an amazing game. Your adventures start in the world of Norrath. You take part in various quests as an adventurer or a tradeskiller, while unveiling mysteries lost in time, exploring places that only myth has referred to, and battling creatures you would never have imagined that you could handle. Filled with rich, extremely inspired lore, Everquest 2 is the among the best for gamers who like to live a game like reading a novel, or watching a movie, and taking part in it. It is a unique mmorpg amongst the thousands of its kind, with not too high pc requirements, simple but beautiful graphics and a vast variety of content, equipment and adventure-wise.
The moon has now crushed on Norrath, dividing it into different shattered islands.
Sentinel's Fate: Strange events open up portals to the long lost land of Ultera.
Age of Discovery: Gnomish pirates sail on their legendary ship, the Icebreaker, and discover Velious, a chuck of the first land (something like the real Pangaia) that existed before the shattering.
Chains of Eternity: Inbalance occurs between Ethernere, the land where the dead go before they face judgement from their gods, and Norrath, the land of the living.
Tears of Veeshan: A prismatic dragon named Kerafyrm, child of fire and ice, takes advantage of his power to conquer the 2 mightiest strongholds of Norrath: Freeport, head of the evil empire, and Qeynos, throne to the good kings and queens, as he challenges the authority of the dragons and their king Lord Yelinak in Skyshrine, the land of dragonkind.
Will you aid the people of this fantasy world to live through these otherwordly challenges or exploit the chaos to your own benefit?
I recommend you play this game if you have no life and no family to care for.

Where do I get off not recommending a game I've played for 240 hours... ??
To be clear, there's plenty to like about Prison Architect. It's rated "Very Positive" for a reason, so obviously you won't be throwing your money away if you purchase it.
So my cavaet here is, if, like -me-, you want a real challenge, you want to have to work hard with your design in order to prevent prisoners escaping, then prison architect isn't really what you are looking for. It's a good simulation, but not really a game in that sense.
The initial concept was super exciting. I got in on early access and started playing, and looked forward to fresh updates each month. I'd try out different base designs, figure out the mechanics, and then do it again when it was updated.
But over time I started to notice a pattern. The basic framework already in place, most updates involved "features", like new room types, that fleshed out what you could do. But I never felt that the game became much more challenging from then on.
I was waiting for staff to be given personalities, like sim hospital. Maybe some of them secretly being corrupt and passing on keys and supplies. I was hoping that prisoners would work together in forming their escape plans, maybe one group making a distraction while another made a break for it. I was hoping that we would get an AI which could analyze the points of entry and exit, figure out what weakenesses existed, and try and exploit those if at all possible.
Thats a tricky thing to do maybe. And to be clear, what the game -does- do, it does pretty darn well. But it's not ultimately what I was hoping for, so it has left me disappointed.

UPDATE:
As of March 2017 the game had been updated a bit since when I first wrote this review, so I thought I would jump back in and see if I could now recommend it. I played with a new prison for a few hours to see if my original issues with the game still held.
Unfortunately it was much as I expected. While there are a bunch of nice new features, the core of the game remains an unchallenging sandbox where it is almost impossible to reach any kind of fail state.
Seeking a challenge, I tried the following setup and house rules.
1. Small map. No trees for selling.
2. No grants. No workshops. The only money I would have is what I started with, and what I would be paid for looking after prisoners.
3. Permanent intake. As per intial settings, that means mostly medium sec, a few min sec. Inevitably you end up with a few people reclassed as max sec after they turn out to be crazed murders. So basically a nice mixture. 10-16 or so per day.
I hoped that at least with these conditions, I could force myself into enough of a challenge that my puzzle solving brain could have some fun. At the very least, when it all went down in flames it would be fun to watch....
Well, that was the idea. 18 days in, I've hit a population of nearly 200, and have a daily income of 11 thousand. Then I also have an extra 5-8k per day bonus when the next batch of prisoners come. It looks likely I could easily continue on in this fashion indefinitely, so I quit in disappointment. No challenge here, even using harsh house rules.
What happened? Basically, I kept the prisoners indefinitely in holding cells. You stuff a few dozen bunk beds in a single room, add some toilets and showers, and voila, you can stuff a hundred prisoners in there, no problem. As the prisoners can sleep when tired in their free time, it doesn't really matter even if you are hot-seating them. The prisoner to bed ratio was maybe 4 to 1. The shower and toilet ratios far worse. Without the need to build cells for your prisoners, you really don't have much in the way of expenses. You just hire a new guard every day, a new cook ever other day, and here and there build extra beds and stoves. Now and then you make a new room to house more people, or you expand on the canteen. It was mind numbingly simple.
Through it all I never had a single real riot. Snitchers were getting killed at a rate of one per day or so, but that had no real negative repercussions, so I didn't mind.
Two things were very clear.
1. The game remains easy to exploit. And without even trying very hard. Prisoners simply shouldn't accept me keeping them in holding cells indefinitely without getting very angry. However they just don't care. This means the game is fundamentally broken, as it makes many other features redundant. Cells? Not needed. Hence money, abundant. And workshops? Also not needed at all. Grants? Unnecessary.
2. Most other game features are also entirely unnecessary as far as keeping your prison going is concerned. Prisoners didn't care that I give them pretty much nothing in terms of services/education/family acces etc. etc. etc. You just put them in a box, give them food, beds, some clothing, heat, etc. and thats it. The only reason to have half of the features of the game (libraries, stores, classrooms, etc. etc. etc.) is for the heck of it. Because you want a better score etc.
So, my original problem with Prison Architect remains. It's fine as a sandbox to mess around in, I guess. But it isn't much of a game. You can't really lose unless you massively screw things up, and over half the features aren't technically necessary. By comparison, you can't finish a map in Theme Hospital without carefully and judiciously using all the rooms avaliable to you. You have to be clever to win at Theme Hospital. Prison Architect is maybe more like keeping some gerbils, and giving them some wheels to run in, and little plastic houses, and other fun little decorations for your own amusement. That's fine I guess, but it's not a game.
Losing is fun, as they say at Bay12. But the opposite is also true.

To completely finish story and everything game has to offer, you may reach up to 50 hours or longer. Cinematics are very enjoyable. Story has surprising events, twists & dramatic ending. You also have big ammount of side missions which often reward with car upgrades.
Gameplay off story is pretty much reducing threat level in regions - you do that by destroying camps, removing snipers & towers in the region, fighting convoys or do a race. Off mission rewards is mostly scrap, which you use to upgrade max & your car. To fully upgrade everything you will need to collect 25000+ scrap which is very long process. Getting all this scrap comes with exploration where you often find not only project parts (which you can use to upgrade friendly camps and get some perks) but also stunning sceneries or camp creations.
Mad Max is open world, where you spend most gameplay off missions (unless you rush the game). Slowly upgrading and weaponizing car is necessary to finish late-story missions, but i think you could go through whole campaign with only half the upgrades ive done. Another fun level adds various car weapons, you can get - my favourite is harpoon that you get early in the game to enjoy. While you are not in car, even tho you have shotgun always with you, your main weapon will always be fists. Fighting is decent, i found it especially hard in the beginning, but as i got used to it, i am often able to fight off everyone without getting hit now... Max's skill upgrades adds some extra moves you can perform during fights. Other upgrades improve fist damage, damage resistance or shotgun upgrades...
+ Flawless optimization

+ Huge map and lot of exploration
+ Best purchase for its price (especially on sales where i got it for 5€)

- May get a bit grindy unless you enjoy a lot of exploring for small rewards.

Super Meat Boy (for those who don't know) is an exciting, and violent 3rd person platformer. It is very simple when it comes to world 1, but once you get to world 2; there is no mercy! It does become difficult, but has the appropriate charm to keep me playing. Would I recommend this? If you're a platformer junky like I am:
DEFINITELY!
It will surely provide a challenge like no other!

Super Meat Boy.  The one and only platforming game I've played in the last two years, and it's very easy to explain why. It's good. In fact it's more than good because it's the most excellently executed 2D platformer since Super Mario World. In fact I'm going to say something about that. Everything in this game is a modern take on the retro style of 2D platform games, but as much as it takes from that time long ago, it doesn't completely thrive off of that. It is its own game too.
The gameplay is by far the first and foremost reason why I played this for two years.The controls are incredibly well done, because I never have to worry about something in the game screwing me over (except occasional lag spikes that can't be helped, I blame that it was meant to be on Flash). Every level is treated like a puzzle, and at points, obstacles in a level are treated as a puzzle. It is at times difficult to solve but never unsolvable. And through that you get into the thought process that it will be possible to beat this level as long as I keep trying new strategies. Which makes it addicting as hell, which I love.
The story is simple, but it allows you to fill in the blanks like most games back in the old days. I'm sure they had this in mind the whole time they were making it, and of course it shows through all of the references to older games it makes in easy and not so easy to reach places. The references range from obvious to obscure, but either way you'll at least find a thing or two you recognize.
The music will take you back just like the story does, but it's so well modernized that you wonder to yourself every now and again if you've heard this music before. You haven't, and it gives the game its own originality and atmosphere that you won't find in another game. Danny Baranowsky, the composer for Super Meat Boy is a legend, and this soundtrack will feel like you're going through one or that you are one yourself. That's one impactful soundtrack if you ask me.

There's plenty to be said against this game, but it's still a thumbs-up game for me.  Yes, it's a step backwards for the series, it has some serious unpatched bugs, and it's generally an unworthy followup to its two predecessors.  But keep in mind that Arkham Asylum and Arkham City were legendarily good games; they left plenty of space for the sequel to be inferior without being downright bad.
Arkham Origins feels primarily like a clumsier, less polished attempt to recreate Arkham City, and I could rhyme off at length the ways in which it fails to measure up to City, but they're already well known.  The critical matter is that Origins is still fun.  Not as fun as City, and sometimes the glitches get irksome, but still fun.  I played all the way through to end, and still liked it enough to want more.
Bottom line; if you haven't played any of the series, start with the older and better ones.  But if you've fallen in love with the amazing gameplay of the series, Origins is still enjoyable.  It can help tide you over until the release of Arkham Knight.  And it's even a little endearing when Batman tries to swoop dramatically off a rooftop, only to have his transition-to-glide animation glitch out, causing him to flap his way down the street like a demented sparrow.

The Good
- Amazing fighting mechanics
- Great gameplay
- Great graphics
- Good all around & fun game
The Bad
- Suffers from a lack of story selection (Explained in the final paragraph)
- Tends to become monotonous
Final Verdict
I would definatly say get the game on offer (a common feature in most of my reviews). The Batman Arkham series has alway been good but this one has sufferd from, someting I call, industrialisation. My favourite part of the game is the fighting mechanic. It has been a fantastic addition to the Arkham series and has only improved. Easy to learn yet difficult to master. But once mastered it feels great to be able to use it properly (my highest combo is 179 or 231 on Arkham City).
From here I'll only go over the bad bits as the good are all fairly self explanatory after the mechanics. I said that BAO suffers from a lack of story selection, what I mean by that is the game just feels......messy. It has far to many villans at a time, 8 to be exact. It introduces all of the familiar villans from the older Arkham series but fails to explain how or what the new ones do (bar 3-4 of them). Don't get me wrong, they all have a purpose in the story and don't spoil it in any way at all. But when you are freely roaming the city, it is as though the developes have added them in to just to be able to put extra side missions in. That is what I mean by the game becoming monotonous. But would I recommend this game, Hell yes! Being honest, I have been nit-picking over the game to give you a good review, it's just that good. A solid 9.5/10.
