is a unique RPG with a cool story behind, although it takes you the whole game to fully understand it.
Unlike most RPGs, on your monster encounters you'll have the option to defeat them by other means than fighting. I followed a neutral path on my gameplay, but you can either go on the genocide or pacifist path, and from what I've read, the story unfolds differently on those three paths. So you basically get three storylines for the price of one. Nice, isn't it?
Its battle system has minigames depending on the monster you're battling against, so I saw myself dying several times, giving up and opening the game again in less than ten minutes 'cause I was really eager to find out how the story ended. It's funny and nice how the struggle filled me with... DETERMINATION.
Puzzles are something they've done well in this game. They are not too hard (none will take you more than two or three attempts to get through), but they still force you to pay attention to details and think a little.
Everything is a surprise in the game, and it has little jokes that made me smile every now and then (like the skeletons and their fonts and personalities - as soon as you play it, you'll understand what I mean).
Another pro that I should write here is that people seem to really like its soundtrack but I personally haven't paid much attention to it, to be honest.
I also enjoyed a lot that the game has some LGBT characters and none of them were stereotyped. You couldn't tell, most of the times, if they were female or male by how they looked, you had to pay attention to their pronouns. This is something I usually value in a game so kudos to you, tobyfox!
As I said, I have finished it on the neutral path and I have no interest on playing it again to see how the genocide or the pacifist routes work. This might be due to the lack of achievements and to how the battles were painful at times (you basically play a minigame to avoid damage, and sometimes they are really hard and repetitive, which ended up being a little bit boring).
I wish I knew better that I could've chosen a different path at the beginning. After reading the game description I thought "hey, I'm gonna go through this without killing anyone, so this will be a really different RPG" but sometimes I felt like I had no option other than fighting (bosses, mostly) and I found out later that I could've been more of a pacifist. I'm not unhappy with the neutral route, though, I just wish I hadn't played it that blindly.
succeeds at being different from most of the games you know, and you'll probably like it once you get through the first one or two hours, but it can be painful at times and you won't find out everything it has to offer unless you fall in love with it (which didn't happen to me, sadly).

Tables come in a wide variety of materials, shapes, and heights dependent upon their origin, style, and intended use. Most tables are composed of a flat surface and a base with one or more supports (legs). A table with a single, central foot is a pedestal table. Long tables often have extra legs for support.
Table tops can be in virtually any shape, although rectangular, square, round (e.g., the round table), and oval tops are the most frequent. Others have higher surfaces for personal use while either standing or sitting on a tall stool.
Many tables have tops that can be adjusted to change their height, position, shape or size, either with foldable extensions or sliding parts that can alter the shape of the top. Some tables are entirely foldable for easy transportation, e.g., camping. Small tables in trains and aircraft may be fixed or foldable, although they are sometimes considered as simply convenient shelves rather than tables.

I love Batman games in general I am going to give my review of the game.
So first of all let’s start with the game mechanics, They are really good and super responsive I have to say that, but there are times when it feels like its requesting more commands and does extra punches or use baterangs or sometimes even change gadgets unwillingly. The controls are easy to use and very customizable indeed. You can have more than one button that executes the same control and/or ability.
Now let’s talk about the A.I thugs and villains. Thy need MAJOR bug fixes some may just keep running straight into the wall and disappear, there was one time where I lost a missions and I restarted and all the thugs I had to knockout just vanished, NOT COOL! I came here for a challenge I'm playing on the hardest difficulty and I'm finding it too easy. I would have to give the mechanics a 7/10.
Let’s talk about the music. I really like the music I mean I do. There's just one problem, the soundtrack is just too short only around about three-four hours. Then it can get really annoying and repetitive. I would suggest make a DLC soundtrack like most games do I don't care if it's from the previous Batman Arkham games, I personally think music from Arkham city would be a great addition! Until that happens I give it an 8/10.
Onto the story line. The story is absolutely MARVOLOUS! I love it, great acting, great modeling, and the music just fits right in, it really does put you into suspense and makes you want to finish the game just to experience the story. I also love the side missions, how you learn more about Enigma, Anarchy, The Penguins A.K.A Cobble pot, is just fascinating. I give it a 10/10.
The upgrade system. This is where it got really disappointing, I thought there would be a bunch more. It's too easy to level up and when I got the last few upgrades I was sad because I couldn't lvl up any higher. I think it would have been better with more customization and at least thirty+ upgrades to unlock. I give this a 6/10.
The map. I personally don't think you can get the map wrong and I mean any game shouldn't, this is where it bothers me a lot. There are some times where I am in in area and it shows me somewhere in the middle of the ocean. I have to say there are long periods of time where I have to wait while I use the Batwing for fast travel I had to wait for three minutes one time! I give this a 9/10.
Multiplayer. All I have to say is that it sucks! no one is on, you have to wait a good five minutes for a full lobby, but I do have to say the idea was good where two people are randomly selected to be Batman and/or Robin, and the rest gets to choose to be either in Joker's crew or Bane's. I give it a 4/10.
The last thing I'm going to talk about are the DLC's, there are some amazing DLC's to get for this game, they are incredible fun and entertaining adds a whole new level of gameplay. I love the challenge maps, skin packs from previous games, different characters to play as all of that. I give it a 10/10.
Overall I do think it's a good Batman game to own, but wait till it's on sale next summer because I got it with all the DLC's for 13$ even though normal price is 87$ I did the math. It's not worth all that money. I will give my overall impression the game deserves a 7/10.

It's not often that a shooter game leaves you feeling gut punched at the end of the story.
When you shoot down enemy soldiers, some of them aren't quite dead and lie on the floor squirming or screaming in agony. Several times I found myself putting an extra bullet in them.
At first I told myself it was out of mercy.
Later I realised it was because watching them crawl away feebly attempting to draw breath through destroyed lungs made me deeply uncomfortable. This typifies Spec Ops: The Line perfectly.
The game is not so much about butter-smooth mechanics or mowing down hordes of enemies, but rather about inviting you to question your decisions, to face the consequences of violence and to think about what it means to leave a trail of corpses like in so many video games before. Of course, we're talking about a videogame, an entertainment product where Hollywood brings out no end of violent films every year; it's fair to say humanity still enjoys violence as entertainment, although we've moved away from slaves fighting lions and have embraced technological substitution to feed our thirst for excitement.
Spec Ops: The Line is no different, where you're faced with wave after wave of enemies to kill and creative ways to dispatch your foes into the afterlife. In this sense violence is glorified, with your character and his teammates calling out succesful kills in increasingly excited tones, and with time slowing down when you hit a headshot allowing you to admire your handiwork as the man who was trying to kill you and your friends drops to the floor in a limp heap. At the same time the cost of warfare is apparent, with your character looking increasingly harrowed and beaten up as the story progresses.
Other reviews have pointed out the apparent hypocrisy in this construct - to present an exposition of violence meant to be enjoyed whilst simultaneously berating the consequences and, by proxy, the player's enjoyment of said violence. This wasn't a concern for me - I was far too busy both enjoying and worrying about the feeling of discomfort I got every time I shot another man down.
The critical look at violence and the way it's juxtaposed with wave after wave of bad guys for you to kill means Spec Ops: The Line is a sublime mix of stereotypical shooter game combat and a deep discomfort that only grows as the story progresses.
Recomended.

Cosmochoria is loosely based on the principles of 4X strategy games, while being a basic rougelite twin-stick shooter. It takes some time to get into the game, since story and gameplay aren't quite clear in the beginning. After surviving the chaos however, a big picture emerges through exploring the world and finding scattered bits of lore.
At first, there seems to be no other purpose than hopping from planet to planet and restoring them to full health by nurturing flora. Enemy aliens need to be eradicated in the process and after a certain amount of recovered planets, boss aliens spawn and overrun the player. Beating these bosses can be hard initially, but once the tactics are set and permanent upgrades from the store are bought, they become a pushover. These permanent upgrades are extremely beneficial for the general enjoyment of the game, providing substantial quality of life and combat enhancements. Still, the increasing amount of enemies keeps the gameplay quick and demanding.
Full of wisdom and nonsense, cutesy graphics and somewhat psychedelic music, Cosmochoria's impact is hard to pin down. It's a mix of a cheerful, relaxing experience and unremitting arcade gameplay. If the mood is right, it's quite fun.

This game delivers in terms of art and music. Some of the most beautiful graphics and art I've seen in a game, and the accompanying score is some of the best music I've heard written for a game resulting in a beautiful game with absolutely gorgeous music. The mechanics of the game is implemented pretty nicely. You jump through the air, jump off of projectiles before travelling through a tunnel of spikes. Everything becomes fluid and multiple skills are used in succession. This game has a tonne of secrets which requires a lot of exploring (and backtracking which can get annoying). Numerous skills (with Bash being a favourite of mine) can be obtained and need to be used in order to beat a lot of the areas. Despite all this, there are some things that are left to be desired. The difficulty spike means that the game can get difficult quicker than other games like this, which will test one's patience. The story, while emotional, is not anything special. The combat isn't as complex and developed (such as the combat system in Dust), instead focusing on platforming and puzzles (with a few time-trials). This means that if your looking for a tear-jerking story and/or intense action, you'll be disappointed.
If you want a story-rich game or a combat intensive game, this probably isn't the game you're looking for. However, if you want a game that looks stunning, has incredible music and/or challenging platforming, this is the game you're looking for.

A well blended and deep FPS-RPG mix. Tons of weapons, enemies, missions, and mods available to alter your gameplay experience or make you feel like a badass. Not many of this kind can say the same thing...at least to my knowledge.

You can't help but like and root for them against oppressive, evil, hilarious, handsom "Handsom Jack". So, the story might not be Bioshock ambitious with social commentary but the enteraining, quirky characters supported the story well.
The game itself never gets stale because not all weapons and enemies are created equal. And sometimes you have to make situational decisions about what to buy/discard to tackle certain enemies. Not only that, you have to decide how to best upgrade your character as you level up. For example, you have a special action skill at level 5 that can assist in mowing down enemies. After that, do you continue upgrading that or do you go for more survivability? The point is: it's not a game with the same sh** over and over again and (sometimes) tough decisions must be made.
Recommended to anyone into the FPS genre or the like.

My Review of the Full Steam Version of Euro Truck Simulator 2
Overview:
Pros :
-	Acceptable and quite realistic graphical fidelity
-	Incredibly relaxing and realistic gameplay
-	A humongous map size with expansions adding to it as well
Cons :
-	AI keeps on crashing into me for no reason(seems only to happen with Peugeots)
-	I have to explain to people why I have nothing better to do than drive virtual trucks around all day
See My Full Review Below:
At the time of the writing of this review, my Steam Library tells me that I’ve pumped approximately 14 hours into ETS 2, and 5 hours is the minimum cut off point for the amount of time I spend in a game before writing a review.
ETS 2 is a game about driving trucks around the entirety of Europe, earning money to build up your empire of trucks to conquer the industry with. At first I was skeptical about how the gameplay would be enjoyable, and not monotonous and boring, but now I realise that it is the main point of the game. I cannot tell you just how relaxing it is to come home after a hard day’s work, to sit down by my desk, sink into my chair, boot up ETS 2 and just drive for an hour or two. What makes this even more palatable is the addition of the radio system, whereby which you can put music on your PC into the game’s built in sound system. As I play without headphones in this game(I use a whole room surround sound setup), I feel that I can enjoy music that I played to death years ago once again, which is so fundamentally pleasing to my soul that it is worth the entire game on its own.
In regards to the gameplay, I have to point out that I have never driven before, let alone a truck, and therefore do not know what it feels like to drive one of the things. However, I should say that when a trailer is attached, the driving mechanics feel weighted and heavy, with me needing to swing out into corners with a lot of momentum to get around some bends. However, with my DualShock 4 in hand, it feels easy to pull off accurate turns, and the vibration allows me to feel the road beneath the truck. The control scheme features dead-zones and wheel support, and I would recommend not using a keyboard and mouse with the game as they do not provide much in the way of accurate turning.
A minor issue is the finicky AI system, which has a tendency to crash into you when taking a turn. For example, I pull out into the bend after waiting for all the traffic to stop and let me through, and a car or van(usually a Peugeot) slams into the side of my trailer(usually filled with noxious chemicals or acid). This is a minor issue with how the AI recognises the player and could be easily fixed by linking all the AI to one mind which stops before the player who is turning. The other issue is of a social matter and will only apply to some people, however, I am often quizzed on why I choose to spend my time in a virtual job that brings in no real income and ‘wastes time’. To them I have to say, “It brings me enjoyment”, and when you look at it in the scheme of things it does seem a little odd!
Overall, I recommend that you purchase Euro Truck Simulator 2 as it provides a relaxing and appealing experience. There is a free demo I recommend you try first, as it is quite lenient until you level up beyond a certain point. Just make sure that you know what you have to say when people ask you, “But what’s the point?”
My Hardware Specs:
-	CPU : AMD 5800K
-	GPU : EVGA Nvidia GTX 960 SC 4GB
-	RAM : 8GB of some random stock Kingston RAM
-	Motherboard : ASUS A-78M
-	Storage : Some kind of Toshiba HDD

If someone had ever told me that I would enjoy playing a game that entailed "driving" around Europe delivering cargo to various cities I would have laughed in their faces. However I am glad to say that no one ever said that to me thus I do not have to admit to anyone that they were right and I was wrong.
This game is brilliant! The scope is amazing, the models used are so smooth and the economic model used seems pretty well thought out. With the need for fuel, rest, (I assume the rest periods are aslo used to make use of coffee and toiltes!), and a lot of other traffic on the roads to make it a nice challenge, the game has been so well thought out. My only slight complaint is that some of the DLC might not qualify, in my mind, as DLC that needs to be paid for. Not the regions additions, for example the Scandanavia addon is well worth it. It's the things like wheel colours and cabin accessories. That said however, these sorts of things are not that expensive and by not having them you are not losing out at all.
The cargoes are very well thought out, I have added the DLC that adds addition cargo types; for instance I have recently delivered a helicopter, a digger, used plastic packing and empty pallets. Each item you are delivering is mounted on a suitable trailer and each seems to model a suitable weight with the cruise control struggling on hills with a heavy load.
The only downside, as far as I can tell, is the way that it is so hard to stop! (Playing that is, not the braking system on the trucks).
There is a huge user base with a multiplayer version available for free. Once you have played for a short while you will be hooked. There's even a free demo available. Go for it. You know you want to find out how anyone can be stupid enough to enjoy a game that has you driving a lorry.
By the way, the horn is very weak sounding. However, the airhorn, key N, is so much more rewarding. :-)
Better get back to it now, those Atlantic cod fillets wont deliver themselves.

Euro Truck simulator 2 runs perfectly on my mid-range laptop, Lenovo G40-80 (Windows 10, Intel Core i7-5500M, 4GB RAM, integrated graphics. The trucks are real and it simulates almost everyting in the trucks (e.g lights, steering, even when the air pressure is low. Gameplay is very stable.

You can drive like a Total Maniac in this game and still have lots of fun! I'm not entirely sure this game includes a difficulty level, but the overall penalties such as Speeding Infractions and Running Red Lights only take out about 5-10% of your paycheck. The game itself has such an amazingly calm and beautiful scenery in contrast to my driving. Cutting the AI off with my trailer is so damn funny. Also, I accidentally took a Highway Exit Loop at about 80KM/H (double the speed limit) and ended up flipping over my trailer. I was in tears laughing for a good 5 minutes while I had to call a service center to tow me away. However, I wouldn't advise you to destroy your truck so quickly because repair costs and maintenance are similar to that of a Second-hand Used German Luxury Sedan notorious for being filled with "reliable" electronics.
Overall, this is a great game if even if you're used to driving as fast as possible in other racing games. This might not be a racing game, but it sure as hell can be one. The in-game Radio Streaming services help set the mood, for whenever I feel like enjoying the drive, or when I need to finish my stupid delivery as fast as possible.
TL;DR: If BMW made Trucks, my driving record would reflect that.

This game was a pleasant surprise coming off of the mediocre Hitman Absolution. To explain, one of the largest issues I had with Absolution was the issue of how linear the experience felt. Areas to kill targets felt too small and cramped to be deemed enjoyable and the variety of kills just wasn't there for me. This game despite the episodic structure which initially made me turn away from it is a fantastic Hitman game and Stealth game as a whole. The maps are extremely open and the amount of content on display makes me still find new things on 5th and 6th runs of the maps. The main downsides of the game are the always online aspects of it which essentially only give you a fragment of the experience if you are not online and the lack of voice actors who fit the place you are. I speculate that the voice acting issue it a result of lacking the budget to pay voice actors to make the areas more authentic, instead focusing on placing those funds into map design. I can't say I disagree with the decision as one is for immersions sake and one is for replayability. I still feel that despite these flaws, fans of stealth games or the prior Hitman games who were turned off by Absolutions flaws should make this a must own. I think it is a diservice to deny oneself this game if you are interested in the social stealth aspect of the Hitman series.
TLDR: This game is phenominal despite certain flaws mentioned above. It's a great return to form and in my opinion on the short list for game of the year due to the sheer amount of content and fun I have had with it in just two weeks. I will be playing this game for quite some time and I feel it is a must have for stealth fans.

(I don't recommend this game. I somewhat-recommend it. There is no in between for Steam reviews, but that is exactly how I feel with this title.)
My initial thoughts on this game were overwhelmingly negative; I found myself uninstalling it after 8 grueling hours of stressing over when the next game breaking glitch would occur and it felt refreshing to rid myself of this game's torture. However, I attempted a new game recently just because I had a hankering for some Batman: Arkham-style combat and here I am now, having just finished the campaign without a single save-corrupting, fall-through-the-floor, get-stuck-in-a-building-glitch occuring. And, I have to say that now that I've experienced the game the way it was meant to be experienced I can say that this is a deserving entry in the Arkham series, from a creative standpoint. Strictly. From a creative standpoint.
Why is it a creative standpoint you ask? Because the developers of Origin are technologically inept and couldn't program better than a monkey with a brain tumor. Okay, that might be a little too much, but seriously, let me tell you about these developers.
Warner Brothers Montreau's first game was Batman: Arkham City Armored Edition. It was a special edition Wii U version of the award winning Batman: Arkham City, and it was alright. It was essentially Arkham City with a little gloss and a dash of confetti to spice it up.
Then they made a web-based game that I don't know anything about.
Then they made Batman: Arkham Origins. This game.
Now get this: The developer has worked with this engine before, with the Armored Edition of Arkham City. Now they're using the same map and the same engine ONCE MORE, except this time their making an entirely new game instead of just an enhanced edition.
So you'd think they'd be fairly competent with their game's techincal quality right?
Nope. Nada. Nuh-uh. Sorry. Zip. Zilch. NO.
The game was released with more bugs than a bug petting zoo set on a planet inhabited entirely by humanoid bug creatures. OK, they were rushed by the publisher! Big deal! Ok, sure, maybe they were "rushed" for the release. HOWEVER, get this, in February the developers stated the following:
"The team is currently working hard on the upcoming story DLC and there currently are no plans for releasing another patch to address the issues that have been reported on the forums,"
and later that the game:
"will unfortunately no longer be addressed."
They did say they would fix gamebreaking and progression stopping issues somewhere during that article, however those issues still exist, so it doesn't matter.
HAHAHAHAHAHAHHAHAHA! YOU'RE NOT GOING TO PATCH YOUR GAME!? HAHAHAHAHAHAHA, OH GOD I'M GOING FULL ON JOKER HERE HAHA HA HA!
Another interesting thing: the game hasn't had a patch since April, if you look at the Steam news under the game. So it's true. The game is forgotten. Completely inexplicably forgotten, for no reason other than that the developers just said no.
Now that this rant is over, I'll tell you why I think Arkham Origins is a good Batman game.
The following pros and cons are in the context of this game being the same game as Arkham City, which it pretty much is, but with a different story. So feel free to add any of the pros and cons for that game into here.
Pros
+ Combat is improved greatly; there are several new enemy types, each a joy to fight. Combat is also smoother, and the animations seem to flow better.
+ Graphics are better. They're not next-gen, in fact they're essentially Arkham City's graphics just enhanced with new visual effects here and there.
+ Story is awesome. As much as I disdain some aspects of this game, notably the developers, I applaud the plot here. It draws heavily upon Batman mythos and one of my favorite Batman graphic novels: The Killing Joke. Though I suppose the writers had nothing to do with the programming so huzzah for the writers!
+ The game is generally more cinematic, with superior cut scenes when compared to the previous two entries.
+ New voice actors for Batman and Joker were well cast and do an excellent job
+ Character design is awesome, Copperhead looks genuinely cool, Bane is actually treated as Bane for once (super strong, but also super smart) Deathstroke looks cool.
An interesting addition to Origins was the detective segments, which are greatly improved over the previous games' attempts. However, I'm not going to add this as a specific Pro since i believe that it's simply not significant enough, they're essentially pseudo-quicktime events that look cool but nothing more.
Cons
- The game is buggy. Very. Very buggy.
- The developers do not care about their customers.
- The game heavily relies on rehashing content from the first two games and rarely adds anything of its own.
- The open world here is empty and less interesting. It may seem like there are more things to do in Origins when compared to City, but in actuallity there isn't a lot. Collecting extortion files is boring compared to solving riddles, the side missions are boring and not as well written, the random goon voices you'll hear throughout the city are downright dreadful to listen to, they never say anything cool or funny and you'll hear the same lines OVER and OVER the entire game. I remember smirking and being genuinely interested in what the goons in Arkham City had to say. Here? Nope. Also, I hate to make this single con in an already long-winded review so long, but the opening of Arkham City was seriously cool, wheareas the opening here is very, very lackluster. Sorry, I just needed to say that.
I'm not going to add a con for this, since it wouldn't really be fair, but I always note when games have Nvidia's Physx technology. Unless you have an Nvidia graphics card or a NASA processor, you can't enable this without suffering massive FPS drops. In game there's lots of cool cloth simulation and papers/flyers flying about among other things when you have it activated. It's been said elsewhere and I'll say it here, my graphics card is capable of these things but Nvidia, being a greedy company made it to where you simply cannot efficiently use this technology on anything other than Nvidia cards. Games should be played the way the developers meant them to be played, not the way greedy companies meant them to be played (yes, Nvidia pun).
In all, I'd give Arkham Origins a 6/10. It's worth a playthrough if you liked the first games, for its story and the improvements made to combat. If you've never played an Arkham title, please go back and play Arkham Asylum or City first.
I'd rate the developers of this game a 4/10. The only reason they don't go any lower is because somewhere within that cesspool of "gaming development" there are writers and creative directors who did a remarkable job trying to follow up an award winning series with their own take. And for that, I feel they deserve a commendation. For the rest of them? Please learn how to program before making a AAA-title, and always put technical stability above more content. How can we play the new content if we can't play the game? Oh, you hear that? I think it's the sound of "logic".
WARNING: Know this if you buy the game, there are still game breaking bugs present. You MAY run into them, and you MAY lose hours of progress, though some people never even experience one of them, others, like myself ran into TWO in my first 8 hours. It took three new games before I finally was able to beat the game. There are some workarounds out there for the majority of them, as well as backing up your saves.
TL;DR: The game is okay and worth it for fans of the series but the developers used mostly rehashed content, then botched the rehashed content somehow producing a truck load of bugs and now refuse to fix it and instead want to make more money with DLC.

Spec Ops: The Line is often quoted as one of the best war dramas which actually makes you feel the impact and the negative sides to what you're doing, and to actually show the horror or war.
Well, not quite. First of all, the game looks beautifull. Set in a Dubai city buried almost completely following mysterious sandstorms, staring a disappeared and apparently now brutally reigning american division as your main opponents, and you sent as a rescue team, this game has great potential, but falls short due to two main errors made.
First of, the storytelling. The way in which you get set up to eventually be shooting (without any attempts of communication) at CIA Agents and american soldiers, is completely unbelievable. It tears a gigantic hole in an otherwise very interesting story, which i particularly liked for its unique setting.
And second, and more importantly, there are ENORMOUS flaws in the gameplay design. Not only is the game the definition of a sloggy tunnel-shooter, it tries its hardest fo fullfill every stereotype possible, from the pinned scenario where you're hiding behind tiny bits of debris taking out 50+ people shooting at you from the remnants of a skyscraper, to the obvious helicopter shooting through the side of a glass window sidescraper, to actually falling off a skyscraper, surviving a 200+ meter fall, and finding yourself in a corner at the start of another level tunnel with nothing but a pistol with 8 bullets in it and 11 enemies facing you down immediatly and simultaneously. The amount of times i had to restart that section to go for a 100% headshot rate and to grab one of their guns before the shotgun-guys ran me over was mildly annoying to say the least.
Enemy AI has massive deficiencies. They will go for certain pieces of cover, and eventually lob grenades at you if you don't kill them, but they keep peaking their heads out without actually properly returning fire, and most of the time they won't react to your grenades and simply die. Their only advantage seems to be their sheer number and considering the setting you could've replaced them with something akin to zerglings instead of american soldiers (FEEL BAD FOR SHOOTING THEM DAMNIT!!)
Lastly and most importantly, we have to talk about the interactive-cognitive dissonance of this game because it sets to bar for it in every video game ever. What is ICD? It's the difference between what the story is telling you, and what you actually do in gameplay. You sneak down a stairway, spotting two US Soldiers discussing how they want to return to their green farm from this desert nightmare and wish to find peace. Then one of them eventually walks up the stairs to you and you have to shoot them both in the face. No disarming, no dialogue, kill only. You find camps of survivors and refugees who have been murdered, just to make sure, yes, those deserted americans you're shooting HAVE to deserve to be killed AND you're still supposed to feel bad about it, but never lets you do anything to avoid confrontation of the bunches of enemies placed in the level tunnels, like talking them into surrender, taking them down in non-lethal ways or disarming them. You can't feel bad for enemies that you can't choose not to kill, which is why the game ultimately fails to be as dramatic and meaningfull as it tries to be. Also, the sheer amount of super soldier stereotypes thrown at you (for example the aforementioned falling off a bloody skyscraper) makes it impossible to relate to the actions of your "heroes".
Based on Setting, optics, graphics and sound design, this game could be a solid 85/100 contender. Unfortunately, the hilarious failures of matching the gameplay to the storytelling, and the frustrating lack of alternatives to shooting everyone in the head discourage taking the game for anything else than a shooting gallery. This game serves pretty much only as a lesson to game designers to match their gameplay and variety up to par with their (in this case pretty good) writing, and because of it's massive flaws, i can not recommend you to pick it up unless it's massively discounted or you want to see how NOT to design your own story to gameplay relationship. Or if you just want to ignore all of the story and play the game like a shooting gallery, i guess it's definitely one of the better looking ones.

This is such a beautiful little game. The classic arcade core with a botanical twist; the cartoony-cute art style; the tone-setting soundtrack that is memorable but unobtrusive, fun and sophisticated; the gentle humor balanced by some existential far-outness in story bits and easter eggs throughout the game—each of these elements is full of personality and together they help to define each other and the game as a whole, making Cosmochoria a unique experience that’s more than the sum of these parts.
Most of the action involves you thrusting around from planet to planet Lunar-Landing-style, planting seeds and briefly nurturing plants while defending them from alien ambushes. When you succeed in healing that planet, you move on to another. Boss fights challenged me but weren’t depressingly frustrating. For me the game delivers something between casual play and old-school arcade grinding, leaning more towards casual.
I liked the designer’s pacing choices. There are at least a few different satisfying endings and you probably won’t find all the hidden artifacts before you beat the game a few times. Artifacts alter certain elements of the game and can be selected or deselected before every session. Apart from that, you also have a running total of little triangular bits (common finds as you fight through alien hordes) that you can use to purchase permanent upgrades for you character stats, weapons, etc.
The music is REALLY well done. All electronic and spacey, sometimes more ambient and other times more groovin, but in like an alien/cyborg kinda way. Perfect for cartoony space exploration. Interesting and awesome final boss theme music too—love how the composer manages to convey such a phat menacing feel in a cartoony way.
This is not just a cute lil game that’s fun to play casually and hard to put down; it’s a creative work with a playful heart and funky soul.

This is a beautiful, but challenging, little game, with atmospheric music that fits the character of each level.  The whimsical and surreal hand-painted backgrounds are reminiscent of a children's story book, of games such as "Machinarium," or of animated shorts such as "La Maison en Petits Cubes."  I'm not ashamed to say I purchased this game solely for the art, and it did not disappoint.
The gameplay consists of a handful of short hidden object levels.  The items you need to find are sneaky: they blend into the background or are hidden in secret compartments, although if you look hard enough you will find all of them eventually.  It felt more like a scavenger hunt than like traditional "stuff-piled-on-other-stuff" HOGs.  The objects you collect can be used to open up new areas, solve puzzles, or unlock mini-games.
Some of the mini-games were easy and straightforward, but I found many of the rest to be quite frustrating.  They require a wide range of skills including superior spacial perception, logic, patience, memory, fast reflexes, luck, keen observation and attention to detail.  Occasionally the built-in hints were helpful, but often they just reiterated information you already knew instead of nudging you toward the next step.  I feel the game did a great job of making the ultimate goal of each puzzle clear with minimal instructions, but I either had physical trouble doing what they asked, as was the case with the "classic console" sections, or I felt like my brain was spinning in circles trying to get pieces to line up properly, as was the case with the "compass" and "globe map" puzzles.
One thing I noticed that may be an issue for some players is the game's heavy reliance on colour-coded puzzles.  If you are colourblind you WILL NOT be able to beat this game without using a walkthrough.
Overall, I would give this game a 7.5/10.  It is short, but meaty and innovative, and is worth picking up just for the art alone.

Undertale (or UNDERTALE), a game in which you control a human who has fallen underground into a world of monsters.
Meet a talking flower, meet a talking goat, meet a ghost, meet a skeleton, meet his brother, meet a dog, meet a fish, meet another dog, meet a dinosaur, meet a robot, meet another talking goat, meet the talking flower, meet a dog.
This game has thousands of characters, and depending on what you do to them, you get a different ending. Unlike Telltale games in which the game "adapts to the choices you choose" or whatever, then you get the same ending even if you didn't save Bob or whatever, Undertale brings a new perspective. If you do one bad thing, you can't take it back and you get a different ending. Killed one thing? There's no max-revive. It's dead.
I highly reccomend you play this game. There is more to it then I mentioned in this review.

I really hate this game!
I'm generally a fan of point and click adventures and yes, I know I just don't have the patience for some of the failings I was used to at their height in the 90s but this game is still horrible! By the end of it I was screaming at the screen in anger and frustration. I then resorted to online walkthroughs so that such a poor excuse for a game did not defeat me.
My main objections are below (warning there are some spoilers):
1. There is no tutorial.
I was just flung into the game and had to guess how to access the inventory and hint system. Perhaps this wasn't a problem when it was originally purchased in a box with a manual, but it's a drag now.
2. Movement/backgrounds/stupid, pointless mazes.
The movement is your standard grid system point and click which wouldn't be so much of a problem if the backgrounds weren't so poorly rendered. This really comes into its teeth-grindingly-frustrating own when the game decides it would be fun to have a largely featureless underwater maze. They then decide to compound this misery in the final section with circular corridors.
3. The hint system is more of an 'I told you so' system.
This includes notes in a diary which sometimes bear some relation to your predicament, sometimes don't. The latter is more often true. It leaves you completely hanging in places for no reason whatsoever.
4. Progression/puzzles are too often stupid.
We're not talking comedy stupid, or one-off perhaps they were having a bad day stupid. We're talking criminally poorly stupid. Why when I want to access the Loch do I have to magically realise I want a garden hose? Why when I want 120ml of a substance do I have to click on a bottle clearly marked as 30ml four times? It just doesn't make sense! Once or twice you can put up with, by the end of the game I felt it was almost constant.
If you're prepared to put up with all of this then please go ahead. All I can say is that it's a good job I'm blessed with a luxuriant mane as by the end of this a more folically challenged person might have had no more hair to pull out!

Do you find driving to be very relaxing but don't exactly want to pay $40 for a tank of gas to drive down the countryside? Have you had passing thoughts such as, "Hey, I kind of like road trips. I wonder if I could be a transport truck driver"? Then Euro Truck Simulator 2 is just the game for you.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is just as realistic as you want it to be, with many modes to choose from; from Automatic (WASD + mouse to look) to fully Manual transmission (most of the keyboard) -- you can even add a steering wheel controller if you wish. In addition to this, there are different types of trucking such as fragile cargo, expensive cargo, long-haul trucking, and 'just in time' jobs. You can even choose your own routes, free-drive, and download or buy mods to make your truck your very own.
You even get penalties just like real driving. 400 Euro tickets for speeding, accidents, and failing to stop at a red light, as well as company and reward penalties for damaging your truck and arriving late, or bonuses for arriving with plenty of time to spare and your truck in pristine condition.
Categorization for routes is possible as well. Don't have much time? Select 'Route Length' and a 500m mission to get your truck across the street and park it. Have plenty of time? Go for the long haul and drive across 3 countries if you want to.
I know what you may be thinking, "A truck driving simulator? Is it really worth it?". Well, that depends. Are you a fan of simulations? Do you find driving fun and relaxing? Ever imagined driving a transport truck? Need something that will help you unwind? Do you like watching grass sway in the wind when you turn your graphics up? If you answer is yes to most of those questions, then yes, you will most likely enjoy the game.
As for myself, I like doing 2 - 3 jobs before bed in order to calm down. Works like a charm, and only takes 30 minutes to an hour depending on the route length you choose.
Tl;DR: This game is zen AF.
Still not sure? Try the free demo, it took me about 2.5 hours to finish (just enough time for me to master the control scheme).

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is all about living the dream that is professional trucking. The game even tells you as you begin that this is your dream job -- and who are you to argue? Armed with little more than enthusiasm, players begin their adventure humbly -- with a decrepit little garage in the home city of their choice, and a company with no trucks to its name.
The player begins by taking jobs for other companies, earning money with fuss-free escorts from one city to another, with an eye toward earning enough cash and purchasing a truck. An owned truck means more freedom, with higher-paying jobs that require more responsibility. When working directly for the player company, cargo is waiting at a select shipping yard and must be hitched to the truck before it can be taken to its ultimate destination. The next step from there is to start upgrading the garage, hiring other drivers to bring in more income, and eventually building a trucking empire that spans all of Europe.
The deeper you go, the more there is to do. Want to expand quickly? You can take out loans that need to be repaid. Want specialized drivers? They each level up the same way you do, and you can dictate the way they do. Of course, you also have to be mindful of expenses, be they repayments to the bank or fuel consumption by employees looking for work. There are a lot of ducks to get in a row, but the interface is user-friendly and information is constantly provided so nothing ever feels insurmountable.
More than simply a game about driving, Euro Truck Sim 2 boasts some roleplaying elements to keep things interesting. Successful jobs earn experience, which leads to skill points. Skill points can be spent upgrading one's proficiency in certain types of jobs, unlocking new types of cargo, or even investing in fuel efficiency. Improving personal abilities and building a business from one lone driver to an entire fleet is just as important as getting from A to B, and maintains a compelling grip on the experience.
That said, driving trucks in as realistic a fashion as possible is the bread and butter of any trucking sim, and Euro Truck will have fans covered. Offering a huge map spanning the length and breadth of Europe, there's plenty of time to be spent on the open road, and lots of distance to cover. Although you won't be undertaking journeys in real-time, a decent paying job is still quite the investment. I often found myself able to only play one job at a time, rather than stay glued to the screen all night long. As outwardly mundane as the experience may appear, it's a time sink that can prove a mental drain, and is best played with breaks in between.
There are a variety of controls and settings allowing for significant flexibility in terms of personal comfort. You can choose how complex your controls are, with automatic settings for those rocking the trusty keyboard, and more involved ones for those wanting to go the whole hog and set up a wheel. Whatever your available input, Euro Truck does a great job of covering you and ensuring you get into the game easily enough.
Accessibility is, in fact, one of its strongest suites. A solid tutorial guides newcomers, and the essential GPS is easy to understand, as is its clear and simple route map. My first job was an absolute disaster, with me getting the trailer stuck a number of times, managing to tip the vehicle over, and even getting so boxed in I had to call for emergency rescue. After my embarrassing first run, however, I quickly found myself getting the hang of things, and was soon bold enough to trek across whole countries in my quest for freight and fortune.
A lot of Euro Truck's experience is, expectedly, rooted in routine, but complacency manages to be quite a dastardly foe. Traffic lights, speed cameras, and the ever-present need to keep one's eyes on the road can always trip up an overconfident player, and as relaxing as long country drives may be, the pressure to avoid mistakes is present throughout. It's very easy to start getting too ♥♥♥♥♥ure, speeding along a motorway without regard to other drivers and strict speed limits. Every mistake translates into a financial penalty, damaged cargo reduces the payday, and dings suffered by an owned truck will have to be paid for at service stations.
When a mistake occurs, it's almost always the player's fault, but there are some moments where the computer-controlled road users compound an issue. Seemingly programmed to only ever drive forward, other vehicles have a nasty habit of doing nothing to avoid their part in a collision, and if you're ever trying to steer your way out of a tight spot, you'll get no help from other cars, willing as they are to close any gap in the road, no matter how minute, even if you were backing up to create the space they just filled. Should you manage to hit them, drivers have a nasty habit of refusing to move thereafter, sometimes causing you to suffer a second collision fine for smacking them again as you drive through them.
These frustrations inevitably pop up, but they're few and far between, and experienced drivers will be able to avoid many of the pitfalls that lead to such trouble. Despite the occasional irritation and the pressure to perform jobs well, Euro Truck Sim is still a largely cathartic experience. There's a therapy to be had in driving through a variety of countries, a sense of joy as you get closer to your destination, and a sense of accomplishment in performing such mundane tasks as refueling at gas stations and finding parking stops at which to grab some sleep. As you build your business up from nothing and take on more of managerial duties, it's hard not to feel pride over rewards well earned.
Although not the most visually advanced game, Euro Truck's believable presentation of Europe's roads and cities are nonetheless impressive. From the shape of the traffic lights to the atmosphere of the backdrops, there's a sense of individuality to each new territory you uncover, and the trucks themselves are lovingly recreated with an intricate level of detail. Owned trucks can be repainted and upgraded with all manner of parts, and as the player levels up, the potential for personalization expands.
Perhaps the most fun aspect of Euro Truck Sim 2, however, comes in the form of its music. With the simple tap of the "R" key, you can open up a menu packed with European Internet radio streams providing a wide variety of tunes. Whether you want some top forty hits or obscure French '80s tunes, you'll be able to find something worth digging. Being able to complete my deliveries with some Peter Gabriel's blasting through the speakers bumps up the enjoyment tenfold. There's also the option to queue up music from one's own PC, for those who don't wish to leave their aural stimulation to chance.
Euro Truck Simulator 2's following is well earned. It's not just a tongue-in-cheek dalliance, but an understandable dedication won by a game genuinely terrific at what it does. Being a simulator, there are inevitable parts of it that feel slow, and sometimes progression can be a bit of a drag, but it nevertheless manages to be an approachable sim with a smart implementation of more familiar "game-like" elements. A far cry from some of the more technical and unforgiving sims on the market, Euro Truck is as welcoming as it is authentic, forgiving while still prepared to reprimand those who fail. It's one of the best jumping points anybody curious about sims could have, and for everybody else, it's still just a fine experience in its own right.

I was very much on the fence whether or not to recommend this game. In the end, I have to give a cautios recommendation.
Main issue is in the core gameplay. It has rogue-like progression element to it, where each time you start a new game, you can buy persistent upgrades and jump past bosses. This means that you end up starting new game rather often (permadeath), and repeating same tasks (plant seeds, build base, kill enemies) over and over again. This means that gameplay may get rather repetitive and grindy, if you don't particularly enjoy the mechanics. I have my gripes with it, but found it pretty fun nevertheless.
In the end it comes down to whether or not you like the core gameplay loop enough to keep grinding. Game is reasonably challenging and somewhat unforgiving, especially in the beginning. A lot of learning is supposed to happen via trial-and-error, and speaking of discoveries, there are a lot of different upgrades to buy and secrets to find.
In some ways, Cosmochoria reminds me of the free flash games I used to sometimes play on Armor Games or similar sites, both in gameplay and aesthetic.
So there you have it, my cautious recommendation.

Overall this game has an interesting idea, but the execution consists almost solely of grinding while fending off annoying enemies.

Rust is a complex game, and if power is your goal, a pretty challenging game.
If you want to dominate your server, you better make some friends, and your friends better be good players.
If you want to dominate gun fights, you better practice, and pick your fights smartly.
If you want to laugh, trolling people can be hilarious, you can use external audio programs to blast music, or use music that fits a particular narrative. Playing songs to troll salty players, or mess with clans is pretty fun. There are voice changers that make you sound like a 5 year old, and other stuff to mess with.
The options are really dependent upon you.
What sets this game apart from others is the fact that your hard work is always on the line, which creates stress, especially during fights. Most players know it as the 'Rust shakes'. I have never played another game with such intense fights, which can be extremely rewarding, or depressing. How you can manage those emotions depends upon your outlook of the game. You can ghost around being sneaky, afraid, cautious, and careful; or you can run full speed through an open field. You will lose your stuff in this game, so if your not having fun getting that stuff in the first place, then you probably wont find the game appealing overall. I can guarantee that you will have much more fun playing with friends, in small groups (max 5) ((larger groups are frustrating due to communication)).
It is completely possible to solo this game, however, I recommend sticking to solo/duo/trio servers. The more time you have put into this game, the better you will become, especially if you come from a fps background. Find good players to play with and learn from them, and you will find yourself stealing AK's with revolvers and pipe shotguns.
On Grinding: You can grind hard in this game, if you wish. You will have to grind to raid bases, if you have at least 4 friends who share in the grind, its not bad at all, but the huge zerg groups obviously will have a monopoly on resources vs the smaller (and usually more talented) small groups. ---OR--- You can grind just enough to get a gun, some gear, and some meds and then farm (kill) other players, basically; farm players. Typically it takes me about 20 minutes to grind out some initial weapons (python, wood armour, face mask, meds...).
It takes time to get skilled at this game, and you never really stop getting better with practice. BUT you dont HAVE to have 1000+ hrs to be good at pvp, some people are just naturals, and some just get lucky.
Love Rust, have wasted WAY too much of my life on it, but it is unlike any other game I have ever played. I have had, and continue to have some pretty great times on it, and have made some pretty good friends.
PS. Yes there are cheaters in this game, but typically are a rarity. If you want to avoid them, stay away from Official servers, and when you encounter them, switch to different servers until they are banned. Facepunch is pretty responsive to actual cheating, and the last cheater I reported was banned in 5 hours. Try not to get attached to your gear, its just data, and don't hate on your friends when you lose. This game can bring the best, and worst out in people.

For new players, I recommend playing Hitman to completion once using "opportunities" to guide you. This 5-6 hour experience will introduce you to many of the stealth mechanics in the game and help you get used to the spaces and characters in play. Though the story is intriguing enough, Hitman shines most when players embrace the emergent gameplay potential of its clockwork worlds. So, aftewards, you'll want to return to the various international settings to complete challenges, escalation missions, and elusive targets--or you can just create chaos by toying with the games mechanics. If you find the game a little easy, you can also disable various help systems and UI to make it tougher on yourself.
For the most part, the game controls well, though Agent 57 can move a little stiffly at times and is certainly not as spry as other video game assassins I could name. You won't be scaling any tall buildings, certainly, and even sneaking around can sometimes be more challenging than necessary. That said, there's nothing more satisfying than sneaking up on an unsuspecting NPC and introducing them to the toilet basin. Once you've got a sense of how the game works, you'll find yourself murdering targets (and non-targets, if you like) with relative ease. In fact, you'll start to look at the worlds as a series of opportunities to rub them out in the most creative ways you can.
There are a few technical issues. Load times on PC are occasionally long enough that they break the flow of the game, and I've had the repeated experience of being dropped from the online service for no good reason, which actually forces you back to the main menu. This is a frustrating experience, and I'm not surprised so many other reviewers respond so negatively here, but don't let it stop you from playing one of the best games of 2016. The frame rate can also drop on occasion, especially in crowded spaces, though it shouldn't be a problem for gamers with better hardware than me.
Some hitches aside though, Hitman is a great entry for the series, and a game that will continue to evolve as the developers add new missions and elusive targets as well as a new narrative in Season 2. It's an achievement in episodic gaming and definitely worth a purchase, especially at a discounted price.

To give this game a bad review would be difficult. It did so many things right that it seems to outweigh the few problems it has. From the small details that make the surroundings gain depth and story. Or to the large areas that explain some of the history to the game/series. The game combines combat and story almost as one. And you can choose just how much you want to do of either. If you want combat and challenges, then you can do them. But if you want to learn more of the stroy and history of the dystopian land, then you are free to wander and explor every crevis you find. Along with the attention to detail and the unique envionment the game puts out there, it also speaks volumes when it comes to the open world stand point. The game doesn't limit you to an area. Once you are out of the gates you are free to drive off and explore the vast wasteland as much as you like.
Furthermore the developers put a lot of effort forth to emphisise story and Max's own motives. And little by little they begin to unravel more of what Max is truley driven by. As said before the envionment is beautiful with details that reveal a world that "once was but now is." It is amazing how they seemed to create their own language and system for the society that is now left. From the "Long Lookers" to the "Huge fans that people used to fly with." All of the wording seems to help build that sense of atmosphere to the game.
Naturally the game does have it's issues, like the leveling system that doesn't seem all that well intigrated due to the requirment of having to finish challenges and other misculanious tasks. Along with the leveling comes the tokens to upgrade Max. When interacting with Griffa you learn more of Max's past, this was a good idea in some ways, but the game eventually gets to repeating itself and the tokens eventually get phased out making it hard to know if you caught all of the bits. Other than some design flaws the game had few glitches in my own play through. (Besides getting stuck on top of a light.)
Overall the game was and is a joy to play, I always seem to find more subtle hints or interesting areas to explore. And if you like the type of game I just describbed then I would highly recommend picking up the game as soon as you can.

Right, this review is late, but sometimes it's good to see a more modern perspective on games.
Spec Ops: The Line is pretty goddamn awesome. If you (yes, you! Reader!) are too lazy to read the blurb, this game is about Captain Walker (voiced by the King of voice acting, Nolan North) and his team of Delta Force operatives who are sent into Dubai to find out what happened to the 33rd Battalion who attempted to evacuate Dubai before lethal sandstorms swept the city. Naturally, the 33rd failed. (If they'd have succeeded, it'd have made for a boring game, don't you think?) When you get there, you find that everything's gone to sh*t and anarchy has ensued, because humans can't help but tear each other apart whenever any form of disaster happens. (Humans, what a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, right?)
I know what a lot of you are thinking, having seen the title and the blurb- yeah, I know it sounds like a mediocre third person shooter with one or two cool parts, nothing to get excited about. That's where you're wrong. This game manages to capture you with a powerful narrative in which you are forced to witness the atrocities that happen in the aftermath of a disaster, and you even do a couple yourself. That being said, this isn't a game where you just see some awful crap and do some yourself, what the game does is show the emotions of Walker and his team. You see the effects that the harrowing scenes have on them and you watch them slowly descend into madness. You can make choices in what you do. Sometimes one choice is the smart thing to do, but is not necessarily the more moral choice. At times, you'll be forced to make the worse choice simply to survive, or to make things easier.
The story isn't just the good thing, although that would have most people hooked. The gunplay is a bit normal, but it's solid. Most weapons have alternate abilities that can change the way you play, or the tide of a battle. For example, the M4, one of the more common weapons. The alternate fire is a suppressor, which allows you to have an element of stealth. You can silently murder enemies, meaning you need to fight less of them when they inevitably catch you, whereas other weapons just make themselves more effective, such as the AK-47, another common weapon. This one has a burst fire mode as well as automatic, meaning you can accurately pick off enemies in a manner that would be difficult with a fully automatic weapon.
The level design is linear, but the beautiful -and wrecked- environments will command your attention. The environment isn't all about looks however, there are many ways you can use it to turn the tide of a battle, maybe by shooting out a window to allow tonnes of sand to crash down upon anyone unfortunate enough to be standing next to it, or by turning around a turret and decimating the enemy forces.
And now, the graphics. The game has aged well, thus far. It won't satisfy graphics wh*res (because they're never satisfied), but they still look pretty amazing, even today.
The game runs like a charm and holds up a solid 60 FPS, and very rarely begins to tank.

:  This game doesn't really add anything new overall compared to the previous ones.  If you liked the way the previous ones played, you'll like the way this one plays.
:  Graphics seem to be on par with the previous Batman: Arkham etc... games.  The snowy weather effects are a nice touch.  (Subjective) -> I found a few (and only a few) of the character graphics to look a little odd.
:  The random snippets of conversation you get from around the city are entertaining, even when they're not story relevant.  The music is top notch, keeping the dark orchestral theme that the Batman franchise uses.  Some of the songs have some Christmassy elements to them that are well incorporated.
:  Voices and acting are top notch.  Zero complaints.
:  This was a dissapointment.  The map is about twice as big as Arkham City, but that's because half of it
the same map from Arkham City.  As the timeline is early in Batman's career, you see Old Gotham as Old Gotham, not as Arkham City.  The new section is well done.  More tall buildings.  Travel times aren't too bad thanks to a waypoint system you unlock as you progress through the game.
:  I don't recall this existing the same way in Arkham City or Arkham Asylum, but there are multiple sets of challenges that you can go through that unlock addional gadgets and techniques (additional items you can get from the levelling system).  Finishing off the challenges definitely adds some more game time for completionists.
:  I played the game on the 'normal' difficulty, and for most of it I didn't have too many issues.  There are a couple of boss fights that can get frustrating (IMO), but most of them are reasonably tough, but not frustratingly so.
There's a 'crime scene investigation' feature that I liked.  You analyze a crime scene, reconstruct it and solve it.  I believe it's new (again, I don't recall ever doing that in City) and it felt like an interesting diversion from the usual stuff, while still keeping everything feeling properly 'Batman'.
One thing I found frustrating is that there are many doors that are locked and cannot be accessed.  This is usually because you need to be at a certain part of the main storyline to access it (or have uncovered a certain side mission).  There's no indication or pointer to let you know this.  I spent a lot of time searching for ways to unlock these doors, but just wasted my time.  I checked online and found out that they were unaccessible until I progressed through the game.
There are a couple of parts of the game where you go into a 'locked camera' style where the camera stays fixed at a distance, rather than the usual 'behind Batman's back' style.  One of these occasions is a little awkward and any difficulty was only because it was harder to move around compared to the rest of the game.  At first I thought my game was bugging out on me (especially because none of the menus came up), but it was designed to be that way.
(
: Minor Spoilers):
The game took me about 40 hours to finish, and that includes solving all the crime scenes, finding all Riddler related materials, finishing the game, capturing all the criminals.  The only side events I didn't do are locating the Anarky tags and finding the Cyrus Pinkney plaques.  I also finished most of the challenges.
At first I was dissapointed that the overall area was 'Old Gotham' plus another section about the same size.  The entire game, you're teased with what I think is Gotham proper accross the river (a very metropolitan skyline).  It's the same view you had in Arkham City, and I remember, when playing that one, that I was hoping I could do 'Batman' stuff on that side of the river next time.  That said, there were many 'inside' zones to explore that seemed to be all new.
As an aside, it's weird hearing the Joker not voiced by Mark Hamill, but the new actor does a good job.  Same with Batman / Kevin Conroy.
From what I read, the main cause for 'so-so' reveiws was that there wasn't enough 'new' stuff compared to Arkham City.  That's more or less true.  Personally, I found the story and characters were enough to overlook those negatives.  I found it was worth the purchase cost.

Here's what made Arkham City amazing for me:
-It introduced new gadgets and associated tasks
-It allowed you to play as Cat Woman and her story meshed very well with Batman's
-The story was even better than the first game
Here's why I feel that Arkham Origins sucks:
-You use the same gadgets for exactly the same tasks as the other games
-The new gadgets introduced are ultimately uninteresting and bland
-The story.....Is there one?
-There's no co-op (for story)
I'll explain. The story is so boring in this installment, that I hardly pay attention. "Black Mask" hires some assassins to take out Batman. And yet, nobody believes the Bat exists at this point? If Batman is not famous enough yet to instill fear in minor thugs, then why is he on the mask's radar? Why would he hire assassins to take Bats out? Furthermore, the side missions are an absolute waste of time. Anarky's was idiocy. You race a timer to reach a bomb. Beat up some thugs. Take out bomb. Then you do it like 4 more times. Voila, Anarky's story complete. Ridler's part in this is inconsequential. You have to destroy relay beakens (much like Joker's balloons in the second game) and disable radio frequency generators or some such nonsense. Boring! Also, the Ridler challenge things are practically the same exact ones from Arkham City. Recycling? Lastly, there's the multiplayer. You play as random thugs, or Batman and Robin. For Batman and Robin it's like playing a predator mission.....again and again......you can unlock either Joker or Bane for the thugs. And they have special abilities you can use....but meh. Simply put, it's just some PvP that does nothing to advance or enhance your gameplay in story. What's the use?
Anyway, this game killed the franchise for me. If the next installment has co-op in story mode, I may check it out. When it goes on sale. But until then, the Arkham games have met their end with this one. At least for me.

Cosmochoria is a science-fiction rogue-like game of exploration from indie developer Nate Schmold.
In Cosmochoria, you play a pants-less little pink guy in a space helmet, spawning on an unnamed planet in the middle of space. Your task is to plant flags to claim planets and grow plants on them, thus restoring them to vitality. As you claim planets, fight off aggressive aliens, meet NPCs, and find weird items, the game slowly reveals its story and your goals.
Graphics are simple, but elegant. The game is two-dimensional, played from a side-on view, with colourful pixel graphics used throughout, and a unique stylised look.
Your character is a chubby little naked person in a space helmet, and he (?) is almost as big as some planets. Planet appearance is variable, with planets ranging from those that look like the leftovers over some sort of nuclear war to some that bear ancient ruins reminiscent of Mayan civilisation. Even the larger planets are only an order of magnitude larger than the main character.
The camera keeps the character in the centre of the screen and, by default, rotates loosely around as you orbit planets (by running around their surface). It works well, although it takes some getting used to as you reorient yourself, especially when jetting off into space.
Special effects are simple, but nicely done.
There are only very limited graphics options related to window mode and screen resolution.
Sound effects are good: well-normalised and used appropriately. The jetpack sound has a nice feel to it, and the pea shooter weapon sounds suitably weak.
Music is good, only occurring in certain situations, such as when a boss draws near. I haven't worked out what causes little bursts of background music in other situations, but the sporadic nature of them adds to the overall weirdness of the game.
There are no voices.
The game is very easy to play, but hard to master. You have only five controls: move/rotate left and right, jump/jetpack, crouch/pick up/use, and shoot.
When on a planet, gravity keeps you on the ground, so your most common actions become running around the planet either clockwise or anticlockwise, shooting enemies, and crouching to plant or build. Once you've restored a planet, you can leap in the air and use your jetpack to escape orbit, then navigate your way to another planet to start all over again.
Control in space is fun, with your escape vector governing your path across the galaxy, and only limited fuel in your jetpack to correct it. Planets all have localised gravity fields, though, which helps to bring you back to ground when you find another one.
Making your job harder are a horde of nasty aliens of various types, who chase and shoot at you, and a 'boss' enemy that gets activated after every few planets that you restore. These become difficult fast, but keep at it and you'll soon learn some tricks to make defeating them easier.
The galaxy is procedurally generated each game, including planet placement and size, and NPC and artefact placement. The game includes three resources: seeds, bricks, and some sort of currency. Seeds are only collected and used in the current game. Bricks and currency are carried over to your next game when you die. Bricks can be collected and used to build towers and other structures on planets. Currency can be used to buy permanent upgrades in the shop before you start a new game. It's a good system. As you play not only do you start to understand and get better at the game, but your character also becomes more powerful and able to do what's required of him.
The game also has a strange collection of unique artefacts that can be collected. Deliver these to the correct NPCs and you end up with another artefact that allows you to change the universe in some way. Again, this is activated or deactivated before each game. Some are beneficial, like a NPC and boss detector, whereas others are downright dangerous, such as one that makes enemies more aggressive.
Unfortunately, though, Cosmochoria either doesn't like new hardware and software (i7, GTX1070, 32 GB RAM, Windows 10), or it's become more buggy since its early days. I first played it about a year ago, then put it away until it was 'finished'. It's in full release now, and is much more fleshed out, but it also seems less stable. A few times an hour the game will just freeze for about 20 seconds, then resume again as if nothing happened; there's no stuttering or other performance-related issues, it just seems to decide to have a rest. I've also had occasional crashes to desktop, with the game giving no warning and no error, and just dropping back to Windows. This has invariably happened while I've been doing very well, too, so it's immensely frustrating.
Pros:
+ Creative universe and plot, with unique interactions and a good sense of humour
+ Rogue-like aspects are well thought out
+ Addictive and very replayable
+ Pleasant pixel graphics used to great effect
+ Nice music and sound
+ Creative Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Buggy: in-game freezing and occasional CTDs
- No save system (which would be almost forgivable if it weren't for the CTDs)
Cosmochoria is a unique rogue-like game of space exploration. If you can appreciate solid design, good pixel graphics, and a sense of humour, then you should definitely take a look. It's just a shame about the crashing.
(-1 for stability issues)
