Euro Truck Simulator 2 is all about living the dream that is professional trucking. The game even tells you as you begin that this is your dream job -- and who are you to argue? Armed with little more than enthusiasm, players begin their adventure humbly -- with a decrepit little garage in the home city of their choice, and a company with no trucks to its name.
The player begins by taking jobs for other companies, earning money with fuss-free escorts from one city to another, with an eye toward earning enough cash and purchasing a truck. An owned truck means more freedom, with higher-paying jobs that require more responsibility. When working directly for the player company, cargo is waiting at a select shipping yard and must be hitched to the truck before it can be taken to its ultimate destination. The next step from there is to start upgrading the garage, hiring other drivers to bring in more income, and eventually building a trucking empire that spans all of Europe.
The deeper you go, the more there is to do. Want to expand quickly? You can take out loans that need to be repaid. Want specialized drivers? They each level up the same way you do, and you can dictate the way they do. Of course, you also have to be mindful of expenses, be they repayments to the bank or fuel consumption by employees looking for work. There are a lot of ducks to get in a row, but the interface is user-friendly and information is constantly provided so nothing ever feels insurmountable.
More than simply a game about driving, Euro Truck Sim 2 boasts some roleplaying elements to keep things interesting. Successful jobs earn experience, which leads to skill points. Skill points can be spent upgrading one's proficiency in certain types of jobs, unlocking new types of cargo, or even investing in fuel efficiency. Improving personal abilities and building a business from one lone driver to an entire fleet is just as important as getting from A to B, and maintains a compelling grip on the experience.
That said, driving trucks in as realistic a fashion as possible is the bread and butter of any trucking sim, and Euro Truck will have fans covered. Offering a huge map spanning the length and breadth of Europe, there's plenty of time to be spent on the open road, and lots of distance to cover. Although you won't be undertaking journeys in real-time, a decent paying job is still quite the investment. I often found myself able to only play one job at a time, rather than stay glued to the screen all night long. As outwardly mundane as the experience may appear, it's a time sink that can prove a mental drain, and is best played with breaks in between.
There are a variety of controls and settings allowing for significant flexibility in terms of personal comfort. You can choose how complex your controls are, with automatic settings for those rocking the trusty keyboard, and more involved ones for those wanting to go the whole hog and set up a wheel. Whatever your available input, Euro Truck does a great job of covering you and ensuring you get into the game easily enough.
Accessibility is, in fact, one of its strongest suites. A solid tutorial guides newcomers, and the essential GPS is easy to understand, as is its clear and simple route map. My first job was an absolute disaster, with me getting the trailer stuck a number of times, managing to tip the vehicle over, and even getting so boxed in I had to call for emergency rescue. After my embarrassing first run, however, I quickly found myself getting the hang of things, and was soon bold enough to trek across whole countries in my quest for freight and fortune.
A lot of Euro Truck's experience is, expectedly, rooted in routine, but complacency manages to be quite a dastardly foe. Traffic lights, speed cameras, and the ever-present need to keep one's eyes on the road can always trip up an overconfident player, and as relaxing as long country drives may be, the pressure to avoid mistakes is present throughout. It's very easy to start getting too ♥♥♥♥♥ure, speeding along a motorway without regard to other drivers and strict speed limits. Every mistake translates into a financial penalty, damaged cargo reduces the payday, and dings suffered by an owned truck will have to be paid for at service stations.
When a mistake occurs, it's almost always the player's fault, but there are some moments where the computer-controlled road users compound an issue. Seemingly programmed to only ever drive forward, other vehicles have a nasty habit of doing nothing to avoid their part in a collision, and if you're ever trying to steer your way out of a tight spot, you'll get no help from other cars, willing as they are to close any gap in the road, no matter how minute, even if you were backing up to create the space they just filled. Should you manage to hit them, drivers have a nasty habit of refusing to move thereafter, sometimes causing you to suffer a second collision fine for smacking them again as you drive through them.
These frustrations inevitably pop up, but they're few and far between, and experienced drivers will be able to avoid many of the pitfalls that lead to such trouble. Despite the occasional irritation and the pressure to perform jobs well, Euro Truck Sim is still a largely cathartic experience. There's a therapy to be had in driving through a variety of countries, a sense of joy as you get closer to your destination, and a sense of accomplishment in performing such mundane tasks as refueling at gas stations and finding parking stops at which to grab some sleep. As you build your business up from nothing and take on more of managerial duties, it's hard not to feel pride over rewards well earned.
Although not the most visually advanced game, Euro Truck's believable presentation of Europe's roads and cities are nonetheless impressive. From the shape of the traffic lights to the atmosphere of the backdrops, there's a sense of individuality to each new territory you uncover, and the trucks themselves are lovingly recreated with an intricate level of detail. Owned trucks can be repainted and upgraded with all manner of parts, and as the player levels up, the potential for personalization expands.
Perhaps the most fun aspect of Euro Truck Sim 2, however, comes in the form of its music. With the simple tap of the "R" key, you can open up a menu packed with European Internet radio streams providing a wide variety of tunes. Whether you want some top forty hits or obscure French '80s tunes, you'll be able to find something worth digging. Being able to complete my deliveries with some Peter Gabriel's blasting through the speakers bumps up the enjoyment tenfold. There's also the option to queue up music from one's own PC, for those who don't wish to leave their aural stimulation to chance.
Euro Truck Simulator 2's following is well earned. It's not just a tongue-in-cheek dalliance, but an understandable dedication won by a game genuinely terrific at what it does. Being a simulator, there are inevitable parts of it that feel slow, and sometimes progression can be a bit of a drag, but it nevertheless manages to be an approachable sim with a smart implementation of more familiar "game-like" elements. A far cry from some of the more technical and unforgiving sims on the market, Euro Truck is as welcoming as it is authentic, forgiving while still prepared to reprimand those who fail. It's one of the best jumping points anybody curious about sims could have, and for everybody else, it's still just a fine experience in its own right.

Alright, I know everyone is gonna say one of two things about this game, and you've probably heard both a million times, but I thought I'd put my two cents in. In all honesty, this is one of the best games I've ever played. It's been a really good couple of years for indie games, but in recent history, only a few stick out in my mind. Sure, you got your Cupheads and your Bendy And The Ink Machines and your Five Nightses, and those all deserve a hardy round of applause for what they've accomplished. Those are by no means bad games. But they don't really hit that spot that I like from indie games. They can get away with so much, why not make full use of it? Why not go all out and really make something awesome that you can enjoy for a long, long time? Undertale hits that spot dead center. Right, this review is late, but sometimes it's good to see a more modern perspective on games.
Spec Ops: The Line is pretty goddamn awesome. If you (yes, you! Reader!) are too lazy to read the blurb, this game is about Captain Walker (voiced by the King of voice acting, Nolan North) and his team of Delta Force operatives who are sent into Dubai to find out what happened to the 33rd Battalion who attempted to evacuate Dubai before lethal sandstorms swept the city. Naturally, the 33rd failed. (If they'd have succeeded, it'd have made for a boring game, don't you think?) When you get there, you find that everything's gone to sh*t and anarchy has ensued, because humans can't help but tear each other apart whenever any form of disaster happens. (Humans, what a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, right?)
I know what a lot of you are thinking, having seen the title and the blurb- yeah, I know it sounds like a mediocre third person shooter with one or two cool parts, nothing to get excited about. That's where you're wrong. This game manages to capture you with a powerful narrative in which you are forced to witness the atrocities that happen in the aftermath of a disaster, and you even do a couple yourself. That being said, this isn't a game where you just see some awful crap and do some yourself, what the game does is show the emotions of Walker and his team. You see the effects that the harrowing scenes have on them and you watch them slowly descend into madness. You can make choices in what you do. Sometimes one choice is the smart thing to do, but is not necessarily the more moral choice. At times, you'll be forced to make the worse choice simply to survive, or to make things easier.
The story isn't just the good thing, although that would have most people hooked. The gunplay is a bit normal, but it's solid. Most weapons have alternate abilities that can change the way you play, or the tide of a battle. For example, the M4, one of the more common weapons. The alternate fire is a suppressor, which allows you to have an element of stealth. You can silently murder enemies, meaning you need to fight less of them when they inevitably catch you, whereas other weapons just make themselves more effective, such as the AK-47, another common weapon. This one has a burst fire mode as well as automatic, meaning you can accurately pick off enemies in a manner that would be difficult with a fully automatic weapon.
The level design is linear, but the beautiful -and wrecked- environments will command your attention. The environment isn't all about looks however, there are many ways you can use it to turn the tide of a battle, maybe by shooting out a window to allow tonnes of sand to crash down upon anyone unfortunate enough to be standing next to it, or by turning around a turret and decimating the enemy forces.
And now, the graphics. The game has aged well, thus far. It won't satisfy graphics wh*res (because they're never satisfied), but they still look pretty amazing, even today.
The game runs like a charm and holds up a solid 60 FPS, and very rarely begins to tank.

Since Gears was the first game to do this covershoot thing, it's allowed to do so and this Spec Ops right here, does have scenery in videogames which you have not seen before. Dubai deserts after sandstorm and thus atleast visually it's something new, even if it rides on the same old gameplay which gets old after 15mins of playing.

(This review is only for the single player part of the game)
I only bought this game because it is available on Linux and I heard it is kind of good. "Kind of good" is an understatement. I was really amazed by this game, it's one of the most profound games I've ever played. It can be seen as an "Anti Call of Duty", because the setting of the game could also be as well the setting of the next Call of Duty edition. But the story develops in a direction where Call of Duty (most likely) never will go: no glory, just madness. Even though the game starts in quite a standard way (not only in terms of story and setting, but also in terms of gameplay), the direction changes quite fast.
Speaking of gameplay: it is a solid cover shooter. The cover mechanics work quite well (most of the time), the shooting part is good and the AI of the enemies is really good. They are more than just cannon fodder and put some real pressure on the player. The gameplay itself might be standard nowadays, but the implementation is top-notch. The overall game experience is what you would expect from a AAA title, which is a big surprise, considering the topics covered by the game's story.
I have a few points of critique, but those points rather fit to modern shooters in general:
This game is one of the most underrated games in recent history. Apart from the story it fulfills all the criteria of a successful AAA title. It is really a pity, since this is the only AAA game (I know) that is brave enough not only to be mature, but also to raise unpleasant questions to the players and it didn't get the appreciation that it deserves. Seems like in future this will be only done by indie games.
Anyway, I was very surprised (in a positive way) by this game and I can recommend to everybody to see, what can be done with the medium computer games.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
Eekeemoo is a 3D action platformer with puzzle elements. The game was developed by Cogg Games, and is their first entry into the gaming market. Eekeemoo follows the journey of a young Eskimo, tentatively named; Eeekeemoo, and his quest to free his friends from the evil Dark Shard. It's a short title that can be completed in under four hours. As the  player traverses each stage of the game, new characters become playable and can be switched between during play. These characters have unique abilities that contribute to solving puzzles, breaching obstacles and even fending off boss creatures during game-play.
--------

The graphical assets of the game are actually quite nice. The unique art style gives the title a lot of charm despite being a bit basic. The character and terrains designs are interesting. Unfortunately the game's combat lacks some visual feedback aside from the main character and enemies glowing red upon taking damage. The game should run fine on any lower tier graphics card and CPU as it is not very demanding.
--------

The sound assets are something left to be desired. There's no real soundtrack to the game aside from a few notes that play throughout each stage. These notes are very dull and become tiresome quickly. The remainder of the sound effects are very basic combat and environmental noises.
--------

The game is a very basic platformer which some character switching mechanics. Throughout each stage the player will fight enemies and complete puzzles until the boss fight at the end. The player may switch between characters during play, with each character having different abilities that effect the terrain around them. This is important as many puzzles and obstacles can only be bypassed by using certain characters. That being said, the majority of these challenges are very simple along with the abilities used to solve them.
The game is playable, but just barely. There is no real way to stop incoming damage from enemies. Mashing the attack button is the best way to defeat hoards of zombies and even some bosses. There is no strategy involved in the combat what so ever, and becomes boring rapidly.
--------
The game lacks a lot of polish and it's combat system is not as solid as I'd like. I really wanted to like the game as the art style was very appealing to me. It is a very short title, and looked like it had the potential to be a good puzzle platformer. The game was just not engaging enough.

Batman: Arkham Origins is definitely a game. But I bet the one person on my friends list who reads these wants more. So in this Batman game you play as Batman. Big surprise there; and I was waiting so eagerly in line for this game so I could play as bloody Catwoman again. The difference is that this time you’re beating up thugs in all of Gotham city instead of just a part of it. Don’t know why because the map is the same size anyway. Obviously the people in charge of Gotham are true visionaries to double the city limits and then section it off. The character list was actually different this time though. Instead of fighting Two Face, Penguin, Bane and the Joker you will be fighting Deathstroke, Penguin, Bane and the Joker. Well I didn’t say it was a big difference. Apparently every villain is supposed to reflect something of Batman; the Joker is his opposite and Deathstroke is his equal in combat. So hell if I know what Penguin reflects. Perhaps it’s Batman’s insecurities or perhaps I’m just trying to make this segment longer. I should remember to cross out the last sentence later.
There are two things to do in Gotham city; king-hit pedestrians and label them as thugs or collect Riddler trophies, but let’s be honest, you won’t do the latter. You can finally traverse the Batcave; a privilege I never collected upon because there was nothing in the Batcave with the exception of clutter. Maybe there was a secret, but bugger if I could be bothered to find it. I now see this series taking the Halo methodology in the sense that the developers said Origins was going to be the final game, but now the Arkham series has been taken back by Warner Bros. who have already announced the next game. So I guess I’ll see you back here when that bolt from the blue arrives. And for the record, this game has the twisted oddity of not having Nolan North voice acting a superhero/villain.

To give this game a bad review would be difficult. It did so many things right that it seems to outweigh the few problems it has. From the small details that make the surroundings gain depth and story. Or to the large areas that explain some of the history to the game/series. The game combines combat and story almost as one. And you can choose just how much you want to do of either. If you want combat and challenges, then you can do them. But if you want to learn more of the stroy and history of the dystopian land, then you are free to wander and explor every crevis you find. Along with the attention to detail and the unique envionment the game puts out there, it also speaks volumes when it comes to the open world stand point. The game doesn't limit you to an area. Once you are out of the gates you are free to drive off and explore the vast wasteland as much as you like.
Furthermore the developers put a lot of effort forth to emphisise story and Max's own motives. And little by little they begin to unravel more of what Max is truley driven by. As said before the envionment is beautiful with details that reveal a world that "once was but now is." It is amazing how they seemed to create their own language and system for the society that is now left. From the "Long Lookers" to the "Huge fans that people used to fly with." All of the wording seems to help build that sense of atmosphere to the game.
Naturally the game does have it's issues, like the leveling system that doesn't seem all that well intigrated due to the requirment of having to finish challenges and other misculanious tasks. Along with the leveling comes the tokens to upgrade Max. When interacting with Griffa you learn more of Max's past, this was a good idea in some ways, but the game eventually gets to repeating itself and the tokens eventually get phased out making it hard to know if you caught all of the bits. Other than some design flaws the game had few glitches in my own play through. (Besides getting stuck on top of a light.)
Overall the game was and is a joy to play, I always seem to find more subtle hints or interesting areas to explore. And if you like the type of game I just describbed then I would highly recommend picking up the game as soon as you can.

This game has a great storyline and a great soundtrack. The story starts out as what seems to be a clear-cut situation, but quickly dissolves into one of the most well-written stories I've seen in a game. It puts an interesting perspective on how someone's mind can deal with extreme trauma or guilt, as to go so far as to fabricate situations to try and justify themselves.
The score is great, with most of the combat tracks fitting really well with the fast-paced action. The licenced soundtrack is great too, with one of the seminal characters to the plot playing backing music during certain firefights and situations, adding a few "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥this is cool" moments.
It's a shame that people mostly see it just as a third-person cover shooter. I just wish they'd added more to the co-op mode, instead of roughly five missions which each take only maybe 10 minutes for a good team to finish. But then again, the whole multiplayer aspect was "required" by the publishers so Yager Development, who didn't even plan on having a multiplayer mode at the cost of improving the single player, just had to throw it in at the last minute to appease 2K.
Still, for the price it's usually at, it's way worth it, if not for the great soundtrack and narrative at the minimum.

I do NOT recommend this game. It's painfully clear that the makers were trying to make a point with the game, story and gameplay. But it's extremely heavy handed, in your face and sometimes makes absolutely no sense.
So let's start from the beginning. The game is a Modern Military Shooter and it's got every single trope from these games, including regenerating health, bland cover mechanics, billions of soldiers, rambo-style firing from the hip, unskippable cutscenes and more testosterone than a juvenile detention camp.
It tries to be dark, realistic and gritty, but then throws you in a situation where you mow down 50-60 enemies all on your own (or with your two teammates). There are even situations where AG (Air-to-ground) missiles strike the ground not five feet from you and all that results in is a bit of an action scene in slow-mo, a building falling apart but you escaping unscathed. It's got a serious problem with keeping it's setting and tone. Is it dark and realistic? Trying to make a moral point? Is it a dumb covershooter? It can't seem to make up its mind about what it's trying to be.
The gameplay is bland, bordering on downright dull. It's just moving to a battle arena area, mow down 30-50 enemies, move to the next cutscene, new arena. Rince and repeat. It's incredibly dull and if it wasn't for the story, I would've quit after less than half an hour. It's that dull.
It's very obvious the point of this game was to make a moral point in killing and what you're actually doing in a game like this. Killing hundreds upon hundreds of soldiers. Yet the game never gives you an option to stop and ponder these things. Nor does it give you any meaningful choices. Oh, so you want to berate me for using white phosphorous on a bunch of american soldiers, and accidently on a bunch of civilians? Sure, but then give me an alternate route! You can't berate me for making a choice where I had no other choice.
Then there's situations which are obvious "shooter traps". At one point, someone you care about is killed by an angry mob of civilians, and you're put in a situation where unless you wait for a few seconds, it's going to be the airport scene all over again. Try to walk through the civilians, they nearly one-hit kill you with a push. It's blindingly obvious that the game wants you to shoot the civilians so that it can complain about what a horrible human being you are later. Now, there's actually a way out of that situation that does not involve massacre, so I'll give the game that.
The game at one point makes a quip at how killing civilians isn't allowed in war and adds a contemptful "But you don't even care". Don't presume to know me, my dear game. It pisses me off.
But on the whole this game is frustrating, extremely heavy handed, DRENCHED in MMS tropes and has bland and dull gameplay. Unless you love these kinds of games, please stay away! It's raising some questions, but it does is so extremely "in your face" that it just becomes tiresome and preachy.

One of the best things of Ori and the Blind Forest is the absolutely amazing soundtrack and the smooth graphic. I love games like this. I even bought the OST and I am listening to it at work because it's so great and helps me concentrate :)
All in all: This game can be pretty annoying on the one hand. On the other hand I had to continue because of story, soundtrack and graphical reasons.
692 deaths later: I DO NOT REGRET PLAYING THIS AWESOME GAME.

Graphics: This game is quite pretty. Nothing spectacular or mind-blowing, but there are moments when you have to balance driving and admiring the scenery without smashing into anything. There are also a few mods that can enhance your experience in this regard.
Audio: The music is pretty standard, but all of the other audio in the game is fantastic. The sounds of the vehicles are very realistic, especially since they have been updated over time. There are videos on the SCS website of how they record the engine noises, and it's very well done.
Gameplay: This is a very relaxing game. Not exciting by any means, but it can be quite satisfying to see your progress over time, and the driving can be enjoyable on its own. The progression itself is quite good. As you earn money, you'll be able to purchase other trucks for your company and hire drivers to operate them while you are on your own job to create additional revenue. You begin to snowball, and you eventually reach the point where money is no longer a concern, but that takes a considerable amount of time. You also earn XP, unlocking the ability to take more jobs. There is a decent variety of trucks in the base game to keep your interest, and this is one of those games that has an absolutely massive modding potential. There is a load of trucks, cargo, maps, truck parts, and more available to download to keep the game fresh. And don't let the DLC turn you away, as the majority of it is paint packs, which aren't necessary by any means. The other DLC, such as the Going East expansion, are superb.
TL;DR: This isn't really a game for everyone, but if you have interest, I do recommend picking it up on sale. It's a high-quality simulator, and it's very satisfying to progress in. Overall a great game to play to relax or chill while watching a video or listening to some music.

My Review of the Full Steam Version of Euro Truck Simulator 2
Overview:
Pros :
-	Acceptable and quite realistic graphical fidelity
-	Incredibly relaxing and realistic gameplay
-	A humongous map size with expansions adding to it as well
Cons :
-	AI keeps on crashing into me for no reason(seems only to happen with Peugeots)
-	I have to explain to people why I have nothing better to do than drive virtual trucks around all day
See My Full Review Below:
At the time of the writing of this review, my Steam Library tells me that I’ve pumped approximately 14 hours into ETS 2, and 5 hours is the minimum cut off point for the amount of time I spend in a game before writing a review.
ETS 2 is a game about driving trucks around the entirety of Europe, earning money to build up your empire of trucks to conquer the industry with. At first I was skeptical about how the gameplay would be enjoyable, and not monotonous and boring, but now I realise that it is the main point of the game. I cannot tell you just how relaxing it is to come home after a hard day’s work, to sit down by my desk, sink into my chair, boot up ETS 2 and just drive for an hour or two. What makes this even more palatable is the addition of the radio system, whereby which you can put music on your PC into the game’s built in sound system. As I play without headphones in this game(I use a whole room surround sound setup), I feel that I can enjoy music that I played to death years ago once again, which is so fundamentally pleasing to my soul that it is worth the entire game on its own.
In regards to the gameplay, I have to point out that I have never driven before, let alone a truck, and therefore do not know what it feels like to drive one of the things. However, I should say that when a trailer is attached, the driving mechanics feel weighted and heavy, with me needing to swing out into corners with a lot of momentum to get around some bends. However, with my DualShock 4 in hand, it feels easy to pull off accurate turns, and the vibration allows me to feel the road beneath the truck. The control scheme features dead-zones and wheel support, and I would recommend not using a keyboard and mouse with the game as they do not provide much in the way of accurate turning.
A minor issue is the finicky AI system, which has a tendency to crash into you when taking a turn. For example, I pull out into the bend after waiting for all the traffic to stop and let me through, and a car or van(usually a Peugeot) slams into the side of my trailer(usually filled with noxious chemicals or acid). This is a minor issue with how the AI recognises the player and could be easily fixed by linking all the AI to one mind which stops before the player who is turning. The other issue is of a social matter and will only apply to some people, however, I am often quizzed on why I choose to spend my time in a virtual job that brings in no real income and ‘wastes time’. To them I have to say, “It brings me enjoyment”, and when you look at it in the scheme of things it does seem a little odd!
Overall, I recommend that you purchase Euro Truck Simulator 2 as it provides a relaxing and appealing experience. There is a free demo I recommend you try first, as it is quite lenient until you level up beyond a certain point. Just make sure that you know what you have to say when people ask you, “But what’s the point?”

I know that Arkham Origins shipped with game-stopping bugs which took a (relatively) long time to patch. I know that this situation angered a lot of people, and turned them against the game. It would've angered me also.
But ... I've only been playing Batman: Arkham Origins recently, now that it's been all patched up ...
And I love it. I really, really love it. This is the best Batman game I've played since Batman: Arkham Asylum, and pound-for-pound I think I like this one even better.
Why? Well here are some of the main reasons:
- The open-world Gotham feels like an open-world this time, not just a "game arena". The city is properly large, and the visual design by WB Montreal is pitch-perfect.
The game takes place in Gotham on Christmas Eve, and anyone who's grown up in an urban cold-weather setting will know, they got it absolutely right -- the lighting, the look of the sky and the weather, all of it.
In short, Gotham in Arkham Origins looks and feels like it could be a real place, a place moody and atmospheric, but real.
Also, the size of the city this time out helps with believability -- I wasn't running into the same seven respawn groups every time I crossed town to undertake a mission, like I was in Arkham City.
There are respawned badguys in Arkham Origins, certainly, but the city is big enough now that you're not seeing the same short-list of respawns every time you travel.
-- The story makes solid sense this time. The storyline of Arkham City made less sense the more you actually thought about it. Even allowing for the fact that it was a superhero game didn't change the fact that the plot was more and more preposterous the more you focused on it.
By contrast, the premise of Arkham Origins is simple but sensible, and the story unfolds very well. The setup is that Bruce Wayne has recently returned to Gotham after his training, and has just started out fighting crime. Batman's already making a dent in the city's corruption, so one of Gotham's crime lords puts a one-night-only price on Batman's head, bringing eight notorious assassins to town. And that's not the story, that's just the setup.
Even the Riddler Trophy collectibles from previous Arkham games are actually worked into the story this time, becoming part of the plot, instead of just an immersion-breaking "mini-game".
Some people have complained about the lack of the familiar voice cast in Arkham Origins, but I found the voice cast surprisingly good throughout. Roger Craig Smith sounds like a younger version of Kevin Conroy, but his version of the Batman tranmits less detached certainty, and more hints of suppressed rage. Likewise, Troy Baker's take on Mark Hamill's Joker is uncannily good, but his younger Joker is less baroque, less droll, and more pointedly dangerous.
Alfred is wonderfully written and voiced. As a friend of mine pointed out, you actually believe that this is the man who raised Bruce Wayne.
The excellent fighting system from previous games is here again in all its glory. Using a game crontroller on your PC, as opposed to a mouse and keyboard, will make the battles in this game much more reflexive, fluid and intuitive, and I recommend that route.
Is the game perfect? Of course not. Some of the assassin "boss battles" can feel a little too easy -- even to an average-skill gamer like myself. But I will say this: even though some of the boss battles were a bit easy, they never bored me, as in Arkham City.
There are probably other minor flaws in the game I've forgotten, because the good really does outweigh the bad here, in my opinion, and by a large margin.
Even the batsuit is cool in Arkham Origins, and reflects the fact that Batman is more of a martial arts brawler than an acrobat in the world of these games. The costume here nods to that difference, but still looks very much like Batman.
TL;DR? It's one of the most enjoyable superhero games I've ever played, and I recommend it highly to anyone who might be interested.

If you already have played some of the other batman games in this sereis, you properly know about the gameplay by now, and therefore you can skip that part, since there have been no big changes on that part.
I have a lot to say to this game, and therefore I`ll split this review into smaller topics.
gameplay:
The gameplay is simple but fun! You use your mouse to curse around, and click the left mouse button in order to attack the enemy you have targeted, you use your right mouse button to counter attacking enemeys. Along the way, you will unlock more items, and therefore more attack options. This is the open combat gameplay, but there is also the stealh element. This means there is normally two ways to do your job, but sometimes the game either gives you a stealh mission, or the open combat system.
The stealh system is just you, the bat, sneaking around taking down your opponents one by one, without getting detcted. If you get spotted the army of enemys will attack you with heavy guns, that hurts a lot.
All in all the combat system has`t change from the last two titels in the sereis, but I personally like this combat system, and this is a part of the game, I would not see any changes of. All in all the combat is great, it`s action packt, and trust me, the bosses makes the combat even more intense.
Bosses:
Speaking of the bosses, they are all great, and diffrent mechanics must be used, to defeat each and evey one, I will of couse not spoil to much, but I can tell you that the game usses known enemys from the batman universe such as Bane and Firefly, and usses lesser known if not new, like Electrocutioner and Cobberhead.
The battles usses diffrent mechanics deppending on the boss. Bane is very strong, and you must be fast, and outsmart him, in order to deafet him. Firefly is flying around and you must pull him down while avoding the bombs he throws. Cobberhead is making you believe there is more of her, and you must fight an army, while searching for the real one. Deathstroke is a boss where you must counter at the right time, while giving deadly blows at the same tme.
There are more bosses but they are all very good, and diffrent to change the gameplay a bit. They are all making your heart pump, and every single blow is satesfieing. The last "boss" is like the fight in Final Fantasy where Cloud uses the omnislash, it`s only for show, but trust me it`s a great ending.
World:
The world is what will become arkham city, in the game before this. The world is very open, and you can do whatever you want like extra missions or just beating up bad guys.
Bonus missions:
There is a lot to do on the side here, there are so many extra things to do, and things to find, just to name some of them, and why I liked them or not, I am going to go through some of the onece, that either was great or disapointed me.
The riddler is back, or accually this is the first time he meets batman. This time, he has found intel on importeant peaople of Gotham, and you must find this intel and stop the Riddler. The diffrence from the other games is, that the intel is a bit easyer to find, and the puzzels are sometimes really lazy made. I was very dissapointed in this part of the game, sure it was fun to find the intel, but not as fun as find the Riddlers ridels as in the first game.
You also get to know when there has been a humerside now and agian, therefroe you go into detective mode, and search for clues. This was a really cool idea and we really get to see batmans detective skills in action here. The only problem is that there is not much to it, you just follow the clues, untill you find the anwser. I thought this part could have been executed better, and made you the one to solve the puzzel not batman.
The Mad Hatter sidequest is really great, he makes the bat enter a dream like stage, kinda like the one Scarecrow makes you go trough in the first game, the inverment is so great, and you get to see the wicked world of the Mad Hatter.
There are also other sidequst, but they are just beat the bad guys sidequests.
The sidequests where very great, and I enjoyed solving most of them.
Story:
The story takes place before the other two games in the series and is therefore a prequal. The game takes of with batman fighting killer Crock and afterwards escapese the police. So this is before the police trusts batman. We find out that there is a bounty on Batmans head, given by Black Mask and batman most now stop Blsck Mask, while avoding the assasins there is trying to kill him. Batman then finds out that someone has taken the mask, from Black Mask. That means someone is pretending to be Black Mask, and is pulling the strings for a plan, there will set Gotham in chaos.
The tvist (spoilers):
Black Mask has been overrun by the Joker, and it turns out he is just using the money he steels later on, to make bombs all over Gotham. We know the Joker, and therefore there is not motevation to blow up the city, other than to see pure chaos. This is also the first time that Batman meets Joker, and we get to relive Jokers tragic story, from a sorry comedian to the criminal he is.
Batman then hunts around to find the Joker, and that makes Blackgate prison there final showdown. There is a final secuence where Batman beats up Joker, in an epic beatdown. This leads up to the rivalship bewtween Batman and Joker.
spoilers over............

Mad Max; open world post-apocalyptic driver with Batman:Arkham/Assassin's Creed style combat.
You start the game driving your classic Interceptor; which is then taken from you in order to start off the main chapter of the game - building your Opus Magnus. Every quest, mission and piece of scrap goes toward upgrading either Max himself or various parts of your new car. This particular economy runs on 'scrap' I should mention; which you will find -everywhere- in small amounts.
This leads to a enormous amount of grinding.
I had in fact not realized how short the main story of the game was until I had finallly given up on the various location clearing missions. While I cIocked in at thirty-three hours a ton of that time was spent shooting the same scarecrow posts, snipers, convoys and minefields over and over again.
There are a number of upgrades for your vehicle including:
Rammer, Armour, Engine, Acceleration, Stabilization, Tires (Handling), Boarder Spikes, Harpoon Gun, Explosive Harpoon, Shotgun upgrades (MAX), side flamethrowers, Nitro and various customization options.
All in all it's not a bad game, but it's incredibly grindy. Get it on sale if you can!

I will start by saying, this game does not want you to buy it. And I am dead serious about that. The developers even said as much themselves.
But lets say you were considering buying it anyway. What is Spec Ops? Its a standard cover based third-person shooter. Ever play Gears of War, Kill-Switch, the recent Ghost Recon games, or GTA5 and you know what I mean. Slow paced, but throws more at you. But that's now why you're considering it anyway, its the story.
Well let me get back to that first statement that may have confused you. This game is about "subverting traditional game tropes" which is an asinine way of saying its story really resonates with people concerned with the surface of storytelling. How it does this is by presenting scripted scenes to the player that are sad, then telling the player its their fault it happened. All this hinges on the player being emotionally connected to what's going on. And by going on, I mean dead civilians. Something which has always felt cheap and uninspired. Especially when you as a playerr know its completely disconnected from what you're doing.
That's the problem here. The game takes a huge gamble on whether you emotionally resonate with fictional people you have no connection to. And does this with scenes it forces you to participate in to progress. Which brings us to the real problem with this game. How you win, is to not play it. This was actually said by their staff. You're meant to buy this game, and if you want to be considered a good person, you'd turn the game off immediately. Yes they are trying to make this into a moral judgement on you as a person.
Keep in mind the pricetag they're asking here. As well as the fact this came out before Steam refunds even existed. At the time you would have had to have bought a retail copy and traded in for either store credit, or not even a 1/5th of what you payed for it. Yet what they're expecting from you, is to enjoy being told something they made is your fault, or spend money to NOT play a video game. Some have called it art because of what they were trying to accomplish. To which i say, making an artistic statement doesn't cost people money to understand it. And if you think it does, you're not an artist worth caring about.
I've avoided spoilers here because they're irrelevant to bring up. They're not what makes this game a waste of time. The game itself does, by existing.

I purchased this game at a friend's recommendation because I was looking for more LGBT content in gaming. When discussing the game after a couple hours of play, he managed to sum up my feelings pretty well: "we are just grasping for straws for the content we want".
The Good: I expected to hate the combat system with its non-violent options, but I ended up feeling like it was one of the best mechanics of the game. It made combat a bit more interesting, and added variety to something that could otherwise be formulaic. I ended up loving the concept.
The characters are quirky and interesting, and I think the retro art style works very well. I also enjoyed pieces of the humor, and the first hour was fun.
The Bad: Too much of my total play time was spent trying to make my Xbox One controller work. And it still doesn't work very well; if I nudge the thumbstick, it tries to automatically move the character down and left until it's nudged back... Going full screen also didn't play nicely with my graphics card, and even caused the card to disable itself until reboot twice.
Normally I enjoy linear games--I grew up on the original Final Fantasy games, Earthbound, Phantasy Star, etc--but this was a really terrible kind of linear. It plays more like one of those boring point and click adventure games. It does nothing to hide that you're locked onto a path; you're just following a single road and don't really diverge from it. Everything you see and do is on that road, and most of your progress is from rather shallow button-pushing. This comes from the "puzzles" having their answers spelled out for you with signs, instead of just having little hints.
Overall, the story and interactions just felt really naive--not in an innocent, childlike sense of Earthbound, but more in a, "you're dumbing it down in a faux sense of cuteness" kind of way. As an example, I was irked at the notion of being able to flirt with someone who's physically assaulting you, and opting to go on a date with them instead of continuing to fight. Interactions like these felt uncomfortable.
Because of the shallow, naive content, I've hit a wall where I just don't feel like continuing the game to completion.

An excellent third person shooter with tons of ability to customize your look and your vehicle. The game consists of two very large (1000+ meters) city maps where many teams of either faction are engaged in missions simultaneously. All in all a fantastic third person shooter that I spent hundreds of hours playing!
Pros
- Full customization of vehicle and character with large multitudes of clothing and the ability to make completely custom designs. Every character and vehicle looks completely unique.
- Large array of guns with custom skins, though most of the skins have to be bought through the in game store.
- Progression system. If you like these, it's there. You get quick access to the base versions of guns, so it's not too bad. Though, things such as the OPGL and OSMAW come much later, as well as a couple of the cars.
- Frequently matched against new people, so you're not playing against the same team over and over again like in other multiplayer shooters.
Cons
- The open world can lead to griefing and "ghosting" on occasion, or just some frustration as you're trying to drive to the next objective as quickly as you can while getting rammed by cars driven by other players.
- Some of the guns in the in game store which cost real money to buy can be considered across the board better than some of the guns available as free to play.

APB Reloaded is a cops and robbers MMO that couldn't quite pull it off. The game has SO much potential that it almost makes me angry when they fall short on almost every game features. The lack of locational damage means accuracy is not needed. Combat often ends in a jumping match, and corner camping is one of the few strategies thanks to the third person camera.
The games micro transaction system and F2P model are majorly flawed. When buying guns in game you rent them allowing you to use it for a set amount of time before you have to rent it again. Buying an account bound weapon costs more but allows any of your characters to use it. This will run you anywhere from 20-55 dollars. You can also purchase character bound weapons for less, these cost about 10-40 dollars. When buying cars you can do the same rent, or own. An account bound car will run you about  15-35 dollars.
All of these prices can be discounted by owning a premium subscription.
Other premium benefits include a 20% off the cost of premium subscriptions, up to a 90% bonus to all Contact Standing (XP) Gains, 125% bonus to all Cash gains, 20% discount in the Armas Marketplace, 50% reduced cool down on activated abilities (Field Supplier / Nitro Booster), advanced access to Customization Suites (50 Symbols per Vehicle / Clothing item. 100 layers per Symbol), removal of in-game premium subscription advertising (which pops up at the end of every other mission), extended duration for Armas Trials for Weapon and Vehicle Trials.
Premium costs about 10 dollars for 30 days and gets cheaper the more time you buy. All in game prices are set in G1C which come in inconvenient amounts to make you buy more or additional packs. An example of this is a non-premium 1 month subscription costs 999 points. You can only get 999 points by buying spending $15 (1200 credits) because $10 is only 800 credits.
The best part of this 3rd person MMO shooter is the customization. While it is extremely limited as a non-premium user you can still add some flavor to your character or vehicle. Premium allows for you to create a truly unique look with 50 Symbols per Vehicle / Clothing item. At 100 layers per Symbol.
The in game missions are not over exciting and after playing for about 2-3 hours you will have played all of the available missions. Other players not in your mission are still in the world and can interact with you. They can do things like ram your vehicle or block you in buildings, but it is difficult for them to directly kill you.
The favored anti-cheat system of APB is Punkbuster. This program doesn't work very well at all and allows hackers to run rampant. In my short amount of play time I had encounter roughly 1 hacker per hour.
Overall this game has such a great idea, yet such terrible terrible execution in nearly everything the developers tried to do.

They made an excellent platformer/metroidvania game even better. Two new areas expand the story of an important character in a simple, yet very poignant manner. There are new difficulty levels for those who found the game too hard or too easy -- even an One Life mode for the brave. Two new skills that open up a lot of possibilities for speedrunning and integrate very well with the original game areas, which have been modified to accomodate them in a way that still allows you to progress through the entire world without them.
You can now teleport to any Spirit Well you found. You can revisit areas that were previously locked. You can continue adventuring even after you beat the final level. Literally everything that could be improved was improved.
Again, the only downside is that if you're here for the experience the game eventually ends. Speedrunners get a lot more out of it, though.

Cosmochoria doesn’t seem to follow a specific linear storyline, instead it is a very do-at-your-own-pace style game. You do unlock snippets of story as you revive more planets but it’s never done in a ‘do this’ or ‘follow this’ kind of layout. The general story behind Cosmochoria is very simple yet very enjoyable. You’re a little astronaut tasked with reviving planets which are dying out across the galaxy. Armed with nothing more than a jetpack, a single seed and a small gun it’s up to you to save the galaxy before it’s too late.
The gameplay is simple, you start on a planet which will vary in size play from play and you must start by planting seeds which you’ll only have one of at first. You must plant and tend to your seed whilst defending yourself from the various enemies you’ll run into with your aforementioned peashooter. Once your seed reaches full sproutyness it’ll give you more seeds and heal that planet a little. After you’ve planted enough seeds the planet will be fully healed and you’ll be rewarded with a chest which can have many things inside ranging from building blocks to random items or snippets or information and tips. Since there is nothing forcing you to leave the planet you are welcome to stay and keep planting there but you’re better off using your jetpack to fly off and find another planet to save.
Each planet has it’s own center of gravity and once you leave you’ll be floating through space using your (limited) jetpack fuel to guide you around. If you decide to fly right out of the edge of the map you WILL die so don't try it like I did. As you’re travelling through spaces you’ll can come across ‘glitches’ which teleport you elsewhere on the map which can be fantastic or really, really awful so use them which caution.
The enemies you encounter start fairly simple but as you progress and heal more planets you’ll find harder enemies. When you kill anything it’ll drop crystals which you’re able to level up yourself with once you die and the bigger the enemy and harder, the more crystals they drop. Bosses will spawn periodically when you heal a certain amount of planets and they are a lot bigger and stronger. It’s usually wise to have a small base on a planet by then to avoid being obliterated right away since bosses can seek you out from anywhere they are. You’re not alone when it comes to killing enemies and defending yourself though! You’ll earn something called ‘building blocks’ which allow you to build various towers on the planets you land on which can range from turrets to healing towers. Building blocks do not seem to be massively common and have to be bought with crystals if you can't find any and run out so spend them wisely.
Since you cannot level up during a run you’ll find yourself dying a bit at first until you manage to get some crystals and get a bit stronger but once you get the hang of it you’ll be able to survive a fair amount of time each time but at first it can feel a little bit grindy. Since you’re able to choose what you spend your crystals on in which order though you can quickly progress the way you want choosing to prioritize health over speed if you’re dying a lot or focusing on jetpack fuel if you find yourself running a little low.
The further you progress and the more planets you heal will allow you to start further in the game each time so you are not constantly having to beat the same bosses over and over. Planets are randomly generated each playthrough so nothing is quite the same and there is plenty for you to explore ranging from NPCs, random backstory snippets and giant bosses so it never feels boring and has high replayability.
--- Addictive gameplay
--- A level-your-own-way system.
--- Randomized world each time for extra replayability.
--- Great graphics with accompanying soundtrack.
--- Wide range of weapons, planets and enemies.
--- Very friendly and active dev who is quick to solve any issues.
--- Can feel a little grindy.
--- Gets a little repetitive after a while.
--- No saving during runs: if you exit you have to start over.
I got Cosmochoria in a bundle and this game alone is well worth the price of the bundle itself. Hours and hours of relaxing gameplay paired with cute graphics and a brilliant little soundtrack makes Cosmochoria a fantastic purchase and a game well worth checking out. Though a little hard at first the game eases up a lot and becomes a very enjoyable and time-consuming game. Well worth grabbing on sale.

This game is phenomenal. That's all that needs to be said, review over...
Ok, just kidding. I'm not the kind of guy who reviews anything with a single sentence or short paragraph (nothing against people that do that, it's just not my thing). If you've read any of my other reviews before, you'll notice that I often end up writing a short story about games that I like. I'll try to keep this shorter if possible, for the sake of conciseness.
At face value, this game might just look like a 2.5D version of Minecraft and upon playing it, it does feel that way at first. However, as you delve into the game, you discover an extraordinary sandbox with countless hours of fun and creativity awaiting you. This game is more than just digging and building in a relatively empty world. Each world you create is unique with countless layers of different biomes and atmospheres. You might be digging down through an average grassy landscape and then come across old mine shafts (with rideable mine carts), ancient temples riddled with monsters, a massive beehive with a gargantuan queen bee boss, occult dungeons or even the underworld, which sits at the very bottom of every world and is extremely dangerous. And later, once your character has grown in power and gotten better gear, you might find your way up into sky islands or space itself, the former of which often has some great loot and scenery.
I've spent just as much time exploring the world as I've spent building my ever-growing castle complex. When you think about it, how is it that a world that was procedurally generated and has absolutely NO story behind it (other than stories you create yourself) is more intriguing and enjoyable to explore than some hand-crafted open world games? Somehow, this game's generation algorithms end up creating worlds that genuinely feel ancient and massive, but also detailed. It's all procedural generation but it FEELS like a hand-crafted world that was created with an impeccable attention to detail.
Despite how fun the game can be in solo play, the game REALLY becomes fun when you play it with friends. I've explored my own home world quite a bit with friends and yet I've barely scratched the surface (literally and metaphorically). There is still so much yet to uncover that even with a whole group of friends, it'd take a long time to explore everything... and that's just in a SMALL world. You can set your world to be small, medium or large with three difficulty modes: soft-, medium- and hardcore. Personally, I don't recommend hardcore until you have a lot of friends to play with and make sure it's a character you can afford to lose. And don't even get me started on how fun boss fights can be, especially with friends. Who knew that a 2.5D building/exploration sandbox could have such enjoyable boss fights?
This game is a prime example of why indie games are often better than AAA ones. Free updates such as seasonal ones (the Christmas one is active as this review is being written) keep the game feeling alive and fresh, and the price of the game itself is not just reasonable... it's an absolute STEAL. You get such a huge bang for your buck with this game. The only "flaw" (if you can call it that) is that it can take awhile to properly get 'into' the game. You start off with pretty much nothing and genuinely have to work, fight and craft your way to the top. Or you can find a multiplayer server where the server hosts are generous, but that's only if you don't mind getting a massive boost right away. There is still something very rewarding about delving into a dungeon and finding a great weapon that, while it may not be the BEST weapon in the game, still makes you feel accomplished and rewards you with a better piece of gear than you had before.
To summarize, if there's only one indie game I could recommend to pretty much anyone, it's this. It takes a little patience to get into at first but once you do, the game opens up and becomes an unforgettable experience that delivers non-stop fun. 10/10 all the way.

APB Reloaded is a cops and robbers MMO that couldn't quite pull it off. The game has SO much potential that it almost makes me angry when they fall short on almost every game features. The lack of locational damage means accuracy is not needed. Combat often ends in a jumping match, and corner camping is one of the few strategies thanks to the third person camera.
The games micro transaction system and F2P model are majorly flawed. When buying guns in game you rent them allowing you to use it for a set amount of time before you have to rent it again. Buying an account bound weapon costs more but allows any of your characters to use it. This will run you anywhere from 20-55 dollars. You can also purchase character bound weapons for less, these cost about 10-40 dollars. When buying cars you can do the same rent, or own. An account bound car will run you about  15-35 dollars.
All of these prices can be discounted by owning a premium subscription.
Other premium benefits include a 20% off the cost of premium subscriptions, up to a 90% bonus to all Contact Standing (XP) Gains, 125% bonus to all Cash gains, 20% discount in the Armas Marketplace, 50% reduced cool down on activated abilities (Field Supplier / Nitro Booster), advanced access to Customization Suites (50 Symbols per Vehicle / Clothing item. 100 layers per Symbol), removal of in-game premium subscription advertising (which pops up at the end of every other mission), extended duration for Armas Trials for Weapon and Vehicle Trials.
Premium costs about 10 dollars for 30 days and gets cheaper the more time you buy. All in game prices are set in G1C which come in inconvenient amounts to make you buy more or additional packs. An example of this is a non-premium 1 month subscription costs 999 points. You can only get 999 points by buying spending $15 (1200 credits) because $10 is only 800 credits.
The best part of this 3rd person MMO shooter is the customization. While it is extremely limited as a non-premium user you can still add some flavor to your character or vehicle. Premium allows for you to create a truly unique look with 50 Symbols per Vehicle / Clothing item. At 100 layers per Symbol.
The in game missions are not over exciting and after playing for about 2-3 hours you will have played all of the available missions. Other players not in your mission are still in the world and can interact with you. They can do things like ram your vehicle or block you in buildings, but it is difficult for them to directly kill you.
The favored anti-cheat system of APB is Punkbuster. This program doesn't work very well at all and allows hackers to run rampant. In my short amount of play time I had encounter roughly 1 hacker per hour.
Overall this game has such a great idea, yet such terrible terrible execution in nearly everything the developers tried to do.

Original Ori Review: First Edition (I have 47+ hours on this edition)
This is one of those games that deserve the 'Perfect Game' category. Perfect balance between action, puzzles, challenges and rewarding cutscenes that will keep you at the edge of the seat. You will end this game with a smile on your face and quite possible, tears.
Congratulations to the devs and thanks for creating a game that can be called without any doubt, a masterpiece.
I have to make a special mention to the Music, since it is a great part of the experience.
Gameplay 10/10
Graphics 10/10
Music 10/10
About Definitive Edition:
Definitive Edition adds background story on Naru and a new map. Both additions have the same level of quality as the original game. Also there are new powers, fast travelling between zones and difficulty levels, which is great because now my 5 yo kid can play the game by himself in the easy difficulty.
Conclusion: DE is great for re-playing the entire game, and the new songs in the soundtrack are really *really* good. Upgrading worths every penny.
*Edit 11/23: Nominating this game for “I'm Not Crying, There's Something In My Eye” Award : )

I bought the "normal version" and this version too.
The thing I've noticed immediately is that in this Definitive Edition, the game seems well optimized. It does not stutter anymore on my pc and I have good fps almost all the time. Since I already had the "normal version", I had the chance to buy it at a small price (it seems like it will stay like that).
The main differences between the normal version and this are new areas, mechanics and artwork.
Now, let's talk about the game itself. And that's the hardest part since I don't know what to say more about it... This is just pure art... Great gameplay, amazing art style, great story and soundtrack, amazing action sequences and beautiful environmental design.
This game gave some awards to the indie company which developed it (awarded by its animation, art direction and music composition, more than one time).
About the story, I only will say this: after like 10 minutes of gameplay, this game already put you on board of the "feels train"...
This game will always have a special place in my heart (along with Unravel). 10/10

But don't let the game's "virtual" simplicity fool you, this game will _punish_ you for not thinking of the actions you take. Growing up, Mad Max was one of my favorite things. It gave birth to an entire genre of entertainment in both film and games. It's hard to imagine another franchise more influential.  Well, Lord of the Rings. Conan definitely, I guess Star Trek. Ok, fine, it's really easy to imagine a franchise that was more influential. But there was nothing quite as novel as the post-apocalyptic Clint Eastwood male-melodrama archetype searching for meaning in a barren, womanless world destroyed by men (oooh, symbols!).
So what I did was watch the cutscene of this game, which was kind of cool I guess. It was like one from the movie. I didn't need it to be excited about Mad Max. In fact, it would have been better to have started in a place of relative safety, and let the arc pick up after 10 minutes of learning about the world.
I found a dog. Then I lost my dog. There was some dog food eating, which was nostalgic. I walked up the dirt, and Gollum came out from LOTR and started yelling at me about a dog. Then I was like "Ok Gollum, I'll help you find some pieces of metal." Gollum was happy about that. Then I walked a bit, and drank some water. The game was insistent that I remember to hydrate, which was really very helpful because dehydration causes all kinds of health problems, including headaches and depression.
So I hydrated, then I walked. There was a bad guy who had spikes, I kinda didn't really care because I had no idea where I was. I killed him though. Then I walked 10 feet and fell off a cliff. I looked at the body of Mad Max, dead at the bottom of a cliff, for 2 minutes. I haven't loaded the game since.
I hope you have lots of fun playing this game.

Probably the best trucking game out there as of yet.
A nicely done game with great optimization and controller support. Had no major problems with playing the game and have enjoyed playing both single player using the steam game and multiplayer with an additional client downloaded from the web.

Graphics: This game is quite pretty. Nothing spectacular or mind-blowing, but there are moments when you have to balance driving and admiring the scenery without smashing into anything. There are also a few mods that can enhance your experience in this regard.
Audio: The music is pretty standard, but all of the other audio in the game is fantastic. The sounds of the vehicles are very realistic, especially since they have been updated over time. There are videos on the SCS website of how they record the engine noises, and it's very well done.
Gameplay: This is a very relaxing game. Not exciting by any means, but it can be quite satisfying to see your progress over time, and the driving can be enjoyable on its own. The progression itself is quite good. As you earn money, you'll be able to purchase other trucks for your company and hire drivers to operate them while you are on your own job to create additional revenue. You begin to snowball, and you eventually reach the point where money is no longer a concern, but that takes a considerable amount of time. You also earn XP, unlocking the ability to take more jobs. There is a decent variety of trucks in the base game to keep your interest, and this is one of those games that has an absolutely massive modding potential. There is a load of trucks, cargo, maps, truck parts, and more available to download to keep the game fresh. And don't let the DLC turn you away, as the majority of it is paint packs, which aren't necessary by any means. The other DLC, such as the Going East expansion, are superb.
TL;DR: This isn't really a game for everyone, but if you have interest, I do recommend picking it up on sale. It's a high-quality simulator, and it's very satisfying to progress in. Overall a great game to play to relax or chill while watching a video or listening to some music.

Rust is a complex game, and if power is your goal, a pretty challenging game.
If you want to dominate your server, you better make some friends, and your friends better be good players.
If you want to dominate gun fights, you better practice, and pick your fights smartly.
If you want to laugh, trolling people can be hilarious, you can use external audio programs to blast music, or use music that fits a particular narrative. Playing songs to troll salty players, or mess with clans is pretty fun. There are voice changers that make you sound like a 5 year old, and other stuff to mess with.
The options are really dependent upon you.
What sets this game apart from others is the fact that your hard work is always on the line, which creates stress, especially during fights. Most players know it as the 'Rust shakes'. I have never played another game with such intense fights, which can be extremely rewarding, or depressing. How you can manage those emotions depends upon your outlook of the game. You can ghost around being sneaky, afraid, cautious, and careful; or you can run full speed through an open field. You will lose your stuff in this game, so if your not having fun getting that stuff in the first place, then you probably wont find the game appealing overall. I can guarantee that you will have much more fun playing with friends, in small groups (max 5) ((larger groups are frustrating due to communication)).
It is completely possible to solo this game, however, I recommend sticking to solo/duo/trio servers. The more time you have put into this game, the better you will become, especially if you come from a fps background. Find good players to play with and learn from them, and you will find yourself stealing AK's with revolvers and pipe shotguns.
On Grinding: You can grind hard in this game, if you wish. You will have to grind to raid bases, if you have at least 4 friends who share in the grind, its not bad at all, but the huge zerg groups obviously will have a monopoly on resources vs the smaller (and usually more talented) small groups. ---OR--- You can grind just enough to get a gun, some gear, and some meds and then farm (kill) other players, basically; farm players. Typically it takes me about 20 minutes to grind out some initial weapons (python, wood armour, face mask, meds...).
It takes time to get skilled at this game, and you never really stop getting better with practice. BUT you dont HAVE to have 1000+ hrs to be good at pvp, some people are just naturals, and some just get lucky.
Love Rust, have wasted WAY too much of my life on it, but it is unlike any other game I have ever played. I have had, and continue to have some pretty great times on it, and have made some pretty good friends.
PS. Yes there are cheaters in this game, but typically are a rarity. If you want to avoid them, stay away from Official servers, and when you encounter them, switch to different servers until they are banned. Facepunch is pretty responsive to actual cheating, and the last cheater I reported was banned in 5 hours. Try not to get attached to your gear, its just data, and don't hate on your friends when you lose. This game can bring the best, and worst out in people.

Don't be deceived by the marketing for this game. This is not your typically shooter.
To be honest, Spec Ops: The Line is not a great Third Person Shooter mechanically, but that doesn't mean it isn't enjoyable. It's just simple, in the way any TPS is.
It can be frustrating during parts, but if you get past that, it's a great experience.
You'll really want to play through this game atleast once for the story. The narrative makes some great statements on games in general, and how they glorify war and violence. It's not perfect, but it's admirable that a developer would take such a risk in storytelling in any case. It's worth supporting this game, at the very least for this.
In general, it's a great PC Port, with only minor stuttering at times. Key rebinding is dodgy though. Definitely a console port.

Short storyline, I beat the game in 8 hours on normal diffculty, but edge-of-your-seat suspense the entire way. I could not put the game down after starting it. I don't generally replay a game's campaign but Spec Ops: The Line was good enough to play through again. You can't regret this purchase.

This game was a really pleasant surprise. It's not a groundbreaking game; the third-person shooter mechanic is pretty average, the AI and the sound aren't necessarily anything to write home about, but what really caught me was the story. It's unlike any shooter I've ever played. I had to get every ending because I wanted so badly to see all possible outcomes. It's an incredibly riveting and original story, and at the end of it, I still don't know what to really think - who were the good guys and the bad guys - and while I probably won't play it again, I'm sure as hell glad I played it at all. Definitely give it a shot. Be warned, it's heavy, but it's fantastic.

I used to play this game with my brother a lot, sometimes late at night. He was always incredibly serious about it for some reason. For an entirely different reason, I just can't take Borderlands seriously at all.
Want guns? Yep, this game has guns. Want humor? Yep, this game has humor. Want characters with incredibly detailed backgrounds? Eh, this game is probably not for you. Roland and Axton are more or less interchangeable, honestly; both of them used to work for major corporations before bailing. Axton wasn't as good as Roland, though; I found Salvador to be much more agreeable.
Alright, rundown of playable characters.
Axton- Former mercenary for Dahl corporation. Decided to hunt the Vault because he wanted fame, fortune, and a challenge. Action skill is a turret that can actually turn 360 degrees.
Salvador- Pandora native. Decided to hunt the Vault because he heard it was dangerous. His action skill allows him to dual wield, which is extremely effective. (The Warrior kind of melted when I dual wielded two machine guns; it was awesome.)
Maya- Former goddess. Decided to hunt the Vault because she wanted an adventure. Her action skill allows her to temporarily incapacitate an opponent, unless it's a boss or something incredibly badass.
Zero- Assassin. Got bored with killing important people, and went looking for a challenge. His action skill makes him invisible, summons a holographic decoy, and amplifies the damage of his next attack.
Krieg- He's pretty much a Bandit Psycho. He's probably the most interesting playable character in the game. I won't go into much detail; I'd hate to spoil it all for you. His action skill gives him a buzz axe, and restores his health to full when he kills something.
Gaige- Former high school student. After a minor accident involving a classmate, she boarded a transport to Pandora because she was interested in Vault hunting. Her action skill summons Deathtrap, which is like Claptrap on steroids.
Well, enjoy Borderlands 2! If you still don't want the game after reading snippets about the characters, you have no soul.

The game has a steep learning curve.  Once you figure out how to play and what you are doing, things get easier.  It is still very repetitive.  Having said all of that, it is still enjoyable.
My advice to new players:
-- You will die a lot.  Buy your upgrades at the start screen between deaths.
-- As soon as you can, buy the map.  It is invaluable since this game does not have and auto-mapping feature.
-- Once you have the map, use it to aim when travelling between planets.  That way you are not floating aimlessly between planets.  It will cut down on your travel time and give you more time for collecting resources.
-- Use the Easter Island monoliths.  After you build up 20+ seeds, build one on each planet as you start to tarraform it.  It helps a lot with the creeps that constantly spawn.
-- When you find the portals, use them in boss fights.  They are especially usefull against the space dragons.  It will let you instantly get way from them.  When they find you again, shoot them as much as you can, then portal away again.
-- While you are using the portals, build pyramids on your portal planets to reinforce them.

First of all, while I've thoroughly enjoyed RockSteady's Arkham series, I have to say that this one, made my WB  Montreal, was actually better realized IMO. While Arkham Asylum and Arkham City was impressive and well done, Arkham Origins had a much cleaner and sophiscated look when it came to visuals. I also enjoyed how the villians in the story were represented and the look of them was much grittier and "realized" than in the previous Arkham series. It was also a pleasure to finally visit the Batcave.
That being said, I had issues with game play. The game was buggy at times during certain fights, when I should have easily taken down enemies and wasn't able to.  I also found takedowns buggy whereas in Arkham City, they were solid every time. I had played Arkham Origins first before I had played Arkham City so I was puzzled why trying to take down a person in AO was so difficult when in AC it was so easy. I was also disappointed with the boss fight with Deathstroke as it really didn't have anything to do with player skill as it did with timing and to me, that makes a boss fight hard but not hard for the right reason. It should be hard due to challenging the player with his player skills but when you have countering disabled then it's not about your ability to take them but about some kind of weird timing that the developers think you should figure out. I wasn't a fan of that.
Finally, because I had played AO before AC, I was a bit disappointed when I started with AC to realize that WB Montreal hadn't brought anything new to the game as far as the game play was involved. You had the same type of riddler clues and types of quests as you did in AC, only this time you had both North and South Gotham to work in. I was also puzzled why the story went back to Batman's origins instead of moving the Arkham story forward. This game could just as easily been called Batman Origins instead of using the Arkham series title.
I would still recommend this game as I've played through it several times but while I think Warners Montreal put out a better game visually, Rocksteady's games have better gameplay. Just keep in mind that some of the skill quests may be hard to complete or impossible (which I found) due to the somewhat buggy nature of the game at times.
