You've heard of hard games, right? Like...games that basically dangle a golden coin at the end of the stage in front of you with 500 lazers and rockets in between you and it? Welcome to the Dark Souls of platformers. SMB is hard. Real hard. I'm writing this review for someone who is looking for a face pummeling and/or controller breaking level of hard. People say that Spelunky is hard. Spelunky's controls are polished to the point that when you mess up, it is usually your fault as to why. SMB is a lot like that, but basically forces you to memorize level layouts through a minimum of 500 deaths.
My biggest gripe with SMB is the fact that a controller is so necessary for it to play properly. The wonky acceleration, jumping, dashing, and wall sticking physics are really cumbersome and it takes a long time to learn the exact precision to which you need to know them in order to get past advanced stages. It can become very frustrating, the levels nonwithstanding, that you say to yourself "I'm sure I pressed the jump button there really hard" but didn't jump and you died 2 feet from the end of the level.
That being said, SMB has good music to listen to whilst getting reamed every 5 seconds. The addition of cloud saves means after you uninstall the game out of pure rage on the final level, you won't have to start from the very beginning and endure the 'fun' all over again. The addition of the user-created levels is a nice touch, too. I think the leaderboard is also great, since comparing speed runs to friends can be its own level of competitiveness.
To sum up, you will need a controller. In fact, you'll probably want to buy 5 or 6 of them, because no doubt at least two will be thrown into a wall and turned into controller confetti from this game.

Let’s start with the positives: This game is really cute. The art style is very bright, colorful and generally happy. (When you're not in the depths of outer space, that is.) Every planet is unique, with its own size, background objects, and possibly water or lava. Each time you play the game you get a randomly generated map, so you’re always exploring new space. The problem is, you’re exploring new SPACE. All of outer space looks just about the same, so unless you have planets evenly spaced, it can get boring. Also, there are some NPCs who, when you talk to them, activate a conversation loop that you can only escape by pausing and killing yourself. The two bosses I managed to fight (before conversation loops) were the exact same; one was big and red, the other small and blue, both of them fire-breathing worms. Another glitch I found while playing is that occasionally, the map won’t show where your planets are, which made navigation a pain. Unfortunately, until there are some updates and bug fixes, this game isn’t worth the ten dollars.

Ever try selling something online only to have a potential buyer haggle over price after meeting to transact so you slam the door in their face and decide you won't settle for a penny less than what you have decided this junked up old cell phone is worth? Don't buy this game on sale, pay full price instead because for once forget about money and other things that cause stress in your life and allow this little hooker to bring you one last true feeling of joy and satisfaction before you lock yourself in your car with a hose redirecting the exhaust into the cabin. Weirdly specific? Don't turn around, but I'm standing right behind you.
Cosmochoria (I pronounce it out loud a few different ways every time I read it, koz-moke-reeah, kosmo-koreeah, koss-mok-♥♥♥♥♥eah, koz-mo-fuggiteeah) is a wonderfully delightful little game. Most of the game is unexplained and as you play, you discover the quaint fun of jumping, flying, and silly jokes about assgas that you suddenly realize is alarmingly absent from anything you've played lately. You'll lose a huge chunk of time mercilessly extinguishing the lives of an alien horde who were probably just trying to provide for a family they were pressured into raising by social conditioning they never thought to question until it was too late. There's also fun to be found uncovering or learning how everything works and unlocking items that alter the game mechanics. Go ahead though, don't find out on your own, look all the stuff up; you're an iconoclast or at least consider yourself one and really like the nice feeling you reward yourself with believing that to be true.  Why not set yourself up for dissatisfaction? You do it in many other aspects of your life. Weirdly specific? That's because your own desire is the cause of your suffering, as desire is the root cause of all suffering.
After carefully considering exactly how far never really taking the advice of others seriously has gotten you in life, should you decide to ignore caution and engage in the ego-driven, hedonistic pleasures in life as I have, and you purchase and play this game, I have one bit of advice: Don't bother tearing your hair our trying to figure out where to buy upgrades, you'll go bald. You have to first play the game and then die in order to access this screen. I spent five hours on my first play without dying and let me tell you I was practically screeching like a banshee after visiting every planet three times without finding a vendor. The loading screen tip I was given was "Buy a new weapon right away. Seriously. What are you waiting for?" My inner monologue became narrated by the Earl of Lemongrab, just a long, high-pitched wail of how unexemplorable (wait, is that it?) this experience was, and it was then that I struggled to recall who it had been narrated by previously. Was it me, I wondered? Why do I talk to myself in my head at all? Weirdly specific? Why do you talk to yourself in your head anyway?
If you read this, honestly ask yourself what you actually get from reading reviews subjective to another's experiences? The experience of consciousness, you know the feeling of being in driver's seat of your own little meat bag, the same feeling responsible for the illusion of "free will", this experience is entirely subjective. The experience of consciousness seems to universally fool people into thinking they are in charge over the course of events in their lives rather than being  instinctive, highly reactionary creatures, who's decisions are entirely based on that subjective experience; an experience that yields a range of reaction based on cultural programming, brain chemistry, and genetically predisposed personality traits. Maybe it's possible to read a review written by a family member whom you understand very well and can somewhat accurately apply the same context to their phrasing, but a person who has lived a substantially different life from you will apply entirely different context to the same phrasing. In order to effectively transplant an idea from another's mind to yours without erroneously interpreting their true meaning, you must have established a common framework of knowledge and understand without assumption what context they may be applying.
But hey, you don't buy any of that... do you? You believe in free will. You believe you can alter your circumstances through rational decision making. Somehow, you are unencumbered by the emotional biases built up in others that accumulate over a lifetime. Somehow, you are not impaired by the impressive array of illogical heuristics that rob others of neutral observance, perceiving without judging, and feeling/thinking without attachment. Okay great, do something that betrays a typically conditioned response.  Do something for someone else completely selflessly without the self-driven motivator of being able to feel good about your altruistic behaviour; buy the game at full price rather than wishlisting it and buying it on sale. Oh, and please, start clicking "no" next to "Did you find this review helpful?" when the review is absolutely useless without the missing context found only in another's subjective experience. Maybe then we can actually use the reviews to inform our opinions on whether to purchase, rather than using this space for jokes phrased like ♥♥♥♥♥ greentext posts, with the same unoriginal ending, time and time again, "10/10 would <do slightly quirky thing in game> again".

Rust is a complex game, and if power is your goal, a pretty challenging game.
If you want to dominate your server, you better make some friends, and your friends better be good players.
If you want to dominate gun fights, you better practice, and pick your fights smartly.
If you want to laugh, trolling people can be hilarious, you can use external audio programs to blast music, or use music that fits a particular narrative. Playing songs to troll salty players, or mess with clans is pretty fun. There are voice changers that make you sound like a 5 year old, and other stuff to mess with.
The options are really dependent upon you.
What sets this game apart from others is the fact that your hard work is always on the line, which creates stress, especially during fights. Most players know it as the 'Rust shakes'. I have never played another game with such intense fights, which can be extremely rewarding, or depressing. How you can manage those emotions depends upon your outlook of the game. You can ghost around being sneaky, afraid, cautious, and careful; or you can run full speed through an open field. You will lose your stuff in this game, so if your not having fun getting that stuff in the first place, then you probably wont find the game appealing overall. I can guarantee that you will have much more fun playing with friends, in small groups (max 5) ((larger groups are frustrating due to communication)).
It is completely possible to solo this game, however, I recommend sticking to solo/duo/trio servers. The more time you have put into this game, the better you will become, especially if you come from a fps background. Find good players to play with and learn from them, and you will find yourself stealing AK's with revolvers and pipe shotguns.
On Grinding: You can grind hard in this game, if you wish. You will have to grind to raid bases, if you have at least 4 friends who share in the grind, its not bad at all, but the huge zerg groups obviously will have a monopoly on resources vs the smaller (and usually more talented) small groups. ---OR--- You can grind just enough to get a gun, some gear, and some meds and then farm (kill) other players, basically; farm players. Typically it takes me about 20 minutes to grind out some initial weapons (python, wood armour, face mask, meds...).
It takes time to get skilled at this game, and you never really stop getting better with practice. BUT you dont HAVE to have 1000+ hrs to be good at pvp, some people are just naturals, and some just get lucky.
Love Rust, have wasted WAY too much of my life on it, but it is unlike any other game I have ever played. I have had, and continue to have some pretty great times on it, and have made some pretty good friends.
PS. Yes there are cheaters in this game, but typically are a rarity. If you want to avoid them, stay away from Official servers, and when you encounter them, switch to different servers until they are banned. Facepunch is pretty responsive to actual cheating, and the last cheater I reported was banned in 5 hours. Try not to get attached to your gear, its just data, and don't hate on your friends when you lose. This game can bring the best, and worst out in people.

In case you didn't already know, Arkham Origins was not developed by Rocksteady (the studio that developed the other two -- soon to be three -- Batman Arkham games. My understanding is that Rocksteady licensed their material out to a third-party studio in order to focus on the upcoming Arkham Knight. That said, Batman: Arkham Origins is not in the same league as Arkham Asylum or Arkham City, though it has the open-world feel of the latter. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed this game, but it has some flaws. For me, the most frustrating part of this game was the unclear objectives: I can't begin to tell you how many times I had to retrace my steps before finding the next door in the campaign. The boss battles are good (most of them), but [MINOR SPOILER] the game hypes itself with eight assassins out to kill Batman only to leave half of them as side missions. And, one of the "bosses" only takes one hit to defeat. I found the voice cast to be surprisingly good (note: this is a different cast than the other Arkham games). The combat isn't as solid as in Arkham City: you will be countering A LOT. All in all, I'd give the game about a 7.5-8 out of 10. Note: I did not play the multi-player mode.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a good casual truck driving simulator developed and published by SCS Software. The game was released in January 2013. You, the player, will create a truck driver that can choose from several generic appearance options and you will create your business with a name and logo. The objective of the game is for you to choose contracts to deliver goods and services to various destinations in return for cash. This review will examine Euro Truck Simulator 2's main features in regards to gameplay, environment in respects to performance.
ETS2 features entertaining gameplay targeted at casual gamers, as players can play, relax, and listen to music. ETS2 features a job market, split into quick job, freight market, and external contracts. The final category is World of Trucks related; therefore I will not cover it. A quick job is for beginning the game. You choose a job and you drive a business-assigned truck to the destination and in return earn cash. A freight market is for when you purchase a truck and complete jobs to grow your business. Furthermore, once you make money you buy more trucks and hire employees that automatically choose and complete jobs on a time-basis and do earn cash for your business. At the end of each delivery, may it be you or your drivers, all earn experience that increases your levels and grants you skills so you can place into one of six categories, which feature diverse attributes. The game features several brands for trucks and there is an upgrade system that allows you to use money to purchase various upgrades for you and your employee’s trucks including wheels, design, and interior. The entire gameplay process is easy to grasp and it was not difficult for me to learn because it is essentially picking a contract, completing that contract and getting money, and so forth. Furthermore, the game is endless through the objectives of growing your business and learning of all the areas in the game, meaning there is replay potential in ETS2. And, the game does feature a very nice variety of trucks, designs, and customisation. The game features an in-game radio system that allows you to download live radio stations from the Internet. For instance, I was playing and listening to BBC Radio 1, which was live and had Emilia Clarke from Game of Thrones in for an interview, so it is a complement to the gameplay. Lastly, the game is very realistic and compares to real-life counterparts through the behaviour of AI drivers and through regulations. The game features speed limits, toll booths, traffic lights, stop signs, basically anything that you see when you drive on so it does add a high level of realism towards the core mechanics of the game. The only negative I have with the gameplay is your truck can only go 90. While this may be realistic, this can be awfully slow when the majority of the game is highways.
ETS2 features an excellent map design that alters depending on what location you are at. For instance, Berlin has a different landscape and bigger cities than Torino, Italy. But overall, I found the variety to be plentiful and the overall landscape and environment beautiful and gorgeous. I loved the autobahn's in Germany to the tons of tolls in France to the countryside of Britain. The game complements the great areas by incorporating further detail through weather and night driving. With weather, AI does not change its behaviour, but the only notable difference is drivers have their lights on, but it does not affect their speed. Likewise, night driving is realistic as there are fewer cars driving and there is lights everywhere to illuminate the area. All countries have diverse road designs and it complements the experience.  Performance-related, the game remains consistent in FPS as I was able to maintain a 48-55FPS playing on max settings with minimal drops under 48 and regular increases over 55. I commend the developers for the effort they have in producing a truly beautiful environment and with the diverse weather affects and how it affects the roads. I also commend them with strong optimisation to make sure lower-end PCs play this with ease. My only wish was for bigger cities, but that is probably something we will see in American Truck Simulator.
ETS2 has very minor bugs and spelling errors. These are not entirely noticeable, but are present in the game. In saying that, I will not detract from the score because SCS Software have been excellent in providing continued support and update for ETS2, even post-American Truck Simulator release.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a gorgeous game that is simple, aimed for driving and simulation fans and for casual gamers. It acheieves a very high level of performance, coupled with excellent design and scenery. It has several features and options to spice up the game and maintain simplicity while driving. It is realistic that it matches real-life experiences of road regulations, traffic lights, and even penalties. The game features 35 DLCs with two major expansions, one cabin accessory DLC and the rest being paint jobs. I highly recommend the Euro Truck Simulator 2 + East/North Expansion bundle for USD$29.99 as the game has high replayability.

This is a close call for me as I have played it through to completion (all acheivments) with several play throughs, so as to call this a bad game would be wrong, it's quite fun but there are a LOT of cons that makes me never want to play it ever again.
THE CONS:
- Multiple actions mapped to one button, this leads to meleeing walls instead of jumping over them and getting me killed. In fact it is the number one cause of me dying and having to restart the checkpoint, it is beyond annoying it's just plain frustrating.
- Terrible cover system, no clear indicator of what you can cover behind including some walls don't allow cover.
- Having to micro manage every single action of your squad gets old fast, team mates won't shoot enemies right infront of them unless told to.
- Crouching is much better that using the cover system if only the walls you were crouching behind offered any cover at all. This leads back to having to use the cover system which as stated sucks.
- A.I. on harder difficulty use cheap tatics like grenade spamming the very little cover the maps offer.
- Maps are as linear as linear gets, with scripted routes and infinate enemies unless you do exactly what the scripts expects you to do. There is no other routes or options to complete a level which is very disapointing sucking all the fun out of replaying the game.
- Stupid friendly A.I. squad members which will constantly die and need rescuing as you only have a limited time to heal them, it feels more like baby sitting than teamplay.
- Lots of glitches but only experienced one crash to desktop.
- Many more..
Why you Should play it:
+ The story is great; 9/10
+ Skipable cutscenes
+ Still a fun shooter
+ Commanding your squad adds a little more stratergy to the TPS genere
+ Good music
I would only recommened getting this game on sale.

That game is one of the whole genres: the repetitive open world.
There are lots of other games which use the same formula: big open world and tonnes of collectables, towers/outposts, upgrades and free-flow combat system. For example, Shadow of Mordor was that type of game, but without a real open world. But what was repulsive about that games is that they quickly become boring. But Mad Max isn't boring and can be enjoyable for a  long time. There are few reasons why that game is the best "repetitive open world" game:
1) Upgrades split into 4 branches: vehicle, abilities, fortress and Max gear.
And if you like cars you will be very happy with such wide upgrade system. Fortress upgrades can be interesting for people who like seeing the collapsed world rise. But every person would like improving Max gear, especially when they will unlock the leather jacket and shotgun from original movies.
2) Routine is rewarding, so it can be enjoyable. You'll do it not for achievements or just simple area control, you'll do it for blueprints for fortress upgrades, for the new car engines, tires and other upgrades or for a new Max gear. The game isn't forcing you to collect all the stuff, you can beat the game playing only story missions and a few side-quests and you will not feel like you should grind some things to beat the game, no. But if you will, it will be a lot easier. You will feel like you are growing as at every good RPG.
3) Atmosphere. One of the best wasteland atmospheres ever created. Depression, thirst, heat, oil and madness. Just melt and play.
4) Graphics and optimisation: the game looks awesome in the open areas (because it's just a big desert) and cars have very good details. And it can be played on a mid-tier PC with ultra settings.
5) Mad Max references are everywhere. The game took many things from Fury Road, but it didn't forget about old movies. So you will find some nostalgia here.
6) Car battles are cool. Intense, beautiful and available for all skill-levels.
TL;DR:
The game is repetitive but rewarding. Awesome wasteland atmosphere, many Mad Max references, easy combat system and amazing car battles. Simple but not bad story.

After beating the original Ori and 100% completing the Definitive Edition, here are my thoughts...
If you've never played Ori and the Blind Forest before, start here. Otherwise, feel free to skip the first little bit.
Ori and the Blind Forest is one of the greatest games I have ever played. Everything about it is beautiful. Its masterfully crafted art style is breathtaking, providing some of the most visually appealing graphics you'll have ever seen. The bright, vibrant palette of colors of the world you have to explore will make you want to stop and take a screenshot everywhere you go. The music perfectly complements the graphics, with strings, winds, and percussion completing the atmosphere and truly immersing you in your surroundings. Ori's light and whismical melodies will fill you with happiness and calm you, while its more aggressive, suspenseful tracks will make you panic and feel fear. On the other side of the audio spectrum, the sound effects are just as good as everything else, further adding to the authenticity of the environment. Finally, the controls are incredibly smooth and precise - exactly what you would want out of an action-platformer such as this game. Whether it be jumping from wall to wall to ascend to a new height, or using enemies' projectiles to propel yourself across a hazardous row of spikes, it just feels right. All of these elements meld together to create an overall feel of beautiful fluidity throughout the game, making it truly unique.
Level design and gameplay are near perfect. The learning curve is spot-on, giving you chances to experiment and familiarize with the new abilities you recieve, then slowly ramping up the difficulty of how the level makes you use that skill as you approach mastery. The one, very minor complaint I have about this are the escape segments. Throughout the game, there are three segments in which you must progress through certain areas while avoiding a danger that will instantly kill you. Basically, you have to run. Fast. However, these segments are significantly difficult and have zero margin for error. One dreaded mistake will lead to your death and force you to restart the entire escape. These are essentially trial and error, unless you have superhuman reactions. Make a mistake, die, restart. Solve mistake, progress slightly further, make another mistake, die, restart, repeat. Don't get me wrong, Ori is not at all an easy game. It's certainly one of the more challenging games that I've played. However, I found these escape segments to be considerably tough and almost unfair at times, given how steeply the difficulty ramps up. Despite that long spiel however, it's really a minor error that doesn't hurt the overall experience you get from the game.
As for the story, it lets down compared to the rest of the elements of the game. It's not bad, but it's not great either. You're told a heartwarming, touching tale, but aren't given much detail. It's not really that big of a deal given the type of game that this is, but it still could have been better.
Overall, Ori and the Blind Forest is an incredibly well executed, charming game that is certainly worth purchasing. Even those who aren't fans of platformers will find enjoyment in it.
Now, onto the Definitive Edition and its additions. The DE adds two new areas that add slightly to the story, multiple difficulties, backtracking support, and two new abilities. The two new areas aren't extremely expansive, but still do add a good amount of extra gameplay. I wasn't a huge fan of the Black Root Burrows because you can't see what's around you for half of the time you'll spend in it, so one little missed jump or slip could send you plummeting to your doom with no idea on how to escape. There were a few times where I didn't know exactly where I was supposed to be going, made a mistake, and fell to the bottom of the area that is filled with spikes. There was nothing I could do but watch my health slowly decrease because I couldn't see my surroundings. Besides that annoyance though, I did enjoy the rest of the Black Root Burrows and the Lost Grove. As you explore said areas, you learn the backstory of Naru, the panda-like creature who cares for you at the beginning of the game. Unfortunately, like the rest of the story, it's rather minimalistic and doesn't really add too much depth. It was still interesting to learn, though. The two new abilities that you obtain in the new areas, Light Burst and Dash, are fun little additions. Dash is exactly what it sounds like, allowing Ori to move across a small distance with a tremendous burst of speed. Light Burst can be used as an attack, but its primary use is to light torches that will unlock certain areas where secrets are hidden (the rest of Nibel besides the two new areas was slightly adjusted to provide this use for Light Burst). Multiple difficulties was a good addition overall, given that the original game is rather challenging. The easy difficulty will very much appeal more casual gamers who want to focus less on the challenge and more on the story. Also, in the DE, you can load completed save files, which you were unable to in the original game, much to my dismay. This gives you the ability to explore any parts of the world you may not have gotten around to before you finished the game, and is a very welcome feature. To sum up, the Definitive Edition provides great new features and some extra gameplay to further improve what was already a fantastic game which both seasoned and new Ori players will enjoy.
TL;DR: It's absolutely beautiful and amazing. Buy it.
EDIT: I've nominated this game for the The “I'm Not Crying, There's Something In My Eye” Award  because it's so beautiful and emotionally moving. I still love it so much.

This was a very good game. The story was very compelling, the characters in it were very developed, and there are plenty of moments that make you think about morale and the "right" path to choose. It also helped that Nolan North voices the main character, who I'm a big fan of. The game play itself is mediocre. It's your typical 3rd person shooter and does not add anything new to the genre. The strongest element of the controls was to be able to command your teammates to focus on an enemy target, but that lost its luster rather quickly.
The best part of the game was the main story. Although it was rather short, the plots of the game was one of the best I've ever played. The story line is very thrilling, and it leaves you wanting to play more to see what happens in the next chapter. The atmosphere of the story is also very dark. If you read the game's description, it mentions showing the horrors of war and battle. This is very true. Many shooter games these days have the main character shoot a bunch of people, but those never emphasize what consequences result due to those actions. This game focuses heavily on those consequences. There are also parts in the game where you can make a decision on what to do, and each decision will have different results which make you think if the choice you made was the right one.
Multiplayer exists, but it's not very lively. I haven't spent much time on it, but from what I've seen so far, it's nothing special. Single player/co-op for the campaign will be a lot more fun. Overall, a great game, and I highly recommend it. However, the campaign is quite short so I would not pay for price for this.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a good casual truck driving simulator developed and published by SCS Software. The game was released in January 2013. You, the player, will create a truck driver that can choose from several generic appearance options and you will create your business with a name and logo. The objective of the game is for you to choose contracts to deliver goods and services to various destinations in return for cash. This review will examine Euro Truck Simulator 2's main features in regards to gameplay, environment in respects to performance.
ETS2 features entertaining gameplay targeted at casual gamers, as players can play, relax, and listen to music. ETS2 features a job market, split into quick job, freight market, and external contracts. The final category is World of Trucks related; therefore I will not cover it. A quick job is for beginning the game. You choose a job and you drive a business-assigned truck to the destination and in return earn cash. A freight market is for when you purchase a truck and complete jobs to grow your business. Furthermore, once you make money you buy more trucks and hire employees that automatically choose and complete jobs on a time-basis and do earn cash for your business. At the end of each delivery, may it be you or your drivers, all earn experience that increases your levels and grants you skills so you can place into one of six categories, which feature diverse attributes. The game features several brands for trucks and there is an upgrade system that allows you to use money to purchase various upgrades for you and your employee’s trucks including wheels, design, and interior. The entire gameplay process is easy to grasp and it was not difficult for me to learn because it is essentially picking a contract, completing that contract and getting money, and so forth. Furthermore, the game is endless through the objectives of growing your business and learning of all the areas in the game, meaning there is replay potential in ETS2. And, the game does feature a very nice variety of trucks, designs, and customisation. The game features an in-game radio system that allows you to download live radio stations from the Internet. For instance, I was playing and listening to BBC Radio 1, which was live and had Emilia Clarke from Game of Thrones in for an interview, so it is a complement to the gameplay. Lastly, the game is very realistic and compares to real-life counterparts through the behaviour of AI drivers and through regulations. The game features speed limits, toll booths, traffic lights, stop signs, basically anything that you see when you drive on so it does add a high level of realism towards the core mechanics of the game. The only negative I have with the gameplay is your truck can only go 90. While this may be realistic, this can be awfully slow when the majority of the game is highways.
ETS2 features an excellent map design that alters depending on what location you are at. For instance, Berlin has a different landscape and bigger cities than Torino, Italy. But overall, I found the variety to be plentiful and the overall landscape and environment beautiful and gorgeous. I loved the autobahn's in Germany to the tons of tolls in France to the countryside of Britain. The game complements the great areas by incorporating further detail through weather and night driving. With weather, AI does not change its behaviour, but the only notable difference is drivers have their lights on, but it does not affect their speed. Likewise, night driving is realistic as there are fewer cars driving and there is lights everywhere to illuminate the area. All countries have diverse road designs and it complements the experience.  Performance-related, the game remains consistent in FPS as I was able to maintain a 48-55FPS playing on max settings with minimal drops under 48 and regular increases over 55. I commend the developers for the effort they have in producing a truly beautiful environment and with the diverse weather affects and how it affects the roads. I also commend them with strong optimisation to make sure lower-end PCs play this with ease. My only wish was for bigger cities, but that is probably something we will see in American Truck Simulator.
ETS2 has very minor bugs and spelling errors. These are not entirely noticeable, but are present in the game. In saying that, I will not detract from the score because SCS Software have been excellent in providing continued support and update for ETS2, even post-American Truck Simulator release.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a gorgeous game that is simple, aimed for driving and simulation fans and for casual gamers. It acheieves a very high level of performance, coupled with excellent design and scenery. It has several features and options to spice up the game and maintain simplicity while driving. It is realistic that it matches real-life experiences of road regulations, traffic lights, and even penalties. The game features 35 DLCs with two major expansions, one cabin accessory DLC and the rest being paint jobs. I highly recommend the Euro Truck Simulator 2 + East/North Expansion bundle for USD$29.99 as the game has high replayability.

Sometimes a game is defined by a single decision. And unfortunately the route the devs decided to take with the story make this a game I cannot recommend to anyone. I'm not even sure if I'll be able to bring myself to finish it. They play out the trope of introducing characters and giving you the spark of hope for a happy ending just to set you up to do the predictable thing games like to do these days where they snuff out those characters in succession to try and be deep and evoke an emotional response. But the emotional con job doesn't hold up in an age where everyone and their brother seems to be doing it, and the ending of the game leads nowhere but misery. For a movie where it's just 2 hours of your time such an outcome can be acceptable. But for a game where you can sink in countless hours for completion and have a real stake in things, taking away player agency and railroading things on a course to absolute misery means the game is an absolute failure.
Within the span of three missions I went from a definite recommendation to truly loathing the game and the people that made it. I feel disrespected and betrayed as a player both for investing my time into this game and for giving the developers the benefit of the doubt.

Im suprised this game isn't as well known or widespread as it should be considering how well done and entertaining it is.
It's basically a roguelike game that takes place in space. Some be gotten evil has destroyed the galaxy and rid it of life. Your task is to hover over to each planet and plant seeds to restore life on said planets while at the same time fending off invaders and monsters.
The monsters start of simple and easy to deal with but increase in difficulty and variety as time progresses (Or as your save more planets, im not particularly sure). Every now and then, a boss has a chance of spawning in an attempt to ruin you for good.
The area you will be playing in is widely blank (It's space lol) save for a few planets here and there, big and small, which you will need to roam around to find, inhabit and restore. While it seems simple, floating in space combined with limitted jetpack fuel actually makes roaming space more lethal than it sounds since you would have to ration your fuel so you are not caught floating in space on an empty backpack towards the edge of the galaxy (Which causes death if that isnt obvious enough)
There are collectibles and artifacts that you can gather and send to the "Wise one" to be examined (Which is basically a way of cashing in your found items to be used in your next playthrough or identifying what it does). Permanent Stat and character upgrades are also available with currency you collect while playing the game which improves your chance of survival each time you traverse the abyss. There's also artifacts in the game which you can activate to change the base game mode either making it easier (Enemies spawn less/do less damage) or harder (Less Jetpack fuel). Top that off with procedurally generated map layouts to the game and you've got yourself a good replay value game.
Overall, the game is completely worth getting and trying out. For the price tag they put on the game (23RM for me), I would say it is actually a pretty good deal considering how well fleshed out the game is. A discounted price is like taking Bacon and Eggs and adding MORE BACON AND EGGS.
Edit: I seem to have forgotten one other thing. Im fairly certain it's obvious enough but the game has a strong childish and cartoon like art style which some might like or not. Personally it gave it a more innocent and simple atmosphere. The game would look more serious and action oriented if it was painted in another way. Like imagine Risk of Rain's explosion, art and chaos in this game. Pretty sure it'd probably be less about saving planets and more about destroying them. (Would be interesting to see the Magma Worm here :D)

Short, but satisfying game. Even after 4 years, the graphics look nice and the engine works well (no bugs encountered). Also, the cinematics are pretty amazing, especially towards the end of the game - destroying buildings whilst flying a helicopter - what more could you want? You're allowed to make multiple choices throughout the game, which affect your sanity. The only drawbacks for me are the 30 fps/720p cutscenes, and the length of the game (6 to 12 hours), but that can be justified by the quality of the game, and the multiple choice scenarios. Overall, it's a great and original TPS, definitely deserving more recognition. If you haven't played it, make sure you get it on a sale, it can go for dirt cheap, and it's definitely worth playing.

Before I begin this feature I feel it is necessary to say that I find it very annoying that a developer wouldn’t take all of ten seconds to see whether or not the title of their game had already been taken by another game on Steam. Call it what you like a rookie mistake, it is after all Spider Key Games’ first game on the Steam platform or just laziness either way it’s not a good look especially with such a name consisting of two fairly common words and the fact that the other, older, Spellbind wasn’t met with raucous critical or player acclaim.
Moving on, this Spellbind is a traditional point and click adventure game made in the Unity 4 engine that first appeared on mobile devices. It progressed through the Greenlight program successfully after being bundled in a Lazy Guys bundle. You play the role of Luppe, a 16 year old boy who is a gang leader. A rival gang leader has issued you a challenge – to steal the most oldest and most expensive bottle of wine from Lord Amatar. An interesting enough concept and if the puzzles and execution of the game were good enough could lead to a memorable experience.
Unfortunately, the English writing within the game appears to be written by someone without a thorough understanding of the language. That it clearly hasn’t been edited by a professional is a further downside. There are simply too many grammatical errors within the game that it detracts from the experience. Unfortunately, Spellbind like many point & click adventure games requires the writing to be at a high level for it to pass muster. This is just something that the game, as is, cannot achieve. It requires a massive editing job from top to bottom. That this game was released onto mobile long before it arrived onto Steam is a sad state of affairs.
This leads into the puzzles. The instructions behind them – from the very beginning of the game – are either not present or are again so poorly presented as to make playing the majority of them not a fun experience. However, there is a light at the end of the tunnel. They are able to be skipped. Unfortunately, a point and click adventure game without well executed puzzles isn’t much of a game even if they are skippable. I just don’t see the point of playing through the puzzles or the game itself while it is in such a sorry state.
The graphics and other presentation values are not up to the standard that we have come to demand from games on Steam. Yes, the game is only $2.99 but this is a game that would struggle to get an audience if it were released as a free to play title. The only thing that makes it a traditional point and click adventure game aside from the mechanics are the graphics. There are games from the last century that have better graphics. While graphics aren’t everything – and I adore many games that don’t pretend to have good graphics – it just speaks volumes as to the presentation value of the game.
Unfortunately, it’s just not a very good game in its present state. The concept and the story have the potential to be enjoyable but not without a massive overhaul.

After completing this game, I can confidently say that it isn't really worth playing. I powered through it hoping it would improve, and it was entertaining enough to finish, but was still consistently frustrating.
There's the combat sections, which are very basic and not nearly as fun as the combat in the Arkham series. In my opinion, they don't add anything to the game. They also protray Max as some kind of martial arts master that can kill 20 men in a single fight, which is silly and antithetical to the story.
There's the driving, which is fairly fun, but there isn't much variation. Your car vs some basic enemy cars. No monster trucks, dirt bikes, or any of the other exciting vehicles from the movie series.
The story is uneven and fairly boring. There's a few memorable characters and scenes, but overall nothing too exciting. The ending is pointlessly bleak, giving no sort of character development or arc.
All these mediocre aspects are then spread extremely thin over the course of the game. Tear down these dozens of scarecrows! Loot these dozens of camps! Drive all the way across the map in this slow moving truck for some reason!
Things seem even worse when you imagine what could have been. What if you could actually customize your vehicle, and choose different play styles? Imagine driving a tricked-out dune buggy that drives circles around foes, or a gigantic bus that plows straight through enemies?
If I could do it again, I would not have bought or played this game.

This is a very poor port of Arkham Origins for PC. Whereas the Rocksteady-developed Arkham games worked perfectly for me on PC, various game-breaking glitches have make Arkham Origins nearly unplayable. The single player game has several bugs that can potentially break your save, and the multiplayer servers fail to create a match more than half the time. Many of my achievements did not properly unlock either, and this was the only game where I experienced this problem. The developer has frankly expressed that they do not intend to fix many of the known glitches with the Steam version of the game. I am very disappointed with the support for this product, and I strongly recommend getting this game on another platform, if at all.

I had previously played Arkham Asylum and Arkham City, both awesome games, so I started playing this game with a certain level of expectation. If you enjoyed the combat and story for the past games, you will probably enjoy this as well. The game provides interesting backstory to some of the characters that appeared in AA and AC. Unfortunately, that is only what it had going for the game.
Firstly, the level of quality in the game is subpar compared to its predecessors. Numerous bugs, glitches, crashes. I can't even play the challenge maps! Most common problem is how Batman gliding animation glitches over and over again. The only fortunate thing for me is I do not experience save game corruptions as experienced by other players. WB Montreal did a very poor job in polishing the game to ensure minimal problems.
Secondly, the combat system, while mostly similar to Arkham City, felt... unsastifying disjointed. In Arkham City, once I got past the learning curve, I'm able to combo perfectly, and you can get the hang of the techniques and movement quite easily. Not so in Origins. The combat does not flow as well and as easily, especially when the counters is problematic in this version. What do I mean? Let's say, just as a criminal was about to hit me while I hit another criminal nearby, AND when click to counter JUST before his punch lands on me, it does not always execute the counter. This could also be attributed to the fact that counter timer seems much faster now, which is a problem especially if the criminal is about to hit you from the back of the camera where you can't see until they get too close to you. This is one example of the frustrating combat tweaks by WB Montreal. I'm not saying that games shouldn't be more challenging but this is more frustrating than anything else. Rocksteady got the timing of the combat in AA and AC perfectly balanced in this regard.
Lastly, the "lesser" details of the game - the menu UI. It feels like a terrible port from consoles, using keyboard KEYS to move between the menu. Seriously, why are we using the keyboard to control parts of menu navigation when we have something called the MOUSE? Navigating the map is another annoyance, you CAN'T use the mouse to scroll around and place waypoints in the EXACT locations you want. No, the developers thought navigating with a keyboard is a good thing, but it is so imprecise and clumsy.
All in all, it's not a terrible game per se, but it is essentially Arkham City 2 but with a whole lot of problems. I won't recommend this game until all the above points are improved and fixed. This also shows that WB Monsteal takes the fans' faith in the series for granted. You'll be better out saving your money for Rocksteady's return with Arkham Knight when it releases.

I used to play this game with my brother a lot, sometimes late at night. He was always incredibly serious about it for some reason. For an entirely different reason, I just can't take Borderlands seriously at all.
Want guns? Yep, this game has guns. Want humor? Yep, this game has humor. Want characters with incredibly detailed backgrounds? Eh, this game is probably not for you. Sure, they do flesh out the character backgrounds a bit, but not too much. Roland and Axton are more or less interchangeable, honestly; both of them used to work for major corporations before bailing. Axton wasn't as good as Roland, though; I found Salvador to be much more agreeable.
Alright, rundown of playable characters.
Axton- Former mercenary for Dahl corporation. Decided to hunt the Vault because he wanted fame, fortune, and a challenge. Action skill is a turret that can actually turn 360 degrees.
Salvador- Pandora native. Decided to hunt the Vault because he heard it was dangerous. His action skill allows him to dual wield, which is extremely effective. (The Warrior kind of melted when I dual wielded two machine guns; it was awesome.)
Maya- Former goddess. Decided to hunt the Vault because she wanted an adventure. Her action skill allows her to temporarily incapacitate an opponent, unless it's a boss or something incredibly badass.
Zero- Assassin. Got bored with killing important people, and went looking for a challenge. His action skill makes him invisible, summons a holographic decoy, and amplifies the damage of his next attack.
Krieg- He's pretty much a Bandit Psycho. He's probably the most interesting playable character in the game. I won't go into much detail; I'd hate to spoil it all for you. His action skill gives him a buzz axe, and restores his health to full when he kills something.
Gaige- Former high school student. After a minor accident involving a classmate, she boarded a transport to Pandora because she was interested in Vault hunting. Her action skill summons Deathtrap, which is like Claptrap on steroids.
Well, enjoy Borderlands 2! If you still don't want the game after reading snippets about the characters, you have no soul.

Yar's Revenge is a modern reboot of a classic atari 2600 game of the same name. This one is a rail shooter that has you flying through levels shooting various bug-like enemies with lasers, missiles, a railgun, and more. It's not a bad game by any means (in fact it's a lot better than I was expecting), but it's not really my cup of tea. It's very easy to lose track of yourself sometimes while trying to aim, so you're trying to hit enemies, dodge projectiles, and not run into the environment, all in a 3 dimensional space. Also, the control options are almost nonexistent. You can rebind things but I couldn't find anywhere to change the mouse sensitivity (just the analog sensitivity for my controller) which is fairly high by default. Like I said, it's not a bad game, in fact it's a pretty decent one, it's just not my kind of game. That being said, if you're a fan of rail shooters you'll probably like this.

This is actually a fairly fun game. Honestly I only bought it because I owned an Atari 2600 as a kid and had Yar's Revenge for that system, and wanted to see what an update / sequel would possibly be like so many years later. It doesn't seem all that related to the original, actually. I mean the story is, very very vaguely, similar, but other than that -- different gameplay, different feel, different tone, different everything. The original was just a masterpiece. It'd be nice if this contained the original as a mini-game or something inside it, but nope, it doesn't. I guess they had the game license and wanted to use it for some slight popularity. And for me it worked. But most Steam gamers are younger than me and never even heard of Yar's Revenge, so I doubt this trick works on most people.
Basically the game is a On-Rails Shooter. If ever played a game where you move along a path and have to shoot everything that appears in front of you, quickly, before it disappears, it's like that. Panzer Dragoon is a good analogy. If you *casually* enjoy that type of game, you might enjoy this. If you think that type of gameplay is stupid and boring, you won't enjoy this. If you are a die-hard fan of on-rails shooters and only look for the best examples in that genre, you also won't enjoy this. It's intended to be a time-waster. I'd say buy it on sale if you are even remotely curious about it, and if you read this review that's probably you. Two dollars (on sale) isn't a big risk. I played it for two hours, and had some fun with it. Two hours of fun for two dollars is an okay trade by me.

Tiny Bang Story Review
Ever felt the need to be totally calm and yet entirely frustrated at once? Neither. But it’s definitely worth the experiment to see what it’s like – and Tiny Bang Story is the ideal vehicle to help you on your journey.
The idea behind the game, apparently, is to
The game starts off entirely unassuming. You’re dumped in front of what looks like a work of art with absolutely no clue on what you’re doing. A little signal shows you to click on certain things and depending on your style of thinking you’ll probably understand fairly quickly that you’ve just embarked on a very long puzzle journey.
Separated into 5 “levels” of sorts, you’re shifted from landscape to landscape by searching out missing pieces of puzzles – which you’ll then complete. But not all of them are jigsaws. You have those of course, but along the way there are also plenty of other mind benders. Slide puzzles, mini-games that look like the dark ages of gaming and so on.
It’s fairly easy to spot which items on your screen will be the ones you need to pick up along the way, they’re slightly less arty-looking. But some are highly difficult to spot, especially as you click back and forth between areas of the screen, most of your items will blend and you’ll miss them terribly easily.
A good feature of each puzzle is the help button, which almost entirely but not exactly tells you how to solve your problem. Good for a jog of the brain but not always enough to take the fun out of it.
It’s quite easy to get frustrated and turn to walkthroughs for help, though sometimes you might be better off just taking a break and coming back to it later with fresh eyes. This helps with your feeling of accomplishment – but unfortunately it is a highly addictive game and you’ll most likely be heading for YouTube quicker than you should.
Once you reach the end of the game, which could be anywhere around 5 or more hours to reach, you’ll come across another peculiar feeling. Satisfaction and dissatisfaction – both at once. It’s excellent to complete the game, to feel like you’ve done what you set out to do. But the ending isn’t entirely forthcoming. It’s like watching a movie where it sort of just ends without feeling like it ends.
The bonus is you’ll be able to do all of those little puzzles and stuff again. The bad part is, it’ll just remind you how you only really did them to move on to the next part because they’re so frustrating.
The soundtrack is excellent, a very calming background tune which while repetitive, isn’t enough to be annoying. Personally, I’m easily irritated at the best of times and playing this game after a particularly bad mood set upon me was still quite welcoming in most aspects. Sound effects are fairly satisfying too, making the right pops and clangs when you click on things.
The thing that threw me for the biggest loop was the distinct lack of instruction or insight into what the heck is going on in the first place. I’m assuming that this is because the game developers, Collibri Games, is from Russia. This makes things a tad confusing for all – but it also means it’s generally going to be a tad confusing for people of any language. Which means you could introduce your best mate in Cairo that doesn’t speak a lick of English to Tiny Bang Story and he’ll get a fairly equal amount of enjoyment.
That said though, your pre-requisite is to know your numbers 1-9 and roman numerals (such as those found on a clock…). Which could be difficult for any intellectually challenged English speaking individuals.

-Great music and atmosphere
-Gameplay has its moments but is generally mediocre and feels unrewarding

-The game does not respect its own premise(see below)
The Tiny Bang Story starts off strong, with the music and art coming together to create a delightful fairy-tale atmoshere. Quickly though, the shiny aesthetic wears off to reveal a disappointing core game. The first level feels like it had by far the most effort put into it-perhaps to entice people with a nice demo?
The gameplay is roughly a 50/50 split between Where's Waldo-esque collection quests and simple logic puzzles. The logic puzzles range from decent to mediocre, with the mediocre ones lacking any way of achieving a solution other than brute force guessing or using a guide. One problem is that it is sometimes unclear what the player has achieved in the world by completing a puzzle. Several times I found myself looking around, trying to figure what had changed in the world as a result of finishing a puzzle. This greatly diminished the satisfaction of completing the puzzle.
The game's biggest flaw, though, lies in its lack of respect for its own premise. The game is divided into five levels, each containing 25 puzzle pieces that, ostensibly, you are supposed to collect in order to repiar the fractured world. On the third level, I neglected to collect several of the puzzle pieces before activating the end-of-level sequence. I was dismayed to discover that not only was there no way to return to the level to collect the rest of the pieces, but the game had progressed as if I had collected them all anyway. This was quite disappointing considering that collecting these pieces has been presented in the opening as the main goal of the game.
Due to this severe problem, combined with the lack of an ending and rampant use of the filler collection quests in a pretty short game, I cannot recommend The Tiny Bang Story. I think you can do a lot better in the adventure genre.

This game is hours of fun and slightly addicting.  It has a challenging edge to it that requires logical playing in order to avoid riots and such.  I currently have a really big prison on one of my maps.  Just after I finished dumping a ton of money to expand it in order to add more prisoners, one of my power stations exploded and burnt down half the prison.  After pouring all my savings into fixing the prison, I was left with very little money and down 84 prisoners (rioting as well as the fire).  Then it happened again...

This is a fun little 2-D sandbox game that is definitely worth the price of admission.  You basically build a prison from scratch with limited funds available to you, and you earn funds through grants, getting more prisoners, etc.  You basically choose the infrastructure of your prison from ground up, and the very layout you choose will have an impact on how well your prison is run.  For instance, it is a very bad idea to let Supermax and Maximum security prisoners come into contact at any time with Protective Custody prisoners, or even prisoners who aren't but should be classified Protective Custody.  I made the mistake of overlooking this once, and my prisoner was killed by the other inmates for it.
You can even choose among several types of wardens for your prison, which each have their own benefits/drawbacks.  This will slightly affect how your prison is run and is a matter of personal preference.  You can also sell your prison after certain conditions are met, and then use these funds to start a new prison with more money than you started the previous prison with.  For such a simple looking game, there's actually quite a bit of complexity to it, and it benefits the game.  All in all, I recommend this game; most people should feel like they got more than their money's worth.

What is Cosmochoria?
Genre: 2D space adventure & shooter
Setting: cartoonish astronaut trying to revive a dying galaxy by planting seeds on small-scaled planets
Difficulty: 5/10 (normal playthrough), 8/10 (going for achievements and how to figure them out)
Length: 5 minutes to 2 hours for a single stint, 5-7 hours for a campaign playthrough, up to 15 for getting all rewards
Mode: singleplayer campaign
The positive aspects:
- fresh and funny gameplay. The player travels through a galaxy of 50 planets, planting seeds, crafting defence towers and shields, battling bosses and probably saves the galaxy by beating the so-called cataclysm
- a variety of powerups and perks. In every stint you do you will gain credits which you can invest in powerups and perks before starting another one. Those will permanently boost your abilities and thus make it easier to progress further. Very motivating!
- neat cartoonish graphics and funny dialogues
- Over 20 "artifacts" (to be randomly found in chests that pop up as rewards for revived planets) to twist gameplay mechanics in either a positive or a negative way, such as half/double damage, no planet healing, fast planting etc.
The negative aspects:
- rather short, repitive gameplay
- simple story (galaxy is dying - please help!)
- lack of content: galaxies are basically the same - not much variation; towers don't have upgrades; boss fights don't require special tactics most of the time
Result (and summary for those who have no time reading):
What a great and cute game cosmochoria is! Saving the galaxy and unlocking perks several times will make you spend hours ingame. If only there was more content, like additional galaxies, upgradable towers and more challenging boss fights! But hey, its an indie game and it does a great job - hopefully there will be a sequel one day!
Definitely worth the buy!

A pleasant, difficult to categorize, little game. Is it an exploration game? Yes. Is it a shooter game? Yes. Is it a funny game, with a little naked cartoon man? Why, yes, it is.
It almost seems like the innovative execution and simple premise of this game would make it a one-time indie game, easily tossed aside when mastered. The trouble is... This game isn't easy to master. At every turn, it is designed to throw a curve ball your way. As of writing this, I've sunk almost five hours into it and not gotten bored at all. There are many things to unlock, many things to explore, and many tasks to complete. I would be willing to bet I could sink another ten hours into it, easily. For a game I spent $3 on during a steam sale? I'll take it. Hell, I'll throw my money at it.
I'll summarize with this: is Cosmochoria going to win the 'OMG BEST GAME EVER!!! STOP MAKING VIDEO GAMES, THIS IS IT, WE'RE DONE" award? No, probably not. But are you going to have a ton of fun while playing it? Yes. Easily. And, honestly, that's all that matters here.

This game is the game equivelent of a mix between 'Predator' and 'Full Metal Jacket' i.e. it's the 'Aliens' of video games.
Sans full-on analogy, basically it's generic and predictable action (yet satisfying, a la 'Predator') but with a very well written narative. While you may initially feel the whole "Been there, done that." gambit, it'll suck you in if you let it, and leave you very satisfied with the [end] experience.
There is a good reason I brought up the aforementioned movies: There are paralells to be drawn; you see, while not a great movie (or even good, by reasonable standards) I can't help but love 'Predator'; it has a certain entertainment quality, that while generic, that just stands out and is entertaining. 'SPEC OPS: The Line' is very much in that vein, with one HUGE difference being it has a very well thoughtout script, or at least they were abitious. The pacing could definitely take a queue from the likes of the 'UNCHARTED' franchise...but then again, what series couldn't? That's why I harken back to 'Full Metal Jacket'. While that film was ultimately a masterpiece, it's pacing (along with all Kubrick films) was somewhat lacking; SO: The Line seems moreso to suffer from frantic pacing rather than the slow-draw of a Kubrick film, yet missed pacing is jarring either way, with similar effect.
Yet...Just like FMJ, the pacing seems to make sense within the source material to deliver an ultimately satifying experience.
Lastly, the 'Aliens' reference. You see, while not a cinematic materpiece, 'Aliens' is enjoyable on almost every level, so long as it isn't taken too critically; sure, it's a 'B' movie wrapped in celeophane, but made with such care it just becomes that much more entertaining; and that's what SO: The Line is -- A generic shooter with an exceptionally encompasing narative that, while not entirely original, is extremely entertaining and engaging.

2-sentence review : I came to that game from the hype about the difficult moral choices, but there was none (the marketing guys probably never played any RPG in their life). However, I got a solid TPS with a lot of action and an incredible scenery, packaged in an intriguing but ultimately disappointing story-telling.
- Amazing & original scenery : Dubai lost in a desert storm
- Even better, the scenery is well exploited and brings a lot in the gameplay
- Solid TPS gameplay ; nothing out of the ordinary, but all the basis are there and well implemented
- Good story-telling, but...
- ... But the story doesn't make much sense (yup, I've read all the explanations and they still don't explain correctly a lot of things ; I guess it's just hard to fit what the authors wanted to do with the mechanisms of a shooter game)
- Worst, the story setting isn't explained clearly, which made me know less than the protagonists and let me wondering what's the heck was going on during almost all the game
- The story setting is actually some kind of Science-Fiction stuff ; it's not bad in itself, but it would have required some clear explanation (in very short : Dubai has been taken in a several months long desert storm and people are going to die soon)
- We have to find some intelligence during the game that explains a bit more what happened in Dubai ; some of this stuff is hidden, which means I missed some and it made the story even more muddy... :-/
- It is in no way tactical (not a con for me, but it's advertised otherwise, so better be clear on that)

Rockstar once again shows that it is master of its craft by creating an amazing character-driven story.  GTA typically gets criticized for its content but the fact remains that Rockstar is a talented team of designers and writers that make quality games.  San Andreas has always been my favorite of the franchise because of its unapologetic wackiness and expansiveness.  There is so much to do.  After playing GTA4 and becoming more aware of the constant "do this" messages on the screen, I do think that the gameplay element is slightly overrated.  However, for me, this is not where the brilliance of GTA lies.  The fun of GTA is vicariously living the adventure of the story's character.  In San Andreas this path begins as a gang-banger, then flawlessly expands into casino ownership, chinese triads, and a story of redemption, all while meeting rich characters along the way.  Highly recommend SA above any of the GTA titles.

This game is hours of fun and slightly addicting.  It has a challenging edge to it that requires logical playing in order to avoid riots and such.  I currently have a really big prison on one of my maps.  Just after I finished dumping a ton of money to expand it in order to add more prisoners, one of my power stations exploded and burnt down half the prison.  After pouring all my savings into fixing the prison, I was left with very little money and down 84 prisoners (rioting as well as the fire).  Then it happened again...

This is a fun little 2-D sandbox game that is definitely worth the price of admission.  You basically build a prison from scratch with limited funds available to you, and you earn funds through grants, getting more prisoners, etc.  You basically choose the infrastructure of your prison from ground up, and the very layout you choose will have an impact on how well your prison is run.  For instance, it is a very bad idea to let Supermax and Maximum security prisoners come into contact at any time with Protective Custody prisoners, or even prisoners who aren't but should be classified Protective Custody.  I made the mistake of overlooking this once, and my prisoner was killed by the other inmates for it.
You can even choose among several types of wardens for your prison, which each have their own benefits/drawbacks.  This will slightly affect how your prison is run and is a matter of personal preference.  You can also sell your prison after certain conditions are met, and then use these funds to start a new prison with more money than you started the previous prison with.  For such a simple looking game, there's actually quite a bit of complexity to it, and it benefits the game.  All in all, I recommend this game; most people should feel like they got more than their money's worth.

I really enjoy Mad Max and it proved to be worth the money. No other game creates a Mad Max unlike the self-titled game, really.
Mad Max is an open world game where you build a car and enhance it with parts so you can fight your way through the wastelands. You collect scrap as a currency in order to further upgrade your car as well as your own personal equipment and skills. The primary game loop consists of driving, fighting off bandits, destroying enemy bases, and trying to make the perfect car for Max. You search for scrap, as well as relics of the past, and look to help out survivor strongholds by enhancing their structures (which in turn provide you a lot of benefits as well).
Upgrading the car proves to be interesting because not every part you unlock could be considered a direct upgrade. Many parts have specialized purposes and sometimes you might not want a part if it makes your car weaker in another aspect. Having a car with little reinforcements and upgrades will give you a faster car as far as acceleration and top speed is concerned, but more armor and stronger engines will make you an absolute war machine and a force to be reckoned with.
Combat is relatively simple and juggles between on-foot combat with simple but enjoyable fist combat, to vehicular combat where you try to fend off attacking vehicles with a wide array of tools, mainly the harpoon which serves to be the most useful and most fun one. Max also comes equipped with his iconic shotgun that can be used to blast enemies and shoot off tires.
Overall the world is massive, and driving out into the world exploring can be fun. Occasionally you'll run into a sandstorm and you can even see it on the horizon (sometimes you'll have to go into structures to hide from them).
Things I enjoyed:
+ Driving is fun and the physics play as you would expect driving in the desert. Mastering driving proves to be enjoyable as you build a vehicle that fits your style.
+ Combat can be tough, specially when it comes to hordes of bandits on foot or a convoy of vehicles. Beating large encounters proves to be enjoyable when you come out on top.
+ The cast of characters are what you would expect from a Mad Max universe, and Max proves to stay true to his character for the entire story.
Things I didn't enjoy:
- disarming all minefields in multiple zones was the most cumbersome aspect as far as freeing all territories from bandit threat. You're forced to use a buggy with a mine detector dog who can sniff out the minefields for you, then will beep as you approach mines. Each mine requires you to hold down the action button to disarm, and there's probably close to two dozen minefields in total. Minefields aren't revealed when you scan entire horizons via map reveal buildings, and you have to drive around the entire map to find them all which proves to be annoying.
- saving enough scrap can be the longest grind if you're keen on unlocking everything. You start off picking up pieces of scrap that'll give you 3-4 scrap, but the largest upgrade is the largest V8 engine which costs 4,400 scrap alone (the V8 engine section probably costs about 10,000 scrap in total to unlock). This is offset a bit by offline scrap generators that will collect scrap for you while you're not in game, so you actually might earn more scrap by not playing sometimes. Bases you defeat will also start to passively generate scrap as well so the more you complete, the more you'll idly earn.
- collecting everything in this game is just painful. There's scrap everywhere, history relics to pick up, and your map will be littered in mostly useless scrap locations that will grant you a feeble amount of scrap. Even inside bases, you'll be offered the ability to collect all scrap on location, but even that gets annoying as bases become more complex in layout and just takes longer to do with each base.
Overall I really enjoyed my experience with the game and loved playing it, despite the minor shortcomings around 100% completion.

Cosmochoria is a game where you heal planets void of all life because of a cataclysm that happened millions of years ago... while fighting off wave after wave of stuff that wants you dead.
In many respects, this game is a rogue-lite. Permadeath, unlockables that can be used over multiple playthroughs, procedurally generated maps, etc.. However, unlike most rogue-likes, the difficulty comes mostly from personal choice. You can unlock artifacts by finding them in the game and having them identified. Half of the artifacts will decrease the difficulty in some way, like, for example, giving you the ability to instantly plant seeds, which is how you heal planets, or have less monsters on screen. The other half will increase your difficulty, like not allowing turrets, or no healing, which will essentially turn the game into a survival.
The story is a nice addition, though not necessary to enjoy the game, and completely optional. You can learn about how the world came to an end by randomly generated messages on planets. The main issue I had with it is that there's a lot of nonsense in between the messages themselves, and while it does actually fit in to the story, it makes it a bit confusing to cope.
When it comes to gameplay, you'll find yourself dying a few times at the beginning. The game has an upgrade/unlock system that you can only access when starting a game. There's a decent weapon variety once you have the currency to unlock it, and there's some costumes you can unlock in game for that added variety, all with their unique benefits.
You might find that a session, once you get used to the combat and pace of the game, takes a long time. A run from start to finish would take 1-3 hours, which is why the game has a milestone system, which will place you after the defeat of each of the bosses.
All in all the game is a good bit of fun. With a nice difficulty range, artstyle that's pleasant on the eyes, decent story, and fantastic soundtrack, I doubt you'd be disappointed.

[Edit: Added a little more below about the weapons]
This is a good game, a very good game.  It's also hard to describe exactly what *type* of game Cosmochoria is.  I hesitate to call it a platformer or a shooter, though both of those are well represented in its design.  I suppose the best thing to do is watch some gameplay videos and see if it's to your liking.  Personally, I've found it strangely addictive.  It has a very charming and very colorful art style, and the background music is quite nice, as well.
The author means it when he says that it is a game of exploration because that includes many of the mechanics as well.  There are ample hints dropped in-game, like what to do with the strange objects you sometimes find, so do pay attention.  One object in the game, the Moai statue, took me until just recently to learn just what it does, and that is only because the game now hints/tells you.  I bought Cosmochoria some time ago on Humble Bundle and the earlier builds gave no clue (that I could find) as to its purpose.  Now that I know what it does, it is *very* useful.
One adjective that goes a long way towards explaining this game is "strange".  The concept, the enemies, the dialogue... all very strange.  But in a good way.  Apparently, there was some drama recently concerning the introduction of a Pewdiepie enemy sprite into the game.  I guess some people felt it didn't belong or it broke the immersion.  Really?  There are plenty of bizarre enemies and nods to other games (Purple Tentacle, anyone?), and *that* is what some people choose to complain about?
The game's difficulty progression is, on the whole, fairly balanced.  The action certainly gets more hectic as you progress, and larger planets have more room which generally means more enemies, too.  Fighting a boss on a large planet can make the battle a lot harder than it might otherwise be as your attention will be divided amongst numerous enemies.
The artifacts that you can unlock during gameplay are pretty neat, as well, because they aren't all good.  Some will give you advantages to make the game easier while others won't.  This is a good mechanic since it means that, later on, you have the option of increasing the difficulty of the game (in some cases, significantly) if you like.
The only major fault I have with the game is actually the weapons.  You start with a wimpy pea shooter, so upgrading your gun ASAP is all but required.  In my game, all of the guns, except for the final two which are still locked, cost 1500.  Now, so far, each gun *has* been very different from the others.  The problem is that, with the exception of the second gun, the blaster, the remaining weapons make the game much more difficult.  They might not be automatic, which means *lots* of clicking, or they might be amazingly weak until leveled up a few times.  So far, each time I buy a new weapon, I always end up switching back to the blaster rather quickly.
Edit (Oct. 19): I've now tried all of guns except for the two that are locked, and I think I can lessen my criticism a little.  The shotgun is actually usable.  It doesn't fire nearly as rapidly as the blaster, but it has a very wide spread and decent power.  I also forgot to mention the sniper gun.  I'm not sure how long I could remain alive while using it, but it is extremely powerful.  The downside, however, is a very slow refire rate and no spread.  Bullet spread is actually rather important because the surface of planets curves, in general, away from your player meaning that hitting enemies on the surface can often be difficult.  One solution is to jump up to give yourself a better line of sight, but if you're using a gun with slow reload, you'd better have a good aim.  For guns that spray out lots of bullets, like the blaster, hitting surface enemies is a lot easier.
One other issue could be, I suppose, the difficulty of the boss enemies.  The first few dragon-like bosses come across as extremely difficult, especially as you encounter them at the beginning of the game.  Expect to die... probably a few times.  That said, it's not *that* bad.  You're going to die plenty of times anyway, and each time you can spend your accumulated crystals for better stats and weapons.
Anyhow, get this game.  It's a lot of fun and I think you'll find yourself spending a lot more time playing it than you might plan on.
