This game is a one eyed man in the land of the blind:
This might be the best (new) city planner in the market right now. Yet, that is not to say that this is a particularly good game.  The genre as a whole is rather starved of quality.
I really tried to get the most 'juice' out of this game, i try to do that with every game i purchase. In the final analysis and to put it succintly there are two flaws with this game; flaws which luckly could be fixed. (I am playing a rather finished version of the game, so i doubt they will be).
First, there is no structured challenge.  Only a sandbox mod which allows you to essential change the difficulty in game.  This greatly reduces the immersion and difficulty to what is already a rather easy game.  There should either be a caimpain that is more than a tutorial with differing challenges and objectives, or at least standarized difficulty levels which may put you in a position of 'holding on' for a long as possible, rather than eternal game seeking ideal prision.
Second, there is no great twist, event, goal or obstacle.  Prison riots is an attempt at such an element (an essential element in city builders; think of Wonders and invasive armies of the Ceasar III and Pharao games).  Instead, if played correctly, the game quickly becomes monotone.  Just search individual cells periodically and frequently and nothing can go wrong...  frankly the riots should be, to a certain extent, depending on difficulty, an integral and inexcapable aspect of the game.  Instead they are merely a side note, that the player by choice can bring about if... well if he or she gets bored.
This game is a lot of fun if you're looking for an interesting twist on a sim game!

Having played APB and this "Reloaded" relaunch, it's really tough to recommend APB Reloaded, but at the same time it's hard to deny that it can be great fun at times.  To get the lows out of the way first: the engine is unoptimized, the community is awful (we're talking Xbox Live Call of Duty levels), there are hackers (the only cheat detection is Punkbuster), players usually want to troll more than they want to play, the reputation grinds can be long and annoying if you don't know what you're doing, new players are typically shunned and treated like crap (it doesn't help that there is little in the way of a tutorial), and the ARMAS shop will rob you blind if you wish to purchase lifetime weapons from it (which some borderline on pay to win).
With all that working against it, you would think it would be pretty cut and dry that the game should be avoided.  BUT, and this is a pretty big one, there are some pretty awesome things about APB.  If you're playing with friends, it can be good fun to just drive around and do a few missions to kill some time.  When you get thrown into a mission with a large group of players, it can be a lot of chaotic fun full of pretty awesome moments and just overall good times.  But those can be far and few in between.
A quote from a friend sums it up nicely: "The highs are very high, and the lows are frequent".  So, ultimately I can recommend this game if you're looking for a third person "cops vs robbers" shooter, but don't expect to have a lot of options when you first start, and don't expect a warm welcome.  Ever.

Call of Duty, one of the most hated and most loved games ever.
I still can't figure out how I have 140 hours on this game. It's fun, but at the same time it's boring, annoying, and straight up horrible.
I personally haven't finished the single-player campaign because I get bored within the first 3 missions, so I won't give my opinion on that.
It's fun for a few hours, I was able to get to the highest rank, that being level 50 without prestiging which is basically reset your rank back to 0 with a cooler looking icon by your level, and a few small upgrades here and there.
The multiplayer is just annoying, child-filled, cheating cesspool, but it is sort of fun when it all works out.
Now this is where buying the game actually makes sense. I love the zombies mode, I wouldn't go buying the game to play alone though, it gets extremely boring if you don't have a buddy to try and get to the high levels with, but it's definetly worth buying if you do have someone to play it with. The DLC maps are best, the original maps that come with the game are extremely annoying and bad, you'll find yourself dying to the lava more then the actual zombies and other enemies.
So now I think it's time to wrap up this review with my final thoughts on the game with some pros and cons listed.
The game is worth buying on sale, but I'd suggest getting the DLC with it, which would be over $100 CAD if you were to buy it not on sale, so try getting the game and season pass on one of the main Steam sales. You'll be really sad when you realize you just spent $100 on a game that you barely squeezed 200 hours out of. The game is very well optimized, probably the best Call of Duty on PC since Call of Duty 4 (Which I do suggest picking up on any sale if you're looking for some Call of Duty.) it runs really well on pretty much and system, if you can't run this game I'd suggest buying a whole new PC, it really shouldn't be that hard.

Arkham Origins is an addicting game, but that doesn't mean it's good. As someone who has put over a hundred hours into Arkham City and has 100% Arkham City and Asylum, I'm not afraid to say that Arkham Origins is an inferior follow-up. Don't get me wrong, the game is fun; the combat is better than ever with the addition of new enemy types and the ability to stack up to 2 special moves. But besides that there isn't really that much the game has going for it. The predator rooms feel uninspered and generic compared to the ones in City, and can be breezed through with the use of Deathstokes grappel gun which basicly allows you to pick off up to three enemies with no challenge to it: it's basicly a ranged Inverse takedown. This eliminates the diffliculty of predator rooms.
Then there's the city, the game's hub world. While it is larger than the one in Arkham City, if I remember correctly I've been told it's atleast 3 times as big as the one in AC, it feels empty. There isn't much to do apart from stopping the same general street crimes that pop-up in the city districts (whether it's fighting mobs or beating up gangs it all ends up becoming the same repitative task after a while). The are no riddler trophies or riddles that unlock bonuses and give winks and nods to the batman lore. I understand Edward Nigma hasn't transformed into the Riddler yet, but the replecement collectibles they have in the game just feel inferior compared to the collectibles of past games. There are side-missions you can do, but half of them are straight up copies of the ones present in AC; Instead of blowing up titan containers you're blowing up drug containers, there's the one where you get sucked into Mad Hatters Wonderland, there's the one where you have to track down Deadshot just like you did in AC.
Speaking of Deadshot, one of the biggest flaws in this game is character development. For a game whose whole premise is based around Batman having to defeat eight assassins, the assassins themselves have barely any impact in this game. Assassins like Deathstroke have little to no screen time, they just show-up, you beat them, and you about never see them again. I'm not talking about B or C list characters here, this is Deathstroke, a major player in the DC Universe, a man who has fought the Teen Titans and had multiple comic series. Instead more emphasis is placed on characters like Bane, who has already had screen time in the previous two games. For the most part it just feels like most of the assassins where just there as fan-service instead of actually having a purpose; it's like how people always joke that the Batman story-arc "Hush" was just an excuse for Jim Lee to draw and include major stars of DC universe, with them having little to add to the overall plot.
But while there's a lot I can criticize about Origins, there are some things it gets right. Like I said earlier the combat is better than ever, not to mention the boss fights, which for the most part, are an improvement over the ones in City and especially Asylum. The voice acting is surprinsgly better than I expected; Troy Baker sounds great as the Joker and overtime Roger Craig Smith starts to grow into the role of Batman, even at some points sounding like a young Kevin Conroy. And while I do think the assassins where underplayed, I'n my opinion James Gordon and Alfred were certainly given the time in the spotlight they rightfully deserve, more so then they were in the past games. But besides that there isn't much I can say good about it.
Like I said from the beginning, Origins is addicting. The comabt is satisfying, I'd dare say even more than City, but it lacks the things AC has that made me 100% it and start on my 5th playthough of it.
It might just be me, I'll admit that. From what I've read in other reviews people have enjoyed this game, and that's good. But in my opinion, as an honest-to-god Batman/Arkham series fanboy, I just can't recommend this game. I wish I could put it into words that would fully convey my dislike towards this game in a way that would allow you to see it the way I do, but I can't. And when I try the only word that comes to mind is the same one I've repeated over and aver again in my review, and that word is "inferior". This game is just inferior.
But I'll say again, that's just the way "I" see it. If you think you'll like it, and it comes on sale, you can buy it and make your own opinion. But if you had to ask me, I would not recommend it.

Arkham Origins is a great game that doesn't deserve the flak it receives from most reviewers. Arkham Origins takes the gameplay mechanics from Arkham City - the responsive freeflow fighting mechanic demonstrating just how badass Batman is and the tightly coordinated predator rooms that allow multiple approaches - and combines it with a great storyline. If you enjoyed Arkham City, you'll enjoy this game.
The gameplay isn’t much different from Arkham City. You’ll have some new/replaced items, some new enemy types are introduced, the city has been expanded and they added a new detective mini-game. Ultimately, these are only minor changes from the solid base that Arkham City created. The game doesn’t offer the revolutionary changes that Arkham City did compared to Arkham Asylum, but rather expands on it.
The story features both well-known (Joker, Penguin, Bane) as lesser-known characters (Firefly, Shiva, Deadshot). Not every character is part of the main story, so it is advised to try and play the Most Wanted side missions for the full experience. The well-crafted Mad Hatter stage deserves a playthrough.
At the time of writing, it appears WB patched most of the bugs. During my three playthroughs (new game, new game+ and I am the night mode, 100%, roughly 70 hours), as well as during the Cold Cold Heart DLC, I experienced only a single non-game breaking bug. This is coming from an inherently more bug-prone Crossfire system. You’ll see most negative reviews because of bugs are pre January 2014.

What a beautiful game.
As I usually do, I tend to read reviews of the games I want, then I wait some time so they update the games properly and lower the price a bit (6 months - 1 year), and I only readed good things about this gem, how it was extremely fun, how it was also challenging, and how it was simply stunning, but I decided to still wait a bit more to pull the trigger, and I finally did it!
Let's start with how well the game runs; my rig is a GTX 770 / i5 4670k / 8GB RAM, so it's pretty beefy, that said, I still had drops of FPS all the time since the start, I did my research and a few people like me got unlucky and it runs like this, I saw a few fixes, forcing d3d11 or d3d9, I didn't bother trying anything because I'm exhausted and tired lately, so I decided to just run the game like this, after an hour I didn't notice the framedrops and I played frankly well! My PC never got above 46ºC playing the game.
The art and graphics are next; stunning visuals, it feels like everything has been hand-made perfectly, everything is charged with love and you can feel it. You can see how the water trembles when something happens, or when something drops in it. The leaves drops gently on the screen, in a realistic and beautiful way. Every single character in the game, either enemies, the protagonist, or NPCs are beautifully crafted, and every movement feels real and well made. The colors are vibrant when they need to be, and off when they have to, every level has a different art style in it, and it shows. You really notice where you are by simply looking at the screen, and that's something that not many games are able to do. Basically, the art is beautiful, well crafted, and stunning, one of the very few games that manage to do it perfect.
The soundtrack, oh boy, the soundtrack is marvelous, if you can, give it a shot and search for it in youtube or in any other place, you'll see how incredibly well put it is, epic and emotive, full of emotions, every place is fit with a perfect soundtrack for it.
The sounds are so good, I was amazed at how realistic it sounds. I mean, I never heard a "rabbit" falling from the sky and trying to break the ground in real life, but it's just like I imagined it, with bass, powerful, noisy; simply perfect, as I said in earlier lines, you can see how they made it with love, everything fits.
The gameplay is... Wow. I started playing the game, and the first 30 minutes I didn't know how to feel about it, I mean, it's not what I imagined (I also tend to not look at gameplays nor information about games except the reviews so I don't get spoiled at all), it's a mix of platforms, action, speedrunning, and being quick as ♥♥♥♥. After 7 hours, I am so much in love with it, you're in total control of your character, and your character will go exactly where you want it to go; it's fun, fast, frenetic, full of action and possibilities, being able to attack the enemy in whatever way you want feels so much fun, it doesn't really get repetitive and at certain moments I wished there were more enemies. The platform feels great, frenetic, fast, and well made, it's very addictive, because it's also a bit challenging, very fun and one of the few games that made me feel great from start to finish!
The story isn't very very good. I mean, it's alright, I didn't really need a big story for the game, but it certainly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off a bit at certain moments, I felt it needed more writing and more reasoning to it, would've loved to learn more about the lore, but being the game it is, it's the least important point of the game.
The longetivity of the game; 7 hours for me, almost every place is at 100%, granted that I am a quick player and I learn really fast, but I felt it was a bit short, I played at medium difficulty, because hard was extremely hard at the start (1 hit 1 kill), but it's a replayable game and as I said before, addictive, so I really don't have problems with the longetivity.
The game is great, fun, full of love and incredibly well made, a gem. I'd gladly put it in my top 20 games I played in my life, it's THAT good.
If you were thinking about pulling the trigger for the game but weren't sure because it might not be the game for you, let me tell you that I hated Super Meat Boy, a platform game, and I loved Dust: An Elysian Tail, so if you have the same likings, maybe this will be the game for you. Pull the trigger, you'll love it!

Ok, I've finally completed the game, so I'm making a review for this. Before I start WARNING: SPOILERS. Now this isn't going to be a review saying something like "BEST GAME EVER 10/10" no, I'm actually going to put time into making this. Now Scott Cawthon, you are a great man. This game is definitely different from the other FNAF games, and you actually took time to make this game instead of the normal 3-4 months of developing. The teasers look great with those special effects, and I love how you tried to keep everything balanced and not show much of gameplay in the trailer. Speaking of gameplay, let's talk about that. Now the only problem I had with the previous FNAF games is that the gameplay was the same thing and repetitive. No matter what in FNAF 1-4 you  are doing the same thing  each night, but just more animatronics. (In FNAF 4's case, one animatronic changes things up.) In this game you're doing something different on EACH night. Now that is what I love to see, a FNAF game that doesn't have repetitive gameplay each night. FNAF: SL also has different elements, instead of waiting until it's 6AM you actually have to keep progressing until your shift is complete, I can say that this game is pretty much faster than the previous games because of that and the fact there isn't any extra nights, but that's if you can. Not only is Sister Location different, but it's more difficult than the other FNAF games (Especially night 4.) so if you're planning on doing a speedrun of this game, you better completely master your skills first, because like I said this isn't your usual FNAF. Now, I'm not gonna go too deep in the story, but I will say that it's very good, of course since it's FNAF, it is dark, but it is also much more interesting than the usual lore. This is by far, the best Five Nights At Freddy's game, it's worth the money, it won't feel rushed, and best of all it has very nice voice acting. The voice acting is absolutely amazing, I love how Baby talks in a calm, monotone voice, and Funtime Freddy sounds like an insane killer clown. Is there things that I don't like about this game? Yes there is, I'm not calling the game bad, these are just a few things I don't like about it. (I won't say Night 4, it's meant to be hard)
The checkpoint system, ok, I understand getting jumpscared is a penalty for dying, but some of these checkpoints are ridiculous. For an example, if you get killed by Freddy in the Breaker room, you have to crawl though Ballora gallery. That's not really how a check point works, what's the whole point of crawling through Ballora Gallery again, why don't we just start over in the Breaker Room?
ULTIMATE SPOILERS AHEAD!
The Worst checkpoint in this game, is dying from Ennard in the Private Room. If you fail to complete the Private Room section, then you have to start all over in the control module and do that code thing with Baby again, and run to the Private room again, I don't understand why we have to go through all of that over and over, when we can just start in the Private room, I mean I love how it's a throwback to FNAF 1, but seriously, why do we have to start all over if we die?
I will give this game a 9.5/10, it would be a 10/10 if the checkpoints were better. Thank you again Scott Cawthon for making all of these games, and this one was definitely worth the wait.

Overall this is a big recommendation. Got it on sale for $8 and I've had a blast with it ever since. I'm about 48 hours into it because I'm literally stopping to do every scavenge area. If you just streamed through the game you could likely finish it in under 20 hours but why do that when there's so much fun?
For me, I’ve reduced Scrotu’s presence in the first two zones to zero. Working on Pink Eye’s territory and done some messing around in Friah’s temple.
Protip #1: Build up your "clean up crew" projects at every stronghold. This frees you to just bash and crash and you won't have to get out of your car every few seconds to clean up. Note, this does not apply to the scarecrows. Only cars you mash and smash.
Visually stunning and immensely satisfying. Get this game. Play it. Play it hard.
I'm now going to list my complaints now which could be seen as spoilers so if that bothers you, don't read further. Rest assured that none of them, in my eye, make this game unplayable. These are merely ways in which Avalanche could have made the game deeper.
Issue #1: Utter lack of car customization. What I mean by this is that literally every aspect of the car can be upgraded. Engine. Tires. Armor. Exhaust. Harpoon. Thunderpoon. Rims. Unfortunately, each level of upgrade has one look and one look only. Let me upgrade my exhaust but get the wicked side pipes earlier. Let me throw a laughingly hideous hood scoop on for nothing other than pure giggles.
Issue #2: Griffa. Heavily involved in the story line up until you max out your character stats then pull a Dodo. Dude just ups and disappears. This is, to me, the point where Avalanche really dropped the ball. Griffa could have been a fantastic storyline throughout the game as he helps Max identify who he really is. Heartless survivor or humanity's last/best hope for redemption?
Issue #3: This plays into issue #2 but the dehydrated desert wanderers you routinely happen across. Stop the car. Hop out. Give water. And.....nothing. These alone could have been a great "personality flag" wherein you gain "good boy" points for helping them and "bad boy" points for not. Heck, you could even direct them to ally camps or stronghold to help build up the population. As it is now, since they really don't have any effect on the story at all, I just use my side flames on them and giggle. What makes these even more maddening is the vague, cryptic things some of them say. Things along the lines of “It’s all used up but maybe you can blah, blah, blah.” It makes it seem as though this was going to be something developed and then Avalanche just said “meh.”
Issue #4: Repetitiveness. This has been said a few times where the quests in one map section are identical to quests in other map sections. That the game is basically Shadows of Modor in cars. Not gonna deny it and this is another place where Avalanche kind of dropped the ball. I’m sure there plenty of other kinds of quest ideas they could have come up with. Dealing with the convoys and clearing the camps are certainly critical but they could have tossed in quests to find sources of clean gas, open trade routes for fuel, etc.
Issue #5: The Big Nothing. Why you gotta hurt us like this? I can’t go far into TBN without instantly and rapidly losing health. Why? Lemme go search. If I want to point my hood ornament south, lemme go south.
That’s all I have for now. Honestly, I hope there is some DLC being developed for future release that will expand on these topics. Don’t just give us more areas to cover with the same quests on repeat. We’ve conquered the lands without.
Now let us conquer the lands within.

Arkham Asylum and Arkham City are tough acts to follow, but I think Arkham Origins manages it okay.
The gameplay is more or less identical to previous games. You are Batman and it's your job to leave a trail of bruised faces and broken bones through Gotham. One gets the impression as you float over the city that maybe this place isn't worth saving, considering that every single citizen of Gotham is some sort of thug or hoodlum that's plotting to rob the local jewelry store. The game tries to sort of justify this by saying there's martial law, but it's a tad ridiculous.
Sometimes Batman even comes across as being the bad guy. A bunch of times I was floating around the city, saw some guys on a street corner and jumped in on them to start punching. Doing that a few times reminded me of Scott Kurtz's "My Parents Are Dead", which I don't think is what the devs were going for.
So for future installments, having some actual civilians in the city (maybe even areas of the city where people don't try to come punch you on sight!) would perhaps be a good idea. Though I think Arkham Knight starts with Gotham being evacuated so I can't imagine that improving.
Overall though, there are some great character moments in here, particularly with the Joker (who completely steals the show from these c-list assassins they have around). And the sneakysneaky/punchypunchy gameplay is just as great as it always is. So grabbing this title is not such a bad idea.
I won't be doing the post-story collectibles though.

The game also toys with the introduction of some major players from the Batman universe while liberally lacing some much minor ones in comparison (at least to non comic book fans such as myself.)
I definitely recommend picking the game up and starting the Trilogy from here (i still consider it a trilogy despite the latter 2 games being from a different developer) if you are a fan of either comics or action 3rd person adventure games.

It was a really clever, fun little game about spreading life and defending planets with plenty of upgrades too.
But on the 15th of October 2015, the developers thought it'd be a good idea to make minuture PewDiePie enemies. Completely out of fit from the rest of the game, essentially mucking it up, and giving us no way to turn it off.
So due to that, I'm going to have to stop recommending this once good game due to the idiocy of adding something which has NOTHING to do with any aspect of the game. It's like adding Ghandi or Hitler as a playable character just because they're also famous the world over. Completely stupid idea.

The game is hilarious, albeit short if you're only going for a single playthrough (7.3 hours for me, but replayability is high) - that said, it's priced very fairly for the gameplay. Love the artstyle, love the humor, the mechanics are very fun, and the devs seem to be active and attentive to player comments.
Looking at the preview video, it looks like a lot has been added since I beat the game - might actually fire it up and try again soon.

You're a naked dude (or dudette, it's not that detailed) colonizing planets by planting your flag and growing seeds... just so you can drain them of health later. And you build weird Illuminati death towers to fight off native bugs. Feels a bit bad, but the art style and music are great. It's slow-paced at the start, but that just ads to the lonely space feel though it's hard to feel sad with all the bright colors around.
I don't like the Rogue Legacy style grind, which reminds me of mobile games. You start out really slow and hard to control, so you need to grind up to move at a decent clip, get more health, etc. It feels really arbitary. It's more fun to get power-ups and items in play.
All that said, it's still  a unique and fun little game and I'm glad I bought it.

After putting lots of time into this game it would likely be more enjoyable, but as is it is too slow, and not very entertaining.
Second look: I replayed the game after there has been many updates. I mostly stand by what I've said. This is a bit more than a flash game, the developer is definitley DEVELOPING the game. The map is lovely, it's nice to see what places have already been settled. Also I'd say this game certainly has more merit as a casual game. Slowly progressing through the improvement system and going through the story, which admittedly I haven't had the patience to do, is likely a rewarding experience. I'd like to elaborate on the VERY SLOW part. RPG elements, and taking a long time to progress because you need upgrades is fine, I just don't prefer those sort of games. My problem with this game is building. Sitting still and planting for a couple seconds is just frusteratingly slow. If we could drop the seeds and watch them auto grow that would be much better. I recognize that may cause planets to get inhabited too quickly, but you could make the gameplay more interesting by growing plants being vulnerable to bullets.
I will keep trying this game as it is updates. I like the how the developer treats his community, and I'd really like to change this reccomendation to a yes.

I find it interesting, that Spec Ops: The Line got "Very Positive" user reviews. People talk about "realistic damage" while complaining about "too long regeneration times". Even though the story seems good - the gameplay isn't.
- The game isn't refined for 3rd person. More than often your character stands in your own way of view resulting in you getting shot from an enemy that would be clearly visible in 1st person.
- Usability is a mess. Sometimes there are cutscenes which you can't skip. The savepoint is right before that cutscene. So, if you die at higher difficulty levels (i.E. "FUBAR") it'll get played over and over and over and over and over again. Yeah, I got it, they're rounding up civilians. Again, and again, and again.
- The AI is very bad. Enemies only try to rush you in groups, or they fall one after another while running up stairs without even reacting. Your team is mainly occupied with blocking your sight or not following you - sometimes they rush forward though and if they weren't almost invincible they'd be dead in a second. Sometimes they even shoot through walls.
- The game is, as it is with many mainstream-shooters today, very unrealistic. The most unrealistic things are theweapon damage and the health recovery. And how the soldiers behave. In fact you play rogue soldiers who fail following orders and then you get blamed for "decisions" in a "all war is bad and you are bad" manner.
I didn't play it for a while... and now I remember why I stopped playing Spec Ops: The Line. The idea was good, but the implementation is a mess. All in all it's a good game with nice textures as long as you don't know anything about weapons, military operations or other stuff. If you have at least a bit of a clue you'll hate the game, because Spec Ops: The Line is very good at one thing: Destroying the high opinions you've may got from all the good reviews. If you're new to the shooter genre or you play mainstream-shooters - go for it, you could happy with it. To the rest: Keep away.

But for right now it is an experience you can't really get anywhere else.

Finally beat the game after more than 25 hours, and at the price I got it I feel really bad about having played it.
The game is probably the most fun I've had in an open world setting in a long time. The story is REALLY engaging and exciting, you will actually grow to love the supporting characters and hate the antagonist. They got the feeling of the Mad Max world down perfectly, you can't trust anyone and the war boys are all bat-s*** crazy. Lots of good dialogue occurs just driving around the world, and I never really had an issue with any of the voice acting in the game.
Gameplay wise, just imagine the Batman: Arkham ____ games melee combat with a cool mix of weapons thrown in. The shotgun is really satisfying to use, and 90% of the time the combat will flow very smoothly (with the other 10% being a broken animation derp fest).
The driving in Mad Max is OK. Other people have said this in their reviews, but, at times the traction on your car feels toyish and the way you bounce of walls is a bit too intense. The road combat is great though, although later into the game you'll find some enemies just become tedious on the road. I advise you upgrade the Thunderpoon as soon as you get it, as it makes dealing with these types of enemies much much easier.
My only real complaint is the way the game leaves you hanging. The entirety of the game has you in pursuit of something Max wants, and once you get it it doesn't really feel worth it. The conclusion happens, and then the game throws you back into free roam directly contradicting the conclusion you just witnessed. I also wish that getting Max's original car back had more oomph, as I would have loved to use it over the Magnum Opus.
All in all though, if you can nab this game on sale DO IT. I can't believe I waited so long to play it.

Mad Max is one of those nice games that you can play easily while doing something else, like listening to a podcast, an audiobook, news, or whatever else you fancy.
The graphics are one of its strong points, with beautiful visuals, a very interestingly designed wasteland, where every zone is different and has a different vibe to it. The skybox is usually awesome to look at any time of day/night.
Sound is also pretty decent, with good sound effects. Music is, unfortunately, not worthy and I would have prefered if they would've gone to something similar to Hans Zimmer's amazing score of Fury Road. I would actually reccommend switching off the music and playing the game with the film's soundtrack in the background. During car chases it works wonders, giving you the thrills you'd expect from a game like this.
Coming to gameplay, Mad Max provides you with a wasteland to explore littered with many things to do. Surprisingly, they are *almost* all quite fun to do, even if repetitive. Upgrading your car, collecting new ones and doing races while destroying other cars is pretty much a Mad Max formula, and it makes sense to be in the game.
The main plot follows events set in the film universe (probably the timeline is immediately before Fury Road) borrowing some character designs and lore. It expands upon the latter as much as it can, altough not nearly enough, given an open-world potential. The story keeps you entertained enough to get you through the end, but don't expect anything too interesting. There are some moments that will surprise you (one scene in particular is very much worthy of praise). All in all, it's a Mad Max story, and anyone familiar with the movies will understand it and easily predict its outcome. For all others, give it a try.
Given the bad reputation games inspired from movies have, this one is an example of a product that actually has some genuine attention put into it, and it can be deserving of a little bit of your spare time.
PROS: Visuals - Gameplay - Some moments in the story - Mad Max lore - Setting
CONS: Music - Repetitivity - Some wasted potential

The long dead genre of turn based RPG's, were in my mind, well, dead. Unfortunatley for the existance of that mindset, Undertale exists. While many such games hold a very special place in my heart because of childhood nostalgia, the reptitive system gets tired and was in need of a desperate change if it wanted to continue, which is nowhere more exemplified than in Undertale. An interesting and interactive battle system continues to challenge the player in new and interesting ways as the game progresses, switching up style of combat while still mantaining the foundation of the mechanics. Aside from the ever important game systems, the other major contributer to this game is the story and the characters. Reminiscent of earthbound or a paper mario game, nearly every character has something interesting and quirky to say which solves another one of the modern game problems, the desire to explore the world you inhabit. You never get tired of looking around the game world because each new area you encounter is full of interesting and deep visuals and characters to talk to and interact with. With the most minor of characters having such depth, there is an obvious extreme effort put into the main characters of the game. Every one of the major characters you meet eventual build a deep emotional connection with you that makes you care about not only the characters themselves but also their endeavors and the story as a whole. At this point nearly unecessary to mention, the soundtrack is perhaps the greatest of it's generation of games, especially for an indie development, but there has been plenty said about it as it is. Overall, Undertale earns its place among the 10/10's, and I absolutley reccomend you pick up and play this game.

NOTE: This review will only address the single-player portion of the game as I have yet to try multiplayer.
As a fan of the Arkham games (I have played through
and
on the Xbox 360), I knew I was going to have to get this one, even though I had read some mediocre reviews about it. One common complaint seems to be that AC was a great improvement and expansion upon the first game, but we don't see that with AO. Well, I guess I can agree that this game is "more of the same" in terms of the whole series of games, but it is very good "more of the same".
I really like the expanded map of Gotham; the city feels huge. Plus, it's cool to be in certain neighborhoods and around specific buildings that I could recognize from
. It's also cool to be able to head back to the Batcave to hang out with Alfred or get some training.
The Freeflow Combat is back and it has always been, for me, one of the things that make the Arkham games so much fun to play. Fighting ninjas and martial artists in AO adds some new twists to the combat since your counters can be countered. I have to say that I really like some of the boss fights in this game; to me they feel more interactive than some of the boss fights in earlier games. I disagree with others who contend that they are basically QTEs. I thought the fight with Deathstroke was exceptionally fun to play.
Overall, I am pretty happy with this game and am looking forward to the next one where I can drive the Batmobile around Gotham.

Bleh, I got this game for under a buck, wish I had never installed it.  At first glance, it looks cool, with some fun little mechanics, and an interesting idea behind it, but it's very poorly executed... It's not even close to being a complete game, and is a beta version, at best.
The entire gameplay mechanic is landing on planets, holding the down key to plant a seed, which takes several seconds (even with upgrades... UGH), while pausing fairly often to shoot completely unchallenging enemies.  Repeat this several times per planet, and you get rewarded with a worthless item that you can carry (only one at a time) that has to be set down to build anything else... there is absolutley no reason you can't do both, it slows the game down even more.  After you plant many seeds, dependent on the planet's size, you "heal" it, and a chest pops up with either resources, or thost stupid do nothing items.
You can blunder your way around space discovering new worlds, which is awful, because the minimap icon is very difficult to read, so often your course takes you off the map, and into the sun (certain death), and the map doesn't even display planet locations, just your x,y coordinates on a blank map... it's nearly worthless, and is, hands down, the worst map function I've ever seen in a game, which is made worse by the fact that you SORELY need it to navigate featureless open space.  Eventually you'll stumble upon less than a handful of worlds with important characters on them, such as the bearded man, who will tell you what those  awful items you've been lugging around one by one do (most SUCK), and if you're lucky, you'll find some teleporters that will enable you to bounce around between planets you've rescued, although there's literally no reason to ever return to them.
The game starts off REALLY slow, since your planting speed is ridiculously slow, your defautl weapon atrocious, and your jetpack fuel limited... one of the least fun things I've ever encountered in a video game is having to blast off into space completely blind, then run out of jetpack fuel, and be left drifting aimlessly until it refills itself ever so slowly.
Oh ,you collect shards or crystals or whatever from killing enemies, and can use them to pay for outrageously priced upgrades between game sessions, none of which even come close to lowering the monotony of gameplay.  I don't care if I could instantly colonize the planets, instantly find worlds, or hell, even had a minimap that served any function at all... this game still wouldn't be fun, even if you removed all the hinderances to gameplay, because there are no fun aspects to be enjoyed... GD, it REALLY is this bad, and it's a shame the cute graphics and nearly free price caused me to squander hours of my life only to be disappointed.
Yeah, so this game has some potential, and is cute-looking, but I doubt it will ever be expanded into anything I would ever recommend to a friend... it's just a hair above what a high school student would make in an into to programming class.

Having just beaten the game, I can say that this is truly a well-thought-out, quality, enjoyable title.
The gameplay is primarily a test of your technical skills (i.e.  your ability to effectively control Ori and utilize his/her abilities to progress and reach new areas).  Though some may be tempted to call this game a RPG, it really isn't - it just has a simple leveling system which gives you some control over your abilities.  The environment and story form a coherent framework that provides sufficient immersion without overbearing you with lengthy "story time-outs."  The game can at times seem almost Metroid-esque in layout and feel, but it's most definitely not a clone.  The game really is a work of art - it ran seamlessly and bug/crash-free for me.
FAVORITE ASPECT:  Perhaps my favorite thing about this game is the quantity and quality of "escape challenges" (this probably screamed "Metroid" to me more than anything else).  The pace and complexity of these form the main challenge of the game, in my opinion.  They are well-done and for most of them I came away thinking, "Wow!"
LEAST FAVORITE ASPECT: This game has almost no real negatives, but if I had a complaint I'd say it has to be about the length.  I beat the game in 11 hours and I was slow about it (looking for power-ups, etc.).  Ideally, this game would be in the 15-20 hour range.
All things considered, I give this game 9.5/10.

First and foremost: The always-on requirement for this game is terrible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If you want to Ex-nay the whole thing for this reason, all power to you. That said, I will only review the game as I have played it myself.
God damn this game is great.
Great
-Level design. Very large & dense levels, lots of NPCs, lots of little side stories, lots of environmental storytelling.. exceptional. Even the worst level in the game is among the most interesting levels I've ever seen.
Good
-Stealth system. There's some reliance here on typical 'stay out of sight' mechanics, and things get tense when you're ducking behind things to dodge a gaurd. However, most of it is 'social' stealth, in having the correct disguise to move through the levels and to nab your target.
-Audio. The music is pretty great. The synths and strings when you get caught, or right after you take out a target are exceptional. Otherwise it does a great job fading in and out of the background as things progress
Meh
-The animations and graphics. I can't play the game above medium settings anyway, but the fine details of the game aren't super. The game looks great overall, when looking at the big picture. But if you're the type to stare at texture quality or expect fluid animation and gameplay, you won't get it here. It's functional at best.
Bad
-No meaningful offline mode. If they wanted to lock online progression to online, sure I get that. They want to keep cheaters off the leaderboard, I can respect that. However, the offline mode has basically no progression at all, so no extra starting locations, suits, guns, gadgets, etc. That is just straight up ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Overall: This is my first real hitman game I've put time into (I played Absolution for like 3-4 hours, it was fine), and I love it to pieces. Each level is a labrynth of interlocking clockwork pieces made of people, objects and events. It's great fun just to knock over the dominoes and see how things fall. 100% recommended.

Spec ops: The Line is a unique Third Person Shooter with a Great Storyline. This is as long as other shooter games but it has better story than most shooter games out there. From the beginning of the game you notice something strange about the characters and you are left with many questions unanswered, but by the end of the game you get a truly amazing story with a great gameplay.

The game has the standard 3rd person cover-based shooter gameplay as many do. It has the nice twist of team commands for sniping, throwing grenades and focusing fire, all context-sensitive. Imho most thrilling are the few situations where you can't use your team early on - thats when the gunplay becomes more intense. Also there is the "drop sand on enemies" mechanic. But thats only useful for about 5 times in the whole game.
The UI is quite nicely done and lacks the health bar or so - everything is more or less focused on the main character. Colours and graphics are nice, and it is quite enthralling to see the characters (and parts of the environment) become more and more ragged, deteriorating with the story progress.
This is where the game shines most. If you watched any of the great (anti-)war movies like Platoon, Apocalypse Now, Full Metal Jacket: this is what the game shows you and lets you experience. The moments of feeling goodlike while you mow down hordes of enemies are halted by scenes which contain everything from moral difficulty to outright horror. Try keeping humanity in an inhuman environment. What can I believe of the things I am hearing (and seeing)? So, a road to hell (paved with good intentions) comes as a playable experience here. Pick  your own flavour of bad outcome.
Nice one. I picked it up during a sale and was smitten with it. It is mostly a one-playthrough thing unless you are completionist and want all the achievements. You can also replay certain chapters, just to see how different choices play out. Surprise: most play out bad. But bad is good when in context of a warzone. Or at least it makes one think. And that it was SOTL does. Recommended!

Nice gritty single player storyline. Standard FPS mechanics with very basic squad control. Failed nearly un-playable sniper/aiming console port. Some rather painful checkpoints behind unskippable cutscenes. Horrible contextual controls (same button to do 10 different things and you hope the game chooses the action you meant to do). The smallest things can be so damaging to an otherwise great game.
Good game; competent gunplay, very well refined and delivered story.

Mad Max is one of those nice games that you can play easily while doing something else, like listening to a podcast, an audiobook, news, or whatever else you fancy.
The graphics are one of its strong points, with beautiful visuals, a very interestingly designed wasteland, where every zone is different and has a different vibe to it. The skybox is usually awesome to look at any time of day/night.
Sound is also pretty decent, with good sound effects. Music is, unfortunately, not worthy and I would have prefered if they would've gone to something similar to Hans Zimmer's amazing score of Fury Road. I would actually reccommend switching off the music and playing the game with the film's soundtrack in the background. During car chases it works wonders, giving you the thrills you'd expect from a game like this.
Coming to gameplay, Mad Max provides you with a wasteland to explore littered with many things to do. Surprisingly, they are *almost* all quite fun to do, even if repetitive. Upgrading your car, collecting new ones and doing races while destroying other cars is pretty much a Mad Max formula, and it makes sense to be in the game.
The main plot follows events set in the film universe (probably the timeline is immediately before Fury Road) borrowing some character designs and lore. It expands upon the latter as much as it can, altough not nearly enough, given an open-world potential. The story keeps you entertained enough to get you through the end, but don't expect anything too interesting. There are some moments that will surprise you (one scene in particular is very much worthy of praise). All in all, it's a Mad Max story, and anyone familiar with the movies will understand it and easily predict its outcome. For all others, give it a try.
Given the bad reputation games inspired from movies have, this one is an example of a product that actually has some genuine attention put into it, and it can be deserving of a little bit of your spare time.
PROS: Visuals - Gameplay - Some moments in the story - Mad Max lore - Setting
CONS: Music - Repetitivity - Some wasted potential

APB, orignaly made by real time world set out to make a great game with the whole GTA style behind it. With such a great idea you would think the game would of been amazing. However whenever the game was out during beta there was countless bugs and problem and faction balancing that was needed. Real time world felt like they would have more than enough time to worry about these problems later. Once it finally came out the game crashed and burned with in a few months. Real time world didn't fix more problems they also had a system in game where you could pay in game money to pay for you account. Real time world planned this game to be pay per month and when you got the game they would "give" you 50 free hours of time to play. The companyed folded and APB was lost.
Then back in 2010, G1 picked up the game few a couple of million. Once in hand they took it on themselfs to fix the bugs and balance the game out. In return they made the game free to play, With the option of pay for a priumere account and get more stuff. G1 overall did save APB as a whole and renamed it APB reloaded for it's re-launch.
APB is a great game. Even though it was very buggy back in 2010 during the beta and release of the game i still enjoyed it alot. I was a bit upset to see the game fall and i was hoping that someone else would of picked it up and fix the game. My wish came true.
APB brings alot to the table. This game has one of the best if not the best costumiztions in any game out there! (hell i tought city of heroes had such an amazing system). This right here alone sold APB to most poeple who wnated to play and who still plays.
The combat in this game is pretty simple, You aim, you shoot, you run, to hide, to blow things up, and you drive around in a 3rd person view. However, every player can buy or "license" a gun for 3day that will give you a better chance of doing more damage to your enemys. Each gun has a "better" version you can unlock threw leveling up your contacts but i will talk about that in a few moments.
Cars! This is one of the other great selling points of this game was the amount of cars you can buy and use. How they look what they can do. You want more speed? you want more ramming power? well there is power up for this! However much like the wepaons you can always buy "better" version of your car by leveling up your contact levels.
Contacts. This is the main thing you do in the game. You have contacts that are spread out threw every city map. When you start off you start with what i call the Tier 1 contacts. This is the basic contact to help get your hands wet to learn the ropes and unlock a few basic things. Every contact has a list of items and upgrades you can unlock from them ranging from New card, New weapons, New clothes, Car and weapon upgrade. However the down side of contacts are that before you can get to the next tier of contacts you must fully have each contact maxed out for that faction. there a few factions in the game each  has there own story and what there role is in the city.
Upgrades. With being able to buy better weapons and cars you are able to add up to 3 upgrade to a single weapon or car. However like i said before every car has an better version out there. You basic weapon or car will not have any slots to add a upgrade to, the next "Better' version you get 1 slot and then the next will be 2 and so forth. Even your charater it's self has upgrade that you get overall.

Gameplay: In apb it's your basic third person shooter, when playing the game you have a few zones to choose from. two combat zone, and one social zone. The social zone is where both factions can rest and change there charaters look, there cars look, or buy things from each other or use the auction house. In the combat zone there are two to choose from, each has there own story and there own style of play. This is where the main action of the game happens. once you are in you are able to que up for missions that are randomly given to you from one of your contacts to gain better exp with them to gain better stuff. the missions  them self can be a number of different task, Raiding, Defusing, PvP, Capture zone, VIP, and many others. The mission do get repeative after awhile since you will be doing the same thing over and over again time after time. However its the player interaction that can make it better or worse.
Ranking: This game works on two type of ranking. There is your level from leveling your contacts and unlocking more. You need to be a certain level rank to before to unlock some things in game or to use things. Then there is Threat level. There are 4 threat levels. Training, Bronze, Silver, and Gold. Each one works off of your skill in game on how well you do on taking out the oppsing team, or finishing missions.
Free to play or pay to win? Now this is a huge thing for this game. Even though this game is free to play you can alway pay to buy better games over all that are alot more powerful than what a free to paly can get. Now with that said. I am not saying to enjoy this game you must pay to win but i'm not saying because if you pay to win you will beat everyone else. It's how you play the game. I've never bought a gun in apb like that. I've gotten free 30 min trial and i gotten gun that lasted for 24 hours to 3 days but never went out of my way to buy them. Some poeple will agrue and say you must pay real money to do well in this game. To be honest if you are skilled enough you don't need to buy a single gun in the game with real money. If you are abel to play taticfully you can get the upper hand on people. The problem with this game is that most players are run and gun players. They will run in not think or check around before tehy go to the point. Then they will get killed and then want to play other people for there lack of skill.
This game still has memory lacks and lag problems that will drive you nuts. the lag can get better bad even higher end computer still has problems. alot of people ends up using costume launchers and/or editing ther config files to make it more playable.
Overall, I really enjoy this game alot. As of right now this is by far my favorite free to play game on Steam.This game isn't for everyone and it's not that noobie friendly either. it's a great game to play at short burst for a few weeks at most then put it away for awhile then come back again.

The art style is really nice and the music is relaxing, but in the end I've found the actual gameplay frustrating. The two main aspects to the game are puzzles, some of which are fairly clever, others of which are annoying and feel like busywork, and item gathering. The latter is, somewhat vexing and the hint system often points things out that you weren't looking for. The hint system itself is designed to be annoying to discourage casual use, but often you'll need to use it several times in a row to get what you want. To me, the game wore out its welcome while also feeling too short. At the end you get a chance to replay any puzzle you want for fun, but I honestly didn't feel like repeating maybe one or two. Death is a great teacher. Failure in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is, as it always has been for this series, the greatest way to learn where you should have gone, what you shouldn't have done, and how you could have done better. Counter-Strike players spend a lot of time learning -- consequently, they are always getting better.
Growth is an important factor in Global Offensive, especially if you're coming into Counter-Strike fresh or after a sabbatical. This is an extremely hardcore, skill-based first-person shooter, and it forces you to think differently than other modern shooters. If you’re a Call of Duty player, you’re going to need to change your play style to succeed here. Counter-Strike also tries developing into something new here as well, despite doing little to push itself beyond what it’s always done best. Global Offensive modifies old maps to keep veterans on their toes, and introduces official new modes that encourage different play styles for the first time in almost 15 years.
For the uninitiated, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a small-scale, team-based first-person shooter with permanent death. When a counter-terrorist kills a terrorist planting explosives in a classic Defusal match, or a CT escort swallows a sniper round in Hostage Rescue, the victim is dead for good and doesn't respawn until the next round. As such, players on both sides must exercise skill and care. The bomb objective, meanwhile, gives everyone a purpose. Of course matches end when everyone on a team is dead, but a clever and coordinated terrorist team will give the CTs the slip, plant their bomb, and protect the bomb site. Between rounds, everyone spends earned cash on better gear and guns, and the cycle continues.
Pieces of the Counter-Strike formula are dated at this point, but the superb heart and soul of Global Offensive is timeless. Teams are small, guns are lethal, and rounds are short. There's an addictive just-one-more-round quality to it, because there's a constant desire to do better than last time, to earn a satisfying kill, or to win in a new way. Call of Duty and Battlefield vets will wonder why they can't sprint to escape enemy fire or look down the iron sights to improve aim; Counter-Strike players will feel like they walked into their redecorated home. Certain map redesigns will catch hardcore fans off guard, but the changes are for the best -- the underpass choke point in de_dust, for instance, has a new escape route.
Even in the face of genre evolution, Global Offensive doesn’t care to adapt. CSGO is so dedicated to Counter-Strike's aging ideals despite market and trend changes that it brute-forces its way to success. Part of what makes it such an engaging competitive game is that killing in Global Offensive requires a wholly different skill set than other shooters. Everyone is limited to what they have and can see, with little room for character modification or on-the-fly advantages. Running and gunning is a useless play style, even if you've bought a helmet and kevlar that round, to the point that someone standing still is more likely to score the kill. Walking, crouching, or standing are your best bets to reduce the inaccurate spray of machine-gun fire.
Consequently, killing in Global Offensive feels good. There's a sickening sensation to dropping someone dead because you know they're not coming back. It's also satisfying knowing you used limited resources to play smarter than your victim. If players aren't watching corners, providing covering fire, or using smoke grenades and flashbangs, they're more likely to take a headshot from a more delicate and patient triggerman. The desire to experience that distinct feeling is a strong motivator to keep playing, even when you're getting steamrolled by an obviously better team.
If you've played Counter-Strike before, Global Offensive probably sounds a whole lot like Counter-Strike. Like Counter-Strike: Source before it, Global Offensive exists simply to modernize the look of the classic competitive shooter, while doing little to disrupt the core form and function. At the same time, it does enough to color outside the lines of tradition to justify your time and effort.
Fire is one of the most interesting new combat variables. Molotov cocktails and incendiary grenades either roast groups of guys or force them in another direction. Flames are a useful distraction or scare tactic, too. They're particularly useful during Demolition matches, which focus the fight at a single bomb site rather than giving terrorists two to pick between. The new and modified maps in this mode aren't as big as classic Counter-Strike arenas – entire sections have been cut off to direct teams toward a central location – but their thoughtful design is as intricate as ever. The Lake map is a standout -- there's a wide open yet densely populated yard around the bomb site, which is inside a sizable lakeside home with plenty of vantage points and hiding spots. To separate Demolition from Defusal, players can't buy between rounds. Instead, it takes a cue from the other new mode, Arms Race, in which each kill unlocks another weapon instantly. The better you do, the more you have to switch up the way you play, and because Demolition is so fast you'll need to be quick on your feet.
Unlike other game types, Arms Race allows for respawns. It's the most chaotic and care-free mode in Global Offensive, with players throwing caution to the wind for the sake of climbing the kill ladder as quickly as possible. It's a shame there are only two maps in Arms Race -- a problem that will more likely persist on consoles than PC.
If you have the option, playing the PC version is unquestionably the best way to experience Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. Mods, mouse and keyboard, and the usual PC-only options are better than the ports. Plus, Valve is much better about long-term PC support -- it abandoned Team Fortress 2 on consoles, and Portal 2's level editor was PC exclusive. They're struggling to get through the cell doors, so you replace them with staff doors to save time. By now you've run out of money so you open up to your grants. "There's a grant to build a hospital and hire doctors," you see. You were going to do that anyway, so why not get paid for it? Now you're scouting out a good location for your hospital. Shoot. You need more guards to patrol the new hospital. Hire a few more guards. The staff is complaining that they're overworked and in dire need of a staff room. Got to keep the staff rested so that they work at top speed! You figure out where you're going to put the staff room and get the workers on the foundation. By then, you're able to go back to the hospital and route power to the new area, not to mention adding the beds and other requirements for a hospital room. You've overtaxed the power station with the new area, and get the workers to add some capacitors to increase the power.
All of a sudden, in the real world, your sister tells you that it's 1:00am and that you should probably go to bed.

I might be a bit biased, seeing as I've watched this game grow from its kickstarter days, but the sheer charm and arcade-esque feel of Cosmochoria is hard not to love. Controls take a bit of getting used to, but before you know it you're rocketing off into parts unknown (or directly into a star, whoops) in hopes of saving the universe!
The goal is to revive planets across the galaxy by planting, protecting, and nurturing seeds. In return, the revived planets heal you as you stand on them and pop out a chest of goodies when they are first revived. If you are easily frustrated by having to start over and over from scratch (but stronger each time) this might not be your game. It's a game that is meant to have multiple takes - you can activate powerups that you've found in previous runs to keep you alive longer and get further towards your goal. Enemies are relentless jerks, constantly spawning in to ruin your day. With good fortifications, you can hold off wave after wave, but eventually you have to venture out to another rock in hopes that you can get it alive and protected before your naked little butt gets spanked.
In summary: challenging, charming, and not-too-serious.
As a side note, this is backed by one of the most dedicated and enthusiastic devs you could possibly ask for. Excellent communication with the backers and community - I mean, you could feel the joy radiating out of every word in the updates - and very quick to address problems and suggestions. Nate, you've done marvelously!

Though I'm actually extremely late to reviewing this game, I'm going to do it anyways. I do recommend undertale.
Now, let it be said that undertale is a bad game and a good game. But it isn't really bad in the aspect most would think it is. It's horrible because of its fandom. Now I know, supporters of the game will strongly disagree with me, but hear me out. Horribly undesireable fanart is cranked out on the daily, questionable cosplays, odd ships, etc. I feel that the main place the game messed up is with its fandom, actually. It's one of the worst (if not THE worst) I've seen, which is truly saddening. This game has TONS of untapped potential that could be easily reached if the fandom wasn't so toxic. I'm not saying that other fandoms don't hold a torch up to undertale, I'm simply saying that this is on the bad side of the spectrum. But if you're able to see past the fandom in general, keep considering buying it.
If you've processed the fact that the fandom is horrible, now we can start looking at the truly redeeming qualities of this game. I would describe undertale as nothing short of a masterpiece. Though I'm not part of the fandom, I do have to take my hat off at a few factors. First, the music is AWESOME. I enjoy most, if not all, of the pieces in the game. Next, the characters and story are absolutely amazing. By the end of the game you truly do feel sad that you have to leave all of the characters (if you choose the pacifist route, that is). I promise you that you'll enjoy ALL of the characters equally by the end of your journey in the underground. With gruling and excruciatingly difficult fights, (looking at you sans and undyne), you'll be kept on your feet all throughout the game. All of the factors of the game somehow blend into an exquisite harmony that comes out to be undertale.
Overall, undertale is an extremely well-made game that I recommend for anyone. Though the fandom's toxicity often gives the game a bad first impression, pushing past that one factor will reward you greatly. I believe anyone who plays undertale will be entranced by it's charm.

When I first heard about this game, I loved the idea. A shooter which forces you to make morally gray decisions while trying to get outta Dodge in one piece. While the game had the core premise well enough, I was sorely disappointed.
PROS
+Cover mechanics and gunplay are mechanically well-fleshed.
+The ending makes a number of things that I scratched my head at make sense. Not all of them, but a number of them.
+There are a number of situations where you do something and just sit there for a minute, amazed at what you did.
+Your AI teammates do actual damage (unlike some other games I know). This may seem like it should be par for the course, but it was refreshing because not enough games have an AI that can actually hurt the enemy.
+Definitely has the atmosphere down pat.
+Game can make you feel terrible early-on for crossing a line, then later forget there was even a line.
CONS
-There's still a lot of things that didn't make sense, even after the end.
-Over-use of Juggernauts. Where they should feel like a mini-boss, they felt like "just another bad guy, but tanky"
-Music didn't help that often. Sometimes, it helps a scene hit home. More frequently, it's annoying background noise, and made me feel annoyed more than anything else.
-One particular character was singled out and it looks like the developers were too eager to make him look like a bad♥♥♥♥♥instead of letting his actions speak for his character.
-Game tried too hard to beat you over the head with "You're bad! You're bad!" instead of taking a subtler approach. Sometimes, it's necessary. More often, it backfires. Again: let the action speak for itself.
-There's a number of things the game made me do that I didn't want to, both good and bad. Then the game tried to make me guilty for stuff I couldn't say "No" to.
-Squad-based combat mechanics weren't fleshed out, and feel completely useless. Just an add-on to try and make the game have more of a tactical feel, which requires more than "Attack this target," "Heal a downed partner," and "Throw a flashbang, but only at certain times."
-Game isn't sure whether to be realistic or "standard Gears of War cover-shooter," and chooses the latter when the former would have served much better.
-Despite numerous decisions to make, only one changes the ending. It would be nice to have it change across numerous endings based on what you did.
I'm seeing a ton of positive reviews, so I'm probably missing something or seeing too much into it. Either way, it felt like an idea that was poorly realized. Hopefully, the sequel will have a more subtle, expansive way of telling a tragic story.

Well, where to start? I'll begin by saying that it's nice for Scott to try and correct the errors of FNaF 4 (the lore being too vague, it simply being a rehash of the first game's mechanics etc), but Sister Location could have been better. In terms of the good, huge steps were indeed taken in the form of voice acting, which adds a new level of both terror and intrigue to the animtronics, as well as actual movement to different rooms. Due to the game's engine, this feature was of course limited to "point-and-click" and basic WASD, but Scott made the most of what he had available. Also, the idea of each night being unique and centred around completing different tasks was a fresh take, something this franchise desperately needed.
However, the great shame comes in the fact that the concept of something different every night, which is the main gameplay aspect of the game, isn't carried out very well. Many of the game's mechanics are either explained poorly, too easy, or too hard. There's no sense of balance or stability for the majority of the nights. For me, sneaking through Ballora Gallery and repairing Funtime Freddy in Parts/Service are the only bits of the game that feel immersive. The rest is a whole bunch of talking, which I understand is for explaining the lore, but again there is no balance between it and the gameplay. Shocking the animatronics could have gone further in terms of a mechanic, but it just feels abandoned, and I feel the same about many other parts of the game. The horror aspect also rarely makes a decent appearance.
Overall, Sister Location is on a 50/50 basis with me. I like how it took the series in a new direction and proposed various new gameplay mechanics or ways to tell the story, but it falls flat in many of these ideas that have great potential on paper. Lately the FNaF games have been declining when it comes to replayability value (to be honest they didn't have much to begin with) but this time it came to a new low. There is virtually no reason to play through all the game's nights from start to finish more than once, especially considering the abomination that has come to be known as...Night 4. Nevertheless, I'll recommend this game since I feel like it will serve as an experiment, to see how people feel about a new take on this game series which, as of now, has an uncertain future.

The bottom line is that APB: Reloaded looked like a good idea on paper, but the execution is horrendous.  The anti-cheat system is basically non-existent, as the engine believes botters to be players with pin-point precision (which, in reality, is virtually impossible). Undertale is a good game. It’s fun, overflowing with many easter eggs, and has genuinely interesting characters with excellent writing. There’s ambiguity with plenty of opportunity for those inclined to game theory, although that can sometimes regress into madness when taken too far. But speculation can be fun, and some level of ambiguity good.
Also the music. The music to this game is genuinely one of my favorite OSTs in terms of its impact upon the story, and I think that the game would be severely lacking without it. I went into Undertale almost blind; I had no knowledge of the plot but some of the premise. If you are able to go into it blind I’d strongly recommend doing so.
I greatly enjoyed the humour in this game. Some may like it less, but this was one aspect that made Undertale enjoyable in my eyes. I really can’t say or judge the absolute quality of this game in terms of how it’s made and how it compares to others, because there are probably better games out there that I am unaware of or that are better in various other respects. What I know with certainty is that this game and its story stayed with me and caused me to care about it for many months after I initially played it, and something about it made it the most memorable game I had played in a long time. Also I remember the value for money that I got from this game being very good, I paid something like £5 for the game and soundtrack when it was on sale, which was money incredibly well spent considering the enjoyment I got out of Undertale.
So in short, Undertale is a game which I would strongly and heartily recommend, and would probably be worth giving a try. If you do go for it I'd recommend getting the soundtrack, I wasn't certain about whether to initially but now have no regrets.

Bought it due to word of mouth, and while it took me a while to feel arsed to start and play it, I found out it delivers and I should have played earlier.
The story as probably everyone says is good (I guess it helps it was a book first, some felt cliché or even lame to me, but all in all it was a strong point of the game, it helps the game doesnt try to extend past its reach, it's compact, does what it needs to do and moves on).
It_is not just story however, the art is so good, and I don't mean LOOK AT THOSE SETTINGS, but the art assets, architecture (so nice, you can look at weird angles you wouldn't usuallly look at, and there's still something to see), art direction, the art team really worked hard. There's the giant towers buried image (like sea level rise, but ground level this time?), the luxurious rooms with aquariums for walls (in the desert), or a favorite of mine, a room that has a beatiful aquarium on its floor, that room is so damn pretty.
Music is also okay, it transmits that you should have fun (due to meta, or because it's a game, maybe both?), there is at least one interesting non-standard choice that stands out. Sfx is also good.
Gameplay is cookie cutter fps but on third person. The ideas are good but I found the most problems here due to "bugs", bug as in the cover system works, but you keep dying because you fail to take cover, or the sprint button works, but you sprint when you dont want to, and dont when you do, all of this due to poor design I believe, or perhaps programming itself (cover and sprint are the same button, if the programming is on point then I would decouple the actions to separate buttons because it messes everything up, but in theory it should work, so the programming could be not as tight as it needs to be for this to work).
I hear you run faster with light weapons, but while perhaps realistic, unnecessary, should have been removed especially since there are sections where you must run fast.
You may get killed instantly at points, at other you may never get shot (cod problem), devs should have added invincibility frames to the single player so that guns didnt have a "shots to kill" (which leads to death in 0.1s) but "time to kill" stat with perhaps that time getting halved if attacked by a number of enemies to give you time to react and hide (like, 1s to die, that's all you need to be fair, sure, not realistic, but its a game).
Some checkpoints are placed with the storytelling in mind but not the replayability, so you get them right before cutscenes or world presentation (a long trek), that works if you quit and start the game another date, but, on the same session, that means if it is followed by a tough fight, it gets annoying fast.
Once you get past the annoyances, firefights are good, and level design helps by not being 100% shooting gallery and giving plenty of alternate ambush routes (which you dont figure until after you get past the shooting gallery so you feel dumb for not taking the clever route, but at least that would help to spice a second playthrough). There's also the sense of game progression, which is also nicely done, the game gives you new weapons (without making a fuss about it) to try and discard at a good pace, almost all of them having 2 (realistic) fire modes, mostly zoom level or select fire mode, with turrets having two stances. Due to the design every weapon actually has uses, there are big health sinks you can use the smgs on, long range enemies for snipers, close range for shotguns (and shotguns can be decent at medium range although aiming may be tougher), big groups with lots of suppression that just require explosives of any kind and so on. You start with the simple weapons, and by the end of the game you are using the one-shot-kill sniper, and pro-rifles with noob tubes or m32 6-round grenade launcher with infinite ammo and short reloads. If you notice, the boss enemies start spawning closer and closer to you, forcing you to stop cowering and learn how to beat them, give you less room to hide, and get more personal as the game goes (you have to be the one that kills them, not your ai allies), that the good progression I felt during the game.
All things considered, remember to buy it.
